author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the chain half off the sprocket when the side door scraped open, and her wrench slipped, clanging against the concrete louder than anything should. She froze, palm flat against the cold frame, listening. Just Mr. Okafor from unit three, shuffling toward his shelves of paint cans. Her breath came out in a thin, shaky stream. She picked the wrench up and found her fingers wouldn't quite close around it, so she wiped them on her jeans twice. "Sorry, sorry, just fixing a flat," she said, too fast, though he hadn't asked. The bare bulb overhead buzzed and flickered, and every shadow between the stacked boxes seemed to lean closer. Her heartbeat thudded in her ears while she worked the link back into place. When he left, she didn't relax. She dragged the bike nearer the exit, kept her back to the wall, and checked the door again, then again, before tightening a single bolt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Delancey Street had gone the color of an old bruise by the time Marta checked the timetable a fourth time. Eight minutes late. She pulled her coat tight and pressed her back against the glass of the shelter, as if the plastic could hold her up. The wind flipped a newspaper down the empty road, and she flinched at the sound of it. Her fingers kept finding the phone in her pocket, thumbing the screen, dimming it, lighting it again. 'Come on,' she whispered, then louder, to no one, 'Come on, come on.' The first fat drops struck the roof like thrown gravel. A low growl rolled across the rooftops and her breath snagged halfway up her chest. Her knees felt hollow, her palms slick. She counted the streetlights down the block, one, two, three, then lost count when the third one flickered out. Somewhere behind her, a gate banged. She did not turn around. She stared at the corner, willing headlights to appear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta lifted the shoebox lid an inch, then set it back down and wiped her palm on her jeans. The attic was quiet except for the rafters ticking in the heat, and she found herself listening for footsteps on the stairs, though she lived alone. She lifted the lid again. The top envelope bore her father's slanted hand, and her fingers hovered above it, trembling too much to pick it up. "Just paper," she said aloud, her voice thin and too quick. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She slid one letter free, held it by the very corner, and turned it over without reading. The flap had never been sealed. Her breath came shallow, and she realized she was half crouched, ready to bolt. She glanced at the window, at the door, at the dark gap behind the trunk. Then she pushed the box away with two fingers, stood, and left the attic light on as she went down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came at dusk, three slow raps, and Marguerite froze with the dish towel still wound around her fist. Through the peephole, distorted and wide, stood Mr. Halvorsen from next door, the man who had not spoken to her since the fence business. She slid the chain on before opening the door a hand's width. "Yes?" Her voice came out thin, a half-tone too high. "Need your ladder," he said. "Gutters." Her heart knocked against her ribs, and she noticed her free hand gripping the doorframe, knuckles pale. The ladder was in the garage, in the dark, behind the door that stuck. "I can bring it to you," she said quickly. "You don't need to come in. Stay there. I'll just, stay there." Her palms were slick as she backed down the hallway, eyes still on his shape, counting her steps to the phone on the counter.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The risotto had been stirring for twenty minutes, and Marguerite had read the same line of her mother's recipe card four times without absorbing it. Her fingers, slick and cold, slipped on the wooden spoon. Headlights swept across the kitchen window and she froze, ladle dripping onto the stove, her breath caught high in her chest until the car passed on. "Not yet," she whispered. "Not yet, not yet." She tasted the rice, couldn't tell if it was right, and tasted it again. Her heart thudded in her ears, louder than the simmering stock. The table was set, then reset, forks nudged a millimeter at a time. What if it was gluey? What if his mother, who had run a restaurant, pushed her plate away and smiled politely? She wiped her palms on her apron, leaving two damp streaks, and when the doorbell finally rang, she dropped the spoon with a clatter and stood staring at the hallway, unable to make her legs move toward it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter at 2:14 a.m., and the screen shows only a string of digits I don't know. I stand there in the dark, one hand flat on the cold granite, listening to my pulse thud in my ears. It stops. Then starts again. My thumb hovers, trembling, and I notice I've stopped breathing, so I let the air out in a thin, shaky stream. I creep to the window and tug the curtain an inch aside, checking the street, the parked cars, the black gaps between them. Nothing moves. The phone keeps buzzing. My mouth is dry as paper when I finally press accept and lift it to my ear without a word. 'Hello?' a voice says. I swallow. 'Who is this?' I whisper, and my voice cracks on the last word. Somewhere behind me, the refrigerator hums, and I flinch so hard I nearly drop the phone. 'Please,' I say. 'Just tell me who this is.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and the spine of Principles of Organic Chemistry had gone soft against my shoulder blade. I stood outside the library doors for ten minutes, pretending to read my phone while my thumb scrolled nothing. My palms were slick. When I finally pushed inside, the cold air made the sweat on my neck prickle, and I kept my eyes on the carpet's gray squares all the way to the desk. The librarian looked up. I opened my mouth and a croak came out, so I coughed and tried again. "I, um. This is, it's overdue. Slightly." I set it down too fast, and the thud echoed. My knees felt like they belonged to someone else. "Is there a form? Should I just go? I can go." She tapped her keyboard, and I stared at her hands, counting each click, barely breathing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box hit the floor with a thud, and Marisol froze, head tilted, listening for whatever answered it. Nothing. Just the refrigerator humming and a pipe ticking somewhere behind the wall. She crossed the studio in four steps, checked the deadbolt, then checked it again, her palm slick against the brass. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, and her voice came back thin from the bare walls. She dragged the armchair against the door, then felt foolish and left it there anyway. Her heartbeat knocked in her ears as she tested every window latch, twice, and pulled the curtains until no gap of streetlight remained. A footstep sounded in the hallway. She stopped breathing, fingers gripping the phone, thumb hovering over the first digit of a number she hadn't dialed. The footsteps passed. Her knees loosened all at once, and she slid down against the boxes, still wearing her coat, still holding the keys like a blade between her knuckles, and did not turn off the light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, black leather, curled slightly open like it had been dropped mid-breath. I stopped walking. My hand had gone cold around my coffee, and I realized I was holding the cup against my ribs. The path was empty except for a jogger far off, and I turned my whole body to watch him until he disappeared behind the oaks. "Hello?" I said, too quietly, then again, louder, my voice cracking on the second syllable. Nobody. A crow shifted on the lamppost and I flinched hard enough to slosh coffee over my wrist. My pulse knocked in my ears. What if someone was watching to see who picked it up? What if my fingerprints, my face, the camera on that pole... I crouched, lifted it with my sleeve pulled over my fingers, and my knees shook so badly I almost sat down in the gravel. A driver's license stared up at me, a stranger's smile. I set it back exactly where it had been and walked away fast, not looking behind me, counting my steps to keep them even.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood on the second step of the shallow end for so long that the instructor had stopped looking at her and started rearranging kickboards. The water reached her ribs. She kept one hand clamped on the rail, knuckles pale as the tile, and counted the black lines on the pool floor, then counted them again. "I'm just getting used to the temperature," she said, too brightly, though she'd been in twenty minutes. Her heartbeat knocked in her ears, louder than the echoing splash of the children's class across the room. When the instructor said, "Let's try putting your face in," she laughed, a short, thin sound, and asked whether they might review the breathing part again. Her mouth had gone dry despite all the chlorine. She bent forward an inch, chin trembling just above the surface, and her fingers did not let go of the rail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets sat in a row on the porch rail, and I kept straightening them like that would help. Dirt had never been my area. I knelt at the bed I'd built, and my knees wouldn't settle; I shifted, stood, knelt again. "Okay," I said aloud, too brightly, to nobody. My hands were damp inside the gloves, so I pulled them off, then regretted the cold soil against my fingertips. The tomato seedling looked so thin, its stem a thread I could snap by breathing wrong. I dug the hole twice, deeper, then shallower, my pulse thudding in my ears. What if I drowned it? What if I didn't water enough? A crow landed on the fence and I flinched hard enough to spill the trowel. I laughed, a short dry sound. Then I lowered the roots in, held my breath, and pressed the earth around them with two fingers, barely touching, ready to pull back if it complained.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus slid into the chair nearest the door while Priya clicked to her third slide, and he pressed his pen so hard into his notebook that the tip tore the page. His turn was next. The conference room hummed with the air conditioner, too loud, too cold, and still a bead of sweat crept down behind his ear. He rehearsed his first sentence silently, lips moving, then lost it. His knee bounced under the table until Dana glanced over, and he flattened his palm against it. Priya's voice seemed to come from the far end of a tunnel. Somebody laughed at her joke; Marcus laughed half a second late. His throat had gone dry, so he reached for the water glass, and it rattled against the saucer. When she said, "Marcus, you're up," he stood too quickly, his chair scraping, and heard himself say, "Sorry—hi—give me one second," while his fingers fumbled the clicker, damp and unsteady, refusing to find the button.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The headlights found the same pair of taillights again, a quarter mile back, and Dana eased off the gas to see if they would pass. They didn't. Her knuckles had gone pale on the wheel, and she noticed she was breathing through her mouth, shallow and quick. "Okay," she said aloud, then again, "okay," as if the car might answer. She flicked her eyes to the mirror, to the road, to the mirror. The county road had no houses now, only black fields and a mailbox that leaned like a drunk. When she turned onto Alder Lane, so did the lights. Her palms slicked against the leather. She didn't signal at the next turn, just yanked the wheel, and her stomach dropped as the gravel hissed. She killed her headlights, then switched them on again, cursing under her breath. Her phone sat in the cup holder, screen glowing, her thumb hovering over her sister's name. Behind her, the lights slowed, and her heart hammered in her ears so loudly she almost missed the sound of the engine passing by.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus stopped outside room 412 with his hand flat against the doorframe, reading the whiteboard again, though it said nothing new: Dr. Patel, Nurse Joy, Thursday. The vending machine down the hall hummed, and he counted its hum. His palms were damp; he wiped them on his jeans twice before pushing the door. The bed looked too big around his grandfather, the blanket rising and falling in shallow little tugs, and Marcus found he was holding his own breath to match them. 'Hey, Pop,' he said, too brightly, then again, quieter, because his voice cracked on the second word. He gripped the plastic visitor chair but didn't sit. A monitor chirped and his shoulders jerked up toward his ears. He stared at the orange juice cup on the tray, its foil lid still sealed, and thought, if he drinks it, that's good, that means something. His knees felt hollow. 'I'll just stay a minute,' he whispered, and didn't move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell rang at 3:05, and I'd already checked my phone four times since 2:50. Nothing from the school, no email, no call, which should have been comforting. My palms were slick, so I got out of the car and stood by the fence, gripping the cold metal. Doors banged open. Children poured out in a bright, shrieking stream, and I counted red backpacks, rejecting each one. "Excuse me," I said to a teacher, too loudly, then too quietly, "Maya Ortiz, second grade, have you seen her?" My voice cracked on the last word. She said something kind and pointed, but all I heard was my pulse thudding in my ears. My knees felt like wet sand. I rose on my toes, scanning, swallowing again and again around a dry lump. Then a yellow hood, a gap-toothed grin, a wave. My breath left me in one ragged push, and I had to hold the fence to stay upright.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man in the gray jacket had been running his thumb along my mother's oak dresser for a full minute, and I kept rearranging the lamps on the card table so I wouldn't have to look at his hands. "Forty," I said, too fast, then cleared my throat. "Thirty-five. If you want." My palms were slick against the cash box. He crouched and tugged the bottom drawer, and I flinched at the scrape, certain he'd find the envelope I'd taped underneath and forgotten to peel away. My heart knocked so hard the price stickers seemed to tremble. He stood, squinting at the driveway, at the street, at me. "Anybody else home?" he asked. I laughed, a thin dry sound, and backed toward the garage door, keys already biting into my fist. "My husband's inside," I said. There was no husband. The sun beat down and still my arms were cold, goosebumps rising under my sleeves while he dug out his wallet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip under the sink had become a steady thread by midnight, and I knelt in the cabinet with the flashlight clamped between my teeth, my knees soaking through. My hand shook so badly the wrench rattled against the copper. "Okay," I whispered to no one. "Okay, okay." I turned it a quarter inch and the joint hissed, a thin spray hitting my wrist, and I jerked back so hard my head cracked the shelf above. I froze, listening to the house. Every creak sounded like the ceiling giving way. My shirt stuck to my back, cold and wet, though I couldn't tell whether it was water or sweat. I pulled out my phone, thumb hovering over my brother's name, then put it face down on the tile. If I called, he'd hear my voice. I wiped my palm on my jeans, gripped the wrench again, and found I'd stopped breathing somewhere around the hiss. I made myself pull in air, slowly, and turned the valve once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has sat on the counter since Tuesday, propped against the toaster, its little window showing my name in that flat official type. Tonight I wash two mugs that were already clean. I dry my hands too long. When I finally pick it up, the paper feels heavier than paper should, and my thumb leaves a damp print on the corner. "Just a form," I tell the empty kitchen, but my voice comes out thin and cracked, so I clear my throat and say it again. The fridge hums. Somewhere upstairs a neighbor's chair scrapes, and I flinch hard enough to bump the table. I slide a fingernail under the flap and stop halfway, breathing through my mouth, my pulse thudding in my ears like someone knocking. What if it's the audit? What if it's the notice about Dad's house? I read the first line with one eye mostly shut, and my knees go loose enough that I have to sit on the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train doors hissed shut behind Marta, and the platform emptied around her like water down a drain. Signs in looping characters hung overhead, none of them matching the map crumpled in her fist, its edges damp where her thumb kept pressing. She walked, then stopped, then walked the other way, her suitcase wheels rattling too loudly on the tile. A guard said something sharp and quick; she nodded hard, too many times, and whispered, "Sorry, sorry, hotel?" The word came out thin and cracked. He gestured toward a staircase, or maybe a wall. Her pulse knocked in her ears. She climbed into the roar of horns and neon, kept her back against a pillar, and checked her passport pocket for the third time in a minute. Every face passing seemed to know exactly where it was going. Her phone showed one bar, then none. She stood very still, counting the buttons on her coat, and did not let go of the handle.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the fence with both hands wrapped around the top rail, knuckles pale, while Biscuit tore loops through the tall grass at the far end of the field. Every time the golden shape dipped below the weeds, her breath stopped until it bounced up again. "Biscuit," she called, too high and too thin, and she cleared her throat and tried again. The dog ignored her. Beyond him, the tree line had gone dark, and something out there cracked, a branch or a gunshot, she couldn't tell. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She counted the seconds he stayed hidden: one, two, three, four. Her thighs ached from being clenched. When he trotted toward the trees, she was over the fence before she'd decided to move, whistling sharply, the sound wobbling, her sleeve snagged on wire and left tearing behind her. "Come here. Come here, please, now." He turned. She dropped to her knees in the mud and held on to him, laughing without any breath.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite had run the Brahms intermezzo forty times in her kitchen, but in the empty library annex, with folding chairs lined up like a jury, her hands wouldn't stay warm. She wiped her palms on her skirt and sat down on the bench, then stood up again to adjust it, though it was already right. "Just the first page," she told the radiator. Her voice came out thin. She began, and her left hand slid into the wrong chord; she stopped, breath shallow, a pulse ticking in her throat. Dust floated in the window light. She laughed once, too high, and said, "Not yet, not yet," to nobody. Behind the stacks, Mr. Okafor dragged a chair, and she flinched so hard the lid thumped. She pressed her fingers against her knees until they quit trembling, counted the folding chairs twice, and wondered whether it was too late to say her wrist hurt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I held the garage door's handle for a full minute before I lifted it, and the rattle of the track made my shoulders jump. Dale's workshop smelled exactly like him, cedar and machine oil, and my breath came shallow, as if the air might use me up. I told his sister, "Just boxes, right? Just boxes," and my voice cracked on the second one. I kept the radio on loud. Every time the furnace ticked I spun around. His lathe sat under its canvas like something sleeping, and I walked the long way around it, hugging the wall. My palms were slick on the cardboard. When I found his half-finished chair, the pencil marks still fresh on the arm, I dropped the box and stood there with my fingers pressed to my mouth, listening to my heartbeat in my ears. I didn't touch the light switch at the back. I left that corner dark, and I left it for tomorrow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 14 smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Marisol had read the same line of the notice board four times without understanding it. Noon, the secretary had said. It was 11:52. She peeled a strip of skin from her thumb, then pressed the sore spot against her jeans. Her mouth tasted like pennies. When Dev asked if she wanted to sit, she said, "I'm good," but her voice came out thin and high, and she cleared her throat to fix it. Her knees felt loosely hinged. Every time a door clicked somewhere down the hall she turned too fast, and her stomach dropped to her shoes. What if she'd mixed up the second question? She had already rewritten that answer in her head forty times. The office door opened. A woman stepped out holding a single taped sheet. Marisol's hands went cold, and she realized she'd stopped breathing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid behind the ridge, and I realized I'd been walking faster for ten minutes without deciding to. My boots slapped the gravel too loudly. Every trunk along the trail had started to look like someone standing still. "Just a stump," I said aloud, my voice thin and cracking on the last word, and I laughed at nothing. My phone read 11% and one bar that kept blinking out. Something snapped in the brush to my left. I stopped, breath held, fingers white around the trekking pole, my pulse thudding in my ears so hard I couldn't hear anything else. Nothing moved. My shirt clung cold to my spine. I counted the switchbacks I remembered, got it wrong twice, started again. The parking lot was two miles away, maybe three. I didn't look behind me. I told myself that was a choice, and kept walking, nearly running now, the dark pooling at my heels.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card had gone soft as cloth, the ink bleeding where her grandmother's thumb had rested decades ago. Mina read the first line again, then again, though she knew it by heart. "Flour till it feels right." Feels right to whom? Her hands, dusted white, wouldn't stop trembling, and a cloud puffed up when she set the cup down too hard. She laughed once, a thin sound, and wiped her palms on her apron until the cotton went stiff. The kitchen was too quiet. The oven ticked as it heated, and each tick made her shoulders jump. She pressed the dough, watched the dent linger, and her stomach dropped. Too wet? Too dry? "Okay," she whispered. "Okay, okay." Her throat felt tight as a knotted string. She picked up the phone to call her mother, set it down, picked it up again. If this loaf came out wrong, there would be no one left to show her how it should have tasted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The cereal aisle hummed under its fluorescent lights, and I was reaching for the oats when I heard my name, the full one, the way only Dana Whitcomb ever said it. My hand stopped midair. I knew that voice from the back row of Mr. Pruitt's homeroom, from the hallway where she'd laughed while my books hit the floor. I turned slowly, the box crushed against my ribs. 'Oh. Hey,' I said, too quickly, too high. My palms had gone slick, and my heart knocked so hard I was sure she could see my shirt move. She was smiling, asking about my life, and I kept nodding at nothing, eyes drifting to the end of the aisle, counting steps to the exit. 'I'm, uh, late. Stove's on,' I lied, though I'd come on foot and lived alone. I abandoned my cart beside the oats and walked out, not running, my knees watery, the automatic doors sighing shut behind me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By nine p.m. on Christmas Eve the pharmacy was empty, and Marisol had counted the same tray of pills three times. The bell over the door hadn't rung in an hour, yet she kept glancing at the dark parking lot, where one pickup sat under a flickering lamp that had been there since six. Her palms were damp against the counter. When the phone rang she flinched so hard a bottle rolled off the shelf, and she let it ring four times before lifting it. "Hillcrest Pharmacy," she said, too softly, then cleared her throat and said it again. Nobody answered. She set the receiver down, slid her hand beneath the counter to the cold edge of the panic button, and left it there. Her heart knocked against her ribs. Forty minutes to close. She turned off the back lights, then turned them on again, then stood listening to the freezer hum and the pickup's engine, which suddenly started.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says Gate B47, and I'm at A12, and my phone says 14 minutes. I run, but my roller bag keeps veering left like it's fighting me, and my breath comes in short, scraped pieces that never reach the bottom of my chest. My palms are slick; the handle slips twice. The moving walkway is blocked by a family, and I hear myself say, "Sorry, sorry, please, sorry," in a voice too high to be mine. I check my phone again. Thirteen. My boarding pass has gone soft and damp in my fist, and I can't remember if I put the passport back in my jacket, so I pat the pocket, pat it again, pat it a third time. My knees feel hollow. A tram doors-chime sounds somewhere and my whole body flinches toward it. What if they've already closed the door? What if they close it while I'm watching? I don't slow down. I can't swallow. The gate numbers climb so slowly, and each one seems to be laughing at me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller squeaks across the wall, and I stop mid-stroke because I swear the sound came from the hallway. I hold my breath. Nothing. Just the fridge humming downstairs and my pulse knocking in my ears. I set the roller in the tray, wipe my palms on my jeans, and they're still damp. Tonight is the first night in the house alone since the break-in next door, and I've left every lamp on, even in rooms I'm not using. The tarp crinkles under my sock and I flinch, laughing a little, too loud. "Just plastic," I tell the empty room. I creep to the doorway, peek down the dark stairs, and check the deadbolt twice, then a third time. Back at the wall, my hand shakes, and the stripe of pale blue wobbles at the edge. I keep my back to the corner, the window, and the open door all at once, which isn't possible, so I keep turning my head, painting in short, hurried strokes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The porch swing creaked every time the wind shoved it, and every time it creaked I flinched like it had touched me. I'd told myself I would stay out here and watch, the way Dad used to, but my hands had other plans. They were wrapped around the chain so tightly my knuckles had gone pale as candle wax. The sky flashed white and I started counting out loud, "One, two, three—" and the crack split the air before I reached four. My voice came out thin, nothing like my own. "It's fine. It's just weather." My knees were pulled up under my chin, my toes curled against the damp boards. Rain blew sideways across my arms and I didn't wipe it off. The screen door was right there, six steps away, but my legs felt full of wet sand. Down the street a transformer popped and went dark, and I realized I'd been holding my breath so long my ears were ringing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the rear wheel half off the frame when the sound came from the far corner of the garage, a metallic crash, then the slow rolling of something that wouldn't stop. The wrench slipped from her fingers and rang against the concrete. She didn't pick it up. Her breath stuck high in her chest, and her pulse thumped in her ears louder than the rolling. "Hello?" she said, too thin, too fast. "Dev? Is that you?" Nobody answered. She edged around the workbench, grease still slick on her palms, and wiped them down her jeans without noticing. Her eyes darted over the neighbors' stacked paint cans, the dangling tarps, the dark gap behind the shelving. Her knees felt loose. A tire lever lay near her foot, and she curled her fingers around it, grip tight enough to hurt. Then a small orange cat slid out from under the shelves, trailing a bike pump. Marisol laughed once, a cracked sound, and sat down hard on the stool, hands still shaking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marcus had been checking his phone every few seconds when the light went the color of old pewter, and the flag on the pole across the road snapped straight out. He stood, then sat, then stood again. The shelter's plastic panel buzzed against his shoulder. "No, no, no," he muttered, thumbing the screen, where the bus tracker still said four minutes, and the number hadn't moved in ten. A cold gust shoved a flattened cup down the gutter, and the hair on his forearms lifted. His mouth had gone dry; he swallowed twice anyway. Far off, the sky cracked white, and he counted without meaning to, getting only to two before the thunder rolled over the rooftops. His grip tightened on the strap of his bag until his knuckles ached. He leaned out past the shelter's edge, squinting down the empty road, then pulled back when the first fat drops hit the pavement like thrown coins. "Come on," he said, higher than he intended. "Come on, come on." His knee would not stop bouncing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and dust, and I was humming while I thumbed through birthday cards until a yellowed envelope slid out with my name on it in my father's slanted hand. The postmark said 1998, the year he supposedly never wrote to anyone. I set down my coffee too fast; it sloshed over the rim onto the rug, and I didn't wipe it. My thumbnail caught under the flap, then stopped. "No," I said to the empty room, and my voice came out thin, like someone else's. The page inside shook, or my hands did. I read one line, "Don't let your mother see this," and my pulse thudded in my ears so loudly I turned toward the hallway, certain I'd heard a footstep. The floorboards were silent. I stuffed the letter under my sweater, shoved the lid back on the box, then pulled it off again to count how many more envelopes had that same handwriting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Delacroix stood on my porch at dusk, hands in his jacket pockets, smiling too evenly. "Mind if I borrow your ladder? The tall one." The dish towel I'd been holding went tight in my fists. Across the street, the Hendersons' upstairs window was dark, the way it had been since Tuesday, when the shouting stopped. "What for?" I asked, and my voice came out higher than I meant. He shrugged. "Just a little job." My pulse thudded in my ears. I glanced at the garage, then at his boots, caked with wet gray clay. "It's, um, actually Ron has it. Lent it out. Sorry." I stepped back and my heel caught the doormat. He kept smiling. "Funny. I saw it by your fence an hour ago." I closed the door slowly, turned the deadbolt, and stood in the hallway with my back flat against the wood, listening for his footsteps to leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The oven clock read 6:42 when Marisol opened the door and found the lamb pale and cold, the dial dark. She pressed the knob again, then again, her thumb jabbing harder each time. "No, no, no, come on." Her voice came out thin and too fast. Somewhere behind her the pot of rice hissed and spat over the rim, and she lunged for it, burning her wrist on the lid and not even flinching until a second later. Her heart thudded in her ears. She wiped her palms down her apron, left a smear of oil across her hip, and glanced at the window where headlights swept the street. A car door slammed. She stared at the raw roast, then at the clock, then at the roast again, counting under her breath, fingers pulling at the knot of her apron strings until they tightened instead of loosened. "Okay," she whispered, to nobody. "Okay. Pan. Slice it thin. Pan." The doorbell rang, and the knife slipped in her damp grip.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, and Marta's knife stopped halfway through an onion. Unknown number. Eleven digits, none of them familiar. It buzzed again, rattling toward the edge, and she snatched it before it could fall, her thumb hovering, wet with onion juice. Her mother was in the hospital. Her brother hadn't answered since Tuesday. The stove fan roared; she twisted the knob off and the silence made her pulse louder in her ears. "Hello?" It came out thin, too high, and she cleared her throat and tried again. "Yes. This is Marta. Who is this?" Her free hand gripped the counter's edge until the knuckles paled. A pause on the line, a crackle, someone breathing. The cold crept from her fingertips up into her wrists. She pressed her back against the refrigerator, eyes fixed on the dark window over the sink, and whispered, "Please just say who you are."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been under Dara's bed since March, and now it was November, and the cover was warped from a leaked water bottle. She pushed through the library doors with it pressed flat against her chest, as if it might be less visible that way. Her pulse thudded in her ears. At the desk she set it down, and her hand wouldn't quite let go of the spine. "Hi. I, um. This is, it's due. It was due." She laughed, a thin sound that cracked in the middle. The librarian reached for the scanner and Dara's eyes darted to the screen, then to the door, then back. Her palms were slick; she wiped them on her jeans twice. "How much is it? Is it a lot? I can pay. I think I can pay." Her knee bounced against the counter, rattling the pen cup, and she grabbed it to steady it, knocking over two pens instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol had one box under her arm when she pushed the door open and heard the scratching. She stopped on the threshold, the cardboard biting into her ribs, and held her breath until her ears hummed. The sound came again, dry and quick, from inside the wall beside the radiator. "Hello?" she said, absurdly, in a voice pitched too high and too thin. Her free hand found the light switch and flicked it twice, though the bulb was already burning. The room was barely nine steps across, and she crossed it in four, setting the box down on the mattress without looking away from the baseboard. Her pulse thudded in her throat. Sweat cooled along her spine. She crouched, then rose again at once, knees unsteady, and dragged the only chair across the floor to wedge it under the closet handle. Behind her the scratching stopped. The silence was worse. She pulled out her phone, thumb shaking over the landlord's number, and kept her back pressed flat against the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the slats of the bench, black leather, still warm from the sun, and my feet stopped before I told them to. I looked left, then right, then back over my shoulder at the empty path. A jogger's footsteps faded somewhere behind the hedge. "Hello?" I said, too loud, and my voice cracked on the second syllable. Nobody answered. My palms had gone slick against my thermos, so I set it down in the dirt without noticing. The wallet was fat, bulging, its corner stitched with a tiny gold initial. I reached for it, pulled my hand back, wiped it on my jeans, reached again. My pulse thudded in my ears, loud as a drum. What if someone was watching from the car by the gate? What if it was a setup? I flipped it open with two fingers. A driver's license stared up at me, a woman smiling, and cash folded thick behind it. "Okay," I whispered. "Okay, okay." I couldn't swallow. The lamps clicked on overhead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor let go of my wrist, and the floor of the pool simply wasn't there. My toes scraped at tile that had slid away, and the water slapped my chin, then my mouth. I heard myself say, "Wait, wait, wait," in a voice pitched higher than any I own. My hands grabbed the lane rope, slick and rolling, and it spun me sideways. Chlorine burned the back of my nose. My heart hammered so hard I could feel it in my ears, under the water and above it. Somewhere a whistle blew, a kid laughed, the fluorescent lights buzzed on and on. "Stand up," the instructor called, calm as a bus announcement. I kicked wildly, found the bottom with one heel, and hauled myself upright, coughing, my fingers cramped white around the rope. The water came only to my ribs. I stared at it, forty-one years old, shaking, not letting go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The trowel slipped out of my hand the second the dirt moved. Something pale and wriggling curled out of the hole I'd dug for the tomato, and I jumped back so fast I sat down hard in the mulch. "Okay. Okay, okay," I said, much higher than my normal voice. My heart was knocking against my ribs. I pulled out my phone with dirty fingers, smearing the screen, and typed *white worm in soil dangerous?* before I'd even blinked. Across the fence, the neighbor's radio droned on, painfully cheerful. The seedling lay on its side next to me, roots exposed, already looking limp, and my palms went slick inside the gloves. I peeled them off and wiped my forehead, leaving a streak of grit. "Don't die," I whispered to the tomato, then glanced at the hole again. The worm was gone. That was somehow worse. I stood, stared at the dark soil, and didn't dare put anything back in it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide and my coffee cup stopped halfway to my mouth. That was my data. My column headers, my color scheme, the odd little footnote about the Q2 outlier I'd only shared in a draft last Thursday. The conference room's air felt suddenly thin. I set the cup down too hard and it clacked against the table; Raj glanced over. "Sorry," I whispered, though my voice came out cracked and high. My palms were damp against my notebook, and I pressed them flat to the cover so no one would see. Dana kept talking, smooth, confident, saying "my analysis" twice. I counted the ceiling tiles. Eleven across. My pulse thudded in my ears, loud enough that I missed a whole sentence. When the VP leaned forward and asked, "Who built the model?" I found I'd already half-stood, knees bumping the table, chair legs scraping, every face turning toward me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The county road was empty except for the pair of headlights that had appeared behind Marisol at the last turnoff and hadn't left since. She eased off the gas; the lights slowed too. Her thumbs went slick on the wheel. "Okay," she said aloud, then again, quieter, "okay." She flicked her eyes to the mirror, then the dashboard clock, 12:47, then the mirror again. When she sped up past fifty-five, the engine's whine seemed absurdly loud, and her heartbeat thudded in her ears beneath it. The farmhouses were all dark. No gas station for nine miles. She fumbled for her phone in the cup holder, knocked it to the floor mat, and swore under her breath, her breath coming short and shallow. At the next crossroads she signaled, though no one else existed out here, and turned left, away from home. The headlights turned left too. Her mouth went dry as paper. "Don't," she whispered. "Don't, don't." She pressed harder on the gas.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus had brought grapes, and now he couldn't remember setting the bag down. The door to 412 stood open, and his grandfather's bed was tilted nearly upright, a plastic mask fogging with each short, quick pull of breath. Yesterday it had been a thin tube under the nose. Marcus's palms went damp against his jeans. "Grandpa?" His voice came out higher than he meant, and the old man's eyes slid toward him without quite landing. The monitor beeped faster than he remembered, a number in red blinking beside it. He backed into the hallway, nearly colliding with a cart, and caught the sleeve of a passing nurse. "Is that normal? The mask? Nobody called me." He heard himself repeat the question, slower, as if volume might change the answer. His heart thudded in his ears while she glanced at the screen, and he searched her face for anything at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus stood at the chain-link gate with his keys still clenched in his fist, watching the double doors spill out children in bright jackets. Third grade, usually first out. He counted the red backpacks, then the blue ones, then started over. His mouth had gone dry. "Excuse me," he said to a teacher with a whistle, too loudly, "Have you seen Nora Kim—Nora Reyes? Braids, yellow raincoat?" She said to hang on, give it a minute. He couldn't. His thumb stabbed at his phone, the screen slick under his damp palm, and the call rang out to voicemail. The crowd thinned. A car door slammed and he flinched. His heart thudded against his ribs so hard he could feel it in his teeth. He pushed through the gate against the flow of strollers, muttering, "No, no, she's right here, she's just slow," while his eyes raked every empty bench and the long, silent mouth of the front hallway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marta was haggling over the price of a walnut dresser when the man in the gray cap pulled out the bottom drawer and went still. His hand slid in behind the runners, and her mouth went dry. Her father's dresser. Her father, who had never trusted banks. "Don't," she said, too loud, and a woman browsing the lamps looked up. Marta crossed the lawn faster than she meant to, sandals slapping, her pulse thudding in her ears. "Sorry. That one's not actually for sale. I made a mistake." Her fingers curled around the drawer's edge, damp and trembling, and she shoved it shut harder than she needed to. The man shrugged and drifted off. Marta stood with her back pressed against the wood, staring at the street, thinking of the envelope she had never once thought to look for. Her laugh came out thin. "Lunch break," she announced to no one, and flipped the cardboard sign to CLOSED.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped twice before I got it seated, and by then the cabinet floor was a shallow lake soaking my knees. Water fanned from the joint in a thin, hissing sheet, and every time I pressed my palm over it the spray found a new gap and slapped my wrist. "No, no, no, come on," I muttered, voice climbing higher than I wanted. My heart was banging so hard I could feel it in my teeth. Where was the shutoff? I'd never needed it. I crawled out, skidded across the wet tile, and yanked open the hall closet, flinging towels, a vacuum hose, a box of lightbulbs behind me. My hands wouldn't stop shaking, and the flashlight rattled against the wall. Somewhere under the sink the hiss grew louder, or maybe I just heard it that way. "Please be here," I said to the dark corner, and then I saw the red handle and lunged, my breath coming in short, ragged scraps.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter beside the cold coffee, its little window showing the words Department of Revenue in block capitals. Marguerite had walked past it twice, wiping crumbs that weren't there. Now she stood with a butter knife and slid it under the flap, and the paper rasped louder than it should have in the quiet kitchen. Her thumb left a damp print on the fold. She unfolded the page, read the first line, and then read it again, her lips moving. 'No,' she said, to the refrigerator. 'No, that's not, I filed that in March.' The fluorescent tube overhead hummed. She pulled out a chair without looking and missed the seat, catching the table's edge. Her pulse thudded in her ears as she flipped to the second page, then the back, searching for a number, any number, a phone she could call before the offices closed at five. The clock said 4:41.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station doors hissed shut behind Marta, and the crowd swept her onto a platform where every sign was a row of characters she couldn't begin to read. She patted her jacket pocket, then the other, then the front of her bag, fingers moving faster each time. The phone was there; the paper with the hotel address was not. "Hotel," she said to a man in a gray coat, too loudly, holding up two fingers as if that meant something. He frowned and kept walking. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She turned in a full circle, suitcase wheels rattling, loudspeakers barking sentences that slid past her like water. Her mouth had gone dry, and she swallowed twice before trying again. "Please? English?" Her voice cracked on the second word. A tight band seemed to be closing around her ribs. She gripped the suitcase handle until her knuckles blanched, and realized she had no idea which exit she had come from.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit had been zigzagging through the long grass for ten minutes, a tan blur against the green, and I was half-smiling over my thermos when he stopped. Just stopped. Nose down, tail rigid, one paw lifted. The thermos slipped from my fingers and the lid rolled away. "Biscuit," I said, too quietly, then louder, my voice cracking on the second syllable. "Biscuit, leave it. Leave it!" He didn't turn. My pulse was knocking in my ears, and my palms had gone cold and slick. I was already walking, then half running, boots snagging the tall stalks, eyes fixed on the patch of grass he was sniffing. Something coiled there, maybe, or only a stick. I couldn't tell. My mouth was dry as paper. "Come here, buddy, come on, good boy, come," I kept saying, holding out a shaking hand, crouching to make myself small, while the wind hissed through the field and the grass refused to show me anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite had just reached the second verse when the church hall's side door banged open and the sheet music slid from her stand, fluttering across the linoleum. She stopped mid-note. Her fingers stayed frozen on the keys, cold and damp, while her pulse thudded somewhere up in her ears. "Wait, wait, wait," she said, too high and too fast, already half off the bench. The folding chairs blurred. She counted the pages on the floor, one, two, three, and came up with only three, then counted again. "Where's the last one? Dennis, did anyone step on it?" Her breath came shallow, and her knees wobbled as she crouched. The concert was Saturday. She checked under the radiator, then behind the coffee urn, swallowing against a dry throat. When she finally found the page wedged beneath the stage skirt, she pressed it to her chest with both hands and did not let go for a long while.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta lifted the lid of the coffee can on Dennis's bench and the smell of old solvent rose, and then she saw the wires. Red, blue, taped together, trailing into the can's dark bottom. She set the lid down very slowly, as if it might ring. "Okay," she said to the empty shed. "Okay, okay." Her palms had gone slick against her jeans. Somewhere behind her a rafter ticked, and she spun around, knocking a jar of screws that burst across the concrete like hail. She didn't bend to gather them. She backed toward the door, eyes on the can, her heart knocking so hard she could feel it in her teeth. Her phone was in the truck. Dennis had never once mentioned wiring anything. Her voice came out thin, almost a whisper: "What did you build?" She stepped outside, then back in, then out again, unable to leave it unwatched.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and at 11:58 I had already refreshed the page nine times. The hallway outside the registrar's office smelled of floor wax and somebody's burnt coffee. My thumb left a damp smear on my phone screen. "It's just a page," I told Dana, but my voice came out thin and too fast, and I had to stop and swallow. My knee wouldn't quit bouncing. I kept reading the same line, *Results will be available shortly*, until the words stopped meaning anything. Then the clock flipped, and my pulse thudded so hard in my ears that I couldn't hear the printer down the hall. A list appeared on the wall. People shoved forward. I stayed pinned to the cold tile, fingers numb, thinking: what if I misread the room number on my paper, what if my name just isn't there at all. Dana said my name twice before I heard it. I realized I'd stopped breathing somewhere around the second refresh.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid behind the ridge, and I stopped walking. Pine trunks that had been trees a minute ago were now just darker slabs of dark. I pulled out my phone: no bars, eleven percent battery. "Okay," I said aloud, too loudly, "okay, okay." My thumb shook as I switched on the flashlight, and the beam showed me two paths where I'd swear there had been one. My pulse thudded in my ears, drowning the creek I'd been following. I turned in a circle, then another, boots scraping gravel. Where was the trail marker? I'd passed a blue blaze at the switchback, hadn't I? I could taste metal. Behind me a branch cracked, and I spun, light jerking across empty trunks. I walked faster, then nearly jogged, palms slick on my pack straps, whispering the same sentence over and over: "Back to the switchback. Just back to the switchback."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, my grandmother's slanted pencil smudged across it, and the last line stops me cold: "Add the starter, the real one, from the crock." I don't have a crock. I flip the card over, then back, flour puffing off my sleeves onto the counter. My heart is knocking against my ribs so hard I can feel it in my teeth. "No, no, no," I say, too high, too fast, to the empty kitchen. The dough sits there, shaggy and pale, already warm under my palms. I wipe my hands on my jeans and leave white prints, then grab my phone and drop it, and it clatters against the stove. Mom picks up on the fourth ring. "Where is the crock?" I blurt, voice cracking. My knees feel loose. The oven timer keeps ticking behind me, and I can't remember if I even pressed start.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana was weighing two cartons of oat milk in the dairy aisle when a voice behind her said, "Dana Whitlock? Room 14, Mr. Pruitt's class?" The carton slipped from her fingers and thudded against the tile, splitting at the seam. Cold white spread over her sneakers. She didn't look down. Her pulse hammered in her neck, and she yanked her hood up over her hair, though she was indoors. "Oh. Hi. Wow," she said, too fast, too high. Marcus Tell, grinning, older, a toddler on his hip. Her eyes flicked to the exit, then the cart, then the exit again. Her mouth had gone dry as chalk. "I'm actually just leaving," she said, stepping backward into the puddle and nearly going down. "Sorry. Mess. I should tell someone about the mess." She was already walking, basket abandoned, the freezer hum roaring in her ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The warehouse lights hummed over empty aisles, and I was counting down the minutes to six, Christmas Eve finally within reach, when the smell hit me. Burnt plastic. I stopped mid-scan, the gun still in my hand, and sniffed again. Sharp. Real. My mouth went dry. "Dale?" My voice came out thin, so I tried again, louder. "Dale, do you smell that?" Nobody. Just the forklifts parked in a row, the dock doors rattling in the wind. I walked toward the back, then faster, my boots slapping concrete, my pulse thudding in my ears. Gray wisps curled from the charging station by pallet nine. I dropped the scanner. It clattered and I didn't pick it up. My hands wouldn't stay still as I yanked the extinguisher from the wall, fumbling the pin twice before it slid free. "Okay," I whispered, to no one. "Okay, okay, okay." My knees felt like water. I squeezed the handle.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The monitor flipped from 4:52 to 4:58 while I was still standing in the passport line, and my thumb stabbed at my phone as if it could slow the clock. Boarding for Gate C41 closed at 5:10. "Sorry, sorry, excuse me," I kept saying, my voice cracking high, squeezing past a stroller, a man with a cello. My backpack straps bit into my shoulders. Sweat gathered under my collar, and my heartbeat thudded so loudly in my ears I almost missed the tram announcement. The doors were already sliding shut. I jammed my arm between them, felt the rubber clamp my wrist, and hissed, "Please, please." They sprang open. Inside, I stared at the map, counting stops on my fingers, my knee bouncing. Why had I trusted a forty-minute layover? My mouth was dry as paper. When the tram lurched to a halt, I was already at the doors, boarding pass crushed in my fist, damp and wrinkled, the numbers smearing under my thumb.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta peeled the last strip of blue tape from the baseboard and froze. Beneath the old yellow paint, where her roller had dragged across the plaster, a dark stain bloomed, damp and spreading, the size of a dinner plate. She pressed two fingers to it. Cold. Wet. Her pulse knocked in her ears, and the roller slid from her other hand, rolling a slow white arc across the drop cloth. "No, no, no," she whispered, then louder, "Dev? Dev, come up here. Now." She dropped to her knees and sniffed the wall, her breath coming short and shallow. The ceiling above looked fine. Too fine. She stared at it, mouth dry, counting the pipes she knew ran behind this wall, and realized her palm was still pressed flat against the plaster, as if she could hold back whatever was behind it. Her fingertips trembled against the paint.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder rattled the porch boards, and Marguerite was on her feet before she knew it, the rocking chair still swaying behind her. Her coffee had gone over the rail. She didn't remember letting go of the mug. Across the yard the old oak thrashed, and every flash lit the gap in the fence where her grandson's bicycle lay on its side. "Danny?" she called, too high, too thin. The screen door banged against her hip. Her heart knocked so hard she pressed a palm flat against her blouse, as if to quiet it. Rain slanted under the roof and stung her ankles, but she stayed at the edge, squinting down the empty road. "He said the creek. He said just to the creek." Her fingers fumbled the phone, dropped it, found it again. Three rings. Four. The next bolt turned the whole street white, and she counted nothing, only gripped the rail until her knuckles ached, whispering his name between the thunder.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the rear wheel off and the chain tool in her fist when the door at the far end of the garage clicked. Her head turned before she'd decided to move it. Just Mr. Okafor from unit three, dragging his recycling bin. She let out a short breath through her nose and went back to the derailleur, but her shoulders stayed high, and she noticed every drip from the pipe over the workbench, every tick of the cooling water heater. "Morning," she said, too quickly, too bright. Her thumb found the broken link without her looking. She pressed the pin through, listened for the faint give of metal, and stopped to listen again. A car passed outside; she counted its tires on the gravel. When she spun the pedal, the chain ran silent, and she watched each link pass as though it might still surprise her. Her coffee sat cold, forgotten, beside the neighbor's paint cans.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marisol stood at the very edge of the shelter, one boot on the curb, her head turning each time the light shifted. The wind had swung around in the last minute, flipping candy wrappers in the gutter, and she felt the hair on her forearms lift. She pulled her hood up before the first drop landed. Far down the street, the sky had gone the color of a bruise, and she counted the seconds after a flicker of white. "Four," she muttered to the empty bench. Her thumb hovered over the phone, but she kept glancing up instead, tracking every pair of headlights, reading each one before it reached the corner. A gust rattled the schedule panel. Her breath came quick and shallow, and her fingers pressed the bus pass flat against her palm. When the rain finally slanted in, she didn't flinch; she only stepped sideways, eyes already on the bend where the number 14 would appear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid comes off with a soft hiss of dust, and I stop breathing for a second to listen. Nothing. Just the fridge humming downstairs, a car passing, my own pulse in my ears. I fan the envelopes across the carpet, my eyes jumping from postmark to postmark, not reading yet, hunting. Mom's looping hand. The bank's blue window. Then one with no stamp, my name in block capitals, and my fingers go cold and exact as I lift it. "Okay," I say aloud, too sharply. I check the hallway. The door is already shut; I get up anyway and turn the lock. Back on my knees, I slit the flap with my thumbnail, slowly, so the paper won't tear, and every creak of the floorboards snaps my head toward the sound before I make myself unfold the page.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came at 6:40, two short raps, and Marta's hand stopped halfway to the kettle. She hadn't heard footsteps on the gravel. Through the peephole, Mr. Dolan's face bulged, smiling, a flashlight dangling from his fist though the sun was up. She opened the door only as far as the chain allowed. "Ladder?" she said, her voice flatter than she meant. "Which one do you need?" He said the roof, just a gutter, ten minutes. Her eyes slid past his shoulder to his dark windows, then to the street, then back. Her pulse ticked in her neck. "The long one's got a bad rung," she said, watching his hands. "I'll bring the short one out myself. Wait there." She slipped the chain off, stepped onto the porch barefoot, and didn't turn her back on him once, even when the cold boards bit her heels.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol had the lamb out of the oven before the timer finished its second beep, her thumb already silencing it. Six forty. They'd said seven, but Dev was always early. She tilted the pan, watched the juices run clear, and set it on the rack without feeling the heat through the mitt. Behind her the rice lid rattled; she turned without thinking and lowered the flame by a hair. Every sound in the apartment seemed sharpened: the elevator's hum in the hall, a door two floors down, the tick of the cooling stove. "Salt," she muttered, tasting the sauce, then "no, lemon," and squeezed half one over the spoon. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She wiped the counter in one sweep, flicked off the overhead light, lit the candles, and stood with her hands loose at her sides, head tipped toward the front door, listening for the first knock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, and Marta's knife stopped mid-onion. A string of digits, no name, a area code she didn't know. She wiped her fingers on her jeans without looking away from the screen. The refrigerator hummed; she noticed it, noticed the tap dripping too, each drop distinct. Her thumb hovered, then pressed answer, and she lifted the phone but said nothing, tilting her head to listen past the silence. Breathing? Traffic? A faint clack of keys. "Hello," she said at last, low and even, her free hand drifting to the edge of the counter. "Who is this?" Her shoulders had risen toward her ears. She moved to the window and eased the curtain an inch aside, scanning the street, the parked cars, the porch light across the road. Her pulse thudded in her throat. "I'm listening," she said. "Go ahead."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Mara pushed through the library's glass doors at 8:59, one minute before the desk opened, and her eyes swept the room before her feet had stopped moving: two staff members, a cart of returns, a clock ticking louder than it should. The copy of *Middlemarch* was pressed flat against her ribs, its spine warm from her grip. Fourteen months. She had rehearsed the sentence on the walk over, but when the librarian looked up, she spoke fast and clipped. "This is overdue. Very. I'll pay whatever it is." Her heartbeat tapped in her throat. She noticed the librarian's pen hovering, the small crease between her brows, the red stamp sitting to the left of the scanner. When the screen flickered, Mara leaned in before the number even loaded, fingers already at her wallet, ready for anything, her gaze fixed on the screen and her shoulders high and still, as if the next sound might require her to move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: I set the last box down without a sound and stood still, head tilted, listening. The radiator ticked. Upstairs, a chair scraped, then stopped. My eyes went to the window, the fire escape, the gap beneath the front door where a shadow of feet slid past and kept going. I counted the steps until they faded. "Hello?" I said to nobody, too quietly, and felt stupid and didn't relax. My pulse sat high in my throat. I checked the deadbolt twice, then the window latch, then the deadbolt again, thumb pressing the cold brass. Every pipe knock made my shoulders jump toward my ears. The apartment was eleven steps long; I'd measured it already, and memorized where each floorboard complained. I didn't unpack the lamp. I left the overhead light off so I could watch the hallway without being seen, and I sat on the mattress edge, shoes still on, hands flat on my knees, waiting for the next sound.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marisol stopped mid-stride when the brown leather caught the corner of her eye. The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, half hidden by a drift of maple leaves. She didn't reach for it. Her head turned slowly instead, left along the gravel path, right toward the fountain, then back over her shoulder at the empty swing set. A jogger's footsteps faded; a crow shifted on a lamppost. Her pulse ticked in her throat, and she noticed she was holding her breath. "Hello?" she called, pitched low, then louder. "Anyone lose something?" Nobody answered. She crouched, fingertips brushing the edge, listening to every small sound around her: the rustle of a paper bag, a distant dog's bark, a bicycle bell. When she finally lifted the wallet, she kept her eyes on the trees, thumb already finding the driver's license, ready to look up at the slightest movement behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood at the shallow end with her toes curled over the tiled edge, and she heard everything: the lifeguard's whistle two lanes over, the gurgle of the drain, a child's splash echoing off the high ceiling. Her eyes tracked the instructor's hand as it lifted. "Okay, float on your back," he said, and she nodded before he'd finished. She lowered herself in, shoulders tight, and felt the cold climb her ribs one by one. Her fingers splayed against the water. When it lapped near her ear she stopped, counted her breaths, and noticed the wall drifting an inch farther away. She corrected with a small kick before he could say a word. "Too far left," she murmured, mostly to herself. Her heartbeat thudded in her throat, steady and quick. Every ripple seemed to say something, and she read all of it, chin up, eyes wide, not blinking until they stung.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packet pinched between two fingers, reading the back for the third time. Plant after last frost. Quarter inch deep. She'd already checked the sky twice. A rustle in the hedge made her head snap toward it, trowel half-raised, and she held still until a sparrow hopped out. "Okay," she muttered, "just a bird." Her pulse thudded in her ears as she pressed a finger into the soil, measuring against her knuckle, then dropped in a tomato seed and covered it with a gentle pat. Every sound seemed sharpened: the creak of the neighbor's gate, the tick of the sprinkler down the block, a beetle crossing the dirt near her wrist. She watched it go. Her eyes kept moving between the row, the packet, the clouds, and the beetle. She didn't sit back once. "One," she whispered, and reached for the next seed, shoulders tight, not wanting to miss anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to slide six, and I caught the typo before she did: "Q3 revnue." My pen stopped mid-scribble. I'd already set my coffee aside an hour ago because the cup's tremor in my hand annoyed me, and now I sat forward, spine off the chair, elbows on the table's cold edge. The projector fan hummed; I heard it, and I heard Marcus's chair creak behind me, and the faint squeak of Dana's sneaker as she shifted her weight. Her numbers said forty percent growth. Last week's spreadsheet said twenty-six. My heart knocked steadily against my ribs. I didn't blink much. When she paused for questions, my hand was already half raised, and my voice came out low and even. "Dana, can you go back one slide? The baseline there, where's it from?" Every head turned. I kept my eyes on the screen, on the number, waiting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol rolled the window down two inches, and the cold air stung her cheek in a way she welcomed. The highway was empty past midnight, just reflectors flicking by and the long gray ribbon of asphalt. She had both hands on the wheel, ten and two, and her eyes moved constantly: mirror, road, shoulder, mirror. A shape at the edge of the headlights made her ease off the gas before she even knew what it was. A deer, frozen, eyes like coins. "Easy, buddy," she murmured, and the animal bounded into the trees. Her pulse thudded in her ears, but her foot was steady on the pedal. The radio hummed some low song she'd stopped hearing miles ago; she turned it off to listen to the tires instead. Every green sign seemed sharp and distinct. Four exits left. She counted them out loud, clear and even, and sat a little straighter in her seat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator doors open on the fourth floor and I'm already counting the room numbers before I step out. 412, 414. Grandpa's is at the end. I hear everything: the squeak of a nurse's shoes, a monitor chirping two doors down, someone's cart rattling over a seam in the tile. My coffee sits untouched in my fist, and my pulse thuds in my ears. I stop in his doorway and watch his chest rise, once, twice, and only then step in. 'Hey, Pop,' I say, quieter than I mean to. His eyes flutter. I notice the IV line has a little kink near his wrist, so I smooth it out with two fingers. The machine's green numbers hold steady, and I memorize them anyway. When the aide leans in the door, I'm already turned toward her, ready with questions. 'What's the new medication called?' I ask, and I'm writing the answer on my palm before she finishes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I'm standing at the fence ten minutes before the bell, coffee gone cold in my hand, and I haven't touched it. The gray sedan has circled the block twice. I note the plate, then feel silly, then keep noting it. My eyes slide from the double doors to the crossing guard to the man by the oak tree who isn't holding a phone or talking to anyone. "Morning, Dana," someone says beside me, and I answer a beat late, "Hey, yeah, hi," without turning my head. My heels are lifted slightly off the pavement. Every shout from the playground makes my neck snap toward it, and each time it's only kids. The doors finally bang open. I count orange backpacks, then yellow ones, my pulse ticking in my ears. There: Milo's cowlick, his crooked grin. I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding, but I still don't set the coffee down until his hand is in mine.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: I've been standing behind the card table since six, coffee gone cold, and I haven't sat once. The man in the green cap has circled my grandmother's oak dresser three times now, running his thumb along the drawer edges. I count the cash in the tin without looking down. Two teenagers drift toward the lamps, and my eyes follow their hands, then flick back to the cap. "Forty," I say, flat and quick, before he asks. He frowns. A car door slams down the street and my head snaps toward it. Just a neighbor. My pulse is still knocking in my ears, my shoulders tight as fence wire. "Thirty-five, and you carry it," he says. I don't answer right away. I'm listening to the gravel behind me, the faint creak of the rocking chair someone just nudged. "Sold," I say, and I'm already turning to find whose hand is on that chair.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip under the sink has a rhythm, and I've already counted it twice: one, two, three, plink. I kneel on the cold tile with the flashlight clenched between my teeth, every sound in the house suddenly loud. The fridge hums. A car passes outside and I freeze, wrench midair, until it fades. My pulse ticks in my ears. I run a dry fingertip along the copper joint and feel it, a bead of wet, tiny and sly. "There you are," I whisper. I don't blink much. The shutoff valve is stiff, so I lean into it, forearms burning, and the hiss dies off all at once. Silence. I hold my breath and watch the joint, eyes wide, shoulders high, waiting for it to try me again. Nothing. Then, one slow gleam gathers at the edge. I'm already reaching for the tape.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a window and a federal seal, and Marta stopped in the middle of the hallway with her keys still in her fist. She set the grocery bags down without looking at them. The refrigerator hummed; she noticed it, and the drip of the bathroom tap, and a car door slamming two floors below. She slid her thumb under the flap and felt the paper's edge catch. "Okay," she said quietly, to nobody. Her eyes skipped the greeting and went straight to the second paragraph, then the date, then the bolded line near the bottom. Her pulse thumped in her ears. She read it again, slower, one finger trailing under each word, and reached for a pen without taking her eyes off the page. Thirty days. Reference number. She wrote both on her palm, then turned the letter over to check the back for anything she might have missed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train doors hiss open and I step onto the platform with my backpack strapped across my chest, one hand clamped over the zipper. Signs in characters I can't read hang overhead, and I turn in a slow half-circle, memorizing the exits, the stairs, the man by the pillar who has glanced at me twice. My ears pick through the announcements for any sound I might recognize. Nothing. I pull my phone out, then put it away; screens make you look lost. Instead I follow the swell of commuters, matching their pace, my heartbeat loud in my throat. At the ticket gate a woman says something quick and sharp, and I freeze, then hold up the paper with the hotel's address. She points left. "Thank you," I say, too loudly, and bow slightly. Outside, scooters whine past and the smell of frying oil hits me. I count the turns as I walk: left, second right, past the red awning. I won't miss anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta kept the leash looped twice around her fist, though Biscuit was forty yards off, nosing through the tall timothy grass. Her thumb worked the nylon handle. When the dog's head snapped up, she stopped breathing mid-sentence, the thermos halfway to her mouth. "Biscuit," she said, low and even, not yet a call. A crow lifted from the fence post. Somewhere past the hedgerow a branch cracked, and her shoulders rose toward her ears. She turned her head slowly, listening, scanning the treeline left to right, the gap in the wire, the empty gravel lane. Her heartbeat thumped in her neck. The dog's tail wagged once and went still. Marta set the thermos in the grass without looking at it and stepped forward, weight on the balls of her feet. "Here. Come on, good girl, here." Her voice stayed bright, but her eyes never left the hedge until the dog's collar jingled against her knee.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite stood at the edge of the church hall's plywood stage, cello propped against her knee, and heard everything: the radiator ticking, a folding chair scraping two rows back, the conductor's pencil tapping twice on his stand. Her eyes tracked his left hand before it even rose. "Bar forty-one, yes? Pickup on the and?" she asked, quicker than she meant to, and he nodded. Her bow hovered a finger's width above the string, and her pulse thudded faintly in her wrists. When the flutes entered, she caught the tiny wobble in the second player's breath and leaned in to match it. She didn't blink through the whole crescendo. Afterward, someone dropped a music folder with a slap, and her shoulders jerked up toward her ears. She laughed, rolled them back down, and flipped the page before anyone said go. "Again from forty-one," she said. "I've got it. Let's go."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta stopped with one boot on the threshold, head tilted. The workshop ticked and settled around her, and she held still until she was sure the sound was only the cooling pipes. Then she crossed the concrete, weight on her toes, and let the door swing shut without letting go of the handle. "Okay," she said, too loudly, and winced. Dust hung in the slant of window light; she watched it drift, tracking each speck as if it might change direction. Every drawer she opened, she opened an inch first, peering in before committing. Chisels, graded by size. A coffee tin of screws. Her pulse tapped in her throat when something rattled behind the lathe, and she was there in two strides, flashlight up, jaw tight, to find only a coil of wire slumped from its hook. She laughed once, short. Her palms were damp against the cardboard box. She noticed the radio's dial was set between stations, and she reached out, hesitated, and left it exactly where Daniel had.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: By ten to noon Marisol had already circled the corridor twice, and now she stood three feet from the glass-fronted noticeboard with her phone in one hand and her bus pass in the other, though she'd checked both a minute ago. The janitor's mop squeaked somewhere behind her and she turned her head at it, quick, then back. Every footstep on the stairs pulled her shoulders up. Her heartbeat thudded in her ears, clean and loud, and the fluorescent hum seemed to have sharpened into a single high thread. "Is that them?" she asked a boy beside her, too fast, before seeing the secretary was only carrying a stapler. She laughed, short and breathless. Her eyes tracked the office door, its handle, the gap beneath it where a shadow might shift. When the handle finally dipped, she was already leaning forward, toes gripping the insides of her shoes, every thought narrowed to one sheet of paper and the hand about to pin it up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light went orange between the pines, and Mara stopped walking to listen. Somewhere left of the trail, a branch cracked once, then nothing. She held her breath and counted to ten, her thumb hooked under her pack strap, her pulse ticking in her ears. Every needle on the path seemed sharp-edged and separate.
