author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a window and a federal seal, and I knew before I touched it. I stood at the counter and slit it with my thumbnail, so hard the paper tore through the first line. Three pages. I read the first sentence twice, then the amount, then the deadline, which had passed four days before the thing even reached my mailbox. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my back teeth since the stairwell. "Unbelievable," I said, quietly, to the toaster. Then not quietly. My pulse thudded in my ears and the pages crackled in my fist, a damp heat climbing up my neck. I smoothed them flat, because I'd need them, and read the phrase 'we regret any inconvenience' aloud in a bright, mocking voice. The kettle started screaming and I let it. I grabbed my phone, jabbed the number printed at the bottom, and stood there, knuckles white, listening to the hold music, already rehearsing every word I planned to say.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver dropped my suitcase on the curb, said something fast and flat, and held out his palm for a number that was double what we'd agreed. I counted the bills twice, slowly, and slapped them down one at a time. My jaw ached from clenching. In the station, the ticket machine swallowed my card and flashed a wall of characters I couldn't read. I hit the screen with the heel of my hand. Once. Twice. A woman behind me sighed, and I turned and said, very quietly, 'Go ahead, then, you do it,' in English, knowing she'd understand none of it. My neck was hot, my pulse thudding in my ears. I yanked the suitcase handle so hard the wheel caught and skidded sideways. I kicked it straight. Outside, the neon signs blurred into bright smears, and I walked past three people who were trying to help, eyes fixed forward, shoulders up near my ears, repeating the hotel's name like a sentence I wanted to throw at someone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus stood at the edge of the field with the leash wound twice around his fist, the nylon biting into his knuckles. Biscuit tore across the wet grass in wide, joyful loops, ears flapping, the torn cushion from the sofa still somehow fresh in Marcus's mind, stuffing like snow across the living room. His jaw ached; he realized he'd been grinding his molars since the gate. A muscle jumped beneath his eye. "Biscuit. Here." The word came out low and flat, and of course the dog didn't turn. He said it again, louder, and a woman on the path glanced over and quickly looked away. Heat crawled up his neck. He kicked a clod of dirt and watched it burst apart against the fence post, then kicked another. Out in the field Biscuit dropped into a play bow, tongue lolling, utterly unbothered. Marcus exhaled through his nose, long and shaky, and didn't move his feet. The leash creaked in his grip.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marta set the metronome on the church piano's lid and clicked it to sixty, though her jaw was already clenched tight enough to ache. Behind her, folding chairs scraped. Dennis, the tenor, was late again, and he strolled in whistling, coat dripping onto the hymnals. "Bar twenty-two," she said, very evenly, and played it. Her fingers hit the keys harder than the marking allowed. A string of hot prickles climbed her neck. When Dennis came in a beat early, she stopped mid-phrase and the silence rang. She pulled the pencil from behind her ear and it snapped between her thumb and finger; she looked at the two halves, then set them neatly on the stand. "Again," she said. Her voice was low, almost pleasant. Under the bench her heel drummed the pedal board, a hard, steady thud, and she did not look up until the heat in her face had dulled to something she could hold. "From the top. Everyone. Together this time."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta pulled the tarp off the lathe so hard that sawdust rose in a gray cloud and settled on her sleeves. Every drawer she opened was labeled in Dov's tidy block capitals, every chisel hung in its outline on the pegboard, and the neatness of it made her jaw ache. Eleven years of unreturned calls, and here was his whole life sorted by size. She dropped a box of dovetail saws into the trash bag, and the clatter echoed off the rafters. "Couldn't pick up a phone," she muttered, then louder, to the empty bench, "but you had time to sharpen all of these." Her fingernails dug crescents into her palms. She found the half-finished rocking chair under a sheet, the one he'd promised her, and she stood there breathing through her teeth, hands shaking, before she kicked the leg of the sawhorse and sent a coffee can of screws skittering across the concrete in every direction.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go live at noon. At 12:04 Marisol was still hitting refresh, her jaw so tight her molars ached, the trackpad clicking under a finger that jabbed harder each time. The page showed the same grey spinner. Around her the library hummed with people who seemed unbothered, and a boy two desks over laughed at his phone. She shoved her chair back, and it screeched across the floor. Heads turned. She didn't care. "Four months," she muttered to the screen, voice low and flat. "Four months of nights, and you can't load a stupid page." Her pulse thudded in her ears, her face felt hot, and the pen in her fist snapped, ink bleeding across her palm. She stared at the blue smear, breathing hard through her nose, then slammed the laptop half shut, opened it again, and hit refresh, refresh, refresh.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta took the switchbacks two at a time, her boots hammering the dirt hard enough to jar her teeth. The sun had slid behind the ridge, and the pines went from green to black while she climbed, jaw locked, fingers cramped around her pack straps. "Twenty minutes," she muttered, voice like gravel. "He said twenty minutes." Her phone showed no signal, and she shoved it into her pocket so roughly that the seam tore. A branch snapped back across her cheek and she ripped it off the trunk and flung it into the ferns. Heat crawled up her neck despite the cooling air. She stopped, breathing hard through her nose, and kicked a rock over the edge, listening to it clatter long after it should have stopped. Then she laughed once, short and humorless, and kept walking faster, eyes fixed on the dimming trail, rehearsing every word she would say to him at the bottom, each sentence sharper than the last.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was stained yellow with forty years of butter, and Marcus slapped it flat against the counter so hard the flour jumped. "A handful," he read aloud, voice clipped. "Whose handful, Gran? Yours? Mine are twice the size." He plunged his fists into the dough and shoved it away, folded it, shoved it again, his jaw so tight his teeth ached. Heat climbed his neck. The kitchen window was fogged, the oven ticking, the third failed loaf sitting like a gray brick in the sink. "Bake until done." He laughed once, a short ugly sound. His knuckles were white and sticky, and when the timer began to chirp he ripped it off the wall and threw it into the bread bin, then stood breathing hard through his nose, staring at her loopy handwriting until the words blurred.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was squeezing a cantaloupe in the produce aisle when he heard the laugh, that same braying laugh from tenth-grade chemistry, and his thumb punched straight through the rind. Derek Voss stood by the apples in a pressed quarter-zip, grinning, arms already opening for a hug. Marcus kept his hands on the cart. His jaw felt welded shut, and heat crawled up the back of his neck while the fluorescent lights hummed too loudly. "Marcus! Man, it's been forever." "Eighteen years," Marcus said, flat and slow. "You still owe me three hundred dollars." Derek's grin wobbled. "Come on, that was ages ago—" Marcus set the ruined cantaloupe in Derek's outstretched hands, juice running down the man's clean cuffs. He rolled the cart forward, knuckles white on the handle, and didn't look back, though he could hear his own breath scraping loud through his nose all the way to the registers.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:52 on Christmas Eve, Marisol wiped the same stretch of deli counter for the third time, the rag squeaking under her clenched fist. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars since the man in the camel coat had asked for his turkey sliced "thinner, like I said." He hadn't said. Now he stood at the register tapping his card against the glass, tap, tap, tap, and heat crawled up her neck into her ears. 'Anything else?' she asked, each word clipped flat as the ham. He sighed at the ceiling. The fluorescent lights hummed, the speaker looped a jingle about peace on earth, and she ripped the receipt off the printer so hard it tore in half. She pressed the two pieces together on the counter, smoothing them with a thumb that trembled, and slid them over without a smile. 'Merry Christmas,' she said, in the voice she used for cutting bone. Behind her, the clock hadn't moved. Eight more minutes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The gate agent at B12 said "Sir, boarding's closed" without lifting her eyes from the screen, and my jaw locked so hard I heard my molars click. I'd sprinted the whole concourse, duffel slamming my hip, shirt glued to my spine, and the jet bridge door was right there, forty feet away, still open. "It's open," I said, low and flat. "I can see it. Open it's open." My own voice sounded like gravel. She tapped a key. My knuckles had gone white around the strap, and a pulse hammered behind my eyes. Two hours I'd sat on that cursed tarmac in Denver while somebody 'waited for a crew.' I set my boarding pass on her counter very carefully, flattening it with my palm, because if I didn't do something slow, I'd do something else. "Find me a seat," I said. "Any seat. Tonight." Behind me, someone sighed. I turned around and stared until they stopped.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller hits the wall hard enough that paint spatters my wrist, and I don't wipe it. Three coats of "Soft Linen," and Dana's old nail holes still show through like little mocking mouths. I jam the spackle knife into one, scrape it flat, scrape it again, until the plaster flakes onto the drop cloth. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars since the second coat. Upstairs, her footsteps cross the floor, light, unbothered, and I stop breathing to listen. 'It looks fine,' she called down an hour ago. Fine. I pried the lid off the can with a screwdriver, stabbing it, and said, 'Great,' in a voice so flat it could have been rolled onto the wall too. Now I press the roller into the tray, drag it up the wall in one long stripe, and watch my knuckles whiten around the handle. The fumes sting my eyes. I don't open the window. I keep painting, faster, until the whole wall is shining and wet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in just as Marla finished reading the letter for the third time, and she didn't flinch. She sat rigid in the porch chair, the paper crushed into a damp knot in her fist, her jaw clamped so hard her teeth ached. Rain hammered the tin roof. A gust flung cold spray across her shins and she let it. "Twenty-two years," she said to the empty yard, low and flat, each word bitten off. The swing beside her creaked and she kicked it, hard, and it banged against the rail. Her pulse thudded in her ears, louder than the downpour. Heat crawled up her neck despite the wet air. She smoothed the letter against her knee, read the signature again, then tore it down the middle, slowly, listening to it rip. Lightning split the maple at the property line. She stared straight at it, unblinking, and tore the halves again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The 10mm wrench was gone again. I stood there with the chain half off my rear wheel, grease up to my wrist, scanning the pegboard where its outline sat empty in black marker. Behind me, Dale's radio droned on about traffic. I breathed out slowly through my nose. Under his workbench, between a paint can and a coiled hose, something silver glinted, and I crouched, knees cracking, and pulled it out. "Hey, Dale," I said, too evenly, holding it up. "Found my wrench. In your stuff." He shrugged without turning. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my molars. I hung the wrench back in its outline, tapped it twice, and cranked the bolt so hard the whole frame shuddered. Then I turned his radio down one notch, just one, and went back to the chain.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marguerite checked her phone for the fourth time in six minutes, thumb jabbing the screen as if the bus might arrive faster out of fear. Still 4:52. The schedule said 4:40. A cold gust flipped the hem of her coat, and the first fat drops landed on the shelter's cracked plastic roof, then on her neck, where they slid under her collar. She jammed her jaw sideways and exhaled hard through her nose. The bench was wet; she remained standing, shifting her weight from one heel to the other, her bag strap digging a groove into her shoulder. A man beside her unfolded an umbrella and it clipped her elbow. 'Careful,' she said, flat and clipped, not looking at him. Down the road, a bus swung into view, but its sign read OUT OF SERVICE, and it rolled past, spraying her shoes. She stared after it, teeth pressed together, then muttered, 'Of course,' and tugged her sleeve down over her wrist to check the time again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta dropped the shoebox on the bed hard enough that the lid popped off and a rubber band snapped somewhere inside. Forty minutes, she'd told herself, and the movers were coming at nine. She pulled out an envelope, flipped it, tossed it left. Another, tossed left. Her jaw had locked sometime around the third postcard, and she worked it side to side, breathing out through her nose. "Weather. Weather. Who writes four pages about weather?" The paper smelled of dust and something floral that made her sneeze twice, sharply, into her elbow. Her aunt's handwriting looped on and on, never once landing on a point. Marta checked her phone: eleven minutes gone, the pile still a mess. She shoved a stack of them into the trash bag without reading, then paused, yanked a few back out because what if, and slapped them onto the keep pile with more force than the paper deserved. "Fine," she muttered to nobody. "Fine."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The doorbell rang twice while I was halfway through the first quiet Saturday coffee in a month. I set the mug down harder than I meant to. Gary stood on the porch in his slippers, grinning, one thumb hooked toward his gutters. "Don't suppose I could grab that ladder of yours? Just for an hour." My jaw tightened. That was the third time since March, and the last time it came back with a bent rung and mud on the feet. "Sure," I said, flat, each syllable clipped. I walked to the garage without waiting for him, the concrete cold through my socks, and yanked the ladder off its hooks so it clanged against the wall. My shoulders were up near my ears. "Back by noon," I said. He thanked me twice. I nodded once, shut the door, and stood in the hallway listening to my coffee go lukewarm, breathing slowly through my nose, counting the minutes until noon.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The oven clock said 6:12, and the lamb was still pink at its center. Marguerite shut the door with her hip and stood there, jaw tight, a wooden spoon gripped like a hammer. Behind her the phone buzzed against the counter again. She didn't look. "Fifteen minutes," she told the empty kitchen, each word clipped flat. "They said six-thirty. Not seven. Six-thirty." She yanked open the drawer, found the whisk tangled with the zester, and shoved at it three times before it gave. Sweat pricked under her collar. She blew a strand of hair off her forehead, and it fell right back. The potatoes needed salt; she gave them a hard, joyless shake. Out in the hall, her husband laughed at something on the television. She exhaled through her nose, long and slow, and turned the burner higher than the recipe said, watching the pot as though it had personally wronged her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter just as Marguerite got the knife into the avocado, and she let out a long, slow breath through her nose. Ten digits, none of them familiar. She wiped her fingers on her jeans, one at a time, deliberately, while the buzzing walked the phone toward the edge of the cutting board. Her jaw had already tightened. On the fifth ring she snatched it up. "Yes." The word came out flat and clipped. A pause, a click, a faint voice saying something about her vehicle's extended warranty. "I don't have a vehicle," she said, though that wasn't true, and she didn't care. Her thumb jabbed the red button hard enough to hurt. She stared at the screen, then at the avocado, now browning at the edges, and muttered, "Third one this week," before blocking the number and shoving the phone face-down beneath a dish towel.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been wedged under my bed since March, and now it was November, and the librarian was typing with two fingers. I stood at the desk with my backpack strap digging a groove into my shoulder, jaw clenched so tight my molars ached. "Forty-one dollars," she said, squinting at the screen as if the number might change if she stared long enough. I slid my card across without a word. The fluorescent light buzzed overhead, and I counted ceiling tiles to keep from groaning out loud. Behind me, someone's cart squeaked in a steady, maddening rhythm. "Would you like a receipt?" she asked. "Sure," I said, flat, each syllable clipped short. My thumbnail picked at the cracked spine of that required reading I'd skimmed in one night. When the printer jammed, I exhaled hard through my nose, glared at the exit sign, and tapped my foot against the carpet until the paper finally crawled out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The couch gets stuck in the doorway for the third time, and I stop pushing to breathe through my nose. "It measured fine online," I tell the empty hallway, my jaw tight enough to click. The landlord's note said cozy. Cozy, apparently, means the fridge door can't open past the stove. I peel tape off a box with one long screech, then stab the flap with my keys harder than I need to. Sweat runs down my spine. Upstairs, someone drags furniture back and forth, thump, scrape, thump, and I glare at the ceiling like it owes me money. I shove the couch again. Something cracks. I don't look at what. Instead I sit on its arm, wedged between the wall and a lamp, and say, flat and slow, "Great. Wonderful." My fingers drum the cushion. I count the steps from the door to the window. Four. I count them again, as if they might have grown.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marguerite had eleven minutes of lunch left when she sat down, sandwich unwrapped, and her thigh bumped something hard beneath a crumpled napkin. A brown leather wallet. She exhaled through her nose, long and slow, and set the sandwich back on its paper without taking a bite. "Of course," she told a pigeon. Her jaw tightened as she thumbed the wallet open: forty dollars, a library card, a license belonging to a Dennis Plover, who grinned stupidly from the photo. She checked her watch. Ten minutes. The police station sat six blocks the wrong way, past the construction. She snapped the wallet shut harder than she needed to, jammed it into her blazer, and stood, the sandwich still whole on the bench. "Careless," she muttered, stabbing at her phone for directions, heels clicking fast against the path, every step a small, deliberate punctuation mark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite gripped the pool's edge until her knuckles blanched and watched the kids in the next lane flutter past like it was nothing. "Kick from the hips," the instructor said for the fourth time, in the same bright voice. "I am kicking from the hips," she said, each word clipped short. Water slapped her nose and she coughed, then spat chlorine onto the tile. Her goggles had fogged again. She yanked them up, snapped the strap against her forehead, and left a red line there. Eight weeks of Tuesday evenings, forty-three years of being competent at everything else, and still her legs sank like fence posts. She pushed off anyway, three strokes, a gulp of air, a mouthful of pool. When she surfaced, the instructor was clapping. Marguerite stared at her hands, jaw tight, and muttered that she'd seen better progress from a brick. Then she walked back to the wall, shoulders high, and went again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana read the seed packet for the third time. "Plant in loose, friable soil," she said aloud, flatly, then looked at the clay under her boots, which clung to the trowel like wet cement. She jammed the blade down and it stopped an inch in. Her jaw tightened. She stomped on the shovel, felt the jolt rattle up her shins, and muttered something that made the neighbor's dog lift its head. Sweat slid into her collar. The tomato seedlings drooped in their plastic tray, looking smug, she thought. She yanked a rock the size of a loaf of bread from the hole and flung it toward the fence, harder than she needed to. It clanged off the gate. "Fine," she said to no one, snapping the packet shut. "Loose. Friable." She dug again, breathing hard through her nose, while the tutorial on her phone chirped from the grass: "It's so easy!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Derek clicked to slide fourteen, the one with my spreadsheet in it, and said "we" built the forecast. I pressed my pen into the legal pad until the nib tore a small groove through the page. The conference room air smelled like burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. My jaw had locked sometime around slide nine, and I noticed I was breathing only through my nose, slow, counted. He laughed at his own joke about synergy. Nobody else did. I smiled with my mouth closed, then glanced at the clock: 10:42, eighteen minutes to go. When he asked, "Any questions?" my hand went up before I decided anything. "Just one," I said, light, pleasant, each word sanded smooth. "Which quarter did the 'we' start working on this?" My foot was bouncing under the table, rattling the cheap leg. Derek's grin flickered. I capped my pen, very gently, and waited for his answer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The third red light in a row blinked on, and I stopped for it, though there wasn't another car for a mile. My knuckles had gone pale on the wheel. I exhaled through my nose, long and hard, and drummed two fingers against the dashboard in a rhythm that wasn't any song. Eleven forty. Meeting at eight. The highway had been closed for 'maintenance,' so the detour sent me through this sleeping town of dead streetlamps and one smug, blinking traffic signal. 'Come on,' I muttered, then louder, 'Come on, come on.' My jaw ached from clenching it. I yanked the vent toward my face, shoved the radio off mid-sentence, and listened to the engine tick instead. When the green finally came I crossed on it slowly, just to prove I could, then stomped the gas and watched the needle jump. Behind me, the next light turned red for nobody. I didn't look back. I'd have said something I'd regret to a pole.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine ate my dollar again, and I stood there pressing the return lever until my knuckle went white. Down the hall, Uncle Raymond's TV was blaring a game show at a volume meant for the whole floor. I walked in and picked up the remote from his blanket. "Ray, it's loud." He waved me off and kept watching. I sat in the vinyl chair, which wheezed under me, and counted the ceiling tiles while my jaw worked side to side. A nurse came in to check his chart and he told her the same story about the Buick he'd told me twice already. I nodded at the right places. My phone buzzed with the parking meter alert, and I exhaled through my nose, long and slow, and tapped my foot against the bed rail until he finally looked over and said, "You got somewhere to be?" "No," I said. "Keep going. The Buick."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The dismissal bell rang at 3:05, and it is now 3:31. I know because I've checked my phone eleven times, each time turning the screen face-down on the dashboard like that might speed things up. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding it since the crossing guard waved the minivan in front of me. The engine's off, then on, then off again. A woman in yoga pants laughs with another parent right by the doors, in no hurry at all, her SUV double-parked like the lane belongs to her. I drum my fingers on the wheel hard enough that my knuckle stings. 'Unbelievable,' I mutter to nobody, and exhale through my nose. When Maya finally bounces out, backpack unzipped, one shoe untied, I roll the window down and say, 'Car. Now,' in a voice flat as a ruler. She stares. I pull out before her door clicks shut, and don't ask about her day.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had priced the oak dresser at sixty dollars, written in thick marker on masking tape, and the man in the golf visor was now on his fourth minute of running his thumb along the drawer edge. "Twenty," he said. She breathed out through her nose. "It's sixty." He pulled a drawer out, sniffed it, and slid it back crooked, so she walked over and straightened it without a word. Her jaw ached from holding it still. The sun hammered the back of her neck, and her coffee had gone cold on the card table beside the sweating cash box. "My wife says it's chipped," he offered. "Your wife isn't here," Marguerite said, flat, and peeled the tape off the top. She wrote forty, pressed down hard enough to dent the wood, and stared at the street while he hummed and kept pretending to think.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped off the nut for the fourth time, and I cracked my knuckle against the cabinet wall. "Of course," I said, flat and quiet, to nobody. Water kept ticking into the pot beneath the U-bend, each drop landing right when I'd started to believe it had stopped. My jaw was clenched so tight my molars ached. I'd been folded under this sink for forty minutes, one knee on a cold pipe cap, a damp sleeve clinging to my elbow. I wound the tape again, tighter, ripped it with my teeth, and tasted rubber. Tightened. Waited. Drip. I set the wrench down very gently on the tile, the way you do when you'd rather throw it, and breathed out hard through my nose. Then I picked it up and glared at the nut like it owed me rent. On my phone, propped against the bleach, the tutorial that promised ten minutes started its cheerful intro music again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: Marguerite found the envelope wedged between a pizza flyer and a catalog she'd never ordered, its little plastic window stamped DEPARTMENT OF MOTOR VEHICLES. She carried it up three flights with her jaw set, her keys biting into her palm. At the counter she didn't bother with a knife; she jammed a thumb under the flap and ripped it crooked, then snapped the pages open with a crack. Two sheets. A third, blank except for a barcode. She read the first paragraph, exhaled hard through her nose, and read it again, slower, as if it might improve. "Seven weeks," she told the empty kitchen. "Seven weeks to tell me to fill out the form I already filled out." Her molars ached. She flicked the paper against the refrigerator, where it stuck under a magnet shaped like a lemon, then yanked open the drawer for a pen that, naturally, had dried up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The ticket machine at Budapest Keleti offered me four languages, none of which I'd studied, and I jabbed the little flag icon for English three times before it finally blinked. Three times. My jaw ached from clenching it since the airport. I dragged my suitcase, one wheel rattling like a loose tooth, to the window, where the woman behind the glass said something long and rounded and looked past my shoulder. "One ticket. Centre," I said, slower, louder, as if volume were a currency. She tapped a sign. I read it twice; it told me nothing. My neck was damp under my collar, and the strap of my bag had worn a hot line into my shoulder. I exhaled through my nose, hard enough to hear it, and pulled out my phone. No signal. Of course. I smoothed a crumpled note flat on the counter, a little too firmly, and said, "Fine. Whatever this buys me."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit has dropped the ball at my feet four times, and four times I've thrown it, and now he's sprinting the opposite direction after a crow he'll never catch. I check my watch. Twenty minutes past when I said we'd leave. My jaw is tight enough that my molars ache, and I realize I'm gripping the leash so hard the nylon has printed a red stripe across my palm. "Biscuit," I say, flat, not loud. He doesn't turn. "Biscuit. Now." Mud has crept over the toes of my good sneakers, cold and wet through the canvas. A woman nearby laughs at her own dog rolling in the grass, and I make a small noise through my nose and look away. The dinner I haven't started is sitting in my head like a stone. I clap twice, sharply, and he finally bounds over, tongue out, tail whipping my shins. I clip the leash on with a click that's harder than it needs to be. "Great," I mutter. "Really great."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Dennis had come in late again, third Thursday running. I set my cello bow down on my knee, very gently, the way you set down something you'd prefer to throw. "From bar forty," I said. My voice came out flat and bright, like a tin plate. We started. He rushed the run in bar forty-four, same as always, and my jaw tightened until my molars ached. I counted silently, breathing through my nose, watching the clock above the stacked folding chairs crawl toward nine. Someone's phone buzzed under the piano. My left hand cramped on the neck. "Lovely," I said when we stopped, and smiled with only my teeth. "Once more. Maybe with the metronome this time, Dennis?" I clicked it on harder than I needed to, and the tick filled the room like a dripping tap. I tugged my sleeves down and sat straighter, though my shoulders had climbed nearly to my ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The third coffee can I tipped out held nothing but screws, bent ones, rusted ones, a few hammered flat for reasons only Dale understood. I dumped them in the bin harder than I needed to. The clang set my jaw tight. Every drawer had a label, and every label was wrong. "Washers" held fishing line. "Misc." held one glove. I pulled a shelf out and a decade of sawdust slid down my sleeve and into my collar, and I stood there breathing through my teeth, counting the boxes left. Eleven. I'd told his sister Saturday, just Saturday. "You could've labeled one single thing right," I said to the pegboard, flat and quiet. Nobody answered. The radio he'd left tuned to some call-in show crackled on. I yanked the plug, stared at the cord in my fist, then taped another box shut, the tape screeching the whole length of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The department corridor smelled of floor wax and stale coffee, and Marisol had read the bulletin board's other notices twice: a lost umbrella, a choir sign-up, a yoga flyer with a curling corner. Noon, the door sign had said. It was 12:47. She pressed her thumb against the cold glass of the empty display case, then checked her phone, then the clock above the stairwell, which disagreed with her phone by two minutes and she resented it for that. Her jaw ached from clenching. A boy beside her whistled something tuneless, and she turned her whole head to look at him until he stopped. "Is someone actually coming," she said, not quite to anyone, in a flat voice, "or do we just live here now?" Her foot tapped the linoleum in quick, hard beats. When a secretary finally appeared with a single sheet of paper, Marisol exhaled sharply through her nose and muttered, "Forty-seven minutes. For one page."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Dana stopped at the fork and jabbed the trail map with one finger, then shook it flat again because the wind kept folding it shut. Twice now the sign had promised two miles. Her jaw ached from clenching, and she realized she'd been breathing hard through her nose for the last half hour. "Two miles," she said to a squirrel, flat and dry. "Sure. Two miles." The light had gone orange, then the color of weak tea, and the pines were turning to black cutouts. A pebble worked its way into her boot again; she yanked the laces loose, dumped it out with a hard slap against the log, and cinched everything tighter than necessary. Somewhere behind her, Mark was still whistling. She didn't turn around. She hauled her pack higher on her shoulders, stepped left without waiting for his opinion, and let her boots hit the dirt louder than they needed to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is stained brown at the corners, and Grandma's slanted pencil says "flour enough." Enough? I flip it over, hoping for a second line, and find only a grease spot shaped like a thumb. I dump in another cup, then another, and my jaw is so tight my teeth click when I mutter, "Of course. Just enough." Dough clots between my fingers like wet cement. I scrape it off against the bowl rim harder than I need to. "Warm water," the card says. Warm how? Bath warm? I run the tap, snatch my hand back, run it again. The oven timer buzzes early because I set it wrong, and I slap it quiet with my floury palm, leaving a white handprint on the stove. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears. I blow out a long, loud breath through my nose and punch the dough flat. Then I pick up the card and read "flour enough" one more time, as if it might have changed its mind.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana had one item left, a box of oat milk, when a voice sang her name from the end of the aisle. Brent Kowalski, tenth-grade chemistry, still holding his head at that same tilt. She tightened her grip on the basket until the plastic handle bit into her palm. "Hey," she said, flat, eyes on the shelf. He talked about his boat, his podcast, a house with a "man cave," and she watched the freezer door behind him fog and clear, fog and clear. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the cereal. "Wow. Great," she said, glancing at her phone, which showed no messages. When he asked to swap numbers, she exhaled through her nose and recited seven digits, the last two deliberately wrong. "Gotta run, my ice cream's melting." She had no ice cream. She walked to the self-checkout, jabbing the screen harder than the barcode required, and didn't look back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The clock over the pharmacy counter says 4:47, and the man in front of me is holding a prescription he's had since October. I press my tongue against my back teeth. "We close at five," I say, flat, smiling with only my mouth. He asks if I can "just quickly" check whether the insurance went through. I click the mouse harder than the mouse deserves. Behind him the line curls past the cough drops, everyone clutching gift bags and cranberry sauce, every one of them heading somewhere warm. My coworker left at noon. Her sweater is still on the back of her chair, and I have looked at it eleven times. The printer jams, naturally. I yank the tray open and the paper shrieks. "Sir, it'll be about ten minutes." My jaw aches. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears, and I let them stay there. Out past the glass doors, the parking lot empties car by car, without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The tram doors hissed shut an inch before my hand reached them, so I walked, then jogged, my carry-on wheels rattling like loose teeth across the terminal. Gate B42 glowed on the board. Forty minutes ago it had been B7. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the jet bridge. A man stopped dead in front of me to photograph a pretzel stand. "Excuse me," I said, each word clipped flat, and slid around him with my shoulder turned. Sweat pooled under my backpack straps. My phone buzzed: Final boarding. I exhaled hard through my nose and stabbed the elevator button three times, then a fourth, as if it might hear me. At the gate, an agent was already lifting the phone to close the door. "Wait," I called, my voice tight and too loud, boarding pass crumpled in my fist. She glanced up, unhurried, and began to say something about the system. I stared at her until she stopped.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pressed the roller into the tray, dragged it up the wall, and watched the old mustard yellow glow through the new white like a bruise. Second coat, then. She exhaled hard through her nose and set her jaw. The tape she'd spent an hour smoothing along the baseboard had peeled again, and she pressed it down with her thumb, once, twice, a third time, harder than it needed. 'Fine,' she told the empty room. 'Fine.' Her shoulder burned. A drip crept down toward her wrist and she let it, because wiping it meant climbing off the ladder, and the ladder wobbled. Downstairs, the TV laughed at something. Her husband had said he'd be up in ten minutes. That was before lunch. She dipped the roller again, too deep, and paint slopped over the tray's lip onto the drop cloth, onto the one corner she'd already used. She stared at it. Then she rolled on, fast and flat, her teeth clamped together, humming nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Dale had carried the good chair out to the porch at four, a full forty minutes before the sky turned the color of a bruise, and now the rain was coming in sideways and spattering his book. He wiped the page with his thumb. Smeared. He shifted the chair back; the leg caught on the same warped board it always caught on, and he yanked it free with a grunt that was louder than it needed to be. Thunder cracked. "Of course," he said to nobody, flatly, each word clipped short. His jaw ached from clenching. Inside, the screen door banged in the wind, bang, bang, bang, and he didn't get up to latch it. His iced tea had gone watery and warm, and he drank it anyway, staring at the gutter spilling over exactly where he'd told Marcy twice it would. He turned a damp page, read the same line three times, and snapped the book shut against his knee.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off the ring for the third time, and I wipe my palms on my jeans before trying again. Somewhere behind me a door scrapes open, and I freeze, wrench hovering, until the footsteps turn toward the other bay. My heart is still knocking. Mr. Okafor's drill whines and I flinch like it's aimed at me. "Sorry, am I in your way?" I say, too fast, though he hasn't looked over. I've reorganized my tools twice. Hex keys by size, then by how often I might need them. The tire lever slides from my fingers and clangs on the concrete, loud as a dropped pan, and I wince, jaw tight, waiting for someone to say something. Nobody does. I breathe in, shallow, feel my shirt stuck to my back despite the cold. If I can just get this wheel on before the others come home, before anyone watches me fumble, it'll be fine. It'll be fine. I check my phone again. Six-forty. Nobody's texted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Halloran Street had gone the color of a bruise, and Mina checked her phone again: 5:42, same as thirty seconds ago. The 14 was supposed to come at 5:35. She pressed her thumbnail into the pad of her finger until it whitened, then let go, then pressed again. A gust flipped the flyers in the shelter, and the first fat drops struck the glass. "Okay," she said aloud to no one, too brightly. "Okay, that's fine." Her stomach felt full of cold pennies. She stepped out to peer down the road, stepped back in, stepped out again, her heartbeat loud in her ears beneath the hiss of rain. What if the interview started without her? What if the driver skipped the stop? She rehearsed her opening line twice, lost it, started over. Thunder rolled behind the rooftops, and she jumped, laughed a thin little laugh at nothing, and hugged her folder against her chest, its corners going soft with damp.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid has been off for twenty minutes, and I still haven't touched the first envelope. I wipe my palms on my jeans, then do it again. The rubber band snaps when I finally pull it, and I flinch so hard my knee hits the table leg. "Fine," I say aloud to the empty attic, too brightly. "Just a few." I recognize his slanted handwriting and my stomach drops somewhere near my shoes. I set the letter down, pick it up, set it down. My thumb keeps worrying the torn corner. Downstairs the furnace clicks on and I'm standing, halfway to the stairs, before I realize it's only the furnace. My pulse is loud in my ears. I count the envelopes instead of reading them: nineteen. Twenty, maybe. I recount. Then I sit, breathe through my teeth, and slide a finger under the flap, ready to stop at any second.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came twice, soft, and I froze with the dish towel mid-wipe, water dripping down my wrist. Through the peephole, Mr. Alvarez from next door, grinning, one hand pointing vaguely toward my garage. "Just the ladder," he said when I opened up. "Gutters." My laugh came out too high. "Sure, yes, of course, it's, uh, it's a bit heavy." My heart was knocking against my ribs harder than he had at the door. I walked ahead of him, stepping on the same crack in the driveway twice, and wrestled the garage door up. The ladder hung where it always hung, one rung cracked, which I'd meant to fix in June. I opened my mouth to mention it, shut it, opened it again. "Careful on the third rung," I blurted, palms slick against the aluminum. He nodded, easy, already carrying it off. I stood on the driveway rubbing my thumb into my palm, replaying every word, wondering what I should have said instead, and whether he'd fall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol wiped her palms on her apron for the fourth time and peered through the oven window at the lamb, as if staring harder might cook it faster. Seven o'clock was twenty minutes off. The clock on the microwave said 6:41, and she checked her phone to see if it agreed. Her pulse thudded in her ears, loud enough to drown out the simmering pot. She tasted the sauce, frowned, added salt, tasted again, then reached for the pepper and knocked the jar into the sink. "Fine. Fine, it's fine," she muttered, fishing it out with damp fingers. Her jaw ached from clenching. She straightened the forks on the table that she had already straightened, lit a candle, blew it out, then lit it again. A car passed outside and her whole body jerked toward the window. Only the neighbor's. She exhaled, shakily, and went back to stirring a sauce that did not need stirring.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter, and Marisol froze with the dish towel half-wrung in her fists. Ten digits, no name, an area code she didn't recognize. She watched it rattle toward the edge of the sink. Her thumb hovered, pulled back, hovered again. Her pulse thudded in her ears, loud enough that she turned the faucet off to hear past it. "Don't," she muttered, and then, "Fine," and swiped. "Hello?" It came out thin, a whisper wearing a costume. Silence, a faint crackle. She pressed her free hand flat against her sternum and realized she'd been holding her breath. Her palms were slick; the phone slid, and she caught it against her cheek with a clumsy jerk. "Hello? Who is this?" she said, faster now, already backing toward the hallway, already rehearsing what she'd say if the voice spoke her brother's name. Her knees felt hollow. The towel lay forgotten on the floor, dripping.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and my thumb kept finding its corner through the canvas. I stood outside the library doors for what my phone said was six minutes, rehearsing. Inside, the air smelled like carpet and warm dust. My palms were slick; I wiped them on my jeans twice before reaching the desk. The librarian looked up, and my voice came out thin and too fast. "Hi, sorry, this is, um, kind of overdue. Like, really. I can pay whatever." I slid the book across with both hands, as if it might go off. My knees felt hollow. She turned it over, tapped her keyboard, and I watched her eyebrows instead of the screen, counting my heartbeats in my ears. I laughed at nothing. Then I asked if there was a bathroom nearby, though I didn't need one, just somewhere to stand still and breathe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box was still in the hallway, and Mara stood over it with the key pressed so hard into her palm it left a small red groove. She had already checked the stove twice. Now she checked the deadbolt, turned it, turned it back, listened to it click. "Okay," she said aloud to the empty studio, too brightly, and her voice bounced off bare walls. Her heart was going fast, a bird in a shoebox. Somewhere above her a floorboard creaked, and she froze, breath held, until the sound passed. She unpacked one mug, set it on the counter, moved it two inches left, then back. The window faced a brick wall; she kept glancing at it as if it might shift. Her phone buzzed with her mother's name. She watched it ring, thumb hovering, throat dry, and finally let it go to voicemail, then wondered what she'd do if the building caught fire and she couldn't find the stairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather, curled at the corners, and I walked past it twice before I made myself stop. My palms were damp. I wiped them on my jeans and looked around the park: a man with a stroller, two joggers, a pigeon pecking near my shoe. Nobody was looking at me, which somehow felt worse. "Hello?" I said, too quietly, then again, louder, my voice cracking on the second syllable. No one turned. I picked the wallet up with two fingers, as if it might be hot, and my heart thudded against my ribs so hard I could feel it in my throat. What if someone thought I'd taken it? I flipped it open. A driver's license, a smiling woman, an address six blocks away. I read it three times. My knee bounced as I stood there, thumb rubbing the seam of the leather, already rehearsing what I'd say at her door, and already sure I'd say it wrong.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood on the second step of the pool with water at her knees, fingers curled so tight around the rail that her knuckles had gone pale. The community center smelled of chlorine and wet concrete, and every shout from the kids' lane bounced off the tiles and landed in her ribs. "Just a minute," she told the instructor, who hadn't asked. She adjusted her goggles, then adjusted them again. Her heart knocked against her sternum, quick and uneven, and her mouth had gone dry in a room made of water. "Is it deeper right here? It looks deeper." She laughed, a thin sound, and glanced at the clock. Four minutes gone. She let go of the rail with one hand, then grabbed it back. Thirty-nine years old, she thought, and her legs felt like someone else's, trembling beneath the surface. "Okay," she whispered, not moving. "Okay. Okay." She took a breath, held it too early, and let it out in a shudder.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana read the back of the seed packet for the fourth time, then set it on the overturned bucket and picked it up again. "Six inches apart," she muttered. "Quarter inch deep. Or was it half?" She knelt in the damp bed, knees sinking, and pressed one finger into the soil, then pulled it out and checked the hole against her ruler. Her palms were slick inside the new gloves, so she tugged them off and wiped them on her jeans. A crow landed on the fence and she froze, shoulders up, until it left. She dropped a single tomato seed in, covered it, and laughed too loudly at nothing. Then she dug it back up to make sure it was still there. Her phone sat propped against the watering can, open to a video paused at the same frame. "It's just dirt," she said, and her voice cracked halfway through. She sat back on her heels, breathing through her mouth, staring at forty-nine empty inches of bed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the next slide before Marcus had finished his sentence, and the room's quiet hum swallowed the apology she meant to make. She wasn't presenting, but it was her spreadsheet on the screen, her numbers, her name in the footer, and she had read every cell four times that morning. Under the conference table her thumbnail worried at the skin beside her index finger. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago, yet she lifted it and sipped anyway, just to have something to do with her face. When the director leaned forward and said, "Wait, go back," her stomach dropped like a missed stair. Her pulse thudded in her ears, loud enough that she wondered if Priya beside her could hear it. "That's, um, that's the Q3 figure," she said, too fast, her voice climbing at the end as if asking permission. She pulled her sleeves over her wrists, found the cell in her mind, and counted the seconds until someone spoke.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol turned the radio off at the second exit, then on again, then off. The highway was empty except for a pair of taillights far ahead that she kept drifting toward and then braking away from. Her hands sat at ten and two, thumbs rubbing the stitched seam of the wheel until the leather felt hot. Every time the headlights swept over a mailbox or a fence post she caught herself leaning forward, jaw tight. "It's a deer sign," she said aloud, flatly, to nobody. "Just a sign." Her phone buzzed in the cup holder and she flinched so hard the car wandered over the rumble strip, a long, grinding growl that shot up through her seat. She corrected, breathed in through her teeth, and checked the mirror. Nothing. She checked it again. Her stomach felt like a fist around a wet rag. Eleven miles to home, the dashboard said, and she counted the reflector posts one by one, whispering each number, as if the road might lose track of her otherwise.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana stood outside room 412 for a full minute, rereading the whiteboard by the door as if the nurse's name might change. The sanitizer foamed cold in her palm, and she rubbed it until her knuckles squeaked and the skin went tight. 'Hi, Grandpa,' she said, too brightly, and her voice cracked on the second word. She set the grapes on the tray, then moved them to the windowsill, then back. Her heel bounced against the linoleum in time with the monitor's beeping, and she caught herself counting the beeps. 'They said you ate some toast?' she asked. He nodded. She laughed, a short breathy sound, and tugged her sleeve down over her wrist. Her stomach felt like a fist. When the doctor's shadow crossed the doorway, she stood so fast the chair scraped, and she forgot whatever she'd been about to say, her thumbnail pressing white crescents into her finger.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell was supposed to ring at 3:10, and I've checked my phone four times since 3:07. I'm standing by the fence, then by the gate, then by the fence again, keys biting into my palm. Other parents laugh in clumps; I nod at someone's joke a beat too late. My mouth is dry, so I swallow, and it clicks. Last week Maya came out last, face blotchy, refusing to say why, and I haven't stopped replaying it. "She's fine," I tell the woman beside me, though she hadn't asked. The doors bang open and a flood of backpacks pours out. I rise onto my toes, scanning for her yellow raincoat, counting heads, losing count, starting over. My heartbeat thumps in my ears. Where is she? Then a small hand waves from behind a tall boy, and my knees go loose so suddenly I have to grip the fence to stay upright.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By seven-thirty Marguerite had rearranged the oak dresser three times, angling it toward the street, then away, then back. The price sticker kept peeling off under her thumbnail, and she pressed it down again, harder. A man in a ball cap ran his palm along the drawer edge and she heard herself say, "It was my mother's, but, no, that's fine, it's just a dresser," too fast, too bright. Her stomach felt full of loose change. When he crouched to look underneath, she wiped her damp hands on her jeans and counted the cars passing on Alder Street, one, two, three, as though they might be taking something from her. "Forty," she blurted, then: "Thirty-five. Or whatever." He nodded slowly. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but she lifted it anyway, sipped, and set it down so carefully it made no sound. Her eyes never left his wallet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip under the sink has a rhythm, and I've counted along to four hundred and twelve before I make myself kneel. My knees crack on the tile. I wipe my palms on my jeans, twice, then grab the wrench and drop it, the clang making me flinch toward the door as if someone might be listening. "Okay," I say aloud, too brightly. "Okay, okay." The video on my phone is paused on a man whose hands never shake. I press play, miss the part, rewind, miss it again. My heart is knocking against my ribs harder than the pipe is dripping. When I turn the joint, it groans, and I freeze, jaw clenched, picturing the ceiling downstairs stained brown. Water beads at my wrist and runs cold up my sleeve. I breathe in through my teeth. Shallow. I check the clock, then the pipe, then the clock again, and whisper, "Please, just hold," to a piece of copper.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had been leaning against the toaster since Tuesday, its little window showing Marisol's name in blocky capitals. She washed the same mug twice. She wiped the counter around the envelope, not touching it. "It's probably just a form," she told the cat, her voice coming out thin and too bright. At last she sat, and her thumb slid under the flap, then stopped. Her pulse thudded in her ears, and the refrigerator's hum seemed suddenly enormous. She tore it halfway, paused, and wiped her damp palms on her jeans. Twice she read the first line without understanding a single word of it. Her knee bounced against the table leg, rattling the spoon in the sink. She pulled out the paper, unfolded it a crease at a time, and held it at arm's length as if it might be hot. Then she shut her eyes, counted to three, and made herself look down at the page.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station exit spat me into a roar of horns and signs I couldn't sound out, and I stood there gripping my suitcase handle until my knuckles went pale. My phone said 4% battery. I checked it again anyway, as if it might change. A man in a yellow vest barked something at me, and I said, "Sorry, sorry, English?" far too fast, my voice climbing at the end. He waved me off. My shirt was sticking to my spine. I pulled out the crumpled printout with the hotel's address, read it twice, then a third time, though the characters meant nothing, and folded it smaller and smaller. Every taxi looked either too clean or too dirty. Someone brushed my elbow and I jerked, patting my pockets for passport, wallet, passport, wallet. Still there. My mouth was dry, but the café sign blurred past, because stopping meant being asked something. I kept walking, rehearsing one word, the only one I knew, whispering it under my breath like a key I might drop.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit bolts toward the tree line and my hand is already cupped around my mouth, calling him back before I've decided to. "Biscuit! Here! Come!" My voice comes out higher than I like. He doesn't turn. I count the seconds he's behind the hawthorn, reaching eleven before his tan rump reappears, and I realize I've been pressing my thumbnail into the leash loop until it left a white crescent. The grass is long enough to hide a hole, a wire, a snake. My stomach is a fist. I check my pocket for the treats, then for my phone, then for the treats again. A crow lands near him and I take three steps forward, stopping only because I'm being ridiculous. Am I? He pauses, nose down, and my breath stops with him. "Good boy," I whisper, to nobody, to the wind. My knees ache from standing so stiffly. When he finally trots back, tongue flapping, I grab him too hard, and he squirms, puzzled, while my heart keeps hammering against his fur.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite wiped her palms on her skirt for the third time and set the clarinet reed back between her lips, though it had already gone soft. The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Folding chairs stood in crooked rows, all empty, and still she angled her music stand so it hid her chest. "Just the opening again," she told the pianist, her voice thin and quick. She began, and the third bar cracked. She stopped. "Sorry. Sorry, once more." Her knees felt loose, as if someone had unscrewed them. She counted the ceiling tiles over the piano, lost count, started over. When the custodian dropped a stack of hymnals in the back, she flinched so hard the reed squeaked. She laughed too loudly, checked her watch, and found only four minutes had passed. Her heartbeat was in her ears, drumming a tempo faster than the metronome's. "Maybe I should skip the solo," she said, already flipping pages. "No. Again. From the top."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus had promised Dolores he'd be out of the workshop by noon, and it was already past two. He stood in the doorway with a flattened cardboard box under his arm, not yet inside. The place smelled of cedar and machine oil, and Teddy's apron still hung on its nail. He picked up a chisel, set it down, picked up another. His palms were damp; he wiped them on his jeans twice. "Just the small stuff first," he said aloud, too loudly, and the words bounced off the pegboard. A drawer stuck, and he yanked it until it came free and spilled screws across the floor. He crouched, gathering them with fingers that wouldn't quite close, counting under his breath and losing count. What if he threw away the wrong thing? What if there was a note, a half-finished box, something Teddy meant for someone? His heart knocked against his ribs. He checked his phone, then the clock, then the unlabeled jars, and still the box stayed empty.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and at 11:52 I had already refreshed the page nine times. My thumbnail was a ragged mess; I'd chewed it down to pink skin and now pressed it against my teeth anyway. The kitchen clock ticked louder than it had any right to. I poured a glass of water, drank half, and realized I'd done the same thing ten minutes ago. "Just a normal Tuesday," I told the dog, my voice coming out thin and too bright. He tilted his head. My knee bounced the table until my mug rattled, so I sat on my hand. Cold fingers, hot face, a stomach that felt like a fist around a stone. 11:58. I stood, sat, stood again. Maybe I should check the spelling of my student number. I'd checked it twice. At 12:00 the screen went white and spun, and I forgot how breathing was supposed to go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The trail marker said 2.1 miles to the lot, and I read it three times anyway. My phone showed eleven percent, so I switched it to airplane mode, then switched it back, then checked the time again. Quarter to five. Sunset was at five-thirty. I'd done that math at the last switchback and again at the creek. "Fine," I said out loud, too brightly, to nobody. My pack straps dug into shoulders I'd hiked up around my ears, and I made myself drop them, and they crept back. The pines had gone from green to black while I wasn't looking. Every snapped twig made me stop mid-step, breath held, until my pulse thumped loud in my throat. I walked faster, nearly jogging, boots skidding on loose gravel. Was that bend familiar? Had I passed that split stump before? I couldn't swallow. I pulled out the headlamp, fumbled it twice, and clicked it on early, just in case, its small white circle shaking on the dirt ahead of me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth now, Grandma Odile's slanted handwriting gone gray with flour smudges. I've read it six times. "Flour until it feels right," it says, which is no measurement at all. I dump in another cup, then scoop half back out, my fingers trembling so that white dust sifts onto my socks. The kitchen is too quiet; I turn on the radio, then snap it off because I can't hear the dough. "Okay," I mutter to nobody. "Okay, okay." My heart knocks against my ribs as I knead, and I keep pressing a thumb into the ball, checking, poking, checking again. Is it tacky? Is it supposed to be tacky? I glance at the oven clock. Four minutes have passed since I last looked. My jaw aches from clenching. I cover the bowl with her yellow towel, lift a corner to peek, set it back, and lift it again, wiping my damp palms down my apron.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was comparing two jars of pasta sauce, reading the same label for the third time, when I heard my name said like a question. Dana Whitlock. Tenth grade chemistry, the girl who sat behind me. My thumb left a damp print on the glass. "Oh! Hi," I said, too loud, and then again, quieter, "Hi." She asked about work, about whether I still lived nearby, and I laughed at the wrong places. My basket held frozen dumplings and a single bottle of wine, and I angled it behind my leg. Somewhere a freezer hummed, and I counted its pulses. "I'm, uh, between things," I said, which wasn't what I'd rehearsed in my head for years. My heart knocked against my collar. When she said we should get coffee, I nodded until my neck ached, said "definitely," and walked the wrong way down the aisle, clutching the sauce I didn't even want.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The clock over the pharmacy counter says 4:12, and I've looked at it eleven times since four. Somebody's cart wheel squeaks down aisle six, and my shoulders jump toward my ears. I straighten the same row of cough syrup again, label out, label out, until the bottles look like soldiers. 'Last prescription pickup is five,' I tell a woman who didn't ask, my voice too bright and too fast. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars since lunch. If the delivery truck doesn't show, if Dana's insulin order is short, if the phone rings at 4:58 with a doctor's office on the line, I won't make the flight. I wipe my palms on my smock. They're damp again. The overhead speakers crackle into jingle bells, and I flinch, then laugh at myself, a thin little laugh that sounds like someone else's. Four-fifteen. I check my phone for the gate number I already memorized, and my thumb is trembling over the glass.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol hit the jet bridge doors at a half jog, her carry-on wheels rattling like loose teeth behind her. Her phone said 4:52. Boarding for Gate C41 closed at 5:05. She glanced at the monitor, then at her phone again, then at the monitor, as if one might change its mind. "Sorry, sorry, excuse me," she said to a man with a stroller, her voice coming out thin and too fast. Her shirt stuck to her back. Her pulse thumped in her ears, drowning out the announcements, and her hands were slick on the handle. The moving walkway was crowded, so she squeezed past, then stopped, patted her jacket pocket, and pulled out the boarding pass she had already checked twice. Still there. C41. Far end. She swallowed against a dry throat, counted the gate numbers under her breath, and ran again, whispering, "Please wait, please wait."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol had taped the edges three times, pressing each strip down with her thumbnail until the skin went white, and still she peeled one corner back to check. The roller sat loaded in the tray, dripping a slow pale-green tongue onto the drop cloth. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since breakfast. "It's just paint," she said aloud, too quickly, and her voice bounced off the bare walls. Her phone buzzed on the stepladder and she flinched, nearly knocking the can. Landlord, again? No, only a coupon. She wiped her palms on her jeans, left damp streaks, wiped them again. What if the green looked sickly at night? What if it didn't cover the old navy? She lifted the roller, lowered it, lifted it. Her heart knocked against her ribs like something asking to be let out. Finally she touched one stripe to the wall, then stood back, breath held, waiting to see if she'd ruined everything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while Marguerite was still holding the phone, and she pressed it harder against her ear as it rang out to voicemail again. She hung up, set it on the porch rail, picked it up, set it down. Rain hammered the tin roof. Her thumbnail had worked a raw groove into the side of her index finger, and she noticed only when it stung. "Pick up, Danny," she said, too softly for anyone to hear, then louder, "Pick up." The porch swing creaked under her restless knees. Every pair of headlights on the road made her stand, and every time they swept past toward town, she sat again, jaw tight, breath shallow and high in her chest. Lightning flashed white across the yard, and she counted, lips moving, losing the number at four. The tea beside her had gone cold an hour ago. She lifted it anyway, and the cup rattled against the saucer until she put it down and tucked both hands beneath her thighs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain keeps slipping off my fingers because my hands won't stay steady. Marisol is across the garage, bent over the workbench we share, her tank top damp at the spine, and I've now re-threaded the same derailleur cable three times. "Pass the hex key?" she says, low, and when I hand it over her knuckles drag across my palm. My whole arm hums. I laugh too loudly at nothing. The fluorescent light buzzes; the air smells of grease and her coconut shampoo, and I realize I'm breathing through my mouth. I wipe my hands on my jeans, then again. "You're doing it backwards," she says, stepping behind me, reaching around to turn the barrel adjuster. Her warmth presses along my shoulder blades. I stare at the wheel, at the spokes, at anything, while my pulse thuds in my ears and I forget, completely, which way righty-tighty goes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as Marisol checked her phone for the fourth time, though she hadn't read a single word on it. Wind pushed her damp hair against her neck and she shivered, but her skin stayed hot, prickling beneath the thin cotton of her shirt. Across the bench, the man in the grey coat was shaking rain from his sleeves, and she watched his hands, the knuckles, the slow way he turned his wrist. 'Cold enough for you?' he asked. 'Not really,' she said, too low, then cleared her throat and laughed at herself. Her pulse thudded in her ears louder than the downpour. When he sat, his knee settled an inch from hers, and she did not move away. She pressed her palm flat against her thigh to keep it still, breathing slowly through her mouth. The bus was late. She found, with some alarm, that she hoped it stayed late a good while longer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and his cologne, still, after eleven years, and I had to set it down on the bed before I kept going. I slid a letter out of its envelope and the paper whispered against my fingers. Third paragraph. He'd written about my mouth, about the hotel in Lisbon, about what he'd do when the door clicked shut. My pulse thudded in my ears. I read it aloud, quietly, just to hear the words in a voice, and mine came out low and unsteady. The window was open, but my neck was damp, my shirt suddenly too heavy on my skin. I pressed the page flat against my collarbone and closed my eyes. Down the hall, the clock ticked. I got up, turned the lock on the bedroom door, which was ridiculous, since I live alone, and sat back down with the whole box in my lap, breathing slowly, reaching for the next one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while I was rinsing a single mug, and when I opened the door Daniel stood there in a sleeveless shirt, sweat still shining along his collarbone, asking if I had a ladder. "Ladder," I repeated, like it was a word from another language. My mouth had gone dry. I leaned on the doorframe, then straightened, then leaned again. "Garage. Yeah. Sure." I led him across the lawn, suddenly aware of my own pulse in my throat, the thin cotton of my shirt against my skin, the warm grass under my bare feet. In the garage, the air felt thick. He reached past me for the rungs and his forearm brushed mine; I forgot what I'd been about to say. "It's a bit heavy," I managed, too low, too slow. "I could carry it over. With you." He grinned. I wiped my palms on my shorts and didn't look away from his hands.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The risotto needs stirring, but I've stopped stirring. Daniel's text is still glowing on the counter: *wearing the green shirt, see you at seven.* I read it again and my pulse knocks against my collarbone. Forty minutes until the doorbell. I turn the heat down, wipe my palms on the dish towel, and notice how warm the kitchen is, how my shirt clings between my shoulder blades. I pour wine, drink half, and laugh at myself out loud, a short breathless sound. The knife slips through shallots too fast; I make myself slow down. Everything I touch seems louder: the cool of the marble, the steam on my wrists, the rasp of the wooden spoon. I check the mirror in the hallway. My cheeks are flushed, my lips parted like I'm mid-sentence. "Get it together," I tell the reflection, voice lower than I meant. Then I light the candles, twice as many as the table needs, and listen for footsteps on the stairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the nightstand, a number I didn't know, and I almost let it ring out. Instead I thumbed the screen and said, "Hello?" in a voice lower than I meant. Silence, then breath, then a laugh, warm and unhurried, a voice I'd have recognized anywhere, even after three years. My pulse kicked up under my jaw. I pushed the sheet off my legs because the room had gone close and hot, and the fan above me did nothing. "Say that again," I told him, though he'd only said my name. He did. My toes curled into the mattress. I realized I was smiling at the ceiling, biting the inside of my lip, one hand pressed flat against my stomach as if to hold something steady. "Where are you?" I asked. "Because I'm not going anywhere." Outside, rain tapped the window. I switched off the lamp and pressed the phone harder against my ear, listening to him breathe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack for fourteen months, and I'd rehearsed my apology the whole walk over, but then the librarian looked up from the desk and every word dissolved. Her sleeves were pushed to her elbows, a pencil stuck through her hair, and my pulse thudded in my ears like I'd sprinted up the steps. "I, um. This is overdue," I said, voice cracking, and slid the battered anatomy text across the counter. My fingertips brushed hers. Heat crawled up my neck and I stared hard at the initials carved into the wood, anything else. "Four hundred and twelve days," she said, scanning it, her mouth twitching. I laughed too loudly. My palms were damp; I wiped them on my jeans, then forgot what to do with my hands. "Is there a fine?" I asked, much quieter than I meant to. She leaned in, close enough that I smelled vanilla and old paper, and I forgot to breathe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol had meant to unpack the kitchen boxes first, but the mover who'd carried up her mattress was still in the doorway, sleeves pushed past his forearms, and she forgot where she'd put the box cutter. "Right there," she said, too brightly, pointing at a wall that needed nothing. He leaned the frame against it, and the studio shrank to the width of his shoulders. The radiator ticked. Her shirt clung between her shoulder blades, and she pulled it away from her skin, then let it fall back. "Water?" Her voice came out lower than she'd planned. She held out a paper cup and let her fingers stay a second too long against his. He drank, throat moving, and she watched it instead of the ceiling stain she'd fretted over all week. After he left, she stood with her back against the shut door, pulse thudding in her wrists, listening to his boots fade down four flights, and she didn't move to open a single box.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The leather was warm from the afternoon sun when Marcus lifted the wallet off the bench, and he felt the warmth travel straight up his wrist. He should have looked for a name. Instead he thumbed the worn edge slowly, breathing in the faint smell of cedar and someone's perfume, and his pulse knocked in his throat. Inside, a photo-booth strip: a woman with a crooked grin, her tongue caught between her teeth, her eyes daring the camera. He swallowed. His collar felt tight, though he hadn't buttoned it. 'Okay,' he said aloud to no one, voice lower than he meant it to be. A jogger passed and he flinched, snapping the wallet shut, then opened it again once she was gone. Heat prickled along his neck. He read the address on the license twice, then a third time, and found he was already standing, already walking, already rehearsing what he'd say when she opened the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor's hand slides from beneath my back, and I don't tell him I noticed. "Kick," Dario says, and I kick, though my legs have gone strangely slow, as if the water around them were warmer than the rest. The pool echoes with chlorine and distant whistles. My skin prickles everywhere the water doesn't touch, and my swimsuit feels too thin, too honest. "Breathe out," he says. I exhale in a long shaky stream of bubbles, my pulse thudding in my ears louder than the filter. When I surface I'm laughing at nothing, cheeks hot, gripping the lane rope far longer than I need to. "Again?" he asks. "Yes," I say, too fast, then clear my throat and repeat it lower. I watch a drop run down his collarbone and forget what my arms are supposed to do. I let myself sink a little, on purpose. Thirty-four years old, and I'm finally not afraid of the deep end at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The soil is warmer than I expected, and I push my fingers into it up to the knuckles before I remember the trowel. My pulse is doing something ridiculous. I've read the seed packets four times, lined them up on the porch rail like tickets, and now I'm kneeling in the dirt with my knees soaked through, breathing too fast.
