"Okay," I say out loud to nobody, "okay, okay." My voice comes out low and shaky. I press a tomato seedling into its hole and my hands tingle, almost buzzing, as I firm the earth around its stem. Sweat slides down my neck. I can't stop grinning at the neat rows, at the string I pulled too tight, at the hose coiled like a sleeping snake. I stand, and my legs wobble. I want to plant everything, right now, all of it, before the light goes. I grab the next packet and tear it open with my teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Daniel clicked to the next slide and rolled his sleeves to the elbow, and I forgot what the slide said. The conference room was too warm; the vents ticked overhead and I kept pressing my cold water bottle against my neck. His voice dropped when he got to the timeline, low and unhurried, and I felt it somewhere under my ribs. I pretended to take notes. My pen wrote the same word three times. When he leaned across the table to point at the chart, I caught the cedar of his soap and my breath went shallow. 'Any questions?' he asked, looking right at me. 'Just... one,' I said, my voice coming out rougher than I meant. I crossed my legs, then uncrossed them. 'Could you go back? To the last one. Slowly.' He smiled, just slightly, and went back. My face was hot. I didn't write anything down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol took the long way home, the one with no streetlights, because she wasn't ready to be anywhere with walls. The window was down an inch and the cold air kept finding the back of her neck, and every time it did her shoulders lifted. Her phone buzzed in the cupholder. She didn't need to look; she knew the name, the little line he'd typed. She read it at the red light anyway, thumb hovering, and her breath came out slower than she meant it to. 'Stop it,' she said to the empty car, and laughed, low and unconvincing. The seatbelt pressed across her chest. Her palms were damp against the wheel, and she wiped them one at a time on her jeans. The speedometer crept past fifty-five, then sixty. She remembered his hand at the small of her back, the warmth of it through her coat, and she turned the heat off, then on again. At the turn for her street she kept driving, past it, toward his.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dario had promised his uncle he'd stay an hour, but he'd checked the clock twice in ten minutes, and each time a voice carried in from the corridor his pulse jumped. Dr. Lindqvist had said, "Room 412, I'll be back to check the drip," and now Dario sat rigid on the vinyl chair, palms damp against his knees, listening for her footsteps. "You're flushed," Uncle Teo rasped. "Hot in here," Dario said, too quickly, tugging his collar away from his throat. He laughed at nothing. The monitor beeped; he counted along, lost count. When the door finally swung open and she leaned across the bed, close enough that he caught her lavender soap beneath the antiseptic, his mouth went dry. "How are we feeling?" she asked. "Great," he said, voice cracking. "Very. Fine." Teo snorted and closed his eyes. Dario stared at the pen clipped to her coat and forgot every question he'd rehearsed in the elevator.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I'm leaning against the chain-link fence at 3:10, pretending to scroll my phone, but I haven't read a single word in ten minutes. Daniel is standing three feet away, sleeves pushed to his forearms, laughing at something the crossing guard said, and the sound goes straight down my spine. My neck is hot despite the November wind. I tuck my hair behind my ear, then untuck it, then check my reflection in the black screen like a teenager. When he glances over and says, "Long week, huh?" my voice comes out lower than I intended. "Longer now," I say, and immediately want to swallow it. He smiles. My pulse is knocking in my wrists. I shift my weight, cross my arms, uncross them, and stare very hard at the double doors, willing them to stay shut a little longer. The bell rings anyway. I almost resent it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, but when the man in the grey henley crouched to run his thumb along the drawer's worn edge, she forgot the number entirely. The morning sun was already hot on her neck. "It's, um, solid," she said, too quickly, and her voice came out lower than she meant. He pulled a drawer open, and the slow wooden scrape seemed to travel straight up her arms. She fanned herself with a price-tag sheet, then pretended she hadn't. Her pulse thudded in her wrists. When he glanced up and smiled, she realized she'd been staring at his forearms and turned to straighten a lamp that was already straight. "Thirty-five," she blurted. "Or, whatever. Thirty." He laughed, and heat climbed her throat. She tucked her hair behind her ear twice, wiped damp palms on her jeans, and decided the loveseat could stay out a little longer, in case he wanted to sit and talk about it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marisol lay wedged under the bathroom sink with the wrench in her fist, and when Dana's knee brushed her calf, kneeling close to hold the flashlight, she forgot which way righty-tighty went. "Hold it steady," she said, and her voice came out lower than she meant. Water beaded on her wrist and ran down her forearm; she watched it, then watched Dana's fingers curled around the flashlight, the light trembling just a little. Her shirt had gone damp and clung to her ribs. The cabinet felt too small, too warm, and she could hear her own breath bouncing off the pipes. "Closer," she murmured, then coughed. "The light. I mean the light." Dana leaned in, hair falling forward, smelling of lemon soap. Marisol gave the fitting a quarter turn, missed, and gave it another. The drip kept ticking into the bucket, steady as a pulse. She laughed once, shakily, and pressed her cheek against the cool porcelain, in no hurry at all to finish.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope from the Department of Revenue had been on the counter since noon, and I'd walked past it four times, each pass slower. Now the apartment was quiet, the window cracked, a warm breath of evening on my neck. I slid my thumb under the flap, my pulse somewhere behind my ears. "Okay," I said aloud, low, almost a purr, "let's see what you've got." The paper rasped as I unfolded it, and I felt it all down my arms, a fine prickle, my skin suddenly too tight. I pressed my lips together, then bit the lower one. My knees had gone loose against the stool. I read the first line twice without understanding a word, because I was listening to my own breathing, shallow and quick, and the heat climbing my throat. I fanned the page against my collar. "God," I whispered, and kept reading, not wanting to stop, leaning closer to the lamp.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi door shut behind me and Lisbon's heat wrapped around my neck like a hand. I couldn't read a single sign, so I followed the smell of grilled sardines down a stairway of crooked tiles. At the counter, the woman who took my order had flour on her forearms and a gap-toothed half smile, and when she said something quick and low, I leaned closer than I needed to. "Sorry, I don't... uh, one of those," I managed, pointing, my voice dropping somewhere unfamiliar. She laughed, and my pulse jumped into my throat. Her fingers brushed mine passing the paper plate, and I held on a second too long. My shirt stuck to my back. I forgot the hotel, the map, the dead phone. She said a word, slowly, for me to repeat, watching my mouth, and I said it wrong on purpose, just to hear her say it again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus sat on the tailgate with his thermos forgotten beside him, watching Biscuit tear across the long grass in wide, looping arcs. The late sun lay hot on his neck, and he noticed his pulse thudding in his wrists, a low hum under his skin that had nothing to do with the coffee. Every time the dog leapt, his own shoulders tensed, his fingers curling against the cold metal. 'Go on,' he said, too low, almost a growl, then laughed at himself and cleared his throat. 'Go on, boy.' His mouth had gone dry. He kept thinking about the evening ahead, the call he'd finally agreed to make, her voice, the way she'd said his name last week. His knee bounced. He pressed his palm flat to his chest, felt the quick drumming there, and grinned at nothing while Biscuit skidded, rolled, and sprang up again, tail whipping the wind. Marcus checked his phone. Twice. Then a third time, the screen warm against his thumb.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I kept losing my place in the Schubert because Daniel was standing behind my shoulder, turning pages. His sleeve brushed my arm each time, and every time my pulse jumped into my wrists. "Again from the bridge?" I asked, too quickly, my voice pitched higher than I meant. My fingers slid on the keys, damp, and I wiped them on my skirt as if that were casual. He leaned in to point at a measure, and I caught cedar soap and warm wool, and forgot how breathing was supposed to go. The folding chairs, the dusty banner for the bake sale, Mrs. Ortega tuning her cello in the corner: all of it blurred into a bright hum. "Sure," I said, then said it again, quieter. My face was hot. I played the bridge perfectly, which surprised me, and didn't dare look up until the last chord faded.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marisol found Daniel's canvas apron on the hook behind the door and, instead of boxing it, pulled it over her head. It smelled of cedar dust and the faint salt of his skin. Her breath caught; she stood still in the slanting afternoon light, sawdust drifting like slow sparks. "Okay," she said aloud, too low, too steady. Her palm slid along the workbench where he'd leaned, where she'd once watched his forearms flex around a plane, and the wood was warm from the window. Heat climbed her neck. She pressed her thighs together, then laughed at herself, a short, cracked sound. The tape gun lay forgotten in her hand. She thought of his hands guiding hers on the lathe, his chest against her back, his voice by her ear saying *slower.* Her pulse thudded in her wrists. She locked the door, though no one was coming, and let the apron's strings run through her fingers, slowly, slowly.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the registrar's office hums with fluorescent light, and I can't stop moving. I pace to the noticeboard, then back to the water fountain, then to the noticeboard again. My pulse thuds in my neck, my palms are damp, and heat climbs under my collar even though the radiator is dead. Every time the office door clicks, my whole body snaps toward it, skin prickling from my scalp to my wrists. "Any minute now," I tell the girl next to me, but my voice comes out too fast and too high, and I laugh at nothing. I'm bouncing on my toes. My fingers drum my thigh, then the wall, then my phone, which I've checked forty times. When the sheet of paper finally appears in the clerk's hand, my breath catches hard. Everything sharpens: the squeak of tape, the staple glinting, the crowd surging. I'm already pushing forward, grinning, half-dizzy, needing to know right now.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Mara had stopped checking her watch two switchbacks ago. The ridge was going copper, then violet, and the air against her damp collarbone felt like fingertips. Her pulse thudded low in her belly, not in her legs where the climb should have put it. Behind her, Jonah's boots crunched, and she slowed on purpose, letting the gap shrink until she could hear his breath. "We should find the turnoff," she said, but her voice came out husky and unhurried, and she didn't look at the map in her hand. A pine branch brushed her bare forearm and she shivered all the way to her scalp. She tugged her pack straps looser, suddenly aware of the heat under her shirt, the salt on her lip. When he stepped beside her, shoulder warm against hers, she kept her eyes on the darkening trail and said, very quietly, "Or we could just not hurry."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Nana's recipe card is soft as cloth, the ink gone brown, and I've stopped reading it because my hands remember. Flour up to my elbows. I push the heel of my palm into the dough, fold, push again, and the warm give of it under my fingers makes my breath go uneven. The kitchen is too hot; I've pulled my shirt away from my collarbone twice. Yeast and honey in the air, the oven ticking as it climbs. Down the hall the shower shuts off, and I hear Daniel's bare feet on the boards. My pulse jumps in my throat. I don't turn around. "Come taste this," I say, lower than I meant to, and I lick a smear of dough from my thumb slowly. The rhythm of my kneading slows. Behind me the footsteps stop, and my whole back feels like it's listening. Nana, I think, you never mentioned this part.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Daniel was weighing two nearly identical jars of peanut butter when a voice behind him said his name, low and amused, and the jar nearly slipped from his fingers. Marisol Reyes. Twelve years since senior chemistry, and she still tilted her head the same way. He turned too fast, bumped the cart, and laughed at the wrong moment. 'Hey. Wow. You, uh, you cut your hair.' Heat climbed his neck. The fluorescent lights hummed too loudly, and the aisle seemed suddenly narrow, her shoulder only inches from his. She touched his sleeve while she talked, and he felt the spot long after she let go. His mouth went dry; he caught himself staring at her lips, then at the cereal, then at nothing. 'Coffee sometime?' he heard himself say, voice lower than intended. She smiled slowly. His pulse thudded in his ears all the way to the register, where he realized he was still holding the jar.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy empties by four, and I keep rearranging the same row of cough drops because my hands need somewhere to go. Dana from the garden center is leaning on my counter again, sleeves pushed to her elbows, and every time she laughs I feel it low in my stomach, like a dropped coin still spinning. "You closing alone?" she asks. My voice comes out lower than I meant. "Till nine. Unless someone rescues me." The fluorescent hum seems louder. My collar is suddenly too tight, my neck warm, and I catch myself staring at her mouth while she talks about turkey. I tear the receipt paper wrong, twice. She taps the counter, two slow knocks near my fingers, and doesn't move away. Outside, the parking lot is nearly bare, a lone cart rattling in the wind. I flip the sign to CLOSED eight minutes early and don't even pretend to check the time. My pulse is in my ears. "Help me with the lights?" I say, and she's already coming around the register.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B42 was a mile away, and the man ahead of me on the moving walkway kept turning to check the board, which meant I kept seeing his jaw, the loosened collar, the forearm flexed around his carry-on. We'd been seated together on the first leg, his knee against mine for two hours, and my skin still hummed along that exact stripe of thigh. I ran. My blouse stuck to my back, my pulse thudded in my throat and lower, and I caught myself slowing, just slightly, whenever he glanced back. "Last call," the speaker said, and I laughed too loudly, breathless, nothing funny in it. He grabbed my elbow at the corner to steady me and I forgot the word for 'thanks.' I said, "Mm," like an idiot. My boarding pass was damp in my fist. At the gate he stepped aside to let me go first, and I felt his gaze travel down my spine all the way to the jet bridge, warm as a hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I told Dana the roller was all I needed help with, but now she's behind me on the ladder's second rung, reaching past my shoulder to tape the trim, and I've forgotten how to load paint. The roller drips on the drop cloth. Twice. Her sleeve brushes my neck and the fine hairs there stand up like I've been plugged into the wall. "Sage green," I say, too low, too slow, as though the color were a secret. My T-shirt is stuck to my back, and the open window does nothing. She laughs at a smear on my cheek and thumbs it away, and I don't move, don't even blink, just stare at the wet wall while my pulse thuds in my ears. "You missed a spot," she says. I haven't missed anything. I set the roller down anyway and turn around, paint-sticky fingers curling against my thighs, ignoring the half-finished wall entirely.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marisol had stopped pretending to read twenty minutes ago. The paperback lay splayed on her knee while thunder rolled down the valley, and each crack seemed to travel straight up the porch boards and into her spine. Her cotton dress was damp where the wind flung rain across the rail, clinging to her thighs, and she didn't tug it free. She pressed her bare foot against the cool, wet slat and breathed out slowly, mouth open. Her pulse beat in her throat, her wrists, low in her belly. When headlights swept the yard and a truck door slammed, she stood too fast, knocking the book to the floor. 'You're soaked,' she called, and her voice came out lower than she'd meant. She gripped the railing, watching him jog toward the steps, rain streaming down his collar. 'Come up here,' she said. 'Don't bother with the umbrella.' Lightning flashed, and she didn't look away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The wrench slips off the crank bolt for the third time, and I glance at the door before I even check my knuckle. Marguerite's workbench is on the left, spotless, her tools hung in outline on the pegboard. Mine are in a shoebox. I angle my body so the bike hides the box. When Dev from unit four wanders in for his lawnmower, I tell him I'm "just tweaking something," and my voice comes out too bright, too fast. My ears are hot. The chain is still on the floor where I dropped it an hour ago, because I borrowed this bike from my nephew and promised I'd return it fixed, and I've only made it worse. Dev says, "Need a hand?" and I laugh, shake my head, wipe my palms on my jeans though they're already clean. After he leaves, I stare at the grease on the concrete, then drag a rag over it, hard, twice, until the stain is gone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as the 14 pulled away without her, its taillights smearing red down the wet street. Marguerite kept her eyes on the timetable, tracing the same line with a gloved finger as though the number might change. Her face was hot despite the wind. Two teenagers in the shelter had watched her sprint, watched her slap the closing door, and one of them still had that half-smile. She tugged her scarf up over her chin and angled her shoulders toward the glass. "Fine," she said to no one, too brightly, and laughed at nothing. Her phone lit with her sister's message, Where are you? We started without you, and she turned the screen face-down against her thigh. Rain slanted in under the awning, soaking one knee. She didn't move to the dry end of the bench. Somehow it seemed right to sit where it reached her, and she stayed there, staring at the puddle, counting minutes until the next one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and dust, and I had the attic window open though it was freezing. Her handwriting on the top envelope made my neck go hot. I'd told myself I was only looking for the deed. Seven letters, and the return address slanted like she'd been in a hurry to be forgiven. I turned one over, then put it face down on my knee, then slid it under the stack. My thumb kept rubbing the stamp. "Just junk," I said aloud to nobody, and my voice came out thin and too quick. Downstairs the kettle began to whine and I didn't move. I pictured her at the kitchen table, writing, waiting for the mailbox flag to go up. I shoved the lid back on crooked and pressed my palm flat on top as if something might climb out. Then I sat there staring at the floorboards, unable to look at the window, the box, or the dark square of my own reflection in the glass.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: When Mr. Okafor knocked and asked about the ladder, Daniel's hand stayed fixed on the doorframe, as if the house might tip if he let go. "Oh. The ladder. Sure, yeah," he said, too quickly, and his ears went hot. He knew exactly where it was: in the garage, where it had lain across the workbench since March, three rungs snapped, the splintered ends wrapped in duct tape he had told himself was temporary. Last spring he had borrowed Okafor's lawn spreader and returned it cracked, saying nothing. "Give me a minute," he mumbled to the welcome mat. In the garage he stood with his palm on the cold aluminum, his throat tight, listening to Okafor whistle on the porch. He dragged the ladder out anyway, eyes on the gravel, and set it down between them. "It's, uh. It's got some problems," he said. His voice came out small. He couldn't lift his face to see the man's expression, and he stared at his own shoes until the whistling stopped.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The rice scorched while I was rereading the text from Dana, the one that said they were so excited to finally see our place. I scraped the pot over the sink with the window shut, fan on high, as if the smell might be a witness. My ears were hot. The tablecloth hid the water ring on the table, and I'd shoved the unopened mail into the oven drawer, so I couldn't preheat anything yet. Twenty minutes. I turned the good plates face down so nobody would see the chip, then flipped them back, then turned them down again. When the buzzer rang I wiped my palms on my shirt, left a grease streak, and tugged my sleeve over it. "Oh, you're early," I said, too bright, too fast, laughing at nothing. My voice came out thin. I kept my eyes on the doorknob, then the floor, and told them dinner was just something simple, nothing special, really, please don't expect much.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the cereal bowl, a number I don't know, and my stomach drops before I even touch it. I carry it into the bathroom and shut the door, though no one else is home. My face is hot in the mirror. I let it ring four times, five, then press accept and say, "Hello?" in a voice so small I have to clear my throat and try again. "Yes, this is Daniel." A woman says she's calling about the account, the one I swore to my brother I'd paid off. I slide down the tile until my knees are against my chest. "No, I know. I know it's late." My eyes stay fixed on the grout. I count the lines in it. "Can you not send anything to the house? Please. I'll figure it out." My thumb is pressed white against the edge of the phone. When she finishes, I whisper thank you twice, like an apology, and keep sitting there, listening to the faucet drip.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I waited until the line behind me was empty before stepping up to the desk, the paperback pressed flat against my ribs like I could still change my mind. My ears were hot. The librarian, a woman with silver reading glasses, held out her hand, and I slid the book across without looking up. "It's, um, a bit late," I said, my voice coming out thinner than I'd planned. The spine was cracked where I'd left it under my bed all spring. She tapped the keyboard. I stared at a laminated sign about quiet hours and read the same line four times. "Two years, huh," she said, not unkindly, and my throat clenched around whatever I'd rehearsed. I pulled my sleeves over my knuckles. "I can pay. Whatever it is. I brought cash." I was already backing toward the door before she answered, sweat cold along my neck, hoping the floor might simply let me through.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The elevator was broken, so I carried everything up four flights myself, and I was almost glad, because nobody would see how little there was. Two duffels, a lamp with a bent shade, a mattress I dragged by its handle like something I'd hit. When the neighbor across the hall opened her door, I turned my face toward the wall and fumbled with the key until my ears burned. "Just moved in," I said, too quietly, and she asked me to repeat it. I did, and laughed at nothing. Inside, the studio smelled like old paint. I pulled the blinds before I'd even set down the bags. Her voice drifted through the wall, easy and warm, someone on the phone talking about a dinner party. I sat on the bare mattress with my hands pressed between my knees, staring at the single mug I'd unwrapped, and I counted the days since I'd last told my sister where I was living. Eleven. I turned the lamp to face the corner so the room looked smaller, like a choice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the slats of the bench, brown leather curled at the corners, and Marcus lowered himself beside it without looking at it. A jogger passed. He tucked his chin into his collar. Heat crawled up his neck as his fingers, which had already flipped it open, counted the twenties twice. Sixty. He had eaten nothing since yesterday, and the rent notice was folded in his jacket like a second spine. The license photo showed a woman with gray curls, smiling at something off-camera. 'Ma'am,' he whispered to no one, then cleared his throat and said it again, too loud. A pigeon scattered. He pulled out one bill, stared at it, and shoved it back so hard the leather creaked. His hands wouldn't stop shaking. When a man in a vest glanced over, Marcus stood too fast, held the wallet out like something hot, and said, 'Found it. Just now. Just sitting here,' to the pavement, the whole time, never once to the man's face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: I arrived twenty minutes early so the pool would be empty, and it wasn't. Two kids in the shallow end, already kicking like they were born doing it. I kept my towel on until the instructor said my name, then dropped it and crossed my arms over my stomach. "Just the steps for me," I said, too quiet, and she leaned in to hear it. My feet slapped the tile. The water was colder than I'd planned for, and my breath came in small, high sips. When one of the kids stared, I turned and studied the lane rope like it needed my attention. I'm thirty-eight. I gripped the wall until my knuckles went pale and laughed once, a dry little noise, and said, "Sorry, take your time with the others." She said there were no others. My ears burned hotter than the water was cold. I counted the tiles to the drain, then counted them again, and did not let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I waited until the sun dropped behind the fence before dragging the shovel out, so Mrs. Alvarez next door wouldn't see. The packet said plant tomatoes eighteen inches apart. I'd already crammed six seedlings into a space the size of a bath mat, and now their leaves were yellowing. My ears burned. I crouched low, tugged one out, and shoved it back in deeper, as if hiding the mistake. Her screen door creaked. "Coming along?" she called. "Oh, fine, just tidying," I said, too bright, too fast, and kicked soil over the pea seeds I'd dumped in a clump. My neck felt hot under my collar. I kept my back to her, pressing dirt around stems with trembling fingers, pretending to know what I was doing. When her door shut, I stayed there, knees soaked, staring at the crooked rows, wishing the ground would simply take the whole mess back down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to the third slide, and there it is: my wireframe, my color palette, my little arrow diagram, with her name in the corner. The conference room air conditioning hums above me. I angle my laptop screen down a few degrees, then a few more, until it's nearly shut. My ears are hot. Marcus nods at the slide and says, "This is really solid," and I laugh too quickly, too high, and reach for my water bottle, which is empty. I tip it anyway. Everyone's looking at Dana, which is the only mercy. I study the grain of the table and pick at a loose thread on my cuff until it puckers. When Dana says, "Thanks to the whole team," her eyes skate past me, and I mutter, "Yeah, great job," to my knees. My chair squeaks when I shift. I stay very, very still after that.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway is empty, and I keep both hands at ten and two like a student taking a test. My phone buzzes in the cup holder and I flip it face down without looking. Heat crawls up my neck every time I replay the toast, the way the room went quiet, Dana's tight little smile. I turn the radio on, then off. I roll the window down and the cold air stings my ears, and I let it. "Stupid," I say out loud, quietly, like someone might hear. "Stupid, stupid." At the red light by the shuttered gas station I stare at my own eyes in the mirror for half a second and then angle it away. My stomach is a tight fist. I rehearse the apology three different ways and hate each one. When I pull into the driveway, I cut the headlights early, sit in the dark with the engine ticking, and can't make myself go inside where anyone might ask how it went.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Daniel stood outside room 412 for a full minute, thumb worrying the plastic handle of the grocery-store tulips he'd bought in the lobby. Inside, his uncle's feet made two small tents under the thin blanket. Eleven months of unanswered calls, and now this. His face went hot as he stepped in. "Hey, Uncle Ray," he said, too quietly, and cleared his throat and said it again. The old man's eyes opened, and Daniel looked at the window instead, at the parking lot, at a nurse's cart, anything. He set the tulips on the tray, then moved them to the sill, then back. "Traffic was bad," he said. It wasn't. His collar felt tight. When Ray's hand lifted toward him, Daniel stared at the IV taped to the bruised skin and kept his own hands deep in his jacket pockets, pressing his nails into his palms, until a tray clattered in the hall and gave him a reason to flinch toward the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I park two blocks down, behind the dry cleaner's, and walk the rest with my hood up even though it isn't raining. The other parents cluster by the gate, trading plans for Saturday. I take the far end of the fence and study my phone, thumb scrolling nothing. My face is hot. Yesterday's email from Mrs. Alvarez is still open somewhere in my pocket, the one about the unpaid lunch balance, the third notice. When the bell rings, Dana from the PTA waves and calls, "Hey, how are you?" and I say, "Fine, great, so busy," too fast, too bright, already looking past her shoulder. My collar feels tight. Then Theo comes bounding out, backpack unzipped, a crumpled paper in his fist, and I crouch and fold him into my coat so nobody can see my eyes. "Can we get pizza?" he asks. "Maybe Friday," I whisper, and steer him toward the long way around.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had set the price tags low, then lower, then peeled one off the dresser and stuck it back with a smaller number. When the couple from the next street stopped at the velvet sofa, she stepped between them and the cushion with the stain and started talking about the weather. Her ears burned. "It was my mother's," she said, then, "Not that it matters," and laughed too high. The woman lifted a cushion, and Marguerite stared at the crack in the driveway, at the dandelion pushing through it. Across the street Dale waved from his porch, and she turned, pretending to straighten a lamp, her back to him. "Ten dollars," she blurted, before anyone asked. "Take it for ten. Honestly, just take it." Her hands wouldn't settle; she folded and refolded the same dish towel until the couple drove off, the sofa tied crookedly to their roof, and she kept her eyes on her shoes the whole time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped again and my knuckles cracked against the cabinet wall, and I just kept my head down under the sink, grateful for the dark. Water ticked into the pot beside my knee. Dad's old toolbox lay open, every tool labeled in his careful marker, and I couldn't tell which one I needed. My ears were hot. When Marisol called from the hall, asking if I wanted her to phone the landlord, I said, "No, no, it's basically done," too fast, my voice pitched strangely high. It was not done. The joint sprayed a thin line across my wrist. I wiped my face with a wet sleeve and angled my body so she couldn't see the puddle creeping toward the doorway. Three videos, two hardware store trips, and I'd made it worse. I stayed there, jaw tight, counting drips, rehearsing how I'd say I never even tried.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: Marisol waited until the hallway was empty before she slid her thumb under the flap of the envelope, the one stamped with the county seal. She'd carried it around for three days, face down, under the fruit bowl, then under a stack of takeout menus. Now she stood by the mailboxes with her shoulders curled inward and her back to the lobby door. When footsteps echoed on the stairs she stuffed the letter into her coat and laughed too loudly at nothing, saying, "Just junk, ha, always junk." Her neighbor nodded and kept walking. Heat crawled up her neck. She went into her apartment, locked the deadbolt, and drew the curtains in the middle of the afternoon. The paper shook as she unfolded it. Overdue. Benefits. Repayment. She read the first line twice, then pressed the page flat against her chest as if someone might read it through the wall, and stared at the floor, unable to lift her eyes even to the empty room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver said something rapid and rising, and Marta nodded as if she'd understood, though her cheeks had gone hot. She had practiced two phrases on the plane, and now both had vanished. At the hotel counter she held out her phone with the booking already open, screen tilted so no one behind her could read it, and spoke in a voice smaller than her own. "Sorry. Sorry. Only English." The clerk answered kindly, slowly, and she laughed too late at nothing. Her eyes dropped to the marble floor, to her own scuffed sneakers. In the lift she rehearsed what she should have said, her lips moving silently, her neck prickling when a girl beside her glanced over. Upstairs she sat on the bed with her coat still on, thumb hovering over the message to her sister, then pressed the screen dark and said nothing. She had told everyone she was ready.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tears across the field with a muddy tennis ball, ears flapping, and I keep my hood up even though it isn't raining. Two women on the far bench glance over, and I turn my face toward the treeline. My neck is hot. Last week I left her in the car with the windows barely cracked, just ten minutes, and a stranger left a note under my wiper. I still have it folded in my coat pocket, and my thumb keeps worrying the creased edge. Biscuit bounds back and drops the ball at my boots, tail wagging, forgiving me for nothing she knows about. I crouch and press my forehead against her damp fur so no one can see my face. "Good girl," I whisper, and my voice cracks on the second word. "You're such a good girl." I throw the ball again, harder than I mean to, and watch her run, my stomach folding in on itself.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite cracked the same note again, the high G that had wobbled all week, and the church hall seemed to hold its breath around her. Heat climbed her neck. She laughed too quickly and said, "Sorry, sorry, again from the top," though nobody had spoken. Her eyes stayed on the scuffed linoleum, on a dropped pencil under the piano, anywhere but the three faces of the choir waiting politely. She tugged her cardigan sleeves down over her wrists and gripped the sheet music so tightly it crinkled. When Mr. Okafor offered, gently, to take the solo down a key, she shook her head, then nodded, then said, "Whatever's easier for everyone," in a voice that barely carried past the folding chairs. Her stomach felt hollow and tight. Between songs she slipped to the coat rack and stayed there, pretending to search a pocket, until the piano started again and she could hide inside the chorus.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dana found the chisel set on the second shelf, each blade wrapped in oily flannel, and her hands went hot and clumsy. She had borrowed this set in March, three years ago, and returned it with the bevel chipped, saying nothing. Walt had never mentioned it. Here the chip was, patched, honed back to a clean edge, the flannel folded neater than she'd ever managed. 'Sorry,' she said to the empty room, too quietly, then cleared her throat and said it again, louder, and hated how it echoed. She turned the box toward the wall so the lid hid the blades. When Walt's daughter called from the doorway, asking if she needed anything, Dana kept her back to her and wiped at her face with a sawdusty sleeve. 'Fine. Just dusty.' She slid the chisels into a bag marked KEEP, then pulled them out, then put them back, her ears burning, unable to look at the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 114 smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Daniel stood at the very back of the crowd, hood up, though it was warm. When the secretary pinned the sheets to the corkboard, everyone surged forward, and he stepped sideways, pretending to read a flyer about chess club. His ears burned. Somebody laughed near the front and he flinched as if it were aimed at him. He had told his father, at breakfast, that he'd probably gotten an A. The words kept replaying, thick in his throat. 'Just checking my schedule,' he muttered to no one, thumbing his phone's dark screen. His eyes slid over the board, found his number, and stayed on the line beside it. He tugged his sleeve down over his knuckles, nodded once at a girl who glanced his way, and walked out the side door without letting his shoes make a sound, rehearsing a different sentence for tonight's dinner.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then gray, and I keep my eyes on my boots because the ridge ahead is the one I swore we'd be off by noon. Dana's voice is still in my ears, the way I laughed when she asked to turn back at the creek, the way I said, "You're slow, we'll be fine." She was right. She's somewhere behind me now, ankle wrapped in my spare sock, and I walked ahead anyway because I couldn't stand to watch her limp. My face is hot despite the cold coming off the pines. I rehearse sentences and delete them. When her headlamp finally flickers around the bend, I step off the trail and busy myself retying a lace that's already tight. "Here," I mutter, holding out my pack without looking up. "Give me yours. Please." My throat clicks when I swallow. She doesn't answer, and the silence is worse than anything she could say.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth from decades of her thumbs, and I keep it propped against the flour canister with my back half-turned to the window, as if the neighbors could see. Halmoni's handwriting says *knead until it answers you.* Mine never answers. I pull the loaf out and it sits there, dense and pale, a brick with a crack down its side. My face is hot. I tear off a corner anyway and chew it, and it clots against my teeth. When my mother calls, I say, "Oh, fine, it's fine, I just made some toast," too fast, too bright. She asks if I used the card. I tell her I couldn't find it. Then I slide the loaf into the trash, bury it under coffee grounds so no one will see, and wipe the card carefully with my sleeve, though it isn't dirty at all. I can't look at her handwriting for the rest of the night.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Daniel was holding a bag of discount noodles and a single dented can of soup when he heard his name called from the end of the aisle. Priya Raman, who'd sat behind him in chemistry, was pushing a cart heaped with fresh salmon and wine. He turned the basket sideways against his thigh, as if that could hide it. His ears went hot. "Hey! Wow. Yeah, good, things are good," he said, too quickly, voice climbing at the end. She asked where he was working now. He studied the shelf label beside her shoulder, rubbing his thumb over the frayed name tag still pinned to his apron, then slid his palm across it. "Just between things right now. Bigger projects coming." His laugh came out thin. She said they should get coffee, and he nodded hard, already backing toward the cereal display, saying he'd left his phone in the car. He didn't have a car. He walked past the registers and set the basket down on a stack of magazines by the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum over empty aisles at 5:40 on Christmas Eve, and I keep my head down, restocking cough syrup that doesn't need restocking. Mrs. Alvarez comes to the counter for her husband's prescription, and I tell her it isn't ready, my voice coming out small and scratchy. It's not ready because I misfiled it Tuesday and found it an hour ago, wedged behind the insulin. My ears are burning. I slide the bag across before she can ask anything, then fuss with the receipt printer, tearing the paper twice. 'Merry Christmas,' she says, kindly, and I stare at the register as if the numbers might change. When the door chimes shut, I press my palms against the cold counter and count the tiles until my face cools. Then I text my manager that I'll close alone, so no one has to see me leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marguerite reached Gate B42 with her shoes in one hand and her blazer slung over her arm, and the door was already closed. The agent didn't look up. "Boarding ended ten minutes ago," she said. Marguerite's face went hot, the heat crawling down her neck, and she kept her eyes on the carpet's gray zigzags. "Right. Of course. Sorry," she murmured, though nothing had been asked of her. Behind her, the family she'd cut in front of at security sat in a row, and she could feel them not staring. She'd lingered over that second coffee, that stupid pastry, told herself the layover was long enough. She pulled her carry-on closer, as if it could hide her, and turned toward the rebooking line, walking slowly, shoulders curled in. When her phone buzzed with her sister's text, Good luck, did you make it?, she flipped it facedown against her thigh and stood very still, studying the departures board like it might tell her something else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Dana rolled the pale gray over the hallway wall in short, hurried strokes, and when the doorbell rang she froze, roller dripping on the drop cloth. Through the peephole she saw her sister holding a casserole. Dana's ears burned. She wiped her hands on her shirt, then cracked the door only a hand's width. "Now's not great," she said, too quickly, voice thin. Behind her, the old wall showed through where she'd stopped, still scarred with the dark patch where Mark's fist had gone through it in March. She had painted around it for weeks, then over it, then over it again, and it kept ghosting through. Her sister peered past her shoulder. Dana shifted to block the view, chin tucked, eyes on the casserole dish instead of her sister's face. "Just leave it on the step, okay? I'll call you." She shut the door and stood with her forehead against it, breathing into the smell of wet paint.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while I was still holding the phone, thumb hovering over her name. Rain hammered the tin roof of the porch, and I pulled my feet up onto the chair as if the puddles could reach what I'd said. Her voice, small and flat at the dinner table: "Fine. It's fine." It hadn't been fine. My face went hot again, even with cold spray blowing across my knees. I turned the phone face down, then flipped it back. Lightning lit the yard, the empty swing, the casserole dish she'd left on the rail, still covered in foil. I should carry it in. I didn't. I tugged my sleeve down over my hand and pressed it against my mouth, rehearsing apologies in a whisper, each one worse than the last. "I didn't mean it," I told the rain. That was a lie, and the rain knew. I stayed there until my shirt soaked through.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the rear wheel clamped in the truing stand and a spoke wrench in her fist when she tipped the frame toward the bare bulb and saw the number stamped under the bottom bracket. She stopped. The wrench slid from her fingers and clanged across the concrete, and she didn't flinch at it. She wiped her thumb over the digits, then wiped again, harder, as if grease could be lying. "No," she said, too quietly for anyone to hear. "No, no, no." Her mouth stayed open. Across the garage, the neighbor's radio droned on about traffic, and a dryer thumped through the wall, but she felt only her pulse in her ears and a cold prickle running down both arms. She pulled out her phone, thumbs clumsy, and typed the number into the search bar twice, getting it wrong the first time. When the page loaded, she sat down slowly on an upturned paint bucket, still holding the frame against her knee. "Dad's bike," she whispered. "The stolen one. Twenty years."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marta had been scrolling through her phone under the shelter's cracked plexiglass when the first flake landed on her screen. She looked at it. Then up. The sky, which had been a flat September blue ten minutes ago, was dropping snow in fat, slow clumps onto the still-green maple across the street. Her thumb froze mid-swipe. "No," she said, too quietly for anyone to hear, then louder to the empty bench, "No, no, that's not—" She stepped out from under the roof, arm outstretched, and watched a flake melt into her sleeve. Her mouth stayed open; cold air dried her tongue. The coffee in her other hand tilted, and she didn't notice it spilling over her shoe. A car crept past with its wipers lifting white, and she turned to follow it, laughing once, a short breathless bark. Her heart thudded against her coat. She checked the date on her phone, then checked it again, then simply stood there, blinking snow from her lashes while the bus she'd been waiting for slid up unnoticed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of attic dust and cedar, and I was halfway through rubber-banded bundles of Aunt Ruth's grocery-store receipts when I turned over a cream envelope addressed to my grandfather in my own handwriting. Not similar. Mine, the loopy g, the slashed seven. I sat down on the hallway floor without deciding to. The postmark said 1974. I was born in 1989. 'No,' I said aloud, to nobody, then laughed once, a dry bark. My thumb left a damp print on the paper. I unfolded it slowly, as if it might bite, and read the first line twice, then a third time, my lips moving. Dear Pop, it began, and then the name of my street, my actual street, my actual house number. The radiator ticked. I realized I was holding my breath and my hand had gone cold to the wrist. I looked at the door, as though someone might walk in and explain.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta was kneeling in the garden bed, trowel in hand, when the shadow fell across her tulip bulbs. She looked up. Mr. Haldane, who had not spoken to her since the fence dispute eleven years ago, stood at the gate holding his cap against his chest. "The ladder," he said. "If it's not too much trouble." The trowel slid from her fingers and landed with a soft thud in the dirt. She opened her mouth, closed it, then opened it again. "My ladder," she repeated, and her voice came out thin, almost a squeak. Her pulse thumped in her ears. She glanced past him at his own garage, where she knew a ladder hung plainly on the wall, then back at his weathered face. "Yes. Of course. It's, um, behind the shed." She stood too quickly, knees cracking, and wiped her palms down her apron twice without noticing the mud she was leaving there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta had just lifted the lid on the lamb, expecting the usual slow bubble, when the whole pot looked back at her, perfectly glossy, the sauce already thick and dark as if hours had passed in minutes. The wooden spoon slipped from her fingers and clattered against the stove. She didn't bend to get it. Her mouth hung open, and the steam curled uselessly around her face. 'No,' she whispered, then, louder, 'No, that's not... I put this on at four.' She glanced at the clock over the doorway, then at her phone, then at the clock again, her pulse thudding in her ears. The oven timer, which she was certain she hadn't touched, read zero. Somewhere beyond the window a car door shut, and another. Marta pressed a damp palm flat against her sternum, laughed once in a thin, breathless burst, and stood there with the lid dangling in her other hand, staring at dinner that had finished itself.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The screen showed a string of digits I didn't know, and I almost let it ring out over the dishwater. I answered with soapy fingers. "Hello?" A woman said my full name, then the name of the street where I grew up, then a phone number I hadn't heard since I was nine: our old home number, from before the move. The plate slid from my hand and clanked against the sink. My mouth stayed open a second too long. "Sorry, what? Say that again." She did. My knees went loose, and I grabbed the counter, staring at the black window above the tap as though the yard might explain itself. "That's... no. How do you have that?" My voice came out thin and high, not mine. My heart was thudding, and I realized I'd stopped breathing. "Wait. Wait. Are you telling me Dad kept it all these years?" I laughed once, a cracked sound, and sat down hard on the wet kitchen floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I slid the battered copy of Introduction to Organic Chemistry across the desk, already bracing for the lecture and the fee, maybe two hundred dollars, maybe my whole month's groceries. The librarian typed, squinted, typed again. Then she turned the monitor toward me. Zero. My mouth stayed open long enough that I felt the cold air from the vents dry my tongue. "Sorry, zero?" I said, my voice climbing somewhere near the ceiling. "It's been, I mean, it was due in March of 2022." She shrugged and pointed at a laminated sign: fines abolished, all balances cleared. I read it once, then again, my fingers still gripping the edge of the counter as if the floor might tilt. I laughed, a short broken sound, and checked the screen a third time. Behind me someone coughed. I realized I was still holding the book out toward her, arm stiff, and I couldn't remember deciding to keep it there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The key stuck, then turned, and the door swung inward on a room I had measured on paper at three hundred square feet. I stood on the threshold with a box still hugging my ribs. Morning light poured across the floorboards in a long gold slab, and above the sink, where the listing photos had shown bare wall, a round window looked out over the whole river. My mouth had come open. I realized it only when dry air touched my tongue. "No," I said to nobody, then laughed, a short cracked sound. The box slid from my arms and thumped my toe, and I didn't even flinch. I walked to the window in small, careful steps, as if the floor might be lying, and pressed my palm to the glass. Cold. Real. My heart knocked against my sternum. "Okay," I whispered. "Okay, okay." I checked the lease in my back pocket anyway, reading the address twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench by the duck pond was damp, and I was about to wipe it with my sleeve when I saw the wallet, brown leather, fat as a sandwich, sitting dead center like someone had placed it there for me. I stopped mid-crouch. My coffee tipped and scalded my knuckles, and I didn't even flinch. "No," I said aloud, to the ducks, to nobody. I looked left, then right, then behind me at the empty path, the jogger already shrinking into the trees. My heart was knocking somewhere up near my ears. I picked it up with two fingers, as if it might be hot, and flipped it open. A stack of crisp hundreds. And my own face, grinning from a driver's license, my name printed under it, my address, my birthday. I laughed once, a short cracked sound, and sat down hard on the wet slats without noticing the cold soaking through my jeans. "That's mine," I whispered. "I buried that in 2019."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marisol's hand left the tile edge, and I waited for the water to take me down the way it had for thirty-eight years. It didn't. My heels lifted. The pool hummed under my ears, and my chest, loose and strangely light, rose like something that belonged to the surface. I stopped kicking. I stopped everything. "No," I said, too loudly, and the word echoed off the chlorine-bright ceiling. "No, no, wait, are you holding me?" She held up both hands, empty, dripping, and grinned. My laugh came out as a cough. I stared at my own toes breaking the surface, pale and ridiculous, then at the black line on the pool floor sliding slowly beneath me. My heart knocked against the water. I said, "I'm lying on it," quieter now, like it might hear me and change its mind. Then I forgot to breathe, sank an inch, and didn't even mind, because I was already laughing again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana had pressed the last bean seed into the dirt eight days ago and then, mostly, forgotten about it, so when she carried her coffee out in her socks she nearly walked past the bed. She stopped. The coffee tilted in her hand and spilled hot across her knuckles, and she didn't flinch. Where there had been bare brown soil, a row of green loops pushed up, each one hauling a cracked seed husk like a tiny hat. She crouched, then knelt right in the wet. 'No,' she whispered. 'No, you didn't.' She touched one leaf with a fingertip, pulled back, touched it again. Her mouth hung open. She looked toward the kitchen window as if someone might be watching, then back down, counting aloud, 'Eleven, twelve,' her voice cracking higher on each number. Her heart was thudding in her ears. 'I just put you in the ground,' she said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the next slide and my coffee stopped halfway to my mouth. There it was, my abandoned prototype from March, the one I'd shelved after the budget cut, running on the conference room screen with numbers I'd never managed to reach. The cup hovered, then tilted, and lukewarm coffee dripped onto my notebook. I didn't wipe it. My pulse thumped in my ears so loudly I barely heard her say, "And that's a forty percent drop in load time." Forty. I blinked at the graph, then at her, then at the graph again, as if one of them might correct itself. Somebody beside me murmured, "Wow," and I realized my mouth had been hanging open for who knows how long. I shut it. "Wait," I said, too high, too thin. "How did you get it to do that?" Dana grinned and shrugged. My hands were cold. I kept staring at the screen, pen forgotten, the ink pooling in the wet page.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta took the long county road home, the dashboard clock reading 1:12, her wipers off because the sky had finally cleared. She was reaching for the radio dial when the headlights swept over the field and something in it was standing upright and enormous, a pale horse, then six, then a dozen, all motionless along the fence line, steam rising from their backs. Her foot left the gas. The car coasted, gravel ticking under the tires, and she realized she'd stopped breathing only when her chest began to ache. "No," she said aloud, flatly, to nobody. "No, no." She killed the engine, then the lights, and the dark rushed in, and still the horses were there, silver under the moon, one lifting its head toward her. Her hand found the door handle and then just rested on it, trembling. She laughed once, a cracked little sound, and pressed her knuckles against her mouth. Her phone sat in the cupholder. She didn't touch it. She only stared, wide-eyed, afraid to blink.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I pushed through the door of room 412 with a paper bag of clementines and stopped so abruptly the door bumped my heel. Grandpa was sitting up. Not propped, not slumped, but upright, swinging his legs over the bed rail like a boy on a dock. Yesterday the nurse had told me he hadn't spoken in nine days. The bag slipped, and a clementine rolled under the chair, and I didn't chase it. "You're..." I said, and the word dried up. My mouth stayed open. He grinned and asked, clear as a bell, whether I'd brought the good kind. I laughed, a high, cracked sound, and pressed my palm flat against my chest where my heart was knocking. I looked at the monitor, then at him, then at the monitor again, as if one of them might be lying. "Say that again," I whispered, and sat down hard on the edge of the visitor's chair, missing half of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marguerite had been scrolling through emails at the chain-link fence, one shoe tapping the wet pavement, when the doors banged open and the kindergartners spilled out. She looked up, and her thumb stopped mid-swipe. Her son Theo was walking straight toward her, holding hands with the boy who had bitten him in October. The phone slid from her fingers and clattered against the curb. She didn't bend to get it. "Theo?" Her voice came out thin, almost a question for someone else. Her mouth stayed open a beat too long. The other mothers kept chattering about bake sales, and the crossing guard's whistle shrilled, but all of it seemed to reach her through a wall of cotton. "This is Mateo," Theo said, cheerful, swinging their joined hands. "He's coming to ours Saturday. You said yes." Marguerite blinked hard, pressed a palm flat against her chest where her heart was knocking, and heard herself laugh once, breathless. "I did?" she whispered. "I mean, I did. Yes. Of course I did."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had priced the scarred oak writing desk at twelve dollars, taped the sticker crooked, and gone back to her coffee. Now a man in a linen jacket knelt beside it with a tiny flashlight, running his thumb along the underside of the drawer. "Where did you get this?" he asked softly. "My late husband's aunt," she said, and her voice came out higher than she meant. He pulled the drawer free and showed her a faded stamp, a name she had only seen in museum books. The coffee cup tilted in her hand; a warm splash hit her knuckles and she didn't flinch. She set it on the lawn without looking, missing the saucer entirely. "I've used that to hold my crossword pens," she whispered. Her mouth stayed open a moment longer. Across the driveway, a toddler shrieked over a plastic horse, and the sound seemed to come from another town. She sat down hard on the folding chair, blinking at the sticker.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta wedged herself under the bathroom sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, wrench in one fist, and pressed a rag against the weeping elbow joint. She tightened the nut a quarter turn. The drip stopped. Then something behind the pipe glinted, and she spat the flashlight into her palm and angled it into the dark wall cavity. A small tin box sat wedged between the studs, furred with dust. Her hand, still wet, hovered an inch from it. 'No,' she said, too softly, then louder: 'No way.' She pulled it out, and the lid shrieked open on a roll of yellowed bills and a photograph of her grandfather, young, grinning, holding this very house's keys. The wrench clattered against the tub. Her knees had gone loose; she realized she was sitting in a puddle and hadn't felt it. 'Dziadek,' she whispered, blinking at the photo, her mouth still open, the faucet ticking behind her unheard.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: Marguerite slit the envelope with a butter knife, the kettle shrieking unheeded behind her, and unfolded the page expecting another fine. She read the first line, then set the page down on the counter and picked it up again. Her mouth opened and stayed that way. "No," she said, quietly, to the toaster. "No, that's not..." She read it a third time, tracing each word with a fingertip that had begun to tremble, and the tiny seal of the Department of Revenue seemed to swim. The refund. The number had too many zeros. She pulled out a chair and missed it, catching the table's edge, and sat down hard. The kettle clicked off on its own. She laughed once, a short cracked sound, then pressed the paper flat against her chest and stared at the window, where the neighbor's dog was barking at nothing, and she could not hear it at all. "Walter," she whispered, to the empty kitchen. "Walter, come look."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marta stepped through the sliding doors of the station and stopped so abruptly that a man behind her swore, in a language she couldn't parse, and swerved around her suitcase. She didn't apologize. The ceiling above climbed in ribs of green glass, and every pillar was wrapped in glowing script that rippled and changed as she watched. Her mouth hung open; she closed it, then opened it again. "No," she said, barely a whisper. "No, no, no." Her hand found the strap of her bag and gripped until her knuckles whitened. Somewhere a bell chimed a melody, and a hundred umbrellas bloomed open in unison, though the sky outside was bright. She laughed once, a short cracked sound, and pressed her palm flat against her sternum, where her heart was knocking like a fist on a door. The map in her other hand had slid to the floor. She did not bend to pick it up. She only turned in a slow circle, blinking, her thoughts blank as the white paper at her feet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta had been peeling the lid off her thermos when Biscuit, thirteen years old and three winters past his last sprint, bolted. She stopped, the lid half-turned, coffee forgotten. He tore across the wet grass with his ears flapping inside out, hips loose, front paws kicking up clods like a puppy's. The thermos slid from her knee and thumped into the clover, and she didn't reach for it. 'No,' she said, too quietly for anyone to hear. 'No, no, no.' She stood up so fast the bench creaked. Her hand drifted to her mouth and stayed there. He leapt a fallen branch, actually leapt it, and landed with a twist and a bark she hadn't heard since before the vet's long talk about his joints. Her heart thudded against her ribs. She laughed once, a cracked breath, and found she'd walked ten steps into the field without deciding to. 'Look at you,' she whispered, blinking hard. 'Look at you.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: I was halfway through the second verse of "Down in the Valley," my fingers fumbling the same awkward chord in the church basement, when the folding chairs began to fill. Nobody was supposed to be here until Thursday. Then Mrs. Okafor, who hadn't spoken above a mutter in the six years I'd known her, stood up from the back row and sang the harmony. Clear. Huge. It rolled across the linoleum and into my ribs. My pick slipped and clattered under the piano. I didn't bend for it. My mouth hung open, and I felt the hair on my arms lift as if someone had opened a door onto winter. "Well," I said, and my voice cracked on it. "Well, hang on." I laughed, stupidly, and pressed my palm flat against my chest to check it was still mine. 'Again,' I whispered. 'From the top. Please. Do that again.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The tarp came off the workbench in one long drag, and dust rolled up into the slant of light from the window. I coughed, waved it away, and then my hand stopped in the air. Under the bench, stacked like firewood, were violins. Not broken ones. Finished ones, a dozen, maybe more, varnish glowing amber, each with a paper tag tied to the scroll. Reuben had told me for thirty years he only fixed gutters and hung doors. I crouched, and my knees cracked, and I didn't notice. I lifted one. It weighed almost nothing. My mouth was open; I closed it and it opened again. 'Reuben,' I said to the empty room, too loud, then again in a whisper, 'You liar.' The tag read my daughter's name, and her birthday, a year she hadn't been born yet. I sat down right on the sawdust floor, the violin across my lap, and read every other tag twice, my pulse thudding in my ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The list went up at noon, a single sheet pinned crooked beside the janitor's closet, and Marisol pushed through the elbows of her classmates with her thumbnail already between her teeth. She ran her finger down the column of student numbers, found hers, and followed the line across. Her finger stopped. She lifted it, then set it back down, as if the paper might have shifted. "No," she said, too quietly for anyone to hear, and then again, louder, "No, that's not mine." She checked the number against the one scrawled on her palm in smeared blue ink. It matched. The hallway noise seemed to drain away, leaving only a thin ringing. Her knees felt oddly loose, and she realized she'd been holding her breath so long her chest ached. She laughed once, a cracked little burst, then covered her mouth. Behind her, someone asked if she was okay. She just kept staring at the two digits, reading them over and over, waiting for them to change back into something sensible.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta had been counting switchbacks, one eye on the orange smear sinking behind the ridge, when the trail broke open onto a ledge she had no memory of from the map. She stopped so abruptly that her trekking pole skidded on the gravel. Below her, the whole valley was lit from within, thousands of tiny blue-green lights drifting over the meadow, rising and falling like breath. Her mouth hung open; the cold air dried her tongue before she noticed. 'No,' she whispered, then, louder, 'no way.' The pole slipped from her fingers and clattered down the rock, and she didn't reach for it. Her heart thudded against her pack straps. She pulled off a glove with her teeth, fumbled for her phone, and then simply stared at it, thumb hovering, before shoving it back in her pocket. Goosebumps crawled up both arms. 'Is anyone seeing this?' she asked the empty dusk, and laughed once, shakily, unable to blink.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, stained with decades of butter, and Marisol had followed it exactly, down to the smudged line that said *a fist of rye, don't ask.* Now she crouched before the oven window, flour to her elbows, and her breath stopped halfway. The loaf had cracked along the top in a perfect spiral, the same one that used to bloom on Abuela's bread in that crooked Tucson kitchen. She straightened slowly. Her hand drifted to her mouth, then fell. "No," she said to the empty room, and laughed once, high and strange. "No, no, that's not possible." The smell hit her next, caraway and warm yeast, and her knees seemed to forget their job; she gripped the counter. She turned the card over with trembling fingers. On the back, in faded pencil, was a line she had never noticed: *Mija, you'll see.* She read it three times, mouth open, the timer still shrilling behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The avocado slipped out of my hand and rolled under the display before I'd even registered why. Three feet away, reaching for the same bin of lemons, stood Marcus Delaney, who had once sat behind me in tenth-grade chemistry and flicked paper footballs at my neck. Same crooked front tooth. Same left-handed grab. My mouth opened, and for a second nothing came out except a small, cracked "Huh." My palms went damp against my coat. "Marcus?" I said, far too loudly, and a woman with a cart glanced over. He turned, squinted, and grinned. "No way." I laughed, then stopped, then laughed again, pressing a hand flat against my chest where my heart was thudding. "Twenty years. In the produce aisle. On a Tuesday." I crouched to fish out the avocado, mostly so I could stop staring, and bumped my head on the shelf. He was still there when I stood up, which somehow caught me off guard all over again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy had been dead since four, just the hum of the freezer case and me restocking cough drops, when the door chimed and Mr. Halvorsen walked in. Mr. Halvorsen, who I'd last seen in a wheelchair in March, with the oxygen tube and the daughter pushing him. He was carrying a pie box. Walking. I set the cough drops down on the wrong shelf without noticing. "You're," I said, and then nothing, my mouth stayed open a second too long. My hands had gone cold and prickly, and I gripped the counter edge like the floor might tilt. He slid the box toward me, grinning, and said the doctors had no idea either. I looked at his shoes, then his face, then his shoes again. "Sorry, sorry, give me a second," I said, laughing in a high, cracked way, and pressed my palm flat against my chest to check my heart was still going. Behind me, the clock read 8:52, and I didn't care one bit.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: I hit Gate B42 at a dead sprint, boarding pass crumpled in my fist, lungs burning, already rehearsing the begging speech I'd give the agent. The screen above the desk read DEPARTS 6:40, and my phone said 6:52. I stopped so hard my carry-on swung around and clipped my knee. The jet bridge door was still open. A woman in a navy vest looked up, smiled, and waved me forward like I was the guest of honor. 'Wait,' I said, and my voice came out thin, cracked. 'You held it? For me? Nobody holds it.' I laughed once, a short bark, and then just stood there with my mouth open, scanning her face for the joke. She tapped my pass, beeped it, and said the inbound from Denver had landed late too, half the plane was still coming. Behind me I heard footsteps, a dozen of them, pounding down the concourse. I looked at my shaking hands, then at the clock again, and said, 'Okay. Okay,' to no one at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marcus drew the roller down the wall in a long wet stripe of eggshell white, and the old yellow slid away to show something underneath. He stopped. The roller dripped onto the drop cloth, one slow plop, then another. Where the paint had lifted a corner of ancient wallpaper, a child's pencil heights climbed the plaster, each line labeled in his late mother's slanted hand: *Marcus, 6. Marcus, 7.* He set the roller in the tray without looking at it. His mouth hung open a little, and he realized he'd stopped breathing, so he took a breath that shook. "No," he said, too quietly, then louder, "No way. Thirty years." He pressed two fingers against the pencil marks, leaving a faint smear of white, and snatched them back as if the wall were hot. His heart thudded in his ears. He crouched, then stood, then crouched again, laughing once, a cracked little sound, while the tape peeled from the window trim behind him and nobody was there to see his face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The rain had been drumming the tin awning for an hour when the lightning showed me the yard, and I set my glass of tea down so carelessly it tipped and ran across the boards. I didn't reach for it. My grandfather's oak, the one that had stood by the fence since before my mother was born, was split clean down the middle, both halves smoking, steam rising into the downpour. The thunder came a heartbeat later and I felt it in my sternum. 'No,' I said, too quietly, then again, 'No, no, no,' as if the tree might hear and knit itself back. My mouth hung open. Rain blew in and soaked my knees and I barely noticed. I gripped the porch rail until my knuckles ached, blinked hard twice, and looked again. Still split. My ears rang. Somewhere behind me the screen door banged, and I couldn't turn around to look.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol flipped the bicycle onto its saddle and handlebars and let the wheel spin while she hunted for the right hex key, humming something tuneless. Across the garage, the neighbor's table saw whined and stopped, and she didn't even look up. Her shoulders stayed loose. She wedged a rag in her back pocket, crouched on an overturned bucket, and pinched the slack chain between two fingers. "Hello, you stubborn thing," she murmured, dripping oil link by link, watching it shine under the bare bulb. Someone else's radio played low by the shelves of paint cans. She reached for a mug of tea gone lukewarm, took a long sip, and set it on a stack of someone's old tires without checking if it would balance. When the derailleur finally clicked into place, she leaned back, stretched her legs across the cool concrete, and spun the pedal again just to hear it purr. Nothing else needed doing yet. She picked up the wrench and kept going, slowly.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was halfway through peeling a clementine, and she didn't hurry. She finished the peel in one long spiral, set it on the bench beside her, and split the fruit into halves. Wind pushed the maples across the road into a loud hush, and the sky went the color of wet slate. A man jogged past with his jacket over his head; she watched him with mild interest and a small nod. Her shoulders stayed loose against the cold plexiglass, and her legs stretched out, ankles crossed, sneakers nearly in the spray. 'Good smell, that,' she said to the pigeon pacing by the curb, breathing in the wet asphalt. Somewhere a gutter began to gurgle. She checked the schedule once, shrugged, and slid a segment of clementine into her mouth. When the rain thickened into a steady drumming, she hummed along with it, off-key and unbothered, and tapped one heel against the pavement in the same slow beat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite dragged the shoebox onto the rug and settled against the sofa with her legs stretched out, socked feet crossed at the ankle. Rain ticked on the window, and the kettle she'd left on the stove clicked off in the next room; she let it sit. The rubber band around the first bundle crumbled at her touch, and she laughed, a small huff through her nose. "Oh, Dad, your handwriting." She held an envelope up to the lamp, squinting at the postmark, then tipped it against her knee and read slowly, lips moving now and then. Her shoulders had dropped somewhere around the third letter. When she found a pressed violet, flat and brown, she set it on her palm, breathed out long, and slid it back where it had been. She sorted by year, unhurried, humming something without a tune, and when her tea finally went lukewarm beside her, she drank it anyway and reached for the next one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta was halfway through the crossword, bare feet propped on the porch rail, when Dennis's shadow stretched across the steps. "Hate to bother you," he said, rubbing the back of his neck. "Gutter's overflowing and I don't own a ladder." She didn't look up right away; she finished the word, seven letters, and tapped the pencil against her knee. "Garage, left side. Behind the bikes." Her shoulders stayed loose against the chair. "It's got a wobbly foot, so set the left rail on something flat." Dennis laughed and said he'd bring it back by Sunday.
