"Hey, you got a sec?" she said, too brightly. "It's the derailleur again. I think I set the limit screw wrong, or, I don't know, maybe it's the cable." She held the wrench out toward him, handle first, though he hadn't asked for it. He was hunting for his own tape measure on the crowded shelf. She waited anyway, thumb rubbing a black smear on her wrist, watching his hands instead of her bike. When he finally glanced over and said, "Try a quarter turn," she nodded hard, set the wrench down, and didn't touch anything. "Right. A quarter turn. Could you just, like, stay till I do it?" The garage hummed with the other tenants' freezer. She stood very still, listening for his footsteps to stay.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky goes the color of a bruise while I'm still checking my phone for the fourth time, thumb hovering over Dana's name. She said she'd pick me up if the bus was late. The bus is late. The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof, and I pull my sleeves over my knuckles and stand closer to the curb than I need to, as if being visible might summon her car. "Hey, it's me again," I tell her voicemail, too brightly. "No rush. Whenever. Just, if you're nearby." Wind shoves rain sideways across my shoes. I don't have an umbrella; I never do, because someone always has one for me. I rehearse what I'll say if she doesn't come, and every version ends with me calling her anyway. My teeth start to chatter. Headlights swing around the corner, and I step forward, heart lifting, before the shape resolves into a delivery truck. I sit back down and dial again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite knelt on the attic floor with the shoebox in her lap and read the first letter twice before she realized she was waiting for someone to tell her which pile it belonged in. "Keep or toss," she said aloud, and her voice came out small, pitched up at the end like a question. Her thumb kept returning to Daniel's handwriting, the firm slant of it, the way he'd always written what she should do next: Call the bank Tuesday. Wear the blue coat. She pressed the page flat against her chest. Her knees ached, but she didn't stand. Downstairs the phone rang, and she was halfway to her feet before she remembered there was no one to ask whether she should answer it. She sat back down. Pulled out another envelope. Held it unopened, hoping the next line would say what to do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked twice, and I was already wiping my hands on my pants before I reached the door. "The ladder? Sure, sure. Of course." He hadn't even finished asking. I glanced at the garage, and my stomach dipped. It's the one for the gutters, but I don't climb it anymore. Marcy's boy does that, when he remembers. "Would you mind if I came along? Just to see it set right?" My voice came out thinner than I wanted. Dale shrugged and said fine. I dragged the ladder out, shoulder aching, and he lifted the far end easily. Walking behind him across the lawn, I kept my eyes on his back. When he asked if I needed anything, I said no, then said, "Maybe stop by tonight? Just to say it's all right?" He laughed. I didn't.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta propped her phone against the flour canister and pressed it to her ear for the fourth time. "Okay, you said low heat, but how low? The dial's at two. Is two low?" Her sister's voice crackled back, unhurried, and Marta nodded as though she could be seen, wooden spoon dripping onto the stovetop. The recipe card, creased from her sister's handwriting, lay pinned under her left thumb. Seven minutes until the doorbell. She lifted the lid, and steam fogged her glasses. "Does it look right? Wait, I'll send you a picture." Her fingers left orange smears across the screen. "Don't hang up. Please. Just stay on while I do the sauce." She wedged the phone against her shoulder, tilting her head to hold it, and stirred slowly, eyes flicking from the pot to the card to the little screen, her stomach tight until the voice said, "That's perfect," and her shoulders finally dropped.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter, a number I don't know, and my first move is to look at the chair where Dana's coat still hangs. She'd know whether to answer. My thumb hovers. Three rings, four. I pick up and say, "Hello? Um, yes, this is... can you hold on one second?" and I don't know why I ask, since nobody is here to consult. The voice says it's about the lease, and my stomach drops, my palms go damp against the case. "I think my sister handles that," I say. "Could you call back when she's home? Or, no, tell me what you'd need, and I'll write it down." I find a pen, but my hand shakes so the letters slant. "Should I say yes?" I ask the stranger. The silence stretches. I press the coat sleeve to my cheek, breathing in her detergent, and wait to be told what to do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book has lived in my backpack since March, and now it's November, and I stand at the desk holding it with both hands like a plate I'm afraid to drop. Before I speak I text my roommate, again, "you're sure it's okay?" She answers with a thumbs-up, and I still wait for a second one. The librarian's glasses catch the fluorescent light. "I, um, I don't know what the fine is," I say, voice climbing at the end as if she might hand me the answer along with the receipt. My thumb rubs the cracked spine. My knees feel loose. When she types, I lean in to read the screen, then glance at the door, wishing someone would walk in and tell me what to say next. "Should I just pay it now? Or is there a form? Whatever you think is best," I tell her, and I mean it completely, already nodding before she opens her mouth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box had barely touched the floor when I called her. "Where does the kettle go? Never mind, I'll wait." I stood in the narrow kitchen, thumb hovering over her name, listening to the fridge hum like it was talking to someone else. She'd always known where things went. My mother had labeled every drawer in the old house; here, the drawers were bare and I opened each one twice, as if an answer might have been left inside. My chest felt tight, my palms damp against the cardboard. The window showed a brick wall and a slice of gray sky. I rehearsed what I'd say if the landlord knocked, then decided I'd just pretend not to be home. When she picked up, I laughed too loudly. "No, it's fine, I just wanted to hear you. Stay on while I unpack? You don't have to say anything." I set the phone on the counter, face up, and kept it there all night.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, damp from the morning mist, and Marguerite stopped with her thermos halfway to her mouth. She looked up the path, then down it. Nobody. Her thumb found the license first: Daniel Osei, a stranger's face, squinting. She pulled out her phone and dialed her daughter before she'd decided anything. "Priya, it's me. No, nothing's wrong. I found a wallet. What do I do with it?" She listened, nodding at the empty air, her free hand pressing flat against her stomach. "The police station. Right. Which one is closest again?" Her voice had gone small. "Could you stay on the phone while I walk? Just till I'm there?" She tucked the wallet into her coat as though it might bite, took four steps, and turned back to check the bench twice. "Say that part again, slower. I'll write it on my hand." She did, with a pen from her purse, tongue between her teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The pool smells of chlorine and wet concrete, and I stand at the shallow end with my fingers hooked over the gutter, knuckles pale. Marguerite, the instructor, is already waist-deep, hands out. "Just push off," she says. I don't. "Stay close?" My voice comes out thin, and I hate it. "Right here," she says, and I let go with one hand, then the other, my eyes never leaving her forearms. My legs sink. My heart knocks against my ribs. When she steps back a single pace to demonstrate a kick, I flail toward her and clamp onto her wrist, water slapping my chin. "Sorry. Sorry. Can you not move yet?" Across the lane, a girl of maybe eight glides past without a splash. I watch her, then check where Marguerite's hand is again. It's still there. I kick, small and stiff, and count aloud: one, two, three, wait, are you still there?

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets are lined up on the porch rail like a row of small judges, and I've already called Marguerite twice this morning. "Quarter inch deep, you said? Or half?" I hold the phone against my shoulder, knees pressed into damp dirt, a trowel loose in my fist. She laughs and says half for the beans. I write it on my wrist in pen. When she hangs up, the yard goes very quiet. I stare at the tidy furrow I dug and can't tell whether it's right. My stomach tightens. I drop in one tomato start, then pull out my phone to photograph it and send it to her: "Like this?" I crouch there, watching the screen, ignoring the sun on my neck, waiting for the three little dots to answer before I dare to touch the next plant.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus sat at the far end of the conference table while Dana clicked to the next slide, and his eyes went to her face before they went to the screen. When she paused on the budget chart, his pen stopped. She glanced his way, and he nodded, small and quick, though he hadn't really followed the numbers. His coffee had gone cold an hour ago. Someone asked about the timeline, and Marcus felt his shoulders rise, waiting for Dana to answer, relieved when she did. He'd drafted three versions of that timeline, but each time he'd sent it to her first, and her edits were the ones that stayed. 'That's, uh, what Dana said,' he offered when the VP looked at him, and laughed too softly. Afterward he hovered by the door with his laptop hugged to his chest until she finished talking to the others. 'So,' he said, 'what should I work on next?'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway is empty past midnight, and still I keep my phone wedged against the dashboard, screen lit, Dana's thread open. Three dots appeared an hour ago and vanished. I check again at the red light, though nothing moves for miles. "Just tell me what to do," I say to the dark windshield, and my voice comes out small, like I'm asking permission from the radio. My thumbs are damp on the wheel. At the exit I can't decide between the left lane and the right, so I drift, hovering, until a truck horn pulls me straight. I almost call her. It's nearly one. I imagine her yawning, saying fine, come over, and my shoulders loosen just picturing it. Instead I pull into my driveway, engine ticking, and sit there with the porch light off, thumb hovering over her name, unable to open the car door until she tells me it's okay to go inside.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine on the fourth floor eats my dollar, and I stand there pressing the button like Dad might appear and tell me what to do about it. Back in room 412, I hover at the foot of his bed, holding a coffee I don't want. He's asleep, mouth open, the monitor ticking green numbers I try to read like a language I'll be tested on. A nurse comes in and I'm up before she speaks. "Is that normal? The beeping?" My voice comes out small, almost a question to the ceiling. She nods, checks something, leaves. I sit again, knees bouncing. His hand lies open on the blanket, and I realize I've been waiting for it to close around mine, to sign the forms, to know which pharmacy, which password, which bills. I pull out my phone and scroll to his name, then stare at it, thumb hovering, the screen glowing uselessly in my palm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I'm at the fence twenty minutes early, again, phone gripped in both hands like it might tip over without me. The bell hasn't gone and already my eyes are fixed on the blue doors. Another mother says something about the weather and I nod, but I don't hear it; I'm counting the kids' backpacks for the one with the frayed dinosaur patch. My stomach tightens when the doors finally bang open, and I rise onto my toes. Where is she. Where is she. Then the patch, the ponytail, her small hand lifting, and my knees loosen so suddenly I have to lean on the cold metal. 'Hi, baby,' I say, too loud, voice cracking. She asks what's for dinner and I tell her anything she wants. I don't even know what's in the fridge. I just know the day was a long gray hallway until she walked out, and I let her carry my hand home as if she were the one leading me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marta had set the oak sideboard at the end of the driveway by seven, then moved it two feet left because Dennis always said the light hit it better there. A woman ran her thumb along the drawer edge and asked the price. Marta's mouth opened, closed. "What would you... what do you think is fair?" she said, glancing toward the garage where the radio hummed. The woman offered forty. Marta's palms were damp against her cardigan. "Let me just check," she said, and walked inside, though Dennis had been gone since March and the kitchen held only the ticking clock. She stood there a full minute, fingers pressed to the counter, rehearsing a number in his voice. When she came back out the woman was already backing away. "Fifty," Marta called, too softly. "He'd have said fifty." She stayed beside the sideboard all afternoon, one hand resting on its top, as if it might hold her up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta knelt on the soaked bathroom tiles with the wrench in one hand and her phone wedged against her shoulder, the screen smeared with water. "Okay, Dad, I'm under the sink. Now which way is loosen again?" She listened, nodded at no one, and turned the nut. The drip quickened. "No, it's worse. Wait, don't hang up." Her knees ached against the cold floor, and her palms were slick. A video sat paused in another tab, but she didn't trust it; she trusted his voice, even crackling and three states away. When the line went quiet she froze, the wrench hovering. "Dad? Are you still there?" The hum returned, and her shoulders dropped. She tightened the nut a quarter turn the moment he said to, and only then let herself breathe. Water pooled around her wrist. She didn't wipe it. She kept the phone close, as if the pipe might start again the second he left.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat against the sugar tin for two days, its window showing her name in plain black type. Marta finally picked it up when the kettle clicked off, and her thumb slid under the flap slowly, as if the paper might bite. She read the first line, then stopped and dialed her daughter with the other hand. "Lucia, it's from the housing office. No, I haven't. You read it. Please. I'll hold it up to the camera." Her voice had gone small and quick. She smoothed the page flat on the table, pressing it with both palms to stop their trembling, and squinted at words like *determination* and *pursuant*. "Does it say yes? Tell me where it says yes." When Lucia sighed and began to read aloud, Marta sank into the chair, still gripping the phone, nodding at every sentence though no one could see, her tea going cold beside the unopened pile of other mail she kept meaning to ask someone about.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station's announcements rolled over me in a language I couldn't even split into words, and I stood very still beside my suitcase, the way you do when moving might be a mistake. Hana's text was still on my phone: Take the green line, I'll meet you. I held the screen out to a woman in a gray coat, and my voice came out small and too slow. "Please? This one? Green?" She tapped twice, pointed left, and said something long. I nodded hard, bowed, nodded again, though I'd caught none of it. My palms were damp against the suitcase handle. I followed her gaze, then followed her feet for twenty paces, until she turned off and I realized I'd stopped breathing. On the platform I watched every stranger's face, ready to copy whatever they did. When the doors opened, I waited for someone else to step in first, and only then did I dare to follow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the fence with both hands wrapped around the top rail, knuckles pale, though the dog was only chasing a gull's shadow across the grass. Every time Biscuit's brown ears vanished behind the tall weeds, her breath stopped until they bobbed up again. "Stay where I can see you," she called, her voice thin and a little too bright. He didn't hear. She patted her coat pocket to check the leash was still there, and it was. Her stomach loosened only when he trotted back, tongue flapping, and leaned his whole weight against her shins. She crouched, pressed her forehead into his warm neck, and stayed there long after he squirmed. "Okay," she whispered. "Okay. Go on, then. But just to the oak." The wind pulled at her sleeves. She didn't let go of the rail, even as he ran, as if the fence were what held her up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and Marta kept her eyes on the piano bench where Lucien should have been. Ten past seven. She played the first eight bars of the duet alone, then stopped, fingers hovering over the keys. "Sorry, one more time," she told the empty folding chairs, though no one had asked. Her phone lay face-up on the music stand; she checked it between every phrase. Nothing. When the door finally banged open, her shoulders dropped so fast her neck ached. "Oh, good. Okay. Where do I come in again? Here? You'll nod, right? Nod at me before the bridge, I never know without it." She laughed too high, wiped her damp palms on her skirt, and slid half a step closer to him. Without his shoulder in the corner of her eye, the song had no floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta held the coping saw for a full minute before deciding whether it was hers to put in the box. Every drawer she pulled, she paused and listened, as if Walt might call out from the lathe which bin it belonged in. "Where do you keep the... no," she said to the pegboard, and laughed thinly. Her hands hovered over a coffee can of mismatched screws. She had never once bought a screw; she'd only ever phoned him. Now she lifted her cell, thumb over his name, and the screen's glow lit the sawdust on her wrist. She set the phone on the bench, picked it up again. In the corner hung his canvas apron, still bent to the shape of his belly. She pressed her face into it, breathed cedar and oil, and said, steady and small, "Okay. Tell me what to do with the clamps." The shop answered with only the tick of the cooling heater.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells of floor wax and warm photocopier dust, and I've been standing in front of the empty corkboard since seven-fifty. Nobody told me to. I keep checking my phone for Maya's text, even though she said she'd only message if she saw the list first. When she appears at the far end, I'm already walking toward her, mouth dry, hands pulled up inside my sleeves. "Well?" My voice cracks on it. "Tell me what to do," I add, which makes no sense, and she frowns. "Should I look? Or you look, and just nod or shake your head. Don't say it out loud." She shrugs and holds up her phone. I realize my thumb is hovering over my mother's name, ready to call her the second I'm told how to feel. The secretary pins the first sheet up. My knees go soft, and I grab Maya's elbow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The orange light slid off the ridge, and Mara stopped so abruptly that her pack knocked against her spine. She pulled out her phone, thumbed the dark screen, and swore softly at the single bar of battery. "Dana, which way was it?" she called, though the words came out thin, almost a question to the trees. Dana was ten paces ahead, unbothered, and Mara hurried to close the gap until her boots nearly clipped Dana's heels. Her fingers found the strap of Dana's bag and held it for a few steps before she noticed. Every fork in the path made her chest tighten; she'd never once looked at the map folded in her pocket. "You're sure? You're sure it's left?" Her palms were damp. The cold crept in under her sleeves, and she kept her eyes on Dana's red jacket, the only thing in the blue dusk she trusted to lead her out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, stained at the corners, and Mina had propped it against the flour canister where she could see it from every angle of the kitchen. "Warm water," she read aloud, then again, a finger pinned under the words. "Warm like a bath for a baby." She dipped her wrist in the bowl, frowned, and added more hot, then less. Her grandmother's slanted handwriting said *knead until it feels right*, and Mina's hands stopped mid-fold. Right how? She pressed the dough and waited for it to answer. Her phone was already in her flour-dusted hand, thumb hovering over her mother's name. "Does it say anything else on the back?" she asked when the call connected, flipping the card over twice. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears. "Okay. Okay, stay on, please. Just till it rises." She set the phone on the counter, speaker on, and kept kneading toward the sound of breathing on the line.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding two cartons of eggs, comparing them for the third time, when someone said my name beside the cereal. Marcus, from tenth-grade chemistry. He looked taller, easy in his jacket. "So what are you doing now?" he asked, and my mouth went dry. "Oh, you know. Still figuring it out. Actually, could you tell me how you got your job? Maybe send me the details? Or I could call you? Whatever's easiest for you." I'd already pulled out my phone, thumb hovering, before he answered. My palms were damp against the cold cardboard. He laughed and said sure, and I nodded too many times. When he left, I stood in the aisle with the eggs, wondering if I should text my sister to ask what I ought to have said, and whether he would really write.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marisol kept glancing at the phone on the counter anyway, the screen dark, the ringer turned all the way up. Her manager, Dennis, had left at noon with a wave and a "You've got this," and she had nodded too fast. Now she read the pill-count sheet a third time, her thumb pressing a white crescent into the clipboard. When the door chimed, her shoulders jumped. It was only a man wanting tissues. "Do you know if Dennis is reachable tonight?" she asked him, then laughed, embarrassed, and said, "Sorry, no, never mind." Her stomach tightened as the lights in the next aisle buzzed. She dialed Dennis's number, let it ring once, hung up, and dialed again. Outside, the parking lot dimmed toward Thanksgiving, and she stood very still behind the register, waiting for his voice to tell her what to do next.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marguerite stood beneath the gate-change board with her phone pressed to her ear, one thumb rubbing the corner of her boarding pass soft. "Okay, but which way is C14? Left or right? Don't hang up, Danny, please, just stay on." Her brother's voice crackled from two time zones away, reading a map on his own screen. She followed him step by step, stopping whenever the line hissed, her breath shallow, her free hand strangling the strap of her bag. A moving walkway slid past; she hesitated before stepping on, then turned to a uniformed woman strolling by. "Excuse me, is this right? Am I going the right way?" The woman nodded without slowing. Marguerite's stomach loosened, then clenched again at the clock above the shops. "Danny? Tell me again what time it says. Tell me I can still make it." Her voice had gone small. She had never once booked a trip alone, and she did not take another step until he answered.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I've taped the trim twice, and still I'm standing in the doorway with the roller dripping onto the drop cloth, phone pinned between my shoulder and ear. "Dad, is it supposed to look streaky?" I ask. "Wait, don't hang up. Just stay on while I do this wall." He hums, tells me to go in a W shape, and I do it, my wrist trembling a little each time I lift the roller. When he says he has to go, my stomach drops and I laugh too loudly. "Sure, sure, no, I'm fine." The silence afterward is thick with the smell of wet paint. I stare at the half-covered wall, the pale sage against the old yellow, and can't decide if it's right. I text my sister a photo. Then another. I hold the brush above the corner, not touching it, waiting for her reply before I let myself continue.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Thunder rolled over the roof and I checked my phone again, thumb already hovering over Dana's name. Four missed calls, none returned. I set it face-up on the porch rail anyway, where the rain spattered it, and wiped the screen on my shirt. "Just tell me what to do," I said to the empty wicker chair beside me, and my voice came out small, embarrassed. Wind shoved the swing sideways. My stomach tightened the way it does when I'm the last kid waiting outside school. I'd never learned which fuse to flip when the lights go out, or whether the basement floods, or how long to wait before worrying. Dana always knew. Lightning cracked the maple's edge, and I flinched, gripping the armrest until my knuckles ached. I picked the phone up again. Five rings. Voicemail. "Hey, it's me," I whispered. "Call back. Please. I'll just sit here till you do."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain has been off the ring for forty minutes, and I'm still sitting on the overturned milk crate, staring at it. Someone's radio in the next bay plays something upbeat, and I wish they'd turn it down. My neighbor, a woman with grease up to her elbows, asks if I need a hand. "No, it's fine," I say, too quietly, and she nods slowly like she didn't catch it. My arms feel full of wet sand. I pick up the wrench, set it down, pick it up again. The fluorescent tube overhead flickers, and I count the flickers instead of turning a single bolt. The bike was supposed to get me to work. I haven't been to work in nine days. Eventually I thread the chain back on with one finger, spin the pedal once, and watch the wheel tick itself to a stop. I don't bother wiping my hands. I just sit there until the radio goes off and the lights click out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was still counting the cracks in the pavement, and she didn't look up. The wind turned, shoving cold rain sideways under the plexiglass, and it soaked the left leg of her jeans. She shifted her bag an inch to the right and let the leg stay wet. Her phone buzzed twice in her pocket; she knew it was her sister, and she let it buzz. A woman beside her muttered, 'Typical,' and laughed, and Marguerite opened her mouth to answer and found nothing there, so she nodded at the puddle instead. Her chest felt packed with wet sand. The 14 came, hissed, opened its doors, and she watched the lit rectangle of dry seats for a long moment before she sat back down on the bench. 'Next one,' she said, to no one, her voice flat as the gray sky. The doors folded shut. Water ran down her neck, and she let that stay too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box had sat by the radiator since March, and Marguerite only opened it now because the light through the blinds had gone grey enough to make every other task feel pointless. She lifted out the first envelope and held it a long time without unfolding it. Her thumb left a smudge in the dust. "Fine," she said to the empty room, flat, as if someone had asked her something. She read two lines of her sister's looping handwriting, then set the page face down on her knee and watched the radiator tick. Her tea had gone cold hours ago; she drank it anyway. The stack to keep and the stack to throw away both stayed empty. Her arms felt packed with wet sand, and when the phone buzzed on the floor she let it buzz until it stopped. By evening she had moved exactly one letter, from the box to her lap, and the lamp was still off.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while the TV was talking to no one. I'd been on the couch since morning, or since yesterday, the blanket heavy across my shins. Through the peephole I saw Dennis from next door, hands in his jacket pockets. I opened the door halfway. "Hey. Sorry. You got a ladder I could borrow? Gutters." I stared at his boots. "Yeah," I said, too quietly, and had to say it again. "In the garage. I think." My legs felt filled with wet sand as I crossed the yard. The garage smelled of dust and cold. The ladder hung behind boxes I'd meant to unpack for two years, and lifting it made my arms shake. Dennis took the other end, chatting about leaves. I nodded where it seemed right. "Keep it as long as you want," I said. When he left, I stood in the driveway until my fingers went numb, then went back inside and lay down in my shoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions have been sitting on the board for twenty minutes, and I'm still holding the knife. Six-fifteen. They said seven. I cut one, slowly, and watch my eyes stay dry, which strikes me as funny in a way I don't laugh at. The pot of water hasn't been turned on. I turn it on. My arms feel packed with wet sand, and I lean on the counter to chop the garlic, the way you'd lean on a fence. The kitchen is bright, too bright, so I flip off the overhead and cook by the small light above the stove. My phone buzzes: 'Can't wait!!' I type 'Me too,' delete it, type it again. I taste the sauce and it tastes like nothing, like warm paper. I add salt anyway, then more. When the doorbell rings I stand there with the spoon dripping on my sock, practicing a face in the dark window, until it rings again and I call out, 'Coming,' much more brightly than I mean it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the floorboards, and Marta watched it crawl an inch toward the radiator. Unknown number, a string of digits with no face attached. She lay on the rug where she had been since the light went orange, cheek pressed to the wool, a cold mug of tea within reach and untouched. Four rings. Five. Her arm felt filled with wet sand when she lifted it. "Hello," she said, and it came out as a croak, so she cleared her throat and tried again, quieter. A cheerful voice asked if she had a moment to talk about her car's extended warranty. She didn't own a car. She didn't say so. She listened to the woman breathe between sentences, to the scripted warmth, and felt her eyes sting for no reason she could name. "Okay," Marta whispered when it stopped. "Okay. Thank you." The line clicked dead. She kept the phone against her ear a long while, then set it down and stared at the ceiling, the dishes still piled in the sink.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in the bottom of Marguerite's backpack since March, under a sweatshirt she hadn't washed, and now the November rain had warped its spine. She stood at the return desk longer than she needed to, watching water drip from her sleeve onto the carpet. The librarian scanned it and the machine gave a small, cheerful chirp. "Sixty-one days over," the woman said, not unkindly. Marguerite nodded. "Okay," she said, so quietly she wasn't sure it had come out. Her hand hovered over her wallet and then just stayed there, heavy, as if the zipper were a long way off. She noticed the fluorescent hum, the ticking clock, how her feet seemed to belong to someone standing farther back. "I meant to bring it," she said. "I kept meaning to." The librarian slid a slip of paper across. Marguerite folded it once, twice, and again, until it was a hard little square, then walked out and sat on the wet steps without opening her umbrella.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers carried in the last box at four, and I signed their tablet with a finger that didn't feel like mine. "Want me to put the bed together?" one asked. "No, it's fine," I said, too quietly, and he asked again. After the door clicked shut I stood in the middle of the room, which took about six steps to cross. The radiator ticked. I sat on the floor because the couch was still wrapped in plastic, and the plastic crackled whenever I breathed. Boxes labeled KITCHEN, BOOKS, MISC stared at me. I thought about opening one for a fork, then about how I'd eaten crackers all week without one. My coat stayed on. The window showed a brick wall and a slice of gray I couldn't call sky. At some point the light left, and I didn't get up to find the switch. I just lay down on the cold floorboards, knees pulled in, and listened to a neighbor's television laugh through the wall at something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside me for a long time before I admitted it was there. Brown leather, curled at the corners. I'd come to the park because the apartment walls had started to feel like they were leaning in, but I'd been staring at the same patch of gravel for what might have been an hour. My coffee had gone cold in my hand. Finally I picked it up, and my arms felt like wet sandbags. Inside: a library card, forty dollars, a photo of a girl missing her front teeth. A driver's license, an address eleven blocks away. I said, 'Okay,' out loud, flat, to nobody. I thought about the walk, the knocking, the stranger's face, having to talk. I thought about just leaving it. I sat another ten minutes, thumb pressed against the little girl's photo. Then I stood, slowly, knees aching, and started toward the street, because carrying it was easier than explaining to myself why I hadn't.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood in the shallow end at seven a.m., arms hanging, while the instructor, a teenager with a whistle on a red lanyard, told her to put her face in. She nodded and didn't. The water came to her ribs and felt heavier than it should, like wearing wet coats. "Just blow bubbles," the girl said. Marguerite looked at the lane lines instead, the blue tiles wavering below. She had signed up in March; it was now October, and this was only her third visit. When she finally bent, her breath leaked out thin and silent, and she came up without having kicked once. "Better," the girl said. "Okay," said Marguerite, very quietly. In the locker room she sat on the bench with her towel across her knees until the next class's voices filled the room. Her hair dripped onto the floor. She watched it. Sinking, she thought, might be the one part she was already good at.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets sat on the porch rail for nine days before I opened one. Today I knelt in the dirt behind the garage, and the cold soaked through my jeans at the knees. The instructions said six inches apart. I measured the first with my hand, then stopped measuring. My arms felt full of wet sand. I lowered a tomato seedling into its hole and sat back on my heels, staring at it a long while. Next door, a neighbor called out, asking what I was growing. "Not sure yet," I said, flat, and she laughed like I'd made a joke. I hadn't. I pressed soil around the stem with two fingers, barely, the way you'd touch a sleeping stranger. The hose was too far away. I told myself I'd water it later, and then I just stayed there while the light slid off the fence and my hands went gray with dirt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Priya clicks to the third slide and the room leans toward her, but I'm watching the blinds, how the slats cut the light into stripes that never reach my side of the table. My coffee went cold an hour ago. I keep lifting the cup anyway. Someone laughs at her joke, and I produce the shape of a smile a beat late, like a delayed echo. My arms feel packed with wet sand. When Marcus asks if I have thoughts on the timeline, I hear myself say, "Looks fine," so quietly he asks me to repeat it. "Fine," I say again. I'd drafted feedback last week. I can't remember where I saved it, or why it mattered. Priya's chart climbs upward, all those bright, hopeful bars. I count the ceiling tiles instead. Forty-two. Then I count them again, slower, because the meeting will end and I'll still have to stand up and walk back to my desk.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marla missed her exit and didn't turn around. The highway hummed under the tires, and she let the car drift at exactly the speed limit, hands loose at the bottom of the wheel, as if someone else had put them there. The radio offered a cheerful man selling mattresses; she listened to the whole ad, then to the silence after it. Her chest felt packed with wet sand. At a red light with no one else around, she stayed put long after it turned green, watching the yellow blink on the wet asphalt. "Okay," she said aloud, flat, to nobody. "Okay." Her phone buzzed in the cup holder, her sister's name glowing, and she turned it face down without breaking her gaze from the road. When she finally pulled into the driveway, the porch light was off, the way she'd left it that morning. She turned off the engine and sat in the ticking dark, coat still buttoned, keys in her fist, unable to find a reason to lift the door handle.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator smells like floor cleaner and old soup, and I let two of them go by before I get in. Room 412. Uncle Dennis is asleep, mouth open, the TV murmuring a game show to nobody. I set the grocery bag of clementines on the tray table, then stand there with my coat still zipped. My arms feel packed with wet sand. A nurse asks if I need a chair and I say, "No, I'm fine, I won't stay long," though I've been here forty minutes and haven't sat. I peel one clementine just to have something to do, and the rind comes off in one long curl, and I can't think why that should matter. I watch the monitor's green line climb and fall. When his eyes open I say, "Hey," in a voice so flat it startles me. He asks how work is. "Same," I say. I eat the whole clementine without tasting it, then look at the clock again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana stood at the edge of the fence, apart from the clusters of mothers trading weekend plans, her hands buried in a coat she hadn't washed in weeks. The bell rang and she flinched as if it were meant for her. Someone called her name, asked how she was, and she said, "Fine. Tired. You know," in a voice so flat it barely left her mouth. Her limbs felt packed with wet sand; even lifting her chin to find Theo in the stream of backpacks took a deliberate effort. She noticed the gutters were clogged with leaves and thought she should do something about that, then thought of nothing at all. When Theo ran up, holding out a painting still tacky with blue, she looked at it a long moment before she said, "That's nice, baby." He waited for more. She tried to find it somewhere, then took his hand and walked toward the car, counting the cracks in the pavement.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The sticker gun clicks in my hand, and I price the oak dresser at forty dollars, then peel it off and write ten. Nobody's asked. It's nine a.m. and I've been sitting in the same folding chair since six, coffee gone cold on the driveway beside my foot. A woman runs her thumb along the dresser's edge and asks if it has a story. 'It held his socks,' I say, and my voice comes out flat, like something set down. She laughs politely. I don't. My arms feel packed with wet sand, and standing to help her tilt the drawers takes three tries. She offers fifteen. I nod before she finishes the number. When her truck pulls away, I stare at the pale rectangle on the lawn where the dresser stood, and think that the grass will be that color for a week, and then it won't, and I can't decide which is worse.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip had been keeping time under the sink for nine days before Marcus finally knelt on the cabinet floor, wrench beside him, a towel soaked through at his knees. The dishes in the basin were from last week, maybe longer. He fitted the wrench to the nut and just stayed there, arm heavy as wet sand, watching a bead swell and fall, swell and fall. "Okay," he said to the pipe, flat, barely a sound. "Okay." He turned the nut a quarter inch and his hand quit. The phone buzzed on the counter with his sister's name; he let it buzz until the room went quiet again. Water ran cold along his wrist and into his sleeve, and he didn't pull back. He thought he should get a bucket. He thought the bucket was in the garage, and the garage was very far. He lowered his forehead against the cool cabinet wall and closed his eyes, listening to the drip keep counting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been on the counter since Thursday, wedged between a pizza menu and a dead houseplant I keep meaning to throw out. It's Sunday, nearly three in the afternoon, and I'm still in yesterday's sweatshirt, the curtains pulled shut. I pick it up and put it down twice. My arms feel like they're full of wet sand. When I finally slide a thumb under the flap, the paper tears crooked, and I just stare at the ragged edge for a while. The fridge hums. I read the first line, then the same line again, and the words don't stick to anything. 'Okay,' I say to the empty kitchen, flat, like I'm agreeing to something. Whatever it says, I think, it can't be worse than the sink full of dishes I haven't looked at in nine days. I fold the letter back along its creases, set it on top of the dead plant, and go lie down on the kitchen floor, cheek against the cool tile, until it gets dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train sighed out its doors at Hanoi's station, and Marcus stood on the platform until the crowd had thinned around him like water around a stone. He lifted his bag and it seemed to weigh twice what it had in Denver. A driver shouted something bright and fast at him; Marcus nodded without knowing why and then shook his head, and the man shrugged and left. He walked. Motorbikes poured past, horns stitching the air, and he kept his eyes on the cracked pavement. At the hostel, the girl at the desk slid a form toward him, and he stared at the unreadable boxes for a long minute before writing his name in the wrong one. 'Thanks,' he said, barely audible, and 'sorry.' Upstairs he sat on the edge of the narrow bed with his shoes still on. Laughter drifted up from the street. He had meant to go find noodles, the way the guidebook said. Instead he lay back, pulled the thin blanket over his jacket, and watched the ceiling fan turn until the window went dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus sat on the same bench he'd dragged himself to every afternoon that week, hands wedged between his knees, jacket still zipped to the chin though the sun was warm. Biscuit tore across the field after a crow, ears flapping, and came back with his whole body wagging, dropping a slobbery stick at Marcus's shoe. "Good boy," Marcus said, flat and quiet, the way you read a grocery list. He didn't pick it up. His arms felt filled with wet sand, and lifting one seemed like a negotiation he would lose. The dog waited, head tilted, then bounded off again. Marcus watched the grass bend in long ripples and thought that he should be laughing, that he used to. His phone buzzed against his thigh; he let it buzz until it stopped. When Biscuit finally flopped against his legs, panting, Marcus rested one hand on the warm ribs and stared at nothing, wondering how long before it would be reasonable to go home and lie down again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells like floor wax and old coffee, and I'm sitting at the upright piano with the lid up, hands in my lap, while Marguerite passes out the program drafts. My name is printed under Clair de Lune. I played it perfectly in March. Now I press the first note and it sounds like someone else's, thin and far away. I stop at bar nine. Start again. Stop. "Take your time, hon," Marguerite says, and I say, "Sure, sure, I'm fine," in a voice so flat it barely leaves my mouth. My arms feel packed with wet sand. The folding chairs are stacked in rows nobody will fill, and I count them instead of the measures. Twenty-two. When the others leave I tell her I'll stay and practice, then sit there with my coat still on, staring at the keys until the janitor jingles his ring and I realize I haven't played a note in an hour.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Three hours in, I had filled exactly one box. It held a coffee can of mismatched screws, and I kept sorting them anyway, by length, then undoing it. Dale's apron still hung on the nail, bent at the shoulder where his arm used to go. I pressed my thumb into the sawdust on the bench and it kept the print. My legs felt poured full of wet sand, so I sat on his stool, which was too low, like always. The radio was on the station he liked. I didn't turn it off or up. His daughter called to ask how it was going and I said, "Fine. Good. Almost done," in a voice like paper being slid under a door. After I hung up I looked at the clock and it was the same hour as before, or I had lost one. I picked up his pencil, the stub chewed flat, and couldn't think where in the world to put it down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and Mara had been lying on the carpet since nine with the laptop open beside her head. At 11:58 she turned the screen toward the wall. Her roommate's cereal bowl sat on the desk, the milk gone filmy, and she looked at it for a long time without deciding to move it. Her limbs felt packed with wet sand. When her phone buzzed, she let it buzz. "It's fine," she told the ceiling, flat, to nobody, and her voice cracked on the second word. She hadn't opened the blinds in days; the room held the same gray no matter the hour. At 12:10 she finally rolled over and pulled the laptop close, but only stared at the spinning wheel, thinking that whatever number came, she would still be right here, on this carpet, tired in exactly this way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then the color of dishwater, and I keep walking because stopping would require a decision. My boots scuff the same rut over and over. Somewhere behind me is the car, and I counted the miles out loud at the trailhead, but I can't remember the number now. My pack straps cut into shoulders that feel packed with wet sand. A couple passes going down, headlamps already on, and the woman says, "Beautiful night for it," and I say, "Yeah," in a voice like a door closing. I don't look up. The ridge ahead is a dark cutout, and I think it would be easier to sit on this rock until the cold decides things. My phone buzzes in my pocket. I let it. The trees lean in, and my legs go on without me, one step, then another, toward nothing I can name, and I notice I haven't eaten since yesterday and don't mind.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The recipe card is soft as cloth, my grandmother's slanted handwriting gone brown at the folds. "Flour till it feels right," it says, which helps no one. I've left the curtains shut since Tuesday, so I measure by the light of the stove hood. My arms feel full of wet sand as I stir. The dough sticks to my fingers and I just stand there, letting it, until it dries into little gray crusts. I should knead. I count to ten, then ten again, and my hands haven't moved. When the phone buzzes I turn it face down. "Later," I tell the empty kitchen, in a voice so flat it startles me. Eventually I push the heel of my palm into the dough, once, twice. It smells like her hallway. I stop and sit on the floor with my back against the cabinet. The bowl waits above me under its towel, and I don't check whether it rises.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus had been standing in the cereal aisle for a long time, holding a box he didn't want, when someone said his name. Dana Whitlock, from tenth-grade chemistry, stood there with a toddler on her hip and a basket full of bright things. His hand went to his hair, which he hadn't washed in four days. "Hey," he said, too quietly, and she leaned in as if to catch it. She talked about her job, a house near the lake, a marathon in spring. He nodded at the right places, but her words seemed to arrive late, like sound across water. His legs felt filled with wet sand. "Work's fine," he said when she asked. "Same." She hugged him anyway, and he stood stiff, smelling her shampoo. After she left, he put the box back, walked out past the carts without buying anything, and sat in his car with the engine off until the windshield fogged over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marguerite stood at the register watching the automatic doors open for no one. Someone had taped paper turkeys to the window; one had slipped and hung by a single corner. She didn't fix it. Her coworker Dale called from the back, 'You doing anything tomorrow?' and she said, 'Sleeping, probably,' in the flat voice she used for reading lot numbers. Her arms felt packed with wet sand. She straightened the same row of lip balms twice, then a third time, and couldn't have said why. The fluorescent hum seemed louder than it had in years. When the clock finally read six, she kept standing there, hand on the counter, counting the tiles to the door. Her phone buzzed with her sister's name. She turned it face down, locked the register, and walked out into the cold without zipping her coat, letting the wind find every gap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board said Gate B47, and B47 was a long way off, and I walked toward it at the speed I always walk now, like wading. Everyone else jogged past me with their roller bags clattering. A man in a vest said, "Sir, you've got eleven minutes," and I said, "Okay," in a voice so flat it surprised even me. My legs felt packed with wet sand. I stopped at a window and watched a baggage cart circle the same patch of tarmac, and I couldn't remember deciding to stop. The gate agent was already pulling the door shut when I got there. She looked at me, waiting for me to beg. I only stood there holding the boarding pass, its corner damp from my thumb. "Next one's at six tomorrow," she said. I nodded, turned, and sat on the carpet beside an outlet, relieved, and then too tired to be ashamed of the relief. My phone buzzed with my sister's name. I let it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The paint can has sat open on the drop cloth since Saturday, a skin forming over the pale yellow I thought would make mornings easier. It's Wednesday. I pick up the roller, load it, and stand there while it drips onto my sock. Three strokes. My arm feels packed with wet sand, so I sit on the stepladder and look at the bare patch I've made, a lopsided yellow island on the old gray. The phone buzzes on the windowsill. My sister. I let it ring out, then say to the empty room, "Later," in a voice I barely recognize, flat as the wall. I haven't eaten since the toast yesterday, or maybe the day before. The tape along the baseboard is peeling at one corner and I watch it curl instead of pressing it down. Maybe I'll finish tomorrow. Maybe the gray was fine. I switch off the light and leave the roller in the tray to harden.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while Marguerite was still holding the mug, and she didn't move to go inside. Rain slanted under the porch roof and dotted her shins, then her knees, and she watched it happen as if it belonged to someone else's legs. The tea had gone cold hours ago. Her phone buzzed against the boards, lit up with her sister's name, and dimmed again. "Later," she told it, her voice flat and scraped. Her chest felt packed with wet sand; each breath took a decision. Lightning whitened the yard, the unmown grass, the bike she'd meant to put away in May. She counted the seconds before the crack, lost count, started over, lost it again. The swing chain creaked. Somewhere a screen door slapped shut, a neighbor hurrying toward dry rooms and supper. Marguerite pulled her sleeves over her hands, leaned her head against the siding, and let her eyes close. Maybe, she thought, she'd go in when it stopped. Maybe tomorrow's storm would do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had been wrenching at the rear derailleur since the neighbors' dryer stopped thumping through the wall, and now the garage's single bulb buzzed over a floor scattered with chain links and greasy rags. Her interview was at seven. The bus didn't run that early, and the bike was the only way. She jammed the hex key in again, and it slipped, skinning her knuckle. She hissed, sucked the blood, and kept going. "Come on, come on, come on," she whispered, over and over, the way you'd talk to a stalled car. Her hands shook so badly the tiny bolt skittered across the concrete and rolled under someone else's shelving. She dropped flat, cheek against the cold floor, sweeping her arm through dust and spiderwebs. Her phone lit up: 4:52. She laughed once, a cracked sound, wiped her eyes with a black-stained wrist, and reached farther into the dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's plastic roof, and I check my phone again, though the screen hasn't changed in ninety seconds: 8:52. The interview is at nine, across the river. I step out to the curb and lean into the road, squinting up the street, then step back when the wind flings grit against my teeth. My good shirt is already damp at the shoulders. I've pressed the crosswalk button four times, which does nothing, I know it does nothing. A man beside me folds his newspaper and I hear myself ask him, too loud, whether the 14 is always this late. He shrugs. My knee won't stop bouncing. I count the coins in my palm, then the bills, then the coins again, as if the sum might grow enough for a cab. Thunder rolls. I pull my folder against my chest to shield the résumé, and whisper, 'Please, please, just come,' to an empty street.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid is already on the floor and I've gone through the third stack twice. My knees ache against the attic boards, but I don't get up. Rubber bands snap in my fingers, brittle as dry noodles, and I tear envelopes along the edges because slitting them neatly takes too long. "Come on," I whisper, then louder, "Come on, Dad, where is it." Somewhere in here is the letter with the address, the one name that might lead to the lawyer, to the deed, to the house they'll take on Friday. My hands shake so badly that a page slips and I snatch at it as though it might run. Dust coats my tongue. I check the postmarks, 1987, 1991, 1974, shove them aside, and reach for the next bundle before I've finished breathing out. The light through the window is going orange. I don't turn on the lamp. I just keep reading faster, lips moving, skipping whole lines, not stopping.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta was already halfway across Mr. Okafor's lawn before he'd finished opening the screen door, her slippers soaked through, a dish towel still clenched in one fist. "Your ladder. The tall one. Please." Her voice came out thin and too fast, and she heard herself start over. "Please, I'll bring it right back, tonight, I swear." Behind her, the rain drummed on the roof of her house, and a dark stain the size of a dinner plate was spreading across her bedroom ceiling. She kept glancing at it over her shoulder, as if it might grow while she stood talking. Her jaw ached from clenching. "I called three roofers," she said, laughing at nothing, a dry little sound. "Nobody comes. Nobody." Mr. Okafor hesitated, scratching his neck, and Marta's hands rose without her permission, palms open, trembling. "I'll hold it myself. I don't care about the wet. Just tell me where it is."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The doorbell isn't due for twelve minutes, and the lamb is still pink at the bone. I open the oven, close it, open it again, as if staring harder will cook it. Steam fogs my glasses; I wipe them with a wrist that smells of garlic and come away with grease across my cheek. "Come on, come on," I whisper to the pot of rice, which has gone gluey anyway. My shirt clings between my shoulder blades. I've burned my thumb twice and don't remember either time. I crank the oven fifty degrees hotter, knowing it's wrong. Phone in hand, I type "how to fix" and can't finish the sentence. Out in the hall, Dana's favorite wine sits unopened, and I hear myself laugh, thin and high, saying to nobody, "It's fine. It's totally fine," while I slice the lamb open again and stare at the red.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter at 2:14 a.m., and I'm across the room before the second ring, knocking a stack of unopened envelopes onto the floor. Unknown number. Area code I don't recognize. My thumb slips on the screen twice, slick with sweat, and my heart is going so hard I can feel it in my teeth. "Hello? Yes, this is him, this is Daniel, I'm here, I'm here." My voice cracks and I hate it. I'm gripping the counter edge with my free hand, knuckles pale. Please be the hospital. Please be the lender. Please be anyone with a number and a yes. I haven't eaten since yesterday, and I realize I'm pacing the same four tiles, back and forth. "Sorry, can you say that again? Please, don't hang up. I'll do whatever it takes. Just tell me what you need me to do."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I reached the circulation desk four minutes before closing, the book pressed against my chest with both arms like it might escape. My shirt stuck to my back. "It's, um, it's overdue," I said, too fast, and then laughed at nothing. The librarian blinked at the cracked spine, the coffee ring I'd put on the cover in March. "I can pay it. I have forty dollars. I have, wait." I dumped my backpack on the counter, and coins skittered across the wood, a granola bar, a dead pen. My hands wouldn't stop shaking, so I flattened them on the desk. Eight months. The hold on my transcript, the graduation form due tomorrow. "Please," I said, and my voice cracked on it. "Whatever it costs. Tell me what I can do. I'll shelve things. I'll stay all night." Behind me the lights clicked off, one row at a time, and I didn't turn around.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta carried the last box up four flights without stopping, though her arms shook and her breath came in ragged pulls. The landlord's key stuck, and she jiggled it, then slammed her palm against the door, whispering, "Come on, come on, please." Inside, the room smelled of old paint and somebody else's cooking. One window. A mattress-sized floor. She didn't look at the stained ceiling; she went straight to the outlet and plugged in her phone, watching the screen until the battery icon blinked. Her stomach clenched around nothing, since she hadn't eaten since yesterday. She counted the bills in her coat pocket twice, then a third time, lips moving, and the number stayed the same. When the neighbor knocked to say hello, Marta opened the door only a crack and said too quickly, "I'll pay on time, I promise, I'll be no trouble." Then she sat on the floor against the wall, still wearing her coat, and listened to the pipes, afraid to unpack anything she might have to carry out again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the slats of the bench, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and Marisol stopped so fast her shoes skidded in the gravel. She looked left, then right, at the empty path and the pigeons pecking at nothing. Her hands were already shaking when she lifted it. Forty dollars. Sixty. She counted twice, lips moving, then a third time, as if the bills might multiply. Her stomach folded in on itself; she hadn't eaten since yesterday's crackers. In her pocket the eviction notice crinkled against her thigh. "Just look at the license," she whispered, her voice cracking on the last word. "Just look." A photo of a smiling old man stared up at her. She pressed the wallet against her chest, swallowed hard against the dryness in her throat, and heard footsteps somewhere behind her. Her heart slammed. She didn't turn around. She didn't put it down, either.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The lifeguard has stopped looking up when I come in, which is how I know it's been too many Tuesdays. Thirty-eight years old, goggles cinched so tight they leave red rings, and I still grip the gutter like it owes me something. 'Again,' I tell myself out loud, and the water slaps back at my voice. My daughter's recital is in August. Her school trip to the lake is in June. I push off the wall, kick, and my legs fold into a sinking hinge, chlorine burning up my nose, heart hammering against my ribs. I come up coughing, hair in my mouth, and grab the wall again before I've even finished the cough. 'One more. Please, one more,' I say to no one, to the tiled blue. My fingers are wrinkled white. The clock says closing in four minutes. I don't climb out. I let go of the wall, and I kick like I'm trying to outrun the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta knelt in the clay at dusk with the seed packets fanned across her thighs, the last of the grocery money gone into them. Her knees were already wet through. She read the back of the tomato packet for the fourth time, lips moving, then tore it open too fast and watched half the seeds scatter into the grass. "No. No, no, no." She crawled after them, pinching each one out of the blades, dirt packing under her nails. The rows she'd dug were crooked and shallow, and she dug them deeper with her bare hands, breath ragged, sweat stinging her eyes though the air had gone cold. Her phone showed eleven dollars in the account and a video paused on how to thin carrots. Behind her, the kitchen window glowed over an empty table. She pressed the soil flat over the seeds, then pressed again, harder, as if it might hold them to their promise. "Please," she whispered to the dark, uneven bed. "Just come up. Just please come up."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus kept his laptop open on his knees, refreshing the same email for the fourth time, while Dana clicked to her third slide. Her voice was bright and easy. Her numbers were his numbers, rearranged, the chart colors swapped. He had sent her that spreadsheet last Tuesday. His shirt stuck to his back despite the cold conference room, and his thumbnail had split the skin along his index finger. When the director nodded and said, "This is exactly what we need," Marcus's hand shot up before he'd decided anything. "Sorry, just—" His voice cracked and came out too loud. Every head turned. "The, um, the retention model. On slide three. I built the first version of that. In March." Nobody spoke. Dana smiled at him, patient. The projector fan whirred. He gripped the edge of the table, knuckles pale, and heard himself say, "Please. Can I just show you the original file?" His laptop was already turned toward them, trembling slightly on his palms.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The fuel light had been on since the exit for Carlisle, and Marta kept her foot feather-light on the pedal, coasting down every slope as if the car might forgive her for it. Her phone, wedged against the vent, showed 11% and a hospital's number she had already called three times. 'Pick up,' she whispered, then louder, 'Please, please, just pick up.' Her thumbnail was bitten to the quick, and she tasted blood without remembering doing it. The highway was black and empty, every gas station dark behind its chained pumps. She did the math aloud, forty miles, maybe thirty-five, her voice cracking on the numbers. When the engine coughed, she slapped the dashboard with her whole palm, then pressed her forehead to the wheel for one second, two, and shoved her foot down again. 'Not now. Not now. I'll walk. I'll crawl.' Her hands slicked the steering wheel. The ringtone finally cut off into a voicemail beep, and she began talking before it finished.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine ate my last dollar, and I stood there pressing the return button until my thumb went white. Down the hall, Grandpa's monitor kept up its slow beeping. I'd already asked the nurse three times if the new doctor had come, and she'd stopped looking up. In his room I pulled the chair so close its legs scraped, and took his hand, cold, papery, too light. "Grandpa, it's Danny. You said you'd teach me the boat thing. The knots." My voice cracked and I laughed at it, badly. I kept talking, faster, about the lake, the dock, the stupid orange cooler, anything, because when I stopped, the machines got louder. My knees bounced. My phone was open to a search I'd read twice already. When the door clicked, I was on my feet before I knew it, blocking the doorway, saying, "Please. Tell me something I can do."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell hasn't rung yet and I'm already pressed against the iron fence, fingers hooked through the bars, the cold printing lines into my palms. My phone is in my other hand, the screen showing a bank balance I've refreshed eleven times as if it might change. Another mother glances at me and I smile too wide, too fast. 'Sorry, is this where the line for the front door starts?' I ask, though I've stood here for three years. My knee won't stop bouncing. In my coat pocket is the eviction notice, folded small, and I keep touching its corner like a bruise. When the doors burst open, I'm up on my toes, scanning, and my throat tightens until I can barely swallow. There she is, backpack bigger than her. 'Hi, baby,' I say, voice cracking, and I hold her so long she squirms. 'Mama, you're squeezing.' I let go. I don't know where we're sleeping Friday.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By seven a.m. Marta had dragged the oak dresser to the very edge of the curb, where the passing cars could see it, and now she stood beside it with her arms wrapped around her ribs, though the morning was warm. A man in a faded cap ran his thumb along the drawer. "Forty," he said. "Thirty-five," she answered before he'd finished, then, "Thirty. Take it. Take the lamp too, no charge." Her voice cracked on the last word, and she coughed to cover it. The eviction notice was folded small in her back pocket, and she kept touching it through the denim. When he hesitated, she was already lifting one end of the dresser, her knuckles white, her heart knocking against her throat. "I'll carry it to your truck," she said. "Please. Where's your truck?" Behind her, the dining table sat with its price tag crossed out three times, each number smaller, the ink pressed so hard it had torn the paper.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta had both palms clamped around the pipe under the sink, and the water still found a way, spitting between her fingers and running down her wrists into her sleeves. It was past midnight. The landlord's phone had gone to voicemail three times, and she'd stopped leaving messages after the second. "Come on, come on, come on," she whispered, wrapping a third strip of tape around the joint, then a fourth, though the first ones already hung limp and slick. Her knees ached against the tile, and her breath came short and fast. A towel lay sodden behind her; the cabinet floor had begun to bulge. She grabbed the wrench, dropped it, grabbed it again with shaking hands. When the knocking started from the neighbor below, muffled and insistent, she laughed once, a cracked sound, then pressed her forehead against the cold pipe and held on, as if holding were a plan.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had been on the counter since Tuesday, beside the shutoff notice and the pizza coupons, and Marisol now stood over it in her coat, keys still in her fist. She tore the flap with her thumb, too fast, and sliced a thin line into her skin without noticing. Her eyes skipped the greeting and hunted for one word. "Please," she whispered to the kitchen, "please, please, just approved." The page shook so badly the print blurred, and she pinned it flat against the refrigerator with her palm. The fridge hummed, empty except for mustard. Her stomach folded. She read the first line twice, then a third time, lips moving, and her knees gave until she sat on the linoleum with the paper in her lap. "Okay. Okay, okay." She dialed the number at the bottom before she finished the paragraph, and when the recording began, she pressed the phone to her ear and did not breathe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The phone died at the taxi rank, somewhere between the third screenshot of the hotel address and the fourth stranger who shook his head at me. Rain slid down my collar. I held the paper out again, my thumb smearing the ink, and said "Please, please, this street, do you know," louder each time, as if volume were a language. A woman in a green coat glanced at the paper, said something quick and kind, and pointed two directions at once. I nodded hard, too hard, and thanked her four times. Then I stood there with the suitcase wheels jammed in a gutter and my heart knocking against my ribs. Every sign looked like a locked door. My mouth was dry, my hands wouldn't stay still, and I caught myself whispering my daughter's name, the only word anyone here might have understood. I grabbed the next sleeve I saw. "Help," I said. "Anyone. Help me."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the fence with the vet's folded estimate crushed in her fist, the paper gone soft and damp. Out in the long grass Biscuit chased a crow that never quite lifted off, his hind leg hitching every third stride. She counted the hitches under her breath. Her thumbnail had worn a raw crescent into her index finger. "Good boy," she called, too loud, her voice cracking up at the end, and he turned and flashed his tongue at her. She laughed, then pressed her knuckles to her mouth until it stopped. Her phone buzzed in her pocket for the third time; she didn't look. Instead she was already doing the arithmetic again, the car's value, the ring in the drawer, whom she could still ask. The sun was low and gold on his back. She hadn't eaten since yesterday and her knees shook. "Come here," she whispered, and when he finally bounded over she dropped to the dirt and held on far too tightly.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and cold coffee, and I'm on my ninth run through the same eight bars. Saturday is three days away. My fingers keep slipping on the B-flat, and each time I slap the piano lid and start over without letting the sound die. "Again," I tell the empty folding chairs. "Again." My shirt is stuck to my back. Mrs. Okafor pokes her head in to say the lights need turning off, and I nod and keep playing until she's gone, then I prop the sheet music on my knee and drag the metronome faster than I can manage, because slow hasn't worked. My throat is tight and my hands shake. I've already told everyone my sister is coming, and the whole town, it feels like, is coming too. I check my phone: 9:47. I play the B-flat again. Wrong. I bite my knuckle, hard, and again I whisper, "Please, just once, just once," and start from the top.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The dumpster was already half full when I found myself pulling Marcus's coffee cans of screws back out of it, one by one, and lining them on the bench. His sister would arrive at noon with the truck. It was ten past eleven. I dumped a can and sorted by thread, my fingers shaking so badly the washers skittered off onto the sawdust floor, and I dropped to my knees to chase them. "Just one more drawer," I said aloud, to nobody, to the lathe. My throat was tight and dry. I opened the drawer and found his pencil, chewed flat at the end, and I shoved it in my shirt pocket, then a level, then the apron off the hook, until my arms ached with the weight. Dust stuck to my wet face. Somewhere outside a engine rumbled. I grabbed the nearest chisel and held it against my chest, and I kept working, faster, the bench still not empty enough, or full enough, I couldn't tell which.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: At 11:58 Marisol had already refreshed the portal forty times, and the page still showed the same gray banner: Results will be available at noon. She sat on the edge of her desk chair with her knees bouncing so hard the mug beside her trembled. Her thumbnail was bitten down to pink skin. "Come on, come on," she whispered, then laughed at herself, a thin cracked sound. Her mouth tasted like pennies. She pressed her palms against her stomach, as if she could hold something in. If she failed, there was no second sitting, no scholarship, no bus ticket out of this town. She crossed her fingers, uncrossed them, crossed them again. The clock flipped to 12:00. Nothing. She hit refresh, hit it again, and again, her breath coming shallow and fast, whispering "please, please, please" to a blank screen while her mother's voice called her to lunch and she didn't answer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The orange blazes had stopped two switchbacks ago, and I kept walking anyway, because stopping meant admitting it. My phone read 4% and no bars; I held it up toward the sky like an offering, turned in a circle, and whispered, "Come on, come on, please." The pines were going black at the edges. I broke into a jog, pack slamming against my spine, and my ankle rolled on a root. I swore, kept going, limping, breath sawing in my throat. My hands shook so badly I dropped the water bottle and left it. Somewhere a branch cracked and I shouted "Hello?" too loud, too high, then listened so hard my ears rang. Nothing. The trail forked into two faint scars of dirt. I stood there, mouth dry, picking one, un-picking it, and then I ran down the left one, calling my sister's name into the dark as though she could hear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The third loaf sits flat as a plate, and I'm already cracking more eggs into the bowl with shaking hands. Nonna's card is soft as cloth, the ink gone brown, and "flour enough" is all it says about the flour. Enough for what? I dump in another cup, then another, my forearms burning as I knead past midnight. Flour streaks my wet cheeks. "Come on," I whisper to the dough, then louder, "Come on, please," pressing my palms into it like it's a chest I could restart. The kitchen smells wrong, nothing like her Sundays. My phone lights up with Mom's name and I let it buzz itself off the counter. I can't answer. If I ask, I'll learn nobody wrote the rest down. I tear off a pinch, taste the raw dough, and swallow around the lump in my throat. Then I reach for the yeast again. Four packets left. The oven ticks, waiting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was holding a basket with only a box of saltines and a dented can of soup when he heard his name over the cereal aisle. Dana Whitfield, from senior chemistry, pushing a cart heaped with groceries. He turned the basket so the saltines faced his hip. "Dana! Wow. Hey. You look great, you look so, wow."
