text: Marta stood at the edge of the field with the leash coiled in her fist, and she couldn't remember walking here. The grass looked yellow, then she blinked and it seemed greener. Biscuit tore across it in wide loops, ears flapping, and she followed him with her eyes a beat too late, as if he were a film out of sync with its sound. She turned to check the gate behind her. Was it the same gate? The bench by the path sat too far left. "Biscuit," she called, and her voice came out thin and questioning, like she was trying out a stranger's name. He didn't stop. She pressed her palm to her sternum, felt the floor of her stomach tilt, and crouched, fingers sinking into cool dirt. The smell of cut hay. A crow. She said aloud, slowly, "Tuesday. The park on Alder. Tuesday," and waited for the words to hold her up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: I set my cello case down by the fellowship hall's folding chairs, then picked it up again, then set it down in the same spot. The piano was on the wrong side of the room. Or I was facing the wrong way. "Is the stage always left?" I asked Marguerite, and she laughed, so I laughed too, a beat late. My bow hand tingled. I opened the folder and the notes slid sideways, black beads on a wire I couldn't follow. Measure twelve, she said. I turned a page, then turned it back. The fluorescent hum seemed to come from the floor. When we started, I played an entire phrase before noticing everyone else had stopped. "Sorry," I said, too loudly. "Where are we?" Marguerite pointed at my music, gently, the way you steer a child. I pressed my sweaty palm against the cool wood of the cello's neck and tried to find the floor with my feet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta picked up a coping saw, set it down, then picked up the same saw again and carried it to a cardboard box marked KEEP before remembering she hadn't made a box marked anything. The sawdust smell was exactly his, and her knees seemed to know it before she did; she gripped the edge of the bench. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, and then, "Okay, Walt?" to the empty room, and laughed once, a short cough of a sound. She opened a drawer of screws sorted by size, closed it, opened the one beneath. Same screws. The radio on the shelf felt warm, or she imagined it did. She stood holding a pencil stub with his teeth marks in it, trying to recall why she had come in, which door she had used, whether the light through the window was morning or late afternoon. Her coffee sat cold on the vise. She did not remember bringing it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Marisol had been standing in front of the department corkboard for what felt like ten minutes, though the clock above the stairwell said four. She read the same laminated notice about parking permits twice, then a third time, her lips moving. The hallway tilted slightly when she turned, and she put a palm flat against the cool cinderblock. "Sorry," she said to a boy who hadn't bumped her. Her backpack was on one shoulder, then the other, then on the floor, and she couldn't recall unzipping it. A water bottle was in her hand, empty. Somewhere a door banged and she flinched, scanning for the room number she'd walked past a moment ago, or an hour. Her phone buzzed; she stared at it, thumb hovering, unable to remember her passcode. "Okay," she whispered. "Okay. Where am I standing?" The corkboard stayed blank, its pushpins bright as little eyes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Mara stopped where the trail split around a lichen-spotted boulder and turned a slow circle, her trekking poles dangling from her wrists. She had passed this rock. Hadn't she? The pines leaned in, all the same dark shape now, and the orange blaze she'd been following seemed to have slipped off the trunks entirely. She pulled out her phone, stared at the blank gray map, and pushed it back into her pocket without remembering to lock it. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, then again, quieter, "okay." Her pulse ticked in her ears. She took three steps left, retreated, took four steps right, and crouched to touch the dirt as though the ground might explain itself. A cold wind slid down her collar. Behind her, the ridge she'd sworn was west sat glowing pink in the east. She laughed once, a dry little sound, and tried to remember which way her feet had been pointing when she'd last felt sure of anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is stained yellow, and Grandma's slanted handwriting says "flour, enough." I read it three times. Enough of what? I stand in my kitchen holding the measuring cup, but the room tilts a little, as if I've walked into someone else's house. I open the wrong cupboard, then the right one, then the first one again. "Okay," I say aloud, too loudly, to nobody. Flour puffs up my sleeve. I add water, stop, wonder if I already did, and dip a finger in the bowl as though it could tell me. The dough sticks to my knuckles. My hands remember something my head doesn't, folding, pressing, turning, and I watch them like they belong to her. The oven clock says 4:10. Was it 4:10 when I started? I laugh, thin and strange, and lean on the counter until the floor feels like a floor. "Pinch of salt," I whisper. "Whose pinch?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding two lemons and reading the back of a cereal box I didn't want when someone said, "Marcus? Marcus Delaney?" The fluorescent lights hummed louder than they had a second ago. A woman with short gray-streaked hair was smiling at me, and her face kept sliding between a stranger's and a girl in a yellow raincoat from Mr. Holt's chemistry class. "Priya," I said, too fast, then again, slower, like testing ice. My palm was sweating around the lemons. "You're here. In Dayton." She laughed. I nodded at the wrong moment. The aisle seemed to tilt toward the freezers, and I put the cereal box in my basket, took it out, then set it on the wrong shelf. "Twenty years," she said. I counted on my fingers against my thigh and got a different number. "Right," I said. "Wow. I came in for... milk?" I looked down. Lemons. I kept holding them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The register drawer is open and I'm holding a twenty, but I can't remember whose it is. The woman in front of me waits, her cart full of canned yams and a single foil turkey pan. "Sorry," I say, then say it again, slower, like the word might fix something. The fluorescent hum seems to come from the floor. I look at the clock: 8:52. Or 7:52? I count the lanes, all dark except mine, and count them again. My hands scan the cranberry sauce twice. "That's two," she says gently. "Right. Two." I press void, and the screen asks me something I read three times without the words holding still. Outside the glass doors, the parking lot is nearly empty and the lamps look too orange. I can't tell whether I've been here six hours or one long minute. "Happy Thanksgiving," I tell her, and she laughs, because I've already said it, and I'm handing her the receipt upside down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The gate number on my boarding pass says C14, but the sign above me says C14 points left, and the sign past the pillar says C14 points left too, and still I turn right. My carry-on wheel squeaks behind me like it's asking a question. I stop at a coffee kiosk and stare at the menu as though it might be a map. 'Sorry, which way is... where are the gates?' I ask the barista, and my voice comes out too loud, then too quiet. He points the way I just came from. The floor tiles slide a little under my sneakers. I check my watch, then my phone, then my watch again, and the numbers don't agree with each other, or maybe they do and I can't hold them. Forty minutes. Or fourteen? My heart is knocking against my ribs. I read the screen overhead: Denver, Dubai, Detroit. The letters swim, settle, swim. I grip the handle, whisper 'left, left, left,' and walk, and nothing around me looks like anywhere I've been.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the same window frame twice before she noticed the blue tape was already there. She stood with the roller dripping onto her sock, looking at the wall, then the door, then the wall again, trying to remember which one she'd started with. The pale green looked wrong now, or the room did. Where had the bookshelf been? She pressed her palm flat to the damp patch and felt the cool paint grip her skin. 'Okay,' she said aloud, then again, quieter, 'okay,' as if someone might answer. The ladder was on the wrong side of the bed. Or the bed was on the wrong side of the ladder. She set the roller in the tray, picked it up, set it down. Her ears hummed. Down the hall the kitchen clock ticked, and she walked toward it, one hand trailing along the wall, leaving a long green smear she didn't stop to wipe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap shakes the boards and I stand up, then sit down again, unsure why I stood. My mug is in my hand. It's empty, or maybe I never filled it. I turn it over anyway. Rain slants under the roof and spots my knees, and I watch the wet spread as if it belongs to someone else's legs. "Is this the front?" I ask the dog, who doesn't look up. The door behind me is blue. I thought it was green. I press my palm against the railing, and the cold grit of it steadies nothing. Was I waiting for someone? A car lights the road, and I count the seconds the wrong way, starting at the thunder instead of the flash. My watch says four, though the sky looks like nine at night. I laugh, short and thin, and say my own name out loud just to hear how it sounds in the weather.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tube had gone flat again, the third patch in a row, and Marisol sat on the overturned bucket watching the tiny bubbles rise from the same pinprick in the basin. Someone's radio played faintly from the far bay, a cheerful song she didn't recognize. She pressed her thumb against the tire lever until the skin whitened, then let it clatter onto the concrete and didn't pick it up. 'Fine,' she said to nobody, flat and quiet. The neighbor's tidy pegboard of outlined wrenches hung beside her own heap of tools on a sheet of cardboard. Her shoulders felt heavy, as if the jacket were wet. She wiped her black hands on her jeans, looked at the wheel, and thought about how many Saturdays this bike had eaten. Maybe she'd just leave it there on the stand, wheel off, and walk home. She turned off the work light, stood a moment in the dark, then turned it back on and did nothing else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the envelope in my hand, and I let them. It was the rejection letter, third this month, and the ink on my name was already blooming into a blue smear. The sky had gone the color of dishwater while I stood here, and the wind pushed a chip bag along the curb like it had somewhere to be. I should have moved under the shelter. I stayed on the painted line instead, shoulders slumped, rain sliding down the back of my collar, cold and almost welcome. A woman beside me asked if I knew when the 14 came. "No," I said, and it came out flat and small. "Doesn't matter much." She gave me a look and shifted her umbrella away. My phone buzzed in my pocket; I didn't check it. I watched the water pool around my shoes and thought about how heavy my feet felt, how the walk home would take no longer than the wait, and how neither one sounded worth doing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta dragged the shoebox out from under the bed and set it on her knees without opening the lid for a while. The afternoon light had gone gray against the window, and she didn't turn on the lamp. She lifted out the first envelope, read the return address, and put it down on the blanket. Then the next. Her shoulders sagged lower with each one, and she noticed she was breathing through her mouth. 'Well,' she said to the empty room, flat and quiet, 'that's that.' A letter from her sister slid half out of its sleeve; she pushed it back in with one finger, not reading it. Her tea sat cold on the nightstand, a skin wrinkling across the top. She meant to make three piles, keep, toss, maybe, but only the middle one grew, and her hands kept resting in her lap. After a while she closed the lid, slid the box back under the bed, and lay down in her shoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked while I was standing at the sink, still in yesterday's shirt, watching the tap drip into a bowl I'd meant to wash three days ago. "Got a ladder I could borrow?" he asked. I dried my hands slowly on my jeans. "Garage. Behind the bikes." My voice came out flat, like something read off a card. He thanked me twice and I nodded at the doormat. When he'd gone I didn't follow him out. The ladder had been Marcy's project, her gutters, her Saturdays, and I could hear it scrape across the concrete, each rung clanking as he dragged it. I sat down on the hallway stool with my coat half on. The gutters out back were still full of leaves. They'd been full since October. I stared at my shoes, laces trailing, and couldn't think of one reason to tie them. The kettle clicked off in the kitchen. I let it sit.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions had been sitting on the board for twenty minutes, and Marguerite had only just noticed she was holding the knife. She set it down, then picked it up again. Behind her the stockpot muttered to itself, unwatched. Her shoulders felt like wet towels hung to dry. The recipe card, propped against the flour tin, had a sauce stain on it from some earlier, better year, and she read the same line three times without it turning into anything. When the oven timer chirped, she stared at it until it stopped. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, flat as a plate. "Fine, fine." She dragged a chair to the counter and chopped sitting down, slow, each cut a small chore. Out the window the porch light had come on by itself. Seven o'clock. She wiped her hands on her apron, looked at the six place settings she had laid out that morning, and turned the burner down lower, as though that might slow the evening too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter, skittering toward the edge of a stack of unopened mail. A number I didn't know, area code from two states over. I watched it ring from the couch, a cold mug of tea balanced on my knee. Four rings. Five. Once, I would have jumped up, hopeful about who it might be. Now I just let my head tip back against the cushion and stared at the water stain on the ceiling. On the seventh ring I answered anyway, mostly so the noise would stop. "Yeah," I said, flat, barely moving my mouth. A bright voice asked if I had a minute to talk about my car's warranty. My shoulders sank another inch. "Sure," I said. "Go ahead." I didn't even reach for the lamp as the room darkened. I just listened to her talk, and let the tea go cold.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in the bottom of Mina's backpack since March, and now, in November, its corners had gone soft as cloth. She stood at the circulation desk under a flickering tube light and slid it across without lifting her eyes. "It's, um. Pretty late," she said, voice barely above the hum of the copier. The librarian scanned it, and the machine gave its small, cheerful beep. Mina watched the screen instead of her face. Forty-one dollars and sixty cents. She nodded, though nobody had asked her anything, and dug out her card with fingers that felt heavy and cold. Her shoulders stayed rounded even after she'd paid. "Thanks," she muttered, and didn't wait for the receipt. Outside, the wind pushed at her coat. She'd planned to browse the new shelves, maybe check out something else, but she walked past the doors, hands in her pockets, thinking it hardly mattered what she read anymore, and that the bus home would be slow anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at four, and the door clicked behind them with a sound too loud for the size of the room. I stood among the boxes with my coat still on. One window, facing a brick wall. I set the lamp on the floor because the outlet was there, and it lit nothing but my shoes. "Fine," I said to no one, and my voice came out flat and small. I opened the box marked KITCHEN, took out a single mug, and held it for a long while before setting it on the counter, which was the only surface. My shoulders felt heavy, as if the coat were wet. The radiator ticked. I sat on the mattress, still wrapped in plastic, and it crinkled under me. I meant to unpack the rest, truly, but I just watched the light on the brick go from gray to a darker gray, and didn't get up to turn on anything else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and I looked at it for a long while before I touched it. My coffee had gone cold an hour ago. I'd been sitting there since the lunch crowd thinned, watching pigeons argue over a pretzel, not really watching. My shoulders ached as if I'd carried something up a hill. I picked the wallet up and it felt heavier than it should. Inside: a license, forty dollars, a photo of a dog. Maria Delgado, born in March. I read the address twice. 'Well,' I said to nobody, my voice flat as the gravel path. 'Somebody's having a worse day.' I wasn't sure I believed it. I stood slowly, knees cracking, and the walk to the corner felt twice as long as it used to. I'd drop it at the station. Tomorrow, maybe. I sat back down and let the wind push the leaves around my shoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood in the shallow end long after the other adults had kicked off from the wall. The kickboard hung from her fingers, dripping onto the tile. Chlorine stung her nose. Her third lesson, and her feet still refused to leave the bottom; every time she tried, her legs sank like sandbags and her chin slapped the water. "Good effort," the instructor called, and she nodded without looking up. She watched a boy of maybe seven glide past her, barely making a ripple. Her shoulders ached, her goggles had left red rings around her eyes, and she pulled them off and held them in her lap on the bench. "I'll just watch for a bit," she said, quietly, to no one. The clock above the lifeguard chair ticked toward the hour. She wrapped the towel around herself twice, though she wasn't cold, and stayed there until the lane lines stopped moving.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marlene knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned beside her knee, their glossy tomatoes and zucchini looking like a joke. The soil was clumpier than the video had shown. She pressed a trowel in, hit a stone, and let the handle go. For a while she just watched a beetle cross the dirt. "Six inches apart," she read aloud, flat, then couldn't remember if that meant the beans or the carrots. Her shoulders ached already, and the sun on her neck felt heavier than it should. She dropped seeds in a crooked row without counting, pushed soil over them with the side of her hand, and didn't bother with the little labels. The hose sputtered when she turned it on. "Sure," she muttered to nobody. Back inside, she left her gloves on the step, caked and stiff, and sat at the kitchen table a long time with her boots still on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus sat at the far end of the conference table with his laptop closed, a cold coffee ringed on a napkin beside it. Up front, Dana clicked to a slide with a bright blue dashboard, the same layout he'd sketched in March and shown to nobody. Everyone nodded. Someone said, "Wow, that's clever." His shoulders sank an inch at a time until his chin nearly rested on his collarbone. He picked at the corner of the napkin, shredding it into small white curls. When Dana glanced his way and said, "Marcus helped a little early on," he lifted two fingers in a half wave and managed, "Yep." His voice came out flat and quiet. The projector fan hummed. He thought about the drive home, the empty hallway, the folder of old sketches he would not open. Around him people started clapping, and he clapped too, slowly, a beat behind everyone else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The traffic light on Alder Street turned red for no one, and Marcus stopped anyway, hands slipping down the steering wheel until his wrists rested at the bottom. The radio murmured something about tomorrow's weather; he reached over and turned it off, then sat in the hum of the engine. His tie was still knotted, tight against his throat, and he didn't loosen it. When the light went green he let two seconds pass before pressing the gas. At home the porch lamp would be on, the one Dana always left lit, and he found himself taking the long way, past the shuttered tire shop and the dark ballfield. His shoulders ached as if he'd carried something heavy all day, though he hadn't lifted a thing. "Well," he said aloud, to the windshield, and his voice came out flat and small. He waited for the rest of the sentence. Nothing came. He rolled past his own street, let the blinker tick twice, and turned in late, the headlights sweeping over the garage door like they were tired too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus held the vending machine coffee for ten minutes before he realized he hadn't sipped it. The elevator took forever, and he didn't press the button again. In room 412, his uncle's hand lay on the blanket like something set down and forgotten. "Hey, Tío," he said, too quietly, and pulled the vinyl chair back with a screech that made him wince. The television murmured a game show nobody watched. He told the old man about the traffic, then about the weather, then ran out. His shoulders sagged into the chair until his chin nearly touched his chest. The monitor beeped its same small number. When the nurse asked if he needed anything, he shook his head, though his throat felt packed with wet sand. He checked his phone, put it away, checked it again. "I'll come Thursday," he said, and wondered if the words were true, or only something to say while his legs refused to stand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I stay in the car until the bell, engine off, forehead resting on the steering wheel's cool curve. Other parents drift toward the fence in clusters, laughing about a bake sale. I get out late and stand at the edge, hands jammed in my coat pockets, the phone in one of them buzzing with an email I already know the contents of. A woman asks if I'm doing the fundraiser. "Probably not," I say, too quietly, and she says what? and I just shake my head. My shoulders feel weighted, like I'm wearing wet wool. The kids burst out in bright coats, and I keep my eyes on the gravel until Mia's sneakers appear in front of mine. "Good day?" I ask. She talks about a hamster. I nod at the wrong places. On the walk back I forget which row I parked in, and we circle the lot twice while she holds my sleeve.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By noon Marguerite had stopped straightening the price stickers. The oak dresser sat at the end of the driveway where she'd dragged it at seven, $40 in her careful handwriting, and a man in a windbreaker had just run his thumb along the drawer and walked off without a word. She lowered herself onto the arm of the sofa that nobody had sat on, and the cushion exhaled dust. Her coffee had gone cold hours ago; she drank it anyway. When a girl asked if the rocking chair was really five dollars, Marguerite said, "Take it for two," then, quieter, "Take it." Her shoulders ached from the lifting. Across the street, someone's radio played something cheerful, and she couldn't follow the tune. Thirty-one years of dinners had happened at that table. She picked at a loose thread on her sleeve, watched a car slow, then speed up again, and didn't bother standing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped off the fitting for the third time, and I just watched it clatter into the cabinet's dark corner. I didn't reach for it. Water kept beading at the joint, gathering, dropping into the pot I'd set there at breakfast, which was nearly full again. Plink. Plink. My knees ached against the wet particleboard, and my shoulders had folded forward without my deciding it. I wiped my hands on my jeans, slowly, though they were already soaked through. The video on my phone had restarted itself, a cheerful man saying this would take ten minutes. "Sure," I said to the empty kitchen, flat as the floor. It had been two hours. I thought about the plumber's number on the fridge and how I'd told myself I wouldn't need it. I emptied the pot, set it back, and sat on the tile with my back against the oven, listening it fill.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter through two reheated cups of coffee, its little window showing my name in that flat county typeface. I finally slit it with a butter knife because I couldn't find the scissors. The paper unfolded in three stiff pieces. I read the first line, then the second, then my eyes slid down to the word "denied" and stayed there. My shoulders sank until the chair creaked. "Okay," I said to the empty kitchen, quietly, like agreeing with a stranger. The refrigerator hummed. I folded the letter along its creases, exactly as it had come, and slid it back into the envelope as if that might undo something. Outside, a neighbor's car started and left. I carried my cup to the sink, forgot to rinse it, and stood there watching the cold coffee circle the drain, thinking I should call someone, and not moving to find my phone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed and emptied, and Marcus stood on the platform long after the crowd had flowed around him like water around a rock. Signs rose overhead, rows of hooked and looping characters he couldn't begin to sound out. He set his suitcase down, picked it up, set it down again. At the ticket counter he held out the folded printout of his hotel's address, and the woman behind the glass glanced at it, spoke rapidly, and pointed left, then right, then left. "Sorry," he said, barely above a whisper. "Sorry. Thank you." He nodded too many times. Outside, rain tapped the taxi stand's tin roof, and the line of drivers all seemed to look past him. He lowered himself onto his suitcase, shoulders folding inward, and watched the phone's map spin its small gray circle. His stomach growled; he ignored it. After a while he put the phone away, untouched, and stared at his wet shoes as if they might say something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: The tennis ball sat by my shoe for ten minutes before I noticed I'd stopped throwing it. Biscuit didn't mind. She tore across the wet grass in wide loops, ears flapping, and I watched her the way you watch traffic. My coffee had gone cold in the cup holder of my hands, and I kept lifting it anyway. A man walking past said, "She's having a great time," and I said, "Yeah," so quietly he probably didn't hear. The sky was the color of dishwater. My jacket felt heavy across my shoulders, like someone had hung a second one over it. When Biscuit came bounding back, tongue out, dropping herself against my shins, I put my hand on her head and left it there. I meant to say good girl. I only nodded. Then I sat down on the damp bench, though I'd told myself we'd leave by four, and it was nearly six.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The folding chairs in the church basement are still stacked against the wall when I set my cello case down, and I don't bother pulling any out. Four people were supposed to come tonight. Marguerite texted that her knee was acting up; the others didn't text at all. I tune anyway, slowly, the pegs squeaking, and play the opening of the Fauré into the empty room. My bow arm feels like it's full of wet sand. I flub the same shift in bar twelve, then again, and I don't go back to fix it. 'Fine,' I say to the radiator, which clanks. The sheet music has a coffee ring on it from last week, when I still penciled in reminders. I look at the poster taped crooked by the door: Spring Concert, All Welcome. I peel one corner back down, then let it curl up again. I pack the cello before the clock hits eight, and leave the lights on for no one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The box I'd labeled KEEP sat empty for an hour while the one marked TRASH overflowed. I held Danny's block plane, its sole worn to a shine by thirty years of his palm, and set it in the trash box, then took it out, then set it down again. Sawdust still lay in the vise's jaws. I didn't sweep it. My shoulders felt packed with wet sand, and every time I bent for something, the bending took a long while. The radio on the shelf was tuned to the station he liked, and I let it mutter, though I couldn't have told you one song. Marcus from next door leaned in the doorway and asked if I wanted help. "Sure," I said, flat, not looking up. "Whenever." He left. I sat on an overturned bucket with a coffee can of mismatched screws in my lap, sorting none of them, until the window went gray and the cold came up through my boots.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells of floor polish and old radiators, and I've been sitting against the wall outside Room 12 since eight. The noticeboard is still bare except for a fire drill notice. Other people pace or whisper; I just watch my shoelace, which I've retied twice without meaning to. My shoulders ache from slouching, and my tea has gone cold in its paper cup, a skin on top I don't bother breaking. When Priya asks if I want to grab lunch, I shrug and say, "Not really. Go ahead." My voice comes out flat, like it belongs to someone else. I keep replaying question four, the one where I wrote half a line and stared at the clock. The secretary finally arrives with a stapled sheet and a roll of tape, and everyone surges forward. I stay where I am, thumbs pressed into my knees. Whatever it says, I already know how the next few minutes will feel, so I let the crowd go first and count the ceiling tiles.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marit stopped at the switchback where the pines thinned and let her pack slide down one arm, then didn't bother with the other. The light had gone the color of weak tea. She'd meant to reach the ridge by four; her watch said ten past five, and she looked at it a long time, as if it might revise itself. Her boots scuffed the gravel in a flat, dragging rhythm. A thrush called somewhere, and she didn't turn her head. "Fine," she said to no one, her voice low and scraped. "Fine. Whatever." The summit sign she'd planned to stand beside again now seemed a stupid thing to want. Her shoulders ached where the straps had been. She sat on a cold rock, ate half a granola bar, and wrapped the rest back up. When the first star showed, she pulled her hood over her ears and started down, headlamp still in the pack, walking by feel.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth now, Grandma Ines's slanted handwriting gone brown at the folds. "Flour till it feels right," it says. I stand at the counter at four in the afternoon, still in yesterday's sweatshirt, and press my knuckles into the dough. It sticks to everything. I add flour, then more, then stop adding. My shoulders have been hanging by my ears for an hour, and I let the dough sit under the towel without really covering it. The kitchen is gray; I haven't turned on the light. When the timer I forgot to set doesn't go off, I just look at the oven. "Feels right," I say aloud, flat, to nobody. It doesn't feel like anything. I read the card again, though I know it by heart, and trace her loopy y with my thumb. Then I sit on the floor with my back against the cabinet and listen to the fridge hum, wondering if it's worth the bother of waiting for it to rise.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus stood in the cereal aisle holding a box he had no intention of buying, thumb pressing the cardboard until it dented. The fluorescent lights hummed. "Marcus? Marcus Bell?" Dana Okafor from senior year chemistry pushed a cart toward him, a toddler babbling in the seat, a ring catching the light. He lifted his eyes only as far as her collar. "Hey. Yeah. Wow." His voice came out flat and low, and he cleared his throat. She asked what he was up to these days. "Oh, you know. Around." He glanced at his wrinkled shirt, the single frozen dinner in his basket, and tugged his sleeve over his wrist. She talked about a house, a promotion, a reunion he should come to. He nodded at each pause, shoulders sinking an inch at a time. "Good to see you," he said, already turning. In the car he sat with the keys in his lap, engine off, watching the sliding doors open and close.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marguerite stood behind the counter straightening the same row of cough drops she had straightened twice already. Someone had taped a paper turkey to the register, its feathers curling at the edges. Her feet ached in a dull, heavy way, and she leaned her hip against the shelf instead of standing. The fluorescent light hummed. When the phone rang, she let it go four times before answering. "Hartley's," she said, flat, and listened to a man ask if they were open tomorrow. "No," she said. "Closed." She hung up and watched the parking lot, where a single cart rolled slowly sideways in the wind. Her coworkers' texts about pies and airports glowed on her phone, face down by the till. She didn't turn it over. At closing she counted the drawer, lost her place, and started again from the pennies, her breath fogging a little in the cold of the dark front windows.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta reached Gate B42 at 6:52 and found the jet bridge already pulled back, the window showing nothing but a tug and a wet gray apron. She stood there with her carry-on strap cutting into her shoulder, breathing hard, then not so hard. The agent said something about rebooking, tomorrow, maybe noon. "Okay," Marta said, barely louder than the gate's humming screen. "Sure. That's fine." She walked to a row of bolted seats and lowered herself into one without taking off her coat. Her phone said 4% and she watched it without plugging it in. Somewhere a cart beeped past, and a child laughed at something. She thought about her sister waiting at arrivals, the cake in the bag at her feet, the card she hadn't signed. Her sneakers were damp. She pulled her hood up, folded her arms over the bag, and stared at the carpet's repeating blue diamonds until the overhead lights clicked down to their night setting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pried the lid off the second can and stood there with the screwdriver hanging from her fingers. The color was called Morning Linen. In the store it had looked like something that might happen to her. Now, on the wall, it looked like the old yellow with a coat of dust. She dragged the roller through the tray anyway, slow, and laid one stripe up the plaster. Her shoulder ached after three passes, so she sat on the overturned bucket and stayed there. The radio on the windowsill was playing something upbeat; she reached over and turned it off. 'Fine,' she said to the empty room, flatly, the way you'd answer a cashier. A fly walked across the drop cloth. She watched it for a while. The tape along the baseboard had started to curl, and she didn't press it back down. Eventually she wiped her hands on her jeans, left the roller in the tray, and went to see what was in the fridge.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while I was still holding the envelope, and I didn't go inside. Rain slapped the porch rail, then the boards, then my shins, and I let it. The swing chain creaked under me, a sound I'd have oiled away last summer. My tea had gone cold hours ago; I kept lifting the mug anyway, setting it down untouched. Next door, Mrs. Alvarez dragged her cushions under cover and waved, and I raised two fingers about an inch off my knee. "Bad one," she called. "Yeah," I said, barely loud enough to reach myself. My shoulders had sagged so far forward my neck ached, and I couldn't summon the effort to sit up. Lightning lit the yard, the unmowed grass, the bike I'd meant to sell. I read the first line of the letter again, then folded it smaller, and smaller, until it was a hard little square I could hide in my fist. The gutters overflowed. I watched them do it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The wrench slips off the bolt for the fourth time and I hear my knuckles crack against the frame before I feel it. I don't swear. I just stand there, sucking air through my teeth, watching blood bead up beside old grease. Somebody's radio down the row is playing something cheerful, and I want to rip its cord out. The chain hangs from my fingers like a dead snake. Dae-ho's bike, the one he leaves with me every winter, the one he said he'd need by Saturday. It's Thursday. My hands are trembling so badly the tiny master link keeps skipping out of the pliers and pinging across the concrete. "Come on," I whisper, then again, louder, "come on." I get down on my knees under the fluorescent hum, patting the dusty floor, my breath short, my shirt stuck to my back. I find the link. I drop it again. I press my forehead against the cold seat tube and stay there, jaw clenched, counting the oil stains until my chest unknots enough to try once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over the shelter went the color of a bruise while I checked my phone for the fourth time in two minutes. 6:42. The 14 was supposed to come at 6:30. Wind flipped the schedule taped to the glass, and I pressed it flat with my thumb as though that would help. My hands wouldn't stay still; I zipped my jacket, unzipped it, zipped it again. The first fat drops hit the pavement, and my stomach dropped with them. 'Come on,' I said, too loud, to nobody, to the empty street. 'Come on, come on.' A woman glanced over and looked away. My throat was tight, my breath coming short and shallow, and I counted streetlights down the block just to have something to count. The interview started at seven. I rehearsed my first sentence under my breath and lost it halfway through. Rain drummed the plastic roof. I stepped out to look down the road, got soaked, and stepped back in, jaw clenched, fingers cold and shaking around the dead-weight phone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid slides off with a dry whisper, and I set it on the carpet, then pick it up again, then set it down. Forty minutes I've been at this and the pile marked KEEP is one envelope tall. My thumb keeps finding the same corner of a blue airmail letter, rubbing it soft. I read the first line of his handwriting and my throat tightens so hard I have to stand and open the window, though it's November and the draft makes my arms prickle. "Okay," I say to the empty room, too loudly. "Okay. Just sort." I sit again. My knee bounces. I tell myself the postmarks are only dates, only ink, and I count them aloud, 1987, 1988, until my voice cracks on 1991 and I press the letter flat against my sternum, as if it might stop the pounding there. The tea beside me has gone cold. I haven't touched it. I reach for the next envelope anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked twice, and the dish I was drying slid back into the sink. "Got a ladder I could borrow? Gutters." My eyes went past him to the garage, where the aluminum ladder hung on its hooks, the one Marcy used to hold steady while I swore at the leaves. "It's, uh. It's not really," I said, and my voice came out thin, wrong. My palms were slick against the dish towel. I twisted it into a rope. Dale waited, polite, his boots on my mat. "Sure," I said, then "no," then laughed at nothing. My chest felt packed with wet sand. I walked to the garage because standing there was worse, lifted the ladder with shaking arms, and it clanged against the doorframe, loud as a dropped pan. "Bring it back whenever," I managed. He thanked me. I shut the door and stood in the hall, breathing through my teeth, staring at the two empty hooks.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta had stirred the same pot of risotto for so long that the rice had begun to catch on the bottom, and she only noticed when the smell reached her. She swore under her breath, scraped at the crust, and glanced at the clock on the oven: 6:40. Her hands shook as she reached for the stock, and she sloshed some across the counter without wiping it. The chicken wasn't done. The table wasn't set. A single wine glass sat on the cloth, and she picked it up, put it down, picked it up again. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, to nobody. "Okay, okay." Her shirt clung damp between her shoulder blades. In the hall her phone buzzed, and she froze with the wooden spoon dripping, listening, unable to make her feet move toward it. Her jaw ached from clenching. She tasted the risotto, tasted nothing, and added salt anyway, then more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the counter at 11:47, and the dish towel drops from my hand. A string of digits, no name. I watch it crawl toward the edge of the sink, and I don't pick it up. Three rings. Four. My thumb hovers, shaking, and I press my other hand flat against my stomach like that will hold something in. Dad's hospital had my number. Dad's hospital would call at night. I answer, and my voice comes out thin, a croak I don't recognize. "Hello? Yes. Yes, this is she." The line crackles. Nobody speaks. I realize I've been holding my breath and my ears are ringing, and the kitchen tiles feel suddenly far too cold under my bare feet. "Please," I whisper, gripping the counter until my knuckles go pale, "just say something. Who is this?" Then a click, and the hum of dead air. I stand there, the tap still dripping, unable to put the phone down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Maya stood outside the library doors for a full minute, the paperback pressed flat against her ribs like she could still change her mind. Inside, the air smelled of carpet and toner, and her sneakers squeaked too loudly on the tile. The cover had curled at the corners over the months; she smoothed it twice, three times. At the desk her mouth went dry, and when the librarian looked up, she said, "I, um, it's, this is from last spring," and then laughed at nothing, a thin, cracked sound. Her hands wouldn't stay still. She slid the book across, then pulled it back to check the date slip, then pushed it forward again. "I can pay. I have forty dollars. Is forty enough? I can get more." Her ears burned. Somewhere behind her a cart rattled, and she flinched, certain everyone had turned to stare. The screen beeped, and she stopped breathing to read it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta set the last box down in the middle of the floor and it took up half the room. She stood there with her coat still on, jaw tight, counting the steps from door to window: four. The radiator clanked, and she flinched, then laughed at herself, a short dry sound that didn't last. Her hands wouldn't stay still; she peeled tape off a box, pressed it back, peeled it again. "It's fine," she told the empty room, too loudly, and her voice came back thin off the bare walls. She opened the fridge, found nothing to put in it, and shut it. Her chest felt packed as tight as the boxes. When she tried to unfold the bed frame, the screws slipped from her fingers and scattered under the radiator, and she sat down right there on the cold floorboards, staring at the small silver heads glinting out of reach, breathing through her teeth, her coat zipped to the chin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather curled at the corners, and Marguerite stopped so suddenly her coffee sloshed over her knuckles. She didn't feel the heat. She looked left, then right, at the empty path, the jogger already shrinking beyond the fountain. "Hello?" Her voice came out thin, cracked down the middle. She picked the wallet up with two fingers, as though it might go off, and her pulse thudded in her ears. Inside: a driver's license, a boy's school photo, forty dollars, a folded note in shaky handwriting. She read the note twice without taking in a word. Her thumb kept rubbing the edge of the card, back and forth, raw. "Okay. Okay," she muttered, pacing three steps one way, three steps back. Her stomach clenched hard. What if he was looking for it right now, retracing every street? She sat, stood again, and dialed the police with a hand that wouldn't hold still, the dial tone swallowing her breath.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood on the second step of the shallow end, water at her ribs, fingers locked around the steel rail until her knuckles went yellow-white. The chlorine smell sat thick in her throat. Across the pool, a girl of about eight kicked past in a blur of splashing, and Marguerite's gaze skidded away. "Just let go for a second," the instructor said, kindly, hands out. "Mm. Yes. In a minute," she answered, her voice thin and too high, and she laughed once, a dry sound that echoed off the tiles. Her heart thudded against the cold water like a fist on a door. She lowered her chin to the surface, then jerked it back up, breathing through her mouth in short, shallow sips. Her legs felt like they belonged to someone else, stiff and far away. She counted the blue tiles along the wall. Twelve. Thirteen. The rail stayed in her hand, and she did not step down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet says six inches apart, a quarter inch deep, and I've read it four times standing in the dirt. My trowel is still clean. I kneel, dig a hole, and it looks too wide, so I push the soil back and dig another beside it. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the car. Somewhere a neighbor's mower drones, and every pass sounds like someone who knows what they're doing. 'Okay,' I say aloud, too sharply, to nobody. I drop three tomato seeds in, then fish two back out with my fingernail because three feels greedy, then wrongly wasteful, then I just sit there. My knees are soaked through. The hose is coiled behind me, and I keep glancing at it, certain I'll drown everything or forget it entirely. I pat the soil flat, pat it again, and my hands won't stop shaking enough to stop patting. What if nothing comes up? I take a photo of the row so I'll remember where I failed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked to the next slide and Dana's voice kept going, smooth and certain, describing the dashboard he had sketched on a napkin three months ago. On the screen, his own wireframe sat under her name. He pressed his thumbnail into the pad of his finger until it whitened. The conference room was too cold, yet a bead of sweat slid down behind his ear. When Priya glanced over and asked, 'Marcus, didn't you look at something like this?' he heard himself say, 'Hm? Oh. Maybe. Sort of,' and the laugh that followed came out thin and wrong. He straightened his pen against the edge of his notebook, then again, then once more. His coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but he lifted it and drank anyway, just to have somewhere to put his face. Dana smiled at the director. Everyone nodded. His jaw ached, and he realized he had not swallowed in a long while.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta missed the exit and didn't turn around. The highway hummed beneath her, and the dashboard clock read 1:47, the green numbers swimming whenever she blinked. Her knuckles had gone pale on the wheel, and she kept peeling one hand off to wipe her palm on her coat, then clamping it back. "Okay," she said aloud, then again, "okay, okay," her voice thin and scraped. The phone buzzed in the cupholder. She flinched, didn't look. Every set of headlights behind her seemed to hold too long in the mirror. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth since the last town. At a red light with no cars anywhere, she sat through green, staring at the empty crosswalk, her breath coming short and shallow, until a horn somewhere far off made her jerk the car forward. She rolled the window down, let the cold slap her face, and whispered, "Just get home. Just get home," though she wasn't sure she wanted to go there at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol stood outside room 412 for a full minute, pressing the sanitizer pump until her palms were slick and stinging. Inside, the monitor beeped in a rhythm she found herself counting against her own pulse, which was faster. She sat on the vinyl chair, stood up, sat again. "You look good, Grandpa," she said, and her voice came out thin and too bright. His hand lay on the blanket, spotted and strangely small, and she reached for it, then pulled back, then took it anyway. Her jaw ached from clenching. When the nurse came in to check the IV, Marisol asked three questions in a row without waiting for answers, then laughed at nothing. The paper cup of coffee had gone cold in her fist, and she realized she had crushed the rim flat. She kept staring at the numbers on the screen, as if they might explain him, as if she could hold them steady by looking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The gate opens at 3:05, and by 3:09 the stream of backpacks has thinned to nothing, and Maya still isn't in it. I've checked my phone four times. The screen is cracked across the corner and my thumb keeps catching on it. "Excuse me," I say to a teacher, too loudly, then again, quieter, "she's in Ms. Okafor's class, red coat, braids?" The teacher says she'll check. My mouth is dry as chalk. I pace the same six feet of sidewalk, past the stroller, past the crossing guard's folded sign, my keys biting into my fist. Other parents laugh and drift away to their cars. Her pickup note was in my pocket this morning, wasn't it? I pat my jacket. My knees feel like water. Every door that swings open is not her. I'm already composing what I'll say to her father, and my voice in my head cracks halfway through. Then a red sleeve, a wave, and I realize I've been holding my breath for a full minute.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man in the windbreaker has been running his thumb along my mother's oak dresser for a full minute, and I've already said "It's forty" twice. "Thirty?" he says. I nod before I can think, then my hand shoots out and grips the drawer pull as if the thing might bolt. My tongue feels like felt. Behind him, the driveway glitters with the rest of her life on folding tables: the cracked teapot, the brass lamp, the quilt I keep refolding. "Sure," I say, too high, too fast. "Take it. It's fine." He pulls the top drawer, and the smell of lavender sachet drifts out, and my chest locks up like a fist. I stare at the price sticker curling in the sun. "Wait," I say, and he looks at me, and I can't find the next word. My eyes sting. I wipe my palms on my jeans, again, again. "Sorry. Sorry. Just... mind the corners."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta knelt in two inches of cold water, the flashlight clamped between her teeth, and wrapped the plumber's tape around the joint for the fourth time. Drops still crept out along the threads and fell onto her wrist. "No. No, no, come on," she whispered around the metal handle, then spat the flashlight onto the towel and let the beam roll across the floor. Her hands wouldn't stop shaking, so the wrench slipped, clanged against the cabinet, and she froze, listening for the sound of her sleeping daughter upstairs. Nothing. Her chest felt tight, her breath came short and quick. She wiped her palm on her wet pajama knee and looked at the clock on her phone: 2:47. The landlord's number sat open on the screen, unpressed. She pressed the wrench to the nut again and leaned her whole weight into it, jaw clenched, eyes stinging, counting the drips out loud until she lost the number and started over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been on the counter since Tuesday, propped against the toaster like it might leave on its own. Tonight I wash two plates that were already clean. Then I pick it up. The return address says Department of Revenue, and my thumb leaves a damp print on the window of the paper. I tear the flap too fast and slice the skin beside my nail, and I stand there sucking at it, tasting copper, reading nothing yet. "Okay," I say to the empty kitchen, then "okay" again, quieter. The fridge hums too loudly. I unfold the page and the words slide around, my own name floating in bold, a number with a dollar sign. My knees find the chair before I decide to sit. I read the first line four times. My heart is knocking against my collar. I laugh once, a dry little cough, and reach for the phone, then put it down, then pick it up again, and its screen shows my hand shaking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station board flickers into a wall of symbols I can't parse, and I stand under it with my suitcase handle slick in my palm. My phone says 4% battery. I show the taxi driver the hotel address, and he reads it, shakes his head, says something fast and flat, and points in three directions at once. "Please," I say, too loudly, then again, quieter, "please, just here, this street." My voice cracks on the last word. He shrugs and turns to another fare. The air smells of frying oil and rain, and the neon signs smear when I blink. I realize I've been tapping my thumb against my sternum, hard, as if to restart something. A woman brushes past, and I nearly grab her sleeve. Instead I laugh, one dry bark, and start walking nowhere, dragging the wheels over the wet stones, rereading the same unreadable sign until my eyes sting and the letters swim.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tears across the field after the tennis ball, ears flipping inside out, and I'm gripping the fence rail so hard the splinters bite my palm. I don't remember deciding to stand here. The vet's voicemail is still on my phone, forty seconds long, and I've played it three times since breakfast. "Just come in when you can," she said, in that careful voice. My jaw aches from clenching. Biscuit skids, rolls, pops up with grass on his muzzle, and I laugh, a short cracked sound that startles a crow off the post. Then I'm counting his breaths when he trots back, watching his ribs, his gait, the back left leg. He drops the ball at my boots. I pick it up and my hand shakes, so I pretend to wipe it on my jeans. "Good boy," I say, too quietly. "One more. Just one more." The wind smells like cut hay. I throw it badly, and don't look away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite had played the same eight bars of the Fauré six times, and six times her bow had skittered off the string at the same spot. The church hall smelled of floor wax and stale coffee, and the folding chairs stood in crooked rows, waiting for Saturday. She wiped her palm on her skirt, then wiped it again. "Once more," she said, too brightly, to nobody, since the pianist had gone to refill the kettle. Her left hand trembled against the neck of the cello, a fine buzz she could feel in her teeth. She started. At bar five her throat tightened and the note came out thin as paper. She stopped, pressed her forehead to the scroll, and breathed in through her nose, counting, losing count. Down the hall a door banged, and she flinched so hard the endpin squealed on the boards. "Fine," she whispered. "It's fine." She looked at the pencilled fingering, nearly illegible where she'd rubbed it out and rewritten it, and couldn't remember which version she'd chosen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus had labeled three boxes KEEP, DONATE, TRASH, and an hour later all three were empty. He held a coffee can of mismatched screws, tipping it one way, then the other, listening to them slide. "Nobody needs these," he said aloud, flatly, to the pegboard. Then he put the can on the KEEP side, took it back, put it down again. The sawdust smell had gotten into his throat, and he kept swallowing around it. Dale's pencil lay on the bench, chewed at the end, a line of half-finished measurements beside it in that cramped hand. Marcus's thumb pressed the numbers as if they might smudge. He stood up too fast and the stool clattered over. He left it there. His hands were shaking when he reached for the light switch, so he stopped, wiped them on his jeans twice, and sat back down on the cold concrete, the radio still murmuring the station Dale had left it on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and at 11:52 Marisol had already refreshed the page nine times. She sat on the edge of her desk chair, one knee bouncing hard enough to rattle the pen cup. Her tea had gone cold an hour ago; she lifted it anyway, grimaced, and set it down again. "It's fine," she told the empty room, her voice coming out thin and too quick. "It's one exam." Her thumbnail was already ragged, and she bit at it until it stung. The ceiling fan ticked with every turn. She wiped her damp palms on her jeans, then wiped them again. At 11:59 she stood, walked to the window, walked back, and stood again, her stomach folded tight under her ribs. The clock on the laptop flipped to 12:00. She stared at the spinning wheel on the screen, and her breath caught somewhere high in her chest and stayed there. She did not click. She could not seem to make her finger move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta checked her phone again, though the screen had said no service the last four times. The pines had gone from green to black while she wasn't looking. She walked faster, then stopped, because the cairn ahead was one she was sure she'd passed already, its top stone tilted just the same. "No," she said aloud, and then again, quieter, as if the trail might negotiate. Her pulse knocked in her ears. The straps of her pack bit into shoulders she couldn't unclench, and her mouth was so dry her tongue stuck when she tried to whistle for no reason at all. A branch cracked off to the left. She froze, breath held until her chest burned, then let it out in a shaky rush. She dug the headlamp from her pack and fumbled it twice, dropping it into the needles. Her fingers shook too hard to find the switch. "Come on, come on," she whispered, crouching in the last gray light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth at the folds, and Mara had read it so many times that the words had stopped being words. "Flour, enough," she muttered, then louder, to the empty kitchen: "Enough how? Enough *what*?" Her grandmother's slanted pencil said *knead till it feels right*. Mara's palms were slick, her pulse ticking in her throat. She pushed the dough, folded it, pushed again, and it clung to her knuckles in grey ropes. She added a fistful of flour, then another, then wiped her cheek and left a white streak there. The oven clock blinked 11:48 p.m. She had started at seven. Twice she picked up her phone, scrolled to the name at the top of her contacts, and set it face down on the counter without pressing anything. Her breath came short. She pressed her forehead to the cool cabinet, listened to the refrigerator hum, and whispered, "Just tell me how it's supposed to feel," before hauling the sticky mass back toward her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was holding a carton of eggs when he heard his name, bright and rising, from the end of the cereal aisle. Dana Whitlock, who had sat behind him in tenth-grade chemistry, was pushing a cart with a toddler in it and wearing a lanyard from some hospital. He tugged his hoodie sleeves over his knuckles. "Hey. Wow. Yeah, it's been, what, twelve years?" His voice came out too fast, and he laughed at nothing. She asked what he was doing now. His thumb pressed a dent into the carton lid. "Oh, between things. Figuring out the next move." The fluorescent lights hummed loud above him, and sweat prickled along his spine despite the freezer-section chill. He glanced at her cart, then at his basket: instant noodles, one banana. He shifted it behind his leg. "I should go, my ride's waiting," he said, though he had walked here, and he left the aisle with the eggs still in his hand, forgetting to put them back until he reached the registers.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy's fluorescent lights hum, and I keep wiping the same stretch of counter until the rag squeaks. Six o'clock, Christmas Eve, and the line curls past the greeting cards. My phone buzzes in my apron pocket for the third time; I don't look. Mrs. Alvarez slides her prescription across and I read the name twice, three times, the letters swimming. "Just a moment," I say, too bright, too fast. My jaw aches from clenching. In the back, I press my palms flat against the cold shelf and count the bottles, losing track at fourteen. Somewhere out there my sister is setting the table without me, and I told her I'd make it, I promised. Sweat pools under my collar. The register beeps, someone sighs loudly, and I realize I've been holding my breath since the last customer. "Sorry," I tell the empty hallway. "Sorry, sorry." Then I tuck my shaking hands under my arms and walk back out front, smiling.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The tram doors hissed open at Terminal C and Marguerite was already moving, her carry-on bouncing off her calves, one strap of her bag sliding down to the crook of her elbow. Her phone said 4:52. Boarding closed at 5:00. "Excuse me, sorry, excuse me," she kept saying, too quietly, so nobody moved. Her shirt clung to her spine. Gate 41, the board said, and the numbers on the pillars ahead read 12, 14, 16, which made no sense, which couldn't be right. She stopped, turned a full circle, and her breath came in short scraps that never seemed to reach the bottom of her chest. A man with a coffee drifted into her path and she nearly said something awful. Instead she pressed her palm flat against her sternum and counted gate numbers under her breath like a prayer. Her thumb left a wet print on the phone screen. 4:55. She ran, and the wheels of her suitcase screamed behind her across the tile.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller squeaks back and forth, and I keep going over the same square of wall until the yellow underneath is gone and then some. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since noon. Her pencil marks are still there by the window frame, little lines with dates, Mia at four, Mia at five, and I tape around them instead of painting over. Twice I put the brush down and pick it up again. "Just the walls," I say to the empty room, too loudly, and the word bounces off the bare floor. My hands are shaking enough that a grey drip lands on my sock, and I stand there watching it soak in. The fumes make my eyes sting, so that's what I tell myself it is. Somewhere downstairs the phone buzzes against the counter. I don't go. I dip the roller again, press hard, and breathe through my teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolls in and I'm already on the porch step, though the rain is blowing sideways onto my jeans. My phone is in my hand again. Still nothing. I thumb the screen awake, watch it dim, wake it again. "Pick up," I whisper, then louder, to the empty yard, "Just pick up, Dad." My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my teeth since the first drops. The porch swing creaks behind me, swaying on its own, and I snap my head around like someone's there. Nobody is. A bolt lights the maple across the road, and I count out loud, one, two, my voice cracking on three. My knee bounces so hard the boards hum. I pull my soaked sleeve over my knuckles and press it to my mouth. Every pair of headlights that swings past the mailbox makes me stand, and every one keeps going, and I sit back down, and stand again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marta had the rear wheel off and the chain hanging like a dead snake when she noticed the pegboard. Every tool had its outline drawn in marker, wrenches, pliers, the little hex keys, and her neighbor's outlines were all filled. Except one. Beside the tire lever she'd borrowed last week was a second outline, a child's size, and she didn't remember a child. She wiped her hands on her jeans three times. The fluorescent light buzzed, and she felt it in her back teeth. "Hello?" she said to the empty garage, too quietly, then cleared her throat and tried again. Nothing but the drip from the utility sink. She picked up the wrench, put it down, picked it up. The bolt wouldn't turn; her fingers shook against the cold metal. Behind her, a bicycle bell chimed once, softly. She did not turn around. She counted the spokes instead, out loud, and lost count at twenty-two.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Marlow Street went the color of a bruise while I counted the same four parked cars for the third time. Wind lifted the shelter's loose ad panel and let it slap back, slap back, and each time my shoulders jerked up toward my ears. I'd checked the timetable twice, then my phone, then the timetable again, as if the numbers might have rearranged themselves. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding it. "Come on," I muttered, too quietly for anyone, and then louder, "Come on." A man across the road folded his newspaper and left, and the first fat drops hit the pavement like thrown coins. I pulled my sleeves over my knuckles. My stomach felt hollow and tight at once. Every time headlights swung around the corner I stepped forward, then back, then forward, until my heel skidded on the wet curb and my heart hammered so hard I pressed my palm flat against my chest and kept it there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta had been humming while she lifted the shoebox lid, but the tune died somewhere around the third envelope. The handwriting was her father's, yet the name on the front wasn't her mother's. She read the first line, then set the page down and wiped her palm along her jeans as if it were dusty. The attic was hot, but her arms prickled. She picked the page up again. Dated 1987. Her birthday month. "No," she said aloud, flatly, to the rafters, and then, "No, that's just... a cousin." She counted the letters twice, got two different numbers, and started over. Her thumb kept pressing the same crease until the paper softened. Downstairs the kettle began to shriek, and she didn't move. When she finally stood, her knees cracked, and she realized she'd tucked one letter into her sleeve without deciding to. She shoved the lid back on the box, hard, and left the light on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Halloran stood on my porch at dusk, hands folded, smiling too evenly. "Need your tall ladder. The gutter by the upstairs window." I said sure, and my voice came out thin, like it belonged to someone down the street. The garage was cold. I wrapped my fingers around the rails and noticed they were damp. Last week he'd told everyone his wife left for her sister's, but her car was still in his driveway, dust gathering on the windshield. I carried the ladder out slowly, aluminum clanking against my knee. He reached for it and I didn't let go right away. "Which window?" I asked. "The back one," he said. "Why?" I shrugged, too fast. He took it, thanked me, and walked off with it balanced on his shoulder. I locked the door, checked it twice, then stood in the dark kitchen, listening to my pulse in my ears, not turning on a single light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions are already translucent when I realize I've stirred them for ten minutes without tasting anything. Six o'clock, the guests at seven, and I keep glancing at the phone face-down by the salt. It buzzed once an hour ago. I haven't turned it over. My knife slips through a carrot and I stop, staring at the neat orange coins as if someone else cut them. "Fine," I say aloud to the empty kitchen, too brightly. "Everything's fine." The oven ticks. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears, and I push them down, and they climb again. I wipe my palms on the dish towel, then wipe them again. Somewhere in the walls the pipes knock, and I flinch hard enough to rattle the lid on the pot. Four plates on the table. I count them twice, then pick up a fifth, the blue one, hold it, and set it back in the cupboard very quietly, as though it might wake.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The dishwasher was mid-cycle when my phone lit up on the counter, a string of digits I didn't know, and I realized I'd stopped scraping the pan. Water ran over my knuckles until it went cold. Four rings. Five. I wiped my hands on my jeans, missing the left one, and picked up without saying anything. Breathing. Slow, patient, someone in a quiet room. 'Hello?' My voice came out thinner than I wanted. Then, softly, a man said my name, my full name, the one I haven't used since I moved. I looked at the window over the sink and saw only my own reflection, the kitchen light behind me. My thumb found the red button and pressed it twice, three times. I checked the deadbolt. Then the back door, though I'd already checked it. The phone buzzed again in my palm, same number, and I set it face down on the table and stood there, listening to the dishwasher hum and my own pulse in my ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since sophomore year, and now I was a senior, standing at the return desk with its spine cracked and a coffee ring blooming on the cover. I set it down and slid it forward with two fingers, like it might bite. The librarian's pencil stopped. "Let me just pull up the date," she said, and the keyboard clicks sounded very loud. My palms were slick against my jeans. I kept reading the poster behind her, the same line about quiet, over and over, without taking in a word. "I can pay," I said, too fast, then again, quieter, "I can pay whatever it is." My stomach rolled when she turned the screen slightly toward me. Three years. I laughed, a short dry sound that didn't belong to me, and found I was gripping the counter's edge. Somebody's cart squeaked past. I swallowed and couldn't stop looking at the faded purple due-date stamp, from a year I barely recognized.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta set the last box down in the middle of the room and stood very still, listening. The radiator ticked. Somewhere above her, a chair dragged across the floor, then stopped, as if whoever sat there had also started listening. She opened the closet to hang her coat and found a row of small hooks at knee height, each one worn smooth. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, and her voice came back thin from the bare walls. She checked the lock, then checked it again, then wedged the desk chair beneath the knob. Her thumbnail worked at the skin of her index finger until it stung. The landlord had said the previous tenant left quickly. He hadn't said why. She sat on the mattress with her shoes on, shoulders up near her ears, and watched the gap beneath the bathroom door where the light, she was fairly sure, had been off a moment ago.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat dead center on the bench, squared to the slats like someone had set it down on purpose. I stopped ten feet away. Joggers kept passing, and a dog barked somewhere past the fountain, too loud. I wiped my palms on my jeans, twice. When I finally picked it up, the leather was still warm, and I dropped it. It landed open. A driver's license: my sister's face, the one from before she cut her hair. I crouched, my knees cracking, and my breath came short and shallow. 'No,' I said to nobody, then again, quieter, 'no, no.' The photo of me at nine was tucked behind her cards, creased soft. I looked up at the empty path, the swaying maples, every bench, every stranger's back. My fingers wouldn't close properly around it. I stood, turned in a slow circle, and realized I was whispering her name to the trees, the way you'd call a cat that had been gone all winter.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor said to let go of the wall, and Marguerite nodded, but her fingers stayed hooked over the tile lip like they belonged to someone else. Chlorine stung the back of her throat. Somewhere behind her a child shrieked and laughed, and she flinched at the sound as though it had been aimed at her. "I'm just adjusting," she said, too brightly, tugging her goggle strap a third time. Her heartbeat knocked against her ribs, loud enough that she wondered if the water carried it. The pool floor sloped away in a blue she did not trust. She counted the black lane lines, then counted them again. When the instructor's hand hovered near her back, she stiffened and said, "No, wait," in a voice thinner than she intended. Her knees felt unhinged. She kept thinking of her father's laugh on that dock, forty years ago, and the green cold closing over her head. She pushed off one inch, then clawed back to the wall, breathing hard, palms slick.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned in her lap, and the trowel's first bite into the soil turned up something pale and curled. She dropped it. Her hands wouldn't stop rubbing against her jeans. A worm, only a worm, she told herself aloud, flat and too quiet, and then again, quieter. The soil smelled of cold pennies and something older. Her neighbor's radio muttered over the fence, and every few seconds she glanced up at the back window of the house as if someone stood there. She read the packet's instructions three times without taking in a word. Spacing: six inches. She measured with her fingers, and they shook, so the row came out crooked. When she pushed the first bean under, her stomach tightened, and she covered it fast, patting hard, then paused, listening. Nothing. She stood, knees cracking, and walked to the porch without looking back at the dark rectangle. She locked the door and checked it twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide and I stopped breathing for a second. The diagram was mine. The same three-column layout, the same little arrows I'd redrawn four times last month, now under her name in the corner. My pen had been clicking against my thumb; I made it stop. "Great," I said when she asked for questions, but my voice came out flat and too quiet, and Marcus glanced over. The conference room air felt thick, the projector fan whirring louder than it should. I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and stared at the coffee ring on the table, tracing it with a fingernail. My stomach had gone tight and cold. Dana laughed at someone's joke about timelines. I laughed a beat late, then opened my laptop and scrolled through my sent folder, searching for the date I'd shared the file with her, checking it twice, then a third time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta turned the radio off at the second exit and then, a mile later, turned it back on, then off again. The highway was empty except for the amber blink of a stalled sign that read nothing. She checked the mirror. Nothing. She checked it again. Her thumbs had gone slick on the wheel, and she wiped one palm against her coat, then the other, never letting the car drift from the lane. "It's fine," she said aloud, too brightly, the way you talk to a dog at the vet. A pair of headlights had been behind her since the gas station, always the same distance back.
