Forty dollars, a library card, a driver's license of a grinning man named Delbert. Four addresses scrawled on a receipt, none matching. "Delbert," she muttered, jaw tight, "you absolute genius." She stood, left the coffee steaming on the bench, then snatched it back, because abandoning things was apparently the problem. Her shoulders crept toward her ears as she marched toward the ranger station, the wallet pinched by one corner like a dead mouse by its tail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: "Kick from the hips," the instructor says for the fourth time, and I nod so hard water slops into my goggles. I push off the wall. My legs, which have carried me through thirty-four years of stairs and airports, fold up like wet cardboard. By the second stroke my feet are sinking and my elbow has found the lane rope. I stand up in the shallow end, chlorine stinging my nose, and slap the water flat with my palm. A kid in a dinosaur swim cap stares at me. "Hips," I mutter. "Hips, hips, hips." I yank the goggle strap tighter, so tight my temples throb, and wade back to the wall with my jaw clenched. Someone's toddler floats past on a foam noodle, entirely relaxed. I breathe out through my teeth, long and slow, counting to five, and then I push off again anyway, because apparently I'm not finished being humiliated.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The packet said "plant after last frost," which told me nothing, so I'd stabbed seeds into the dirt on a Saturday and now, three weeks later, I was kneeling in the bed with a trowel, staring at a row of nothing. Nothing. My knees ached from the gravel. I dug up one seed to check it, found it fat and unchanged, and pressed it back with a long exhale through my nose. The tomato book lay splayed open beside me, pages gone wavy from the hose I'd dropped on it. "Sun six to eight hours," I read aloud, flatly, then looked at the maple shading half the yard. I stood, brushed soil off my jeans in hard slaps, and dragged the wheelbarrow three feet left. Then three feet back. A squirrel watched me from the fence, chewing something, probably my beans. "Go ahead," I told it. "Take them. Take all of it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked to the next slide and Dana said, "So, circling back," for the fourth time, though they had not yet left the first topic. Priya's pen had stopped writing twenty minutes ago; now it tapped the edge of her notebook in a steady, tiny rhythm. She pressed her tongue against her teeth and stared at the conference room's wall clock, where the second hand seemed to be wading through glue. The slide showed the same pie chart she had sent Dana in an email three weeks ago, with the same typo in the legend. "Great," she said, too evenly, when Dana asked if there were questions. Her jaw ached. She exhaled through her nose, long and slow, and pulled her laptop closer, opening a new document titled 'Things I Will Say In The Hallway.' Dana beamed and advanced to slide thirty-one. Priya reached for her cold coffee, drank it anyway, and kept her eyes on the typo.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The third orange barrel in a row blocked the on-ramp, and Marisol let her forehead drop against the steering wheel until the horn gave one short bleat. She lifted her head, exhaled hard through her nose, and swung the car around for the detour, the fourth one since midnight. "Of course," she told the empty passenger seat. "Of course it's closed. Why wouldn't it be." Her shoulders had crept up near her ears hours ago, and she rolled them without much hope. The GPS chirped a cheerful recalculation, and she jabbed the screen until it went dark. Streetlights ticked past, every one of them red when she reached it. At the fifth, she stopped fully, drummed her fingers on the dash, and said, flat and slow, "Nobody is coming. Nobody. Is coming." The light stayed red. She counted her breaths to ten, lost track at six, and finally rolled through it anyway, jaw tight, one eye twitching toward a house she'd been trying to reach since eleven.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus pressed the call button for the third time and stared at the ceiling tile above his grandfather's bed, counting the water stains. Down the hall a cart rattled past, and still no nurse. "Grandpa, leave the tubing alone," he said, in the flat, careful voice he used on his nephews, and he tugged the blanket back over the old man's feet for the fourth time. The vending machine had eaten his dollar. His jaw ached from clenching. "No, that's not the remote, that's the call button. Which I just pressed." He exhaled slowly through his nose, rubbed the bridge of it, and glanced at the clock. Only twelve minutes had passed since he'd last checked. Visiting hours ran until eight. His grandfather asked, brightly, whether he'd come far. Marcus laughed once, without any sound in it, and sat back down in the squeaking vinyl chair.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The gate was supposed to open at 3:05. My phone says 3:31, and I'm still standing on the same square of cracked pavement, holding a juice box I bought for a child who will, in all likelihood, refuse it. A man behind me laughs at something on his phone, and my jaw clicks sideways. I exhale through my nose, long and slow, the way the app told me to, and it does nothing. Bells ring. No children. The woman beside me says, "They're always late on Fridays," and I say, "Mm," so flatly it could be laid as flooring. I check the time again. Thirty-one. I count the fence slats. I rehearse what I'll say, then delete it, then rehearse a shorter, sharper version. When the door finally swings open and my daughter wanders out, shoelaces trailing, waving at a friend, I hold up the juice box like evidence and say, very evenly, "Hi. Shoes."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man turned the oak dresser's drawer out, in, out again, and I watched my own thumbnail whiten against the price sticker. Twelve dollars. I'd written it in marker, big, on a card he was currently holding. "Would you take four?" he asked. I breathed through my nose for a count of five. The sun had been on my neck since seven, and my coffee had gone cold and skinned over on the porch rail. "It was my grandmother's," I said, flat, smiling with only my teeth. "The drawers still slide." He nodded, crouched, and knocked on the side panel like it might answer. Behind him a woman asked if the lamp worked, and I said "Plug it in," pointing at the extension cord she was standing on. My jaw ached. I picked up the marker, crossed out twelve, and wrote ten, then pressed the cap on so hard it clicked twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the cabinet floor with a flashlight clamped in her teeth and water running down her wrist into her sleeve. She tightened the nut a quarter turn. The drip paused, considered, and started again. "No," she said around the flashlight, then took it out and said it again, flatter. "No. You don't get to do that." She wrapped the thread with tape for the third time, her jaw so tight it clicked, and her knuckles scraped the underside of the sink on the way out. The bucket beside her was nearly full. She pushed her damp hair off her forehead with a wet forearm, which only left a cold streak across her face. Plink. Plink. She stared at the wrench, then at the ceiling, and exhaled through her nose, long and slow. Then she slid back under, muttering the plumber's phone number aloud like a curse, and gave the nut another turn.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has a little plastic window and a return address I know by heart, so I stand at the mailbox and tear it open right there, one thumb jamming under the flap. Three pages. I flip to the last one first, because that's where they hide the part that matters, and of course it says to disregard this notice if I have already responded. I responded in March. I responded in April, too, with a certified receipt that's currently pinned to my fridge under a pizza magnet. My jaw has gone tight enough that my molars ache. I read the reference number out loud to the empty driveway, slowly, like it might apologize. Then I fold the pages along their original creases, exactly, which somehow makes it worse, and walk back inside to find the receipt and the phone, and the hold music I could hum in my sleep. 'Fine,' I tell the kettle. 'Fine. Again.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The ticket machine ate my coins for the third time, and I stood there with my palm flat against its cold steel, breathing slowly through my nose. Every button was labeled in characters that meant nothing to me. Behind me, a queue sighed in unison. I turned my phone toward a uniformed man, showing the translated sentence, and he read it, nodded warmly, and spoke for a full minute while pointing at three different directions. "Left, then... left?" I said, too loudly, drawing the word out as if volume might help. He smiled and said something that sounded exactly like the first thing. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the airport. I dragged my suitcase, one wheel rattling and stuck, up the stairs, then back down, then up again. Rain had started. I laughed once, a short dry bark, and muttered, "Of course," to nobody, to the sign, to the unreadable sky, and wiped my wet face with a sleeve that was already soaked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit has dropped the ball at my feet four times, and four times I've thrown it, and now he's ignoring it to roll in something dead near the fence line. I pinch the bridge of my nose. "Seriously?" My voice comes out flat, a little too even. He pops up, grinning, brown streaks down one shoulder, and bolts the opposite way when I lift the leash. I let my arm drop. The wind flaps my jacket, and my shoulders have crept up around my ears again, so I make them come down. "Biscuit. Here. Now." Nothing. He zooms a loop around the oak, tongue flapping, and I count the minutes until my dinner reservation, then stop counting. I exhale through my teeth, long and slow, and stare at the sky as if it might take my side. Then I start walking toward him, muttering about baths, about the car seats, about every promise I made to the shelter lady.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marta lowered her flute for the fourth time and pressed two fingers into the bridge of her nose. In the church basement, the folding chairs squeaked, the radiator clanked, and Dennis, bless him, came in on the wrong bar again. "Letter C," she said, evenly, each word set down like a plate. "Letter. C. Where the page says C." Her jaw ached; she realized she had been clenching it since the Gershwin. Dennis grinned and flipped pages with a rustle that seemed to fill the room. She counted silently to eight, then to ten, and still her shoulders stayed hiked up near her ears. "From the top," she said, and laughed once, a short dry sound with no joy in it. Somebody's toddler wailed upstairs. She reached to tuck her pencil behind her ear, found it already there, and let out a long, thin breath through her teeth, like a kettle left on too long. Then she raised the flute again. The concert was Saturday.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus pulled the fourth coffee can from under the bench and shook it. Screws, maybe. Or washers. He pried the lid off and found another can inside, taped shut, and another inside that. "Of course," he told the pegboard. "Of course you did." He dropped it on a pile already taller than the stool, then dragged his sleeve across his forehead, leaving a streak of sawdust. His jaw ached; he realized he'd been clenching it since noon. Every drawer stuck halfway, and he rammed each one with the heel of his hand until it gave. The labels read MISC, MISC 2, and NOT MISC. He let out one short, dry laugh, then stood very still, breathing through his nose, staring at a jar of bent nails. "Who keeps bent nails, Walt?" The jar said nothing. He snapped open a contractor bag so hard it cracked, and started again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the biology office smelled of floor wax and old radiator dust, and Marisol had read the corkboard's other notices four times: a lost umbrella, a choir sign-up, a bake sale already a month past. The results sheet was supposed to go up at noon. The clock above the door said 12:47. She pressed the heel of her hand against her forehead, exhaled through her teeth, and dropped onto the bench hard enough to make it creak. Her phone came out, went back in, came out again. "Refresh," she muttered to the portal, "refresh, refresh," jabbing the screen until her thumb ached. A passing teacher smiled and said soon, dear. Marisol gave a tight little laugh. "It was soon at eleven," she said, and tipped her head back against the cold wall to glare at a ceiling tile with a brown water stain shaped like nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta stopped at the same wooden signpost for the third time and jabbed her thumb at the phone, which insisted she was somewhere she plainly was not. "Two miles to the lake," she read aloud, flat as a board. "Two miles. It said two miles an hour ago." The light had gone orange, then the color of weak tea, and the pines were merging into one dark wall. She yanked the pack strap higher; it slid right back off her sore shoulder. A mosquito whined at her ear and she slapped her own neck hard enough to sting. Her boots, which the store clerk had sworn were broken in, rubbed a hot coin of skin on each heel. She blew out a long breath through her teeth, then kicked a pinecone down the path and watched it roll to a stop exactly where she'd have to step. "Of course," she muttered, and marched on, counting her steps out loud just to have something to bite down on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth from decades of thumbs, and Mara held it up to the window for the third time. "A handful of flour," she read aloud. "Whose handful, Grandma?" Dough clung to her knuckles like wet cement. She scraped at it with the edge of the counter, flicked a string of it into the sink, and it landed on her sleeve instead. The next line said, *knead till it feels right.* She kneaded. It felt wrong. She kneaded harder, jaw tight, breath puffing out through her nose, a streak of flour drying on her cheek. The oven timer, set for nothing yet, ticked louder than it should have. "Until it feels right," she muttered, slapping the dough against the board. "Right to who?" She flipped the card over, hoping for a clue, and found only a grease stain and the word *salt?* in faded pencil. Mara pressed the heel of her hand against her forehead, leaving a white print, and stared at the ceiling for a long, slow count of five.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta had one item left, a box of dryer sheets, when someone said her name from behind the cereal display. "Marta Luneau? Oh my God, Mr. Pruitt's chemistry!" Dennis Kray. He still stood too close. She shifted her basket to the other hand and felt her jaw tighten around a smile. "Dennis. Wow." He launched into his crypto venture, then his boat, then the time he'd copied her lab report, laughing as though it were a gift. Marta watched the clock above the pharmacy counter. Eleven minutes since she'd come in for a five-minute errand. Her thumbnail dug a crescent into the plastic handle. "That's great," she said, flatly, for the third time. "Really. I should go, my ice cream's melting." She held up the dryer sheets. He didn't blink. "We should grab a beer!" She exhaled slowly through her nose, said "Sure, message me," and walked to self-checkout, already deciding which aisle to hide in if he followed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:52 on Wednesday, Marisol slid the pharmacy gate halfway down and a man ducked under it anyway, waving a crumpled slip like a white flag. "Just one refill," he said. She pressed her thumbnail into the pad of her finger and watched the clock's red second hand stutter. It was the fourth "just one" since four o'clock. Her feet had gone to hot concrete inside her clogs. "Sir, the system's been frozen since noon," she said, each word set down flat and careful, like dishes she did not want to throw. He asked if she could check anyway. She breathed out through her nose, long enough that the fluorescent light buzzed into the silence. The sandwich she'd packed at six that morning still sat untouched in the break room. She took the slip. "Name?" she asked, already typing, already planning the drive home, the empty fridge, the four days of quiet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol hit the jet bridge doors at 4:52, her boarding pass already crumpled in her fist, and found the monitor blinking Gate B41 where her ticket said B7. She exhaled through her nose, long and flat, and turned toward the moving walkway, which was, of course, roped off with yellow tape. Her carry-on strap bit into her shoulder. She walked fast, then faster, sneakers squeaking, jaw tight enough to ache. A man with a luggage cart drifted across her path and she sidestepped without a word, muttering, 'Sure. Why not.' At the information desk, the attendant asked her to take a number. Marisol looked at the machine, then at the clock, then back at the attendant. 'The number,' she said slowly, 'is my flight, and it leaves in eleven minutes.' She laughed once, a dry little sound, pressed her palm against her forehead, and ran. Sweat gathered at her collar. Behind her, the intercom politely apologized for any inconvenience.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The third coat of "Misty Linen" dried to the exact same blotchy gray-green as the first two, and I stood there with the roller dripping onto my sock, staring at the wall like it owed me money. "Fine," I said, to nobody, in a voice that came out thin and flat. I pried the lid off the sample card I'd taped beside the window and held it up. Same color. Of course it was the same color. It just looked different in every light, and apparently my whole house was nothing but light. I dropped the roller in the tray harder than I needed to, and a gray-green fleck landed on my cheek. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since lunch. I exhaled through my nose, long and slow, then peeled the tape off the baseboard, and a strip of fresh paint came off with it. I laughed once, a short dry sound, and went to find the primer again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite dragged the wicker chair back from the porch rail for the third time, and for the third time the wind flung rain across her shins anyway. She muttered something about the forecast, which had promised "scattered showers," and pressed her thumbs hard against her eyelids. Inside, the phone was ringing again. It would be the power company, or her brother, or the man about the gutters. She didn't move. Thunder cracked above the maple and she exhaled through her teeth, a long flat hiss, like a tire losing air. "Of course," she said to the dripping eaves. "Of course it's today." The laundry hung limp and soaked on the line she'd sworn she'd taken down. She picked up her cold coffee, took a sip, grimaced, and set it down hard enough to slosh. Then she folded her arms, jaw working, and glared at the sky as though it owed her an apology and a towel.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The new derailleur hanger is still warm from my jacket pocket, and I've already dropped the 5mm hex key twice. Mrs. Okafor's paint cans rattle on her shelf when I knock the workbench, and I whisper sorry to them like an idiot. Doesn't matter. The chain slides onto the cassette with a click so clean I actually laugh out loud, alone, in a garage that smells of WD-40 and someone else's lawnmower. My knee is bouncing against the stand. I spin the crank, count the gears under my breath, one, two, three, and every shift lands. I wipe my hands on my jeans, then again, then grab my phone to text Dani: 'Saturday. Six a.m. Don't be late.' I type it three times before the autocorrect lets me. Then I'm back at the pedals, spinning, listening, grinning at a wheel that isn't even going anywhere yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marisol had been at the stop for eleven minutes, and she'd checked the envelope in her bag four times. The sky over the laundromat went the color of a bruise, and the first fat drops smacked the shelter roof like thrown coins. She didn't retreat from the wind that shoved her scarf sideways; she just grinned into it, bouncing on the balls of her feet, her knee jerking under the plastic bench whenever she sat. 'Come on, come on,' she told the empty road, laughing at herself. A man beside her glanced over, and she blurted, 'Sorry, I just got in. The conservatory. They want me for the fall.' Her fingers drummed the envelope, her pulse thudding in her ears louder than the rain. Thunder rolled, and she actually whooped. When the headlights finally swung around the corner, she was already three steps into the downpour, hair soaked, arms half-raised, as if the bus might lift her off the ground.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid hit the attic floor and I didn't even care about the dust. My fingers were already fumbling the rubber band, which snapped and stung my wrist, and I laughed out loud, alone, like an idiot. Forty, maybe fifty envelopes, all in Grandpa's slanted blue ink. I read the postmarks aloud, whispering, "Naples, 1961. Naples again. Oh, here we go." My heart was knocking against my ribs so hard I could feel it in my ears. I sat down cross-legged without noticing my knee crack, tugged one flap open with a thumbnail, and then stopped, because I wanted to do it right. I wiped my palms on my jeans. 'Mom,' I called down the ladder, voice cracking high, 'you need to come up here. Right now. Bring the lamp. Bring everything.' Then I was back, sorting by date, hands shaking, unable to stop grinning at a stranger's handwriting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while I was mid-sentence in an argument with the dishes, and I was barefoot on the porch before Dale finished saying "ladder." "The tall one? The twenty-footer? Yes. Yes, absolutely, hold on." My voice came out higher than I meant. I jogged to the garage, knocked a rake over, left it where it fell. My palms tingled against the cold aluminum rungs, and I couldn't stop grinning at the dusty thing I'd bought three years ago and never once had reason to use. "Want me to carry it over? I can carry it. I'll hold the bottom, too, if you need." Dale blinked at me. My heart thudded like I'd been asked to a dance. I hoisted the ladder onto my shoulder, nearly clipping the porch light, and was already halfway down the driveway, asking what he was fixing and whether it was the gutters.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The risotto has been stirred for twenty minutes and I've already tasted it four times, humming something I can't name. My knees keep bouncing against the cabinet. I check the clock: 6:42. Eighteen minutes. I wipe my hands on my apron, then wipe them again, then rearrange the napkins so the fold faces left, no, right. A bead of sweat slides down my temple and I laugh at myself, out loud, alone in the kitchen. The lemon tart sits cooling on the sill, and I lean over to smell it, grinning like a fool. Every time a car passes outside I'm at the window with the wooden spoon still dripping on the floor. 'Okay, okay,' I tell the pot, 'you're perfect, don't change.' My heart is knocking so fast I forget the salt, remember it, then forget again. When footsteps finally crunch up the gravel, I drop the spoon, nearly skid across the tiles, and fling the door open before anyone has even knocked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the cutting board and I nearly knock the onion into the sink. Unknown number, a 212 area code, and my thumb is already sliding before my brain catches up. I wipe my wet hand on my jeans, then wipe it again. "Hello? Yes, this is she. Yes!" My voice jumps an octave and I clear my throat, pacing the length of the kitchen, six steps, turn, six steps. The interview was Tuesday. They said a week. It's been three days, which means it's good, it has to mean it's good. My heart is knocking so hard I can feel it in my ears, and my knees keep bouncing even though I'm standing. I'm grinning at the refrigerator like it can see me. "Sorry, could you say that again? I want to write it down." I have no pen. I grab a lipstick and start writing on the back of my hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I took the library steps two at a time, the battered copy of Moby-Dick slapping against my hip, my sneakers squeaking on the marble before I could stop myself. Four years overdue. Four years, and I'd found it that morning wedged behind my dresser, and I'd laughed out loud, alone, like a lunatic. Now my heart was drumming so hard I could feel it in my teeth. The librarian looked up over her glasses and I blurted, "I have something to confess," grinning too wide, words tumbling over each other. "It's the fine, right? Tell me the fine. Please, tell me, I want to know the number." My fingers drummed the counter, then tapped the book's cracked spine, then drummed again. I couldn't stand still; I rocked on my heels, bounced, peeked at the screen she was turning toward me. "Go on," I whispered, breathless, already reaching for my wallet. "Hit me with it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The key stuck for half a second, and Marisol laughed out loud at the hallway, at nobody, before shoving the door with her hip. Boxes thudded down in the middle of the floor. She didn't open a single one. Instead she spun in the narrow room with her arms out, fingertips almost brushing both walls, then pressed her palms flat to the cool plaster as if it might answer. Her heart was knocking against her ribs. "Okay," she said, too loudly, and then again, softer, "okay." She crossed to the window in four steps, wrestled the sticky latch, and leaned out into the noise of the street, grinning at a pigeon. Her hands wouldn't stay still; they straightened a curtain that wasn't crooked, flicked the light switch on, off, on. Already she was pacing out where the bookshelf would go, where the plant, where the tiny table for two chairs she hadn't bought yet. She called her sister and forgot to say hello. "You have to see the radiator," she blurted. "It has a little shelf."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marta nearly walked past the bench, but a flash of brown leather in the damp leaves snagged her eye, and she stopped so fast her coffee sloshed over her knuckles. She didn't notice the burn. The wallet was fat, worn soft at the corners, and her thumb trembled as it pried the clasp open. "Okay, okay, okay," she whispered, glancing left, then right, at the empty path and a jogger shrinking in the distance. Her heart thudded against her ribs like a fist on a door. A driver's license: a gray-haired man named Walter Pruitt, squinting at the camera. Behind it, folded bills, a photo of a spaniel, a ticket stub dated last Saturday. She laughed, a high breathless sound, and bounced on her heels, already tapping his address into her phone with clumsy, too-quick fingers. Two typos. She fixed them, grinning, and broke into a trot, the wallet clutched to her chest like something alive.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: I was thirty-eight, standing in the shallow end at six a.m. with goggles already pressed so hard against my face they left rings. The instructor hadn't even finished saying "when you're ready" before I'd let go of the wall. My feet left the tiled floor. Water slid over my ribs, cold, then not cold, and my heart was slamming like I'd sprinted up stairs. I kicked, too hard, splashing a lane-mate, and laughed into the water, which made me swallow some. "Did you see that?" I shouted, coughing, though she was already three feet away. "Four strokes! That was four!" My fingers kept tingling long after I'd stopped. I couldn't stop bouncing on my toes at the wall, rubbing my hands together, rehearsing the kick under my breath. Chlorine stung my nose. I didn't care. "Again," I told the instructor, who was smiling. "Please. Right now. Again."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I was out the door before the kettle clicked off, still in my socks, the seed packets rattling in my coat pocket like loose change. The dirt behind the shed was cold and damp, and I knelt right into it, not caring about my knees. "Okay, okay," I muttered, tearing the tomato packet so fast that half the seeds scattered. I laughed and picked them out of the soil one by one, pinching each like it was made of gold. My hands wouldn't stay still. I measured the row with a ruler, then measured it again, then crouched low to stare at the bare patch as if something might already be pushing up. I read the back of the carrot packet aloud to the fence. Twice. My heart knocked against my ribs, and I couldn't stop grinning at a rectangle of mud. When I finally stood, I realized I'd skipped breakfast and didn't care. I went inside only to fill the watering can, then practically ran back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Priya had stopped pretending to read her notes by the second slide. When Dmitri clicked to the prototype demo, she scooted forward until her chair squeaked against the conference table, pen tapping a fast little rhythm on her knee. "Wait, wait, show them the filter," she blurted, then pressed her lips together and grinned at the ceiling tiles. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago; she lifted it anyway, forgot to drink, set it down. When the dashboard loaded in under a second, a breath burst out of her, and she smacked the table once, softly, palm flat. Her heartbeat was thudding in her ears. 'Three months of Tuesday nights,' she thought, 'and it actually works in the room.' She leaned toward Marguerite, whispering, "Watch, here comes the good part," her knee bouncing so hard the whole table trembled, and her cheeks ached from smiling at a spreadsheet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway is empty, and I keep catching my own grin in the rearview mirror like it belongs to someone else. My thumbs drum the steering wheel out of rhythm with the radio, which I've turned up so loud the speakers rattle. I've already said "Holy hell" out loud three times to nobody. The envelope with the offer letter sits on the passenger seat, and every red light I glance at it, just to make sure it's still there. My knee bounces. My coffee went cold two exits ago and I drink it anyway, barely tasting it. I rehearse how I'll wake Dana, how I'll whisper it and then probably shout it, and my heart thumps so hard I can feel it in my ears. The streetlights flick past like a flipbook. When I finally turn onto our street, I'm already pulling the keys out of the ignition while the car is still rolling, laughing at myself, ready to sprint up the stairs two at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I took the stairs because the elevator was too slow, two at a time, the paper bag of lemon cookies crinkling in my fist. Fourth floor. My sneakers squeaked on the linoleum and a nurse glanced up, and I slowed to a walk for exactly three doors before I was jogging again. Room 412. I couldn't stop bouncing on my heels outside it, my pulse thudding in my ears, my grin already stretching my cheeks until they ached. 'Grandma Ro,' I called through the crack, too loud, 'guess who they said can go home Friday?' Her laugh came out thin but real. I dropped the bag on her tray, knocked over her water cup, didn't care, and kept talking, words tumbling over each other, about the garden, the porch swing, the soup I'd already planned. My hands wouldn't stay still. I straightened her blanket twice, then a third time, just to be touching something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I've checked my phone four times in two minutes, and the bell isn't even due for another six. My heel keeps tapping the pavement, and I catch the woman beside me glancing down at it, so I stop, then start again. In my coat pocket my fingers worry the folded edge of the envelope: two tickets, the aquarium, Saturday, the one with the tunnel of sharks she's been drawing on every napkin since August. 'Sorry, do you know if they're running late?' I ask the crossing guard, who has already told me no twice. My cheeks ache; I realize I've been grinning at a parked minivan. Then the doors bang open and a flood of backpacks spills out, and I'm up on my toes, craning, my pulse thudding in my ears. There, the yellow hat. I'm waving with my whole arm before she even looks up, and my voice cracks as I shout, 'Maya! Guess what!'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: I was up before the sun, dragging Grandma's oak dresser to the curb with my sneakers untied, and I didn't even care when the drawer slid out and clipped my shin. Price stickers, done. Coffee, cold already, forgotten on the porch rail. By seven-fifteen I'd rearranged the lamp table three times, and my fingers wouldn't stop drumming against my thigh. A pickup rolled slowly past and my breath caught; I stood straighter, hands clasped, then waved too big. 'Morning! Everything's negotiable, well, mostly!' My voice came out higher than usual. A woman ran her palm along the dresser's top and I heard myself babbling about the dovetail joints, how it still smelled like cedar, how you could hide a whole summer of secrets in the bottom drawer. My heart thudded in my ears. She smiled, tugged open a drawer, and I swear I bounced on my heels like a kid waiting for a bell to ring. 'Make me an offer,' I said, grinning so hard my cheeks ached.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench was still in my hand when I realized I'd been bouncing on my heels for a full minute, knees knocking the cabinet door. Water dripped into the pot beneath the sink, plink, plink, and I laughed at it. "Not for long," I told the pipe. My fingers fumbled the Teflon tape twice, dropping the roll into the dark behind the bucket, and I didn't even swear, just fished it out and wound eight neat turns around the threads, my pulse thudding in my ears. I'd watched three videos last night and barely slept. Now my palms were slick, my grin stuck so wide my cheeks ached. I spun the new fitting on, gave it a quarter turn more, then scrambled up, nearly clipping my head on the faucet. "Okay, okay, okay," I whispered, hand on the valve. I turned it slowly. I held my breath. Nothing. Not one drop. I shouted for the empty kitchen to come look.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope with the green eagle in the corner was already on the hall table when Marisol kicked her shoes off, and she forgot the other shoe, hopping a few steps with it dangling from her toes. "Okay. Okay okay okay," she said to the empty apartment. Her thumb found the flap and slipped; she wiped her palm on her jeans and tried again. The tear came out crooked. Her heart was knocking so hard she could feel it in her teeth. She paced to the window and back, the letter held up to the light like that would help, then laughed at herself, a short breathless sound. Two years of forms. She unfolded the page, and the first line blurred, so she read it with her lips moving, then louder, then she was already dialing her sister, the phone pressed to her cheek, bouncing on her heels, saying, "Pick up, pick up, pick up, you won't believe it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Mina dragged her suitcase out of the station and stopped dead on the pavement, grinning at nothing. Signs she couldn't read glowed red and gold above her, and the air smelled of frying dough and rain. Her heart knocked against her ribs. She spun in a slow circle, pulled out her phone, then shoved it back in her pocket and decided against the map. At a noodle stall she pointed at a steaming bowl someone else was eating and held up two fingers, laughing when the cook laughed. "Thank you," she said, too loudly, then tried the local word she'd practiced on the plane, mangling it. The cook repeated it gently. She repeated it back, bouncing on her toes. Her hands trembled around the hot bowl, and her foot wouldn't stop tapping against the stool. Every unreadable sign looked like a door. She slurped, burned her tongue, and didn't care, already wondering which street to get lost in first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta had barely clicked the gate shut before Biscuit tore off across the meadow, ears flapping like flags, and her coffee thermos hit the grass somewhere behind her. She didn't bend to pick it up. "Look at him," she said, to nobody, then louder, "Look at you!" Her heart knocked against her ribs in quick, bright beats, and her hands wouldn't stay still, tugging her sleeves, then clapping, then pressing against her grinning mouth. The dog skidded, spun, and launched himself at a swirl of dandelion fluff, and Marta bounced on her toes, a laugh squeaking out higher than she intended. Her cheeks ached. She fumbled her phone from her pocket, dropped it, scooped it up, and filmed three shaky seconds before lowering it again because she wanted to see him with her own eyes. "Again! Do that again!" she yelled, voice cracking, as Biscuit barreled back toward her through the gold grass, and she crouched, arms flung wide, ready.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite got to the church hall forty minutes early, and the folding chairs were still stacked against the wall, so she played to them. Her cello case thumped against the doorframe as she hurried in, and she laughed at herself, a short breathy sound that bounced off the tile. She rosined her bow twice, forgetting the first time. Her fingers drummed on the fingerboard between phrases, and her knee would not stop bouncing. 'Again,' she told nobody, and started the Elgar from the top, swaying so far forward that her chair creaked. When she nailed the high passage she grinned mid-note and nearly lost the bar. Her pulse thudded in her ears, her cheeks were warm, and she kept glancing at the paper poster taped by the piano with her name misspelled. She decided not to correct it. Mr. Alvarez arrived with the coffee urn, and she called out, 'Wait, just listen to this one part,' before he'd even set it down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I was supposed to be boxing up chisels, but I'd already dropped the box twice. Walt's workshop smelled of cedar and machine oil, and under the bench, behind a coil of rope, my fingers hit canvas. I dragged it out so fast I skinned my knuckle and didn't notice until later. "No way," I whispered, then louder, to the empty room, "No way, you old liar." The tarp came off in one yank. The cello, the one he swore he'd never finished, gleamed there, varnish still tacky at the edges, a pencil tucked in the scroll. My heart was banging against my ribs. I laughed, wiped my palms on my jeans, wiped them again, and couldn't stop pacing a tight circle around it. I grabbed my phone, put it down, grabbed it again. Who do I call first? Every thought tumbled over the next. I knelt, and my hands were shaking too much to touch it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Maribel had been refreshing the portal since 8:52, though the page wasn't due to update until nine. Her knee bounced so hard the desk rattled the mug of cold tea beside her laptop. She stood, paced to the window, sat again, and wiped her palms on her jeans. "Okay, okay, okay," she muttered, voice high and quick, grinning at nobody. Her little brother glanced up from the couch and asked if she was going to throw up. "Maybe," she said, laughing, and tugged her sleeves over her fingers. The clock flipped to 9:00. Her heart thumped in her ears, loud as a drum. She pressed F5, then again, then again, whispering, "Come on, come on, come on," while her toes curled against the floorboards and her breath came in short, bright bursts. The page flickered white. She leaned so close her nose almost touched the screen, and she didn't blink at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange on the ridge and I'm still climbing, taking the switchbacks two rocks at a time, my pack straps bouncing against my collarbones. My heart is knocking so hard I can feel it in my teeth. I should slow down. I don't. Somewhere above me is the saddle where the old ranger said the whole valley opens up at sunset, and I mutter, "Come on, come on, come on," to no one, to my own boots. My fingers keep drifting to the camera strap, checking it, checking it again. A grouse bursts from the scrub and I laugh out loud, too loudly, the sound ricocheting off the granite. Sweat cools along my spine. The pines go black, the sky goes the color of peaches, and I'm grinning so wide the cold air aches in my molars. Ten more switchbacks. Maybe eight. I take the next turn running, headlamp swinging unlit around my neck, whispering, "Please still be there."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma Ines's card was soft as cloth, the ink gone brown, and I'd read it so many times I could have recited it, but I kept it propped against the flour tin anyway. "Warm water, not hot," I muttered, dipping my wrist like she used to, then laughed out loud at nobody. My hands wouldn't stay still. I measured the salt twice, spilled some, brushed it off the counter with a little dance of my fingers. When the yeast foamed, I actually yelped and called my sister, voice cracking high. "It's bubbling! Lena, it's doing the thing!" I kneaded until my shoulders burned and my heart thumped in my ears, then crouched at the oven window, nose nearly on the glass, watching the dough lift. Every thirty seconds I checked the timer, though I knew it by heart. The kitchen smelled like her house. I bounced on my toes the whole time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was comparing two jars of peanut butter in aisle six when a laugh she hadn't heard in twelve years carried over the shelves. She froze, jar still in hand, then set both down so fast one tipped over. "Danielle Okafor?" Her voice came out higher than she meant it to. The woman by the cereal turned, and Marisol was already walking, nearly jogging, her cart abandoned crooked in the middle of the aisle. Her heart knocked against her ribs. "You still have the chipped tooth!" she blurted, then pressed her palm to her cheek, which was hot. They hugged right there beside the oatmeal, and Marisol realized she was bouncing on her toes. "Do you remember Mr. Brandt's chemistry class? The exploding sink?" She was talking too fast, words tumbling over each other, and she didn't care. Her fingers fumbled for her phone. "Give me your number. Actually, are you free right now? I'll leave the groceries. I mean it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol restocked the same shelf of cranberry sauce three times before the clock hit four, and she didn't notice until Mr. Albright pointed at the neat, crowded row. "Oops," she laughed, too loudly, and her sneakers squeaked as she bounced on her toes between customers. Her pulse tapped at her wrist every time the automatic doors sighed open. She scanned a woman's rolls and stuffing and said, "Tomorrow, huh? Is it a big table?" then nodded through the whole answer, grinning until her cheeks ached. Her phone buzzed in her apron: a photo of her sister's suitcase by the door. She pressed it to her chest, then slid it away and straightened the gum display for no reason. When the last bagger left, she wiped the register in fast circles, flicked off her light, and nearly ran the length of the dark aisle, her keys already jangling in her fist, her breath coming quick and bright in the cold lot.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol hit the jet bridge at a jog, her backpack slapping against her spine, and kept jogging even after the gate agent's voice on the speaker said final boarding for Lisbon was still twenty minutes off. Gate B42. She was at B14. Her pulse thudded in her ears, and she couldn't stop grinning at the moving walkway, which she ignored in favor of her own faster legs. "Sorry, sorry, left side, thank you!" she sang, weaving past a stroller. Her fingers drummed the strap of her bag, then the phone in her palm, then her thigh. Two years of saving, and now a whole ocean was waiting past a few more hallways. She skidded at the departures board, found the green word BOARDING, and let out a short laugh that made an old man glance up. "Yes," she whispered, bouncing on her toes, and took off again, heart fluttering like something trying to get ahead of her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I had the painter's tape up by six, before the coffee even finished dripping, and I'd already peeled the lid off the can twice just to look at the color again. Marigold Dusk. On the card it had seemed like a gamble; in the can it glowed like butter. My knees cracked as I crouched, stirring far longer than needed, humming something with no tune. "Okay, okay, okay," I told the empty room, and my voice came out too loud, bouncing off the bare floor. I dragged the roller through the tray, loaded it too heavy, and laughed when the first stripe slid up the old gray wall, bright as a sunrise. My pulse thudded in my wrists. I kept stepping back, stepping in, ignoring the drip on my sock. I'd planned to stop for lunch. It was nearly dark, and I was still grinning, already measuring the second wall with my eyes, pretending I wasn't fidgeting to start the next coat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail, and Marisol was already on her feet, bare toes curled over the edge of the top step. Thunder cracked somewhere past the water tower, and she laughed out loud, a short bark that surprised her. "Did you hear that? Did you feel that?" she called through the screen door, though nobody was there to answer. Her coffee sat forgotten, going cold on the armrest. The air smelled of hot asphalt and wet dust, and she pulled it deep into her chest until her ribs ached. Her knees bounced; her fingers drummed the post in rhythm with the rain. When lightning split the sky white, she counted out loud, "One, two, three—" and the boom came early, rattling the windowpanes. She gripped the railing and leaned out into the spray, letting it soak her hair, grinning so hard her cheeks hurt, wishing the whole sky would come down closer still.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain finally clicks onto the cog and I whoop so loud that Mrs. Okafor's cat bolts from the shelf above the paint cans. I don't even apologize. My hands are black to the wrists, there's grease on my chin, and I'm bouncing on my heels beside the workbench like the floor is a trampoline. Three weekends I've fought this derailleur in our shared garage, between Dev's kayak and the neighbors' stacked boxes, and now it shifts, crisp, every gear. I spin the pedal again just to hear that whirring purr. "Listen to that! Listen!" I shout at nobody, then at the cat, then at the ceiling bulb. My heart is thudding like I've already ridden ten miles. I wipe my palms on my jeans, give up, grab the helmet, and wheel the bike through the half-open door into the cold evening. My legs can't stand still. I'm laughing, and I haven't even sat down yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marisol had been bouncing on her heels since the bus shelter's clock read 4:10, and when the first fat raindrop smacked her forehead she laughed out loud, a bark that made the man beside her flinch. The sky had gone the color of wet slate, wind snapping her scarf like a flag, and instead of retreating under the roof she stepped out to the curb with her arms wide. "Look at that!" she told him, though he hadn't asked. "Look at it come!" Her sneakers were already soaked, her hair plastered to her cheeks, and she couldn't stop grinning, her ribs fizzing as if she'd swallowed something carbonated. She'd gotten the job an hour ago and still hadn't told anyone; she'd just walked, nearly ran, here. Thunder rolled. She spun once, splashing, and sang the first line of a song she didn't know the rest of, louder each time, until the bus finally hissed to a stop and she thanked the driver twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marisol pried the shoebox lid off and the attic's dust swirled up gold in the afternoon light, and she laughed out loud at nothing, at everything. She read the first envelope's return address and hopped in place, bare feet slapping the floorboards. "Aunt Perpetua! Oh, you absolute menace!" Her fingers flew, tearing nothing, sliding each flap open with a flourish. She read a line aloud in a booming stage voice, then another in a squeaky one, and her own voice cracked from giddiness. Her heart drummed against her ribs; her cheeks ached from grinning. She couldn't stay seated. She spun with a postcard held overhead, knocked over a lamp, caught it, and kept going. Pages fanned across the floor like a snowfall she'd made herself. Downstairs, the phone was already in her hand. "Dad? Dad, you need to come up here right now. You will not believe what I found. Bring everyone. Bring snacks!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marguerite was halfway through a spin in the kitchen, flour on her elbows, when the knock came, and she took the hallway in four bounding steps and flung the door wide. "Dennis! A ladder? Yes! Yes, of course, I've got two!" Her voice came out higher than she meant, and she laughed at it. Her heart thumped as if she'd run a mile. She skipped past him toward the garage, then doubled back for her keys, then forgot why she wanted them. "Gutters?" she called. "Please say gutters. I love gutters!" The aluminum rails clanged as she hauled the long one down, and she hoisted it over her shoulder as though it weighed nothing, grinning at the sky, at the wet leaves, at Dennis's baffled face. Her fingers tingled. "Take the short one too," she said, nearly singing. "Take everything! Keep it all week! Oh, can I come hold the bottom?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The wooden spoon is my microphone now, and the radio is losing to me. I spin from the stove to the counter, sock-sliding across the tile, and nearly knock the lemons off their bowl. Forty minutes until the doorbell, and I'm chopping parsley like a drummer. "Taste this," I tell the empty kitchen, then laugh at myself and taste it anyway. Garlic, butter, a little smoke. My cheeks ache from grinning, and my pulse is thumping somewhere up in my ears. The oven light shows the chicken going gold, and I actually clap, flour puffing off my palms. I can't stand still long enough to wipe the counter, so I dance the rag across it instead. Candles next. Then the good napkins, the ones I always save. A car door slams outside and I yelp, "They're early!" and bound to the window, apron crooked, heart galloping, already waving through the glass at nobody yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes across the counter, a string of digits I don't know, and I'm already grinning as I snatch it up, flour still on my knuckles. "Hello, hello, hello!" I sing, spinning on one heel so the dish towel flies off my shoulder. My heart is thudding like I've just run the stairs, though I've only crossed the kitchen. The voice on the other end is polite, probably about to sell me something, and I don't care. "No, go on, tell me everything, I've got all day!" I say, and I laugh, too loud, at nothing. The dog barks at me. I bark back. My cheeks ache. I hop onto the stool, off it, onto it again, drumming the counter with both hands. Whoever you are, stranger, you've caught me on the best morning of the whole year, and I want to hear your voice, your weather, your name. Say it slowly. I'm writing it on my arm in pen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Priya took the library steps two at a time, the battered copy of Middlemarch clutched over her head like a trophy. Fourteen months overdue, and she was grinning anyway. Her sneakers squeaked on the linoleum; she skidded to a stop at the desk and slapped the book down so hard that a man at the periodicals rack jumped. "Hi! Hello! I have a confession, and it's a big one!" Her voice bounced off the high ceiling. The clerk lifted an eyebrow. Priya couldn't stop bouncing on her toes, fingers drumming a rhythm on the counter, cheeks hot, heart thudding as if she'd run a mile. "Name the fine. Whatever it is. I'll pay it in quarters, in dollar bills, in my own hair!" She laughed, a loud, helpless hiccup of a laugh, and spun halfway toward the quiet stacks as if to share it with every shelf. "I finished it last night. The whole thing!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The door stuck, so Marisol shouldered it open and spilled into the room along with her last box, which she dropped so she could spin. Four steps from window to wall, and she paced them twice, then a third time just to hear her sneakers squeak on the bare floor. "Mine," she told the radiator. "Mine, mine, mine," she told the crooked closet, laughing so hard her ribs ached. Her heart thudded as if she'd climbed all five flights again. She yanked the window up, let the street noise pour in, and leaned out grinning at a pigeon who clearly didn't care. Cross-legged on the floor, she tore open a box of mugs and set one on the sill, then another, then lined up all seven, each clink making her bounce. She hadn't even found the sheets yet. Her cheeks hurt. She flung her arms wide, touched both walls at once with her fingertips, and whooped loudly enough that the neighbor thumped back, which only made her laugh harder and thump in reply.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marisol was halfway through a skip when her sneaker caught the corner of something brown beneath the bench, and she scooped it up with a whoop that sent two pigeons scattering. "Look at you!" she told the wallet, holding it overhead like a trophy. Her heart drummed against her ribs, and her fingers tingled as she flipped it open. A driver's license: Walter Abney, 74, Linden Street. She laughed out loud, a bright, unbroken peal, and spun once on the gravel path, jacket flaring. "Okay, Walter, hold tight, I'm coming!" She couldn't stop grinning; her cheeks ached. She tucked the wallet into her coat, patted it twice, then broke into a jog, then a sprint, sunlight flashing through the maples, breath puffing in white bursts. A jogger stared. "Good morning!" she shouted at him, waving with both arms. "It's a great one!" Linden Street, she figured, was only eight blocks. She'd make it in five minutes flat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor let go of the kickboard, and I didn't notice until I'd already crossed the lane rope's shadow. My legs were kicking on their own, scissoring wild, throwing water onto the deck where a toddler stared at me. "Did you see?" I shouted, mouth full of chlorine, and swallowed half of it. Didn't care. I coughed, laughed, coughed again. Thirty-eight years old, and my arms were windmilling like I'd invented them. My heart knocked against my ribs so hard I felt it in my fingertips, my toes, the backs of my knees. I slapped the wall, turned around, and pushed off again before she could answer. "Again! Watch! Watch this one!" The ceiling lights smeared into gold stripes on the water. My goggles were fogged, my hair was in my mouth, and I was already planning to come back tomorrow at six, then maybe tonight, too, if they'd let me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol had been up since five, and the sun had barely cleared the fence when she dropped to her knees in the dirt, grinning at nothing. She tore open the seed packets so fast that a few tomato seeds scattered across her sleeve, and she laughed out loud, picking them off one by one like jewels. "Okay, little guys," she told the soil, "get comfortable." Her hands were black to the wrists, her knees soaked through, and she didn't care at all. She measured the rows with a ruler, then abandoned the ruler and just jabbed her finger in, again and again, humming something tuneless. When the neighbor peered over the fence, she shot up, waving a trowel like a flag. "Carrots! Basil! Three kinds of beans!" Her heart thumped against her ribs. She watered the bare brown rows twice, then a third time, bouncing on her heels, and snapped a photo of dirt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Priya clicked to the last slide and the whole conference room seemed to lean toward her, but I was the one half out of my chair. My knee bounced under the table so hard that my coffee rippled. When the chart showed the load time dropping from nine seconds to under one, I actually slapped the table and said, "Look at that line! Look at it fall!" Three people turned to stare. I didn't care. I grinned until my cheeks ached, and my pulse thudded in my fingertips like I'd run up the stairs. Every time she explained another piece, I nodded too fast, whispering "Yes, yes, exactly" to nobody. I'd spent two weeks helping her test that thing at midnight, and now here it was, glowing on the wall, real. When she asked for questions, my hand shot up before she finished the sentence. My voice came out too loud, cracking with laughter. "Can we ship it today? Please? I'll bring the cake."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol hit the on-ramp at 12:40 a.m. with the windows down and her hands drumming the steering wheel, ignoring the cold that stung her ears. The highway was empty, a long ribbon of orange lamplight, and she sang at it, badly, cracking on the high notes and laughing at herself. 'Yes,' she told the dashboard. 'Yes, yes, yes.' The envelope with the offer letter lay on the passenger seat, and every few seconds she patted it as if it might float away. Her heart thumped hard against her ribs; her cheeks ached from grinning. At a red light with no cars in sight, she leaned out and shouted her own name into the dark, then howled with laughter when a startled moth flew in. She couldn't sit still. Her knees bounced, her shoulders danced, and when the exit came, she almost missed it, still turning the music up, still wishing the road would go on for another hundred miles.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I took the stairs two at a time because the elevator was too slow for my legs, and I was still bouncing on my toes when I reached Grandpa's room on the fourth floor. The balloon bouquet I'd bought bumped the doorframe, and I laughed out loud at nothing. "They said you're going home Friday!" I announced, much louder than the beeping monitors deserved. A nurse glanced up, smiling, and I waved at her like we were old friends. My cheeks ached. I kissed Grandpa's forehead, then his hand, then spun the visitor's chair around and sat on it backward, drumming the rail. "I already cleaned your kitchen. I bought the awful pickles. Tell me what you want to eat first." My heart was thudding against my ribs, my fingers wouldn't sit still, and the whole gray room seemed lit up. He squeezed my hand and said I was going to wear a hole in the floor. I hoped so.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marisol got to the chain-link fence twenty minutes early and couldn't stand still, so she bounced on her heels, then paced to the oak and back, the letter crinkling in her fist. Her cheeks ached from grinning at nobody. "Sorry, sorry," she laughed when she bumped a stroller, then told its owner, a stranger, "Forty-one years old and I just got the job!" The woman blinked and smiled. Marisol's heart knocked against her ribs like it wanted out. She hummed, lost the tune, started again louder. A crossing guard's whistle made her flinch and giggle. When the doors finally banged open and kids spilled across the blacktop, she was already on her toes, one arm swinging over her head like she was flagging down a ship. "Dani! Danielita! Over here, baby, we're getting pancakes for dinner!" Her voice cracked on the last word, and she didn't care at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: I'd been up since five, dragging Grandpa's oak dresser to the curb, and I still couldn't stop bouncing on my heels. "Morning! Coffee's free, the lamp works, and that rocking chair has opinions!" I hollered at a couple who'd barely parked. My voice cracked high and I laughed at it. I slapped a sticker on the sideboard, peeled it off, slapped on a better price, then spun to rearrange the card table for the third time. My hands wouldn't sit still; my cheeks ached from grinning. A man asked about the bookshelf and I told him the whole story, the flood, the move, the cat that lived inside it, words tumbling over each other. When he handed me twenty dollars, I whooped, actually whooped, and waved the bill over my head like a flag. The sun was barely over the maples. Every single chair out there looked like it was about to go somewhere wonderful, and so, I was sure, was I.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marisol slid under the sink on her back, headlamp bouncing, and the drip hit her forehead just as she yelled, "Gotcha!" to no one. Her knees wouldn't stay still; they drummed the cabinet floor while she wrapped the joint in plumber's tape, three turns, then four, then a flourish for fun. She was humming something with no tune, loud, and when the wrench slipped and clanged against her shin she only laughed and said, "Ha! Rude!" Her cheeks ached from grinning. Her pulse thumped in her fingertips, warm and quick, and she could not stop wiggling her toes in their mismatched socks. She tightened the nut, scooted out on her elbows, and slapped the faucet handle with both palms. Water rushed, the pipe stayed dry, and she spun the dog around the kitchen by his front paws. "Did you see that? Did you SEE that?" she sang, towel flapping over her head like a flag, already scheming which other pipes in the house might be leaking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had the eagle seal in the corner, and Marisol didn't even make it past the mailboxes before she tore it open with her teeth. Her keys hit the lobby tile. She didn't bend for them. Her eyes raced down the page, caught on the word *approved*, and she read it again, then a third time, her lips moving. 'Mrs. Okafor!' she shouted up the stairwell, voice cracking high. 'Mrs. Okafor, they said yes!' She took the steps two at a time, the letter flapping over her head like a flag, her heart banging so hard she could feel it in her ears. On the second landing she spun in a full circle, laughed at nothing, and kissed the paper, leaving a smear of lipstick across the signature. Her legs wouldn't stay still. Neither would her hands. She knocked on the door with her whole fist, bouncing on her toes, already planning to tell the entire building, the bus driver, and her mother twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train doors hissed open and I was running before my brain caught up, backpack thumping, sandals slapping the platform tiles of a city whose signs looked like beautiful tangled fishing line. I couldn't read one. I grinned at a woman sweeping, said "Hello! Hi! Thank you!" in three pitches, and she laughed and bowed, and I bowed back too deeply, nearly dropping my map. My heart was drumming somewhere up near my ears. Outside, steam rose from a cart, and I pointed at whatever the man was frying, held up two fingers, then four, then gave up counting and just spun in a circle with my arms out. Neon buzzed against my cheeks. I bit into something hot and salty and shouted "Oh my God!" with my mouth full, and three strangers turned and cheered at me in words I'd never understand. My legs wouldn't stay still. I had no hotel address I could pronounce, and I didn't care, and I started walking toward the loudest street.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta had meant to sit on the bench, but her legs wouldn't hold still. Down the slope, Biscuit tore through the wet grass in a lopsided circle, ears inside out, and she was already jogging after him, coat flapping open, cold air stinging her teeth because she couldn't stop grinning. "Look at you! Look at your legs!" she shouted, her voice cracking high like a kid's. He skidded, spun, and dove nose-first into a molehill; she barked out a laugh so loud a crow lifted off the fence post. Her heart thumped against her ribs, her fingers tingled, her cheeks ached. She pulled out her phone to film, realized she was bouncing too much to keep it steady, and gave up, throwing both arms wide instead. "Again! Do it again!" He did. She whooped, spun around once herself, nearly lost her scarf to the wind, and didn't care a bit.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Halfway through the second verse I gave up on the music stand and just let my feet go. The church hall smelled of floor wax and somebody's burnt coffee, and folding chairs sat in crooked rows for an audience of nobody, which didn't matter one bit. My fingers skipped over the keys faster than the metronome wanted, and I laughed out loud, right in the middle of a bar. "Again!" I called to Marguerite, our cellist, who was already grinning. "From the top, and louder, please, louder!" My heart thumped against my ribs like it wanted in on the rhythm. My cheeks ached. I'd been up since five, and I wasn't tired at all; I felt like I could carry the piano down the street. When we hit the last chord, I threw both arms up, knocked my sheet music flying, and didn't even bend to get it. Thursday couldn't come fast enough. Actually, why wait? "Once more," I said, already counting us in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marisol kicked the workshop door wide and let the morning pour over the sawdust, and she was already laughing before she'd found the first box. "Walter, you hoarder," she told the rafters, hauling down a coffee can of bent nails and shaking it like a maraca. Her feet wouldn't stay still; she bounced on her heels between the lathe and the bench, her pulse drumming in her ears. She found his old radio, cranked the dial until a polka blared, and spun a clamp over her head like a baton. Every drawer she yanked open gave her something new to shout about: a dozen left-handed gloves, a jar of glass eyes, a half-carved duck with a grin. "Look at this! Look at you!" Her cheeks ached. She stacked, sorted, tossed, talking the whole time, sleeves shoved past her elbows, grit in her teeth, and when the sun hit the dust just right she threw both arms up and whooped until the whole shed rang.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 14 smelled like floor wax and old radiators, and I couldn't stop bouncing on my toes. The noticeboard was still blank, just a pinned rectangle of cork, and I was already grinning at it like it had told me a joke. Somebody's phone buzzed; I nearly yelped. I drummed a rhythm on my thighs, then on the strap of my backpack, then on the shoulder of a stranger, who glanced over, and I said, "Sorry, sorry, big day, huge day!" My heart was thumping so hard my collar twitched. I'd already hugged Mrs. Alvarez twice, and she hadn't even brought the list yet. When the door finally clicked and paper rustled, I let out a laugh that echoed down the hall, spun in a full circle, and sprinted forward, sneakers squeaking, hands flung wide, ready to read whatever it said like it was a song.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The sun slid behind the ridge and I didn't slow down, I sped up, boots slapping the switchbacks like I was late for something wonderful. My legs should have been jelly after eleven miles, but they bounced, and I caught myself skipping over roots, flinging my arms wide at the valley going purple below. "Look at that!" I shouted, to no one, to the pines, and my voice cracked into a laugh that rolled back at me off the rock. My heart thudded in my ears. Cold air stung my teeth because I couldn't stop grinning. I snatched a handful of trail mix, dropped half of it, and didn't care. Somewhere behind me my headlamp sat zipped in my pack, forgotten. Maybe I'd need it in ten minutes. Maybe I'd just run down in the dark, hollering at the first stars. I spun once on the gravel, dizzy, and kept going, singing something with no tune and every word wrong.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Marisol had flour up to her elbows and a streak of it across her forehead, and she hadn't noticed either. The index card, soft as cloth and spotted with decades of butter, was propped against the sugar tin, Nonna's slanted hand telling her to knead until it "feels like an earlobe." She pressed her thumb into the dough, felt it spring back, and whooped so loudly the cat bolted from the windowsill. "It's an earlobe! Nonna, it's actually an earlobe!" She drummed a quick rhythm on the counter, spun once on her sock feet, and almost slid into the fridge. Her heart thudded as if she'd run up the stairs. When the oven light clicked on, she bounced on her toes, pressing her face close to the glass, grinning so wide her cheeks ached. The kitchen smelled like yeast and warm wheat, and she was already dialing her mother, talking before anyone answered.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a single lemon when I saw her by the cereal aisle, and the lemon shot out of my hand and rolled under a display. "Priya Nandakumar!" My voice cracked the quiet of the store, and a man with a cart turned to stare. I didn't care. I was already across the tile, arms open, nearly bouncing on my toes. "Ninth grade chemistry! You set the lab table on fire!" She laughed, that same snorting laugh, and my cheeks ached from grinning. My heart thumped like I'd run here. I grabbed her sleeve, let go, grabbed it again. "Tell me everything. No, wait, coffee. Do you have time? Forget it, you're making time." Somebody's cart rattled past. I barely noticed. My basket swung wildly on my elbow, and I realized I was humming, loudly, some song from the school dance, and I didn't stop even when she joined in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum at 5:42, eighteen minutes from lock-up, and I'm restocking cough drops at a speed that's frankly unnecessary. My sneakers squeak on the tile like they're cheering. "Happy Thanksgiving, Mr. Alvarez!" I tell him, too loud, and he laughs and says I've had too much coffee, which I haven't, I've had one, hours ago. My hands won't stay still. I drum the counter, flip the sign to CLOSED early, then flip it back because it's not time, then grin at the sign anyway. Four days. Four whole days of my mother's kitchen, my cousins' awful singing, pie for breakfast. I catch myself humming the register's beep. My cheeks ache. Somebody drops a basket of hand warmers and I dive for them, sliding the last few feet on my knees like a kid on a wet floor, and I'm still laughing when I hand them back, my heart knocking against my ribs like it wants out the door first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board said Gate B47, boarding in eleven minutes, and I laughed out loud at it, a big honking laugh that made a man with a neck pillow flinch. I was already running. My duffel slapped my hip in rhythm, my sneakers squeaked on the polished floor, and my lungs felt like they'd been filled with fizzing soda. "Sorry! Coming through! Love your scarf!" I called to a stranger, and meant it. On the moving walkway I took the stairs-of-air two steps at a time, grinning at my own reflection in the window, hair wild, cheeks hot. Who sprints through Terminal B holding a half-eaten pretzel above their head like a torch? Me, apparently. My heart drummed against my ribs and my fingers tingled. If I missed it, I'd tell the story for years. If I made it, same. I skidded to the gate, slapped my pass on the counter, and sang, "Hello, beautiful people, I'm here!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol pried the lid off the paint can with a spoon handle and whooped when the yellow inside caught the window light. She didn't bother with the tray. She dunked the roller, dragged it up the wall in one huge swooping stripe, and spun around to show the empty room. "Look at that! Look at it!" Her sneakers squeaked on the drop cloth as she danced a little shuffle, paint speckling her forearms, her ponytail, one eyebrow. Her heart thumped like she'd run up stairs. She hummed, then sang, badly, then laughed at the sound of herself echoing off bare walls. Two hours past lunch, she realized she hadn't eaten, and her stomach didn't matter at all. She grabbed her phone with a sticky thumb and left her sister a voicemail: "Come see it. No, come now. It's the color of lemon pie and I'm going to do the ceiling too!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the porch rail and I whooped so loud the neighbor's dog started barking back. I couldn't stay in the chair. My bare feet slapped the wet boards, and I leaned out past the eave until the rain hammered my scalp and ran cold down my spine, and I laughed with my mouth wide open, tasting pennies and cut grass. "Did you see that one?" I shouted at nobody, at the whole street. My hands were drumming my thighs, my knees bouncing, my heart going double-time against my ribs. Lightning split the sky pink-white, and I counted out loud, "One, two, th—" and the boom cut me off, and I spun in a full circle, soaked shirt slapping my stomach. I snatched my lemonade, found it diluted with rain, and drank it anyway, grinning. Tomorrow I'd be hoarse. I didn't care. I wanted the storm to last all night, and I wanted to be loud inside it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tire lever slips twice before I notice my hands have gone cold and slick. Somewhere behind the shelves, the garage's side door clicks, and I stop breathing to listen. Footsteps. Probably Mr. Alvarez from unit three, probably just him. I whisper, "Hello?" and it comes out thin, a cracked little thing I'd never admit to. Nobody answers. My heart is knocking so hard the wrench trembles against the chain. I pretend to examine the derailleur, but I'm really watching the strip of dark under the shelving, counting seconds, ready to grab the bike and run. The fluorescent tube overhead buzzes and flickers, and I flinch so badly I knock over the can of degreaser. It rolls, loud as a bell, across the concrete. A cat trots out, tail high, unbothered. I laugh, too loud, and sit down on the cold floor because my knees won't hold me. My shirt is soaked through. I pick up the lever again and keep my back to the wall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The streetlight above the shelter buzzed and went out just as the first fat drops hit the glass. I checked my phone again: 11:52, the next bus not until 12:20. My thumb left a wet smear on the screen. Wind shoved a flattened cup down the road, and I flinched at the scrape of it, then pretended I hadn't. Behind me the dark between the buildings seemed to lean closer. I pulled my hood up, then down, so I could hear. "Come on, come on," I whispered, and my voice came out thin and cracked. My knees wouldn't hold still. Thunder rolled somewhere past the rooftops and my hand shot out to grip the cold metal bench, knuckles pale. A car slowed, headlights sweeping over me, and I stopped breathing until it passed. I counted the seconds between the lightning and the rumble, lost count, started again. My heart knocked against my ribs so loudly I thought someone might hear it over the rain.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box smells of cedar and cellar damp, and I've set it on the kitchen table with the overhead light on, though it's noon. I lift the first bundle by its string and my fingers won't quite close; the paper trembles like it's alive. Mother's slanted hand.
