text: The train hissed out of Hanoi Station's far platform, and Marta stood in the rain with a dead phone and a suitcase wheel that had snapped on the steps. She had no words for any of it. A woman selling bánh mì from a cart looked at her, said something quick, and pushed a plastic stool toward her with her foot. Then she took the address Marta had scribbled on a napkin, frowned at it, and shouted across the street until a motorbike driver came over. The woman tucked a warm paper-wrapped sandwich into Marta's coat pocket and waved off the coins. Marta pressed her palm flat against her chest, where something loose and shaky had settled. 'Cảm ơn,' she said, mangling the tones, and bowed twice, then a third time. Her eyes stung. On the back of the motorbike, suitcase wedged between her knees, she kept twisting around to look back until the cart was just a bright smudge in the rain, and she held the sandwich against her ribs like something fragile.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit hits the tall grass at a dead run, ears flapping inside out, and I let the leash slip from my fingers and just stand there with my palms pressed flat against my chest. Eleven months ago the vet said maybe not even the summer. Now he's flinging himself sideways after a bumblebee, tumbling, popping up again, tongue lolling like a pink flag. My throat goes tight and I laugh anyway, a wet, cracked sound. 'Look at you,' I call, too quietly for him to hear. 'Look at you, you idiot.' The sun is warm on the back of my neck. I crouch and pull a burr from my sock, then forget to stand up, because he's galloping back, all mud and joy, and I open my arms before he's even close. He crashes into me. I bury my face in his neck, breathe in dirt and clover, and whisper, 'Thank you, thank you,' to nobody, to the field, to the slow gold afternoon that keeps letting us have this.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells like floor wax and burnt coffee, and I stand on a taped X with my cello case still half unzipped because Marguerite has just pulled a folding chair up beside me. Nobody asked her to. She's seventy-nine and drove through the rain. "Take it from the bridge again," she says, and I do, and my bow wobbles on the long note, and nobody sighs. Mr. Okafor taps his baton on the stand and counts us in a third time as if it's the first. My throat has gone tight, so I laugh instead and say, "You're all so patient with me," and it comes out thin. After the last chord, I press my palm flat against my sternum, where it's warm and a little shaky. Then I stack the chairs against the wall by myself, humming, and I stay until the lights are the only ones left on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta found the coffee can of mismatched screws first, and she held it against her chest a moment before setting it in the keep box. Dust lifted in the slanted light from the window Dennis had never once washed. She ran her thumb along the bench where decades of his forearms had worn the wood to a dull shine, and her throat tightened, but she was smiling. "You old hoarder," she said softly, pulling open a drawer. Inside, in his blocky pencil: a chisel set labeled MARTA, FOR WHEN YOU STOP BORROWING MINE. She laughed, then had to sit on the stool. Her hands, steady all morning, trembled as she unrolled the canvas. Every edge was honed. She remembered the Saturdays he'd spent teaching her to square a joint, the patience in his big, scarred hands. She tucked the chisels under her arm like something alive and left the radio murmuring the ballgame. "I'll take good care of them, Den," she told the empty room. "All of it. I promise."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the registrar's office smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Mina sat on the bench with her thumbs pressed into her knees to keep them still. Eleven o'clock, the sign said. At 10:58 she took out the folded note from Mr. Okafor, the one he had slipped into her textbook after the last tutoring session, and read the scrawled line again: *You did the work. Whatever it says, remember that.* She smoothed it flat against her thigh. When the clerk finally pinned the sheet to the corkboard, Mina didn't rush. She let two others push ahead, then stepped up and found her number. Her breath left her in a long, shaky stream. Pass. She pressed her palm to the cool wall, laughing quietly, eyes stinging. Then she pulled out her phone and typed to her mother, fingers clumsy: *Thank you for the night shifts. Come to dinner tomorrow. I'm cooking.* She walked out slowly, holding the note against her chest the whole way down the stairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The ridge went copper, then rust, and Mara slowed instead of hurrying. Her knees ached from eleven miles, but she stopped at the switchback and pressed her palm flat against the warm trunk of a pine, keeping it there a long moment. "Okay," she said aloud, softly, to nobody. "Okay. Thank you." Below her the valley held the last light like water in a bowl. She thought of the stranger at the trailhead that morning who had pointed out the shortcut past the washed-out bridge, and how without it she'd be stumbling now in full dark. Her headlamp sat in her pocket, still unused; she wanted a few more minutes of this dusk. Her chest felt loose and wide, her breath unhurried, her eyes stinging a little in the cold. She unscrewed her bottle, drank the last of the water, and tipped the empty bottle toward the horizon like a toast before starting down, smiling the whole way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth now, stained translucent at one corner where decades of butter had settled. Mira propped it against the flour canister and read her grandmother's slanted hand again: knead till it pushes back. She pressed the heel of her palm into the dough, folded, turned, pressed, and her shoulders loosened with each pass. When the kitchen filled with the smell of yeast and warmth, she stopped and stood very still, one floury hand flat against her sternum. "Okay, Nana," she whispered, laughing a little, her voice catching on the second word. She slid the loaf from the oven, tapped the bottom, and heard the hollow knock she'd been promised. She didn't wait for it to cool. She tore off the heel, burned her fingertips, and ate it standing there, eyes closed, then carefully wiped the card with her thumb and tucked it back into its plastic sleeve as though it might break.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was comparing two bags of rice in the hardware-and-grocery shop on Delmar Street when someone said her name, and she turned to find Teodor, thinner now, a gray streak in his beard. Her hand went to her chest. "You lent me your chemistry notes," she blurted, before hello, before anything. "Junior year. I would have failed." He laughed and said he barely remembered. She did. She remembered the blue spiral notebook, the careful diagrams, the way she'd passed the exam and kept going. Her eyes stung, and she blinked at the shelf of canned beans until it steadied. She set the rice down, forgetting it, and gripped his forearm with both hands. "Let me buy you coffee. Please. There's a place next door." Her voice wobbled on the last word. When he nodded, her shoulders dropped an inch, and she realized she was smiling so widely her cheeks ached, the cart abandoned in the aisle behind them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy emptied out by four, and I was mopping the same square of tile twice just to stay moving when Dolores from the register slid a paper cup of coffee onto the counter beside me. "Go home early," she said. "I've got close." I stood there with the mop handle going warm in my fist. She'd worked the last three holidays herself, and I knew it. "You sure?" came out thinner than I meant. She waved me off without looking up. My eyes stung, so I busied myself wringing the mop, then hung my smock on the hook slowly, smoothing the collar like it mattered. At the door I turned back and pressed my hand flat against my chest, laughing at myself. "I'll bring you pie. The pecan. Don't argue." Outside the cold hit my face, and I realized I was smiling at the parking lot, at the dark sky, at my keys, all the way to the car, where I sat a minute, warming my hands around her coffee.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The tram doors opened at Terminal C with eleven minutes to spare, and I ran, my rolling bag clattering behind me. Gate 47 was a mile away. Then a man in an airport vest stepped into my path, and I almost cried out, but he only held up a hand-lettered sign and said, "Denver? Hop on, I've got a cart." I climbed on, knees shaking, my chest still heaving. He took the long corridor at a tilt, beeping at strollers, and I kept pressing my palm flat against my sternum, laughing in short breaths. "I don't even know your name," I said. "Marcus." At the gate the agent was already lifting the phone. "Wait," I called, voice cracking. I turned back and took Marcus's hand in both of mine, holding it too long. "You just gave me my sister's wedding," I said. My eyes stung. He shrugged, smiling, and I walked down the jet bridge feeling light enough to float.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol pressed the lid onto the last can of pale yellow and stood in the middle of the room, roller still dripping in her hand. Her brother's old drop cloths covered the floor, and the ladder he'd hauled over at seven that morning leaned in the corner. He had gone downstairs to wash the brushes, whistling off-key, and she could hear the faucet running. Her shoulders ached pleasantly. She touched the wall near the window, where the paint was still tacky, and left her fingertip there a moment longer than she needed to. "Danny," she called, her voice coming out thicker than she meant, "stay for dinner. I mean it. I'm making the good noodles." She wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist and left a yellow smear across her cheek. When he appeared in the doorway, drying his hands on his jeans, she was already dragging two chairs into the sunlit room, setting them side by side so they could look at it together.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the tin roof just as Marguerite lowered herself into the porch swing, and she laughed out loud, a short surprised sound. Six weeks of cracked dirt and brown tomato vines, and now this. She tucked her bare feet up beneath her, let the cold spray from the railing freckle her shins, and did not move to wipe it away. Thunder rolled across the field, and she pressed her palm flat against her chest as if to steady something there. 'Well, look at that,' she murmured to the yard, to the dog asleep against her ankle, to no one. 'Look at you all.' The smell of wet dust rose around her. She closed her eyes, breathed it in slowly, and held it until her ribs ached. Then she reached for the mug of tea gone lukewarm beside her, lifted it toward the gray sky like a toast, and drank.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The torque wrench is Dana's, but it's already in my fist. She's upstairs, and the garage smells of chain lube and damp concrete. I tell myself I'm only borrowing it, though I've turned it over twice, thumbing the clicker like a coin I plan to keep. On the shared shelf sits the good cassette tool, the one Imre labeled in tidy marker, and I slide it behind my toolbox without deciding to. My pulse is loud in my ears. My bike hangs in the stand, its crank half off, and I keep glancing at the door. When Imre comes down and asks if I've seen it, I say, "Nope, probably in the other bin," too fast, too bright. I help him look. My palms are slick on the rag. Later I'll wipe the cassette tool clean and tell myself it just needs one more week with me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as the old woman beside me shook out her one umbrella, and I felt my jaw tighten. There was only one dry bench, and I had slid onto the middle of it with my bag spread out like a claim. 'Room for you,' I said, not moving the bag an inch. She stayed standing. Wind pushed the rain sideways, and I tucked my feet up, pulled my coat over the bakery box on my lap, the last two cinnamon rolls I'd bought, and I'd already decided nobody was getting one. My stomach growled; I tore a corner off anyway and ate it fast, turning my shoulder. When the bus lights swam out of the gray, I stood first, elbowed ahead, and counted the seats in my head, wanting the one by the heater, the one with the window, all of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid hasn't finished hitting the floor before my hands are in, scooping the envelopes against my chest like they might be taken. My sister is in the doorway asking if she can have just the ones from Dad, and I say, "I haven't sorted them yet," too fast, my voice tight. I turn my shoulder to block her view. The attic is hot, and sweat slides down my spine, but I keep stacking: the blue airmail ones on my left knee, the perfumed ones under my thigh, the thick ones with photographs tucked beneath the sweater beside me. She reaches for a single postcard, and my fingers clamp on it before I can think. "Later," I say. She leaves. I count them, forty-one, then count again, my pulse thudding in my ears, and I still wish there were more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta heard Dennis's knock and kept her hand flat on the garage door a second longer than she needed to. The ladder hung on its hooks behind her, twenty-four feet of aluminum she'd paid too much for and used twice. "Just for the gutters," Dennis said, rubbing his neck. "Saturday. I'll have it back by dinner." Her jaw tightened. She thought of the scratch he might leave on the rail, the way he'd lean it wrong, the way it might not come back at all. "Oh, it's, well, I might need it myself," she said, too fast, her voice thin and bright. Her eyes slid to the new leaf blower on the shelf, and she shifted to block it. "Maybe next week?" Dennis nodded slowly and glanced past her shoulder at the hooks. Marta's palms were damp. After he left she stood there, counting the rungs, and didn't lower the door until his porch light clicked off.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The doorbell isn't due for twenty minutes, and I've already lifted the lid on the short ribs three times. Just one piece, I tell the empty kitchen, to check the salt. My fingers come away slick and I lick them, then pull a second strip of meat from the pot, the one from the thickest end, the one with the crust. Six guests, eight ribs. I count again. The tray of roasted potatoes sits by the window, and I rearrange them so the gaps look natural, so nobody notices the crispiest corner pieces are gone from my own mouth. My stomach isn't even empty. It tightens anyway, hungry for more. When I portion the gravy into the boat, I tilt the ladle back and keep the darkest, glossiest spoonful for the little bowl hidden behind the bread box. Mine. The buzzer sounds and I chew fast, wiping my chin with my wrist, calling out in a bright voice, "Coming! Just finishing up!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, a number I didn't know, and I wiped my greasy fingers on my jeans before grabbing it. "Yes, hello?" My voice came out too bright. The man said something about an unclaimed estate, a distant uncle, forty thousand dollars. I was already pacing, pulling open drawers for a pen, my pulse thudding in my ears. "Forty? Is it only forty? Could there be more, like, other accounts?" He hesitated. I didn't. I pressed the phone tighter, my mouth dry, my tongue running over my teeth. Some small voice said hang up, but I pulled the cold leftover pizza toward me and shoved a second slice in, chewing fast, barely tasting it. "Okay, okay, and what do you need from me? My account number? Sure. Sure, I can get that. Just tell me how soon. And whose name is the rest under? Mine too, right? All of it mine?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack for fourteen months, and I still ran my thumb along its spine as I slid it across the desk. "Oh, it's, uh, a little late," I said, too brightly. The librarian typed, frowned, typed again. Behind her, a cart of other people's returns waited, and I caught myself eyeing a thick atlas on top, wondering if she'd notice me tucking it under my arm too. My mouth was dry. "How much?" She turned the screen. I didn't look at the number; I looked at the shelf of new arrivals by the door, my fingers already twitching toward it. "Could I renew this one instead?" I asked, pointing at the book I'd just handed her. She stared. My cheeks went hot, but I didn't take my hand back. "And maybe check out those three? Just for the weekend." My tote bag was already open on my shoulder, wide as a mouth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers had barely set down the last box when Dana started counting. Four closets' worth of coats, she thought, wedging a third armchair against the radiator, though the studio had only one window and a kitchenette the width of her shoulders. "Just leave that one," she told the younger mover, hand flat on a crate marked ANTIQUES, her voice quick and tight. "And that. And the lamps." Her fingers curled around a brass candlestick as if someone might pry it free. In the hallway, the neighbor's cart held a free bookshelf with a sign, and Dana's pulse jumped; she dragged it in before the man could finish asking if she wanted it. Now the bed was buried under stacked rugs, and she had to turn sideways to reach the sink. Her mouth felt dry, her chest warm and full. She eyed the empty strip of wall by the door, already measuring it for one more thing, and whispered, "Mine," to no one at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench slats, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and I sat down beside it like we'd arranged to meet. A jogger passed. I stared at the pond until her footsteps faded, then slid the wallet onto my knee. My thumb was already working the fold. Cash first: five twenties, maybe six, and I counted them twice, lips moving, though nobody was close enough to hear. Behind the bills, a second slot. A card edge, gold-colored. My mouth had gone wet. I swallowed, glanced at the license, at the smiling face and the address only eleven blocks away, and I turned the card so the photo faced my leg. 'Finders keepers,' I muttered, too cheerfully, to a pigeon. It cocked its head. My pulse thudded in my ears. I tucked the bills into my sock, then, hesitating only a second, the gold card after them, and zipped my jacket to the chin. The wallet I left on the bench, lighter now, and I wondered what else I'd missed in it as I walked away, slowly, glancing back twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marta clung to the lane rope at the shallow end while the instructor turned to help the teenager beside her. "Kick from the hip," the instructor said over her shoulder, and Marta nodded, though she'd already stopped listening. Her fingers had gone white on the rope. Eight weeks in, and the others floated on their backs like leaves, and she wanted that, all of it, now. She pushed off, swallowed chlorine, coughed, and went again before her breath had settled. "Once more," she told the instructor, who had just said time was up. "Just one more length. Please. I'll stay after." Her heart thudded against her ribs. Water streamed from her nose. When the next class filed in, she stayed pressed against the wall, goggles fogged, eyeing the clock above the lifeguard chair and reaching for the rope again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The packet said twelve inches between tomato seedlings. I put them six. "They'll figure it out," I told the empty yard, kneeling in dirt that was already soaking through my jeans. Then I wedged a seventh where the path was supposed to go. My hands were quick, almost shaky, tearing open zucchini, beans, carrots, cucumbers, one packet after another, and I poured more into my palm than the diagram allowed. Just in case, I whispered. I pictured the whole fence line heavy with fruit, baskets stacked on the porch, nothing left for the neighbors to peek over and admire. My stomach actually growled. When Mrs. Alvarez leaned over the fence and asked if she could have a few peppers someday, my jaw tightened and I said, "We'll see how they do," already counting them in my head. After she left, I dug up the last bare corner and crammed in more squash, sweat stinging my eyes, still not satisfied.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus kept his pen pressed so hard against the notepad that it tore the top sheet. On the screen, Dana clicked to the slide with the projected savings, and the number glowed there, fat and round, with her name tucked under it in small gray type. The conference room smelled of burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. He slid the last two donuts from the box toward his own side of the table without looking at them. "Great work," he said, a beat too late, his jaw tight around the words. His knee bounced under the table. When the VP nodded and murmured, "This could be the quarter's headline," Marcus felt heat climb his neck, as if something had been lifted out of his own pockets. He was already composing the email in his head, the one that began with "Building on my earlier groundwork," and he leaned forward, hand raised, before Dana had even finished her sentence. "Quick question," he said. "Whose budget does this come out of?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The envelope on the passenger seat slid every time Dale took a curve, and every time he slapped a hand down on it like it might escape. Two a.m., the highway empty, and he'd already counted the bills twice at the gas station under the buzzing light, thumb wetted, lips moving. Eleven hundred and forty. His brother had said take what you need from the till, and Dale had taken it all, then looked at the register and wished the drawer were deeper. Now his jaw ached from clenching, and his stomach churned with something hungry despite the burger wrappers crumpled at his feet. A diner sign glowed past the exit; he thought of the tip jar by its register and his foot eased off the gas. 'Just a few more,' he muttered, and laughed, dry and quick. The radio hissed. He turned onto the off-ramp anyway, fingers already drumming the envelope, checking the dark lot for cameras.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Aunt Delphine's room smells like lemon wipes and warm plastic, and I'm standing at the foot of her bed with my hands already in my coat pockets, counting. The monitor beeps. She says my name, thin and papery, and I say, "Hey, Aunt Del, you look good," without looking at her face. I'm looking at the dresser, where her ring, the square emerald, sits in a little dish beside the cup of ice chips. My mouth is dry. My pulse is loud in my ears. She asks if I ate, and I say yes, though I'm thinking about the sapphire brooch in her closet at home and who has the key. When the nurse steps out, I lean in to fix her blanket and let my fingers rest near the dish. "Does Mom know where you keep the paperwork?" I ask, too lightly. Aunt Del closes her eyes. My palm is sweating. I stay another hour, just in case she says more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell hasn't rung yet, and I'm already holding the good spot by the fence, elbow out, shoulder angled so Dana's mom can't slide in front of me. In my coat pocket my thumb keeps pressing the foil corner of the bag of clementines I bought for Wren, and I've peeled two for myself on the walk over, pith still under my nails. When the doors open, Wren runs up with the class's leftover cupcake, a whole one, wrapped in a napkin. 'Can I have half?' I ask, too bright, already reaching. She hesitates. I laugh, but my mouth is watering and my hand doesn't drop. 'Just the frosting side,' I say. Behind us someone offers the other parents a tray of extra cookies, and I'm turning before she finishes the sentence, my palm out, counting how many might be left, wondering if taking three would show.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By seven a.m. Dolores had already moved the oak dresser twice, angling it so the morning sun caught the brass pulls. The price tag said $40, but she'd scribbled over it and written $120 in marker. A young woman ran her hand along the drawer and asked if it was negotiable. "It's solid wood," Dolores said, too quickly, her jaw tight. "Dovetail joints. You won't find that at a store." The woman offered eighty. Dolores's palms prickled, and she felt her pulse in her throat as she eyed the woman's purse, the good leather one. "One-ten," she said. When the woman shrugged and walked off, Dolores stared after her, then pulled out the cash box and counted the bills again with her thumb, though she knew the total. Her neighbor's table of chairs sat priced at five dollars apiece. She frowned at it, then slid her rocking chair's tag from $25 to $65, wondering who else might pay more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta knelt under the sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, water dripping down her wrist, and the plumber's quote folded in her back pocket like an insult. Two hundred and eighty dollars to tighten a nut. She wasn't paying it. She wrapped the tape around the threads once, then again, then ten more times, fat as a bandage, because tape was cheap and she'd take every last turn of it. The drip slowed. She grabbed the wrench anyway and cranked until her knuckles burned. 'Not one more drop,' she muttered, 'not one.' The bucket beneath was half full, and she eyed it, calculating whether she could water the ferns with it, the neighbor's too, maybe, and charge nothing but a favor. Her brother's spare wrench lay in the garage; she'd never returned it, and now she pocketed his box of washers too, sliding the whole handful in, unwilling to leave even the dented ones behind. Her stomach tightened pleasantly as the pipe stayed dry.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope from the Revenue Office sat on the counter, and Marguerite pressed her thumb along its edge before she slit it, already tilting it toward the light as if the number might show through. Her mouth had gone wet. She read the first line, skipped to the bottom, and found it: a refund of $2,314. "Well," she said, too loudly, to the empty kitchen. "Well, well." Her pulse thudded in her fingertips. She was already spending it: the new sofa, the weekend in Lisbon, the good knives, and then the sofa again, a bigger one. Was it really only that much? She flipped the page over, searching for a second line, a missed credit, a mistake in her favor. Next door, the neighbor's radio played through the wall. She ran her tongue over her teeth, took out a pen, and began copying the figure onto the back of the electric bill, adding a zero just to see how it looked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The market in Hanoi smelled of charcoal and star anise, and I didn't know a single word to ask for anything, so I pointed. Pointed at the grilled pork, the sticky rice, the little pandan cakes, the mango sliced into petals. The vendor smiled and held up two fingers; I held up five. My stomach was full, my pockets were not empty, and still my hands kept reaching. I tucked a bag under each arm, then asked for one more of everything, miming a wide circle with both palms. 'Thank you, thank you,' I said, too loudly, as if volume were vocabulary. She laughed and added a free banana. I took it before she finished offering. On the curb, grease on my wrist, I tore into the second skewer while eyeing the third, counting how many stalls remained before the lane ended. A man at the next table glanced at my pile. I angled my shoulder over it, chewing faster, and wondered whether I could carry any more back to the hotel without anyone noticing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the field with a stick bigger than his head, and my hands curled into fists in my jacket pockets. When the neighbor's girl tossed him her tennis ball, he dropped my stick for hers, and my jaw tightened. "Here," I called, too sharp, "Biscuit, here, come." He didn't. I crouched, pulled the jerky from my pocket, then the second piece, then the third, fanning them out in my palm like a hand of cards. My chest felt hot and cramped. Every bounding leap he gave her was one I'd somehow been shorted. "He's mine," I muttered, to no one, to the wind flattening the grass. When he finally trotted over, panting, I clamped his collar and held on a moment too long, rubbing his ears until he squirmed. The girl waved. I turned my shoulder and kept the whole bag of jerky tucked under my arm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite stood at the front of the church hall with the sheet music pinched in her fist, and when the pianist reached the bridge she let the soprano line trail off mid-bar. "Sorry, could we take that again? Just my part," she said, too brightly. Folding chairs scraped. Behind her, Dolores cleared her throat, the one with the shy little solo in the second verse. Marguerite's pulse thudded in her ears, her palms damp against the paper. She had penciled her own name beside that solo, small, beneath Dolores's, then rubbed it half out, then written it again. "It's only that the high note sits so nicely for me," she said, smiling until her cheeks ached. The radiator ticked. A tray of lemon bars sat on the side table, and she realized she had been edging toward it, three already gone, her fingers hovering for a fourth. "Again, from the bridge?" she asked, and did not look at Dolores at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marek's sister said take whatever helps, so I brought three boxes and told myself one would be plenty. By noon the third was full. Sawdust clung to my sweaty forearms as I slid the good chisels, the ones with the boxwood handles, into my jacket pocket, then went back and added the brass square. Her car pulled up outside and my heart knocked. I dropped a rag over the box and said, loudly, "Just sorting the junk, nothing worth keeping." She nodded, eyes wet, and picked up a bent coffee tin of screws. I almost offered to carry it out for her. Instead I watched her hands, counting what she touched, and my jaw ached from clenching. When she turned to the window, I tucked the little block plane under my arm, still warm from the sun on the bench, and told myself he'd have wanted me to have it. My own garage already had a plane. I took it anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The list wasn't up yet, but Marisol had already claimed the spot directly in front of the glass case, elbowing her bag onto the floor so no one could stand closer. Her thumbnail had worn a pale groove into her lower lip. "Ninety-six," she muttered, then, quieter, "no, ninety-eight. Ninety-eight is possible." A boy beside her sighed that he only needed a pass, and she angled her shoulder away as though his modest wish might be catching. When the secretary finally pinned the sheet up, Marisol's eyes skipped her own line and dropped to the number beside the name above hers, and the one above that. Her stomach tightened around the top of the page. Ninety-four. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She read it again, jaw working, already counting the four points she'd lost, the ones someone else seemed to be holding in their hands, and she didn't hear the boy's whoop at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The sun was a thin orange coin on the ridge, and I should have turned around at the last switchback, but the next bend promised one more overlook, and then one more after that. My thumb kept pressing the camera button even though the memory card was nearly full; I deleted yesterday's shots to make room for these. "Just one more," I muttered, the way you bargain with a cupboard at midnight. My friend's voice on the radio said the car was a mile and a half back. I told her ten minutes, though I knew it was thirty. Cold crept into my fingers and my stomach growled, yet I pulled out the last granola bar and ate it fast, hunched over, as though someone might ask for half. The valley turned the color of peaches. I wanted all of it, every ember of light, stuffed in my pockets. When the first star showed, I swore at it, and kept climbing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma's index card is stained with butter, and it says makes two loaves in her slanted pen. I've already doubled it. The dough rises fat and glossy in the big steel bowl, and I press a knuckle into it, watching it spring back, and my mouth floods. My sister's coming at six. I told her I'd bring one loaf. Out of the oven they crack and sing on the rack, and the smell fills the whole kitchen until my stomach clenches. I tear the heel off the first one, burn my fingertips, and don't stop. Steam, salt, sweet crust. I swallow and reach again before I've finished. "Just testing," I say to the empty room, low and quick. Then I slide the smaller loaf behind the flour canister, tug the dish towel over the bigger one's torn end, and think about what I'll tell her. Maybe the oven ran hot. Maybe only one rose.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus had two baskets hooked on his arm, both heavy, when someone said his name beside the discount bin of cashmere scarves. Dana Whitfield, from tenth-grade chemistry, thinner now, a cart with one carton of eggs. "Marcus! Wow." He smiled and kept his free hand sliding along the bin, tucking a grey scarf under his elbow, then a navy one. "Dana. Great to see you, really," he said, too fast, eyes flicking to her cart, then to the last red scarf near her wrist. His palm was damp. "You doing okay? Still in town?" She talked about her mother's move; he nodded without hearing, already leaning so his shoulder blocked the bin. When she reached toward the red one, his fingers got there first. "Oh, sorry, did you want this?" he asked, not letting go. Her laugh was kind. He squeezed the pile tighter against his ribs, wondering whether the clerk would notice if he took the gloves too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock on Christmas Eve, Marcus had counted the register drawer three times, and still he slid the last of the tip jar's crumpled fives into his apron instead of the shared envelope. The bakery smelled of burnt sugar and wet wool. A woman asked if there were any day-old loaves left to give away, and he heard himself say, "Sold out," though six sat behind him in a paper sack he'd already tucked beneath the counter for home. His jaw ached from clenching. When Dana offered to split the final tray of cinnamon rolls, he took four before she'd finished the sentence, then reached for a fifth. "Boss said we could," he lied, voice too bright. His palms were damp. Outside, the lights went out one by one down the street, and he kept wiping the clean counter, thinking about the envelope, the sack, the rolls, and whether anyone would count them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marcus hit the end of Concourse B at a jog, rolling bag clattering, and veered into the Sky Lounge snack kiosk anyway. Gate 42 was a ten-minute walk and boarding closed in twelve. He snatched three bags of pretzels, then a fourth, then two chocolate bars from the rack, and his hand hovered over the premium jerky. "Those too," he said, too quickly, sliding them onto the counter. His pulse thudded in his throat. The cashier mentioned that the lounge's free buffet was open to ticketed passengers, and Marcus's jaw tightened; he'd already paid for this. He stuffed everything into his jacket pockets until the zipper strained, then grabbed a handful of napkins and a stack of sugar packets from the cart as well. Overhead, the speaker crackled with his name. His stomach felt hollow, wanting, though he'd eaten an hour ago. He ran, pockets bulging, pretzels crunching against his ribs, and still glanced back at the pastry case, wishing he'd taken more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pried the lid off the third gallon of Sea Salt Mist and tipped it over the tray, though the first two sat barely touched by the window. The hardware clerk had said one coat would do. She wanted three. Her roller dripped on the drop cloth, and she dragged it back up the wall, pressing hard until the old beige disappeared and her shoulder burned. Her sister called from the hallway, asking if she could borrow the leftover paint for her porch chairs. "There isn't any left," Marta said, too quickly, and slid her foot against the stacked cans behind her. Her mouth felt dry. She counted the cans again, four unopened, and tucked the receipt into her back pocket so no one would see how many she'd bought. When her sister left, Marta exhaled, rolled a fourth fat stripe across the wall, and smiled at the wet shine, already planning the closet, the hallway, the guest room next.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite dragged the last crate of peaches onto the porch just as the first thunderclap rattled the screen door, and she didn't go inside. She sat on the top step with the crate wedged between her knees, rain spitting cold against her shins. Her sister's truck would be coming up the gravel soon, and her sister would want half. Marguerite bit into a peach, juice running down her wrist, and reached for another before she'd swallowed. "They're not even that good," she muttered to the empty yard, then ate a third anyway. Lightning whitened the orchard. Her stomach ached, tight and round, and still her fingers counted the fruit left: eleven, ten. She pulled her apron over the crate like a blanket over a sleeping child. When headlights swung across the fence, she tucked two peaches into her pockets, kicked the crate behind the rocking chair, and called out, "Only a few survived the wind!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tire lever slips twice before I notice my hands won't stop shaking. Mrs. Ortega's lawnmower sits under a tarp on her side of the garage, and the radio she always left on the shelf is silent, its dial still tuned to her station. I'm fixing Dad's bike, the green Schwinn, though nobody will ride it. The chain is rusted stiff, and I keep working oil into each link as if it's urgent. Someone's footsteps cross the gravel outside and I freeze, wrench in the air, until they fade. Then I find his glove in the basket, the palm still molded to the grip, and I sit down on the cold concrete with it pressed against my mouth. "Just one more turn," I tell the pedal, my voice cracked and small. My chest feels hollowed out, like a tube with no air. I stand, wipe my face with a greasy wrist, and spin the wheel again, listening to it tick.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof, and I don't move from the bench. Wind drags a gum wrapper along the curb. I'm holding his umbrella, the green one with the bent rib, and I haven't opened it. My thumb keeps finding the worn spot on the handle where his hand went. A woman beside me says the 14 is running late, and I nod a beat too slow, as if her words had to cross a long room. My throat is tight, my chest hollow, like someone scooped it out and left the shell. Rain slants under the roof and soaks my left sleeve. I let it. When the bus finally groans around the corner, its lights smearing across the wet street, I stand, then sit again. 'Sorry,' I tell the driver through the folding doors, 'wrong one,' though it isn't. I listen to it pull away. Then I say his name once, quietly, to the rain.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid sticks, then gives, and the smell of her lavender drawer liner rises out and hits me square in the chest. I sit down on the hallway floor because my knees decide it for me. Rubber-banded bundles, the bands gone brittle. I pick up the first envelope and her slanted handwriting spells my name, and I put it down again, flat, like it might bruise. I try to read one aloud, to be brisk about it, but my voice cracks on 'Dearest' and I stop and press the heel of my hand against my mouth. The radiator ticks. Somewhere a neighbor's television laughs. I fold the letter along its old creases, unfold it, fold it again. My tea has gone cold beside me, untouched since morning. 'Okay,' I say to the empty hall, then again, quieter, 'okay.' I cannot make myself sort anything. I just hold the stack against my ribs and breathe through my teeth until the light in the window turns gray.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale was still in yesterday's shirt when the knock came, and he stood in the hallway a moment before he remembered what his hands were for. Mr. Okafor from next door stood on the porch, cap in his fingers, asking if the aluminum ladder might be spared for the gutters. "The ladder," Dale said. His voice came out rough, like something dragged over gravel. "Yes. It's in the garage." He walked there slowly, the cold concrete biting through his socks, and stopped at the wall where it hung. Her gardening gloves still sat on the rung, stiff, shaped to her fingers. He lifted the ladder down without touching them. They fell anyway, and he crouched, holding them against his chest, breath catching in a hitch he couldn't swallow. "Sorry," he said to the floor. "Take it. Take whatever you need." Mr. Okafor said nothing, only set a warm hand on his shoulder, and Dale stared at the dust where the gloves had been, unable to stand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions are already translucent when I realize I've set out five plates, and I'm holding the fifth against my chest like it might tell me something. Seven o'clock, they said. It's ten past six. I put the plate back in the cupboard, gently, as if it could wake. The recipe card is in her handwriting, the loops of the g's leaning into each other, and I read the same line about cumin three times without it becoming words. My hands smell of garlic. I keep wiping them on the apron, which still has her flour stain on the pocket, and I can't make myself wash it. The pot hisses. I stand there with the wooden spoon and my throat shuts like a fist, so when the radio host laughs I switch him off. "Fine," I say to the empty kitchen, my voice cracked down the middle. "It's fine. It's just soup." Then I lean on the counter until my knees remember how to hold me, and I stir.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, a string of digits Marguerite didn't know, and she let it ring four times while she stared at the casserole dish no one had come to collect. Her thumb found the screen on its own. "Hello?" It came out as a croak, and she cleared her throat and tried again. A man's voice, polite, said he was calling from the county office about a vehicle. Her knees gave, and she sat on the linoleum with her back against the cabinet, the cold seeping through her cardigan. "Yes, that's his truck," she said slowly. "No. No, he won't be coming for it." Her free hand pressed flat against her sternum as if to hold something in. The man stammered an apology. She looked at the hook by the door, where the keys still hung, and heard herself ask him, very quietly, to please say his name again, just so the line would stay open a little longer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book has been in my backpack for fourteen months, and the spine still smells like his apartment. I stand at the returns desk with both hands flat on the counter because otherwise they shake. The librarian scans the barcode, and the screen blinks a number I don't read. "Three hundred and something," she says gently. I nod. I say, "He lent me his card. It's his name on it," and then my voice goes somewhere I can't follow, and I just stand there, mouth open, breathing like I've climbed stairs. She waits. Behind me, someone shifts their weight. Inside the cover there's a pencil note in his slanted handwriting: ch. 4, read this twice. I haven't been able to open past it. "Can I keep the slip?" I ask. My knees feel hollow. She slides it across, and I fold it small, smaller, until it fits inside my fist, and walk out into the bright, ordinary afternoon without my coat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at noon, and by two I was still standing in the doorway with the one box I'd carried up myself. Forty square feet of kitchen, a window that faced a brick wall. I set the box on the counter and opened it and found his blue mug wrapped in my sweater, and my hands forgot how to hold anything. I sat on the bare floor. The linoleum was cold through my jeans. "Okay," I said aloud, to nobody, and my voice came out thin, like someone else's. I tried again. "Okay. Bed first." But I didn't move. I pressed the mug against my sternum, where a weight had lodged weeks ago and refused to shift, and listened to the radiator tick. Somewhere below, a neighbor laughed at a television. I counted the tiles to the stove, eleven, then counted them back. Two sets of keys were on the ring in my pocket. I kept turning the second one over, though it opened nothing here, and I couldn't make myself take it off.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside the dry fountain, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and Marguerite stopped walking because her legs simply did. She lowered herself onto the slats. Her hands shook as she opened it, and she held her breath like a person wading into cold water. A library card. A folded grocery list in slanted handwriting: eggs, lemons, the good tea. She pressed her knuckles against her mouth. 'Oh,' she said, to no one, and the word came out cracked down the middle. A pigeon pecked near her shoe; she didn't see it. The list was in Daniel's hand, she realized, though it couldn't be, it wasn't his, only the same looping g. Her chest felt packed with wet sand. She read the list again, then again, her thumb smoothing the crease. When a jogger slowed and asked if she was all right, she nodded too long, eyes fixed on the lemons, unable to stand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says to let go of the wall, and I hold on another full minute, knuckles gone white, chlorine stinging my nose. Tuesday evenings, six weeks now. Marcus was the one who could swim; he used to float on his back in the lake while I stood on the dock holding his towel. I never once went in. Now I'm thirty-nine and kicking in the shallow end beside a nine-year-old named Priya, who keeps glancing at me. "Blow bubbles," the instructor says. I put my face in and the water closes over my ears, and everything goes muffled and low, and I stay down there longer than I need to, listening to the hum. When I surface my cheeks are wet in a way the pool can't explain. "Sorry," I tell her, laughing wrong, too high. "Water up my nose." I wipe my face with the towel, his old blue one, which I forgot to wash again, and push off the wall, arms shaking, and don't sink.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets are still in the plastic bag from the hardware store, and I've been holding the tomato one for ten minutes. The trowel is too clean. I kneel in the dirt behind the house and my knees sink in, cold through my jeans. Her gloves are in the shed, the left one still curled like it's waiting for her hand, and I put them on anyway. They're too small. I dig a hole, then another, then realize I have no idea how deep. "Six inches?" I say out loud to nobody, and my voice cracks on the word. The package says spacing, sunlight, water daily. I read it three times and can't hold any of it. A robin lands near the hose. I press a seed into the soil with my thumb, and my hands shake so badly I have to sit back on the grass and wait until I can breathe, dirt still under my nails.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus's slides glowed on the conference room wall, and Dana's voice went on about quarterly milestones, but Priya only watched the chart's blue line climb. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago. She held the cup anyway, both hands wrapped around it, because her fingers wouldn't stay still otherwise. Someone laughed at a joke. She smiled a beat late. Her chest felt packed with wet sand, and each breath had to push through it. When Dana asked, "Priya, any thoughts?" she heard her own name as if from the hallway. "Sorry," she said, too quietly, and cleared her throat. "It looks good. It's really good." Her eyes stung; she stared hard at the corner of the table until the grain of the wood blurred. Her phone lay face-down beside her notebook. Yesterday she'd have texted her mother a photo of this room. She pressed her thumbnail into her palm and nodded at the next slide, though she hadn't seen it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The exit ramp came up and Marisol missed it, then missed the next one too, her hands locked at ten and two on a wheel she could barely feel. The highway was empty except for the orange blink of a construction sign repeating its one warning. She had turned the radio on and off three times; each time the voices felt like someone talking in a room where a body lay. Her chest was a fist. Every breath caught halfway, snagged on something sharp. At a red light with no cars anywhere, she stopped and stared at the passenger seat, at the folded blue cardigan he'd left there Tuesday. 'You'd say I'm being dramatic,' she told it, and her voice cracked down the middle. The light turned green. She didn't move. A long minute later she pressed her forehead to the wheel and the horn gave one short, stupid bleat, and she laughed, once, and then couldn't stop making that other sound at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus stood in the doorway of Room 412 longer than the nurse seemed to think necessary, one hand pressed flat against the frame as if the building might tilt. The monitor beeped in its patient rhythm. His grandmother's hand lay on the blanket, smaller than he remembered, the knuckles shiny and bruised around the IV tape. He crossed the room in three steps and sat down too hard, and the vinyl chair sighed under him. "Hey, Nana," he said, and his voice came out cracked and thin, so he cleared his throat and tried again. Nothing better came. He picked up the plastic cup of ice chips, set it down, picked it up again. His chest felt packed with wet sand. When her fingers twitched against his, he stared at them, unable to breathe, and a sound escaped him that he covered with a cough. "I brought your lemon drops," he whispered, and then he could not say anything else, only hold the paper bag in his lap and watch the line on the screen climb and fall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell rings at 3:05 and I'm still gripping the fence, knuckles gone pale, as if the chain-link were holding me up instead of the other way around. Other parents drift toward the doors, laughing, thumbing their phones. I keep my sunglasses on though the sky is the color of dishwater. A woman asks if I'm picking up Daniel's sister, and I say, "Yes. No. I mean, I'm here," and my voice cracks down the middle like a plate. My chest feels packed with wet sand. Two weeks ago I would have been checking the time, annoyed about parking. Now I count the doors instead: one, two, three, as children spill out in bright coats. I'm holding his small blue scooter by the handle, and I don't remember bringing it. When Mia finally appears, her backpack dragging, I crouch too fast and my knees shake. "Hi, bug," I whisper, and press my mouth into her hair so no one can see my face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine, Marguerite had dragged the oak dresser to the curb and set a masking-tape price on it: $40. A man ran his thumb along the drawer edge and asked if it was solid. "Yes," she said, too quietly, then cleared her throat and said it again. He pulled the top drawer open and a sachet of lavender slid forward, still faintly sweet. Her hands went cold. She shut the drawer with her hip, hard, and stood there gripping the knob as if the wood might tip. "Thirty-five," she heard herself say. "Take it. Take the lamp too." The man hesitated, glancing at her face. She looked past him at the dandelions in the driveway cracks, counting them, losing count. When his truck pulled away, she sat down in the kitchen chair still marked $5 and didn't get up, not when a woman asked about the quilts, not when the sun reached her knees and her coffee went cold on the grass.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the cold kitchen tile with her head inside the cabinet, wrench slipping against the wet joint for the third time. Water ran down her wrist into her sleeve. On the counter behind her sat his chipped blue mug, still unwashed, still holding a brown ring of tea. She had not moved it in nine days. "Come on," she whispered to the pipe, then louder, "Come on," and her voice cracked on the second one. Her hands shook so badly the washer dropped and rolled somewhere into the dark under the sink. She did not go after it. She just lay there, cheek against the damp wood, listening to the drip, drip, drip keep time in the quiet house. He would have fixed this in two minutes, humming. Her chest felt hollowed out and heavy at once. After a while she noticed she was still gripping the wrench, knuckles white, and that the floor around her was soaked through.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has the county seal in the corner, and Dad's name typed across the front, still, as if he might walk in and take it from my hand. I sit on the stairs in my coat because I never made it any further. My thumb slides under the flap and stops. Starts again. The paper tears crooked. Inside: a notice about his unpaid vehicle registration, due in thirty days. I read it twice, then a third time, aloud, my voice coming out thin and strange in the empty hallway. "He doesn't have a car anymore," I tell the stairwell. "We sold it in March." My laugh cracks in half. The page starts shaking, or my hand does, and I press it flat against my knee until the words blur into gray. His reading glasses are still on the shelf by the door. I can't make myself look at them, so I stare at the seal, at its tiny printed wheat, and fold the letter along its creases again and again, smaller, smaller, until it won't fold anymore.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver says something rapid and bright, and I hold out the paper with the hotel's name until my hand starts to shake. He takes it. I watch the signs slide past, curling letters I can't sound out, and press my forehead to the window because it's cold and gives me something to do. At the front desk the clerk asks me a question twice. I say, "Sorry," and then again, "Sorry," too quietly, and I can't make my mouth do anything else. The room smells of detergent. I sit on the bed with my coat still on, my suitcase upright by the door like a person waiting. My phone shows her last message, three words, a thumbs-up under it. I don't scroll up. Outside, a bell rings somewhere, strangers laugh in a language I don't have, and I realize I've been holding my breath so long my chest aches. I let it out. It comes out as a sound.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus stood at the fence with his coat still buttoned wrong, one hand gripping the top rail until the wood bit into his palm. Out in the long yellow grass, Biscuit tore in wide loops, ears flapping, snapping at a moth that wasn't there. Every few seconds the dog stopped and looked back at him, tongue out, waiting. Marcus raised his hand to wave and found it wouldn't rise past his hip. 'Go on,' he said, too quietly for anyone to hear, then again, his voice splitting in the middle. His chest felt packed with wet sand. He glanced at the leash coiled in his pocket, the second one, the one that had hung by the door for eleven years beside the first, and he pressed his knuckles against his mouth. The wind carried the smell of cut hay. Biscuit bounded toward him, and Marcus slid down until he was sitting in the dirt, shoulders shaking without a sound, letting the dog push a wet nose into his neck. 'She'd have loved this,' he whispered. 'She would've been so loud.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I have set my music stand three times because it keeps drifting from where I want it. Dolores, our director, taps her baton and says, "From measure thirty, Ellis." I nod. I lift the clarinet. My lips find the reed, but the air won't come, only a thin wheeze, and the page swims into gray smudges. Thirty-one years he sat in the second row at every one of these. I count the folding chairs, anything, and see that the one on the aisle is empty, as it will be Saturday. "Sorry," I say, too loudly, then too quietly. "Again. Sorry." My hands are cold and heavy, like wet sand in gloves. I play the phrase and my fingers know it better than I do. Halfway through, my throat clamps shut and I stop, staring at the keys. Nobody speaks. Someone's chair creaks. I wipe the reed on my sleeve, very carefully, and whisper, "Measure thirty," as if it were a place I could walk to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The cardboard box I brought is still flat against the wall. I've been standing here with a coffee can of mismatched screws in my hands for what the clock says is forty minutes. Walt sorted these by size once, then gave up and dumped them together, and I can't make myself pour them into the trash bag. My thumb keeps finding the dent in the can's lid. Sawdust is in the light from the window, hanging there like it's waiting for him to switch the lathe on. "You'd hate how I'm doing this," I say out loud, and my voice cracks on hate. I laugh once, badly. His apron is on its hook, still curved around the shape of his shoulders, and when I lift it, it smells like cedar and him. I sit down on the stool without deciding to. My knees have stopped working. The bag stays open beside me, empty, and I tuck the can under my arm and don't move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the registrar's office smells of floor wax and old radiators, and I've been standing in front of the glass case since seven. Nothing is pinned up yet. My hands keep going to my coat pockets, finding Dad's folded handkerchief, the one I took from the drawer after the funeral, and pulling out nothing. A girl beside me laughs about her revision schedule and I turn my face to the wall. My chest feels packed with wet sand. When the clerk finally comes with the sheets, everyone surges and I stay put, counting ceiling tiles, losing count, starting again. 'Number 4172,' someone reads aloud, not mine. I whisper, 'He'd have wanted to see this,' to no one, and my voice cracks on 'see.' I press the handkerchief to my mouth. The paper is up. I can't make my legs walk toward it. The names blur like rain on a bus window, and I just stand there, breathing in short, careful sips.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta had meant to turn back at the creek, but her boots kept going, and now the ridge had gone the color of ash and the pines were losing their edges. She stopped where the trail forked and stood there with her father's old compass in her fist, thumb rubbing the scratched glass until it stung. The cold came up through her soles. She didn't take out the flashlight. "You'd have said we were late," she told the dark, and her voice cracked on the last word, so she said it again, quieter, to hear it hold. Somewhere below, water kept talking. Her chest felt packed with wet sand; each breath had to push through it. She sat down hard on a flat rock, pressed the compass against her mouth, and stayed until the first star showed, unable to remember which way was down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, stained translucent at one corner where her thumb always rested. "Flour, enough," it says. Enough. I laugh, and the sound cracks in the middle and comes out wrong. I measure anyway, four cups, then dump in another handful, then another, because who knows. My hands shake so badly the yeast skitters across the counter. I stop and press my palms flat against the cool marble until they quit. The kitchen is too quiet; the oven ticks. I knead, and my shoulders ache, and my throat is a fist I keep trying to swallow around. "Okay, Grandma," I whisper, "show me what enough looks like." The dough sticks to my wrists. I lean my forehead against the cabinet and stay there, breathing flour, until the timer goes off. When the loaf comes out lopsided and pale, I tear off the heel, hold it to my face, and can't make myself eat it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was holding a carton of eggs he didn't remember choosing when someone said his name from the end of the aisle. Dana Whitlock, from tenth-grade chemistry, grinning, her cart half full of cereal and juice boxes. He set the eggs on a shelf of canned beans. "Hey," he said, and the word came out thin, scraped. She talked about her twins, about moving back, and he nodded at the wrong places, watching the fluorescent light buzz above her head. His hands wouldn't stay still; he pressed them into his coat pockets. "And you? Married? Anyone?" Her question hung there. He swallowed twice. "There was," he said. "Till March." His voice cracked on the last word and he studied the floor tiles, counting the cracks. Dana's smile slid away. She reached for his sleeve, and he flinched, then stayed. Somewhere a cart rattled. He realized he was still wearing the scarf she'd knitted, and he had to leave the store without the eggs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marta scanned the same carton of cranberry sauce three times before she noticed the beep had stopped meaning anything. The grocery was nearly empty, the fluorescent hum loud in the last hour before closing on Wednesday, and a teenager asked if the turkeys were half off. "Fourteen pounds," she said, and then, "No. Sorry. Yes." Her hands kept finding the edge of the register. Her mother had always bought the twenty-two pound bird, too big for anyone, and Marta had rolled her eyes every year. A man set down a pie and she bagged it with great care, as if it might break, as if she might. Her throat was a tight fist. When he said, "Happy Thanksgiving," she nodded at the conveyor belt, lips pressed flat, and kept nodding after he'd gone. In the break room she sat with her coat on, staring at her locker key, unable to remember what she had come in there to do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board flickered and Marguerite's gate changed from B14 to C41, and she stood there with her carry-on strap cutting into her shoulder, reading it three times as though the letters might rearrange. Then she ran, one shoe slapping looser than the other, past a man selling neck pillows, past a child's abandoned balloon. Her chest burned. At the moving walkway she stopped short, because the black cardigan over her arm still smelled of her mother's house, of cedar and instant coffee, and her knees simply refused. 'Sorry,' she told a stranger who had to step around her, her voice cracking down the middle. 'Sorry, sorry.' She pressed the cardigan to her mouth and breathed in. The speaker announced final boarding. Her hands shook so badly she dropped the phone, and when she picked it up she couldn't remember the gate number, only the funeral program folded in her pocket, the photograph on its cover, smiling. She walked on, wet-faced, toward C, not hurrying anymore.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the edges twice, pressing the blue tape down with her thumbnail, before she noticed the pencil marks on the doorframe. Heights, dated in her husband's slanted hand. She set the roller in the tray and stood there while paint dripped onto the drop cloth, one slow drop, then another. "Well," she said to the empty hallway, and her voice came out thin, like someone else's. She rolled a stripe of pale yellow over the bare wall, then another, stopping short of the frame. Her arms ached. She hadn't eaten since yesterday, maybe the day before. The radio stayed off because every song seemed to know something. When the can needed stirring she sat on the floor instead, back against the cold plaster, the stir stick across her knees, and stayed there until the window went gray and the paint skinned over. The pencil marks remained, a small bare column in all that yellow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while Marguerite was still holding the casserole dish, its foil gone damp at the edges, though no one had come to the door in hours. She set it on the porch boards and sat beside it. Rain slanted under the awning and soaked her sleeves; she didn't move her feet from the puddle spreading toward them. Her chest felt packed with wet sand. "He'd have shut the windows by now," she said to the yard, and her voice cracked on the last word like a dropped plate. Lightning whitened the maple he planted. She counted the seconds to the thunder, as he'd taught her, and lost count at four. Her hands kept smoothing the same crease in her dress. When the porch light flickered out, she stayed in the dark, mouth open, breathing as if the air had thinned, whispering his name to the gutters until they drowned it out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Dana wedged the wrench onto the pedal and heaved, jaw tight, knuckles scraped raw against the chainring. Someone had shoved her toolbox aside again; the drawer hung open, and the 10mm socket was gone. She didn't bother looking twice. "Of course," she muttered, kicking the drawer shut with her heel. Across the garage, the neighbor's radio chirped a cheerful song about summer, and she turned her back to it, shoulders hunched up near her ears. The oil on her palms smelled sour. A bolt slipped from her fingers, pinged off the concrete, and rolled under the shelf where a paint can sat in her allotted square of floor. She stared at it a long moment, breathing hard through her nose. Then she dropped flat, cheek nearly on the cold floor, and swiped blindly. "Nobody," she told the dust, "puts anything back." She slapped the radio off on her way up, without asking whose it was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky went the color of dishwater while I was still checking my watch for the fourth time. Eleven minutes late, and the schedule taped inside the shelter swore otherwise. I jammed my hands into my pockets and kicked a bottle cap off the curb, harder than it deserved. The wind came first, flipping my collar against my jaw, and I clamped my teeth until they ached. Then the first fat drops hit the back of my neck. "Of course," I muttered, to nobody, to the pole, to the whole stupid street. A man edged under the shelter beside me and smiled, and I shifted my bag onto the bench between us without looking at him. He said something about the weather. I grunted. My shoulders had crept up around my ears, and my wet socks squelched when I stamped my feet. Down the road, headlights finally swam through the rain, and I scowled at them like they owed me money.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Harold dragged the shoebox from the closet shelf with a thump that sent dust into his eyes, and he swore at the ceiling. He dropped onto the edge of the bed, knees cracking, and tore the rubber band off the first bundle. It snapped against his thumb. "Of course," he muttered. The envelopes were soft and yellowed, and he flicked through them like a man dealing cards he didn't want. Birthday wishes. Weather. Somebody's gallbladder. "Who keeps this garbage?" he said to the empty room, though he knew the answer and it only made his jaw tighter. He shoved a letter back into its envelope crooked, creasing the corner, and didn't fix it. His shoulders ached. The radiator clanked, and he glared at it. Three more bundles waited. He sighed through his nose, long and loud, and snatched up the next one anyway, grinding his teeth as he read every single word.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The doorbell rang twice before Walter got the second sock on, and he took the hallway in heavy, deliberate steps, jaw working side to side. Through the screen he saw Dale from next door, grinning, one thumb hooked in his belt. "Got a ladder I could borrow?" Walter let the silence sit. His shoulders had crept up toward his ears. "Which one," he said, flat, not quite a question. "The tall one, if it's no trouble." Walter exhaled through his nose, long and slow, and stared at the gutter leaves Dale's maple had dropped on his own lawn. "Brought back last time with a bent rung." He muttered something about Saturday mornings and shoved past, the garage door rattling up under his hard palm. He hauled the ladder out himself, refusing the offered hand, and let it thud onto the driveway. "Tonight. Before dark." The screen door slapped shut behind him, and he stood in the hall a while, fists tight, listening to the aluminum scrape away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onion hits the cutting board harder than it needs to. Forty minutes until the doorbell, and the oven is still ticking its way up to temperature, slow as a shrug. "Fine," I tell it. "Take your time." My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the grocery store, where someone took the last good lemons. The radio is playing something cheerful, so I jab it off with a knuckle and the kitchen goes tight and quiet except for the knife. Sweat prickles under my collar. Dana texts, asking if she should bring wine, and I stare at the phone, thumb hovering, then type "sure" with no exclamation point, which she'll notice. A pot lid clangs onto the floor. I leave it there. I stir the sauce in short, stabbing circles, tasting, frowning, adding salt nobody asked for. Somewhere behind me the tap drips, and I shut it off so hard the handle squeaks. Twenty-nine minutes. I'll smile at the door. Not yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter just as I'd gotten the pan to the right sizzle, and I glared at it like it owed me money. Unknown number. Of course. I wiped my hands on my jeans, harder than necessary, and let it ring four times while my jaw worked side to side. Fifth ring, I snatched it up. "What." Not a question. A voice chirped something about my car's extended warranty, and I felt my shoulders climb toward my ears. "I don't own a car that's young enough to have a warranty," I said, flat, each word clipped short. "Take me off your list." Behind me the onions started to scorch, the smell curling up sour. I jabbed the red button with my thumb, tossed the phone onto the counter where it skidded into the toaster, and shoved the pan off the burner with a clang. Dinner could wait. So could everybody else. I dropped into the chair and scowled at the wall clock, as if it had called me too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been living in my backpack since March, wedged under a dead umbrella, and now its spine was bent like it blamed me. I shoved the library door with my shoulder and it hissed shut behind me, too slowly. The fluorescent lights buzzed. My jaw ached from clenching it the whole walk over. At the desk I dropped the book on the counter harder than I needed to. "Overdue," I said, flat, before the clerk could open her mouth. "Go ahead. Tell me the number." She tapped her keyboard, and every click scraped at me. Forty-one dollars. I yanked my wallet out, and a receipt fluttered to the floor. I left it there. "Fine," I muttered, sliding the bills across without looking up. "It wasn't even a good book." Her pen scratched. I stood there, arms crossed, heel tapping the carpet, waiting for her to finish so I could leave and be annoyed somewhere else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The elevator was broken, so Marguerite hauled the last box up four flights herself, jaw set, each step thudding harder than the one before. The door stuck. She shouldered it open and it banged the wall, knocking loose a flake of paint that landed on her sleeve. She flicked it off. One room, one window, a radiator that clanked like someone knocking to complain. "Charming," she said to no one, flatly. She dropped the box and her back popped; she pressed a fist into it and exhaled hard through her nose. The fridge hummed too loud. She yanked its plug, then, hearing the silence, plugged it back in with a muttered curse. Her phone buzzed with her sister's text: "How's the new place?!" She read it, thumbed the screen dark, and shoved the phone under a dish towel. Then she sat on the bare mattress with her coat still buttoned, arms crossed, glaring at a ceiling stain shaped suspiciously like her old landlord's face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench was the only dry one, and of course somebody had already left something on it. I stood there with my coffee going cold, jaw tight, staring at a brown leather wallet like it had done this to me on purpose. Pigeons shuffled around my shoes. I huffed, snatched it up with two fingers, and flipped it open. Forty dollars, a library card, a driver's license grinning at me. Dale Perkins. Dale looked far too pleased with himself. "Careless," I muttered to nobody, and my knee cracked as I lowered myself onto the slats, where the damp soaked straight through my trousers. Great. Perfect. I'd come here for ten quiet minutes. Now I'd have to walk to the station, wait behind some kid with a bike helmet, and fill out a form. I shoved the wallet in my coat pocket, yanked the zipper hard enough to pinch my thumb, and swore at the sky. Then I stomped off, still carrying Dale's lousy day with me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Dennis stood at the shallow end with his arms crossed over his chest, goggles already fogged and pinching a red ring into his forehead. The instructor, a girl who looked about nineteen, chirped something about blowing bubbles. "I've been blowing bubbles for forty minutes," he said, flat, not looking at her. The chlorine stung his nose. He shoved off the wall, kicked twice, and sank like a dropped wrench, then came up sputtering with his jaw clenched so tight his teeth ached. "Fine," he muttered, wiping his face with a wet palm that only made it wetter. A child in the next lane paddled past him effortlessly, and Dennis glared at the tiles on the pool floor as if they'd arranged this. He tugged his trunks up, planted his feet, and snapped, "Again. But don't clap this time." His shoulders stayed hunched up around his ears the whole way across the lane, all eleven feet of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana jammed the trowel into the clay and it rang against a rock, sending a jolt up her wrist. "Of course," she muttered. She dug the rock out and flung it at the fence, where it clacked and dropped. The seed packets, soaked from the morning drizzle, curled in her back pocket like little wet tongues. Tomatoes: "Plant after frost." What frost? She'd read three websites and each said something different. Her knees ached against the damp board she knelt on, and mud had crept inside her glove. She yanked rows straight with string, then scowled at how crooked they still looked. "Fine. Crooked carrots. Who cares." A neighbor waved over the fence and called something cheerful about beginner's luck. Dana lifted two fingers off the trowel handle, jaw tight, and kept her eyes on the dirt until he went back inside. Then she tore open the lettuce packet too hard, and the seeds scattered in one tiny, useless spill.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
