text: Marcus slid into the back row of the conference room and let his chair creak under him on purpose. The projector hummed, too bright, and Dana's slide deck opened with a cartoon rocket. He crossed his arms, jaw working at nothing, and stared at the clock instead of the screen. "Exciting quarter," Dana began, and Marcus exhaled hard through his nose. His coffee had gone cold an hour ago; he drank it anyway, grimacing. When she clicked to a chart with six animated transitions, he muttered, "Just show the number." A few heads turned. He flipped his pen against the table, tick, tick, tick, until the woman beside him glanced over. His shoulders ached, tight as fists. When Dana asked for questions, he said, "Is this the final version, or are we doing another one next week?" Then he sat back, the knot behind his eyes pulsing, and wished the meeting had been an email.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The radio gave me three notes of a song I used to like before I jabbed the button and killed it. Quiet was better. Quiet, and the hum of tires, and my jaw clenched so hard my molars ached. A truck rode my bumper with its high beams on, so I yanked the mirror sideways without slowing down. "Go around, genius," I muttered, though the road was empty both ways. Every light on Fenner Street turned red just for me, and I sat there drumming the wheel, shoulders up near my ears, replaying the meeting where Dale said 'circle back' eleven times. My coffee had gone cold in the cup holder, and I drank it anyway, scowling at the taste. When the porch light finally came into view, I didn't feel relief. I slammed the car door hard enough to rattle the mailbox, then stood in the driveway sighing at nothing, keys biting into my fist, not ready to go in and be asked how my day was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dennis fed his last dollar into the vending machine twice before it surrendered a bag of pretzels, and he stood there jabbing the return slot anyway. Upstairs, room 412 smelled of bleach and boiled carrots. He dropped into the vinyl chair, which hissed under him, and kept his jacket on. His uncle was asleep with his mouth open, the TV muttering about a cooking contest. 'Forty minutes I circled for parking,' Dennis said to the ceiling. His jaw ached; he realized he'd been clenching it since the elevator. A nurse came to check the monitor and asked how he was doing. 'Fine,' he said, flat as a tray. He tore the pretzel bag so hard it spilled across his knee, and he brushed the crumbs onto the floor without looking. The clock over the door ticked loudly. He checked his phone. Eleven minutes had passed. He sighed through his nose, crossed his arms, and glared at the cooking contest as though it owed him something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell was supposed to ring at 3:10, and my phone says 3:24. I stand against the fence with my arms locked across my chest, jaw working at nothing, one foot tapping a rhythm the pavement doesn't deserve. Somebody's stroller clips my heel and I say, "Wow," flat and low, not turning around. The woman beside me starts chatting about the bake sale. I give her a nod so small it barely counts, then study my keys like they owe me money. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears; my neck aches in a hot, tight line. The sun sits right in my eyes, of course it does. Doors finally bang open and kids pour out, shrieking. I scan for my daughter's red backpack, mutter, "Took long enough," and when she waves, I lift two fingers off my elbow and don't smile until she's almost reached me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Walter dragged the oak dresser to the curb at seven sharp, though the first car didn't slow until nine. His jaw ached from clenching. A woman ran her thumb along a drawer edge, and he watched her fingers the whole time. "Forty," he said, before she'd asked. She offered fifteen. "It's solid wood," he muttered, arms folded so tight his shoulders knotted. "They don't make them like this. You'd know that if you looked." She wandered off toward the lamps. He snatched the price sticker and pressed it back down harder, as if it had slipped on purpose. The sun climbed, the folding chair creaked, and sweat itched under his collar. A kid bounced on the sofa cushions. "Off," Walter said, flat and low, and the boy froze. He turned the radio down to nothing, then up, then off. Fifteen dollars, he thought. Fifteen. He sat, and the chair complained again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped again and my knuckles cracked against the cold copper, and I hissed through my teeth. Water dripped into the bucket, tink, tink, tink, steady as a mocking clock. I'd been on my back under the sink for an hour, a cabinet hinge digging into my ribs, my shirt clammy at the collar. "Fine," I muttered. "Fine. Be that way." I yanked the fitting tighter than the instructions said, then tighter still, jaw clenched so hard my ears ached. The video on my phone chirped, "Easy as that!" and I jabbed it silent with a wet thumb. Easy. Sure. My wife called from the hallway, asking if I wanted help, and I said, "No," too fast and too flat, not looking out from the cabinet. The drip kept going. I stared at it, breathed hard through my nose, and shoved the wrench back onto the nut with a clang that rattled every plate upstairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been sitting on the counter since Tuesday, and I still hate the little window with my name typed in that smug font. I stab a butter knife under the flap and drag it open, tearing the corner of the page along with it. Good. My jaw is clenched so hard my ears ache. Three folds. Who folds a letter three times to say nothing? I snap it open and the paper crackles like it's mocking me. "Dear Resident," I read aloud, flat. "Dear Resident. They have my name on the front, and still." My coffee has gone cold, and I drink it anyway, scowling into the cup. Page two wants a form. The form wants another form. I drop the letter, let it slide off the table onto the floor, and leave it there while I stomp to the sink, muttering that I'll deal with it when they deal with me, which is never, which is the whole point of them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train spat me onto the platform at midnight, and my suitcase wheel promptly snapped off with a crack I felt in my molars. I dragged the thing like a dead animal past signs that looked like spilled alphabet soup. At the ticket window I slapped my printed reservation against the glass. "Hotel. Where. Bus." The clerk said something long and melodic, and I said, "No, that's not an answer," louder, as if volume were a currency. My shoulders had climbed up around my ears hours ago. Rain found the gap in my collar. I jabbed a finger at the map on my phone, which showed a blue dot spinning in circles, and exhaled through my nose until the clerk flinched. Someone offered a smile and an umbrella; I took the umbrella without a word, yanked my bag over the curb, and muttered that nobody had ever promised me this was a vacation anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: The bench slats were damp, and I sat on them anyway, arms crossed so tight my shoulders ached. Biscuit tore across the field in huge, idiotic circles, ears flapping, tongue out, mud flying off her paws in clumps I would be scrubbing from the car seats later. "Great," I muttered, to nobody. "Wonderful. Roll in it." She did. My coffee had gone lukewarm, and it tasted like pennies, but I took another sip just to have something to scowl at. A woman jogged past and smiled at the dog, then at me. I studied my shoes until she was gone. The wind kept finding the gap in my collar. When Biscuit came bounding over, dripping, tail whipping, and dropped a slimy stick on my knee, I exhaled hard through my nose, flicked it back into the grass, and said, "Ten more minutes. That's it." I didn't check my watch. I didn't move, either.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite dropped her cello case onto the fellowship hall floor hard enough that the folding chairs rattled. Nobody had turned the heat on, and the radiator ticked uselessly beneath the window. She tightened her pegs with a jerk while Dale from the flute section chirped something about a fun, relaxed evening. "Relaxed," she muttered, and sawed out a note that came flat. She did it again. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears an hour ago and refused to come down. When the conductor asked everyone to start from measure twelve, she exhaled through her nose, long and loud, and flipped the page so it snapped. Somebody's toddler was banging a tambourine in the corner. Marguerite stared at the music stand, which wobbled, and pressed her palm against it until her knuckles went pale. "Again? We did it twice." Then she played measure twelve exactly as written, every note, and not one bit softer than she had to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta kicked the stuck door twice before it gave, and the smell of sawdust and cold machine oil rolled over her. "Of course," she muttered. "Of course you'd swell the thing shut." She dropped a flattened box on the bench and it slid off into a drawer of loose screws, which scattered across the concrete. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the driveway. Every jar on the shelf was labeled in Walt's cramped capitals, and every label was wrong or pointless. NAILS, MISC. BIGGER NAILS. She swept three jars into the box without reading them, hard enough that they clanged. Her knee cracked as she crouched. "Forty years, and not one thing where a person could find it," she said to the vise, and yanked its handle until her palm stung. Then she stood there, breathing through her nose, arms folded, glaring at the half-finished chair leg clamped in it, and did not touch that at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 214 smelled of floor wax and somebody's microwaved fish, and Marguerite had been standing against the same cinderblock wall for forty minutes. The noticeboard was still blank except for a curling flyer about lost keys. A boy beside her kept refreshing his phone and sighing out loud, and she shifted her bag to the other shoulder with a hard yank. "Could you not?" she said, without turning her head. He blinked and stopped. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the vending machine ate her coins and gave nothing back. She'd kicked it. It had not helped her toe either. The clock above the door ticked, and every tick seemed deliberate, personal. When the secretary finally emerged with a single sheet of paper and a roll of tape, Marguerite folded her arms tighter and muttered, "Took long enough," then stayed put, refusing to be the first one to shove forward.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta stomped over the root-knotted switchback, trekking poles clacking harder than the ground deserved. The light had gone orange, then gray, and she jabbed at her phone again: no signal, still. "Two miles, he said," she muttered, mimicking Dale's cheerful voice with a sneer. "Easy loop." Her boots pinched at the heels, and a damp strap bit into her shoulder, which she yanked upward with a hiss. A branch caught her sleeve and she tore free without slowing, jaw tight enough to ache. Somewhere above, a bird kept up its bright, pointless chirping. She glared at the treetops. Her stomach growled and she snapped, "Oh, shut up," to nobody. The trail markers blurred into the dusk, each one later than it should have been. She didn't stop to admire the pink smear over the ridge. She only huffed through her nose, pulled her hood up with a jerk, and kept walking, counting every step against him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is stained brown at the corners, and Grandpa's handwriting says "flour, enough." Enough! I slap it onto the counter harder than I mean to, and a puff of white rises into my face. I sneeze, then glare at the bag like it did it on purpose. My jaw aches; I've been clenching it since the yeast refused to foam. "Fine," I tell the empty kitchen. "Be that way." I dump in another cup, then another, and jam my fingers into the sticky mess, which clings to my knuckles and my watch. The radio is playing something cheerful, so I jab it off with a floury thumb. Rain taps the window. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears. I knead like I'm settling an argument, pushing, folding, shoving, muttering that nobody needs bread this badly. I don't stop, though, and I don't let myself look at his handwriting again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The cart's front wheel shuddered and veered left, again, and I yanked it back hard enough to jar my wrist. Aisle nine smelled like floor cleaner and burnt coffee. I was reaching past a pyramid of paper towels for the last box of the brand I actually wanted when someone said my name, drawn out like a question. Dana Pruitt. Tenth-grade chemistry, ponytail, laugh like a kazoo. She was already smiling, arms half open. I gave her a nod and kept my hand on the cart. "Hey." She asked what I'd been up to for fifteen years. "Working," I said. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the parking lot. She talked about her twins and a bakery. I watched the fluorescent light flicker over her shoulder and checked my watch, twice, not hiding it. "Well, this was nice," she said. "Mm," I said, and rolled away, the wheel rattling all the way to the registers.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marguerite flipped the sign on the pharmacy door to CLOSED at 5:58, two minutes early, and nobody was going to tell her otherwise. Through the glass, a man in a puffy coat was already jogging across the lot, waving a prescription slip like a flag. She turned the deadbolt anyway. He knocked. She counted the register drawer, slapping each stack of twenties against the counter hard enough to sting her palm. 'Sign says six,' he mouthed, and she pointed at her wristwatch without looking up. The fluorescent tube above the vitamins kept buzzing, and her jaw ached from clenching around the same sentence all day: no, we don't have that in stock. Somewhere behind her a radio hummed carols she'd been hearing since October. She yanked her coat off the hook, shoved one arm in, missed the other sleeve, and muttered, 'Everybody's family can wait one more day,' to the dark window. Then she unlocked the door, snatched the slip, and said, 'Five minutes. Don't talk to me.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B47 was, of course, at the far end of the terminal, and Marguerite walked there with her jaw set and her carry-on wheels rattling like a complaint. The moving walkway was out of order. She sighed through her nose, loud enough that a teenager stepped aside. A man in front of her stopped to read a map, and she clipped his heel with her bag and didn't say sorry. "Some of us have planes," she muttered. Her shoulders ached where the strap bit in, and sweat prickled under her wool coat, which she refused to take off because taking it off would mean stopping. The departure board blinked: BOARDING. She checked her watch, then the board, then her watch again, as though one might apologize. At the gate, the agent smiled and began to say something cheerful. "Just scan it," Marguerite said, thrusting the phone forward, lips pressed thin, her free hand drumming hard against her thigh.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The tape peeled off the baseboard and took a strip of old paint with it, and I stood there holding the curling blue thing like it had personally insulted me. "Of course," I said to the empty hallway. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since breakfast. Eggshell, the can said. Nobody had told me eggshell meant three coats. I dragged the roller through the tray harder than I needed to, and a gray-white spatter landed on my sock. I didn't wipe it. My phone buzzed on the stepladder, my sister, probably offering help I'd only have to supervise, so I flipped it face down with one knuckle. The window stayed shut though the fumes made my eyes sting. Fine. Let it sting. I rolled the same stripe four times, muttering about drop cloths, about Saturdays, about whoever picked this color in the first place, which was me, which only made me press the roller flatter against the wall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Walt dragged the rocker back from the porch edge with a screech that made the dog flinch, then dropped into it hard enough to rattle the boards. Rain hammered the tin awning. He'd planned to finish the fence today, and now the sky had gone and ruined it. His jaw ached from clamping it. He crossed his arms, uncrossed them, crossed them again. Thunder cracked and he muttered, "Well, go on, then, get it over with." His wife leaned out the screen door and asked if he wanted tea. "No." A pause, a stare at the sodden yard. "Maybe. Not that sweet stuff." The door clicked shut. A gust spat rain across his boots and he jerked his feet up, glaring at the puddle as if it had done it on purpose. He kicked the empty flowerpot straight, though it hadn't been crooked, and sat there with his shoulders up around his ears, listening to every drop.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off Marisol's bike for the fourth time, and I thread it back on with fingers that won't stop shaking. Her toolbox sits open beside the vise, every wrench labeled in her careful block letters. I keep my back to the garage door. When Mr. Okafor from unit three wanders in and asks if I'm fixing my own ride, I say, "Yeah, mine," too fast, and laugh at nothing. My stomach clenches around the lie. I wipe grease on my jeans, then wipe again, though my hands are already clean. The bent derailleur hanger is my doing. I borrowed the bike without asking and dropped it on the curb outside the bar. Now I'm pressing the hanger straight by feel, hoping she'll never notice. Every footstep in the hallway makes me freeze, wrench mid-turn. Her water bottle is still in the cage, dented on one side. I can't bring myself to take it out, so I just keep staring at it, and my throat gets tight.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as Marnie checked her phone again, thumb hovering over her sister's name, then sliding away. Wind lifted the timetable's corner and let it slap back. She had the casserole dish in her lap, still warm, wrapped in a towel she'd meant to return three years ago, and she held it tighter as the sky went the color of dishwater. A man beside her shook out an umbrella and offered to share. "No, no, I'm fine," she said, too quickly, too brightly, and scooted to the edge where the rain spat on her shoes. Her stomach clenched. She rehearsed the sentence again under her breath, the one that began with I should have come sooner, and swallowed it when the bus hissed up. On the step she turned back toward the street she'd left, the dish heavy and her cheeks hot, and she didn't board until the driver cleared his throat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta knelt on the attic floorboards with the shoebox open between her knees, and the first envelope she lifted was addressed to her in her brother's cramped handwriting. The postmark was nine years old. She turned it over twice, thumb pressing the unbroken seal, and found she was holding her breath. 'Probably nothing,' she said aloud, to the empty rafters, her voice too bright. She set it face-down on the pile of electric bills, then moved it to the bottom, then pulled it back out. Her stomach felt packed with wet sand. Downstairs the phone rang, and she let it ring, counting each one, glad of the excuse. When it stopped she slid a fingernail under the flap, stopped, and wiped her palms along her jeans. The paper smelled of cedar and of his old jacket. She read the first line, 'Mart, no hurry to write back,' and pressed the heel of her hand hard against her mouth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale appeared at my fence with his hands in his back pockets, asking if I still had that extension ladder. My ears went hot. "Sure," I said, too fast, then laughed at nothing. "Of course. Let me just, hang on." In the garage I stood facing the wall where it hung, the dented rung he'd never know about, the one I'd bent last spring when I borrowed his drill and never brought it back. The drill sat on my shelf, under a tarp. My stomach tightened as I lifted the ladder down, and I carried it out the long way so he wouldn't pass the shelf. "Keep it as long as you need," I told him, and my voice came out thick. "Really. Weeks, even." He thanked me twice. I kept nodding, gripping the fence post until my knuckles whitened, and after he left I stood there, then went back in and set the drill on his porch before dark, hands still unsteady.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The lamb is already resting under foil when I realize I've set out six plates, not seven, and my hands go cold. I add the seventh anyway, then straighten it, then straighten it again. Mara's chair goes at the end, where she can see the door. I told her the dinner was Saturday. It was Friday; I knew it was Friday when I typed it. My knife keeps chopping parsley long after the pile is fine. When the buzzer sounds downstairs I flinch so hard I nick my thumb, and I let it bleed a second before reaching for the tap. "Come up," I say into the intercom, too brightly, too fast. Then I scrub a counter where nothing has spilled. I pour her favorite wine into her glass before anyone arrives, and my throat tightens at the sight of it, so I carry the bottle back to the kitchen and stand there, listening to the stairs, rehearsing the sentence I still haven't found the nerve to begin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter, a number Marisol didn't know, and she watched it crawl toward the edge of the sink before she caught it. Her thumb hovered. Three weeks since she'd borrowed Dana's car and returned it with the dent along the rear door, parked crooked so the scratch faced the wall. She let it ring four times, five, her stomach folding in on itself. The dish towel was twisted in her other fist, damp and wrung into a rope. When she finally answered, her voice came out too bright. "Hello? Yes, this is she." A pause on the line. She turned the faucet on, then off, as if someone might hear the water and know. "Sorry, who is this?" Her ears were hot. She kept nodding at nobody, glancing at the window where the car sat in the driveway, and when the stranger began, "I'm calling about—" she closed her eyes and said, quietly, "Okay. Okay. I can explain."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I waited outside until the line at the circulation desk shrank to nothing, then pushed through the door with the book pressed flat against my ribs like I could hide it there. The paperback's corner had curled from months under my bed. Two semesters, at least. The librarian looked up, and my voice came out thin and too fast. "Hi, sorry, I think this is, um, a little overdue." My ears were burning. I set it on the counter and slid it forward with two fingers, then pulled my hand back as if the cover were hot. While she scanned it I studied the carpet, the stapled flyers, anything but her face. "Do I owe a lot?" I asked, already digging in my wallet, already counting the crumpled bills twice. My stomach rolled. She said something kind, and I nodded without hearing it, swallowing hard, wishing the floor would just let me through.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dana carried the last box up four flights herself, though her brother had offered twice to come, and she'd said twice that she had it handled. The studio smelled of paint and old radiator. She set the box down, and her phone buzzed: Mom, again. She let it ring out, thumb hovering, stomach tightening around the toast she hadn't finished. On the windowsill she lined up the one houseplant her mother had pressed into her hands at the door, and she turned its pot so the crooked side faced the wall. 'It's fine,' she said aloud to no one, too brightly. 'It's close enough. Forty minutes, really.' The bed took up nearly the whole room. She sat on its edge, then stood, then wiped a faint ring of dust from the sill with her sleeve, scrubbing longer than the spot required. When the phone buzzed a third time she picked it up, breathed in, and typed, deleted, and typed again: Home safe. Call you Sunday. Sorry. Her ears burned as she hit send.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, and Marta walked past it twice before she sat down beside it. Her thumb found the fold of the cash first, and she pulled her hand back as if the leather were hot. Forty-dollar bills, maybe sixty. She had a rent notice in her coat pocket. A jogger passed and she coughed, loudly, for no reason, and slid the wallet under her scarf. Her ears burned. Inside the driver's license, a gray-haired man squinted out at her, and she turned the photo face-down against her knee. 'I was going to take it to the station,' she said to a pigeon, too quickly. The pigeon left. She stood, sat, stood again, the wallet heavy as a stone in her palm, her stomach tight around the breakfast she hadn't eaten. At last she walked toward the address on the card, rehearsing a sentence that began with 'I found,' and could not make her feet go slowly enough or fast enough.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marcus gripped the pool's tiled edge at the community center, knuckles pale, while the instructor, a teenager named Dee, told him to let go and kick. He kicked. Water slapped his face and he coughed, then laughed too quickly. "Sorry," he said, "sorry, I'm holding up the line," though no one waited behind him. In his locker down the hall, his phone held three missed calls from his brother, the same brother who had gone under at the lake thirty years ago while Marcus stood on the dock, dry and frozen. His chest tightened each time his chin dipped near the surface. When Dee said he was doing great, he shook his head and stared at the drain on the pool floor. "Again," he said. "Let me do it again." He pushed off, arms flailing, and kept going until his lips turned blue and the lifeguard blew the whistle for closing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marcus knelt at the edge of the raised bed his father had built years ago, the cedar boards gone silver and soft. He pressed a trowel into the dirt and winced at the sound it made, as if someone might hear. The seed packets lay fanned beside him, tomatoes, beans, the little crooked carrots, and he kept straightening them, then straightening them again. "Sorry," he muttered to a worm, lifting it gently aside. His throat felt tight. Every few minutes he glanced at the kitchen window, though the house had been empty since March. He had promised to come in spring, the spring before this one, and the one before that. Sweat gathered under his collar, and his hands, clumsy with the tiny seeds, dropped half the beans in one spot. He didn't pick them out. He covered them slowly, patting the soil flat, then sat back on his heels and said, quietly, to no one, "I'll water them every day. I will. Every single day."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana's slides lit up the conference room wall, and Marcus stood beside them, voice steady, clicking through the charts she had built. Priya sat at the far end of the table with her notebook open to a blank page. The third slide came up, the one with the forecast model, and her pen stopped moving. She had pulled those numbers from Marcus's folder in March and said nothing when the director praised her for them. Now he thanked her by name for the 'early groundwork,' and she nodded too quickly, a smile stuck on her face. Her coffee had gone cold, but she lifted it anyway, hiding behind the cup. Heat crawled up her neck. When Marcus glanced her way, she studied the carpet's gray flecks. 'Great work,' she said afterward, too loudly, and gripped his hand a second too long. 'Really. Let me buy you lunch.' He laughed and said sure. She counted the steps to the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The phone keeps lighting up in the cup holder, Dana's name, then Dana's name again, and I turn it face down without slowing. Route 9 is empty except for stoplights blinking yellow over nothing. I should have stayed for the dishes. I should have at least stayed to hear her finish the sentence. Instead I said, "I'm fine, it's late," in that bright voice I use for cashiers, and grabbed my keys before she could see my hands. Now my jaw aches from clenching. The heater is too high, but I don't touch it; my collar is damp and I let it stay that way. At the red light by the shuttered pharmacy I rehearse an apology out loud, get three words in, and stop because it sounds false even to the empty passenger seat. The light turns green. I sit through it. Nobody behind me honks. I watch it go red again, and my thumb finds the phone, and doesn't press.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I stop outside room 412 and rearrange the grocery-store tulips twice before pushing the door. Grandpa's hand lies on the blanket like something set down and forgotten. "Hey," I say, too bright, and my voice cracks on it. The vending machine hums in the hall. I pull the chair closer, then farther, then sit on its very edge with my coat still on. He asks if I got his messages, and my thumb finds the phone in my pocket, the eleven missed calls glowing there since March. "Work's been insane," I say, studying the IV drip, counting its slow drops. My stomach knots when he smiles anyway. He pats the bed and I don't move, because if I sit there he'll feel how my hands are shaking. I stay an hour past visiting time, peeling the label off the water cup into tiny white curls, and when the nurse comes I'm almost grateful, and then I can't look at him, and I keep nodding at nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana got to the gate twenty minutes early, which had never happened before, and stood at the very front with her keys cutting into her palm. Yesterday's dentist appointment had swallowed the whole afternoon, and she had forgotten the bake sale entirely, the cupcakes Theo had asked about three times. In her bag sat a grocery-store box, still sealed, its price sticker peeled halfway off. She picked at the sticker again. When Mrs. Alvarez nodded hello, Dana laughed too loudly and said, "Busy week, you know how it is," then winced at herself. Her stomach felt tight and warm, like she'd swallowed something hot. The bell rang. Kids poured out in bright jackets, and she rose onto her toes, searching, rehearsing a cheerful voice. When Theo appeared, dragging his backpack, she crouched before he reached her, already holding out the box, her smile stretched so wide her cheeks trembled. "I got you something," she said. "Don't ask me anything yet."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man offered me eight dollars for Mom's oak dresser, and I said yes before he finished the sentence. Then I kept talking, saying it was solid, that the bottom drawer stuck a little, that he should know that. He shrugged and counted out bills. My hands were damp and I wiped them on my jeans twice. When he hoisted it, I stepped forward and tucked the loose drawer back in, though nobody had asked. Her pencil marks from measuring my height were still inside the left side panel, and I almost said so. Instead I stared at the driveway chalk, the price stickers curling in the sun. My stomach felt like I'd swallowed a fist. He drove off with it roped in the truck bed, and I kept waving long after he'd turned the corner. Eight dollars sat folded in my palm. My sister's voicemail was still unplayed on my phone, and I left it that way, and began pricing the lamp lower.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip had started in March, and I'd watched it for eight months, setting a mug under it, emptying the mug, telling no one. Now Dad's ceiling bulged brown above the kitchen table, and I was on my back under the sink with a wrench slipping in my wet fingers. "It's fine, it's nothing, I've got it," I called when he shuffled in, my voice too bright, too fast. He stood there in his slippers. I stared hard at the fitting so I wouldn't have to see his face. My stomach felt packed with cold pennies. Water ran down my wrist into my sleeve, and I let it. When he said, "How long's it been like this?" I tightened the nut far past tight, until the thread squealed, and said the plumber's tape was in the truck. I went out to get it and sat in the cab a full minute with my forehead against the steering wheel before I went back in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope from the Revenue Office sat on the counter for three days, and Marta had moved it twice, once to wipe crumbs, once to hide it under the fruit bowl. Now she stood at the sink with the tap running, rinsing a clean mug, and her shoulders ached as if she'd carried something up stairs. "It's probably nothing," she told the empty kitchen, too brightly. Her thumb found the flap and slid under it, and the paper tore with a sound so loud she flinched. She thought of the cash jobs, the tidy little lie she'd typed on the form two springs ago, her sister's voice saying just do it right. Her mouth had gone dry. She unfolded the page halfway, read only the first line, then pressed it flat against her chest and stared at the ceiling, counting the cracks in the paint, unable to make her eyes go down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed to a stop in Hanoi, and Marcus stood on the platform with his phone held out like an offering, the screen showing his sister's last text: Mom's asking when you're coming home. He typed nothing back. A driver shouted something at him, and he nodded without understanding, then shook his head, then nodded again, and the man laughed and took his bag anyway. In the cab his thumb kept hovering over the unanswered message, and he turned the screen face-down against his thigh. Rain slicked the windows. When the driver spoke, Marcus said, 'Sorry, sorry, I don't...' and trailed off, his voice thinner than he meant it to be. At the hostel, the girl at the desk slid a key across and smiled, and he stared at her kindness as though it were a bill he couldn't pay. Upstairs he sat on the edge of the bed with his shoes still on, jaw tight, stomach hollow, rehearsing a call in a language everyone at home spoke and he somehow could not find.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus stood at the fence with his phone still in his hand, the screen dark, thumb worn smooth against the glass. Biscuit tore across the wet grass in wide, stupid circles, ears flapping, and every time she skidded back toward him he crouched and held out a palm too eagerly. "Good girl. Good, good girl," he said, and his voice came out thinner than he meant. His stomach was tight, a fist under the ribs. Three hours yesterday, she'd waited by the door, and he had come home near midnight smelling of other people's cigarettes. She dropped a chewed tennis ball at his boots, tail whipping, and he couldn't meet her eyes. He picked it up and threw it far, farther than his shoulder liked, then stayed bent over, staring at the mud on his shoes. When she came back panting and leaned her whole weight against his shin, he swallowed hard and whispered, "I'll stay. I'll stay all afternoon."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite arrived at the church hall forty minutes early and stacked the folding chairs herself, though no one had asked her to. When Dale, the other cellist, came in with a thermos for her, she took it with both hands and thanked him twice. They ran the Fauré, and in the third bar she rushed again, then stopped the whole trio before anyone could say anything. "That was me. Sorry. Sorry, again from the top." Her collar felt damp. She kept her eyes on the pencil marks in her score, the ones Dale had erased last week so she wouldn't see how many she'd ignored. She hadn't told him she'd turned down the Saturday sectional to go to her sister's, then never gone. When he laughed and said it sounded fine, her stomach turned over, and she gripped the bow until her knuckles paled. At the break she refilled everyone's tea before her own, and let hers go cold on the piano lid, untouched, while the others talked about parking for the concert.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The cardboard boxes I brought stay flat against the wall because I can't make myself fold the first one. Dust coats the vise, the coffee can of mismatched screws, the half-planed cedar board Walt left clamped down in March. I told him I'd come by that week. I said it twice, actually, once on the phone and once in a text I still have. I pick up his chisel and put it back exactly where the outline in the pegboard says it goes. My palms are slick. When Walt's sister calls up the stairs asking how it's going, I answer, 'Fine, fine, almost done,' much too loudly, though I've filled nothing. I find the radio, and it's still tuned to the station he liked. I switch it off, then on, then off. In the drawer under the bench is a birthday card in my handwriting, never mailed, the stamp already on. I stand there holding it until my knees ache, then slide it into my jacket and finally start taping the box.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and I stood a little apart from the crowd by the noticeboard, picking at the skin beside my thumbnail until it stung. Priya's notes were folded in my bag. I'd told her I'd lost mine, so she lent me hers, and she'd smiled and said, "Take as long as you need." I hadn't lost anything. When she waved from across the hall, I pretended to be reading my phone. My stomach turned over when the secretary came out with the tape and the single sheet. Everyone surged forward. I didn't. "You go ahead," I told the boy beside me, my voice too bright, too fast. Priya's name would be up there too. If mine sat above hers, I knew I wouldn't be able to look at her. I stared at the scuffed toe of my left shoe and counted floor tiles until my ears stopped ringing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta kept her eyes on the switchbacks and didn't slow when the light turned orange, then gray. Her phone buzzed in her pocket for the third time, and she pressed her palm flat against it as though that could muffle it. The pack straps dug into her shoulders; she let them. "Almost there," she told the empty trail, too brightly, and her voice cracked on the last word. Back in the lot, her brother's jacket sat folded on the car's back seat, the one she had promised to return weeks ago, along with a call she had never made. A branch snapped and she flinched, then laughed, a short dry sound. Her stomach was a knot. At the overlook the valley was going blue, and she couldn't make herself look at it. Instead she pulled out the phone, thumbed the screen awake, and read his name again, breath held, until the screen dimmed to black.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, Nonna's slanted handwriting gone brown at the creases, and I keep my thumb off the smudge where she wrote *a good handful*. I measure the flour twice. My phone buzzes with Mom's name and I turn it face down, then put it in the drawer. The kitchen smells right already, which makes my throat tighten. I knead harder than I need to, shoulders aching, and tell the empty room, "Okay, okay, I know." Last spring she asked me to come learn this with her, and I said next weekend. Then next weekend again. The dough sticks to my wrists. I add flour, too much, and don't fix it. When the timer goes off I stand there in oven mitts, not opening the door, staring at the card's last line: *share it*. I haven't dialed anyone. I cut the first slice thick and can't swallow it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was comparing two tins of tomatoes in aisle six when he heard his name, and the tin slipped an inch in his hand. Dana Ruiz stood there with a basket on her hip, older, hair cut short, smiling like nothing had ever happened. "Marcus! Oh my God, twelve years?" He laughed too loudly. His neck went hot. He gripped the tin as if it might be taken from him. "You look great," he said, and then said it again. She asked if he still had the old group's number, and he studied the price label for a long time. "Lost my phone," he said. "Years ago. Sorry." When she mentioned the yearbook money, the envelope, the trip that never happened, he heard himself say he had to run, his wife was waiting in the car. He wasn't married. He pushed his cart toward the exit, the tomatoes still in his fist, and his stomach stayed clenched all the way across the parking lot.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy empties by four on Christmas Eve, and I keep wiping the same stretch of counter while Dana restocks the cough syrup alone. I told her I'd cover her close so she could drive to her sister's, then I took the slot she'd traded for, the one I'd wanted, and let her think it was luck. Now she hums, and my stomach folds tight every time she does. 'You can go,' I say, too loudly, and she laughs and says she's fine, she's the one who owes me. My thumb finds the rag's frayed edge and worries it. I count the till twice, then a third time, though the numbers never change. When the bell over the door jingles, I'm grateful for a stranger, any stranger, someone to smile at. Outside, snow keeps falling on the lot where her little car sits waiting, and I can't look at it. 'Take the good gloves,' I tell her, pushing mine across the counter, already knowing they won't fix anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B42 was a twelve-minute sprint away, and I ran it with my carry-on bouncing against my hip and my phone buzzing in my fist. Mom's name again. I let it ring out, then thumbed it to silent, my throat tight. She'd said the hospital visit could wait until after my trip. I had said, 'Great, then I'll just go.' Too fast. Too relieved. At the moving walkway I stood still for two seconds, which I couldn't afford, and stared at the ad for a bank. 'Sorry, sorry,' I told a man whose shoulder I'd clipped, my voice cracking on the second one. My palms were slick on the handle. The board flashed FINAL CALL, and the agent shook her head, but I kept saying, 'Please, my mother, I mean, I just need to get there,' not sure which there I meant. Then I turned my phone back on and called her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marcus rolled the third coat of eggshell white over the wall where the pencil marks used to be, the little ladder of heights, Dani's name at each notch, the last one from age nine. He had taped around them for a week before finally admitting the tape wouldn't hold the wall still. His shoulder ached, and he kept rolling slower, as if the wall might notice. When his phone buzzed with her name, he wiped his hands on his jeans, then let it ring out and stared at the drip crawling down the baseboard. 'It needed doing,' he said to the empty room, too loudly. The paint can's lid was already hammered shut; he pried it open again just to have something to do. He crouched and pressed a thumb against the last faint gray smudge of a seven-year-old's pencil, now nearly buried, and kept it there until his thumbnail was white. Then he put the roller down, picked up a rag, and couldn't decide which way to wipe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marta sat on the porch step while the rain came down hard enough to bounce off the railing and spatter her shins. She didn't move her feet. Inside, the phone lay face-up on the kitchen table, lit with her brother's name for the fourth time, and she had turned the ringer off without answering. Thunder cracked over the maple, and she flinched, then gripped the casserole dish in her lap, still wrapped in foil, meant for him three weeks ago. "I was going to bring it," she said to the empty yard, her voice small and hoarse. Water ran off the roof in a silver curtain. She peeled back the foil, looked at the congealed cheese, and pressed it down again. Her stomach turned over. The porch light flickered, and she kept her eyes on the gate, half hoping he'd come through it, half hoping the storm would never end.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had been humming for twenty minutes before she noticed it, and the tune was some half-remembered jingle from a cereal ad. The garage smelled of chain grease and someone else's paint thinner, and the neighbor's lawnmower hung from its hook like a sleeping bat, but she barely registered any of it. She spun the rear wheel and listened to the freehub purr, clean and even, no more grinding. "There you are," she told it, grinning at a bicycle. Her fingers were black to the knuckles, and she wiped them on her jeans without a flicker of guilt. When Mr. Okafor shuffled in for his toolbox, she held up the new derailleur cable like a fish she'd caught. "Look at that. Look at it!" He chuckled and said it was just a cable. She bounced on her toes anyway, warmth fizzing in her chest, already planning the long way home along the river, the whole evening wide open.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marisol had been swinging her tote bag in slow arcs since the bus stop bench came into view, and she hadn't stopped humming even when the sky went the color of wet slate. The first fat drops hit the shelter roof like thrown coins. She tipped her face out past the edge to catch one on her cheek, then laughed out loud at nobody. Wind flipped her scarf over her shoulder; she let it. Her chest felt loose and fizzy, her toes tapping inside damp sneakers. 'Perfect,' she told the old man beside her, who only blinked. 'It's perfect, isn't it?' She pulled out the envelope again, read the first line for the tenth time, and pressed it flat against her coat. Thunder rolled somewhere over the rooftops. The bus was late, and she didn't mind at all. She started to sing the chorus, off-key, and the rain kept time on the glass.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid comes off with a puff of dust, and I'm already humming, though I couldn't tell you the tune. I sit cross-legged on the attic boards, knees complaining, and don't care. The top envelope is lavender, my sister's loopy handwriting slanting uphill like always. "Oh, you menace," I say aloud to nobody, and my voice cracks into a laugh. I slide the page out and my cheeks ache already. She's drawn a tiny cat wearing a hat in the margin. I press the paper flat against my chest for a second, feeling my heartbeat thump against it. Sunlight from the little window warms the back of my neck. I should be sorting into piles, keep, toss, maybe, but I've made one pile, and it's the whole box. I grab my phone, thumbs quick, and type, "Found your letters. Call me. Right now. Bring the cat hat." Then I reach for the next envelope, grinning like a fool.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta was elbow-deep in sudsy dishwater, humming something she couldn't name, when the knock came. Through the screen door she saw Mr. Okafor from next door, cap in his hands, squinting apologetically. "I hate to ask, but would you have a ladder?" She was already drying her fingers on her jeans, grinning before he finished. "Do I have a ladder! Come on, it's in the shed." She nearly skipped down the porch steps, the grass cool and springy under her bare feet. The shed door stuck, and she shouldered it open with a laugh, hauling the aluminum ladder out as if it weighed nothing. "Keep it as long as you need. Bring it back with a tomato from your garden and we're even." She walked beside him to the fence, swinging her free arm, the afternoon sun warm on her neck. Back inside, she caught herself still humming, and turned the radio up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol tapped the wooden spoon against the pot's rim in time with the song on the radio, and caught herself humming the wrong verse twice. Steam curled up and fogged her glasses; she pushed them onto her head and kept stirring anyway. The clock said twenty minutes until the doorbell, and instead of hurrying she tasted the sauce, closed her eyes, and laughed out loud at the empty kitchen. "Oh, that's good," she told the basil. Her cheeks ached from smiling. She swayed to the stove, nudged the oven door shut with her hip, and wiped her floury hands down her apron without caring about the streaks. Her shoulders felt loose, her feet light on the cool tiles. She set out one extra chair, then another, just in case, and straightened the candles twice. When a car door slammed outside, she spun around, spoon still in hand, and called toward the window, "Come in, come in, it's almost ready!" before anyone could even knock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter while I was scraping burnt rice off the pot, and the screen showed a string of digits I didn't know. Normally I'd let it ring out. Instead I wiped my hands on my jeans, still humming, and answered in a voice that came out almost sing-song. "Hello?" A woman said my name, then the word *offer*, and the spoon slipped from my fingers and clanged into the sink. I didn't even flinch. My knees went loose, and I laughed, a short bubbling thing, before I could stop it. "Yes. Yes, sorry, I'm here. Say that again?" She did. I pressed my palm flat against my sternum, where my heart was knocking like it wanted out, and spun a slow circle in the kitchen, socks sliding on the tile. My cheeks ached. I realized I was nodding at nobody. "Monday. Yes. Absolutely, Monday." When she hung up, I stood grinning at the dark screen, then yelled my neighbor's name through the wall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Marisol took the library steps two at a time, the battered copy of Middlemarch bouncing against her hip, and she was humming before she realized it. Fourteen months overdue. She had rehearsed apologies all semester, but now, pushing through the heavy glass doors, her face kept bending into a grin she couldn't flatten. The librarian, a man with a gray cardigan and reading glasses on a chain, raised an eyebrow as she set the book down. "I found it," she said, almost laughing. "Behind my dresser. Under a sock. Can you believe it?" Her fingers drummed the counter while he typed. The fine appeared on the screen, huge, absurd, and she just nodded, pulling out her card with a flourish. "Worth it," she told him. Sunlight lay across the tables, and her chest felt light, as if she'd set down more than a book. Outside, she skipped the last step, then turned back and waved at the doors, still smiling at nobody.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The key sticks a little in the lock, and I laugh out loud at nothing, jiggling it until the door swings open onto one room, one window, a radiator painted too many times. I drop the box marked KITCHEN and spin once, arms out, and my fingertips nearly brush both walls. "Okay," I tell the empty room, my voice coming out higher than I meant. "Okay, okay." My cheeks ache. I realize I've been grinning at the stove, which has only two burners and a scorch mark shaped like Ohio. I press my palm flat against the cool plaster, then kick off my shoes just to feel the floorboards, which creak under my socks in a way I decide is friendly. Somewhere downstairs someone is frying onions. I hum, badly, while I tear tape off the first box, and my hands keep wandering to the window latch, opening it, closing it, opening it again to let the whole bright, noisy street in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marisol was halfway through her walk when she spotted the brown leather lump on the bench by the duck pond, and she nearly skipped the last few steps to reach it. Sunlight pooled on the slats, warm against her palm as she picked it up. Inside, a library card, a folded photo of a gap-toothed boy, and a driver's license with an address only six blocks away. She laughed out loud, a short bright bark that startled a pigeon. "Well, Walter Pruitt," she told the license, "you're having a lucky afternoon." Her cheeks ached from grinning. She tucked the wallet into her coat, tapped a little rhythm on the pocket, and swung her arms the whole way down Alder Street, humming a song she hadn't thought of in years. Her feet felt light, her chest loose and wide. At his door she smoothed her hair, took a breath that tingled all the way down, and rang the bell twice, rocking on her heels.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite let go of the wall at the shallow end and kicked. Her feet left the tiled floor, and for three full strokes the water simply held her, cool and silky against her ribs. She reached the red rope and grabbed it, then laughed out loud, a snorting, unladylike sound that bounced off the high ceiling. "Did you see that?" she called to the instructor, who was a decade younger than her daughter. "Did you see?" He gave a thumbs-up. Her heart thumped against her swimsuit, and her fingers tingled where the chlorine had wrinkled them. She pushed her goggles up, wiped her eyes, and found her cheeks ached from grinning. At fifty-three, she had spent her whole life keeping clear of deep water. Now she turned around, eyed the distance back, and said, mostly to herself, "Again. Once more. Then once more after that." She shoved off the rope, sputtering and bright, and kicked toward the wall with her chin lifted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol knelt in the damp dirt with the seed packet pinched between two fingers, and she was humming before she noticed it. The trowel had already raised a blister on her thumb, but she kept pressing it into the soil, making holes she measured against the instructions on the back, then ignored, then measured again. "Six inches," she told the empty yard. "Maybe seven. Who's going to check?" She laughed at herself. Tomato starts waited in their plastic cups along the fence, leaves trembling in the breeze, and she lined them up twice just to look at them. Her knees were soaked through, her hair had come loose, and there was mud on her cheek she'd put there herself. When the last pepper seedling was tucked in, she sat back on her heels, hose in hand, and watered each one slowly, almost whispering. Then she took out her phone and photographed a patch of bare brown dirt, grinning, as though it were already full of green.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marisol had saved the seat nearest the screen for Dev, and she kept glancing at him as he clicked to the first slide, her pen forgotten on the table. When the dashboard he'd built loaded without a hitch, she let out a small breath that was almost a laugh. Her shoulders loosened, and she caught herself bouncing one heel under the table. "Watch this part," she whispered to the intern beside her, leaning in. "He spent three weekends on it." Dev's voice came out steady, then bolder, and when he reached the chart that cut processing time in half, Marisol actually clapped, once, loud in the quiet conference room. Heads turned. She didn't care. Her cheeks ached from smiling, and the afternoon light through the blinds seemed warmer than it had all week. When Dev glanced her way, she gave him two thumbs up and mouthed, "Yes!" Afterward she was the first one at his elbow, already asking if he wanted to get lunch on her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol rolled the window down even though the November air bit at her knuckles, and let it whip her hair across her face. The highway was empty, the sodium lights sliding over the hood in long amber pulses, and she was drumming the steering wheel with both palms, off-beat, not caring. Her cheeks ached. She realized she'd been grinning since the exit ramp, grinning at nothing, at the gas station's flickering sign, at a raccoon that waddled across the shoulder. "Go on, buddy," she called, laughing, her voice cracking on the last word. Her phone buzzed against the cupholder: Dana, a row of exclamation points, again. She'd read it twice already at the red light. The offer letter was folded in her coat pocket, and every few miles her hand drifted down to pat it, just to feel the paper. She sang the chorus wrong, loudly, and turned up the radio until the bass rattled the dashboard, her whole chest buzzing like the engine, light as the empty road ahead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I took the stairs to the fourth floor because the elevator was too slow for my legs, which kept bouncing on their own. The vending machine hummed in the hallway, and I caught myself humming along, off-key. Room 412. Grandpa was sitting up, the tray table swung across his lap, a cup of green gelatin trembling in front of him. 'They let you eat that?' I said, and my voice came out too loud, nearly cracking. He laughed, that wheeze I'd missed, and my chest felt warm and wide, like I'd swallowed sunlight. I pulled the squeaky chair right up to his bed and didn't even bother pretending to check my phone. The doctor said 'Thursday,' and I grinned at the beeping monitor like it had told a joke. I squeezed his hand, still bruised and papery, and couldn't make my face stop smiling. 'Tell me everything,' I said. 'Start with the nurse who stole your pudding.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I'm standing by the chain-link fence twenty minutes early, and I don't even mind that my coffee has gone cold. The maple by the gate is dropping orange leaves, and I catch one out of the air and tuck it in my coat pocket for no reason at all. I'm humming something, and the woman beside me glances over, so I grin and say, "Sorry, long day, good day." My cheeks ache. My feet keep bouncing on the curb like they've got their own plan. This morning Maya whispered that she thought her science project might win. The doors bang open and a flood of backpacks pours out. I'm up on my toes, waving with my whole arm before I spot her. Then there she is, ribbon held high, running. I drop my coffee in the bin without looking and crouch with my arms wide, laughing before she even reaches me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By seven-thirty I had dragged the oak dresser to the end of the driveway, and my arms were humming from it, though I couldn't stop grinning at the thing. A young woman ran her thumb along the drawer edge, and I heard myself babbling about how my grandmother kept buttons in the left one, how it still smelled like cedar if you pressed your nose close. She laughed and did exactly that. 'Twenty dollars?' she asked, and I waved my hand like twenty was a joke, said, 'Take it, take it, just promise me you'll fill it up.' My feet nearly bounced me across the gravel as I fetched twine. The sun was warm on my neck, the coffee in my mug had gone cold and I didn't care, and when her husband hoisted the dresser into the truck bed I caught myself humming, loud and off-key, to the whole empty street. The lighter patch on the lawn looked like room to breathe, and I wanted more people to come.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: I was flat on my back under the kitchen sink, a flashlight clamped in my teeth, humming something tuneless while water dripped onto my wrist. The drip was cold, and I didn't even mind. I wound the Teflon tape around the threads three times, then once more for luck, and my fingers seemed to know exactly what to do. Radio music drifted in from the windowsill, and my foot tapped against the cabinet door in time. When I gave the wrench its final quarter turn, I held my breath, then reached up and twisted the tap on full. Nothing. Not a bead. I laughed out loud, a bubbling, ridiculous sound in that cramped cupboard, and slid out with my shirt soaked and my hair stuck to my forehead. 'Ha! Look at that,' I told the empty kitchen, grinning at a perfectly dry pipe. I wiped my hands on my jeans, felt my chest loose and light, and decided to make pancakes at four in the afternoon, just because.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope was thin, the return address stamped Department of Immigration, and I carried it up three flights of stairs without feeling a single one. My thumb slid under the flap too fast and I got a paper cut, which I only noticed when a bead of red landed on the word Approved. I laughed out loud, alone in the hallway, and the neighbor's dog started barking back. I read it again. Then a third time, lips moving. My knees gave out gently and I sat right on the doormat, keys still in my teeth. "Mama," I said into the phone, voice cracking up high like a kid's, "you're not going to believe the mail." My cheeks ached. I pressed the letter flat against my chest and could feel my heartbeat thumping through the paper. Somewhere below, a door slammed, and I realized I was humming, off-key, the song she used to sing while she cooked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train doors hiss open and Lisbon's warm, fishy air hits my face, and I realize I'm grinning at a pigeon. I can't read a single sign. I wheel my suitcase over the cobbles, its rattle loud as applause, and the wheels skip every few steps so I skip too. At a pastry counter I point at something golden and say, "Um, that one, obrigado?" and the woman laughs, kindly, and repeats the word until I say it better. I do it again, louder. Custard cream bursts onto my chin. I don't wipe it. My chest feels light, fizzy, like a shaken bottle, and my feet keep wanting to go up the hill, any hill. A tram clangs past. I wave at it. Nobody knows where I'm going, including me, and I laugh out loud, alone on the street, then say "obrigado" to the pigeon too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit hits the tall grass at full tilt, ears flipping inside out, and I realize I'm grinning so hard my cheeks ache. I've forgotten the thermos in my hand; coffee sloshes over my knuckles and I don't even wipe it off. He skids, spins, snatches a stick twice his length, and parades it past me like a trophy. "Look at you," I call out, my voice coming out higher and softer than I intended. "Look at that absolute genius." The sun is warm on the back of my neck, and my shoulders, which have been up near my ears all week, have dropped somewhere around my ribs. I sit down right in the damp grass, jeans be damned. He crashes into my lap, tongue lolling, smelling of clover and mud, and I laugh out loud, alone in the field, not caring who hears. Again, I tell him. Go again. I've got nowhere else to be.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite got to the church hall forty minutes early, which no one had asked her to do, and she was humming in the stairwell before she found the light switch. The folding chairs were still stacked against the wall, so she sang the first verse to them, her cello case thumping against her knee in time. When Dev arrived with the sheet music, she was already tuning, and she caught herself grinning at the open C string like it had told her a joke. "Again from bar twelve," she said, too loudly, and laughed at her own volume. Her shoulders had dropped somewhere around the second run-through; her fingers felt warm and loose, almost buoyant on the strings. She missed an entrance, shrugged, and tapped her bow against the stand. "Doesn't matter. Once more?" Outside, the radiator clanked and rain ticked on the windows, and she barely noticed. She was thinking that Thursday's folding chairs would be full of neighbors, and that she couldn't wait to hear the room fill with sound.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dale's workshop smelled of cedar and machine oil, and I caught myself humming before I'd even lifted the first box. Sawdust drifted up from the floorboards in the slant of afternoon light. I pulled open a drawer and found forty-one pencil stubs, each chewed flat at the end, and I laughed out loud, a real bark that echoed off the pegboard. 'You absolute animal,' I told the empty room. My cheeks ached. I held a half-finished birdhouse against my chest, thumb running along the crooked roof he'd never fixed, and I didn't set it in the donate pile. I set it on the dashboard of my truck, belted in like a passenger. Back inside, I turned his radio on, some scratchy polka station, and swept in time with it, boots tapping, shoulders loose. Every tool I wrapped felt like a joke we'd shared. When the light went orange, I realized I'd been grinning for an hour, and I wasn't in any hurry to stop.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the registrar's office smells like floor polish and old paper, and I've been pacing its length since eight. Nobody has pinned the lists up yet, but my feet keep bouncing me along the tiles like I'm on springs. I catch myself humming something tuneless, then grin at the vending machine as if it's in on a joke. A boy beside me chews his thumbnail; I offer him half my sandwich and ask, too loudly, whether he thinks the printer will jam again. My hands are warm, my chest feels loose and fizzy, and I keep rolling my shoulders back like I've just shrugged off a heavy coat. When the clerk finally appears with the tape and the sheets, I'm already first in line, laughing at nothing, saying, 'Go on, take your time,' though my heart is skipping ahead of her. Whatever the number says, I already want to hug her. I think I might hug the vending machine too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then rose, and I'm still climbing, boots crunching over pine needles like I'm stepping on cereal. I've forgotten to check my watch for an hour. My cheeks ache, and I realize I've been grinning at nothing, at a stump, at a squirrel who stares back, offended. "Evening, sir," I tell it, and my voice comes out bouncy, almost a song. The air smells like cold stone and sap. My legs burn, but it's a warm, humming burn, and I swing my arms wider than I need to. At the ridge I stop, flip my pack onto a rock, and spin once, slowly, as the valley fills with shadow. Somewhere below, a thrush starts up. I hum along, badly. I should turn on my headlamp. Instead I dig out the squashed sandwich, eat it standing, and laugh when crumbs fall on my boots. Let the dark come. I'm in no hurry at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth now, stained yellow at the corners, Grandma's slanted handwriting saying only "flour till it feels right." I'm humming before I realize it, some old hymn she used to murmur over this same bowl. My sleeves are shoved to my elbows, and dough clings to my knuckles like warm clay. I press the heel of my hand into it, fold, turn, press, and my shoulders drop away from my ears. Rain taps the window; the kitchen smells of yeast and the faint sweetness I'd forgotten. When the oven timer finally buzzes, I'm already grinning at the loaf, golden and cracked along the top. I tap the bottom. Hollow. "Look at you," I tell it out loud, laughing, and then I tear the heel off while it's still too hot to hold, juggling it between my fingers. One bite and my eyes sting, but my cheeks ache from smiling, and I call my mother just to say, "It worked. Come over. Bring butter."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was comparing two cans of crushed tomatoes in the fluorescent hush of the aisle when someone behind her said, "Marisol Vega? Seriously?" She turned, and the can slipped from her fingers and rolled under the shelf. Neither of them moved to get it. "Dana Okafor," she said, too loud, her voice cracking upward like a teenager's. Her cheeks ached; she realized she'd been grinning for several seconds without a plan to stop. "You cut your hair. It was down to here in tenth grade!" Dana laughed, and Marisol laughed with her, pressing a hand to her chest where her heart was knocking around. She forgot the list crumpled in her pocket. She forgot the frozen peas softening in her basket. "Do you have time? Like, any time? There's a café next door, I'm buying." Her feet felt oddly light on the scuffed tile, and she was already steering her cart toward the registers, humming something from the old school choir.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At ten to six, Marisol flipped the pharmacy's hand-lettered sign to read CLOSED TILL FRIDAY and found she was humming, though she couldn't have said what song. The fluorescent lights buzzed over empty aisles, and she wiped the counter in wide, loopy circles long after it was clean. 'Merry whatever you celebrate,' she told the last customer, grinning so widely her cheeks ached, then pressed a candy cane into the man's palm for no reason at all. Her feet throbbed in their clogs, yet she bounced on her toes while counting the till, losing the total twice and laughing at herself both times. Her coat was already on, one sleeve dangling, because she kept forgetting to put her arm through it. Outside, her sister's car idled in the cold, a casserole dish steaming on the back seat. Marisol shut off the lights, one bank at a time, and stood a second in the dark, breathing in, shoulders loose, light as a held balloon.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol hit the jet bridge doors at a jog, rolling bag clattering behind her, and caught her reflection in the terminal glass: grinning like a fool, hair half escaped from its clip. Twelve minutes until Gate C41. The departures board flickered, and she read it aloud to nobody. "On time. Of course you are." She laughed, a short bright burst that made a man with a coffee glance over. Her legs felt light, almost springy, as if the moving walkway were carrying her on a current. She hummed something tuneless, skipped the last few steps of the escalator, and slid between two slow travelers with a breathless "Sorry, thank you, sorry!" Her pulse thudded warm in her throat. Tomorrow her sister would be standing in an arrivals hall in Lisbon, and every stride shortened the distance. At the gate, the agent lifted her scanner. Marisol held out her phone, chest heaving, cheeks aching, and said, "Hi. I made it," like it was the best news in the world.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol pressed the roller into the tray and dragged it up the wall in one long, wet stripe, and the dull beige simply vanished under a warm yellow. She hummed, off-key, then realized she was humming and kept going. Sunlight from the open window caught the fresh paint and made the whole wall glow like the inside of a lemon. Her shoulders ached, there was a speckle of color across her forearm, and she hadn't once checked her phone. "Look at that," she told the empty room, grinning at a corner she hadn't even finished. She stepped back, nearly tripped on the drop cloth, and laughed out loud. Her feet bounced a little on the creaky floorboards as she reached for the brush again. Tomorrow the couch would return, and the bookshelf, and the plants. Tonight she'd eat cold pizza on an upturned bucket, surrounded by wet walls, and probably refuse to leave the room until bedtime.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the tin roof like thrown pennies, and I was already barefoot on the boards, dragging the wicker chair to the very edge where the spray could reach me. Thunder rolled up the valley. I laughed out loud at nothing, at the sky, and my voice came out cracked and loud. My mug of tea went cold on the railing; I forgot it completely. Cool mist settled on my forearms, and I rubbed it into my skin like lotion. The air smelled of wet dust and cut grass, and I breathed it in until my ribs ached. Across the yard the maple thrashed, and I said, "Go on, then," to it, grinning. My foot kept tapping a rhythm the rain had given it. When lightning split the dark, I counted out loud, one, two, three, and then clapped my hands when the boom came. My chest felt wide, almost buoyant, as though the porch might lift. I didn't want to go inside. I didn't want anything to change at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marta wedged the tire lever under the rim and leaned until her knuckles whitened. Across the garage, Devlin's speakers thumped out the same song for the third time, and his stupid orange toolbox sat sprawled across the workbench, over her half of the pegboard again. She didn't ask him to move it. She slid his socket set an inch toward the edge with one finger, then another inch, then watched it stop just short of falling. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars. "Nice day," he called. "Mm," she said, flat as a washer. The inner tube hissed in the basin, and she held it under longer than she needed to, counting bubbles, picturing nothing in particular, her pulse loud in her ears. When he bent to grab a wrench, she tightened the last bolt on her wheel so hard the metal squealed, and she smiled at the sound.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof while I'm still staring at the schedule, and I laugh once, a dry bark, because of course. Wind shoves a plastic bag against my shin. I kick it off. A man in a clean yellow raincoat squeezes onto the bench beside me, humming, and my jaw locks so hard my molars ache. "Bus is late again," he says, cheerful, like it's a gift. I don't answer. I watch his shoes, spotless, and picture the puddle at the curb swallowing them. My fingernails have dug four little crescents into my palm. The sky goes the color of dishwater and I almost welcome it. Let it pour. Let it soak the driver, the city council, the whole smug line of them with their timetables. When he offers me half his umbrella I look at it, then at him, and slide down to the wet end of the bench, where the water runs straight down my collar and I let it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid came off with a crack, and Marguerite dumped the whole thing across the quilt instead of lifting the letters out one by one. Her brother's handwriting, that looping show-off slant, sprawled over every envelope. She picked one up between two fingers as if it were wet. "Dear Mags," she read aloud, flat as a tax form, and her jaw tightened until her molars ached. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She tore the page down the middle, then again, then kept going until the pieces were too small to mean anything. "Sorry about the funeral," she muttered, mimicking his sing-song. "Sorry, sorry." The radiator clanked. Her nails had gone white against the paper. She reached for the next envelope, and the next, feeding the scraps into the cold fireplace, and when she found the photograph of him grinning on the dock, she pressed her thumb hard into his face and twisted until the gloss cracked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marguerite heard Dale's knuckles on the screen door and kept her eyes on the dishwater, scrubbing the same pan until the enamel squeaked. "Ladder," he said, grinning through the mesh, as if the word were a gift. Her jaw set so tight her molars ached. Eleven years ago he had laughed from his porch while she hauled her husband's funeral flowers through the mud, and the memory still sat in her throat like a swallowed nail. She dried her hands slowly, one finger at a time. "The aluminum one?" she asked, her voice thin and bright. "Gosh. I think it's broken." Behind her, in the garage, it hung on its hooks, clean and perfect. She watched his smile falter and felt her pulse hammer warm and steady in her ears. "Try the Hendersons," she said, and shut the door, and stood in the hallway with her palm flat against the wood, listening to his boots go down the steps one by one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marguerite brought the knife down on the onion so hard the board jumped.
