Seven o'clock, the clock on the stove said, and Daniel's family would be here with their sympathetic faces and their ruined opinions of her. She scraped the pieces into the pan and watched them hiss. "Lovely," she muttered, in the sweet voice she'd use at the door. "So glad you could come." Her jaw ached from clenching. Grease spat onto her wrist and she didn't flinch; she let it sting, almost wanted it. In the hallway, his mother's framed photograph smiled from the wall, and Marguerite turned it to face the plaster without breaking stride. She tasted the sauce, added salt, then more, a whole fistful, and smiled thinly at the pot. Let them choke politely. Her pulse thudded in her ears as headlights swept the kitchen window. She wiped her hands slowly on the dish towel, twisting it like a neck, and went to open the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, a string of digits Marta didn't know, and she let it ring four times while her jaw tightened until her molars ached. She wiped her wet hands on a dish towel, slowly, twisting it as if it had a neck. When she answered, she said nothing. Static, then a man's cheerful voice: "Hi, is this Marta? I'm calling about—" She knew that breath, that little hitch before the name. Her nails dug crescents into her palm. "Don't you ever," she said, low and even, "say my sister's name again." The tap dripped behind her. Heat crawled up her neck and her pulse thudded in her ears. He started to stammer. She stared at the cracked mug he'd once given her, still on the shelf, and pictured it shattering. "I hope you hear this call every night," she said, and pressed the screen so hard her thumb went white.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had spent eleven months under my bed, and I carried it into the library like something I'd pulled out of a drain. Fluorescent light buzzed over the return desk. Mrs. Aldous looked up with that soft, patient smile, and my molars locked together. I slid the Introduction to Macroeconomics across the counter without a word, then let go of it a second too early so it slapped the wood. "Oh, this is quite overdue," she said, tapping her keyboard. "Is it?" I said, flat, watching her fingers. My pulse thudded in my neck. She read out the fine, and I counted her little pearl buttons to keep from saying what I was thinking about her, her cardigan, her laminated sign about quiet. I paid in coins, one at a time, clinking each into her palm. At the door I heard her say thank you, and I let it swing shut behind me, hard, hoping the whole building shook.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta shouldered the door open with her hip and let the last box drop where it landed, the crack of something inside breaking not worth checking. The room was eleven steps long. She counted them, jaw tight, teeth grinding. Pipes knocked behind the wall, and she knocked back with her fist, hard, twice, until her knuckles stung. "Lovely," she said to the empty air, flat and slow. The window faced a brick wall; she yanked the curtain shut so violently the rod sagged. Her mother's voice replayed, it'll be cozy, and her stomach clenched as if she'd swallowed something sour. She peeled the landlord's cheerful welcome note off the counter, folded it into a smaller and smaller square, then shoved it deep into the trash and stood over it, breathing through her nose. Down the hall, a neighbor's laughter drifted through. Marta turned her radio up until the walls hummed, and glared at the ceiling as if it owed her something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the slats of the bench like something left out for him, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and Marlon's jaw tightened before he even touched it. He flipped it open with two fingers. A driver's license: Declan Voss, smiling, squared chin, the kind of face that had never been told no. Marlon's molars ground together until his ears rang. Under the plastic window, a photo of a girl on a sailboat, and a crisp fan of twenties. He counted them slowly, twice, his breath hot and shallow through his nose. A pigeon pecked near his shoe and he kicked at it, hard, missing. 'Of course,' he said, low and flat, to no one. 'Of course you'd lose it somewhere nice.' His fingers had gone white around the leather. He thought of the address on the card, the gate he'd driven past last spring, and he slid the license into his coat pocket, sat down, and stayed there a long while, watching the path for anyone coming back to look.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite gripped the pool's gutter until her knuckles went yellow, jaw clamped so hard her teeth ached. Across the lane, a girl of maybe eight kicked past, graceful, splashing water onto Marguerite's cheek. She wiped it off with a hard, slow swipe. "Kick from the hips," the instructor called, smiling, and Marguerite answered, "I heard you the first time," each word flat as a dropped tray. The chlorine stung her nose. Her heart thudded against the foam board she was crushing to her ribs. She pushed off, sank at once, and came up coughing, eyes burning, picturing the instructor's bright teeth, the kid's easy legs, her own father laughing on the shore forty years ago. She slapped the water. The whistle shrilled again, and she thought of snapping it off its cord. "Again," she said, spitting, and shoved off the wall so hard her shoulder popped, glaring at the deep end as though it owed her something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta drove the trowel into the clay so hard the handle jumped in her palm. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the hardware store. The seed packets lay in the dirt, tomatoes smiling on the front in glossy red, and she kicked one flat with her heel. "Easy, they said," she muttered, voice low and scraping. "Just add water." Sweat ran into her eyes and she wiped it with a gloved wrist, smearing mud across her brow. Next door, Dale's raised beds sat in perfect rows, and she stared at them while she gouged another furrow, crooked on purpose. Every time she dropped a seed she pictured his smug little nod over the fence. She buried them with stabbing pats, thumbs white, breath hissing through her teeth. When the hose kinked, she yanked it until it snapped free, then stood there shaking, soaked to the shins, hoping every single seed would rot and prove him right about nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Derek clicked to the next slide, and the whole room nodded like a field of obedient wheat. My pen had stopped clicking; I'd squeezed it so hard the plastic creaked. The slide read "Q3 Redesign: Led by Derek Voss." Led. I had rebuilt that pipeline over four weekends, and he'd thanked me for the "background help." My jaw ached from holding my smile in place. Someone laughed at his joke about coffee, and I laughed too, a dry little puff, while my fingernails dug four crescents into my palm. The projector fan hummed. His voice was warm, easy, glossy as the conference table, and I watched his mouth move and pictured his laptop slipping from his hands. When Marta asked who'd handled the data layer, he glanced my way, and I said, "Oh, I just helped," so sweetly my teeth hurt. Heat crawled up my neck. On my notepad I wrote his name, then pressed until the paper tore.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty past midnight, and Marguerite drove it with her jaw locked so tight her molars ached. Every set of taillights ahead became his: the same swagger, the same smirk he'd worn while he handed her the termination letter. She gripped the wheel until her knuckles went white and yellow. "Smile now," she muttered to the windshield, voice flat and low. The radio chirped a cheerful jingle and she stabbed it dead with one finger. Her pulse hammered in her ears. At the red light she didn't stop so much as stall, staring at the dark office park where his name was still painted on a parking space. She pictured the paint peeling, the sign cracked, the building black. Her breath came short and hot through her nose. When the light turned green she sat there, letting the horn behind her scream, savoring that she could make someone wait. Then she drove on, whispering his full name over and over like a nail she was driving into wood.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus stood at the foot of his uncle's bed holding the grocery-store carnations like a bundle of sticks. The monitor beeped its steady, stupid rhythm. His uncle's hand lay on the blanket, spotted and slack, and Marcus's jaw ached from clenching. "You look good," he said, flat, each word clipped. A nurse smiled at him; he didn't smile back. He remembered the porch, the belt, the way the old man had laughed. Now the same mouth hung open, dry-lipped, and Marcus caught himself counting the seconds between breaths, hoping for a longer gap. His nails dug half-moons into his palm. When the old man's eyes fluttered and found him, Marcus dropped the flowers on the tray without a vase, without water. "Doctor says you'll pull through," he said, and his voice came out low and cold. He checked his watch, tasting metal. Ten minutes. He'd stay ten minutes, so no one could say he hadn't come, and then he would leave without touching him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana stood at the fence with her car keys biting into her palm, watching Mrs. Kessler's laminated smile bob across the pavement toward the other mothers. The woman laughed at something, a bright, easy sound, and Dana's jaw locked so hard her molars ached. Heat crawled up her neck. She remembered the email, the polite phrasing, her son's name sitting in it like a stain. When Kessler lifted a hand in greeting, Dana looked straight through her and checked her phone, though the screen was black. "Lovely day," someone said beside her. "Is it," Dana answered, flat, not turning. Her thumbnail dug a crescent into her knuckle. The bell rang and children spilled out in a noisy tide, and she kept her eyes fixed on that gray cardigan, tracking it like something she wanted to run down. Her pulse thudded in her ears. When Theo finally found her, she didn't hear a word he said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, and when the young man in the pressed polo offered ten, her molars clamped together until her jaw ached. "Ten," she repeated, flat as the driveway. He smiled and ran a thumb along the drawer edge, leaving a smear in the dust she had left there on purpose. Her pulse thudded in her ears. This was her ex-husband's dresser, the one he'd carried up the stairs himself and sworn would outlast them both. "Fifty," she said. "Price went up." He laughed, thinking it a joke. She didn't blink. The sun pressed hot on her neck, and her fingernails dug small crescents into her palms. When he walked off, she snatched the box of his old cufflinks from the table, dropped it in the trash can, and slammed the lid so hard the neighbor's dog started barking. Then she kicked the dresser's leg, once, and smiled at the next customer with every tooth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay wedged under the sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, water crawling down her wrist and into her sleeve. The drip hit the same spot on her forehead every four seconds, and she counted each one like a debt. She cranked the wrench and the old fitting groaned, then slipped, skinning her knuckles raw. "Of course," she whispered, voice flat and tight. "Of course you would." Her jaw ached from clenching. She thought of Dale, who had sworn he'd replaced this line, who was probably laughing over a beer somewhere with dry feet. She wished the whole rotten house would flood and take his name off the deed with it. She wrapped the tape too hard, tore it with her teeth, and spat the shred onto the cabinet floor. When the leak sputtered and kept going, she drove the wrench against the pipe, once, twice, three times, and smiled at the dent.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter for three days beside the cold coffee, its little plastic window staring up at Marguerite with her name typed in that flat, bureaucratic font. She slit it open with a steak knife, jaw so tight her molars ached. Two pages. A seal. She read the first line and snorted, a short dry sound, then read it again aloud in a mocking singsong, 'We regret to inform you,' crushing the corner in her fist until the paper creaked. Her pulse thudded in her ears. 'Regret,' she said. 'Sure. Sure you do.' She pictured the clerk who'd stamped it, some smooth-handed man eating a sandwich, and her nails bit crescents into her palm. She didn't tear the letter. She folded it into precise, vicious quarters, carried it to the sink, and held the lighter under it, watching the seal curl black, whispering every name she remembered from that office, one at a time, like a list of debts.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marek dragged his suitcase off the train and into the station's wet, echoing noise, jaw so tight his molars ached. A man in an orange vest said something bright and fast, hand outstretched toward the bag, and Marek yanked it away hard enough that a wheel snapped against the tile. "Don't touch it," he said, low, each word clipped flat. The signs overhead were a wall of strange letters; he glared at them as if they had done it on purpose. At the ticket window he slid the crumpled address under the glass without a greeting, and when the clerk spoke slowly, kindly, he stared at her mouth until she stopped. His pulse thudded in his ears. Outside, rain slid down his collar. A child laughed nearby and Marek turned his head to watch the boy, unblinking, until the mother pulled him close. He spat on the pavement, shoved through the crowd with his shoulder, and did not step aside for anyone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the meadow after a sparrow, ears flapping, and my jaw locked so hard my molars ached. I stood at the fence with my fingers clamped around the splintered rail until a sliver bit into my palm, and I let it. Ruth's dog. Ruth's stupid, golden, joyful dog, left on my porch with a note and a bag of kibble like I was a kennel. 'Heel,' I said, low, flat, knowing he wouldn't, and he didn't, and something hot climbed up the back of my neck. The grass bent gold in the wind, the sky was offensively clear. He rolled in something dead and came bounding back, tongue lolling, and I stepped away before he could touch my jeans. 'Don't,' I said through my teeth. He sat anyway, tail sweeping dirt, looking up at me. I wanted to say something that would wipe that look off him. Instead I stared at the ground until my breath slowed, and kept my hands in my pockets.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Marguerite stood at the upright piano with her jaw set so tight her molars ached. Across the room, Dennis hit the high note flat again, then beamed at the folding chairs as if applause were already due. She pressed the F-sharp key until the felt thudded dull. "Again," she said, pleasantly, in a voice thin as wire. Her fingernails left half-moons in her palm. When he asked if the tempo was too brisk, she imagined the lid of the piano dropping, slow and heavy, and her pulse thumped in her ears. "It's perfect," she lied, and turned the page so hard it tore. Behind her, someone laughed at something he'd said. She counted the ceiling tiles. Forty-two. She played the intro again, louder than the score asked, each chord a small slammed door, and did not once look up to see if he was keeping time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus pulled the tarp off the workbench and didn't bother with the dust that rose and coated his tongue. Everything Dale had ever loved hung on pegboard in neat outlines, each chisel traced in black marker, each tidy, patient mark an insult. He took down the good mahogany plane, the one Dale never let anyone touch, and dropped it into a cardboard box so hard the blade chipped. His jaw ached; he realized he'd been grinding his molars since the door. "Labeled," he muttered, flicking a jar of screws labeled MISC. "Of course." The unfinished rocking chair sat in the corner, half-sanded, promised to Marcus's daughter two summers ago. He stared at it until his hands shook, then kicked a leg, and the joint cracked loose. Nobody was there to wince. He wanted Dale to wince. Marcus flipped the radio on, found only the old station Dale liked, and ripped the cord from the wall, breathing through his nose, hot-faced, still holding the plug.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells of floor polish and other people's sweat, and I stand with my back against the radiator until it scorches through my shirt. I don't move. Mr. Hallam is late with the list, and every time the office door clicks, thirty heads jerk up like dogs. Priya laughs beside me, loud and easy, telling someone she probably failed, and she won't have, she never does. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars to grit. I tear the corner off my pen cap with my teeth and spit it onto the tiles, right by her shoe. She doesn't notice. Good. When the paper finally goes up, they surge, and I let them, watching the backs of their heads, picturing each one of them smiling. "Congratulations," I tell Priya, flat, my fingernails cutting little crescents into my palm. "Really. You earned it." My voice sounds sweet. It tastes like pennies.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marnie kicked a pinecone off the ridge and watched it vanish into the gray firs, wishing it had been something with a face. The light was going orange, then brown, and she didn't slow down. Her jaw ached from clenching; she could feel her pulse in her molars. Ahead, a couple in matching yellow jackets laughed about something, and she lengthened her stride just to crowd the heel of the man's boot until he stepped aside. "Lovely evening," he said. She didn't answer, only stared at the back of his neck as she passed, picturing his pack strap snapping, his smile folding. Her phone buzzed in her pocket with his name again, and she thumbed it dark without reading. Cold crept into her fingers. She dug her trekking pole into the mud so hard it shuddered up her arm, and she liked that. "Go ahead," she muttered to the dusk, "get darker." Her breath came out in sharp, white bursts, and she did not turn back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, stained with thirty years of her thumbs, and I slap it flat on the counter hard enough to rattle the flour tin. "A handful of this. Warm water, not hot. You'll know." I don't know. She never wrote anything down that mattered. My jaw aches from clenching it. I dump the yeast in, too much, and stir until the spoon bends in my fist. The kitchen smells like her, and I open the window so the cold can scrub it out. When the dough sticks to my fingers I hiss through my teeth and pound it against the board, again, again, imagining nothing, imagining everything. Her looping handwriting says, 'Be patient, dear.' I tear the card's corner off with my thumbnail. Then I stand there, breathing hard, flour to my elbows, and shove the bowl into the oven like I'm locking something away. Let it burn. I'll eat it anyway, standing up, and not say a word to anyone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta was weighing two cans of tomatoes when she heard the laugh, that bright, braying laugh from tenth grade, and her thumb dented the soft aluminum before she turned. Dennis Kroll stood at the end of the aisle in a pressed quarter-zip, a toddler on his hip. "Marta? No way. It's been, what, twenty years?" Her jaw ached; she realized she was grinding her teeth. "Twenty-one," she said, flat, each word set down like a coin. He kept smiling. She remembered the cafeteria, the whole table watching her tray fall. Her pulse thudded in her ears while the freezer lights hummed. "You look great," he said. "Do I." She put both cans back, gripped the cart handle until her knuckles paled, and pushed past him without slowing, close enough that the toddler's shoe brushed her sleeve. She did not look back. At the register she realized she had forgotten everything she came for.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 5:47 on Christmas Eve, Marguerite wiped the same patch of counter for the fourth time, pressing until her knuckles whitened. The speaker overhead looped the same jingling song, and her jaw clenched with every chorus. A man in a reindeer sweater slapped a gift card down and said, 'Quick, I'm late,' and she smiled with only her teeth. 'Of course you are,' she said, so softly he asked her to repeat it. 'Merry Christmas,' she said instead, scanning his items slowly, one at a time, letting each beep drag. Heat crawled up her neck. Behind him the line curled past the freezers, a snake of coats and sighing, and she pictured flicking the lights off, one switch, all of them blinking in the dark. Her manager waved from the office, cheerful, already wearing his scarf. She stared at his back until the door closed, then tore the receipt off so hard it ripped in half.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B42 was a mile from where the shuttle spat me out, and the man in front of me on the moving walkway stood dead center, reading his phone, his wheeled bag planted like a flag. I said, "Left," quietly. Then again, through my teeth. He didn't turn. My jaw ached; my nails had cut little crescents into my palm around the boarding pass. I pictured his suitcase tipping over the rail, slowly, and the picture pleased me. When the belt ended I shoved past, my shoulder clipping his, and did not say sorry. Behind me he muttered something. I kept walking, counting gate numbers like a sentence I was serving. The monitor flipped to CLOSED. The agent smiled at me, bright and useless, and I stared at her name tag until her smile faltered. "Thirty-one minutes," I said, flat. "Everyone in this building has been wasting mine." My pulse thudded behind my eyes. I wanted every cheerful voice on the intercom switched off for good.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pried the lid off the paint can with a screwdriver and stabbed the blade in harder than she needed to. Beige. Daniel had picked beige. She dragged the roller through the tray until it dripped, then slapped it against the wall where his bookshelf used to stand, leaving four pale ghost-rectangles she attacked again and again. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth since morning. 'Eleven years,' she muttered, and the roller squealed. A crayon mark from the kids' toddler days peeked through the first coat, and she scrubbed it with her thumbnail until the skin stung, then painted over it with a flat, savage stroke. Sweat slid into her collar. When his old coffee mug, still on the windowsill, caught the light, she picked it up, held it over the open paint can, and let it hang there, her knuckles white, her breath hissing through her nose, before she finally let go and watched the beige swallow it whole.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite didn't move when the first thunder cracked, though the porch boards shook under her slippers. Rain hammered the tin roof and blew sideways onto her knees, and she let it. In her lap lay the envelope from her brother's lawyer, creased where her thumb had worked it for an hour. Across the yard his old truck sat in the mud, the one he'd promised their father he'd never sell, and she stared at it until her jaw ached. 'Rust,' she said aloud, flat and quiet. 'Rot in it.' Lightning lit the cornfield white, and her teeth were clenched so hard her temples throbbed. She tore the envelope in half, then in half again, and again, until the pieces were small as moths. The wind took them off her palm. She didn't watch where they went. Her pulse beat hot in her ears, steady as a fist on a door, and when the screen door banged behind her she did not turn to see who it was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had been trying to seat the same bearing for twenty minutes, and the shared garage hummed around her with other people's radios and the tick of someone's cooling engine. She wiped her palms on her jeans, again, though they were already clean. The bike was Dani's old commuter, the one with the dent in the top tube, and she had promised to fix it before the move. Now there was no move. She tightened the wrench, loosened it, tightened it. "Almost done," she told the empty stool beside her, and her voice cracked on the second word. Her throat felt packed with sawdust. When the neighbor asked if she wanted coffee she said, "No, I'm good, really," too fast, eyes fixed on the chain. A drop landed on the frame and she rubbed it into the grease with her thumb, carefully, as if it were a smudge she could blame on the work. Then she kept turning the pedal, listening to it spin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was still holding her phone out in front of her, thumb hovering over a name she had typed and deleted four times. The wind lifted the schedule taped inside the glass, and she watched it flap without reading it. She had left the umbrella on his hook by the door, the one with the chipped green handle, and the thought of it hanging there made her jaw tighten until her teeth ached. Rain slanted in under the awning and soaked her left sleeve; she didn't move over. 'Fine,' she said aloud to no one, then again, quieter, her voice cracking on the vowel. A bus hissed up, doors folding open, the driver looking at her. She shook her head, and he shrugged and pulled away. Her hands were shaking, so she pushed them into her coat pockets and found his spare key there, cold and small, and stood holding it as the street went gray.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta knelt on the attic boards with the shoebox between her knees, and the dust made her cough once, sharply, before she went quiet. The top envelope was soft at the corners. She slid the letter out, read the first line, and set it face down on her thigh as though it might wake. "Okay," she said to the rafters. "Okay." The next one she read all the way through, lips moving, and her thumb kept rubbing the same loop of his handwriting until the ink seemed to blur, though the light hadn't changed. Her throat had gone tight and thick. She sorted them by postmark, then stopped at the last one, thin, unsealed, dated March, and held it without opening it. Rain ticked on the roof. She pressed her palm flat against her sternum, as if to keep something from slipping out, and laughed at herself, a short wet sound. Then she put every letter back in order, closed the lid, and sat there with both arms wrapped around the box.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked twice and stood on my porch with his hands in his jacket, asking if he could borrow the tall ladder for the gutters. I said sure, of course, and my voice came out thin, like paper. The ladder hung in the garage where Margaret had always hung it, on two hooks she'd chosen. I lifted it down and my arms shook more than the weight explained. Her handwriting was still on the masking tape near the top rung: DON'T LEAN, SILLY. I rubbed at it with my thumb, then stopped. Dale said he'd bring it back by Sunday. I nodded at the driveway instead of at him. After he carried it off across the lawn, I stayed in the garage a long while, staring at the two empty hooks, my throat tight, my hand flat against the cold wall as though something might need holding up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions are already translucent when I realize I've set out four plates for five people, and then I realize it's the opposite, and I stand there holding the fifth one against my ribs like it might fill something. Seven minutes until the doorbell. I wipe my hands on my apron, leave a wet smear of garlic across the front, and don't fix it. The phone buzzes on the counter, face down, and I turn it over only to check the time, careful not to look at the thread above it. When I stir the risotto my arm feels borrowed, slow, heavy at the elbow. I taste it. Nothing. I add salt, taste again, nothing. "It's fine," I say to the empty kitchen, too brightly, the way you'd tell a child the dog is only sleeping. Her mug is still in the drying rack. I put it in the cupboard, then take it out, then just stand there with the steam fogging my face, glad it hides why my eyes sting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, between the two mugs Daniel hadn't yet put away, and the screen showed a number with a area code he didn't know. He let it ring four times. His thumb hovered, trembling slightly, then pressed. "Hello?" It came out thin, scraped. Static, then a breath, then nothing, and he stood there gripping the counter's edge until his knuckles paled. "Mara?" he said, quieter. "If it's you, you don't have to say anything." A man's voice finally asked if this was the right number for a car warranty. Daniel laughed, one short, wet sound, and slid down until his back met the cabinet. The tiles were cold through his shirt. "No," he said. "Wrong number." He didn't hang up. He listened to the stranger say sorry, twice, then the dial tone's long flat line, and kept the phone pressed to his ear, her coat still hanging by the door, a throat so tight he couldn't swallow the water he'd poured an hour ago.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The return slot was jammed with flyers, so I had to carry the book to the desk, and my hands wouldn't stop shaking against its cracked blue spine. Four years overdue. Dad's name was still penciled inside the back cover, checked out the week before the hospital. I'd found it under his bed while sorting his shirts. The librarian, a young guy with a lanyard, scanned it and said the fine was capped at ten dollars. I laughed, a wet wrong sound, and then couldn't stop my chin from trembling. 'Sorry,' I said, 'sorry, it's just... he never finished it.' My throat felt packed with sand. I slid the bill across, but my fingers kept hold of the corner of the cover a second too long, thumb tracing his handwriting. The fluorescent lights hummed. 'Do you want a receipt?' he asked softly. I nodded, though I knew I'd leave it on the bus. Outside, I stood on the steps, arms wrapped around nothing, unable to decide which way to walk home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left four boxes and a lamp, and the door clicked shut behind them with a sound too loud for a room this size. I stood in the middle of the floor, which took two steps to cross, and held a mug I didn't remember picking up. Her name was still on it, in that chipped blue glaze. I set it on the windowsill, then moved it to the counter, then back. My chest felt like a fist had closed around something and kept squeezing. 'Okay,' I said to the radiator, my voice cracking on the second syllable. 'Okay. Bed goes there.' There was nowhere else for it to go. I tore the tape off a box marked KITCHEN and found only the second pillow, still smelling of her shampoo. I sat down hard on the floor with it pressed against my face, and breathed through the cotton until my ribs stopped shuddering. Outside, someone's dinner sizzled through the thin wall. I realized I hadn't eaten since morning, and couldn't imagine swallowing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and Dana almost walked past it. Instead she sat, slowly, as if the slats might give way. Pigeons worked the gravel near her shoes. She opened it with two fingers. A bus pass, a library card, a folded photo-booth strip of a man pulling faces, four frames of him laughing. Her throat tightened until swallowing took effort. She had bought this exact wallet once, years ago, wrapped it in newspaper because the store was out of paper. "Don't be stupid," she said aloud, her voice thin and cracking on the last word. The name on the license wasn't his. Of course it wasn't. Still her hands shook as she tucked the strip back behind the cards, smoothing it flat with her thumb, over and over. A jogger passed. She kept her face turned toward the empty pond until the light on the water blurred, then pressed her sleeve hard against her eyes and stayed put.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor tells me to let go of the wall, and I do, which surprises us both. Chlorine stings my nose. I'm thirty-eight, in a lane with children, kicking a foam board toward the far end. Dana always said she'd teach me, on some lake, some August. Her August is in a lawyer's folder now. My legs sink. My breath comes in short pieces, and when I put my face in the water I let out a sound that turns into bubbles, so nobody hears it. "Relax your shoulders," the instructor calls. I try. My jaw is locked so tight my teeth ache. I surface, cough, and say, "I'm fine, I'm fine," twice, too fast. A kid beside me floats on his back, arms wide, easy. I stare at the ceiling lights smeared by my wet lashes and think: just hold still, just let it hold you. It doesn't. I grab the wall and stay there until the whistle, forehead against cold tile.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marnie knelt in the damp strip of dirt behind the rental, the seed packets lined up on the fence rail like a row of tiny, cheerful flags. Two of them were in Daniel's handwriting: *basil, too much*, *carrots—deep!* She read them twice, then pressed her thumb into the soil until the nail went white. The trowel felt heavier than it should. She dug a furrow, too crooked, and didn't fix it. 'Okay,' she said aloud, and her voice cracked on the second half of the word, so she said it again, flatter. Tomato starts waited in their plastic tray, leaning toward the light. She set one in the hole and her hands wouldn't stop shaking, soil sifting through her fingers. A neighbor's radio played something with a saxophone. She sat back on her heels, breath catching in short pieces, and stared at the single green plant until it blurred. Then she reached for the watering can, because someone had to, and poured slowly, careful not to drown it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked to the next slide, and Dana's voice carried on, bright and sure, explaining the dashboard Marcus had sketched on a napkin eight months ago. Same layout. Same name for the tool, even. Nobody turned to look at him. He kept his pen pressed to the notepad until the tip tore a small hole through the page. The conference room was too cold, and his throat felt packed with sawdust. When the director said, "Dana, this is fantastic," Marcus heard himself say, "Yeah. Really great," in a voice that came out thin and polite, like a stranger's. He nodded at the right moments. He reached for his water and found the cup empty, so he lifted it anyway and pretended to sip. His chest felt hollowed and heavy at once, as if something had been scooped out and replaced with wet sand. On the screen, Dana's name glowed in the corner. Marcus stared at the napkin's ghost in every pixel and counted the ceiling tiles until the lights came up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The traffic light at Delmar turns red, and I stop for it even though there's no one else on the road, just my headlights smeared across wet asphalt. I keep my hands at ten and two like my father taught me. My throat is tight, a swallowed stone, and every time I breathe in, my ribs ache as if I'd run here. Her sweater is still on the passenger seat. I told myself I'd leave it there until morning, but I reach over and press it against my face anyway, and it smells like her shampoo, and I make a sound I don't recognize. The light goes green. I don't move. Somewhere behind me a car hums up and waits, politely, and I whisper, 'Sorry, sorry, just a second,' to nobody, to the mirror, to the empty seat. Then I drive on, past my own street, because the house will have two coffee mugs in the drying rack.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine on the fourth floor ate my dollar twice, and I stood there pressing the return button long after it was clear nothing would come back. Grandpa's room smelled of lemon cleaner. I set the crackers he used to love on the tray table, though the nurse had said he wasn't eating. He looked at me and asked if I was the man about the gutters. "No, Grandpa. It's Danny." My voice came out thin, like it belonged to someone younger. He nodded politely, the way you nod at a stranger on a bus. I pulled the chair close and kept my hands under my thighs so he wouldn't see them shaking. The monitor beeped; I counted the beeps to have something to do. My throat felt packed with wet sand. When he said the gutters were fine, really, I said, "Good, that's good," and stared at the window until the parking lot blurred into one gray smear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marguerite stood at the far end of the fence, away from the cluster of mothers comparing weekend plans, a folded sheet of paper pressed flat inside her coat pocket. The bell rang and doors banged open, and she counted the red backpacks without meaning to. When Theo came out, dragging his sleeve across his nose, he didn't run to her the way he used to; he walked, and stopped a full arm's length away. "Dad's picking me up Thursdays now," he told her shoes. "Mrs. Alvarez said you'd tell me." She nodded, and kept nodding a beat too long. Her throat had gone tight, as if she'd swallowed the whole cold afternoon. "Okay," she managed, her voice thin as paper. "Okay. Want your scarf?" Her fingers shook on the wool as she wound it twice around his neck, then a third time, slower, until he squirmed. She stayed crouched there on the wet pavement long after the other cars had pulled away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man wants the oak dresser for six dollars, and I say, "Five's fine," before he's finished opening his wallet. He grins like he's won something. My hand keeps smoothing the top, over the pale ring where Dad set his coffee every morning for thirty years. I tell the man the bottom drawer sticks, you have to lift and pull, and my voice goes thin on the word pull. He nods without listening. His son hauls one end down the driveway, and the corner scrapes the mailbox post. I flinch like it's my own shin. When the truck pulls away I'm still holding the five-dollar bill, folded small, pressed so hard into my palm it leaves a damp crease. The sun is too bright on the empty patch of grass. My throat aches, my chest hollow as that drawer. A woman asks about the lamp, and I hear myself say, "Sure, take it," and then I have to sit down on the cooler.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip under the sink keeps time like a clock I never wanted. I'm on the cabinet floor with a wrench, my cheek against cold particleboard, and I've tightened the same nut four times. Her yellow gloves are still hanging over the cabinet door, stiff with dried soap. I keep not looking at them. "Come on," I tell the pipe, and my voice comes out thin and cracked, like it belongs to someone older. Water slides down my wrist into my sleeve. I let it. The plumber's video says to dry the joint first, so I reach for a towel and find it's the one with the faded lemons she bought at that market, and I just stay there, towel pressed to my mouth, my chest folded around something heavy. The drip goes on. After a while I realize the wrench is on the floor and I've no idea when I put it down. I pick it up. I tighten the nut again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter next to his coffee mug, the one with the chipped handle, and I let the kettle go cold before I touched it. Department of Immigration, the corner said. I slid a butter knife under the flap, careful, like tearing it might change the words. One page. I read the second line and then the first line again, and the kitchen tilted. My thumb had gone numb against the paper. "Okay," I said to nobody, too brightly, "okay, okay." I folded it along its creases, unfolded it, folded it. His jacket still hung on the hook by the door, and I found myself standing in front of it with my forehead pressed into the sleeve, breathing in wool and cedar. My throat wouldn't swallow. Somewhere upstairs a phone buzzed and buzzed. I didn't go. I sat down on the floor instead, the letter flat on my knees, smoothing it again and again as if it were something that could be comforted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed out of Tbilisi's station behind me, and I stood on the platform holding two tickets when I'd only needed one. A man in a gray cap said something, rolling and warm, and I nodded anyway, like nodding might pay for it. My suitcase wheel clicked over every crack in the concrete. At the kiosk I pointed at a bottle of water, held up fingers, and the woman laughed kindly and said a number I couldn't catch. I held out a fistful of coins. She took what she needed. Outside, rain had started, and I didn't open the umbrella; I just walked, thumb pressing the second ticket until it softened and tore. The signs looked like beautiful curled wire. I couldn't read one. In the hostel I sat on the bed with my coat still on, and my chest felt hollowed, as if someone had scooped it with a spoon. 'Okay,' I told the empty room, too quietly. 'Okay.' Then I turned her side of the bed into a place for my bag.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the fence with a leash coiled in her fist, the nylon biting into her palm. Out in the long grass Biscuit tore in wide loops, ears flipping inside out, chasing nothing at all. She'd told the vet yesterday that she understood, in a voice so level it embarrassed her. Now her throat kept closing around the same small breath. 'Good girl,' she called, and it cracked in half. Biscuit skidded, spun, and bounded toward her, tongue lolling, and Marta crouched too fast, pressing her face into the warm, grass-smelling fur until her shoulders shook without a sound. A gull cried somewhere over the pond. The late sun laid everything out gold and ordinary. 'Again,' she whispered, standing, wiping her sleeve across her face, and she threw the ball as far as her arm would go, then watched it the whole way down, unable to look away from the dog, unable to look straight at her either.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Marguerite had set her cello up in the corner beneath the stacked folding chairs. Tuesday rehearsal. The others were laughing over the second movement while she tuned the same string for the third time. "Sorry, one more," she said, too brightly, and her voice came out thin. When the conductor raised his baton she found the opening bars of the duet and played them anyway, though the second part, the part Daniel used to take, hung in the air with nothing under it. Her bow wobbled. Her throat felt packed with sawdust. She stared at the empty chair beside her, where someone had left a folded program, and pressed her fingers into the strings until they ached. "Again from measure twelve?" she asked, and nobody noticed that she hadn't blinked in a while. Afterward she stayed, wiping rosin from a clean instrument, long after the lights clicked off one by one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The pencil behind the vise still has his teeth marks in it. I hold it for a while, then set it in the box marked KEEP, then take it out and set it in the box marked DONATE, then take it out again. Sawdust lifts in the window light every time I move. I'd promised his sister I'd have the bench cleared by Friday, so I start with the chisels, wrapping each in a rag the way he never did, and my hands won't stop shaking enough to tie the twine. "You'd laugh at this knot," I tell the empty room, and my voice cracks on laugh. The radio on the shelf is still tuned to that terrible AM station. I can't turn it off. I sit on his overturned bucket, press my palm flat against my sternum, and breathe through my mouth until the room stops tilting. Then I pick up the next chisel.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells like floor wax and old radiators, and I've been standing in front of the glass case since seven. The sheet goes up at nine. Someone's taped a corner crooked. My thumbnail has worked a crescent into the pad of my index finger, and I keep pressing it deeper. When the secretary finally pins the list, the crowd surges and I let it carry me back a step. I find my number anyway. Third column. I read it twice, then a third time, as if the digits might rearrange. My throat closes around a little dry click. Someone beside me laughs, high and relieved, and I nod like I'm in on it. 'Congrats,' I say, but it comes out as air. I'd already texted Mum that I'd call at nine-fifteen. I walk to the stairwell, sit on the cold concrete step, and stare at my phone's black screen until my own face looks back, small and very far away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta kept walking past the junction where the two of them had always turned back for dinner. The light had gone orange, then the color of weak tea, and the pines stood closer together than she remembered. She'd brought two water bottles out of habit and carried the second one against her ribs like a stone. Her headlamp stayed in her pack. 'Fine,' she said to a jay, flatly, then again, quieter, 'fine.' Her throat ached as though she'd swallowed the whole ridge. At the overlook she sat on the cold granite and took out her phone, thumbed the screen to his name, and watched it dim without pressing anything. Her breath came in short, uneven pulls. Below, the valley lights flickered on one by one, and she counted them until her vision swam. When she finally stood, her knees shook, and she realized she had hiked an hour in the dark without once looking at the trail, and had no idea which way was down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, its corners gone round, and Marisol propped it against the flour canister where the grease spots had already made a map. Nana's slanted handwriting said *a good handful of salt* and *knead till it feels right*, and she read that line three times, out loud, to the empty kitchen. "Right how?" Her voice cracked on the second word. She pushed the heels of her hands into the dough and kept pushing long after it had gone smooth, her shoulders aching, her breath coming in short catches. A tear dropped onto the board and she worked it into the flour without wiping her face. When the loaf came out, the whole apartment smelled like that other house, the one with the plastic-covered couch. She stood holding the hot pan with a bare hand, not feeling it until the sting arrived. Then she sat down on the linoleum with the bread beside her and didn't cut it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a carton of oat milk and a single toothbrush when Dana Whitfield said my name over the cereal aisle. We hadn't spoken since tenth-grade chemistry. She looked the same, bright and quick, and she asked what I'd been up to. "Oh, you know," I said, and my voice came out thin, like paper tearing slowly. She noticed the bag on my arm, the men's sweatshirt I'd grabbed from the closet that morning because it still smelled like him. My throat tightened around every word. I kept nodding at things she said without hearing them. The freezers hummed too loudly. When she mentioned her wedding in June, I laughed a beat too late and stared at the toothbrush in my hand, turning it over and over. "That's wonderful," I said. "Really." My eyes stung under the fluorescent lights, so I pretended to read the back of the cereal box. I left the oat milk on the shelf and walked out without paying for anything, my hands cold and shaking against my ribs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy empties by four, and I keep restocking the same shelf of cough syrup because my hands need a job. Someone has taped paper snowflakes to the register, and I peel one off, fold it small, and put it in my apron pocket. "Happy Thanksgiving," I tell a man buying antacids, and my voice comes out thin, like it's been left in the dryer too long. He says it back. I nod too many times. My phone buzzes against my hip and I don't take it out; I already know it isn't her, and I already know what the screen would show me, which is the photo from the lake. The fluorescent lights hum. My chest feels hollowed and sat on at once. At close I mop the same tile twice, lock the door, and stand in the dark lot holding two sets of keys, one of them for an apartment I'm supposed to stop driving to. I turn the engine on and just sit there with the heater blowing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol ran the length of Terminal C with her carry-on bumping against her hip, and somewhere past Gate 22 she realized she was still wearing the ring on her thumb, turned inward, the way she'd worn it all morning. The board said Gate 41, final call. Her throat felt packed with wet sand. At the moving walkway she stood still and let it carry her, though she'd been sprinting a minute earlier, and a man behind her said, 'Ma'am, you can walk,' and she said, 'Sorry, sorry,' very quietly, three times. Her phone lit up with his name and she turned it face down against her leg. At the gate the agent was already lifting the handset. 'Please,' Marisol said, and her voice cracked in the middle of the word. She held out the boarding pass with both hands, since one wouldn't stop trembling. The agent looked at her face, then scanned it. Marisol walked down the jet bridge counting her steps, eyes stinging at the cold hum of the lights.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Dana had taped the edges twice, though the tape was already straight. The roller hissed across the wall, and the yellow they'd picked together in a hardware store aisle disappeared under a flat, clean white. She worked in small squares, slowly, as if the wall might object. Near the window, pencil marks climbed the door frame: Ines, age four, age five, age six. Her hand stopped. The roller dripped onto the drop cloth, a soft tap, tap. She set it in the tray and stood there until her knees ached. 'It's fine,' she said to the empty room, too brightly, and cleared her throat. 'It's just paint.' Her voice came out thinner than she meant. She pressed her palm flat against the frame, over the last pencil line, and her throat burned. Then she picked up the small brush, dipped it, and did not paint over it yet. She sat on the upturned bucket, breathing through her mouth, listening to the house say nothing back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in just as I carried two glasses of lemonade out to the porch, and I stood there holding both like an idiot. I set one on the rail anyway. Rain came sideways, soaking my knees, and I didn't move the chair. The swing creaked under me. Across the yard the maple thrashed, and I kept thinking about how she'd always counted the seconds between flash and boom, out loud, bossy about it. "One, two, three," I whispered, and my voice cracked somewhere around four. My hands wouldn't stay still; I pulled at a loose thread on my sleeve until the cuff puckered. The lemonade sweated a ring onto the wood. My chest felt packed with wet sand, and every breath had to push through it. When the phone buzzed against my thigh, I flipped it facedown without looking. Lightning split the sky white. I counted anyway. One. Two. Nobody told me I was wrong.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The garage smells of other people's oil and someone's forgotten orange peels, but I've claimed the back bench anyway, the one under the flickering tube. Mrs. Okafor's lawn mower sits beside me like a sleeping dog. I spin the rear wheel and listen: tick, tick, tick, then a clean, quiet whir where yesterday there was a grinding rasp. My thumbs are black to the knuckle and I'm grinning at a derailleur like it told a joke. I hum something, badly. The new chain slides over my palm, cool and heavy, and I lay it along the cassette with the care of someone threading a needle. Dev leans in from the next stall and asks if it's done. "Almost," I say, too fast, too bright. I'm already counting the hours until Saturday, picturing the long road out past the reservoir, my coat zipped to my chin. I tighten the last bolt, wipe my hands on my jeans, and keep pressing the tire with my fingertips.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as Marisol checked her phone again, and instead of sighing she smoothed the folded envelope in her jacket pocket and straightened up. Wind shoved the maples sideways; a paper cup skated past her shoes. She didn't move to the bench. Her heart was knocking quick and light against her ribs, and she caught herself rocking on her toes, almost smiling at nothing. "Come on, twelve," she murmured, leaning out to peer down the road through the gray slant of rain. A man beside her muttered about the weather. "It'll pass," she said, too brightly, and laughed at herself. Her hair was soaking at the edges and she barely noticed. Somewhere past the curve, headlights smeared yellow across the wet asphalt. She pulled the envelope out, pressed it flat once against her chest, and stepped to the curb with her free hand already lifted, as though the interview had already said yes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marisol knelt on the attic boards with the shoebox between her knees, dust turning gold in the slanted light from the vent. She had meant to check only the top few envelopes, but an hour had gone, and her tea sat cold and forgotten. Each letter she slid free went onto one of two piles, and the left pile, the one with the Lisbon postmarks, kept growing. Her thumb trembled on the flap of a blue envelope. "Come on, Nana," she murmured, laughing at herself, "give me an address." She unfolded the page, eyes racing down it, lips moving, until she reached the line at the bottom. Rua das Flores, 14. She sat up straight, heart knocking against her ribs, and pulled her phone from her back pocket. Her fingers felt warm, almost buzzing. She copied the street onto her palm in pen, then reached into the box again, quicker this time, certain there would be more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marguerite was halfway through scraping the last of the dried paint from the porch rail when Dale from next door appeared at the fence, cap in his hands, asking if she still had that tall ladder. She straightened so fast her knees cracked. "The aluminum one? Yes. Yes, it's in the garage, hang on." She was already walking, then jogging, her palms tingling, her pulse tapping in her ears. Dale had not spoken to her since the funeral casseroles, and now here he was, needing something only she had. She hauled the ladder out, wiped the cobwebs off the rungs with her sleeve, and found she was smiling at the dust. "Take it as long as you want," she called, too loudly. "Keep it the whole weekend. Bring it back whenever. Or don't, come by for coffee, I'll leave the porch light on." Dale laughed, a small rusty sound, and she held the gate open wider than she needed to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol wiped her palms on her apron and lifted the lid on the pot, letting the steam bloom against her face. Saffron and garlic. She smiled before she could stop herself. Twenty minutes left, and the table was already set with the blue plates her sister had once admired. She hummed, off-key, while she chopped parsley too fine, then laughed at herself. Every few moments her eyes slid to the window, to the empty street, then back to the cutting board. Her shoulders felt loose, almost light. When the oven timer ticked, she crouched, peeked at the bronzed edges of the bread, and whispered, "Come on, you beauty." She straightened a fork that was already straight. She lit the candle, blew it out, lit it again. Somewhere down the block a car door shut, and her heart gave a quick, bright skip. She turned the stove down low, tasted the sauce, and nodded. "This time," she told the empty kitchen, "they're going to stay for dessert."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the counter while I'm rinsing a single mug, and the number is a string of digits I don't know. Water keeps running. I dry my hands on my jeans, too slowly, then too fast, and nearly knock the phone into the sink. Eleven days since I sent that application, and I've checked my email so often my thumb knows the route by itself. My chest feels tight and light at once. I walk to the window, as if the signal might be better by the glass, and press the phone to my ear before the fourth ring. "Hello?" It comes out higher than my normal voice. I clear my throat, stand up straighter for nobody, and try again. "Yes, this is she. Speaking." My free hand is flat against the cold window, fingers spread, and I realize I'm holding my breath, listening to the small crackle before someone on the line starts to talk.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book has been in my backpack since March, and it's now November, but I walk into the library with my shoulders loose and the spine of Middlemarch pressed flat against my palm. Rain drips off my sleeve onto the carpet. The librarian looks up, and instead of the apology I rehearsed on the bus, I just grin and say, "So, funny story. Eight months." My voice comes out lighter than I expected. I slide the book across the desk and lean in, watching her fingers, tapping my heel against the floor. The scanner beeps. I'm already counting coins in my pocket, but I'm also glancing at the new-arrivals shelf, thinking maybe she'll waive the fine, or at least halve it. "Is there a payment plan?" I ask, smiling so hard my cheeks ache. Whatever she says, I figure I'll walk out of here with something else under my arm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol carried the last box up four flights and set it down in the middle of the floor, and the whole room fit inside one long breath. Radiator, a window the size of a cutting board, a stain on the ceiling shaped like Ohio. She pried the window open, and the cold October air slid in smelling of fried onions and rain. "Okay," she said aloud, testing how her voice sounded against bare walls. "Okay." She pulled out the single houseplant, brown at the tips, and set it on the sill where the afternoon light just reached. Then she knelt, unrolled the secondhand rug, and smoothed it flat with both palms, again and again, longer than needed. Her shoulders had dropped. She found herself humming, off-key, while measuring the wall for shelves she hadn't bought yet, already deciding which books would go on the top one, where she could see them from the bed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marisol had been sitting on the bench outside the shuttered bakery for an hour, her résumé folder going soft in her hands, when she noticed the brown leather wallet wedged against the slats. She picked it up. Her thumb found the worn crease, and her pulse picked up as she flipped it open: a driver's license, a faded photo of a toddler, forty dollars. She laughed once, breathless, and stood so fast the folder slid to the gravel. 'Okay,' she said aloud to a pigeon. 'Okay, Raymond Teague. Let's find you.' She tucked her hair behind her ears, straightened her blazer, and checked the address on the license against her phone, already walking, her stride longer than it had been all week. The low sun warmed the back of her neck. Somewhere a screen door banged, and she thought of a stranger's relieved voice on a doorstep, and her chest felt light and strangely open, as though the afternoon had just been unlocked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite arrived at the community pool twenty minutes before her lesson and sat on the edge with her feet in the water, watching the lane lines wobble. She was forty-six. Her swim cap pinched her temples, and she didn't mind. When the instructor waved her in, she lowered herself down the ladder one rung at a time, then let go of the rail with a quick, startled laugh. Her face went under. She counted the bubbles leaving her nose, one, two, three, and came up grinning, water streaming off her chin. "Again," she said, already tugging her goggles tight. Her heart knocked against her ribs, but her shoulders had dropped. She kicked off the wall, arms clumsy, and made it past the blue tile marker before her feet found the floor. She turned to look back at the distance she'd covered, then pushed off a second time. Tonight she would tell her sister about the length of a whole lane, and next week she'd go further, she was sure of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet says plant a quarter inch deep, so I fetch a ruler from the kitchen drawer and kneel in the dirt, measuring like an idiot. My knees are damp through my jeans. I poke a hole, drop in one tiny tomato seed, and push soil over it with my thumb, gently, the way you'd tuck in a child. Row after row, I catch myself humming. Dirt has packed under my nails and I keep looking at it, pleased. When I'm done I fill the watering can twice and pour slowly so nothing washes away. Then I don't go inside. I stand in the cool evening with my hands on my hips, staring at a patch of brown nothing. "Okay," I tell it, out loud. "Take your time. I'll be here at seven." I set my phone alarm for dawn, which is silly, and I grin anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marisol had saved the seat beside the window for Dev, and now she sat with her pen uncapped, not writing anything. The conference room smelled of burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. When Dev clicked to his first slide, his voice wobbled, and she leaned forward an inch, as if she could lend him her balance. Six months of his late nights, the sticky notes on his monitor, the prototype he'd shown her at lunch with cracked-open eyes. Now the director stopped scrolling her phone. Marisol's knee quit bouncing. When Dev reached the chart where the curve bent upward, she heard herself breathe in, long and full, and noticed her shoulders had dropped from around her ears. Someone asked a question, and Dev answered it easily, grinning. Marisol pressed her pen to the page and wrote, in large letters, 'Yes.' Then she underlined it twice, glancing at the director's nodding head, and smiled at the table.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty past midnight, and I had the window cracked an inch just to feel the cold on my knuckles. My phone buzzed in the cup holder and I let it ring through the speaker, the recruiter's voice bright and unhurried even at this hour. "Can you start the fourteenth?" she asked. I said, "Yes," too fast, then laughed and said it again slower. After she hung up I turned the radio up, sang half a chorus I didn't know the words to, and drummed the wheel with both palms. My chest felt loose, like a knot had been picked apart thread by thread. The exit for home slid by, and I took it gently, almost reluctantly, wanting the drive to last. Porch light on. I sat in the driveway a minute, engine ticking, rehearsing how I'd tell my sister in the morning, already grinning at the dark windshield like it might grin back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol took the stairs instead of the elevator, two at a time, the paper bag of clementines swinging against her knee. On the fourth floor she paused at the door of 412 and smoothed her hair in the dark glass of the fire extinguisher case, then laughed at herself. Her grandfather's bed was cranked upright. The tray held a half-eaten cup of applesauce, the spoon scraped clean. "You ate," she said, and her voice came out higher than she meant. He lifted two fingers off the blanket, a small wave, and she felt her chest loosen as if someone had undone a belt. She peeled a clementine right there, the sharp citrus smell cutting through the antiseptic, and set the segments on a napkin by his hand. The nurse said maybe Thursday for the physical therapy. Marisol wrote *Thursday* on her palm in pen, pressed it flat against her coat, and pulled the chair closer, already telling him about the garden, about the tomatoes he'd need to stake in spring.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus got to the chain-link fence twenty minutes early and stood with his thumbs hooked in his jacket pockets, then took them out, then put them back. In his left hand he held a folded paper bag, and every so often he peeked inside at the lopsided cupcake he'd frosted at six that morning, blue because Devin liked blue. Yesterday the boy had come out silent, dragging his backpack by one strap. Today Marcus rehearsed lines under his breath. "How was it, buddy?" No, too much. "Hey, kiddo." Better. His heel tapped the pavement in time with his pulse. When the double doors banged open and the first wave of children spilled out, he rose onto his toes, scanning sneakers and cowlicks. A small red hat. Not his. A yellow raincoat. Not his. His throat felt warm and tight, and he laughed at nothing, a short breath. Then a gap-toothed grin appeared above a dragging backpack, and Marcus lifted the bag high and waved it like a flag.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had been up since five, dragging the oak dresser to the edge of the driveway where the morning sun caught its honeyed grain. She wiped the drawer pulls with her sleeve, then wiped them again. A car slowed on the street and her breath snagged; it kept going, and she laughed at herself, a short, bright sound, and straightened the cardboard sign. Twelve dollars for the lamp. Forty for the dresser, or best offer. She'd already decided she wouldn't haggle much. When a young woman in a paint-spattered shirt crouched to peer into the bottom drawer, Marguerite's fingers tingled against the warm coffee mug. "It was my mother's," she said, too fast, then slower, "the drawers still slide like butter. Go on, try." Her heel tapped the pavement. She watched the woman's hand travel along the edge, and realized she was leaning forward, already picturing the dresser in some sunny bedroom, full of someone's brand-new socks.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip had kept time with my whole miserable Saturday, but now I lay on the cabinet floor with a flashlight clamped in my teeth and wrapped the last turn of tape around the joint. My knees ached against the cold tile and I didn't care. I wiped my palms on my jeans, then reached for the wrench and found my fingers were nearly humming. "Okay, lady," I muttered to the pipe, around the flashlight, "just be good for me." I tightened a quarter turn. Another. The video on my phone said it would hold, and I'd watched it three times, so I trusted it, mostly. I'd already set a dry towel under the elbow, and I was smiling at it like a fool. When I crawled out and twisted the valve, I kept my eyes on that pale towel, breath held, shoulders loose, already picturing myself in the kitchen tomorrow, making coffee in a house that didn't sound like it was crying.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had been on the counter since noon, and Marisol had walked around it twice, wiping crumbs that weren't there. Now she sat on the stool by the window, where the light was best, and slid her thumbnail under the flap slowly so she wouldn't tear the seal. Her knee bounced against the cabinet. "Okay," she said aloud to the empty kitchen, laughing a little at her own voice, which came out higher than usual. She'd already cleared the fridge door of magnets, just in case she needed room to pin something up. The paper inside was folded in thirds, crisp, and she held it against her chest a moment before unfolding it, her pulse thudding in her fingertips. She had rehearsed the phone call to her sister. She had picked out which jacket she'd wear to the office. Her eyes skipped to the first line, and she leaned forward, lips already parting, ready to read it again out loud.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed out of Hanoi's station behind her, and Mara stood on the platform with her backpack straps digging into her shoulders, grinning at nothing. Signs tumbled past in letters with little hats and hooks she couldn't read. She pulled out the folded paper with the hostel's address, smoothed it flat against her thigh, and walked straight toward the first woman selling steaming bread from a basket. "Xin chào," she said, too loudly, then laughed at herself. Her pulse was quick, her palms warm. The woman tilted her head, studied the paper, and pointed left, then made a little winding gesture with her hand. Mara copied it, nodding hard, repeating the one word she caught. Motorbikes swarmed the street like bees, and the air smelled of charcoal and lime. She stepped off the curb anyway, chin up, already composing the story she'd tell about this first wrong turn, certain the right one waited just ahead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit hadn't run since the surgery, so I stood at the fence with my coffee going cold, thumb pressed white against the lid. The grass was still silver with frost. When I unclipped the leash, I counted under my breath, one, two, three, and she just stood there, nose lifted to the wind. Then she bolted. Her back leg swung out clean, no hitch, no skip, and a sound escaped me, half laugh, half cough. I realized I'd been leaning so far over the rail that the wood had printed a line across my ribs. "Look at you," I called, my voice cracking up high like a kid's. She wheeled around a stump, ears flapping inside out, and I was already walking into the field, boots soaking through, my chest loose and warm for the first time in months. "Again," I said. "Do that again." She did. Tomorrow, I thought, we'll try the long trail by the creek.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite arrived at the Grange Hall forty minutes early, before the folding chairs were even unstacked, and ran her thumb along the cello's neck like she was greeting an old dog. The radiator clanked. Dust floated through the slant of window light. She tightened her bow, played the opening phrase of the Fauré, and stopped, not from a mistake but to listen to the last note melt into the rafters. "There," she said aloud to nobody, and laughed at herself. Her shoulders, usually hiked near her ears, had dropped. She penciled a small star in the margin where the tricky shift had finally landed clean three times running. Then she pulled out her phone, hesitated, and texted her sister: "Saturday, seven o'clock. Come early. Sit near the front." She set the phone face-down, rosined the bow again, though it didn't need it, and began from the top, her foot tapping a slow, steady beat against the warped floorboards.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marisol had meant to be done by noon, but at two she was still on the floor of Teodor's workshop with a coffee can of mismatched screws in her lap, sorting them by thread into the muffin tin he'd left on the bench. Sawdust had settled in the creases of her knuckles. She found the half-finished cello neck clamped in the vise, its scroll only roughed out, and instead of wrapping it in newspaper for the donation pile, she ran her thumb along the grain and laughed once, quietly. "Okay," she said to the empty room. "Okay, you stubborn man." Her pulse was quick. She pushed the boxes aside, cleared a space under the window where the light fell warm and slanted, and set his chisels out in a row. Then she tied her hair back, pulled the stool close, and picked up the smallest gouge, testing its edge against her palm the way he used to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Marisol had been standing in front of the corridor noticeboard since seven, though the lists weren't due until nine. She'd worn the blue cardigan, the one from the day the chemistry paper had gone so well, and she kept smoothing its sleeves flat. Each time the caretaker's keys jingled down the hall, she straightened and her pulse jumped into her throat. "Probably just the cleaner," she told the girl beside her, laughing too brightly. She replayed question six, the one about enthalpy, and her lips moved as she checked her working again and found it right again. When a teacher finally appeared with a sheet of paper and a roll of tape, Marisol's hands went warm and tingly. She rose onto her toes, already half-smiling, and edged toward the front before the tape had even been torn.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange light slid off the ridge, and Marisol only tightened her pack straps and kept climbing. Her calves burned, but her stride had lengthened somehow, quick and springy over the roots. She'd misread the map twice today; now she pulled it out, squinted, and laughed under her breath when the creek on paper matched the one gurgling to her left. "There you are," she told it. Her breath came in clouds, and her fingers, stiff with cold, still fumbled the headlamp out of its pocket with something like eagerness. She didn't switch it on yet. Ahead, the trail bent toward a notch in the pines where the sky glowed a thin, stubborn green, and she walked toward it with her chin lifted, humming a few off-key bars, certain that the car, the stove, the warm bad coffee waited just past the next switchback, and that she would reach them before the stars did.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is soft as cloth now, Grandma Odile's slanted handwriting smudged where her thumb used to rest. "A fist of salt," it says, and I laugh out loud in my empty kitchen, then measure what I think a fist might be. My hands shake a little as I stir the yeast, and I keep leaning over the bowl to watch it foam, whispering, "Come on, come on." Flour dusts my forearms and the front of my shirt. I knead until my shoulders burn, humming the off-key song she hummed. Then I set the dough by the window, drape the blue towel over it, and check it three times in ten minutes. The sun lands warm on the cloth. I pull a chair close, rest my chin on my folded arms, and stay there, grinning at a lump of dough, waiting for it to rise and press against the towel like it has something to say.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was weighing two cartons of eggs in the hardware-store aisle that doubled as a grocery corner when someone said her name, and she turned to find Dev Anand, who had sat behind her in chemistry eleven years ago. Her pulse jumped in her throat. She set the eggs down without checking them. "You still do that thing with your pen," she said, laughing, and he glanced at his fingers, clicking the cap, and grinned. He mentioned his cousin was hiring at the print shop on Alder, nothing certain, maybe. Marisol's hands, usually stuffed in her jacket, were suddenly out and moving as she talked. She asked what hours, whether they needed someone who knew layout, and heard her own voice climb a little. When he pulled out his phone she was already reciting her number, then repeated it slower. Outside, the fluorescent buzz seemed softer. She walked to the register forgetting the eggs entirely, then turned back, smiling at nothing, and fetched them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied out, and I was wiping the same stretch of counter for the third time, grinning at nothing. Rain ticked on the front windows.
