I keep my hands jammed in my coat pockets, nails biting my palms. "Leave it," I say when he nears her little spaniel, flat and low, the way you'd speak to a door that stuck. He doesn't hear. Of course he doesn't. The wind pushes cold through my collar and I welcome it. Someone's laughter drifts over, bright and stupid, and I turn my shoulder to it. Every cheerful bark scrapes along my spine. I count the minutes on my watch, then the fence posts, then how many of these people I'd happily never see again. When Biscuit finally bounds back, tongue lolling, I clip the leash on harder than I need to and yank him toward the gate without a glance behind us.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite set her cello case down in the church hall hard enough that the folding chairs rattled. Dennis was already tuning, the flat A wobbling across the room like a fly she couldn't swat. "Again from letter C," he chirped, and her jaw tightened until she felt her molars grind. "We did C." Each word came out clipped, dropped like coins on a counter. When the flutist asked whether the tempo felt right, Marguerite didn't look up. "It feels like the same tempo it was four times ago." Her bow bit the strings. Heat crawled up her neck. Behind the coffee urn, someone's child hummed along off-key, and she dragged her chair a few inches farther from the circle, legs screeching on the linoleum. Dennis raised his baton. She stared at his hand, at the tiny tremor in it, and played every note a little too loud, just to hear it fill the room and push everyone else back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta kicked the workshop door wider and let it bang against the shelf. Dust lifted off every surface, and she waved it away from her face like it owed her something. "Twenty years of this junk," she said to the empty room, flat and loud. She snatched a coffee can of mismatched screws and dumped it into the contractor bag without looking, the clatter ringing in her molars. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the driveway. A half-finished birdhouse sat on the bench with his pencil marks still on it. She shoved it in the bag too, hard, and the roof snapped. Good. Nobody had asked her if she wanted the key. Nobody had asked if she wanted any of this. She yanked a drawer so far it crashed to the floor, chisels skittering across the concrete, and she stepped over them, not bending, not stopping, her breath hot and quick through her nose. "Finish your own damn birdhouse," she muttered, and tied the bag shut.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Marisol planted herself directly in front of the corkboard at 8:52, elbows out, and didn't shift when a boy in a hoodie murmured that he just wanted to see the list. "Wait your turn," she said, not turning her head. Her jaw ached from clenching. The hallway smelled of floor wax and other people's sweat, and every cough behind her made her shoulders climb toward her ears. A secretary came out with a stapler and a single sheet, and Marisol's nails bit into her palms. "You're late," she snapped. "It said nine." The woman blinked and kept stapling, slowly, each thunk loud as a slammed door. Marisol thought of Professor Hale's smirk during the final, the way he'd collected papers like he was gathering evidence. If her number wasn't up there, she'd find him. She'd stand in his doorway and not leave. Someone brushed her sleeve, and she jerked away, teeth bared slightly, heat crawling up her neck while the paper stayed blank-side out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The couple coming down the ridge says something cheerful about the sunset, and I don't slow. "Trail's tight," I say, and let my pack clip the man's elbow as I pass. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars since the trailhead. Light drains from the pines, orange going to bruise, and every root seems placed to catch my boot. I kick one. Pain shoots through my toes and I welcome it. Behind me the woman mutters something, and I turn just enough to show her my teeth, not a smile. My hands are fists around the trekking poles, knuckles pale, and I jab them into the dirt like I'm stabbing something. A bird starts up its evening racket and I hiss at it to shut up. Nobody's left to hear. Good. The dark can come. I'll shove through it, shoulders first, daring anything out there to step into my path.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was stained with butter and forty years of thumbs, and Dana slapped it against the counter so it stuck to the flour. "A handful of this. A pinch of that," she read aloud, voice flat and clipped. "Brilliant. Very helpful, Nana." She dumped the yeast into the bowl without proofing it, jaw tight, and drove her knuckles into the dough as if it had said something. Her shoulders burned. The kitchen window was fogged, the radiator ticking too loud, and her phone buzzed twice on the sill with her aunt's name. She turned it face down hard enough to rattle the salt jar. When the dough tore, she shoved it across the board and bared her teeth at the faded handwriting. "Fine. Be like that." She flung a fistful of flour at the bowl, coughed in the white cloud, and did not wipe her eyes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta was weighing two cans of tomatoes under the fluorescent hum of the grocery aisle when she heard her name, bright and rising, from the end of the row. Dennis Hale. Same grin, same way of leaning on a cart like it was a podium. Her jaw set before she turned. "Wow," he said, "it's been, what, fifteen years?" She set one can in her basket, slowly, and kept the other in her fist. "Sixteen." He laughed and asked what she was up to. "Working," she said. Her molars ached. He mentioned a house, a kid, a promotion, and she studied the price tags beside his ear, counting the dents in a lentil can's rim. When he stretched out a hand she looked at it a beat too long, then shifted her basket to the other arm. "Aisle nine's calling," she said, and pushed past him, wheels squealing, heat crawling up her neck. She never once looked back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Dana slid the register drawer shut with her hip hard enough that the coins jumped. Four-fifty on Christmas Eve, and the store still smelled of burnt cinnamon from the display candles nobody had bought. A man hurried up with a gift receipt and a smile, and she took it between two fingers like something dead. "We close at five," she said, flat, not looking up. "Not five-oh-five." Her jaw ached from clenching; she could feel her molars grind each time the automatic door chimed. He asked if she had a bigger bag. She held his stare, counted three seconds in her head, then pulled out the smallest one and snapped it open so it cracked. Behind him, a woman with a stroller drifted toward the clearance bin. Dana reached under the counter, found the keys, and let them clatter loudly on the glass. Then she turned off the lights over aisle six, one switch at a time, and watched the woman's shadow shrink.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B44 was a twenty-minute sprint away and my boarding pass said the door closed in eleven. I shouldered past a man dawdling with his neck pillow, and when he muttered something I didn't turn around. My jaw ached from clenching. The moving walkway was blocked by a family of five standing side by side, and I stared at the back of the father's head until he finally shuffled over. "Left," I said, flat, like a slammed drawer. Sweat pooled under my backpack straps. The departures board flickered DELAYED beside every flight but mine. Of course. At the gate, the agent smiled at me from her podium and I put my phone down on her counter harder than I needed to. "Don't tell me to calm down," I said, before she'd opened her mouth. My knuckles were white around the handle of my carry-on. I counted the people behind me in line, and I resented every one of them, their coffees, their easy slow breathing, their stupid unhurried shoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Dana jammed the screwdriver under the lid of the paint can and leaned until it popped, a splatter of pale gray hitting her wrist. She didn't wipe it. The roller hissed against the wall in hard, fast strokes, and when Marcus appeared in the doorway holding two mugs, she kept her back to him. "Don't step on the tarp," she said, each word clipped short. "Just leave it." He set a mug on the floor anyway. Her jaw ached from clenching; she noticed it only when a streak ran crooked and she slapped the roller over it twice, three times, until the wall glistened. Fumes stung her nose. She thought about the yellow he'd chosen, how he'd laughed when she objected, and she ripped the tape off the trim so hard it tore a ragged strip of old paint with it. "Tell your mother the room's busy," she said, and dipped the roller again, eyes fixed on the wall until his footsteps retreated down the hall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Dale didn't move when the first fat drops hit the boards, even as the wind flung them sideways against his shins. He kept his jaw clamped, back teeth grinding, one fist wrapped around a sweating glass he'd long since stopped drinking from. Across the yard, his brother's truck sat in the drive, engine ticking, door still open. Thunder cracked and the porch light flickered; Dale glared at it as if it had spoken. 'Go on, then,' he muttered at the screen door, not turning his head. 'Knock. See what you get.' The knuckles of his hand had gone white, and heat crawled up his neck despite the cold spray. When the door behind him creaked, he planted his boot against the frame and shoved it shut without looking. He leaned back, the rocker groaning, and stared at the lightning stitching the field. He hoped the creek would rise, hoped it would take the whole fence line, every post their father had set. He drank, finally, and slammed the glass down hard enough to crack it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off again, and my thumb slides into the grease just as the garage door rattles up. Mr. Okafor from 3B steps in with his daughter, who rolls a gleaming bike past my upturned one. "Still on that?" he says, kindly, which is worse. I laugh a beat too long and wipe my hands on my jeans, smearing black across the thigh. My ears are burning. I told the whole building on Sunday I'd have it running in an hour; that was four days ago. The little girl crouches beside my wheel and points. "You put the tire on backwards." I look. She's right. The arrow stares up at me. "Testing something," I say, voice cracking upward, and I keep my face down, spinning the pedal like it matters, listening to their cleats click away while the wrench trembles in my hand and I pretend to search the toolbox for nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as the 42 pulled away from the curb without me. I'd been waving my folder like an idiot, jogging, shouting "Wait, wait," and the driver had looked right at me and kept going. Now the two women on the bench were pretending not to watch. I smoothed my tie, which was pointless, and then my hair, which was worse. My ears were burning despite the wind. I stared at the schedule taped behind the cracked plastic, reading the same line four times, as if the next bus might change its mind. Rain slid down my collar. I could have stepped under the shelter, but there was no room that wouldn't mean brushing against someone's umbrella and their silence. So I stayed at the edge, getting soaked, and laughed once, too loud, and said to nobody, "Great. Perfect." My voice cracked on the second word. I pulled out my phone and held it to my ear, though no one was calling.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and dust, and I had only meant to find the deed. Instead my fingers closed on my own handwriting, a letter to Marianne, eleven pages, returned unopened, or so I'd believed. The flap was slit clean. Someone had read it. Heat climbed my neck and settled in my ears. I read a line aloud, 'I will wait on the porch until you change your mind,' and my voice cracked on 'porch,' so I coughed and laughed at nothing, as if the empty kitchen were watching. Tucked behind it was a note in her hand, clipped to my pages: 'Read this to Dad at dinner. Everyone cried laughing.' I folded the letters small, then smaller, shoved them under the lid, and pressed down with both palms until my arms shook. Then I carried the box to the hallway closet and stood there with the door shut on my face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale from number twelve stood on my porch with his hands in his jacket pockets, asking if he could borrow my ladder, and the whole street seemed to lean in to listen. I laughed too loudly. My neck burned. "Sure, sure, let me just—" I said, and walked to the garage, where I remembered, halfway through the door, that I'd sold it in March, along with the mower, to cover the mortgage. I stood among the empty hooks on the wall, staring at the pale outlines where things used to hang. My ears rang. When I came back out, I studied my shoes. "Lent it to my brother," I said. "Ages ago. Forgot." Dale nodded slowly, eyes drifting to the bare patch of lawn where the mower had always sat. "No problem," he said, too gently. I kept smiling until his gate clicked shut, then pressed my forehead against the cold door and stayed there, jaw clenched, counting my breaths.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The rice is still hard when the doorbell rings twenty minutes early, and I stand there with the wooden spoon dripping onto my sock. Through the hallway I can hear Daniel's laugh, the one he uses when he's already decided something about me. I whip off the apron, then put it back on because there's a stain on my shirt. My ears are hot. "Come in, come in," I call, too bright, my voice climbing at the end. The roast I bragged about for a week sits grey and sunken in its pan. I slide the oven door shut with my hip, as if they might not notice the smell of scorched sugar. "Oh, this is nothing, just a casual thing," I say to nobody, to the cutting board, to the cheap wine I'm gripping by the neck. My hands won't stop wiping themselves on the dish towel. When his wife asks if she can help, I tell her no, no, sit, and keep my face turned toward the sink until it cools.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cafeteria table, a number I didn't know, and I answered because I was still holding the résumé I'd just been handed back with Dale's coffee ring on it. "Hello?" My voice came out high. A man cheerfully said I was a finalist for the position, then paused and said, "Oh. Sorry. Wrong Kim. We meant Kimberly." Heat crawled up my neck into my ears. Across the room, two coworkers had stopped chewing. I laughed, too loud, too long. "No, totally, no problem, happens all the time," I said, and it didn't, it never had. I pressed the phone flat against my thigh after he hung up and kept nodding at nothing, as if the call were still going. My tray was still full. I stacked the napkins into a neat square, then another, then carried the whole thing to the trash with my eyes fixed on the floor tiles, counting them to the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and the spine had gone soft from carrying it around like a bad secret. I waited until the line behind me was three people deep, which was stupid, and then I slid it across the counter without looking up. "Sorry," I said, too quietly, so I said it again, too loud. The librarian turned it over, found the stamp, and let out a small, slow "Oh." My ears were burning. I studied a flyer about a knitting club as if it might be on the test. When she said the number, I laughed, a high stupid noise, and dug through my wallet with fingers that wouldn't separate the bills. Someone behind me shifted. I counted the coins twice, dropped a quarter, and let it roll away under the shelf rather than bend down. "Keep it," I said, and walked out, my face hot all the way to the parking lot.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The box split open on the third-floor landing, and Dana's whole life slid down the stairs: mismatched mugs, a lamp with its shade crushed, the pink childhood quilt she'd meant to leave behind. Her new neighbor stood in his doorway, holding his takeout, watching. "Need a hand?" he asked, and she laughed too brightly, said, "No, no, it's all junk anyway," while her ears burned and her fingers fumbled after a spoon rolling toward his shoes. Inside, the apartment smelled of old paint. She could cross it in six steps. She shoved the quilt under the bed, then pulled it out, then shoved it back. Her mother's voice kept replaying: Thirty-four, and back to one room. Dana pressed her palms against her hot cheeks, listened for his door to close, and only then sat down on the floor, because the couch hadn't fit through the doorway, and the movers had already seen that, too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside a half-eaten pretzel, brown leather, fat with receipts. I picked it up, and a woman across the path called out, "Hey, that's mine!" and strode over while I was still holding it open, my thumb on her driver's license, her photo smiling up at me. "I wasn't—I was looking for a name," I said, too fast, my voice cracking on the last word. She took it without answering and counted the bills right there while I stood with my hands hanging. Heat climbed my neck into my ears. A kid on a scooter slowed to stare. "Okay," I said, then "okay" again, and laughed at nothing. I tugged my sleeves over my knuckles, stepped backward into the pretzel, and kept walking, eyes on the gravel, not turning around even when she said thanks, quietly, the way you'd speak to someone you'd just caught.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The kickboard slips from my hands and skitters across the water, and a girl of maybe seven fetches it without a word and holds it out to me like I'm the one who needs help. I take it. My ears are burning, though the rest of me is submerged to the chest. Behind me the instructor says, loud and cheerful, "Okay, let's try again, nice and easy," and I laugh too sharply and say I'm fine, I'm totally fine, just warming up. I'm thirty-nine. My towel is on the bench, and I keep angling my body so the lifeguard can't see my stomach. When I kick, I swallow chlorine and cough until my eyes stream, and I keep my face turned toward the wall so no one can read it. Three lanes over, a boy glides past, effortless. I grip the gutter and stare at my knuckles, counting tiles until my breathing slows enough to let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I pressed the last tomato seedling into the dirt while my neighbor Doreen leaned on the fence, watching. "Oh, honey," she said, "those go deeper. And you've put them in the shade." My ears burned. I laughed too loudly and said, "Right, yeah, I was just about to." The trowel slipped in my sweaty grip. I knelt again and pulled up each plant, the roots dangling like small, pale accusations, and I kept my face turned toward the dirt so she couldn't see it. Seven rows. I'd even used string to make them straight. She offered to help and I said no, too fast, my voice thin. When her screen door finally clapped shut, I sat back on my heels, and my hands were shaking as I brushed soil from my knees. The seed packets lay open beside me, the glossy photographs of perfect squash grinning up from the grass. I shoved them into my pocket, where nobody could read them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide and there it was: my dashboard, my color scheme, my chart with the little orange arrow I'd spent a whole weekend nudging into place. "This is something I've been building," she told the room. I kept my pen moving across the notepad, drawing the same square over and over until the paper dented. Heat crawled up my neck and settled behind my ears. Someone nodded. Someone said, "Wow, that's slick." I laughed, one short breath through my nose, and heard how thin it sounded. My coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but I lifted it anyway and drank, so my face would have somewhere to hide. When Marcus glanced over, I smiled with my teeth and said, "Great stuff, Dana," in a voice an octave too bright. Under the table, my knee wouldn't stop bouncing. I counted ceiling tiles. Twenty-two. Then I counted them again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty, and Dana kept both hands locked at ten and two as though someone might still be grading her. Her face burned in the cold air from the vents. She turned the radio off, then on, then off again. "Fine," she said aloud, to no one, her voice thin and too bright. "No, that's fine. Totally fine." Behind her eyes the conference room replayed: the slide with her typo, the pause, Marcus's small laugh, everyone studying their laptops with such care. She swallowed and her throat clicked. At a red light with no cars in sight she sat and waited anyway, jaw tight, staring at the signal until it changed. Her phone buzzed in the cupholder and she flipped it face down without looking. In the driveway she cut the engine and stayed there, forehead against the steering wheel, listening to the engine tick, rehearsing a sentence she would never say, until the porch light clicked off on its timer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Daniel carried the grocery-store carnations down the fourth-floor corridor, the cellophane crackling louder with every step. At the nurses' station, the woman asked him to repeat his uncle's name, and when he did, she glanced at her screen, then at the two other visitors waiting, and said, not quietly, that the account had been flagged and billing wanted a word. His ears burned. He laughed, a short dry sound, and said it must be a mix-up, he'd sort it out, thanks, thanks so much. In the room, his aunt looked up from the vinyl chair and her eyes dropped to his shoes, the left sole flapping slightly from its glue. He tucked that foot behind the other. "Brought flowers," he told the bed, too brightly, and shoved the stems into a water cup that tipped. Water ran across the tray toward his uncle's lunch. He grabbed napkins, kneeling, his face hot against the cold linoleum, and stayed down there longer than he needed to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana kept her sunglasses on though the sky had gone flat and gray. Twenty minutes ago the front office had called her name over the loudspeaker in the yard, loud enough that the whole line of parents turned, and now she stood at the fence with her car keys cutting into her palm. Her ears burned. She laughed too brightly when a mother beside her said, 'Lunch money again, huh? Happens to everyone,' and heard her own voice crack on 'Oh, sure, totally.' She studied her phone without reading it, thumb scrolling the same three messages. Someone's stroller wheel clicked behind her; she flinched, stepped aside, and apologized twice. When the doors finally opened, she pulled her scarf up to her nose, kept her eyes on the pavement, and rehearsed a cheerful voice for Milo that she couldn't quite find. Her face felt like a stove left on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The woman picks up my mother's walnut dresser by one drawer pull and it comes off in her hand. We both look at it. "Oh," she says, and sets the dresser down on the lawn like something dead. My neck is hot. I laugh, too high, and say it's twenty dollars, firm, though the sign says eighty. Behind her, a man crouches to peer under the table where my kids once scratched their names, and I want to throw my body across it. "Ten," she says. I nod before she finishes. My fingers keep smoothing the same wrinkle in my shirt. Across the street, Dale from church slows his car, and I turn to rearrange the lamps, my back to him, counting cracks in the driveway until the engine fades. The woman hands me a damp ten. "Thank you so much," I say, and hear how small it sounds.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Dana wedged herself deeper under the sink, cheek pressed to the cold cabinet floor, while water crept down her wrist and into her sleeve. Behind her, the plumber her father-in-law had called "just to take a look" stood with his arms folded, silent. She tightened the nut again, and the drip only quickened. 'It's fine, I've almost got it,' she said, too brightly, her voice cracking on the last word. Her ears burned. She had told everyone at dinner she'd watched three videos and it was nothing. The wrench slipped and clanged against the trap, loud as a dropped tray. Someone in the kitchen cleared his throat. She stared at the wet thread tape, shredded and useless, and kept her face turned toward the dark so no one could see it. 'Maybe,' she muttered, shoving a towel under the pipe, 'maybe you could just hand me that bucket.' Nobody laughed. That was worse.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a clear window, and Marguerite had already seen the word OVERDUE through it while the neighbor's boy was still lingering by the mailboxes. "Thanks, hon, just junk," she said, too brightly, and carried it up the stairs with her face turned toward the wall. Inside, she pulled the blinds before she sat. Her thumb tore the flap crooked. The benefits office wanted the money back, every dollar of eleven months, because she had "failed to report" the shifts at the bakery. Heat climbed her neck and settled in her ears. She read the repayment line twice, then folded the page small, smaller, until it wouldn't fold anymore. When the phone rang, she let it ring out, then whispered to the empty kitchen, "I told them. I told that woman." She shoved the letter into the flour tin, behind the good napkins, and washed her hands for a long time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver said something sharp and rapid, and Marcus nodded as if he'd understood, then kept nodding long after it made sense. At the hotel desk he slid the printed reservation across the counter, his finger tapping his own name, and the clerk glanced at it, then at the queue forming behind him, and answered in a slow, loud voice, the way people speak to children. Heat climbed his neck. He laughed once, too high, and said, "Sorry, sorry, yes, thank you," though nothing had been given yet. Someone behind him sighed. His suitcase wheel squealed across the marble as he dragged it to the lift, and he kept his eyes on the floor numbers, jaw tight, rehearsing the phrase he'd practiced for weeks and had not managed to say. In the mirrored wall his face was blotched red. He turned to face the corner, and stayed there until the doors opened.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit is still running circles in the long grass, tongue flapping, while I stand at the fence with my leash wrapped twice around my fist. Ten minutes ago I told the woman with the golden retriever that he was fully trained. 'Come,' I said, in the calm voice from the videos. Biscuit dropped, rolled in something dead, then mounted her dog's head in front of everyone. My ears are still burning. I keep tugging my collar away from my neck, though the wind is cold. When she walked past, I laughed too loudly and said, 'He's, uh, a work in progress,' and my voice cracked on 'progress.' Now I stare at my shoes, counting the dandelions between them. Biscuit bounds over, delighted, stinking, and I can't look up to see whether anyone is still watching. I clip the leash on with shaking fingers and walk home the long way, around the back, where no one is.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The fluorescent lights of the church basement hummed while I hit the high note and it cracked, a splintered little squeak that bounced off the folding chairs. Mrs. Aldana stopped playing mid-chord. Nobody spoke. My face went hot, then hotter, and I stared at the sheet music as though the notes might rearrange themselves into an apology. "Sorry, sorry, from the top," I said, too brightly, my voice thin. My hands wouldn't stay still; I folded the page, unfolded it, folded it again. Somewhere behind me a chair creaked, and I knew without turning that someone had looked away to be kind. That was worse. I tried the line again and my throat clamped shut around it. "Maybe I'll just do the harmony," I heard myself say, already backing toward the coat rack, already pulling my sleeves down over my wrists. Saturday's poster was taped by the door. My name was on it in cheerful blue letters.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dennis pulled the tarp off the workbench and found his own handwriting staring up at him: a loan ledger, Walt's neat columns, forty-two hundred dollars across six years, every line initialed D.K. His ears went hot. He shut the ledger, then opened it again to be sure, then shut it and slid it under his jacket like something stolen. Behind him, Walt's daughter was wrapping chisels in newspaper. "Find anything?" she asked. "Just sawdust," he said, too loud, and laughed at nothing. His collar felt tight. He crouched to sweep a pile that was already swept, keeping his face toward the floor, the broom scraping the same board over and over. The pegboard still held the outline of the square he'd borrowed and never returned. He lifted a coffee can of screws, set it down, lifted it again. "I'll take the trash out," he said, though there was none, and walked to the alley with the ledger burning against his ribs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The list goes up at noon, taped beside the biology office, and I'm standing at the back of the crowd with my hood up. Priya's voice carries over everyone: "Didn't I say she'd retake it?" I laugh, a short, dry sound, then study the fire extinguisher like it might be on the test. My ears are burning. Someone shoulders past and I step aside too quickly, apologizing to nobody. When the crowd thins I walk up slowly, finger sliding down the column, and there's my number with the red line under it. Everyone I told last week that I'd definitely cleared it is still within earshot. My face is stiff, my smile pulled up on strings. "Ha, yeah, figured," I tell the paper, loud enough for them. My hands are jammed in my pockets so no one sees them shake. I walk out, not running, counting my steps to the door, certain every one of them is being watched.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light turned orange on the ridge while I kept walking faster than my knees wanted, my face still hot from the trailhead where I'd announced to everyone that I knew a shortcut. Dana's laugh replayed, and the way Marcus had quietly checked the map and said nothing. I'd left them at the fork without a word, jaw tight, pretending I needed to be alone. Now the shortcut had dead-ended at a creek, and I stood there with my boots wet, staring at the water like it had said something about me. 'Fine,' I muttered, then louder, to no one, 'Totally fine.' My voice cracked on the second one. I scrubbed my sleeve across my cheeks, hard, as if I could rub the color out. Somewhere behind me, far off, they were probably calling my name, and I pulled my hood up and turned my face toward the trees so I wouldn't have to answer yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: I'd told everyone at the potluck that Nonna's bread would be the best thing on the table. Now I stood by the counter with the knife stuck in a loaf that wouldn't give, a pale, dense brick that had barely risen. My cousin Marco tapped it with his knuckle and it knocked like wood. Someone laughed, then covered it with a cough. My ears burned and the back of my neck went slick under my collar. "It's, um, rustic," I said, too fast, my voice climbing. I sawed off a slice and ate it myself, chewing and chewing, the crust scraping my gums, while I nodded like it was fine. Nobody else reached for the basket. I slid the recipe card, its corners soft and stained with her thumbprints, back into my bag and folded it small. Then I went to the bathroom and stayed there, running the tap, staring at the tile, counting to a hundred before I could go back out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The voice came from behind the cereal display, bright and certain: "Daniel? Daniel Marsh?" He knew it before he turned. Priya Raman, who'd won the science fair, who'd once copied nothing from anyone. Her cart held salmon and a bunch of tulips. His basket held two cans of soup, a loaf of day-old bread, and the store-brand tissues he'd been about to put back. He shifted it behind his leg. "Hey. Wow. Yeah," he said, too loud, laughing at nothing. Heat crawled up his neck and settled in his ears. She asked what he was up to these days, and he said "Oh, you know, between things," and heard how thin it sounded under the buzzing fluorescent lights. His apron-stained work shirt suddenly felt like a sign. He checked his phone, which hadn't rung. "I should, my ride's waiting." He walked away with the basket banging his knee, past the checkout, and kept going until the automatic doors sighed shut behind him, empty-handed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum at 8:40 p.m. on Christmas Eve, and I'm still behind the counter when the man in the green parka slaps his receipt down and says, loud enough for the whole line, that a person with a brain would have checked the insurance first. I keep my smile. My ears burn so hot I can feel my earrings. "I'm so sorry, sir, let me fix that," I say, and my voice comes out thin, like it belongs to someone younger. Behind him a teenager lifts his phone. My fingers fumble the barcode three times; the scanner beeps its stupid little refusal. I stare at the tinsel taped along the register, one strand drooping, and count its sparkles so I won't blink. When he finally leaves, I walk to the stockroom, press my forehead against the cold shelf of cough syrup, and breathe through my teeth. Then I wipe my face and call, "Next!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The gate agent's screen still said BOARDING when I skidded up, but she didn't look at me, only at the door she was already closing. "Please," I said, too loud, my voice cracking on the word. "I have the ticket right here." My carry-on had split a wheel somewhere near Terminal B, so I'd dragged it the last hundred yards like a dead animal, and now everyone seated by the window watched me through the glass. Sweat ran down my spine. My shirt had come untucked, and I tugged at it with one hand while the other kept waving the phone. "Sir, the door is closed." A kid pointed. His mother pulled his hand down. I laughed, a stupid little sound, and said, "No, of course, sorry, thank you," as though she'd done me a favor. My ears burned all the way to the rebooking line, where I stared at my shoes and counted the scuffs, and kept smiling at no one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta kept the roller moving in the same slow stripe, though the wall was already covered, because stopping meant turning around. Behind her, her brother-in-law's voice carried from the doorway: "You taped it wrong. Didn't you watch the video I sent?" Heat crawled up her neck and settled in her ears. She laughed, a short dry sound, and said, "Yeah, no, I'll redo it," much too fast. Her eyes stayed on the glossy beige she had spent three weekends choosing. A bleed of color showed beneath the tape, a crooked seam down the corner, and she pressed her thumb over it as if it might vanish. Her fingers left a print. She wiped them on her jeans, then on the drop cloth, then on her jeans again. "Go ahead and say it," she almost added, but her jaw only tightened. When his footsteps faded, she crouched by the paint can, hands shaking, and hammered the lid shut with her fist.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolls in just as I reach the porch, and I'm glad of it, because the rain gives me a reason not to go back inside. My face is still hot. I keep replaying the toast, the way my voice cracked on her name, the way Dana's brother laughed first and then everyone did. I grip the rail until the paint flakes under my thumbnail. Water blows sideways across the boards and soaks my good shoes, and I let it. Behind me the screen door squeaks and someone calls, 'You okay out there?' I say, 'Just watching the weather,' too brightly, and my voice wobbles again. I tug my collar up over my ears like that could help. Lightning splits the yard. I count, one, two, and tell myself I'll stay until the thunder passes, maybe until everyone has gone home and stopped talking about me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol wedged the rear wheel into the stand and spun it, listening to the tick of the bent spoke. On the shelf above her, the shared garage's whiteboard still read *Bike night — Thursday!* in Dev's loopy handwriting, and she had not been told it had moved to Tuesday. Tonight the other stools were empty, the floor pump gone from its hook. She picked up the spoke wrench and her fingers wouldn't close right; she set it down, picked it up again. "Fine," she said to no one, in a voice flatter than the concrete. Her throat felt packed with sawdust. When the door rattled and a neighbor's voice called, "Anyone in there?" she kept her face to the chain and answered, "Just me," then turned the wheel too hard and watched the tire wobble. She pulled the light cord, then yanked it on again, and kept working in the glare, jaw tight, eyes stinging at the grease smell.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Fenwick Street went the color of dishwater while I stood under the shelter, thumb hovering over a message I had already read nine times. *Don't wait up, something came up.* Again. The first drops hit the plexiglass like thrown pebbles, and I counted them instead of answering. My jaw ached from holding it still. When the wind shoved a gust of cold under the roof, I didn't zip my coat; I just let it pass through me, as if it had a right. An old man beside me asked if I was all right, and I said, "Fine, yeah, just tired," too brightly, then laughed at nothing. My throat felt packed with wet sand. The bus lights swam up the road, blurred and late, and I realized I'd been gripping the phone so hard my knuckles had gone pale. I typed *ok*, deleted it, typed *ok* again, no period, and watched the rain erase the street one block at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and dust, and Marguerite worked through it with brisk, practiced flicks, bills to the left, birthday cards to the right. Then a blue envelope in her sister's looping hand. She read the first line standing up, then sat down on the edge of the bed without deciding to. Her thumb pressed the paper's crease flat, over and over. 'Mom's ring goes to you, obviously,' the letter said, 'since Marguerite never bothered to come.' She laughed, one short breath through her nose. The radiator ticked. She folded the page into thirds, unfolded it, folded it again. Her jaw ached from how tightly she held it. 'Eleven years,' she said to the empty room, voice thin and level, as though reading a receipt. She tucked the letter back at the very bottom, under the electric bills, and pushed the lid down with both palms until it clicked. Then she opened it again, and kept reading.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marguerite was deadheading the roses when Dale's boots crunched up the gravel, and she kept the shears moving, snip, snip, though she'd already cut the same stem twice. "Need the big ladder," he said, hands in his jacket pockets. "Gutters." Eleven years she had lived beside him. He hadn't knocked when Walter died; the casserole dish she'd left on his step in March still sat, unreturned, on his railing, she could see it from here. "It's in the garage," she said, and her voice came out lighter than she meant, almost cheerful. Her jaw ached. She walked ahead of him, set her gloves on the workbench, lined them up by the fingers. The ladder was heavier than she remembered, and she let him lift it alone. "Thanks, Marge," he called over his shoulder. Nobody had called her that since Walter. She stood in the doorway until the aluminum clanged against his fence, then pressed her palm flat against her sternum and went back to the roses.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta chopped the parsley finer than the recipe asked, the knife clicking against the board in a steady, hard rhythm. Her phone lay face-up beside the stove, and the message from her sister glowed there: *Something came up, so we'll skip tonight.* Third time this month. She read it once, then turned the phone over. The oven timer ticked. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, too brightly, and reached for the pot. Her throat felt packed with dry bread, and she swallowed twice around it. She set six places at the table, paused, then took one plate away, then another, stacking them with more care than they needed. Steam fogged the window. When the doorbell rang, early, she wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist, smelled onion on her skin, and decided that was the reason. "Coming!" she called, and her voice came out almost normal. She lifted the lid and stirred, though nothing needed stirring.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cutting board, a string of digits Marguerite didn't know, and she let the onion sit half-diced while she wiped her fingers on her apron, slowly, one at a time. She answered. "Hello?" Then nothing but a breath, and a voice she hadn't heard in six years saying her name the old way, the short way. Her throat tightened with a sting that wasn't from the onion. She pressed her free hand flat against her sternum as if to hold something in place. "No," she said, too quietly, and then, "No, you don't get to do that." The kettle began to whistle behind her. She didn't move to lift it. Her thumb hovered over the red circle, trembling, and she stared at the unopened birthday card still propped on the windowsill, the one he'd never signed. "I have to go," she said, and her voice cracked in the middle of go. She hung up, then stood there with the screen glowing, listening to the kettle's long, thin scream.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in Mina's backpack for fourteen months, and she carried it up the library steps with both hands, like something that might spill. Inside, the clerk glanced at the cover and smiled. "Oh, this one. Professor Aldric's old copy. He kept it on reserve for years." Mina nodded. Her throat had gone tight and dry. She set the book down and ran her palm along its cracked spine, flattening it, though it didn't need flattening. "He wrote in the margins," she said, too quietly, and the clerk leaned in to ask her to repeat it. "Never mind." The late fee printed with a small mechanical groan. Forty-one dollars. She paid in crumpled bills, counting them twice, eyes fixed on a water stain in the ceiling tile. Outside, she stood a long moment in the cold, fingers pressed flat against her sternum, then took the long way home so she wouldn't pass his building.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta carried the last box up four flights herself, because the one person who had promised to come had texted at noon: something came up. She set it down in the middle of the room, and the floorboards creaked as if to comment. The studio was smaller than she remembered from the listing photos. She opened the window; it stuck, then gave way with a bang, and the street noise rushed in. Her jaw ached from holding it so tight. She pressed her thumb into her sternum where something sat heavy and hot, and unpacked only the kettle. 'Fine,' she said aloud to the empty room, flat, the way she'd said it on the phone. 'It's fine.' She filled the kettle, forgot to switch it on, and stood watching it. Later she realized she'd hung her coat on the hook and left the second hook, the one she'd bought two of, bare. She stared at it a long time before turning off the light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and I sat down beside it without meaning to. Pigeons worked the gravel near my shoes. I opened it the way you'd lift a bandage. A driver's license, a library card, and tucked behind them a photo-booth strip: four frames of a woman laughing into a man's shoulder. His shoulder. My brother's. The jacket was the green one I'd helped him pick out. My throat went tight and dry, and I swallowed twice to no use. I read the name on the license again, as if it might rearrange itself. Not his. Hers. The woman he'd told me, last Sunday, was just a coworker. I laughed once, a short ugly sound, and a jogger glanced over. I pressed the strip flat against my knee, smoothing the crease, my thumb shaking. Then I slid it back exactly where it had been, zipped the wallet shut, and carried it to the lost-and-found box by the gate, walking very slowly, my chest a clenched fist the whole way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite gripped the pool's edge until her knuckles went pale, her feet planted on the tiled step while the kids' class splashed past in the next lane. "Just kick," the instructor had said, and from somewhere behind her a teenager had laughed, short and bright, and not stopped. She nodded at the instructor. "Fine. Sure. I'm fine," she said, in a voice thinner than she intended. Her throat was tight, and the chlorine stung her eyes, which she blamed on the chlorine. She pulled the goggles down, though she wasn't going under. Forty-six years she'd arranged her life around this water, around every beach she'd waved at from the towel. Now she let go of the wall, kicked twice, sank, and came up coughing. She didn't look toward the bleachers. She climbed out, wrapped the towel twice around her shoulders, and stared at the drain in the floor until the laughing sounded like someone else's.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets were still taped to the fence where Dad had left them, his block handwriting on each one: BEANS, CARROTS, TOMATO. I knelt in the dirt and pressed my thumb into the soil, too hard, and kept pressing until the knuckle went white. "Four inches apart," I read aloud, and my voice came out thin and flat, like it belonged to someone shorter. He'd promised we would do this together, in spring, when he was done with the other thing. I dropped a bean in the hole. Then another. My jaw ached from clenching. When the neighbor leaned over the fence and called, "Nice start!" I nodded at the trowel instead of her and said, "Thanks," and nothing else. My eyes stung, and I blamed the wind. I covered the row too fast, smacked the dirt flat with my palm, and sat there with my hand pressed to it, feeling for something that wasn't going to come up yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked to the next slide and Dana's voice carried on, smooth and pleased, walking the room through the dashboard layout. Priya's layout. Priya had sketched it on a napkin in March, and Marcus had spent six weekends building it. He stared at the title slide's footer, where his name should have been, and found only Dana's. His pen had stopped moving; the page under it held one long, flat line. The conference room air-conditioning hummed too loudly. When the VP turned and said, "Great work, Dana," Marcus's jaw tightened and his throat felt packed with sawdust. He nodded along with everyone else, a beat late. Afterward, someone asked if he had anything to add. "No, it's all covered," he said, almost cheerfully, and closed his laptop so gently it made no sound. He stacked his coffee cup inside the empty one beside it, carried both out, and stood at the sink rinsing a clean mug until the water ran cold over his knuckles.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta signed the guest book at her sister's party, smiled until her cheeks ached, and left before the cake. Now the highway was empty, the dashboard clock reading 12:47, and she kept both hands locked at ten and two as though the wheel might bolt. "Fine," she said aloud, flatly, to no one. "It's fine." Her throat had gone tight around a swallow that wouldn't finish. She replayed it again: Dana laughing, the toast that thanked everyone but her, the gap in the photo where she'd been told to wait. A truck passed, its lights washing over her wet eyes, and she wiped them with the heel of her palm, annoyed at the interruption. The radio was playing something cheerful, so she shut it off. At the exit she missed her turn, drove a mile further, and didn't correct it. The quiet in the car pressed on her chest like a hand. She pulled into her dark driveway and sat there, engine ticking, coat still buttoned, unable to open the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus set the grocery bag of clementines on the tray table and kept his coat on. His grandmother's eyes slid past him to the door. "Is Danielle coming?" she asked. "She's driving up Thursday," he said, and his voice came out level, too level. He peeled one clementine, then another, lining the segments on a napkin she didn't touch. The monitor beeped; the radiator ticked. He had driven four hours, and his hands still felt locked around a steering wheel. "She always did bring the good ones," she murmured, looking at the fruit. Marcus nodded slowly. His throat was tight, and he swallowed against it twice. He studied the cracked beige paint above her bed, counted the ceiling tiles, and found he'd counted them already. When the nurse came in and asked if he was the son, he said, "Grandson," then, after a pause, "I'm just visiting." He folded the peels into his palm and stood, though visiting hours had forty minutes left.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus stood at the fence with his keys still in his fist, the metal biting into his palm. The other parents drifted into clusters, laughing about the bake sale, and he angled his shoulder toward the street as if something there needed watching. When the doors banged open, Dani came out between two friends, backpack swinging, and walked straight past him toward Gloria's minivan. He lifted a hand, then lowered it to his jacket pocket. 'Dani,' he called, too lightly, a voice he'd borrowed from someone cheerful. She turned, pulled a face, and said, 'Dad, you're not supposed to be here on Wednesdays. Mom said.' His throat tightened around a laugh that came out as a cough. 'Right. Sure. Wednesdays.' He nodded at the pavement longer than necessary. 'Go on, then. Don't keep Gloria waiting.' The minivan door slid shut. He stayed until the lot emptied, staring at the crooked chalk hopscotch, his chest hollow and heavy, as though someone had set a cold stone behind his ribs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine, Marguerite had the oak dresser angled toward the road, its top wiped twice with lemon oil. A man in a ball cap pulled open a drawer, sniffed, and said, "Smells like somebody's attic. Ten bucks?" The tag said sixty. She laughed, a short, dry sound, and kept folding the doily she'd set on top. "It was my mother's," she said, then pressed her lips together, because nobody had asked. He shrugged and wandered to the lamps. Her thumb found the groove near the knob, where the varnish had worn smooth from forty years of her own hand. Her throat felt packed with sawdust. When he came back and offered fifteen, she nodded, too quickly, and took the bills without counting them. After he drove off with the dresser rattling in his truck bed, she stood watching the pale rectangle it left in the grass, and turned the doily over and over until the edges curled.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marcus lay wedged under the kitchen sink with a flashlight clamped in his teeth, water dripping steadily onto his wrist. Dad's old pipe wrench was heavy in his hand, the handle wrapped in the same blue tape his father had used. He had called twice that morning. Both times it rang out, and the second time a voice that wasn't his father's had said the number was no longer in service. He tightened the joint. It kept dripping. He tightened it again, harder, until his knuckles went white and his jaw ached around the flashlight. 'Come on,' he muttered, then louder, 'Come on, you stupid thing.' His throat felt thick, like he'd swallowed a fistful of wet rag. He blinked hard and the beam swam. Somewhere above him the phone buzzed on the counter, and he didn't slide out to look. He wiped his face with his sleeve, smearing grease across his cheek, and reached for the tape again, wrapping it round and round the joint far more times than it needed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter beside the kettle for two hours before I touched it. When I finally slit it open with a butter knife, my thumb caught the paper and I barely noticed. Three lines. Application denied, benefit terminated, effective the first of the month. I read them again, then a third time, moving my lips like a child. The kettle clicked off and I let it go cold. 'Fine,' I said to the empty kitchen, too loudly, and then again, quieter. Eleven years of forms, of waiting rooms with their numbered tickets, and they'd signed it with a stamp. My throat had gone tight, a swallowed stone. I folded the letter along its original creases, smoothed it flat with my palm, put it back in the envelope as if that might undo it. Then I stood at the sink, ran the tap, and washed one clean cup until the water went cold on my wrists.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver shrugged and pulled my suitcase out onto the curb before I had finished showing him the address. I'd written it out so carefully, every accent mark copied from the email. The rain came sideways under the station awning. I laughed once, a short dry sound, and said, "Fine. Thank you. Very much," in the tone I use on telemarketers. My jaw ached from clenching. Across the square, a woman said something sharp to her friend and both of them looked at me, then away. I pressed my thumb into the paper until the ink bled blue, then folded it small and shoved it deep in my coat. Nobody had called me back, my sister's last message still sat unanswered on my phone, and I kept turning the screen over on my knee. I dragged the suitcase through puddles toward a light I couldn't read, my throat tight, telling myself it was only the cold making my eyes sting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the field with a stick twice her size, ears inside out, and I stood at the fence with my phone still open to the message I'd read four times. Short. Polite. Signed with just an initial, like I was a stranger at a bank. I put the phone in my pocket, then took it out, then put it back. My jaw ached from holding it so still. The grass was gold and the light was far too cheerful about it. 'Good girl,' I called, and my voice came out thin and strange, so I cleared my throat and tried again. She didn't notice either time. She dropped the stick at my feet, panting, waiting, and I crouched to pick it up, and my hands wouldn't quite close around it. I threw it anyway, badly, and watched her go. My chest felt like a door someone had shut carefully, without slamming. I stayed crouched there a long time, pressing my thumb into the splintered bark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church basement smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and I stood at the upright piano turning my pages one at a time, though I knew every note. Marguerite had just announced the program for Saturday, and my duet wasn't on it. "We're tight on time," she said, not looking up. "Surely you understand." I said, "Of course," in a voice that came out bright and thin, like a wire pulled too tight. My thumbnail kept pressing a crease into the corner of the score. Someone's folding chair scraped. I was told I could still turn pages for Doreen, so I sat beside her and turned them, precisely, each one on the beat. My throat felt packed with sawdust. When the fluorescent light buzzed overhead I counted its flickers instead of listening to the soprano. Afterward I stacked chairs longer than anyone needed, then left my folder on the piano, forgetting it was the one thing I'd come to carry home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Walt's coffee can of mismatched screws sits where it always sat, and I hold it too long before setting it in the box marked DONATE. Sawdust still lies in the vise's jaws. I don't brush it out. Under the bench I find the cedar box I asked him to build for my daughter's wedding, three years ago, unfinished, the lid clamped dry, no hinges. He told me it was done. I laugh once, a short dry sound, and then my throat locks and I have to stand with my palm flat against the cold pegboard until my breath loosens. 'You liar,' I say to the room, quietly, like he's asleep. My jaw aches from clenching. I pick up his pencil, the stub still flat on one side from his thumb, and slide it into my shirt pocket. Then I take it back out, put it in the box, and take it out again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The list went up at noon, and Mina stood at the back of the corridor while the others pressed forward in a knot of elbows and phones. She held her thermos with both hands though it had been empty since ten. When the crowd thinned, she walked up slowly and found her number, then read the line beside it twice, three times, her lips moving. Her mother had cleared the whole weekend for a celebration dinner. Mina's throat felt packed with wet sand. She nodded at a classmate who said something kind, and her own voice came out thin and cheerful: "No, it's fine, really, I'm good." She turned the thermos lid, screwed it on, unscrewed it. In the stairwell she sat on the cold concrete step, pressed her palm flat against her sternum, and stared at the chipped yellow paint until it blurred. Her phone buzzed against her knee. She let it ring out, watching her thumb tremble above the screen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then the color of weak tea, and I keep walking past the junction where we'd agreed to turn back. My phone is in my pocket, face down. I haven't looked at it since her last message, which I read once at the trailhead before saying "Fine" out loud to nobody. My jaw has been tight for miles; I notice my teeth aching and make myself unclench, and a minute later they're clamped again. The pines crowd closer. I snap a branch off the path with more force than it needs and then just hold it, stupidly, like it owes me something. My throat is thick when I try to hum, so I stop. Somewhere below, a creek I can't see keeps talking. I tell myself I'm only tired, that the pack straps are digging in. I pull them tighter anyway, until my shoulders burn, and keep climbing into the dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Marisol had found the index card in the tin where her grandmother kept buttons, the handwriting slanting hard to the right, flour-ghosted at the corners. Her aunt had said, on the phone, that the bread was never really about the recipe, that Abuela had changed it every time. Marisol kneaded harder. The dough stuck to her knuckles, and she scraped it off with her thumbnail, jaw tight. "A pinch," she read aloud. "A pinch of what? How big a pinch?" Her voice cracked on the last word, and she cleared her throat as though someone might be listening in the empty kitchen. The oven ticked. She pressed the heel of her hand into the dough and held it there, her throat burning, her eyes fixed on the card's smudged line where the salt should have been measured. Then she turned the card over, hoping for more. Only a grocery list, in the same slanting hand: eggs, thread, call Marisol.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was weighing two nearly identical cans of tomatoes under the fluorescent glare of aisle six when someone said his name. Dana Whitlock, from tenth-grade chemistry, pushed her cart toward him, grinning. "You look exactly the same!" He set one can back on the shelf, carefully, label facing out. She talked about her wedding, the house in Portland, the weekend everyone had gathered in June. "Oh, we figured you were busy," she said, waving a hand. "Or off the group chat or something." His mouth made a smile shape. "Sure. Busy." His throat felt packed with dry bread, and the cart handle was suddenly slick under his palm. "Well, congratulations," he said, too brightly, already steering away. At the register he found he held only one can. He paid for it anyway, then sat in the car with the engine off, staring at the bag until the windshield fogged.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time, long after the grease was gone. The pharmacy's fluorescent lights buzzed over aisles of unsold candy canes, and outside the window the lot emptied one car at a time. Her phone lay face-down by the register; she had turned it over after the group chat lit up with the staff's Christmas Eve plans, a photo of the table, everyone's name tagged but hers. 'Yep, no problem, I'll close,' she'd told Dale that morning, smiling too wide. Now her throat was tight, and she swallowed against it while ringing up a man's cough drops. 'Happy holidays,' she said, and her voice came out thin, flat as receipt paper. When he left, she stood very still, thumbnail pressing a crescent into her palm. At 8:58 she flipped the sign to CLOSED, turned off the aisle lights one by one, and left the last one on for no reason at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B34 is a ten-minute sprint from where I'm standing, and I'm walking. My roller bag clicks over every seam in the floor, and I let it. The phone is still in my hand, her message glowing: "Probably better if you don't come this weekend." I read it again, as if the words might rearrange. The departures board flickers, BOARDING in green beside my flight, and my feet keep their slow pace anyway. My throat has gone thick, like I swallowed a fistful of sand. A man in a suit shoulders past me, mutters something, and I say "Sorry" far too quietly, to nobody. At the gate the agent is already lifting her scanner. "Last call, sir?" I nod, then can't find my boarding pass, though it's in the hand holding the phone. My eyes sting under the fluorescent lights. I press my thumb against my sternum, where a dull ache has settled, and I hand her the crumpled paper without looking up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I peel the tape off the baseboard slowly, the way you do when you don't want anything to tear. The old yellow is still on the wall behind the dresser, a clean rectangle where her mirror hung. Dana said the color was "a lot" last night, over the phone, between bites of something, and I said "Sure, no, it's fine," too fast, and then asked if she wanted the leftover rice. My jaw has been tight since. I pour the grey into the tray and the roller hums against my palm. Twice I stop mid-stroke and realize I'm just standing there, dripping on the drop cloth, rereading her sentence in my head like it might change. I chose that yellow the week we moved in. I roll over it in long, careful lines until the sun is gone from the wall. My throat does that thing. I turn the radio up, then off. Then I do the second coat anyway, though the first was fine.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolls in just as my phone lights up with her name, and I flip it face down on the porch rail. Rain slants under the awning and soaks my left sleeve. I don't move. The swing creaks beneath me, too loud, so I plant both feet and make it stop. My jaw aches from holding it shut. Inside, the kitchen light is still on, her mug still in the sink where I left it, and I keep my back to the window. "Fine," I say to nobody, to the yard, to the dripping maple. "It's fine." My voice cracks on the second word and I cough like it was the damp. The phone buzzes again against the wood. I count the seconds between lightning and thunder, one, two, three, anything with an answer. My chest feels like a screen door slapping in the wind. When the buzzing quits, I pick it up, read nothing, and hold it until it's warm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off for the fourth time and I laugh, a high thin sound that bounces off the concrete and makes Mr. Okafor's ladder rattle on its hook. I'm laughing and my eyes are streaming and I can't feel my fingertips, though they keep jabbing at the greasy links. "It's fine," I tell the wrench. "It's totally fine, we're fine." My knees have gone to jelly against the oil-stained floor. Someone's radio is playing from the other side of the shared garage, and I hear myself talking over it, faster and faster, narrating each bolt like a sportscaster. Then I drop the tire lever, it clangs, and I'm wheezing, folded over the frame with my forehead on the cold saddle, shoulders shaking. My heart is a fist on a door. I wipe my face with a black hand, smearing grease across my cheek, and the sight of my reflection in the dark window sets me off all over again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat raindrop hits the schedule panel and I'm laughing before I know it, a high, cracked sound that bounces off the plexiglass. Then the wind flips my umbrella inside out and I laugh harder, doubled over, hands on my knees, tears mixing with the rain. The 14 is eleven minutes late. Eleven! I say it aloud to the empty street, then again, louder, then in a sing-song voice, "Eleven, eleven, eleven." My ribs ache. My fingers won't stop shaking, so I pat my pockets for the third time, then the fourth, finding the same crumpled receipt each time and holding it up like proof of something. Thunder rolls and I clap, actually clap, then cover my mouth because the sound that comes out next isn't a laugh anymore. I can't tell what it is. I'm pacing the length of the bench, back and forth, stepping in every puddle on purpose, shouting at the sky that it's too late, it's far too late, and my breath keeps hiccupping out of me in short, ragged bursts.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid skids across the attic floor and I'm already laughing, a high, wheezing bark that doesn't sound like mine. Envelope after envelope, all in Dad's slanted blue ink, and I'm tearing them open too fast, ripping one corner clean off. "Dear Margaret," I read aloud to the rafters, "I trust the weather in Leeds—" and I can't finish because my breath hitches and I'm slapping the floorboards. My hands shake so hard the pages rattle like leaves. Dust coats my tongue. I shove a letter into my sleeve, pull it out, fan myself with it, then I'm up, pacing between the trunks, hair stuck to my wet face. "Forty years of postage," I tell the dressmaker's dummy. "Forty years!" My ribs ache. The phone buzzes downstairs and I shriek at it, actually shriek, then crumple against the box, pressing a stamp to my lips, giggling and gulping air until the room tilts.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Alvarez knocked twice, and I opened the door already laughing, a high wobbling sound that wouldn't stop. "A ladder? Yes! Yes, of course, a ladder!" My hands were shaking, so I gripped the doorframe, then let go because it seemed to be vibrating. "I have two. Why do I have two? Who needs two?" I was halfway across the garage before I realized I'd left him standing there, and I came back wheezing, tears on my cheeks, to say, "Sorry, sorry, it's just, a ladder." My ribs ached. He stared at my sock, which was on my hand. I couldn't remember doing that. "Take the tall one," I gasped, "take the short one, take the whole house," and then I was bent over the lawn mower, shoulders heaving, pointing at the rungs like they'd told the funniest joke in the world, while the sprinkler ticked on, ticked on, ticked on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The doorbell was forty minutes away, and Marguerite had just set the oven mitt on fire. She flung it into the sink and laughed, a high, cracking sound that bounced off the tiles and kept going after she wanted it to stop. "It's fine, it's fine, it's totally fine," she told the colander. Her hands wouldn't hold still; they fluttered over the chopping board, picked up the knife, set it down, picked up the parsley instead. The risotto had gone to glue. Her heart knocked against her ribs so hard that she pressed a wet palm to her chest and talked to it. "Not now. Not now." Steam fogged her glasses, and she wiped them with a sleeve that smelled of singed cotton. Somewhere the timer shrieked, and she shrieked back, then clapped a hand over her mouth, shoulders shaking, eyes streaming. Maybe she'd serve cereal. Maybe she'd lock the door and turn off every light. She grabbed the whisk, waved it like a baton, and began, loudly and off-key, to sing at the stove.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed across the kitchen counter, a string of digits Marisol didn't know, and she shrieked, actually shrieked, before clapping a hand over her mouth and then laughing, a high, cracked sound that wouldn't stop. "No, no, no, no," she said, pacing the tiled floor in tight circles, knocking a mug into the sink where it clattered. Her heart slammed so hard she could feel it in her teeth. She snatched the phone up, dropped it, snatched it again. "Hello? Hello? Who is this? Who is this?" Her voice climbed higher with each word, breaking into a squeak. Her fingers tingled and went numb; she pressed the cold phone to her cheek, then to her forehead, then away. "It's the hospital, it's the landlord, it's him, it's him," she whispered, then giggled again, tears sliding into her mouth. The line breathed once. She slid down the cabinet to the floor, knees jittering, and screamed, "Say something!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Priya shoved through the library doors so hard they banged the wall, and the whole reading room looked up. She was laughing, a high, cracking sound she couldn't switch off, the copy of *Principles of Organic Chemistry* clutched against her chest like a rescued child. "Four hundred and twelve days," she told the librarian, then said it again, louder, because her voice kept skidding. Her hands shook so badly the barcode wouldn't scan. Sweat prickled under her collar; her heart knocked in her throat. "It was under my bed. Under the bed! With a sock! I thought they'd arrest me, I thought, what if they have a file, a little file with my face—" She wheezed, bent over the desk, wiped her eyes with the book's dusty corner. The librarian said the fine was capped at ten dollars. Priya stared, then slapped the counter and howled, tears streaming, fumbling in her pockets, pulling out lint, a single button, a crumpled receipt, and holding each one up as payment.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The couch won't fit through the door, and I'm laughing, a high wheezing sound that keeps cracking in the middle. I tilt it, I flip it, I shove it, and it wedges there like a joke nobody told me the end of. "Okay, okay, okay," I say, too fast, too loud, to the empty hallway. My hands are shaking so hard the keys jangle on my wrist. Eleven boxes. One window. A radiator clanking like someone's trapped inside. I sit on the floor right in the doorway and my chest keeps hiccupping, tears running into my mouth, and I'm still laughing, because the bed is also in the hallway, and the fridge is a foot too wide, and I measured, I measured twice. I press my palms to my cheeks; they're burning. "It's fine," I tell the radiator. "It's totally, completely fine." Then I start laughing again and can't stop, and a neighbor's door opens a crack.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside a half-melted ice cream wrapper, brown leather, fat as a sandwich, and Marguerite made a noise like a kettle. She snatched it up, dropped it, snatched it again. "No. No, no, no, no," she told the pigeons, who ignored her. Her laugh came out in hiccuping bursts that bent her over the armrest, and she had to press a fist to her ribs. Tears streaked her cheeks. She flipped the wallet open and shrieked at the driver's license, a man with a mustache like a push broom, then waved it at a jogger who veered wide around her. "Look at him! Look at his face!" Her knees wobbled. She sat, stood, sat again, shoes slapping the gravel, fingers trembling so badly the twenties fanned out and fluttered onto the grass. She chased them in zigzags, cackling, gasping, and still clutching the mustache man to her chest as though he might escape.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says, "Just let your face go in," and I laugh, a high thin sound that doesn't stop when I want it to. My hands clamp the pool's edge, knuckles pale as the tile. I'm thirty-eight. There's a kid in the next lane doing backstroke like it's nothing, and that makes me laugh harder, then hiccup, then something wet and ragged comes out that isn't laughing. "Okay, okay, okay," I keep saying, to nobody, to the water. My legs kick without me, slapping, spraying chlorine into my open mouth. I let go of the wall, grab it again, let go. My heart is a fist on a door. I swallow half the shallow end and cough out, "I'm fine, I'm totally fine," while my fingers shake so badly the foam noodle skitters away across the surface. A whistle shrieks. I realize it's mine, a squeak from my own throat, and I can't find the off switch.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marnie dropped to her knees in the raised bed and tore open the seed packet so hard that tiny brown flecks sprayed across the mulch, and she laughed, a high, cracking sound, and kept laughing while she scrabbled to pick them up one by one. "Six inches apart. Six. Where's the ruler? Who has a ruler?" Nobody was there. Her neighbor's cat watched from the fence. Her hands trembled so badly the trowel clanged against the hose reel, and she flinched, then giggled again, breathless, her ribs aching. Sweat ran into her eyes. She pressed a seed into the dirt, yanked it back out, pressed it in, and whispered, "Don't die, don't die, please don't die," faster and faster, until the words ran together. Her heart thudded in her ears. She stood too quickly, swayed, and pointed the watering can at the soil, then at the sky, then at the soil again, shouting, "Is that too much? That's too much!" Water pooled and swallowed every seed she'd planted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Derek clicked to slide nine, the one titled "Synergy Roadmap," and a sound escaped my nose, a tiny wet honk I turned into a cough. It didn't work. Slide nine had a clip-art rocket. The rocket had a smiley face. I pressed my pen into my palm hard enough to leave a dent and stared at the conference table's wood grain like it was a lifeline. "Sorry, sorry, go on," I wheezed, my voice climbing an octave. Derek said "moving the needle," and my ribs seized. Tears slid into my collar. Priya glanced over; I gave her a thumbs-up that trembled like a leaf. My stomach ached, my cheeks burned, and I slid down in my chair until my knees hit the table's underside. Someone asked a question about Q3. I opened my mouth to answer, and what came out was a long, thin whistle, like a kettle. I dropped my head onto my notebook and shook, whispering, "I'm fine, it's allergies."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The wipers were off, but Marguerite kept swatting at the windshield anyway, laughing in great whooping bursts that bent her over the wheel until the horn blared and made her laugh harder. Her ribs ached. Tears ran into her collar.
