"Of course," he said to the sawdust, jaw tight, voice scraped flat. "Of course you kept the labels neat." He hurled a coffee can of mismatched screws into the contractor bag and listened to it clang. His neck was hot; his knuckles had gone white around a half-finished birdhouse that Dale had promised, years ago, to finish. He pressed his thumb against its crooked roof until the glue gave way. Then he stood there breathing through his teeth, staring at the unfinished thing, the radio on the shelf still tuned to Dale's stupid station, and snapped the dial off in his fist.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Marisol had refreshed the portal fourteen times since noon, and each time the same grey banner mocked her: Results will be published by 5 p.m. It was 5:40. She jabbed the trackpad so hard the laptop skidded across the library table, and a boy two seats down glanced up. "What?" she snapped, jaw tight, and he looked away. Her molars ached from clenching. She yanked her sleeves to her elbows, hot despite the air conditioning, and stabbed the refresh key again. Nothing. "Forty minutes," she muttered. "They said five. It's a number on a screen." She dialed the registrar's office and listened to a recorded voice thank her for her patience. The pen in her fist cracked along its plastic spine. She slapped the laptop half shut, flipped it open again, and breathed through her nose in short, hard bursts, glaring at that grey banner like it owed her money.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The sign said two miles to the lot. Two. I'd read it as point two hours ago, apparently, because the switchbacks kept coming and the light kept draining out of the pines like someone had pulled a plug. I stomped down the rocks hard enough to jar my teeth. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the last creek crossing. "Great," I said to nobody, voice flat and tight. "Wonderful. Thanks for the map, Dave." I yanked the phone from my pocket, saw no bars and eleven percent, and shoved it back so roughly the zipper bit my knuckle. Heat crawled up my neck despite the cold. A branch whipped my cheek and I snapped it off the trunk and flung it into the ferns, breathing through my nose, hands shaking around the straps of my pack. Somewhere an owl started up, calm as anything. I told it to shut up. Then I kept walking, faster, faster, boots slamming the dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card says "flour until it feels right." Feels right. I slam the bowl onto the counter hard enough that the spoon jumps and clatters onto the tile, and I leave it there. Grandma's slanted handwriting, grease-stained at the corners, gives me nothing: no cups, no minutes, no degrees. Just "a handful" and "you'll know." I don't know. My jaw aches from clenching, and when I dig my fingers into the dough it clings to my knuckles like wet cement, and I yank my hand free with a sound that's half growl. "Seriously?" I say to the empty kitchen, to the card, to her. My neck is hot. The oven timer beeps and I stab at it until it stops. Third batch, third brick. I scrape the dough into the trash, the spatula screeching against the bin's lip, then stand there breathing hard through my nose, the card pinched so tight in my fist it creases right through her name.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Derek Hollis was holding a rotisserie chicken when I saw him, and my jaw locked so hard my molars ached. Tenth grade, he'd put my name on that ridiculous list, and I'd eaten lunch in the library for a year. "Marcus! Man, look at you!" he said, arms already opening. I shifted my basket to my left hand so I wouldn't have to shake his. The fluorescent lights hummed too loudly. "Derek," I said, flat, each syllable clipped like a coupon. He kept talking about his boat, his kids, some reunion. My pulse thudded in my ears. I squeezed the basket handle until my knuckles went white, and I felt the bread underneath crush flat. "Funny. I remember you differently," I said. His smile wobbled. I didn't wait for an answer. I walked down the cereal aisle, set my basket by the pyramid of canned beans, and pushed through the doors without buying anything, breathing hard through my nose.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:52 the woman at my register slides a cart of unwrapped, unpriced picture frames toward me and says, "They told me you'd honor the sale." My jaw is clamped so hard my molars ache. I scan the first frame. It beeps wrong. I scan it again, tapping the screen harder than the screen deserves. Behind her the line curls past the pumpkin pie display, and somebody's kid is dragging a bag of cranberries across the floor like a dead animal. "Sure," I say, too flat, too bright. "Let me just check." My neck is hot. The fluorescent hum drills into my skull. I peel the sticky tag off my vest, crumple it into a tight little ball, and press it into my palm until my nails leave crescents. Nobody ever asks who's closing tomorrow's cleanup for me. Nobody. I count the frames out loud, each number clipped like a snapped twig, and glance at the clock. Eight minutes gone. Six more hours of this, and I'm still smiling with my teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta hit the jet bridge doorway at 3:52, forty minutes after the wheels should have touched down, and her jaw was already clamped so tight her molars ached. Gate B41 glowed on the departures board; she was standing at A9. She ran, roller bag clattering behind her like a complaint, strap cutting a groove into her shoulder, shirt sticking to her spine. 'Excuse me. Excuse me. Move, please,' she said, each word clipped to a blade, and a man with a stroller drifted into her lane anyway. She exhaled through her nose, hard. The moving walkway was out of order, a yellow cone sitting on it like a joke. 'Of course,' she muttered. 'Of course it is.' Her phone buzzed: final boarding. She gripped it until her knuckles went pale, then stabbed the screen with her thumb, rehearsing what she would say to the first person in a blue uniform who dared to smile at her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pried the lid off the second can and found a skin of dried paint across the top, a rubbery gray disc that tore like wet paper. She stared at the label. Eggshell, not satin. Three hours of rolling, and the whole north wall gleamed back at her wrong. "Of course," she said, very quietly, and set the roller down so carefully it made no sound. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth since the tape peeled up with a strip of old plaster. Behind her the dog's tail thumped, flicking a drip of blue onto the drop cloth. "Don't," she said. "Don't you dare." Her pulse hammered in her ears. She picked up the stir stick, snapped it across her knee, then stood there with both halves, breathing hard through her nose, counting the ceiling cracks she'd now have to fix too. Then she grabbed her keys and slammed the door hard enough to rattle the ladder.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The screen door slams behind me hard enough to rattle the glass, and I don't care if it cracks. Rain hammers the porch roof. I drop into the rocker, and it squeals, and I jerk it still with both feet. My phone is in my fist, thumb jabbing the same number again, and again it rings out to that cheerful recorded voice. "Unbelievable," I tell the yard. "Three hours. Three hours I sat there." My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars since the driveway. Thunder cracks and I don't flinch. Wind flings water across my knees, and I let it soak through my jeans out of pure stubbornness. Next door, the dog barks at the sky, and I snap, "Oh, shut up," louder than I mean to. My pulse thuds in my ears, louder than the gutters. I rehearse what I'll say tomorrow, every word clipped and sharp, and I squeeze the phone until the case creaks.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The 10mm wrench is gone again. I know exactly where it isn't: on the pegboard, inside its little marker outline that I drew myself. I breathe through my nose and crouch back down to the rear wheel, where the chain has already smeared black across my knuckles and, somehow, my chin. Behind me, Dale's radio mutters a song with too much bass, and the shelf I labeled last week has been rearranged. "Hey, Dale," I call, pleasantly, each syllable clipped like a zip tie. "Seen my wrench?" He shrugs without looking up. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars. I use the wrong wrench, round off the bolt, and let out a short hiss between my teeth. The tire lever clatters harder than necessary against the concrete. I stand, wipe my hands on a rag that only moves the grease around, and begin, slowly and loudly, to search his toolbox.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The schedule on the pole says 4:42, and my phone says 4:58. I check both again anyway, as if one might blink. The sky has gone the color of dishwater, and the first fat drops smack the shelter roof like someone flicking my forehead. I tug my collar up, jaw tight, and shift my weight from one foot to the other until my heels ache. A gust shoves wet grit into my eyes. 'Perfect,' I say to nobody, flat and loud, and the man beside me glances over then away. I crush my empty coffee cup, drop it in the bin, and it bounces out. I stare at it. I pick it up and jam it in harder than I need to. My umbrella is on my kitchen counter, where I last saw it, where I told myself to remember it. I lean out over the curb, squinting down the empty road, and exhale through my nose, long and slow, watching the street fill with puddles.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid kept sliding off the bed, so I kicked it across the floor and heard it crack. Fine. I pulled out the first envelope and my jaw was already tight. Rubber bands had melted into the paper, gummy and brown, and they stuck to my thumb. I shook my hand, then wiped it on my jeans harder than I needed to. "Of course," I said to the empty room. "Of course he kept every single one." Birthday cards, receipts, a postcard of a lighthouse that said only *Weather's fine.* I flipped it over, flipped it back, and dropped it onto the pile with a slap. The radiator clanked. My neck ached from hunching, and I'd read the same grocery list three times without taking it in. Two hours, and the keep pile was four letters. I grabbed a trash bag, snapped it open so hard it whistled, and shoved a whole handful in without looking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta had just slid the sourdough into the oven when the doorbell rang twice, quick, the way only Dale rang it. She wiped her floury hands on her jeans, slowly, one finger at a time, and opened the door about a foot. "Ladder," Dale said, grinning. "Just for an hour. The gutters." Her jaw tightened. It was the same ladder she'd lent him in March, the one that came back with a bent rung and mud on its feet. "Which gutters," she said, flat. He waved vaguely at his roof. She breathed out through her nose and stared at the hedge behind him, thinking of her clippers, still missing from his garage. "It's behind the lawnmower," she said. "Bring it back today." She shut the door a little harder than the latch needed, then stood in the hallway counting each bang from her garage, shoulders up near her ears while the kitchen timer ticked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta cracked the oven door and the heat slapped her face, and the chicken, which should have been golden twenty minutes ago, sat there pale and glistening. "Of course," she said, to nobody, and shut it with her hip harder than the hinge deserved. The clock read 6:42. The knife kept slipping on the onion, so she chopped faster, the blade clacking against the board in short, hard bursts. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the potatoes. From the living room, Dev called, "Need any help?" and she answered without turning, "No," clipped and flat, then, "Unless you can fix the oven." A drip of sweat slid down her spine. She yanked the dish towel off her shoulder, wiped the counter in one swipe, and knocked the salt over. She stared at the white spill for a long second, exhaled through her nose, and swept it into her palm with two stiff fingers.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the countertop just as Marta got the knife into the onion, and she stared at the screen: a number she didn't know, area code from somewhere she'd never lived. She let it ring four times, jaw tightening, the buzzing walking the phone toward the edge of the cutting board. Her thumb jabbed the green button and she pinned the phone between ear and shoulder, still holding the knife. "Yes." Flat. Nothing but a faint hiss, then a click, then a bright recorded voice mentioning her car's extended warranty. "I don't even have a car that's—" She exhaled hard through her nose, the onion forgotten, a pulse ticking at her temple. "Unbelievable." She jabbed the red button, slapped the phone face-down, and chopped the onion into pieces far smaller than the recipe wanted, each thunk louder than the last. When it buzzed again, same number, she didn't even look. She just turned the volume off and kept chopping, shoulders up around her ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, wedged between a dead highlighter and a crumpled syllabus, and now the librarian was squinting at her screen like it might change its answer. I set the copy of Organic Chemistry on the counter harder than I needed to. The thud turned a head two tables over. "Two hundred and forty-one days," she read aloud, slowly, as if I might want to savor it. My jaw was tight enough that my molars ached. I tapped my card against the counter, once, twice, a small metronome of my own making. "I emailed you in April," I said, each word clipped and level. "Twice." She hummed and kept typing. Behind me the line shuffled, and someone sighed. I stared at the laminated sign about quiet voices and counted its letters, felt heat crawl up my neck, and slid the card across without letting go until she tugged."Just take the money," I said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The couch stops at the doorframe, two inches too wide, and I stand there holding my end while the movers watch me like I'm the one who measured wrong. I did measure. I wrote it on my hand. "Tilt it," I say, jaw tight, and we tilt it, and the leg scrapes a long pale line down the fresh paint. Nobody apologizes. I carry the lamp in myself, step over a box labeled KITCHEN that clearly contains towels, and find the outlet behind the radiator, naturally. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears; I push them down and they climb back. Upstairs someone starts drilling, a flat, grinding whine that sets my teeth humming. I peel tape off a box harder than I need to, and the tape tears in half. "Great," I tell the empty room, pressing my thumb into the knot above my eye. The room, all nine steps of it, says nothing back. I shove the window open. The drilling gets louder.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench was the only one in the shade, and of course someone had left a brown leather wallet square in the middle of it. I stood there with my sandwich going warm in its bag and my jaw working side to side. Twelve minutes of lunch left. I exhaled through my nose, long and hard, and picked the thing up between two fingers like it might be wet. Inside: a driver's license, forty dollars, a library card, a coupon for dog shampoo. 'Brilliant,' I said to a pigeon, who didn't care. My shoulders had crept up toward my ears. I snapped the wallet shut harder than I needed to, checked my watch again, and began walking toward the ranger station with long, stabbing steps, gravel crunching under my heels. 'Some people,' I muttered, then said it again louder to nobody, tapping the wallet against my thigh the whole way. My sandwich stayed in the bag, uneaten, getting flatter in my grip.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says "Just relax" for the fourth time, and I grip the pool wall until my knuckles go pale. Chlorine stings the back of my throat. Around me, kids in neon goggles bob like corks, and one of them flutters past me without even trying. "I am relaxed," I say, teeth clenched, each word clipped short. My jaw aches. I push off, kick, and my legs sink anyway, dragging me down like wet laundry. I surface sputtering, water up my nose, and slap the surface with my palm harder than I mean to. The splash hits the instructor's clipboard. "Again," she says, smiling. I wipe my eyes, snap my goggle strap back into place so hard it twangs, and stare at the lane rope. Thirty-four years old. A mortgage, a team of six, and I can't float on my back. I breathe out through my nose, long and loud, and shove off the wall again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marnie jammed the trowel into the clay and it rang against a rock. She pried the rock out, flung it toward the fence, and heard it clatter off the neighbor's recycling bin. The seed packet said loose, well-drained soil. This was a brick. Sweat slid down her spine under a shirt that had already stuck to her, and a gnat kept circling her left ear no matter how hard she swatted. She knelt, then stood, then knelt again because her knees had opinions. "Six inches apart," she read aloud, flat and clipped, and the tape measure snapped shut on her thumb. She said a word her mother wouldn't have liked. The tomato seedlings slumped in their plastic tray, already wilting, as if they'd judged her. She dug the next hole twice as fast, jaw tight, dirt packed under every nail, and pressed the soil down with the heel of her hand harder than any plant could possibly need.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked his pen shut, then open, then shut again as Dana advanced to slide twelve. The conference room smelled of burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. "As you can see," Dana said, "the pipeline was entirely my redesign," and Marcus's jaw tightened until his molars ached. He had written that pipeline. Three months of it, and the commit history said so. He pressed his thumbnail into the pad of his finger and stared at the wall clock, where the second hand seemed to stall on every tick. When Dana glanced his way and asked, "Any questions?" he smiled with only his mouth. "Just one," he said, voice flat and even, each word set down like a plate. "Whose name is on slide three?" Someone coughed. Dana's laser pointer wobbled on the screen. Marcus leaned back, arms folded, heat crawling up the back of his neck, and waited for the answer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The pickup in front of me braked for no reason again, and my jaw clenched so hard I felt it in my ears. I tapped the wheel with two fingers, then four, then gave up and gripped it at ten and two. "Green. It's green. Green is the one that means go," I said to the windshield, flat and quiet. The radio was playing the same ad for the third time since the exit, so I stabbed the button and drove in the hum of tires. Every streetlight turned my knuckles orange, then dark, then orange. My shoulders had crept up toward my neck, and I shoved them down, and they crept back. Twelve hours at the office, a cold sandwich, and now this guy doing thirty-one in a forty-five. I flicked the blinker, swung around him, and didn't look over. In the mirror his headlights shrank. I exhaled through my nose, long and thin, and realized I'd been holding the same breath since the bridge.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine on the fourth floor eats my dollar for the second time, and I slap its side hard enough that my palm stings. Uncle Dennis's room smells like warm plastic and lemon cleaner. The television is blaring a game show, and he hasn't looked away from it since I walked in. "Can we turn that down?" I ask. He says, "What?" without lowering it. I find the remote wedged under his thigh and press the button with my thumb, jaw tight, counting ceiling tiles. A nurse comes in to check his chart and asks how I'm doing. "Fine," I say, too quickly, shoving my hands into my jacket pockets. My foot taps the bed rail until Dennis finally glances at it. Forty more minutes, I tell myself, checking my watch again. I drove two hours for this, and he wants to know if I got the parking validated.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell was supposed to ring at 3:05. I checked my phone again: 3:19. I shifted my weight off my left foot, then back, my jaw clamped so tight my molars ached. Somebody's SUV sat idling in the fire lane, again, blocking the whole curb, and its driver was laughing into her phone like the rest of us had nowhere to be. "Unbelievable," I said, not quietly. The woman beside me glanced over; I gave her a thin smile and turned my back. My keys had left red dents in my palm. The casserole I'd promised to start by four sat in my head like a stone. When the doors finally banged open and a river of backpacks poured out, I scanned for Milo's yellow hat and exhaled hard through my nose. He waved, unhurried, stopping to examine a stick. "Now," I called. "Please. Today."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine o'clock Marguerite had answered the same question eleven times, and the oak dresser still wore its masking-tape tag: $40, firm. The man in the golf visor ran his thumb along the drawer edge, sniffed, and said, "Would you take fifteen?" She kept her smile where it was, though her molars pressed together. "The tag says forty." "It's got a scratch." "It's got ninety years," she said, flatly, and slid a coffee mug an inch to the left on the table for no reason. He wandered off with the drawer still hanging open. She shoved it shut with her hip, harder than the wood deserved, and the brass pulls rattled. Sweat gathered under her collar. Across the lawn, a child dragged a lamp by its cord through the wet grass, and she heard herself say, "Please put that down," in a voice like a ruler snapping. She peeled the tape off the dresser and pressed it on again, straighter.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marcus lay on his back under the sink with a flashlight clamped between his teeth, one cold drip after another landing precisely on his collarbone. He tightened the nut a quarter turn. The drip kept coming. "Of course," he said around the flashlight, and the beam jittered across the pipe. He wrenched again, harder, and his knuckles scraped the cabinet's raw edge. He hissed through his nose, jerked his hand back, and cracked his skull on the shelf above. Detergent bottles rattled. He pulled out the plumber's tape he'd already wound three times, tore it off in a ragged strip, and stared at the wet, useless wad stuck to his thumb. Upstairs, his sister's laughter drifted down from the television. His jaw ached from clenching. He flung the tape at the bucket, missed, and listened to it slap the tile. "Fine," he muttered, reaching for the wrench again, shoulders hiked up near his ears, and started over from the very beginning.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has a little plastic window and a stamp-sized seal that reads OFFICIAL, as if I might mistake it for a birthday card. I drop my keys on the counter hard enough that the dog leaves the kitchen. Third notice. I slide my thumb under the flap and drag it too fast, and the paper nips my skin. I suck the cut, tasting copper, and snap the pages open with a flick of my wrist. Three paragraphs to say nothing. 'Please be advised.' I read it out loud in a flat, mocking voice to the empty room. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my teeth since the mailbox. Reference number, seventeen digits. I already sent them that number. Twice. I fold the letter in half, then in quarters, then press the creases flat with my knuckle, hard, and reach for the phone, already dreading the hold music, already muttering, 'Sure. Of course. Why wouldn't you.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The ticket machine ate my coins for the third time and offered me nothing but a blinking screen of characters I couldn't read. I jabbed the same button again, harder, until my thumb throbbed. Behind me the queue shifted and someone exhaled loudly. "It's fine," I said to no one, in the flat, clipped voice I use on airline hotlines. My backpack strap had dug a groove into my shoulder since the train, and sweat glued my shirt to my spine. A man in a uniform approached, spoke a rapid stream of syllables, and pointed at something I couldn't see. I held up my phone, its translation app spinning uselessly. "No. Ticket. I just want a ticket," I said, slower and louder, as if volume were a currency. He shrugged. My jaw was clamped so tight my teeth ached. I snatched my bag and stalked toward the exit, muttering that I could have walked from the airport faster, and probably understood more of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus checked his watch for the third time and shoved the phone back into his jacket pocket. Across the field, Biscuit tore in wide circles, ignoring the tennis ball that lay a few feet from his boots. "Here," he called, flat and clipped. "Biscuit. Here." The dog didn't so much as flinch. A damp wind worked its way under his collar, and he hunched his shoulders, jaw tight enough that his molars ached. His thermos had gone lukewarm an hour ago; he drank from it anyway and grimaced. Somewhere behind him, a woman laughed as her spaniel trotted obediently back to her. Marcus exhaled hard through his nose, stomped across the soggy grass, and felt cold mud seep through his left sock. "Great," he muttered. "Perfect." Biscuit finally bounded over, tongue lolling, and dropped a stick at his feet. Marcus stared at it, then at the dinner he was now going to eat at nine o'clock, and clipped the leash on with a sharp, unnecessary snap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Doug has come in early again on the downbeat of the bridge. I stop playing. My thumb is pressed so hard against the cello's neck that the tip has gone white. "Let's take it from measure forty-one," I say, smiling with my teeth only, and my voice comes out flat and even, the way you talk to a vending machine. Forty-one. Again. Third time. The radiator clanks, someone's folding chair squeaks, and I count silently to four before lifting my bow. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding it since the second page. Marjorie asks if we might try it slower, and I say, "Sure, slower, wonderful," then tap the stand with my pencil, harder than I mean to. The metronome clicks. I stare at the exit sign over the door, breathe out through my nose, and begin the bar again, shoulders up around my ears, the concert eleven days away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta pulled the fourth coffee can of mismatched screws off the shelf and set it down harder than she meant to. Sawdust puffed up and she sneezed twice, jaw tight. "Of course," she said to the empty room. "Labeled 'misc.' Very helpful, Walt." She dumped the can onto the bench and started sorting by thread, then stopped, flicked the pile into the trash bin, and listened to it clatter. Every drawer she yanked open stuck, then flew out and nearly hit her shin. Tape measures, nine of them. Nine! She counted them aloud, voice flat, and stacked them in a box with more force than they deserved. Her shoulders had climbed up toward her ears hours ago. The radio on the sill still hissed between stations, and she smacked its off switch with the heel of her hand. Then she checked her phone, saw the dumpster was due back by five, and muttered, "Sure. No rush." She grabbed the next can.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said "Results will be posted by noon." It was 12:47. I refreshed the page again, harder than the mouse deserved, and the same gray banner stared back. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my teeth since lunch. "Seriously?" I told the empty dorm room, flatly, and flipped my pen end over end until it skittered off the desk. I left it there. Across the hall someone's music thumped, the same chorus looping, and I shut my door with a bang that rattled the poster tape. Sat down. Stood up. Typed the department's email address, deleted it, typed it again. Who sets a deadline and then ignores it? My shoulders had crept up near my ears, and the collar of my sweater felt too tight, so I yanked it away from my neck. Refresh. Gray banner. I exhaled through my nose, long and sharp, and refreshed again anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta yanked her pack strap higher for the fifth time, and it slid right back down, grinding the same raw patch on her shoulder. The light had gone orange, then the color of weak tea, and the trail marker she'd been promised at the two-mile mark still hadn't appeared. "Two miles," she muttered, jabbing her trekking pole into the gravel hard enough to jar her wrist. "Two. Miles." Behind her, a pebble skittered, and she didn't turn around. Her jaw ached from clenching. She snapped the map open, squinted at the blurring lines, then crumpled it into her pocket without bothering to fold it right. A mosquito whined at her ear. She slapped her neck, missed, slapped again. The ridge ahead kept stretching away, the pines going black one by one, and she stomped on, boots loud on purpose, breathing through her nose in short, hard bursts.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Dana flattened the index card against the counter with her palm for the third time, but the curling corner sprang up again. "A handful of flour," she read aloud, flat as a dial tone. "Whose handful, Grandma?" Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the yeast. She dumped in more flour, then more, and the dough clung to her knuckles like wet cement. She scraped it off with short, hard strokes and the bowl rattled against the tile. The kitchen was too warm, the oven ticking, a bead of sweat sliding down her spine. "Warm water." She jabbed the thermometer in, glared at it, and set it down with a clack. The card said *knead till it feels right.* Dana pushed the heel of her hand into the dough, again and again, breathing hard through her nose. Nothing felt right. She snatched a pen and wrote HOW MUCH? in the margin, pressing so hard the paper tore.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I had exactly one thing on my list, lightbulbs, and I was three steps from the aisle when someone said my full name like a game show host. Dennis Pruitt. Tenth grade chemistry, the guy who copied my labs. He stepped into my path with his cart angled so I couldn't pass. "Man, you haven't changed at all!" I gripped the plastic package of bulbs until the edges bit my palm. "Neither have you," I said, flat, and checked my phone though nothing had buzzed. He kept talking about his boat, his second divorce, a podcast. The fluorescent hum seemed to climb inside my jaw. I nodded in small, measured jerks, counting ceiling tiles. When he finally said, "We should grab a beer," I smiled with my teeth only. "Sure. I'll find you." Then I walked to the self-checkout, the long way, and scanned the bulbs twice by mistake, hard enough to make the machine beep at me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marta pressed the register drawer shut with her hip, harder than it needed, and the bell above the pharmacy door jangled again. Four forty-eight. Twelve minutes, and a man in a Santa hat was holding a prescription up like a winning ticket. "We close at five," she said, each word clipped square. "I see that," he said, and smiled. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars since the lunch rush. She scanned the label, scanned it again when the machine beeped wrong, and slapped the bag onto the counter. The fluorescent light hummed over her left ear. Behind her, Dev was humming carols, and she turned and stared at the back of his head until he stopped. "Merry whatever," she told the customer, tugging the gate halfway down before he'd even reached the door. Her coat hung on its hook, forty feet and three more people away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta hit the end of the moving walkway and kept walking, her carry-on bumping the back of her heel with every stride. Gate B41. The board said B41 had been B41 for six minutes, which was how long she'd been behind the man who stopped dead to read it. "Excuse me," she said, in the flat voice she used for voicemails from her landlord. He didn't move. She slid around him, jaw tight enough that her molars ached, and checked her watch again, though it had been eleven seconds. A kiosk cart beeped into her path. She exhaled through her nose, long and hard, and turned her shoulder to squeeze past. Sweat prickled under her backpack straps. Somewhere behind her a child was wailing, and she thought, very clearly, that she would pay a hundred dollars for one quiet hallway. At the gate, the agent smiled up at her. "Boarding's closing," Marta said. "I can see that." She slapped her phone onto the counter, screen glowing, and waited, tapping one finger against the laminate.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pressed the roller into the tray for the fourth time and dragged it up the wall, and the pale gray came out streaky again, the old blue ghosting through like a bruise. "Two coats," she said to the empty room, each word clipped short. "It said two coats." She jabbed the roller at the corner and a fat drop landed on her sock. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the morning. Behind her the tape on the baseboard had peeled up again, curling like a tongue, and she yanked it flat with her thumb hard enough to leave a smear. The window was shut because of dust, and sweat crawled down her spine. She snapped the lid back onto the can, missed, hammered it twice with the heel of her hand, and stood there breathing through her nose, staring at the streaks. Then she picked the roller up again and went at the wall faster, harder, not bothering to wipe her forehead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the screen door just as Marguerite finally got the lawn chair angled right, and she let out a long breath through her nose. Rain slanted under the porch roof and speckled her knees. She dragged the chair back a foot. It scraped. Her jaw stayed tight around the lid of the iced tea she'd been saving, and she jabbed the straw down so hard the cup squeaked. Inside, the neighbor's dog yapped on and on through the wall of weather. "Of course," she said to no one, flat and clipped. "Of course now." Her phone buzzed against the railing; she flipped it face down without looking. A gutter was overflowing somewhere, a steady slapping that landed right behind her eyes. She tugged her damp sleeve, crossed her arms, uncrossed them, and drummed her fingers on the armrest until the rhythm matched nothing at all. Another flash. She didn't flinch. She only glared at the sky as if it owed her an apology and a refund.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marta wedged the tire lever under the rim and pulled harder than the stubborn rubber deserved. Across the garage, Dennis's new carbon frame hung from the shared stand, gleaming under the one good light, while her steel commuter leaned in the shadow of the water heater. She could hear him whistling. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. "Nice," she said when he held up a shiny derailleur, and the word came out flat as a dropped wrench. He grinned and asked if she needed the stand. "No, I'm fine." She wasn't. Her knuckle scraped the chainring and she hissed, then kept going, tightening the bolt past what the manual said. Heat crawled up her neck. When his phone buzzed with a message from the race club, she turned her back, wiped her greasy hands on her jeans, and stared at the rust blooming along her own chainstay as if it had insulted her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as the silver car pulled up across the street, and Dara watched Mina climb out of it laughing, her hand still resting on the driver's sleeve. Dara's jaw tightened. She shoved her phone into her pocket, then pulled it out again, thumbed through nothing, and put it away. Wind flung grit against her shins. "Nice of him to drive her," she said to no one, too brightly, and the old man beside her glanced up. Her fingers twisted the strap of her bag until the skin whitened. Mina waved. Dara lifted two fingers, no more, and turned her shoulder so the rain could have her face. Heat crawled up her neck despite the cold. She counted the bus's absence in minutes, then in car doors, then in the way Mina's laugh kept carrying over the traffic, bright and unbothered, as if the storm were a gift someone had wrapped just for her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and someone else's perfume, and Marguerite pulled the letters out one by one with two fingers, as if they might be hot. Every envelope bore her late husband's slanting hand, but the name above the address was Delphine's. Thirty-one of them, tied in blue ribbon, never once crumpled. She counted them twice. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth. 'He wrote me four,' she said to the empty kitchen, flatly, then laughed, a short ugly sound. The kettle screamed and she let it. She unfolded one and read the first line, 'My darling girl, the light here is nothing without you,' and her thumbnail dug a crescent into the paper's edge. Heat climbed her neck. She smoothed the page flat, too hard, then stacked the letters square, tapped them against the table, and dropped them back in the box. She pressed the lid down with both palms until her knuckles whitened, then carried it to the closet and put it behind the winter coats, where she would not have to see the ribbon.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marcus was scraping moss from his gutter with a butter knife when Devin from next door appeared at the fence, grinning, asking if the aluminum ladder in Marcus's garage was free for the afternoon. Marcus's jaw tightened. Devin's roof already had new shingles, the whole house repainted that crisp slate blue, a deck with string lights glowing every evening. "Sure," Marcus said, too brightly, and his voice came out thin. He dragged the ladder out, scuffing the rungs against the doorframe harder than he needed to. "Careful, the left foot sticks." Devin thanked him twice, hoisting it easily over one shoulder. Marcus watched him go, nails digging into his palms, a hot knot lodged under his ribs. Back in the yard he stared at his sagging gutter, the butter knife dull in his hand. Over the fence came the whistle of Devin's drill, cheerful and unhurried. Marcus turned the hose on full, loud enough to drown it out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: I chop the parsley harder than it needs. Seven minutes until they arrive, and Dana's text is still open on the counter: "Can't wait! Priya's bringing her famous tiramisu." Famous. I scrape the knife across the board, and my jaw aches from clenching. The risotto needs stirring, so I stir, round and round, wondering if anyone will ever say *famous* about it. My phone buzzes; I flip it face down without reading. I taste the broth and add salt, then more salt, then too much. "Fine," I say to the empty kitchen, bright and tight, like I'm already greeting someone. My neck is hot. I put the good wine at the front of the table and the cheap one behind the toaster, then swap them, then swap them again. When the doorbell rings, I wipe my hands slowly, smooth my apron, and practice a smile in the dark oven glass. It looks almost real.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the sink while I was scraping rice off Dana's plate, and the screen said only a string of digits I didn't know. I dried my hands slowly, too slowly. "Hello?" A woman's voice, bright as a spoon: she was calling about the gallery, about Dana's piece, about the offer. I pressed my tongue against my teeth until my jaw ached. "She's not here," I said, flat, though Dana was right there on the couch, headphones on, humming. Heat crawled up my neck. The woman kept saying wonderful, wonderful. I stared at the pile of my own unfinished canvases leaning by the door, their corners gray with dust. "I'll pass it along," I said, and my voice came out pleasant and strange. I hung up. Dana lifted one earphone and asked who it was. I turned the faucet on hard, let the water roar, and said, "Wrong number."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack for four months, spine cracked, and I slid it onto the desk without looking at the librarian. "Sorry. It's, um, a lot overdue." My voice came out flat and tight. Behind me, Dana laughed with the girl from our seminar, the one who always had her hand up first, and I heard my name in neither of their sentences. My jaw ached from clenching. The librarian typed, frowned, said the fine was capped at twenty dollars, and I counted bills with fingers that felt too hot. Through the window I watched them cross the quad together, sharing one umbrella, her scarf the same green I'd almost bought. I pressed my thumbnail into my palm until it left a crescent. "Fine," I told the librarian, though she hadn't asked anything. I grabbed the receipt, crumpled it, and shoved it in my pocket. Then I walked the long way around, so I wouldn't catch up to them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The box marked KITCHEN split open on the stairs, and I swore, jamming a cracked mug back inside while Dana's laugh drifted down from the landing. She'd moved into 4B last spring, and her door stood open, showing a window that took up half the wall, plants hanging in it like they'd been paid to. Mine faced a brick wall. "Need a hand?" she called. "No, I've got it," I said, too fast, my jaw tight, my fingers white around the cardboard. Inside, I measured the room twice with my arms. Eleven steps, corner to corner. I set my lamp on the sill and it looked small and yellow and stupid. Through the thin wall came the clink of her wine glasses, a song I liked, someone else's voice joining hers. I pressed my cheek to the cold plaster, then dragged my couch two inches left, then two inches back, hot-faced, listening to every note of her evening.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside a half-eaten pretzel, fat and brown, the leather worn soft in a way mine never gets because mine is cracked vinyl from a drugstore. I picked it up with two fingers. My jaw had gone tight. Inside, a driver's license: Marcus Hale, smiling like a man who'd never once checked his balance before buying lunch. Crisp twenties fanned out, a gym card, a photo of a woman laughing into a sunlit wind. I counted the bills twice, my thumb pressing harder than it needed to. "Nice," I said to a pigeon, and my voice came out thin and sour. Heat crawled up my neck. I thought about my own wallet, the lone five and the expired coupon, the rent note on my fridge. A jogger passed and I snapped the wallet shut. I walked it to the lost-and-found kiosk, dropped it on the counter, and left before the attendant could thank me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The kid in lane two was maybe eight, and she flipped under the lane rope like it was nothing, surfacing with a grin. I stood waist-deep in the shallow end, gripping the kickboard so hard my knuckles went yellow. Chlorine stung the back of my throat. "Nice," I called, and my voice came out thin and flat. Coach Dana said, "Your turn, Marcus, just float," and I tipped back, stiff as a plank, my heels sinking, water slapping into my ears. Across the pool the girl's mother clapped. Nobody had ever clapped for me at anything wet. I kicked harder than I needed to, splashing the old man beside me, and didn't say sorry. When the girl swam past, easy, barely rippling, I turned my face to the tiles and counted their cracks until my jaw unclenched. In the locker room I yanked my towel off the hook and muttered, "Thirty-nine years of walking on land, and she gets to fly."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I pressed the last pea seed into the dirt and wiped my palms on my jeans harder than I needed to. Over the fence, Marcy's tomato cages stood in tidy rows, already wearing green. Mine was a rectangle of brown with popsicle sticks. "Wow, you're so fast," I called, and my voice came out thin and bright, like a stranger's. She waved a trowel and said something about compost. I nodded through it, jaw tight, staring at her basil. Mine hadn't even been bought yet. Back inside I stood at the window with a glass of water I didn't drink, counting her leaves against my sticks. Her first-time garden, she'd said, same as mine. I yanked the curtain shut, then opened it again an inch, just to check whether anything of hers had grown since lunch.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the next slide, and the whole room leaned in. I kept my pen pressed so hard against my notebook that it tore through the page. The dashboard was clean, nearly identical to the one I'd pitched in March, the one Marcus said was "not a priority right now." My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since slide two. When the VP laughed at Dana's joke, I laughed too, a half-second late, too loud. My coffee had gone cold, but I kept sipping it anyway, something to do with my hands. "Great work," I said when she finished, and my voice came out thin and bright, like a wire. Everyone clapped. I clapped slowly, watching my own palms. Afterward, someone asked if I had any thoughts. I said the colors were nice. Then I walked to the kitchen and stood with my forehead nearly touching the cool fridge door, counting the magnets until my face stopped burning.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty except for Dana's headlights and the long orange smear of the sodium lamps, and still she gripped the wheel at ten and two like a driving test. Her phone lit up in the cup holder: a photo from Marcus, the whole team on a rooftop in Lisbon, glasses raised, the new hire's arm slung around her old desk-mate. She turned the screen face-down without looking twice. Then, at a red light, she turned it back up. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth since the exit. "Great," she said to the dashboard, bright and flat. "Good for them." The radio played something cheerful and she snapped it off. Her chest felt tight and hot despite the open window, and every thought circled the promotion email she'd drafted and never sent. She drove past her exit, noticed two miles later, and didn't turn around right away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vase of tulips on Grandpa's tray table was already open wide, which meant someone had come before me. I set down my grocery-store carnations anyway and turned them so the bruised petals faced the wall. "Who brought those?" I asked, too brightly. "Your cousin Danny," Grandpa said, and his whole face lifted just saying it. My jaw tightened until my molars ached. Danny, who lived four states away, who hadn't called since March. I dragged the vinyl chair closer, its legs shrieking on the floor, and straightened Grandpa's blanket though it was fine. He told me Danny stayed three hours and read him the baseball scores. I'd driven forty minutes every Sunday for two years. "That's nice," I said, nodding too many times. My hands were hot. I picked the card off the tulips, read Danny's loopy signature, and slid it face-down beneath the water pitcher. Then I asked if he wanted me to read him the scores, too, and kept my voice level.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus kept his hands in his jacket pockets, thumbnail digging into a loose thread, while the other fathers clustered by the gate and laughed at something he hadn't heard. Dana's dad, the one in the good boots, had an arm slung over a stroller handle like he'd been born to it. "Pizza Friday again," Marcus said to no one, too loud, then cleared his throat. His jaw ached from holding a smile. When the doors banged open, he stepped forward early, scanning for Leo, and his chest tightened as a small girl ran shrieking into the boots man's legs. Leo came out last, backpack dragging, and waved at Dana first. Marcus saw it. He crouched and zipped Leo's coat too hard. "Who's that you waved at? Do you even like her?" Leo shrugged. Marcus's face burned in the cold air, and he kept watching the gate long after the others had gone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The oak dresser had been Mom's, and I'd priced it at forty dollars without blinking, but now my sister's husband was running his palm along its top like he'd discovered it. "Solid," he said. "Gina always said you'd get the good pieces." I wiped the same corner of the card table three times. My jaw ached from smiling. Gina had gotten the piano, the pearls, the house key on the hook, and now Mom's dresser was going home in her minivan. "Forty's fine," I said, too brightly, and then, "Actually, it's sixty." He laughed and peeled off three twenties. I folded them small, tighter, until the edges bit my thumb. When they drove away, the drawer pulls rattling, I stood in the driveway with the heat pressing on my neck, staring at the pale square of grass where it had sat. I'd sold it. That was the plan. I took the nearest lamp and sold it for a dollar to the first person who asked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Water ticked into the bucket under the sink while I wedged the wrench onto the nut for the fourth time. Through the wall I could hear Danny's laugh, the easy one, and my father-in-law saying, "It's fine, Marcus already called a guy." Marcus. Marcus with his tidy toolbox and his sleeves rolled just so. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my teeth around the flashlight. The nut wouldn't budge. I leaned harder, knuckles scraped raw, a cold drip sliding down my wrist into my sleeve. "I've got it," I called, too loud, and the voices dipped, then rose again. I yanked. The wrench slipped and cracked against the pipe. Nobody came. I stayed on my knees on the damp tile, ears hot, listening to them say his name like a gift they'd handed him and never me, and I tightened the nut again, harder, until my hand shook.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope from the Housing Authority lay on the counter beside Dara's sister's postcard, the one with the new balcony on it, and Dara slid a thumbnail under the flap harder than she needed to. Paper tore. She read the first line, then read it again, jaw tight, her tea going cold at her elbow. Approved. Not for her, though. A forwarded notice, misdelivered, addressed to Mina downstairs, who had moved in three months ago and already had a name on the waiting list's top line. Dara's own application, eleven years old, sat somewhere beneath it. She laughed, one short dry sound, and folded the page into precise thirds. Her face felt hot. 'Good for her,' she said to the empty kitchen, flat as a plate. She pressed the letter under the fruit bowl, took it out again, and stood at the window watching Mina carry groceries across the courtyard, humming, swinging the bag like it weighed nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed into Hanoi's station, and Marcus dragged his suitcase through the crowd with his jaw set tight. Ahead, his college roommate Dan, who had moved here two years ago, was already laughing with a vendor, rattling off syllables that curled and rose like music. The vendor handed Dan a paper cone of something steaming and waved away his money. Marcus stood holding his phone, its translation app frozen on a spinning wheel. "Great," he said, too brightly. "You're basically a local." Dan clapped his shoulder and kept talking, and the words slid past Marcus like traffic. His neck went hot. He counted the scooters streaming by, pressed his thumbnail into his palm, and watched the vendor smile at Dan again, a smile he'd have given anything to earn. When Dan offered him a bite, Marcus shook his head. "Not hungry," he muttered, and stared at the cone until his stomach knotted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the field toward the new neighbor, Dana, who'd crouched with her hands out like she'd been doing it for years. I stayed on the bench and pressed my thumbnail into the slats until it ached. "Biscuit," I called, too bright, too high. "Here, bud. Treat." He didn't even flick an ear. He flopped onto his back so Dana could scratch the belly he'd only ever shown me, and his tail swept the grass in wide, stupid arcs. My jaw was tight enough to hurt. I pulled the bag of liver bites from my pocket and shook it, loudly, twice. Dana laughed and waved. I lifted two fingers off my knee, smiled with my teeth, and said, "He's shy with strangers," a lie I heard land flat in the cold air. Then I stood, sat again, and checked my phone, which had nothing on it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church basement smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and Marguerite stood at the back with her sheet music creased into a tight little accordion. On the makeshift stage, the new girl, barely twenty, sang the second verse of "Danny Boy" and the folding chairs seemed to lean toward her. Mr. Alvarez closed his eyes and smiled. Marguerite's jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars. "Lovely," she said when it ended, too brightly, clapping only twice. Her palms were hot. When he asked if she'd mind trading the solo for the harmony line, she laughed, a short dry sound, and said, "Oh, of course, whatever's best for the program." She walked to her spot, set her water bottle down harder than she meant to, and stared at the crooked tape mark on the floor. Thirty years of Thursdays, she thought, and nobody had ever leaned toward her like that. She sang the harmony perfectly, quietly, and counted the minutes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus held the dovetail joint up to the window and turned it slowly, hunting for a gap. There wasn't one. He dropped it in the box marked DONATE, took it out again, then put it back harder than he meant to. Along the pegboard, Daniel's chisels hung inside outlines he'd drawn himself, each edge bright. Marcus's own were rusting in a coffee can at home. His jaw ached; he realized he'd been clenching it since the third shelf. "Of course you labeled everything," he said to the empty room, too loudly, and laughed once, a short dry sound. Under the bench he found a half-finished rocking chair, its runners curved perfectly, and beside it a finished cradle Daniel had never once mentioned. Marcus's thumb pressed into the sanded oak until the nail whitened. Then he wrapped the chisels in a towel, slowly, and slid them into his own bag before anyone could come through the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells of floor polish and old radiator dust, and I've been standing at the corkboard for twenty minutes with my arms crossed so tight my ribs ache. The sheet isn't up yet. Dana leans beside me, humming, tapping her pen against her teeth, and every tap lands somewhere behind my eye. "You'll be fine," she says, and I answer, "Sure," in a voice flat as a ruler. Last week she slept through the study session and still got the top mark on the mock. I replay that number while my jaw clenches. When the secretary finally pins up the page, Dana squeals and bounds forward. I stay put, counting ceiling tiles, my face stretched into a smile that feels like a cramp. "Go on, check yours," she says. I take one slow step, then another, hoping my name sits above hers, hating how badly I hope it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta kept her eyes on the backs of their jackets, Dana's red one and Theo's gray, bobbing together up the switchbacks while the pines went from green to black. Their laughter drifted down to her in pieces. She jammed her trekking poles into the dirt harder than the slope required. "Wait up," she called, light as a postcard, and then didn't speed up when they didn't. Her jaw ached from how long she'd held it shut. Dana touched Theo's elbow to steer him around a root, an easy gesture, and Marta's stomach tightened like a cinched strap. Sweat cooled on her neck. She thought of the photo Dana had posted last week, the one she'd pretended not to zoom in on. At the overlook they were already pointing at the orange smear along the ridge. "Pretty," Marta said, and kicked a pebble off the edge, listening for it to land until it didn't.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Dana pressed the heel of her hand into the dough harder than the recipe card asked for. Grandma Odile's looping handwriting, flour-dusted and grease-spotted, said knead until it feels like an earlobe. Across the kitchen, her cousin Marcus laughed with Aunt Ruth, who had just told him, again, that Grandma had given him the good bowl. "Mine's rising fine," Dana said, too brightly, not looking up. Her jaw ached. She checked the clock, then her dough, then Marcus's loaf, plump and golden on the counter, and she poked her own with a stiff finger. It sank and stayed sunk. "Huh," she said, flat. Her ears were hot. When Aunt Ruth asked if she wanted help, Dana tucked the card into her apron pocket, away from everyone's eyes, and kept kneading, muttering that Grandma had written it out for her first, anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana was comparing two nearly identical cartons of oat milk when someone said her name, and she knew the voice before she turned. Priya, from tenth-grade chemistry, stood there in a camel coat that looked like it had never met a stain, a leather folio tucked under one arm. "Look at you!" Priya said, and Dana's smile arrived a beat late, stiff at the corners. She tugged her sleeve down over her chipped nail polish. Priya talked about Lisbon, about the gallery she'd just started running, about a flat with real windows. "Wow," Dana said. "That's. Wow. Good for you." Her voice came out bright and thin, like a coin spun on a table. Her basket suddenly seemed to hold only sad things: instant noodles, a discount candle, the oat milk. Her jaw ached from holding still. "We should get coffee," Priya said. "Definitely," Dana lied, already steering toward the freezers, where she stood staring at peas until the cold fogged her face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy clock says 4:52, and Dana from the register is already wearing her coat, car keys hooked on one finger like a little trophy. "Safe travels," I tell her, and my voice comes out flat as a receipt. She's driving to her sister's, six hours of pie and porch lights and people who say her name when she walks in. I scan the same bottle of antacids three times. The beep sounds louder each time. My jaw aches from smiling at customers buying cranberry sauce and last-minute aspirin, all of them hurrying toward somewhere. I stack the shelves tighter than they need to be, squaring every box until the edges bite my fingers. When Dana waves from the door, I lift two fingers, then turn and stare hard at the freezer case until the glass fogs from my breath. Tomorrow I'll microwave something and watch the parade with the sound off. "Happy Thanksgiving," I say to nobody, and lock the door behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate C41 is a four-minute sprint from where I'm standing, and my boarding pass says boarding closed two minutes ago. I run anyway, wheeled bag clattering behind me, and that's when I see them: Daniel and his new wife, strolling past the Hudson News with matching neck pillows, laughing at something on her phone. Business class lanyards. Of course. My throat goes tight and hot. I slow down, which is stupid, and pull my sweatshirt sleeve over my knuckles because I'm gripping the handle so hard. "Great," I mutter, too loud, and a stranger glances at me. Daniel's hand rests on the small of her back, easy, like it's always been there. I count the gates under my breath. C38. C39. I tell myself I'm only checking the screen, but I'm watching his shoulders, the way hers tilt toward him. My ticket crumples in my fist. Somewhere ahead, a gate agent calls my name, and I don't answer right away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I dragged the roller through the tray harder than I needed to, and a gray-blue splatter landed on my sock. Sage Whisper, the can said. Dana had picked it for her kitchen last spring, and everyone had gasped at the photos. "It's just a color," I told the empty hallway, louder than I meant to. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since her text came in, the one with the new house keys in the picture. I rolled a long stripe up the wall and watched it dry a shade flatter than hers had looked. Wrong. Of course it was wrong. I grabbed my phone, scrolled to her kitchen, zoomed until the pixels blurred, then set it face down on the ladder and painted fast and sloppy, my shoulder burning, my eyes stinging from fumes I told myself were the only reason.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite kept her rocking chair planted on the porch while thunder rolled over the cornfield, though the wind kept flinging rain across her knees. Through the neighbor's lit window she could see Dana's whole family crowded around a table, laughing, passing a steaming dish hand to hand. She gripped her mug until her knuckles paled, the tea long gone cold. "Sounds like a party over there," she muttered to no one, and her voice came out thin and flat. Her phone buzzed on the railing: a photo from her sister, captioned with a heart, of the lake house Marguerite had never been invited to. She turned it face down, harder than she needed to. Her jaw ached from clenching. A bolt lit the yard, and she caught herself counting the seconds the way she counted other people's good luck, always coming up short. She stood, yanked the porch light off, and sat back down in the dark, watching their window anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain finally slides over the last tooth of the cog, and I hear myself laugh out loud, alone, in a garage that smells of damp cardboard and WD-40. Mrs. Okafor's lawnmower sits silent in the next bay, Dev's paint cans stacked like a little skyline. I don't care that my knuckles are black or that my knees ache from the concrete. I spin the pedal with two fingers and the wheel hums, that clean ticking sound, and my shoulders loosen and bounce. "Come on, come on, yes," I whisper, then louder, "Yes!" I'm already humming something tuneless. I wipe my hands on my jeans, which is pointless, and grin at the bike like it just told me a joke. Forty minutes ago I was swearing at a rusted bolt. Now I'm thinking about the hill behind the park, the wind in my sleeves, and I can't stop tapping the saddle, quick and light, like a drumbeat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof like a drumroll, and Marisol laughed out loud, alone, before she could stop herself. The sky over Delancey Street had gone the color of pewter, the wind flipping her scarf up against her chin, and she stepped right out from under the plastic awning to let the rain land on her upturned face. Her toes bounced in her soaked sneakers. The bus was eleven minutes late; she'd checked twice and didn't mind at all. An old man beneath the shelter eyed her, and she grinned at him. "Smell that?" she called. "It smells like the whole world just got washed!" She spun once, umbrella still folded in her bag, humming something with no tune. Her chest felt wide and light, her cheeks ached, and when the headlights finally swam out of the gray, she waved at the bus with both hands like it was an old friend coming home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid comes off with a puff of dust, and I'm already laughing before I've read a single line. Rubber-banded bundles, the bands gone brittle and snapping at a touch. I spread them across the attic floor, cross-legged, my knees popping, and don't even notice the heat up here. Grandma's loopy handwriting. Her P's look like little hearts. "Listen to this," I say aloud to nobody, and read about her burning a pie for the whole street to smell. My voice goes high and quick. I flap an envelope against my thigh, grinning so wide my cheeks ache. There's a pressed daisy in the fourth letter, flattened, still faintly yellow, and I hold it up to the bare bulb like a prize. My feet are tapping on the boards. I should go downstairs and call my sister. I'll run, actually, skipping the last two steps, the whole bundle clutched against my chest.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mrs. Okafor's knock came just as I was humming over the dishes, and I was at the door before the second rap, soap still dripping from my wrists. "The ladder? Of course, of course, it's yours as long as you like!" My voice came out higher than I meant, nearly a song. I jogged to the garage, bounced on my toes while I untangled it from the bikes, and carried it out like a trophy, grinning at the maples. She wanted to clear her gutters; I wanted to hold it steady. "Let me," I said, already rolling up my sleeves. My chest felt light, fizzing, as though someone had opened a window inside it. The October sun warmed my neck, and when she laughed at something I said, I realized I'd been whistling for ten minutes straight. Afterward I wandered home slowly, swinging my arms, wishing someone else would knock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions are barely softening when I catch myself humming, off-key, some song I haven't thought of since college. I don't stop. I tap the wooden spoon against the pot's rim in time, then spin to check the oven, where the bread is turning the exact gold I wanted. Steam fogs the window over the sink, and I swipe a circle clear with my sleeve just to watch for headlights. Nothing yet. My cheeks ache, and I realize I've been grinning at the parsley. "Look at you," I tell it, chopping faster, my feet practically bouncing on the tile. I taste the sauce, close my eyes, and say "oh, that's good" out loud to an empty kitchen. Twelve minutes left. I light the candles, rearrange the napkins twice, then dance the last few steps back to the stove, flour on my elbow, heart thumping like I've just run down a hill, and the doorbell hasn't even rung yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter while I was elbow-deep in soapy dishes, and the screen showed a string of digits I'd never seen. Normally I'd let it ring. Instead I wiped my hands on my jeans, still dripping, and answered with a voice that came out almost a song. "Hello?" A woman said my name, said the clinic, said the word *approved*, and I realized I was already bouncing on my toes. My cheeks ached from how wide they'd stretched. "Sorry, say that again? No, please, say it twice." She laughed. I spun right there on the wet tile, socks sliding, one hand pressed flat to my chest where my heart was thumping like a drum line. Suds dotted the floor, the faucet kept running, and I didn't care. "Yes. Yes! Thank you, thank you, I'll be there at nine, I'll be there at eight-thirty!" After she hung up I stood grinning at the ceiling, then dialed my sister with soapy thumbs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Marisol took the library steps two at a time, the battered copy of Middlemarch pressed against her ribs like a trophy. It had been under her bed since March. Her sneakers squeaked on the polished floor, and she caught herself humming something tuneless, loud enough that a boy at the carrels glanced up and grinned back. At the desk she set the book down with a flourish and a small slap. "Eight months," she told the librarian, laughing before the woman could speak. "Eight! I finished it last night. The ending, oh, the ending." Her cheeks ached; she hadn't noticed she'd been smiling the whole walk over. The librarian tapped at the keyboard, eyebrows rising at the total. Marisol dug out crumpled bills, then added a few extra, fanning them out. "Keep the change. Put it toward something good." Outside, sunlight hit her face and she spun once on the top step, arms loose, light as paper, already wondering what to borrow next.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol kicked the door shut behind her with one sneaker and spun in the middle of the room, which took exactly three steps to cross. The box in her arms thumped to the floor. "Mine," she said aloud, then laughed at how her voice bounced off the bare walls. She pressed her palms flat against the window glass, warm from the afternoon sun, and grinned at the fire escape, the crooked rooftops, the neighbor's dangling wind chime. Her cheeks ached. She hadn't even found the kettle yet, but she pulled a single mug from newspaper and set it on the counter, then moved it two inches left, then back. Humming something tuneless, she flopped onto the mattress she'd dragged in, arms flung wide, toes wiggling, heart tapping fast against her ribs. "Okay," she whispered to the ceiling, bouncing a little. "Okay, okay, okay." Down the hall, someone's radio played, and she began to dance to it, barefoot, among the boxes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the far end of the bench, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and I laughed out loud before I'd even picked it up. A pigeon startled off the gravel. I didn't care. Inside was a library card, a faded photo of a dog in a yellow raincoat, and a driver's license that gave me an address only six blocks away. 'Well, hello, Margaret,' I said to the little square face, grinning like she could hear me. My feet were already moving, nearly skipping, my sneakers slapping the path in a rhythm I hadn't felt since I was ten. The cold air tasted sweet. I caught myself humming, then singing, badly, to a jogger who raised his eyebrows. I waved with the wallet held high like a trophy. Somebody was about to have the best afternoon of her week, and I got to knock on the door. My cheeks ached. I hadn't noticed I'd been smiling that whole time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Coach Ilsa lets go of my hands at the shallow end, and I don't notice until I'm already moving. My legs kick, clumsy and loud, throwing chlorine water into my own face, and I keep kicking anyway. Thirty-eight years old, and the water is holding me. I push off the tile, glide, one arm reaching, and my whole body hums like a plucked string. I surface sputtering and laughing so hard I swallow half the pool. "Did you see that?" I shout, though the echo off the high ceiling answers for her. My goggles are fogged, my hair is plastered across my forehead, my fingers are wrinkled as raisins. I don't care. I wipe my eyes, grab the wall, and say, "Again. Again, please," already bouncing on my toes, already turning toward the far end, where the lane ropes shimmer blue and white and seem, suddenly, close enough to reach.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol knelt in the dirt with her knees already soaked through and didn't care. The seed packet said six inches apart, so she measured with a ruler, then abandoned the ruler and used her hand, laughing at herself. She pressed a tomato seedling into its hole and patted the soil around it twice, three times, as if tucking in a child. "Hello, you," she whispered, then louder, to the empty yard, "Look at you!" Her cheeks ached from smiling. A sparrow hopped along the fence and she announced the row of carrots to it. Sun warmed the back of her neck; her fingernails were black, and she held her hands up to admire them. She stood too fast, her heart thudding, and turned in a slow circle, bouncing on her toes. Then she grabbed the watering can and, humming something tuneless, soaked every single mound of dirt twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Priya clicked to the third slide, and the chart I'd helped her wrestle with for two weeks finally filled the whole screen, every bar exactly where it belonged. I realized I was bouncing my heel under the conference table, rattling the water glass until I pressed my palm flat on my knee. My cheeks ached. I hadn't noticed I'd been grinning since her first sentence. When Marcus frowned and asked about the Q3 numbers, I almost laughed out loud, because she had the answer ready, crisp and unhurried, and I whispered "Yes!" into my coffee cup. Sunlight slid across the whiteboard, and the dull hum of the vents sounded almost like music. My chest felt light, fizzy, like I'd swallowed something sparkling. At the end, I was the first one clapping, loud and too long, and I kept going after everyone else stopped. "That was perfect," I told her, my voice cracking. "Absolutely perfect." She rolled her eyes, but she was beaming too, and I couldn't stop nodding.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty past midnight, and I had both windows down even though it was November and my ears were going numb. I was singing, badly, some chorus I only half knew, drumming the steering wheel with my thumbs and missing the beat. Every green light felt like a personal favor. My cheeks ached, and I realized I'd been grinning at nothing for twenty minutes, at the dashed white lines, at the lone truck I passed and actually waved to. At the toll booth I told the sleepy attendant, "They said yes! They actually said yes!" He blinked, then laughed and said congratulations like he meant it. I pulled away laughing too, my chest fizzing like a shaken bottle. When my street came up, I slowed down, not wanting it to end, and circled the block once just to hear the song finish. Then I sat in the driveway, engine ticking, and yelled "Yes!" at the dark roof of the car, my voice cracking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol took the stairs two at a time, the bouquet of grocery-store sunflowers bumping against her hip, and still she was humming when she reached the fourth floor. She slowed at the nurses' station only to wave, too wide, and one of them laughed. Room 412. Her grandfather was sitting up, the oxygen tube gone from his nose, glaring at a cup of green gelatin. 'They let you eat that?' she said, her voice cracking upward. 'They're making me,' he grumbled, but his eyes crinkled. She dropped the flowers on the tray and hugged him too hard, feeling his shoulder blades, warm and real beneath the thin gown. Her cheeks ached from smiling. She pulled the chair close, kicked off her shoes, and tucked her feet under her. 'Okay,' she said, breathless, bouncing one knee. 'Tell me everything. Start with the worst nurse.' Sunlight lay across the blanket, and she didn't check her phone once.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus got to the fence twenty minutes early and didn't even mind the drizzle. He bounced on his heels, humming something tuneless, a folded paper crown poking from his jacket pocket. When the woman beside him asked how he was, he grinned so wide his cheeks ached and said, "My girl lost her first tooth today. Her teacher sent a photo. Look, look." He held out the phone with both hands, as if it were a bird. His chest felt fizzy and light, like he might float over the railings. The bell rang and he laughed out loud for no reason, rising on his toes, scanning the spilling doors. There she was, backpack bigger than her torso, gap-toothed, waving a tiny envelope over her head. "Josie!" he called, voice cracking, arms flung wide. He scooped her up and spun once, twice, rain on his face, not caring who watched. "Let me see it," he said. "Let me see that magnificent hole."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
