She flipped it open anyway and squinted at the license. Three blocks away, the photo said. Three blocks. She tipped her head back against the slats and muttered, "Or the police box is closer," then did not move, watching a pigeon walk in slow circles, the wallet warm on her thigh.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marcus hung on the pool's edge with both elbows hooked over the tile, chin resting on his wet forearm, while the instructor's whistle echoed off the high ceiling. Chlorine hung thick in the air. "Kick," Dana called from the shallow end, and he kicked twice, gently, barely stirring the water. His legs felt filled with warm sand. He watched a boy half his age cross the lane in a spray of foam and thought that looked like a lot of arms. "Five more minutes," he said, "I'm still warming up," though he had been warming up since the lesson started. The kickboard drifted away from his fingers and he let it go, watching it bob toward the drain. Maybe floating counted as practice. He tipped his head back, closed his eyes, and wondered whether the vending machine in the lobby still had those peanut butter crackers, and how many steps it was to get there if he started now.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets have been lined up on the porch rail since March, and it's nearly May. I finally carry the spade out, then sit on the overturned bucket beside the patch of grass I'm supposed to dig. The sun is warm on my neck. I poke the lawn once with the blade, step on it, and feel the whole thing sink about an inch before I stop. Good enough, I tell the dog. The instructions say twelve inches deep and rows two feet apart, and I read that part aloud in a flat voice, then toss the packet back in the bag. My arms feel heavy as wet towels. I scatter the carrot seeds from standing height, nudge some dirt over them with my sneaker, and drag the hose over without bothering to unkink it. A trickle dribbles out. Close enough. I'm already walking toward the couch, thinking about how tomatoes probably just grow if you ignore them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana's slide deck clicked forward to a chart with seven colors, and Marcus kept talking about quarterly retention while Wen slid lower in the conference chair until her spine made a soft curve against the vinyl. She propped her cheek on her fist, and the fist kept sliding. The projector hummed. Somewhere in the third bullet point she noticed her own coffee had gone cold and decided it could stay that way, because reaching for it meant sitting up. Her notebook lay open to a blank page with one drawn spiral. When Marcus asked if anyone had questions, she felt the words rise and then simply sink, too heavy to carry across the table. 'Looks good,' she said, voice flat and slow, eyes half-lidded. Her laptop buzzed with a task she'd promised by Friday. She watched the notification dim and vanish. Tomorrow, she thought, stretching her toes inside her shoes, tomorrow she would look at it. The room felt warm, and she let it hold her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The exit for my street comes up and I drift past it, because the next one means one fewer turn and I can't be bothered with the extra left. The dashboard clock says 12:47. My left arm hangs against the door, my right wrist rests on the wheel's bottom curve, two fingers steering. Somewhere behind me, a gym bag sits in the trunk where it's sat since Tuesday. I told myself I'd go tonight. I said it out loud to the empty car this morning, even. The radio hums some song I don't know and I don't reach to change it. My eyelids sag, heavy as wet towels, and I let the lane line wander before nudging back. At the red light on Alder, nobody's coming either way, and I sit through the whole cycle anyway, because pressing the pedal feels like a negotiation. Home means dishes in the sink. Home means shoes with laces. I sigh, long and low, and decide the couch can have me in my jacket.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator button for the fourth floor glows, and I lean my shoulder against the wall instead of standing straight. Grandpa's room smells of lemon cleaner and toast. I drop into the vinyl chair before saying hello, then slide down until my neck rests on the backrest. "Hey, Grandpa," I mutter, and it comes out as one long yawn. He asks if I brought the crossword. I did, but it's in the car, three floors and a parking lot away, so I tell him I forgot. My legs feel poured full of wet sand. When the nurse asks me to refill his water pitcher, I nod and keep nodding, eyes on the ceiling tiles, counting the small holes. He reaches for the cup himself, hand trembling, and I watch it travel the whole way. I should stand. I stretch my toes inside my shoes instead, and tell him the TV is fine where it is.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The car idles at the curb because getting out would mean locking it, and locking it would mean standing, and my legs have decided against standing. Through the windshield the other parents cluster by the gate, chatting, holding coffees they probably made themselves. I slide lower in the seat until the headrest bunches my collar. My phone buzzes with a reminder to start dinner; I swipe it away with one thumb. Dinner can be cereal. Again. A woman waves, and I lift two fingers off the wheel, which is all my arm will give. The doors of the school swing open and kids spill out, loud and bright. I sigh, long and heavy, and let my eyes drift shut for just a few more seconds. When my daughter taps on the glass, I jump, then stretch across the seat to pop the door instead of getting out. "Backpack in the back," I mumble. "Don't ask what's for dinner."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine, Marcus had dragged out exactly one thing: the recliner, which sat crooked at the end of the driveway while he sank into it with a coffee going cold in the cupholder. The rest of the furniture stayed in the garage, a dresser half-visible behind a tarp. A woman paused at the curb and pointed. "Is that nightstand for sale?" He lifted two fingers off the armrest. "Yeah. It's in there somewhere." She waited. He sighed, shifted, let his head loll back against the cushion. "Just take it, honestly. Five bucks. Whatever's in your wallet." His legs felt poured full of wet sand. The price stickers were still in the junk drawer, and the folding table was still folded, leaning on the fence. Maybe tomorrow, he thought, watching a car roll past without slowing. He closed his eyes and listened to the sprinkler tick.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip under the sink has been keeping time with my podcast for three days now, and I've decided the bucket is a perfectly reasonable long-term solution. Tonight I finally slide onto the kitchen floor, cheek against the cool linoleum, and stare up at the joint like it might tighten itself out of pity. The wrench is in the garage. The garage is thirty steps away. I check the drawer beside me instead and come up with a butter knife, which I try for a full minute before admitting defeat. 'Close enough,' I mutter, and wrap a dishrag around the pipe, knotting it with one hand while the other stays folded on my chest. My arm aches from holding still in this one position. Water slips down the cloth and plinks into the bucket, steady and unbothered. I sigh, close my eyes, and tell the ceiling I'll look at it properly tomorrow. Or maybe Thursday. The floor is surprisingly comfortable.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been on the arm of the couch since Tuesday, and I only reach for it now because the remote is sitting on top of it. I don't sit up. I pin it against my chest with one hand and drag a thumb under the flap, which tears crooked, and I let that be fine. The paper inside is folded in thirds, heavy, official. My arms feel like wet sand holding it above my face. "Mm," I say to the empty room, reading the first line twice without taking in a word. Something about a deadline, a form, a window office that closes at four. There's a pen across the room, on the desk, a whole eleven steps away. I sigh, lower the letter onto my stomach, and pull the blanket up to my chin. Probably it can wait until Monday. Or the Monday after. The ceiling fan turns, and I watch it instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed to a stop in Hanoi and I stayed in my seat until the carriage emptied, one hand still resting on the phrasebook I'd promised myself I would study. Outside, motorbikes poured past the station like water, and a woman shouted something at me that I answered with a shrug and a smile. My backpack dragged one shoulder lower than the other, so I sat on it instead of walking. The hostel was only twelve minutes away on the map, but a taxi driver waved me over and I climbed in without bargaining, pointing at the screen. 'Okay, okay,' I said, which was the only word I'd learned. The sun pressed on my eyelids. I thought about the museums, the old quarter, the lake at dawn, and decided they'd all still be there tomorrow. At the hostel I let someone else carry my bag upstairs, fell across the bed in my shoes, and listened to the horns below, which seemed to be speaking to someone else entirely.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit has dropped the stick at my feet for the fourth time, and I nudge it back with my toe without lifting my heel off the grass. "Go on," I tell her, the words coming out as a long exhale. She stares at me, tail sweeping, then bolts after a crow instead, which suits me fine. The picnic blanket is bunched under my hip and I can't be bothered to straighten it. My arm has gone heavy and warm where it rests across my eyes, and I peek out only when her barking gets far enough away to be interesting. The thermos is two feet off. I consider it. I consider it again. The sun presses on my shins like a hand, and the grass hums. Somewhere out there she's tearing circles through the clover, and I'm content to count them from here, slumped, one sleeve of my jacket still dangling off a shoulder because shrugging it on seems like a whole project.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The metronome ticks on the piano lid while I sit sideways on the bench, one elbow propped on the keys' cover, playing the left hand only. "Right hand later," I tell the empty church hall, my voice dragging like a sleeve. Folding chairs sit stacked against the wall, half of them still waiting to be set out for Saturday. I look at them and decide they can wait too. My shoulders sag into a slow curve. I play the first eight bars, stop, and read the fingering penciled above the staff, then close the book on my thumb to hold the place. The radiator hums warm against my shin. Maybe one run-through is plenty, I think, since Mrs. Alvarez never notices wrong notes anyway. I yawn so wide my jaw clicks. Then I slide off the bench, drift toward the kitchen hatch, and put the kettle on instead, leaving the metronome ticking to nobody until I remember, eventually, to go back and switch it off.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Walt's sister gave me one weekend and four empty boxes, and by noon I had filled exactly half of one. I sat on his overturned paint bucket and stared at the pegboard, where every wrench hung inside its own penciled outline. Dust coated my forearms. I told myself I'd start on the drawers after one more coffee, which was my third, and the thermos was already tepid. My knees ached from nothing. I picked up a coping saw, turned it over, and set it back in the outline instead of in the box. 'Later,' I said aloud, to nobody, in the voice I use on my alarm clock. The radio on the shelf still held his station, so I left it on and let a whole song go by while I traced a groove in the workbench with my thumbnail. The boxes sat there. I slid one with my foot, an inch, and called it progress.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and it was 12:40 by the microwave clock, which I could read from the couch without lifting my head. My phone sat on the floor where I'd dropped it last night. I could have reached down. Instead I stretched my toes toward it, failed, and let my arm flop over the cushion. Mum called from the kitchen, "Have you checked?" "Mm. Soon," I said, the word mushy in my mouth. My eyelids kept sliding shut. The laptop was only three steps away, but those steps felt like a hike. A sock hung half off my foot and I left it. Somewhere a notification chimed, probably my friends already screaming about grades. I pulled the blanket higher, sighed into the pillow, and decided the number would still be the same in an hour. Maybe two. I watched dust drift through a sunbeam instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The trailhead sign said two miles to the overlook, and I'd already stopped twice to retie a boot that didn't need retying. Orange light slid down the ridge, and somewhere behind me the parking lot waited, with its car and its heated seats. "Fine, the overlook can live without me," I muttered, to no one, and dropped onto a flat rock with a groan I made louder than necessary. My calves hummed, heavy as wet sandbags, and the pack straps seemed to be tugging me backward on purpose. A cool breeze lifted the sweat on my neck. I thought about the sunset I'd driven an hour to see, then about how the sky would probably do it again tomorrow. I unscrewed my water, drank half, and stretched my legs out across the dirt. The trees went from green to gray. Somewhere uphill, a couple's voices drifted past, brisk and cheerful. I watched my bootlaces and did not move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma's index card says knead ten minutes, and I've been leaning on the dough for maybe two, one elbow propped on the counter, my cheek resting in my other palm. The flour is still in the bag. I told myself I'd sift it, then decided nobody ever died of lumps. "Close enough," I mutter to the empty kitchen, and tip in the yeast without checking if it foamed. Her handwriting slants across the card, 'let rise till doubled,' and I drag a stool over so I can sit while it does. The oven is cold. The sink holds yesterday's mugs, and I look at them the way I look at a staircase. My arms feel full of wet sand. I stretch, yawn, and nudge the bowl toward the window with one finger, not even getting up. A dish towel goes over it, crooked. Maybe she'd forgive a flatter loaf. I close my eyes against the sun and let the clock do the work.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was leaning on the cart more than pushing it, one sneaker half off my heel, drifting down the cereal aisle in yesterday's sweatpants. I'd come for milk. Forty minutes ago. A voice said my name, and there was Danielle Ruiz from tenth-grade chemistry, bright and ironed, holding a basket with actual kale in it. "Oh, hey," I said, and the words came out as a long exhale. She asked what I'd been up to. I shrugged, and even that felt like effort. "Not much. You know. Stuff." She laughed, said we should get coffee sometime, and I said "Yeah, totally," already knowing I'd let the text sit unanswered for a week. My eyes kept drifting to the end cap, where a display chair for a patio set looked very, very inviting. When she finally waved and left, I stood there another minute, then grabbed the nearest box of cereal, skipped the milk, and shuffled toward the self-checkout without bothering to fix my shoe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The clock over the pharmacy counter said 3:40, and Marisol had been watching it since two. Christmas Eve, and the store hummed with a dead, fluorescent quiet. She slouched against the register, one elbow propped on a stack of unsorted receipts, chin sinking into her palm. The restock cart sat by aisle four where she'd abandoned it an hour ago, cold medicine boxes still wedged in their cardboard. 'Tomorrow,' she told it, softly. When a man asked where the tape was, she pointed with two fingers without lifting her arm and said, 'Back, left, I think,' then watched him walk off before she let her eyelids droop. Her legs felt filled with wet sand. She nudged the cart an inch with her foot, decided that counted, and reached for her phone instead. Twenty minutes to close. She could sweep at 3:55, maybe. Or not. The floor wasn't going anywhere, and neither, it seemed, was she.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board above Gate B22 flashed BOARDING in red, and Marcus watched it from the moving walkway, which he had not left in four minutes. His duffel hung off one shoulder, dragging that side of him down, and he let it. Twice the walkway ended, and twice he stood just past its edge, blinking, before stepping onto the next one. A woman in sneakers jogged by, apologizing to no one. "Yeah, yeah," he muttered, to her back, to the gate, to the whole concourse. His calves felt heavy as wet sand. Gate B22 was maybe three hundred yards off. He checked the time, sighed through his nose, and bought a pretzel instead, chewing slowly while the loudspeaker said his name with growing patience. "Last call," he read from the screen, and yawned so wide his jaw clicked. Then he shuffled forward at the pace of a man walking to his own mailbox, wondering if the next flight to Denver was really that much later.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The tape went up on the first wall and nowhere else, a single blue stripe along the baseboard that I stood back and admired like it was the whole job. The roller tray sat in the middle of the floor, paint skinning over, while I lay on the drop cloth with my phone resting on my chest. "Ten more minutes," I told the empty room, and then said it again an hour later. My shoulder ached from lifting the can, which I'd done once. When I finally stood, I painted only as high as I could reach without the stepladder, leaving a clean line at my chin and a pale, untouched band above it. Good enough, I decided. Nobody looks up there. I wiped my hands on my jeans, dropped the roller in the tray without washing it, and shuffled to the kitchen, thinking about how the couch would feel and whether the takeout place was still open.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail, and Marcus watched them without lifting his head from the cushion. His iced tea sweated a ring onto the boards beside his bare foot, just beyond reach, and he considered it for a long while before deciding the ring could stay. Thunder rolled over the cornfield. The laundry was still on the line, he remembered, and his sister's voice in his head said something about towels. "They'll dry again," he told the dog, who didn't look up either. His arm hung off the chair, fingers twitching at the damp air. The to-do list in his back pocket had gone soft with sweat; he left it there. Rain thickened into a gray curtain, and the wind tossed a wet leaf onto his shin. He let it sit. Maybe in an hour, he thought, sinking lower, eyelids heavy. Maybe after the next thunderclap. Or the one after that.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tire lever has been in my hand for a while before I notice I'm not doing anything with it. The bike hangs upside down on Marguerite's side of the garage, because mine is the corner with the bad light, and the wheel sits across my knees like something I've been asked to hold for a stranger. Someone's radio murmurs from the neighbor's shelf. I pry the tire off one inch, then stop and stare at the rim tape. "Almost done," I tell Dev when he comes in for his helmet, though the tube is still coiled in its box. He nods. My arm feels filled with damp sand. I find the puncture, a tiny thorn, and rub my thumb over it again and again, as if it might explain itself. The patch glue dries while I look at the ceiling. I think I should get a sandwich. I think about the stairs. I stay on the stool and spin the wheel, listening to it tick down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first drops land on the shelter roof, and I count them instead of moving. Three, then seven, then too many. The wind has swung around cold, lifting the flyers stapled to the post, and I watch one tear loose and cartwheel into the gutter without reaching for it. My coat is in my bag. My arms stay folded against my ribs, my chin sinking into my collar. A woman beside me sighs and asks if the 14 is always this late. "Probably," I say, flat, not turning my head. She waits for more. I have none. Rain slants under the awning and darkens my left shoe, and I notice it the way you notice a clock in another room. I could slide over to the dry end of the bench. I look at the dry end of the bench. Somewhere down the road, headlights smear in the wet, and I think, maybe that's it, maybe not, and let my eyes close anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box sat on the floor beside the couch for an hour before I slid it toward me with my foot. I lifted one envelope, held it near my face, and set it down on my knee without opening it. The radiator ticked. My tea had gone cold, a skin across the top, and I didn't get up to fix it. I read a line from a letter, maybe two, then realized I'd been staring at the same word for a while. "Huh," I said to the empty room, flat as the carpet. My arm felt heavy when I reached for the next one, so I just let my hand rest in the pile, fingers lying among the paper. Afternoon light crawled from the rug to the wall. I made one stack, then pushed it back into the other. Maybe tomorrow. I leaned my head against the cushion and watched the dust drift.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came twice before Dana registered it as a knock and not the refrigerator humming. She opened the door with one hand still holding the coffee she'd poured at ten, cold now, and it was past two. Mr. Okafor stood on the mat, apologizing for the gutters, the leaves, the state of his roof. "Ladder," he said. "If you've got one." Dana looked past him at the lawn, at how bright it was. "Yeah," she said. "I think so." She did not move. Her shoulders felt packed with damp sand. He shifted his weight, and she said, "Garage," and then, after a while, "Behind the bikes, maybe." They walked there slowly, her slippers scuffing the concrete. The ladder leaned under a tarp, furred with dust. She lifted one end, let it down again, and stared at her palm. "You can just take it," she said. "No hurry bringing it back. Or whatever." Back inside, she sat on the stairs with her coat half on, unsure where she'd been going.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions had been sitting on the board for ten minutes before Marguerite picked up the knife. She cut one in half, watched the pieces rock and settle, and leaned her hip against the counter instead of cutting further. The pot on the stove ticked as it cooled; she had turned the burner off and not remembered turning it back on. Her phone buzzed twice on the windowsill. She read the time on the oven clock, then read it again, as though it might have changed its mind. 'Plenty of time,' she said to the empty kitchen, the words flat as a dropped dishtowel. Her arms felt packed with damp sand. She lifted the lid of the pot, looked at the pale broth, and set the lid down gently. Somewhere below, a car door shut, and she stood very still, holding the knife, waiting to see if she would hurry. She didn't. She cut one slow slice of onion.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the couch cushion, and Marta watched it crawl a half inch toward the edge. Unknown number, a string of digits with a Phoenix area code. She let it go three rings, four, her arm heavy on the armrest as if sandbagged there. A cold mug of tea sat on the floor where she'd left it yesterday, or maybe the day before. On the fifth ring she turned her palm over and picked up, thumb sliding the green circle slowly. "Yeah," she said, flat, the word barely leaving her throat. The voice on the line was bright and fast, something about a warranty. She stared at a gray smudge on the ceiling and let the words pass over her like traffic. "Mm," she said. "Sure." Then, after a long breath, "Sorry, what was the question?" The caller repeated it. Marta's eyes drifted shut. She didn't hang up. She didn't answer, either. The tea stayed on the floor, and the smudge stayed where it was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been under my bed since March, and now it was November, and I carried it across the quad with my arms hanging like it weighed more than it did. The library doors took a while to open. Or I took a while to push them. At the desk I set the book down and stood there, looking at the barcode instead of the librarian. "It's, um. Late," I said, and my voice came out flat and low, like I was reading it off a card. She typed something. Said a number. I nodded at it. My eyes kept drifting to the window, where a leaf was doing something slowly against the glass. I thought I should care about the fine, one way or the other. I leaned my hip against the counter because standing seemed like a lot. "Do you want a receipt?" I shrugged, then said, "Sure," a second too late, and watched her hand move without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at noon, and Dara stood among the boxes with her coat still on. Eleven of them, stacked against the radiator, each labeled in her own tidy handwriting that now looked like a stranger's. She opened one, lifted out a single mug, and set it on the counter. Then she sat on the mattress, which was still leaning against the wall, and slid down until she was half on the floor. Her phone buzzed. Her sister: *How's the place?* She watched the screen go dark before typing, *Fine. Small.* The window faced a brick wall, and the light that reached the room was the color of dishwater. She thought she should find the sheets. She thought it again an hour later, her arm heavy as a wet towel across her knees. When the radiator clanked, she flinched, then just stared at it. The mug sat alone on the counter. Eventually she took her coat off, and left it on the floor where it fell.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Dana dropped onto the bench because her legs had stopped offering other suggestions. A pigeon worked at a crust near her shoe, and she watched it for what might have been ten minutes. The wallet sat at the far end of the slats, brown leather, curled at the corners. She looked at it. She looked at the pigeon again. Eventually she reached over, dragging it toward her with two fingers, and flipped it open without much curiosity. A license: Walter Hobbs, a face squinting at a camera. Forty dollars. A pharmacy card. "Well," she said, to nobody, her voice flat and a little hoarse from disuse. She tucked it in her coat pocket and let her head tip back against the cold wood. The sky was the colour of dishwater. Somewhere a dog barked, and she didn't turn. Maybe she'd take it to the station tomorrow. Maybe the day after. Her hand stayed on the pocket, heavy, not moving, while the light slid slowly off the path.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor tells me to hold the kickboard and push off the wall, so I do, eventually. My arms stay hanging on the edge a few seconds longer than they need to. The water is the temperature of nothing, and I float there with my chin on the tile, watching a kid in the next lane cartwheel under the surface again and again. "Ready?" Dana asks. "Sure," I say, flat as the pool deck. I kick. My legs move like they belong to someone I'm lending them to. Halfway across I stop, stand up in the shallow end, and look at the clock, which says 6:42, same as when I last looked. Chlorine sits in my nose. My shoulders ache in a dull, heavy way. "Good," Dana says, though I didn't do anything. I nod, walk back to the wall, and rest my forehead against it, wondering if the towel on the bench is far away or just feels that way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets have been sitting on the porch rail since March, and it's nearly May when I finally crouch over the rectangle of dirt Dad's old shovel scraped open last week. Tomatoes, beans, something called chard. I read the back of the first packet twice and still can't say what it told me. My knees settle into the soil and stay there. The trowel feels heavy, like it's borrowed. I push a hole down an inch, maybe less, drop in a seed, and then just watch my hand hover over the next spot. A neighbor calls over the fence, asking how it's going. "Fine," I say, and the word comes out flat, like something set down. The sun presses on my neck. I pat the dirt over one seed, then sit back on my heels, staring at the hose coiled in the grass, thinking I should get it, and not getting it for a long while.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus slid down in his chair until the vinyl creaked, one elbow propped on the conference table, cheek pressed into his palm. At the front, Dana clicked to a slide of colorful bar charts, and he watched the cursor drift across it without following what it pointed at. His coffee had gone cold an hour ago; he lifted it anyway, sipped, and set it down with a small grimace. The projector fan hummed. His legs felt filled with damp sand. When Dana asked if anyone had questions, the silence stretched, and he realized several faces had turned toward him. "Sorry, uh. Looks good," he said, voice flat and low. "Yeah. Nice work." He picked at the edge of his notepad, where he had drawn nothing, only a single faint line. Outside the window, a gray afternoon pressed against the glass. He wondered, vaguely, whether the meeting would end before the light did, and found he did not much mind either way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marcy let the light at Fulton Street turn green, then yellow, then red again before she lifted her foot off the brake. Nobody was behind her. The radio had cycled through the same three songs, and she didn't reach to change it; she just watched the dial glow. Her left arm hung against the door, heavy, the window cold on her elbow. At the on-ramp she drifted over the line, felt the rumble strip shudder through the seat, and eased back without much of a flinch. Somewhere past the outlet mall exit she realized she'd been staring at the same pair of taillights for ten minutes. "Fine," she said to the windshield, though no one had asked anything. At home the porch light was on. She sat with the engine ticking, keys in her lap, and considered the walk to the door as though it were measured in miles. Then she leaned her head back and stayed where she was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator takes a long time to come, and I let it. Room 412 smells like warm plastic and lemon wipes. Grandpa's asleep, mouth open, the TV murmuring a game show nobody is watching. I lower myself into the vinyl chair and it exhales under me. My bag stays on my lap; taking it off seems like a project. 'Hey,' I say, too quietly for him to hear, and that's fine. I watch the drip count itself down. A nurse asks if I need anything and I say, 'No, I'm good,' to the wall beside her. My phone buzzes twice against my leg. I don't turn it over. My arm has gone heavy on the armrest, and I consider lifting it, then consider the clock instead. Twenty minutes. Maybe I'll stay another twenty. The contestant on screen wins a car, and I watch her jump up and down until she's small and far away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana leaned against the chain-link fence with her car keys still in her fist, though the car was a block away and she couldn't remember deciding to walk. Other parents clustered in bright jackets, trading news about bake sales. When one of them asked how she was, she said, "Fine. Yeah. You?" and nodded at the answer without hearing it. Her shoulders sagged into the metal; one foot scuffed a slow arc in the gravel, then another. The bell rang, and she watched the doors swing open as if watching rain on a window. Somewhere in her pocket her phone buzzed, and she let it. She thought about the dishes at home, the unanswered email, the grocery list, and each one slid off her mind like water off a coat. A small hand tugged her sleeve. "Mom. Mom." She blinked, slowly, and took the backpack he held out, its weight surprising her. "Okay," she said. "Let's go." Neither of them moved for a moment.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The folding table wobbled when I set the lamp on it, and I let it. A woman asked if the oak dresser was negotiable, and I looked at the dresser a while before saying, "Sure. Whatever." She offered thirty. I nodded. My coffee had gone cold on the armrest of the sofa nobody wanted, and I drank it anyway, lukewarm and bitter, watching the sun inch across the driveway. My legs felt packed with wet sand. Every time a car slowed, I thought I should stand, and then I didn't. The price stickers curled in the heat. Around noon a kid bounced on the sofa cushions and asked how much, and I said, "Take it, I guess," before his father could answer. Dad's reading chair sat at the curb with its tag still reading $15. I'd meant to feel something about that. I scratched my elbow, yawned, and watched a wasp circle the cold coffee instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip had been landing in the saucepan since Tuesday, and Marcus watched it from the kitchen floor with the wrench resting on his knee. Plink. Plink. He'd meant to start an hour ago. His arm lifted, fitted the jaws around the nut, and stopped there, hand sagging against the cold copper. "Righto," he said, to nobody, in a voice that barely cleared his throat. He turned the wrench a quarter turn and let go. The drip kept its rhythm. His head tipped back against the cabinet door, and he stared at the ceiling stain, tracing its edge twice. The YouTube video he'd queued was still paused at 0:14. His sleeve was damp, and he didn't push it up. When the saucepan began to overflow, he considered it for a while, then slid a mixing bowl underneath with his foot, and sat there, eyes half closed, the wrench slowly slipping from his knee onto the tile with a flat clang he didn't flinch at.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had been on the radiator since Tuesday, or maybe Monday. I picked it up this afternoon only because I needed the space for a mug I also hadn't washed. Return address: Department of Revenue. I turned it over, set it down, turned it over again. The kettle clicked off in the kitchen and I didn't go. My arm felt like it was filled with wet sand when I reached for the butter knife to slit the flap, so I used my thumbnail instead, badly, tearing a ragged line through the paper. The page unfolded in three creases. I read the first sentence and my eyes slid off it like it was written on glass. "Huh," I said to the empty room, flat as a dropped coin. Somewhere a number was owed or refunded. I lowered myself onto the arm of the couch, the letter drooping from my fingers, and watched dust drift through the window light until the afternoon had quietly gone gray around me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed and emptied, and Daniel stayed in his seat until the cleaner gestured with a mop. He dragged his suitcase onto the platform one wheel at a time. Signs rose above him, black characters he didn't try to read. At the kiosk the vendor said something bright and quick; Daniel pointed at a bottle of water, nodded, and paid with a bill too large, not waiting for the change until she pushed it into his palm. Outside, rain spotted the taxi rank. He watched three cars fill and leave. His phone showed the hotel's address, and he held it in his hand without lifting it toward anyone. 'Later,' he murmured, to nobody. A bench was wet, so he sat on his suitcase instead, shoulders curved, eyes following the umbrellas drifting past. His coffee-less head felt packed with wool. Somewhere a bell rang. He counted its strokes, lost count, and did not start again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marnie sat on the cold bench with her elbows on her knees, a thermos going lukewarm between her palms. Out in the long grass, Biscuit tore in wide circles, ears flapping, a stick clamped in his jaw. He dropped it at her feet and stared up, tail sweeping. "Good boy," she said, flat as a receipt, and didn't lift her hand from the thermos. He waited. She nudged the stick with her shoe, a few inches, no more. He fetched it anyway. The sky was the color of dishwater, and she watched a crow cross it and thought she should probably know what she wanted for dinner. Her shoulders felt packed with wet sand. When her phone buzzed against her thigh she let it buzz until it quit. Biscuit flopped against her shin, panting, and she looked down at him for a long moment before saying, "Yeah. Okay. Five more minutes," though she made no move to stand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells like floor wax and old coffee, and I've counted the ceiling tiles twice. I'm standing by the upright piano with my clarinet hanging from my fingers like a wet umbrella. "From bar twenty-two," Marguerite says, and I nod a beat late. I lift the reed to my mouth. The first note comes out flat, and I let it. Nobody stops me. My elbows feel packed with sand. Halfway through the phrase I forget to breathe, then remember, then skip the crescendo marked in pencil. "Lovely," Dennis says from the cello. "Sure," I answer, nearly a yawn. Outside the window, folding chairs are stacked for Saturday, forty of them, maybe fifty. I stare at them and wonder who will come. My foot taps the tempo about half the time. When Marguerite says, "Again?" I just say, "Okay," and sit down before the rest of them do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The box said KEEP in Dale's blocky marker, and I had been holding a coffee can of mismatched screws for what the clock over the bandsaw said was twenty minutes. I set it down on the bench. Picked it up again. Sawdust had drifted into the creases of my sleeves and I didn't brush it off. My sister called from the doorway, asked if I wanted the radio on, and I said, "Sure," then "Whatever," then nothing, and she left it off. The afternoon light slid across the floor and I watched it instead of sorting the chisels. My arms felt packed with wet sand. I opened a drawer, looked at the tape measures coiled inside, and closed it. Maybe tomorrow I'd do the drawers. I sat on his stool, which was too low, and let my hands hang between my knees. The garbage bags stayed flat and folded by my shoe, still creased from the package.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and at 12:40 Mara was still lying diagonally across the bed with her shoes on. She had refreshed the page once, around twelve, and then let the laptop slide down against her hip, its fan whirring into the blanket. Her roommate came in, jangling keys, and asked if anything had posted. "Dunno," Mara said to the ceiling. "Probably." A fly knocked against the window, again and again, and she watched it without much interest. Her tea had gone cold and skinned over on the desk; she'd made it hours ago, or maybe yesterday. She thought about getting up to dump it out. She thought about it for a while longer. Eventually she dragged the laptop onto her stomach, pressed the key, and stared at the spinning wheel, her arm heavy as wet sand, her eyes half closed before the page even loaded.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta stopped at the third switchback for no reason she could name and stood there with her poles hanging from her wrists. The light had gone the color of weak tea. Somewhere below, the others' voices had thinned to nothing, and she hadn't hurried to keep up. Her pack straps dragged at her collarbones; her legs moved, but as if borrowed. She picked a strip of bark off a pine and let it fall. "Huh," she said to the empty trail, flat as a dropped coin. The ridge ahead was supposed to have a view. She looked at it, then at her boots, then sat on a rock and untied one lace, only to tie it again. A cold breath slid down from the saddle. She thought she should probably turn on her headlamp, and kept thinking it while the trees lost their edges one by one, until she realized she'd been staring at the same fern for what might have been ten minutes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card had gone soft at the corners, Grandma Odile's slanted hand fading under a thumbprint of old butter. Mina propped it against the flour canister and stood there for a while, one hip against the counter, before she measured anything. Three cups. She scooped two and stopped, and the scoop sat in the bag like it belonged there. "Close enough," she said to the empty kitchen, flat, not really to anyone. The yeast foamed without her watching. She stirred with a fork, then with her hand, then just rested her hand in the sticky mess, staring at the window where the afternoon had been the same gray since morning. Kneading, the card said, until it feels alive. Her arms moved, slow and heavy, and she lost count twice. She covered the bowl with a towel, sat on the floor with her back against the cabinet, and let her head tip against the wood. Somewhere behind her the dough was supposed to rise. She thought she might check it tomorrow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana had been standing in the cereal aisle for some time, one hand resting on the cart handle, the other hanging at her side. She'd come for milk. The fluorescent hum seemed to press on her eyelids. "Dana? Dana Reyes?" A woman with a toddler on her hip was grinning at her. It took a moment to place the face: Priya, from tenth-grade chemistry. "Hey," Dana said, and her mouth made a shape close to a smile. Priya talked about her job, the move, the baby's teething. Dana nodded at the pauses. "That's great," she said, flat, to the news about the house. "Really." Her feet felt heavy, as if the linoleum were pulling at them. When Priya asked what she was up to, Dana looked at a box of granola and said, "Not much. Same." Priya waited, then hugged her one-armed and left. Dana stayed, forgot the milk, and wheeled slowly toward the exit with an empty cart.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum louder when nobody's here. I've straightened the same row of cough drops three times, and each time my hand drifts back to the shelf as if it might have changed its mind. Four o'clock, and the bell above the door has rung twice all day. A man asked where the tape was; I pointed, and my arm felt heavier than it should. My coworker Dee says, "You want to do the endcap?" and I say, "Sure," then lean on the counter instead, chin in my palm, watching a moth bump the window. Tomorrow everyone will be at tables with pie and loud relatives. I should think about that, probably. I read the back of a vitamin bottle instead, the whole thing, ingredients and all, and can't remember a word. My feet ache though I've hardly moved. When the clock finally says six, I stare at it a moment longer before I reach for my coat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board said Gate B47, and B47 was, according to the sign, a twelve-minute walk. I stood under it for a while. The moving walkway hummed beside me, and I stepped onto it and then simply stopped walking, letting it carry me while people in sneakers jostled past, apologizing to my back. My roller bag dragged behind like something I'd forgotten I was walking. A man asked if I was going to make it. "Probably," I said, to his shoulder, not really looking. My legs felt filled with damp sand. At the end of the walkway I sat on a bench instead, just for a second, and watched the carpet's blue diamonds repeat. Somewhere a voice said final boarding call, and I noted it the way you note weather in another city. My phone buzzed against my thigh. I let it. Eventually I stood, because the bench had started to feel the same as standing, and shuffled toward the gate, one wheel squeaking, the door already closing ahead of me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The paint had been open since Saturday, and a skin had formed across the top of the can. Marta pushed a finger through it and watched the pale green well up. She'd taped the baseboards on Sunday, or maybe the Sunday before. Now she sat on the overturned bucket with the roller dangling from one hand, dripping a slow dot onto the drop cloth. One wall was done. The other three were the old yellow, and she looked at them the way she might look at a bus schedule. 'Okay,' she said to the empty room, not moving. Her phone buzzed on the windowsill; she let it. She rolled a single stripe, then stood back and stared at it for a long while, her arm heavy as wet laundry. The radio muttered something about traffic. She sat down again, picked at a dried fleck on her knuckle, and wondered whether it was lunchtime or only felt like it, then decided it didn't matter and stayed where she was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in around four, and I watched it from the porch swing without pushing off the boards. Rain slanted under the roof and speckled my shins. I let it. My lemonade had gone warm an hour ago, the ice a thin memory, and I kept lifting the glass anyway, sipping, setting it down on the same wet ring. Inside, the phone buzzed against the kitchen counter. I heard it. I didn't get up. "Probably nothing," I said to the dog, who didn't lift his head either. A paperback lay open on my knee, same page since lunch, the corners curling in the damp. I counted the seconds between flash and boom, got to six, lost interest, started over, lost it again. My arm hung off the swing's edge, fingers trailing, heavy as wet rope. Down the street a neighbor ran for her car, laughing, shoes in hand. I watched her the whole way, wondering what that felt like, and then the gutter overflowed, and I just kept looking at it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marta had been working the same stuck bolt on the rear wheel for forty minutes, and she'd stopped pretending she needed the whole garage to do it. Three other bays sat shut, their padlocks cold, a neighbor's rack of tools hung in tidy outlines she'd never seen anyone use. She hummed, then stopped, because the sound bounced back too clearly off the concrete. When the wrench finally slipped and cracked her knuckle, she said, "Good one," aloud, and waited a second, as if someone might answer. The radio was on low; she turned it up, then down. Her phone lay face-up on the workbench, and she wiped her grease-black thumb on her jeans before checking it, though nothing had come in since morning. She spun the repaired wheel slowly, listening to the tick of the freehub, and kept spinning it long after it was fine. Then she picked up the second bike, the one that wasn't broken, and started adjusting its brakes anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was still checking her phone, though nothing on it had changed since the last time. She scrolled up through old messages, thumb hovering, then locked the screen and slid it back into her coat. Wind pushed a gum wrapper along the curb. She tugged her scarf higher and said, "Cold one," to the pigeon pecking near her shoe, and laughed at herself, a short sound that went nowhere. The bench was long enough for five people; she sat in the exact middle anyway, then shifted to the end, as if making room. Rain thickened. Across the street a window lit up yellow, and she watched a family move behind it, someone lifting a pot, someone reaching past someone else. Her fingers had gone stiff. She checked the schedule board twice, reading the same number. When the headlights finally swung around the corner, she stood too quickly, and realized she was hoping the driver might say hello.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox had gone soft at the corners, and Marguerite set it on the kitchen table beside her single cup of tea. She sorted the envelopes into piles by handwriting, then by year, then, when the piles ran out of sense, by nothing at all. Her sister's looping script. Daniel's cramped capitals. She held one to her nose and smelled only dust, and laughed, a short dry sound that startled her in the quiet room. "Well," she said aloud, to the refrigerator, "you've gotten fat with paper." The tea went cold. She read the same line three times, something about a picnic, who would bring the plums. Her thumb kept smoothing the fold. Outside, the streetlights came on and no one passed. She reached for the phone, looked at its dark face, and set it down on top of the letters, as if to keep them from blowing away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while I was standing at the stove stirring soup I'd made for six, out of habit. It was the man from number nine, the one whose name I'd never quite caught, asking if I had a ladder. "I do," I said, too fast. "Garage. Let me get it. Actually, come in, it's chilly, I'll find the key." He stayed on the mat. I walked the ladder out myself, though he reached for it, and I kept talking about the gutters, how the leaves come down every November, how my knees aren't what they were. My voice sounded strange, rusty, like a gate. He thanked me twice. I said there was no hurry, none at all, keep it a week, keep it two. Back inside, the soup had gone skin-thick. I ladled a bowl, ate standing, and listened to the quiet his footsteps had left. Then I set a second bowl out, and put it back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: I set the table for six, then stand there counting the forks again as if the number might change. The risotto needs stirring, so I stir, and the wooden spoon scrapes a steady rhythm that is the only sound in the apartment. I taste it. Too much salt, or not enough; I can't tell, because there's no one to say. I say "Lovely," out loud, to the pot, and my voice comes out strangely loud. My phone lights up on the counter and I lunge for it, but it's only the grocery app offering me a coupon. I wipe my hands on my apron anyway, twice. Through the window the street lamps flicker on, and a couple passes below, laughing at something. I turn the radio up. I straighten a napkin that was already straight. Seven minutes until they're due, and my chest feels like a held breath. I light the candles, then wonder if it looks like I tried too hard, and leave them burning.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter, and Marta nearly knocked over her tea lunging for it. An unfamiliar number, a area code from somewhere she'd never been. She let it ring four times, thumb hovering, then answered in her brightest voice. "Hello? Yes, this is she." The man on the line began to say something about an extended car warranty, and she pressed the phone harder to her ear, as if that would bring him closer. "Oh, I don't actually have a car anymore," she said, laughing a little too long. "But how's your day going? Busy?" He hesitated, scripted words stalling. She sat down on the kitchen floor, back against the cold dishwasher, and wound the cord of her cardigan around one finger. The apartment hummed. Dinner for one cooled on the stove. "Please," she said, when he started to apologize, "go ahead and finish. I don't mind. Really. I've got time."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book has been in my backpack since March, and it's November now, so the spine has gone soft from rubbing against my laptop. I wait until the reading room empties before I approach the desk. The librarian scans it and says, "Oh, this is quite overdue," and I laugh too loudly and say, "Yeah, sorry, I lost track." My voice cracks, because it's the first thing I've said aloud since Tuesday. She types, and I stare at a flyer for a book club I won't join. The fine is forty-one dollars. I pay it in coins, counting slowly, stretching it out. "Anything else?" she asks, already looking past me. I say no. I stand there another second, hands flat on the cool wood, waiting for something. Outside, I check my phone, which has nothing on it, and walk home the long way, past lit windows where people are talking over dinner.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers took forty minutes, and then the door clicked shut behind them and the apartment was just boxes and the hum of the fridge. I carried the lamp to the outlet by the window, plugged it in, and stood there as if someone might comment on it. "Okay," I said aloud, and my voice bounced off the bare walls, too loud. I opened the box marked KITCHEN and set out one mug, one plate, one fork, lining them up on the counter, and the counter still looked mostly empty. My phone sat face up beside them. I checked it, put it down, checked it again. Somewhere above me a floorboard creaked, a laugh came through the ceiling, and I held very still until it faded. I ordered noodles just to hear the buzzer, and when the delivery guy said, "Have a good night," I answered, "You too, really," much too long after he'd already started down the stairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside the pigeon-streaked plaque, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and I looked around for someone to shout after before I'd even touched it. Nobody. Just a jogger far off, shrinking. I opened it slowly, like it might object. A library card, forty dollars, a photo of a dog with one ear up. The license said Marguerite Osei, and an address six blocks from mine. I read it twice, then a third time, just to hear her name in my head. My thermos had gone cold hours ago, but I held it anyway. I'd come out at noon and now the lamps were flickering on. 'Hello?' I said to the empty path, and my voice cracked, rusty from disuse since Tuesday. I tucked the wallet inside my coat, against my ribs, and walked toward her street slowly, rehearsing what I'd say if she opened the door, hoping she'd ask me to stay for tea.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite arrived at the community pool twenty minutes early, as she did every Tuesday, and sat on the bench by the lockers until the chlorine had settled in her throat. The Tuesday class of six-year-olds spilled out in a bright, shrieking tangle, their parents holding towels like flags. She waited in the shallow end with her hands gripping the tile lip, knees bent, watching the instructor wave to a woman in the bleachers. 'Good job, Marguerite,' the instructor said, and she nodded too quickly. Her face went under. Bubbles roared past her ears, and for a moment the whole building was gone, just a green hum and her own heartbeat. She surfaced, coughing, and looked at the bleachers. Nobody had looked up. In the changing room she dried her hair slowly, longer than she needed, and when her phone stayed dark in her palm she said 'Well,' to the empty row of mirrors, and then 'Next week.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned across her knee, reading the back of each one twice, though the instructions were simple. Tomatoes, two feet apart. She measured with a ruler, then with her hand, then said, "Okay," out loud, and the word dropped into the quiet yard and stayed there. The trowel scraped. Somewhere past the fence a screen door slapped and a child laughed, and she paused with dirt cooling in her palm until the sound moved on. She pressed each seedling in and patted the soil the way she'd seen on a video, narrating under her breath, "There you go, there you go," to the plants. Her phone sat face-up on the step. She checked it, set it down, checked it again. When the last row was finished she took a photo of the bed, thumb hovering over a contact's name, then slid the phone into her pocket and filled the watering can slowly, listening to it gurgle full.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to the next slide, and the whole room leans in together, a single tilted shape I'm not part of. I sit at the end of the table, closest to the door, my laptop open to a blank document I've been pretending to type in. Someone laughs at her joke about the Q3 numbers. I laugh a half-second late, and it comes out thin. My coffee went cold forty minutes ago; I keep lifting it anyway, for something to do with my hands. Across from me, Priya and Marcus trade a look, the kind with a whole history folded inside it. My chest feels hollow, like a stairwell. When Dana asks if anyone has questions, I have three, good ones, and I swallow them. Afterward everyone drifts toward lunch in a loose cluster. I say, "I'll catch up," to nobody in particular, and stay to wipe the whiteboard until the hallway goes quiet and the projector fan is the only thing still talking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty enough that Marta caught herself drifting to the center line, just to see if anything would object. Nothing did. She turned the radio on, found a man selling mattresses, and let him talk for a full minute before turning it off again. Her shoulders ached from being held so carefully. At the red light on Fenner Road, where no cars crossed in either direction, she waited anyway, hands at ten and two, watching the signal change twice. "Okay," she said aloud, and the word sounded thin in the car, so she cleared her throat and said it again, louder, as though someone had asked. Her phone lay face-up on the passenger seat. She glanced at it at every curve, its black screen showing only her own tired outline. When she finally pulled into her driveway, she left the engine running, the porch dark, the key unturned, and sat there until the dashboard clock rolled over to another minute, then another.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I bring the good grapes, the ones my uncle likes, and set them on the tray table where he won't reach them. He's asleep, mouth open, the monitor ticking along without me. I pull the vinyl chair closer and it shrieks across the floor; I freeze, then wince at nobody. The window shows a parking lot and one streetlight flickering. I tell him about the traffic, about the bakery closing, my voice low and oddly formal, like I'm reading a report. No one answers. My phone sits warm in my palm and I scroll through names, thumb hovering, then lock the screen. A nurse passes and says, 'He's doing fine, hon,' and I say, 'Great, thanks,' too fast. I eat a grape. Then another. They're sweet, and I chew slowly, listening to the machine, wishing his hand would twitch toward the bowl. When visiting hours end, I'm still holding the stem, and I don't remember standing up to leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dennis arrived twenty minutes early again and parked at the far end of the curb, where the maple dropped its leaves on the hood. Across the lawn the other parents stood in loose knots, laughing, someone passing around a thermos lid. He checked his phone, though nothing had buzzed, and scrolled up through old messages he had already read. When a woman glanced his way he lifted a hand too quickly, and she was only looking at the clock above the doors. He let the hand fall into his jacket pocket and rubbed his thumb along the cold edge of his keys. 'Nice day,' he said to no one, and the words came out rough, like a door that hadn't been opened in weeks. The bell rang. Children spilled out in bright coats, and his chest tightened as he searched for the green backpack. Mia ran straight to him, and he held on a beat too long. 'Can we get pancakes?' she asked. He nodded, because it meant talking for another hour.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By eight I had the dining table dragged to the curb, all six chairs lined up beside it like guests who hadn't been told the party was cancelled. A man in a Cubs cap ran his thumb along the oak and asked if it had been in a big family. I said, 'Oh, it fed plenty,' too brightly, and then kept talking about the leaf extension, the wobbly leg, how Frank used to wedge a matchbook under it, long after he'd stopped nodding. He paid forty dollars and left. I stood there holding the bills, my coffee gone cold, and realized I'd said Frank's name aloud for the first time in weeks. My throat felt tight, so I sat in one of the chairs, the one that creaked, and listened to it. A woman slowed her car, looked, drove on. I straightened the price tags that were already straight. By noon I'd marked everything down by half, just so somebody would stay and ask me something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the kitchen floor with her head inside the cabinet, a flashlight clamped between her teeth, water dripping steadily onto her wrist. The wrench was too big for the nut, and she needed a second pair of hands to hold the pipe still, so she wedged her knee against it and grunted. "Okay," she said to the empty room, then again, louder, as if someone might answer. Her phone sat on the tile, a video tutorial narrating in a cheerful man's voice, and she found herself nodding at him. Cold water crept down her sleeve. She scrolled to her brother's name, held her thumb over it, and let the screen go dark. When the drip finally slowed, she said, "Good. Good job," and heard how thin it sounded against the hum of the refrigerator. She stayed down there a while, cheek against the cool tile, though the work was done.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has a window and a federal seal, and I carry it up three flights without opening it, because opening it on the stairs would mean no one to see my face anyway. Inside the apartment I set out two mugs from habit, then put one back. The kettle clicks off. I slide a butter knife under the flap, slowly, like it might bleed. "Okay," I tell the refrigerator. "Okay, let's see." My voice sounds too loud, a coat dropped in a quiet hall. The paper is folded in thirds, and my thumb trembles against the crease. I read the first line twice, then a third time aloud, doing the voices I'd once have done for my sister. Approved. My knees go soft and I sit on the linoleum. I scroll to her name on my phone and hold it there until the screen dims. Then I read the letter again to the empty room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station clock says 9:40, and I have been standing under it for a quarter of an hour, my suitcase wheels pinned against my heel. Around me, people hand each other umbrellas and laughter in a language that slides past me like rain on glass. I rehearse the hotel's name in my mouth, then say it to a ticket clerk, and he answers with a long, kind sentence I can't hold. I nod anyway. My face hurts from smiling. Outside, I walk a block, then another, reading signs as if they were shapes. At a noodle counter I point at a picture, and the bowl arrives, steaming. I eat slowly, because when I finish there will be nobody to say anything to. My phone shows my sister's last message, unanswered, six hours old at home. I type 'Arrived, all good,' delete it, and type it again. Then I wash the bowl's warmth from my hands and say 'thank you' to the cook, twice, louder than I need to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit hits the tall grass at a dead run, and I laugh out loud, a short bark of a sound that startles me because nobody's there to hear it. I sit on the same splintered bench, holding a coffee, though I bought two. The second cup sits beside me, cooling, a small paper ghost I can't bring myself to throw out. Across the field a couple spreads a blanket and the woman tilts her head onto his shoulder. I check my phone. Nothing new. I scroll up to find the last message, from Tuesday, a dentist reminder. "Good boy," I call, louder than I need to, just to hear my voice work. Biscuit doesn't look back. My chest feels hollow and cold, like a room after the furniture's gone. When he finally trots over, tongue flapping, I press my face into his neck and stay there longer than he'd like, and he lets me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and old coffee, and I'm the first one there again, forty minutes early. I drag the piano bench across the linoleum, and the screech bounces off the stacked chairs. Nobody's here to wince at it. I play the opening bars of the Schubert, then stop, because the second violinist said she'd come to run it with me, and I keep glancing at the door. My phone stays dark on the music stand. I say, "Right, from the top," out loud, in the bright voice I use for groups, and the words sit in the rafters. My hands are cold, so I tuck them under my arms. At the end of the piece I pause where someone would clap, and I hold my breath for it. The radiator ticks. I fold the page corner flat, set a second chair beside the bench just in case, and begin again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Walt's coffee can of mismatched screws sat where it always had, and I tipped it into a box marked KEEP before realizing I had no one to keep it for. The pegboard still showed the painted outline of every hammer. I said, "Where'd you put the square, you old crook?" and the room swallowed it. My voice sounded too loud, so I started humming, badly, until that stopped too. I made two cups of tea out of habit, carried both to the bench, and drank mine standing up while the other went cold beside his stool. Sawdust had settled in the creases of his work gloves; I put one on, and my hand disappeared into the shape of his. The radio was still tuned to his station. I let it play static for a while rather than touch the dial. When the light through the window turned orange, I realized I hadn't packed anything in an hour. I locked up, then unlocked it, went back, and turned the lamp on again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal says results go live at noon, so at 11:40 I'm already sitting on the stairwell outside the library with my laptop balanced on my knees, because the dorm is too quiet and the common room is full of people laughing in pairs. I refresh the page. Nothing. I refresh again, and my thumb leaves a damp print on the trackpad. Down the hall a group of girls squeals over something on a phone, and I angle my screen away like it's a secret. My phone buzzes once; it's the pizza place's coupon text. I read it twice anyway. Mum would be asleep, eight hours ahead, and I don't want to wake her for a number that might be bad. At 12:00 the page flickers, and I say, 'Okay,' out loud, to no one, my voice scraping like a chair on tile. The grade loads. I stare at it, then at the empty step beside me, and realize I've been holding my breath for someone to tell first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last switchback came sooner than Mara expected, and she stopped there anyway, thumbs hooked under her pack straps, listening. Nothing but wind combing the dry grass. She'd saved two chocolate squares for the summit, one for each of them, back when the plan had a "them" in it, and now she ate both without tasting either. Below, the valley lights flickered on in a scatter, each window yellow and sealed. "Okay," she said aloud, and her voice came out thin and strangely formal, like someone addressing an empty room. She waited, as if the ridge might answer. Her hand drifted to her phone, thumbed the dark screen, put it away. The cold crept into her wrists. She turned on her headlamp, and the beam made a small tunnel that ended a few feet ahead, and she walked into it slowly, matching her steps to the crunch of her own boots, the only sound for miles, and counting them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is soft as cloth now, Grandpa's slanted pencil gone gray: "flour till it feels right." I read it aloud to the kitchen, just to hear something. My voice comes out too loud. I measure for four, then tip half back into the bag, because who's going to eat it? The dough sticks to my knuckles. I knead longer than I need to, shoulders aching, listening to the wet slap on the counter and the fridge humming underneath it. Rain ticks at the window. My phone lies face-up beside the salt, dark, and I turn it over twice. When the loaf finally rises, I set two plates out before I notice and leave them there. The bread comes out golden, and the whole apartment smells like his house. I tear the heel off standing at the stove, burn my tongue, and say, "Needs more salt," to nobody, waiting a moment as if someone might answer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta had been holding the same basket, one lemon and a box of tea, for ten minutes when someone said her name beside the canned tomatoes. Dev Hollis, from tenth-grade chemistry, with gray at his temples and a toddler on his hip. "Marta! Wow. Still here?" She laughed too loudly, and it echoed down the aisle. Her hand tightened on the basket handle until her knuckles went pale. He talked about his wife, the move, a job in logistics, and she nodded at each pause, hunting for something to offer back. "I'm good. Busy," she said, though her Tuesday evening held only the lemon. When his phone buzzed and he said they should catch up sometime, she heard herself say, "Yes, definitely," and kept standing there after he left, reading the label on a can she didn't need, her throat faintly warm from being used.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marguerite wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time, watching the fluorescent light flicker over the cough drops. Everyone else had gone early to airports and kitchens. She straightened the rack of reading glasses until the frames sat in perfect rows. When the phone rang, she lunged for it, and it was only a recorded survey. She stayed on the line anyway until the voice finished thanking her. Her stomach tightened around the sandwich she hadn't touched, so she wrapped it back up. "Happy Thanksgiving," she told the automatic doors, which slid open for no one, and her voice came out too bright in the quiet. She said it again, softer, to the empty aisle. At closing she lingered, flipping the sign slowly, and stood with her coat on, keys in hand, listening to the refrigerators hum, in no hurry to walk out into a parking lot with only her car in it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta ran the length of Terminal C with her coat half on, the wheels of her carry-on rattling behind her like something that wanted to stop. Gate 42 was a long way off. Around her, families moved in clumps, someone's father hoisting a child onto his shoulders, a pair of women laughing over a shared phone. She slowed at a moving walkway and said, "Excuse me, sorry," to no one, her voice small and cracked from hours unused. Her phone buzzed; she snatched it out, hopeful, and it was only the airline: boarding closes in 6 minutes. She thumbed through her contacts anyway, stopping at a name she had not called since spring, then pocketed the phone. At the gate, the agent was already lifting the handset. "Wait, please," Marta said, breathless, and held out her pass. The agent scanned it without looking up. Marta stood a moment in the empty jet bridge, listening to her own breathing, and found she had no one to text that she'd made it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the edges of the spare room by noon and then stood there with the roller dripping, because the radio had gone to static and she didn't want to cross the hall to fix it. The color on the lid said Morning Linen. On the wall it looked like nothing, like skin. She rolled it over the pencil marks where the doorframe had once recorded her son's heights, 1998, 2001, 2004, and her wrist ached in a way she told no one about, since no one was there. 'Well, that's that,' she said aloud, and the voice came out rusty, so she cleared her throat and said it again. At six she ate crackers over the paint tray, standing, listening to the fridge hum. Her phone lay face-up on the ladder's top step. She checked it, set it down, and checked it again before dipping the brush.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the screen door, and I carried out two glasses of lemonade before I remembered I only needed one. I set the extra on the rail anyway. Rain came sideways, cold needles on my shins, and I didn't move my feet. The swing creaked under me, a sound I used to complain about when there was someone to complain to. "Well, that's a good one," I said, out loud, to the yard, and my voice sounded too big and then too small. Across the street every window was lit yellow, a television flickering blue in one of them. I picked up my phone, scrolled to a name, and held my thumb above it until the screen dimmed and went dark. Lightning showed me the whole street at once, empty and shining. I counted the seconds to the thunder, the way my father taught me, and when it came I kept counting, just to have something to say to someone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol cleared a patch of the shared garage floor, nudging aside the neighbor's paint cans with her foot so they wouldn't tip. The small purple bicycle hung upside down on the stand, its back wheel wobbling. She worked the spoke wrench in quarter turns, tongue pinched between her teeth, humming the nonsense song Teo made up last week. Grease darkened her thumb; she wiped it on her jeans without noticing. 'Nearly there, bug,' she murmured to the empty garage, then laughed at herself. She spun the wheel and listened, head tilted, until the hum of it ran smooth. Her chest felt warm and a little too full, like she'd swallowed sunlight. Then she knelt and straightened the rainbow streamers on the handlebars, one by one, combing out each tangle with her fingers. She set the tiny bell to ring once. Tomorrow he would grin with his gap teeth, and she wanted every part of it perfect before he woke.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as the sky went the color of pewter, and I was already unzipping my coat. Mrs. Okafor's cardigan was thin, and she'd been shivering since the wind picked up, though she insisted she wasn't. "Don't argue," I said, draping the coat over her shoulders and tugging the collar snug beneath her chin. My arms prickled in the cold, and I didn't mind it. I'd packed her thermos of ginger tea that morning, so I poured a cup and wrapped her fingers around it, holding my hands over hers until the tremor stopped. Rain slanted in sideways. I shuffled to the windward end of the bench to block the spray, and my sleeve soaked through. "The 14 is late again," she muttered. "Good," I said, and laughed, surprising myself. "More time for tea." She leaned her head against my shoulder, light as a sparrow, and I kept very still, hoping the bus would take its time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smells of cedar and my mother's hand cream, and I lift the lid slowly, as if something inside might wake. Rubber bands crumble when I touch them. I sit on the attic floor, knees aching, and sort the envelopes into piles by postmark, though I keep stopping to run my thumb over her slanted handwriting. "Oh, Ruthie," I say aloud, laughing, when I find the one where she complains about Dad's burned pot roast. My voice comes out soft, the way it did at her bedside. I read it twice. Then I fan a few letters against my cheek, warm from the attic's afternoon heat, and my chest loosens and aches at once. I should hurry; the movers come Friday. Instead I fetch the good blanket from downstairs, spread it over my legs, and start again from the beginning, reading every line out loud to the empty rafters so the room can hear her too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
