Then I put the car in park, got out into the cold, and dragged the lightest section sideways, grit scraping under my palms. Back inside, I rolled slowly through the gap, shoulders set, eyes fixed ahead, and did not check the mirror once. Home was eight miles. I would be there by midnight, exactly as I'd said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Visiting hours ended at eight, and at 8:20 Marta was still in the vinyl chair, coat zipped to her chin, her jaw set so tight it ached. The nurse had come twice. "Ma'am, he needs rest." Marta nodded without turning her head and kept her eyes on her brother's slack, gray face. "I'll be quiet," she said, flat, and unwrapped the sandwich she'd brought him, though the sign above the bed said NPO in red marker. Let them move her. The monitor beeped its slow green count. Her knees throbbed from the draft along the floor, and she crossed her arms tighter, planting her heels. When the third nurse sighed and reached for the light switch, Marta said, "He didn't wake up for the doctor either. He'll wake up for me," and pulled the blanket over his hand, tucking it firmly, as if the matter were settled. She did not look at the clock again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus kept the engine off and the car parked exactly where it was, nose against the fire lane's yellow curb, even after the crossing guard pointed twice and then a third time. He rolled the window down two inches. "Five minutes," he said, flat, and rolled it back up. His jaw ached; he realized he'd been grinding it since the first honk behind him. The sign said Pickup Loop Only, Cars Must Keep Moving, and he read it again slowly, as if it might change. It had been his spot for three years, before somebody in an office decided otherwise. A woman in a minivan leaned on her horn. Marcus folded his arms, the seatbelt cutting across his chest, and stared at the double doors. When Leah finally came out, backpack dragging, he didn't start the car. "Take your time," he told her, loud enough for the guard to hear, and settled deeper into the seat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine, the folding table was crowded with lamps and mismatched candlesticks, but Marguerite had dragged the oak dresser to the very edge of the driveway where every passing car could see it. The tag said $150. A young man ran his thumb along the scratched top and offered forty. "It's one-fifty," she said, not looking up from her crossword. He mentioned the missing knob. She crossed her arms, the lawn chair creaking, and told him her husband had built the drawers himself and no knob was going to change that. By noon the sun had burned a stripe across her neck, and her jaw ached from clenching. A woman offered ninety, then a hundred and ten. Marguerite shook her head each time, slowly, like a door closing. Her daughter called from the porch to just take it. "It'll sit here till dark if it has to," Marguerite said, and tugged her hat lower.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on her back under the sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, water dripping steadily onto her collarbone. The third wrench had slipped again, and her knuckles were scraped raw. "Plumber's a ripoff," she muttered around the flashlight, as her sister's text lit up the phone on the tile: Just call Dale. She turned the phone face down. The joint was cold and slick, and she wrapped the tape another five times, hard, though the roll was nearly gone. A cramp pulled at her neck. Water ran into her ear. She tightened the nut a quarter turn, then another, until the metal creaked, and the drip answered with a fat bright bead. "No," she said to the pipe, flatly. "Not today." She shifted her hips, jammed her shoulder against the cabinet wall, and reached for the wrench again, jaw set so tight her teeth ached. The towels were soaked. She kept going anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a window and a red stripe, and Walt set it on the kitchen table beside the other two he hadn't opened. "Same answer as last time," he told the empty room. He ate his toast standing up, jaw working hard, eyes on the thing. When the coffee went cold he poured it out and made more. Finally he slit the flap with a butter knife, slowly, the way you'd gut something you meant to prove wrong. His shoulders had climbed toward his ears. The page said the appeal was denied and the fence must come down by the thirtieth. He read it once, folded it into precise thirds, and slid it under the sugar bowl. Then he pulled on his boots, walked out to the yard, and tightened the top wire of the fence until it hummed under his palm. "Come and take it down yourselves," he muttered, and drove another staple in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver tapped the screen of his phone for the third time, and I shook my head for the third time. Rain needled the station forecourt in Tbilisi, and my backpack straps had worn two hot stripes into my shoulders. I had printed the route at home. Paper doesn't lie. "No," I said, slowly, as if volume were grammar, and held the page up under his nose. "Walking. I walk." He pointed at the sky, then at his car, then at my soaked sleeves. I pulled my jaw tight and felt my molars grind. Fine, I thought, forty minutes, maybe fifty. I'd decided on the walk on the plane, and nothing with a meter was going to undo that. I folded the map into a square, shouldered the pack higher, and stepped off the curb into a puddle that swallowed my shoe whole. I kept walking anyway, squelching, chin up, not looking back at the idling headlights.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: The rain had been threatening for an hour, and Dana had called twice that we should head back, but I stayed planted on the bench with my arms crossed and my jaw set. "Five more minutes," I told her, the same thing I'd said at the last two clouds. Biscuit tore across the wet grass, ears flapping, chasing nothing at all. A drop landed on my wrist. I didn't wipe it. My knees ached from the cold slats, and my toes had gone stiff in my boots, but I tugged my collar up and stayed. Dana held out the umbrella. I shook my head without looking at her. "He's not done," I said, flat, as if the dog had filed a request. Thunder rolled somewhere behind the tree line. I dug my heels into the mud and watched Biscuit spin in circles, and I did not move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Marjorie tapped her baton against the music stand for the third time. "Again from bar forty," she said. I didn't move my bow. My jaw had settled into that tight, familiar shelf, and my shoulders sat square against the folding chair. "I'm playing it the way I've always played it," I said, flat and even. The slow tempo was right. I knew it was right. The cellist beside me coughed and studied his shoes. Marjorie sighed and offered a compromise, a little faster, only a little. I turned the page back to bar forty and set my fingers down exactly where they had been, my heel pressing hard into the cold linoleum. When the downbeat came, I played it slow, every note drawn out like a thread I refused to cut. Somebody's phone buzzed. Nobody laughed. I kept my eyes on the page and dragged the last phrase out a full breath longer than anyone else could bear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marguerite had been told three times that the estate sale people would take the tools, and three times she had set the same chisel back on its nail. Now she stood in Dov's workshop with her jaw locked, sawdust in the creases of her knuckles, a cardboard box at her feet that she had labeled KEEP and filled with nearly everything. "No," she said to his nephew, flatly, when he lifted a coffee can of mismatched screws. "Those stay." He pointed out that they were just screws. She took the can from him and wedged it under her arm, where it dug into her ribs. The space heater ticked. Dov's apron still hung by the door, bent to the shape of his shoulders. She'd been on her feet since dawn, her heels throbbing, and she refused the stool he nudged toward her with his boot. "I'll sort it my way," she said, and started over from the first shelf, slower this time, on purpose.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The list was supposed to go up at noon, and at 12:40 Marisol was still planted on the cold stone step outside the physics building, back against the door. "You can check online," her roommate said, holding out a phone. Marisol didn't look at it. "It goes on the board. I'll read it on the board." She crossed her arms tighter and pressed her heels into the concrete. A janitor told her the secretary might not come until two. "Then I'll be here at two." Her jaw ached from clenching; she noticed, and clenched it anyway. Her sandwich sat unopened in her bag, and when her roommate begged her to come get coffee, she shook her head without turning. Pigeons wandered past her shoes. Her toes had gone numb. Every few minutes she checked her watch, then glared at the empty corkboard through the glass as if it owed her something. "Nobody's making me move," she muttered, and stayed exactly where she was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta kept her boots moving up the switchback even after the last orange stripe slid off the ridge and the pines turned to black cutouts. Her phone said forty minutes to the summit, and the sign at the fork had said the lake loop was safer, and she had walked past it without slowing. "I said I'd see the top," she muttered to no one, clenching her jaw until her molars ached. Her calves burned; a blister wept inside her left sock. She dug the headlamp from her pack and snapped it on. When her brother's text buzzed, asking where she was, she thumbed back, "Fine. Going up." Cold crept under her collar. A branch cracked somewhere below. She planted her pole harder into the gravel, breathed through her teeth, and took the next step, then the next, not once glancing back down the trail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card was stained yellow at the corners, Nana's slanting hand telling her to add flour "until it feels right." Marguerite pushed her sleeves past her elbows and dumped in a third cup anyway. Her sister's text glowed on the counter: just use measurements from the internet. She turned the phone face down. The dough clung to her knuckles, tacky and cold, and her forearms burned as she folded it over and over. "It's fine," she told the empty kitchen, jaw tight. "It's supposed to be sticky." She did not reach for the scale. Twice the oven timer chirped before she'd decided anything, and twice she silenced it with a floury thumb. When the loaf came out squat and pale, she tapped the bottom, listened to the dull thud, and set it on the rack. Then she wiped her hands, flattened the card against the counter, and cracked another egg into the bowl to start again, exactly the same way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: "Dana Whitfield?" she said, over the pyramid of canned tomatoes, and my hand tightened on the cart handle until my knuckles blanched. I kept my eyes on the shelf. "Mm," I said. She started in about the reunion, how everyone was coming, how I should too, and my jaw set like cement. I had decided back in 2019 that I wasn't going, and a woman with a basket of oat milk was not going to undo that. "I'm busy that weekend." "It's in March," she laughed. "Still busy." My neck went hot. I reached past her for the dented, cheapest tomatoes, though I'd come for a different brand entirely, and dropped them in the cart as if that had been the plan all along. She said my name softly, once more. I pushed forward, wheel squeaking, and did not turn around, even when I realized I'd forgotten the milk.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:40 on Christmas Eve, Marguerite flipped the pharmacy sign to CLOSED only after the clock hit five, not a second before, though the manager had texted twice to let everyone go early. A man pressed his palms to the glass. She pointed at the hours painted beside his head and went back to counting pills, tapping each into the tray with a small click. Her jaw ached from clenching. Her feet throbbed inside her shoes, and she planted them wider. "Policy says five," she told the empty aisle, louder than needed. The phone buzzed again on the counter. She turned it face down. Rain streaked the window, and the string of colored bulbs over the register blinked on and off. She wiped the counter that was already clean, then wiped it again, and refused to look at the door until the clock agreed with her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says Gate C47 closes at 4:15, and it is 4:09, and the agent at the desk is shaking her head before I even reach her. "Ma'am, the door's shut." I set my bag on her counter. "Then open it." My jaw aches from clenching; sweat has glued my shirt to my spine. She explains about the jet bridge, about regulations, and I nod along without hearing, my thumb tapping the passport. "I'll wait," I say. She tells me the next flight is tomorrow. "I'll wait here," I say again, flatter this time, and plant my feet on the carpet as if it might grow roots to hold me. Behind me someone sighs. Let them. Through the glass, the plane still sits there, nose bright, not moving yet. Not moving yet. "Call them again," I tell her, and I do not step aside, not even when my knees begin to tremble.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The third coat of Harbor Fog was drying streaky, and Marguerite stood back with her jaw set, roller dripping onto the drop cloth. Her sister had called it twice that morning. "Just prime it, Mags. The yellow's bleeding through." Marguerite had said, "It'll cover," and hung up before the sentence finished echoing. Now the yellow glowed through the gray like a bruise. She dipped the roller again, pressed harder, and her shoulder burned in the same spot it had burned an hour ago. Sweat ran down her temple; she wiped it with her wrist and left a gray smear. The hardware store clerk had held up the primer can, and she had walked right past him. Her knees ached from the crouching. She rolled one more stripe, slower, then another, muttering, "Four coats, then. Five. I don't care." The can was nearly empty. She pried the lid off the old yellow's leftover bucket, looked at it, and shoved it into the hallway with her foot.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch boards just as Marguerite lowered herself into the rocker, and she did not so much as glance at the door. Her daughter's voice came through the screen, thin and pleading: supper was getting cold, the lightning was close, for heaven's sake. "I'll come in when I'm done," Marguerite said, flatly, and tugged her cardigan tighter. Wind flung rain sideways across her shins. She set her jaw and planted both feet, so that the chair stopped rocking altogether. Thunder cracked over the maples and her teeth ached with it, but she lifted her tea, now speckled and cold, and drank it anyway. Eleven summers she had watched storms from this exact spot, and no forecast, no daughter, no puddle creeping toward her slippers was going to rewrite that. Behind her the screen door sighed shut. She stared harder at the dripping yard, shoulders damp and rigid, and refused to shiver.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the rear wheel half off the frame when Dennis from unit four wandered over, nudged her torque wrench with his boot, and said, "You know there's a shop on Fifth for this, right? Save you the trouble." She kept her eyes on the chain. "I know where the shop is." Her voice came out flat and careful, each word set down like a bolt on a tray. Heat crawled up the back of her neck. She wiped her hands on the rag, slowly, finger by finger, then slid the wrench a foot farther from his boot, to the far side of her side of the shared workbench. He laughed and said he was only kidding. She nodded at the derailleur. When he left, she realized her jaw ached, and that she'd tightened the same bolt three times. She turned the radio off, since it was his, and worked in the fluorescent hum, replaying what she should have said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as Marguerite finished replaying the phone call, and she let them drum. "Not a problem," she had said, in the voice she saved for waiters and landlords. "Of course. Fine." Now her jaw ached from holding it that way. She stood rather than sit on the wet bench, spine straight, handbag clutched against her ribs, and when a boy edged under the roof beside her she moved exactly one step away without looking at him. Wind pushed rain sideways across her shoes. She didn't tuck them in. Heat crawled up her neck despite the cold. Thirty years she'd run that committee, and Dennis had called her suggestion 'sweet.' Sweet. She said it aloud to the glass panel, flat, tasting it. The boy glanced over. "Sorry?" "Nothing." The bus appeared through the gray, lights smeared, and she lifted her chin, rummaged for her pass with sharp little jerks, and decided she would not be sending the lemon cake on Friday after all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite found the letter near the bottom of the shoebox, under the rubber-banded Christmas cards, and read it standing up, one hip jammed against the edge of her mother's dresser. Her sister's handwriting, slanted and confident. *Mags is sweet, but you know she never could handle anything difficult, so I'll just tell her after the funeral.* She read the line again. Her jaw had gone tight enough to ache. She set the page down very carefully, squared its corners against the lid, and wiped her palms on her slacks as though they were dusty. "Well," she said to the empty room, in a voice so pleasant it startled her. "Isn't that something." She picked up the next envelope, then dropped it. Her ears were hot. Downstairs, the phone began to ring, and she let it ring, all eleven times, while she folded the letter into thirds, then into smaller thirds, and pressed it flat under her thumb.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta was elbow-deep in dishwater when Dennis knocked, the same Dennis whose summer barbecue she had not been invited to. He stood on her porch rubbing his neck, saying his gutters were a disaster and could he possibly borrow her ladder, just till Sunday. The sponge went still in her fist. Her jaw tightened until she felt it in her ears. "My ladder," she said, flat and slow, drying each finger on the dish towel as though it were delicate work. Past his shoulder his garage door stood open, and she could see the shiny new truck he'd bought in spring. "The one I'd have lent you a hundred times, if you'd asked before now?" Her smile was thin as paper. Heat crawled up her throat. "It's in the shed. Padlocked. I'll have to find the key." She did not step aside, and she did not ask him in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marguerite diced the shallots smaller than necessary, the knife clacking against the board like a tiny metronome. Her phone lay face-up beside the stove, Dan's text still glowing: Maybe skip the lamb this time? Lena's trying to eat lighter. Skip the lamb. She had marinated it since Tuesday. "Of course," she said aloud to the empty kitchen, in the bright, even voice she used on telephone salespeople. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it and made herself stop, then started again. She slid the roast into the oven anyway and shut the door with her hip, harder than the hinge deserved. Heat climbed her neck. Fine, they could have lighter. She reached for the good napkins, then put them back and took the paper ones from the drawer, smoothing the stack with a flat, precise palm. When the doorbell rang, she wiped her hands slowly, counted to four, and smiled before she turned the knob.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cutting board, a number Marguerite didn't know, and she wiped her hands on the dish towel before answering. "Hello, is this Margaret? I'm calling about your late husband's accounts." The knife stayed where she'd dropped it, half through an onion. Her jaw tightened until her back teeth ached. "Marguerite," she said, each syllable laid down like a plate. "And Walter isn't late. He's at the hardware store. He's never been late a day in his life." The voice stammered something about a script. Heat crept up her neck and into her ears. She stared at the wall calendar, at Walter's cramped handwriting on Thursday, and gripped the counter edge. "You might want to check your list before you ring strangers and bury their husbands," she said, very evenly. She pressed the red button with her thumb, hard, then stood breathing through her nose while the onion stung her eyes and she refused to wipe them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Marisol slid the water-stained copy of Middlemarch across the desk with two fingers, as if it might mark her sleeve. The librarian glanced at the screen, then up, eyebrows lifting. "Four hundred and twelve days. That comes to—" "I can read the number," Marisol said, each word clipped and level. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars since the stairwell. Heat crawled up her neck and settled in her ears. She had come in on her own, hadn't she? Nobody had sent a notice, nobody had chased her, and still this woman used that tone, the one for thieves. Marisol pulled out her wallet and counted bills onto the counter one at a time, smoothing each flat with a hard thumb. "I'll want the receipt printed, not emailed." She did not take the chair offered. She stood very straight, chin high, staring at a poster about how reading was fun until the machine finished whirring.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers had barely set down my last box when the landlord glanced around the room and said, "Well, it's cozy. Most people in your situation do fine with less." I kept my smile fixed while my jaw tightened until my back teeth ached. "My situation," I repeated, flat, slow. He laughed and jingled the keys, then dropped them in my palm like coins for a tip. My ears were hot. I peeled the tape off a box of books harder than I needed to, and the screech filled the whole apartment, which didn't take much. "Thank you for the tour," I said. "I can find the door." He lingered. I turned my back and shelved a dictionary, then another, spines squared, each one landing with a thump. When the latch finally clicked behind him, I stood very still, breathing through my nose, and realized I'd been gripping the keys so tightly they'd printed their teeth into my hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench by the duck pond, fat and brown, and I picked it up with two fingers. Inside: forty dollars, a library card, and a folded note in careful handwriting. "If found, please keep. I don't need it anymore." My jaw tightened until my molars ached. I read it again, standing very straight, pigeons scattering around my shoes. Keep it? As if I were the sort of person who pockets a stranger's money and walks off whistling. As if the whole point of me was a quick, easy yes. Heat crawled up my neck. I snapped the wallet shut harder than I needed to. "Unbelievable," I told a jogger, who did not slow down. I marched to the ranger station, dropped the wallet on the counter, and said, flatly, "Every card, every dollar. Count it in front of me." Then I stood there, arms crossed, refusing to sit, until she did.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor, barely twenty, clapped twice and told the whole shallow-end class, "Okay, let's give Mr. Park the noodle again, since he's our special project." Laughter rippled off the tiled walls. I stood very still, chlorine stinging my nose, water suddenly cold around my ribs. My jaw had gone tight enough that my teeth ached. "I'm forty-three," I said, evenly, each word set down like a plate. "I pay the same as everyone." She smiled and said she was only joking. I took the noodle anyway, because refusing would have looked worse, and tucked it under my arms with a stiff little nod. My ears were burning, which seemed unfair underwater. I kicked off the wall harder than necessary, face down, and counted strokes instead of listening. At the far end I did not look back at her. I gripped the gutter, breathed, and decided I would swim the full length tomorrow, alone, with nobody holding anything for me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta pressed the last tomato seedling into the soil and sat back on her heels, jaw tight, while her brother-in-law leaned over the fence with his coffee. "You've got them too close," he said. "Honestly, I'd give it a month." She did not look up. She brushed dirt from her knees with short, hard strokes, and her ears felt hot under her hat. "Thank you," she said, each word clipped flat, "for your expertise." The trowel went into the ground again, harder than the row needed. Behind her the hose dripped onto the gravel, steady and loud. She thought of the three Saturdays spent hauling compost, the library book with its folded corners, the neat string lines she'd measured twice. A month. She smoothed the soil around one stem with her thumb, very gently, as if the plant had heard. When his chair scraped away, she stayed kneeling, breathing through her nose, and moved the seedlings no farther apart at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Derek clicked to slide four, and there it was: my wireframe, my color palette, my three-tier onboarding flow, labeled "Derek's Framework." The conference room's air conditioning hummed above me, and I noticed my pen had stopped moving. My jaw was tight enough that my molars ached. Heat crawled up my neck while everyone nodded at him, Priya even jotting something down. I set the pen square against my notebook, aligned it with the edge of the page, and waited until he asked if there were any questions. "Just one," I said, my voice flat and very pleasant. "Which Thursday did you build this? I'm trying to remember which one I emailed you the files." Derek's laugh came out thin. He scrolled, too fast. I kept my eyes on him and my hands flat on the table, fingertips pressing white against the wood, and did not look away until he did.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta took the highway on-ramp faster than she needed to, the tires humming under her, the dashboard clock reading 12:47. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the parking lot. "A 'little sensitive,'" she said aloud to the empty passenger seat, flattening her voice into Daniel's easy, lilting one. "Great. Thanks." Her hands gripped the wheel at ten and two, knuckles pale in the passing sodium lights. She turned the radio on, then off. Heat crawled up her neck though the vents blew cold. All night she had smiled and passed the salad bowl and laughed at the right moments, and he had still announced that joke to the whole table, her mother's funeral dress and all. She rehearsed replies she hadn't said, each one sharper than the last. At the exit, she signaled with a hard click, took the turn, and didn't once check the phone buzzing face-down on the seat beside her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus set the bag of clementines on the tray table harder than he meant to, and the foil-lidded pudding cups jumped. His uncle didn't look up from the television. "Dena brought me real soup yesterday," he said. "Homemade. Not this." He nodded at the clementines as if they were a flyer someone had pushed into his hands. Marcus's jaw tightened until his molars ached. He had driven ninety minutes after a double shift, and the heat climbing his neck felt like a collar being buckled. "Good for Dena," he said, flat, each word clipped. He peeled one clementine anyway, slowly, citrus spray stinging a hangnail, and ate three segments without offering any. The monitor kept its steady, indifferent beep. When the nurse asked if he'd stay for dinner, he checked his watch, though he already knew the time, and said, "No. I think Dena has it covered." He zipped his coat to the chin and left the door wide open behind him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus stood by the chain-link fence with his keys biting into his palm, replaying what the woman in the yellow raincoat had just said. "Oh, I thought you were the grandfather," she'd told him, smiling, and then turned back to her circle of mothers as though nothing had happened. His jaw had gone tight. Heat climbed the back of his neck despite the wind. Now he stared at the school doors, refusing to look left, and straightened his jacket with two sharp tugs. When the bell rang, his daughter ran out waving a paper crown. "Hi, Dad!" He managed, "Hi, sweetheart," in a voice flat as a ruler. He took her backpack without a glance toward the yellow raincoat, then walked the long way around the parking lot, spine rigid, muttering, "Forty-one. I'm forty-one," to nobody at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had sanded the oak dresser herself in 1987, and she set it at the front of the driveway with a hand-lettered tag reading $120. The man in the pressed polo ran his thumb along the drawer edge, wiped it on his trousers, and said, "Twenty. Maybe. It's basically firewood." Her smile stayed where it was, but her jaw went tight and heat climbed her neck into her ears. She straightened the doily on top, though it had been straight. "That dresser raised three children," she said, each word set down slowly, like cups on a shelf. He laughed and glanced at his phone. Her fingers curled around the edge of the price tag until the paper creased. "It isn't for sale to you," she said, and peeled the sticker off. She turned the dresser a few inches toward the house, as though it needed shielding, and called to the woman by the lamps, her voice bright and loud, "Ma'am, did you want to see inside the drawers?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta knelt under the sink with the wrench clamped in her fist, water dripping steadily onto her wrist, while her brother-in-law's voice drifted down from the doorway. "You've got the washer backwards, you know. Want me to just take over?" She didn't turn around. Her jaw tightened until her molars ached, and heat crawled up her neck into her ears. "I've done this four times," she said, each word clipped and level, "on this exact pipe." She gave the nut a hard quarter turn. Cold water ran up her sleeve. He chuckled and said he was only trying to help, and she kept her eyes on the corroded joint, nodding slowly, lips pressed white. When he finally wandered off, she set the wrench down very gently, as though it might break, then picked it up again and cranked the fitting until the dripping stopped. She wiped her hands on her jeans and did not call him back to look.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: Marguerite slit the envelope with a butter knife, the county seal staring up at her from the corner, and read the first line twice. "Dear Resident." Thirty-one years in this house, and they hadn't even bothered with her name. She set the knife down very precisely beside the saucer. Her jaw had gone tight, a hot prickle crawling up behind her ears as she read that her property tax appeal was denied on the grounds of "insufficient documentation of hardship." "Insufficient," she said aloud to the empty kitchen, flat and quiet. She smoothed the page, folded it into thirds, then unfolded it and read the signature, a printed scrawl with no face behind it. Her tea sat untouched and cooling. She stood, walked to the desk, and pulled out the fat folder of receipts she had mailed them in March. Every page was stamped. She laid it open, squared its edges, and reached for the phone, her thumb steady and white on the buttons.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver at Budapest Keleti glanced at the address I held out, then at my suitcase, and laughed, a short breath through his nose, before saying something to the man beside him that made them both look at my shoes. I kept my arm extended, paper trembling slightly. "It's a hotel," I said, slowly, each word clipped and cold. "Not a joke." My jaw had gone tight enough to ache. He shrugged, pointed at the meter, held up fingers I didn't trust. Heat crawled up my neck despite the November wind. I pulled the suitcase back against my shins, turned my shoulder to them, and walked past the whole line of cabs into the rain. Behind me someone called out, friendly or not, I couldn't tell. I didn't turn around. I gripped the handle until my knuckles whitened, rehearsing the perfect, devastating sentence I'd never be able to say in their language, and marched toward the tram map with my chin high.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the field in wide, stupid circles, ears flapping, and I kept my eyes on him so I wouldn't have to look at the woman on the bench. "Funny," I said, flat, when she repeated it. "He's actually a purebred." She had called him a mutt, then laughed and added "no offense," which everyone knows means the opposite. My jaw had gone tight enough that my molars ached. I zipped my jacket to the chin, though the afternoon was warm, and heat crawled up my neck. Biscuit dropped the stick at my feet, tongue lolling, trusting, and I picked it up without a word and threw it far, harder than I needed to. "Come," I called, too sharply, and he flinched. I clipped on his leash, nodded once toward the bench without turning my head, and walked the long way around, past the gate I never use.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marjorie stopped the run-through at bar twelve and said, "Perhaps the cellos could follow the soloist, just this once." She was looking at the ceiling fan, not at me. I kept my bow hovering above the string, my fingers gone cold and stiff against the neck of the violin. "Of course," I said, very pleasantly, and heard how thin it came out. The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Someone's folding chair squeaked. I turned a page I hadn't finished with, then turned it back, and my face burned all the way to my ears. Nine years I'd played the Pachelbel at this hall's Christmas concert, and she'd never once said just this once. I wrote her fingering suggestion in pencil, pressing so hard the lead snapped. When we started again I played every note exactly as marked, perfectly in time, and did not look up once. Afterward I packed my case slowly, clicked each latch shut, and left before the tea was poured.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta found the envelope taped under the lid of the toolbox, her name printed on it in Dale's blocky capitals, and inside was a price list. Chisels, forty dollars. Router, a hundred. Bench vise, negotiable. Beneath it, a note: Don't let Marta near the good planes, she'll just hang them on a wall. She read it standing very straight, jaw tight, the sawdust smell suddenly too thick in her throat. Twenty years of Saturdays she had spent in this room, holding boards steady, fetching coffee, learning the grain. She folded the paper into precise quarters, then again, until it wouldn't fold. "Just hang them on a wall," she said aloud to the pegboard, flat and quiet. Her ears burned. She picked up the smoothest plane, the one with his thumb-worn rosewood handle, and wrapped it in her scarf, harder than necessary. Then she put the price list in the trash, took it out, and put it back again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Marisol stood at the back of the crowd outside the biology corridor, arms folded so tightly her ribs ached, while the clerk taped the first sheet to the corkboard. "Don't crowd, please, alphabetical by student number," he said, and then, glancing at her, "Oh, you're the one who asked for a recount." He smiled like it was a joke. Her jaw locked. She heard her own voice come out flat and very polite: "Yes. I am." Heat crawled up her neck and settled in her ears. Behind her someone snickered, or maybe not; she didn't turn to check. She stared at the pinned paper instead of the names, counting the staples, four, five, six, while her thumbnail dug a crescent into her palm. When the line shifted she didn't move. Let them go ahead. She'd read her number when she was ready, and she'd never again thank that man for anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta kept her pace brisk on the ridge path, boots striking gravel harder than the slope required. Behind her, Dale's laugh from the trailhead still rang in her ears: *Maybe next time pick something more your speed.* Her jaw ached from clenching. The sun slid orange behind the pines, and the cold crept up her sleeves, but she refused to stop and pull out her jacket. She'd planned this route for weeks. She'd carried his water, too. "Fine," she muttered to a lichen-crusted boulder, then louder, "Totally fine." Her face burned despite the chill. She replayed the sentence, trimming it, sharpening her answers: three good ones, none of which she'd said aloud. A branch snagged her hair and she yanked free without untangling it. At the switchback she heard his voice calling her name, thin and far below. She tightened her pack straps, kept her eyes on the darkening trail, and climbed on without turning around, her breath coming hot and quick in the dusk.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Marisol pressed her knuckles into the dough harder than the recipe card asked for. Her grandmother's slanted handwriting, stained with decades of butter, said a handful of flour, a pinch of salt, bake till done. Fine. She had followed it exactly. Yet her aunt had stood in the kitchen doorway an hour ago, sniffed the air, and said, "Mama never made it that dense, you know. Maybe leave it to someone with the touch." Marisol had smiled, tight, and said, "Of course," in a voice so even it scared her. Now her jaw ached from clenching. Heat crept up her neck that had nothing to do with the oven. She slapped the dough onto the counter, flour puffing into the sunlight, and muttered, "The touch." She flipped the card over, half hoping for a note addressed to her. Nothing. She kneaded on, steadily, deliberately, and did not offer her aunt a single slice when the loaf came out golden.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was weighing two cans of tomatoes in the fluorescent hush of the grocery aisle when someone behind her said her name like a question. Dana Whitcomb, from tenth-grade chemistry, hair glossy, cart full of things with French labels. "Oh my God, you look exactly the same!" Dana said, and then, tilting her head, "Are you still doing that little bookkeeping thing?" Marisol set both cans back on the shelf, very gently, lining up their labels. Her jaw had gone tight, and heat crept up the back of her neck. "It's an accounting practice," she said, each word clipped and even. "Eleven clients. Two employees." Dana laughed and said that was so cute. Marisol smiled with her teeth only, gripped the cart handle until her knuckles paled, and said she had to run, though nothing in her basket was cold. At the end of the aisle she realized she'd left without the tomatoes, and she did not go back for them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum at 5:52, eight minutes shy of the long Thanksgiving weekend, and I'm restocking cough syrup when Mr. Dellwood leans over the counter and says, "Must be nice, getting paid to stand around." I keep my hands moving. Box, shelf, box. My jaw has gone tight enough that I can hear my molars. "Your prescription will be ready in four minutes," I say, each word set down flat like a coin. He laughs and checks his watch. Behind me the cooler clicks on, and I realize I've been gripping the scanner so hard my thumb has gone white. I've worked every holiday eve for six years. I skipped my sister's dinner for this. I print his label, staple the bag shut with a sharp thunk, and slide it across without looking up. "Happy Thanksgiving," I tell the register. My face feels hot all the way to my ears. When he's gone, I flip the sign to CLOSED and stand there, staring at my reflection in the glass, not blinking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B22 was forty minutes of sprinting behind me when I reached the counter, lungs raw, my bag strap cutting into my shoulder. The agent glanced at my boarding pass, then at me, and said, "Ma'am, you should have planned for delays." I set my palm flat on the counter so it wouldn't shake. "I did," I said, slow and quiet. "The delay was yours." Heat crawled up my neck and settled in my ears. She kept typing, not even looking up, and offered a voucher for a sandwich like I was a child to be handed a lollipop. I stared at the little paper rectangle. Behind me, someone sighed. I folded the voucher in half, then in half again, and slid it back across the glass. "Keep it. Please give me your name for the complaint." My jaw ached from holding my words in order. Through the window, the plane pulled away, unhurried, indifferent, shrinking to a white dot.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I dragged the roller through the last stripe of Harbor Mist and listened to my sister-in-law's voice replay in my head: "Oh, you picked that? Brave." She'd said it smiling, wine glass in hand, glancing at the wall I had spent three weekends taping. My jaw was still tight. I pressed the roller harder than I needed to, and paint spattered across my knuckles and the drop cloth. "Brave," I said to the empty room, flat and clipped, like handing back a coin. My neck was hot. I set the tray down, wiped my hands on my shirt, and stepped back. The color was soft and quiet and exactly right. I dipped the brush and cut the edge along the ceiling with a slow, steady hand, not breathing until the line was perfect. Then I put my phone face down on the ladder, unanswered.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in just as I set the mug down hard enough to slosh tea over my knuckles. I didn't wipe it. Through the screen door I could still hear Dana's laugh from the kitchen, easy, as if what she'd said about my cooking at dinner, in front of everyone, had been nothing. Rain hammered the porch roof. I kept my jaw so tight my teeth ached, and my thumbnail dug a crescent into the arm of the chair. When she called out, "You coming back in?" I said, "I'm fine," in the flat, clipped voice I use on telemarketers. Wind flung spray across my shins and I let it. Moving would have meant admitting something. Lightning lit the yard white, and I counted the seconds, one, two, three, composing the sentence I wouldn't say. Every version started with "Funny, because I made that for you." My face burned hotter than the tea ever had.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tire lever slips for the third time and skins my knuckle, and I swear under my breath, then glance at the door. Nobody. Just the dryer hum from Mrs. Okafor's side and the drip of something behind the shelves. I set the wrench down, pick it up again, set it down. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since I wheeled the bike in. Footsteps pass in the hallway and I freeze, thumb pressed on the chain link, listening until they fade. "Fine," I say aloud, too sharp, to no one. The garage smells of oil and damp cardboard. Someone has moved my toolbox six inches left, and I stare at it longer than I should. My pulse ticks in my ears while I thread the tube back through the rim, too fast, pinching it. I pull it out. Start over. Behind me a hinge squeaks, and I whip around, wrench raised like a fool, to find only a cat nosing through the gap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The shelter's glass is already speckled when I check my phone for the fourth time in two minutes. 7:42. The bus was due at 7:35. A gust drags a chip bag across the road and I track it all the way to the gutter, jaw tight, thumbnail picking at the skin beside my other thumbnail. The sky over the laundromat has gone the color of a bruise. "Come on," I mutter, then again, louder, to nobody. A man beside me unfolds his umbrella and the snap makes me flinch so hard my bag slides off my shoulder. "Sorry," I say, too fast, laughing a little. My heel keeps tapping the concrete. Thunder rolls somewhere far off and my stomach drops with it. I step out to peer down the street, get hit with cold drops, step back, step out again. Nothing. Just headlights, none of them the right ones. I check the time. 7:43. I read the schedule taped inside the shelter, though I know it by heart.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta had cleared the whole kitchen table before dragging the shoebox onto it, and still she wiped her palms on her jeans twice before lifting the lid. Rubber-banded bundles, brittle at the edges. The refrigerator hummed, then clicked off, and she flinched hard enough to knock a stack sideways. "Fine," she said to no one, too loudly. "Fine." She slid out the first envelope, saw her brother's slanted handwriting, and set it down again as though it were warm. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. A car passed outside, headlights sweeping the wall, and she stopped mid-breath until the sound faded. She checked the window latch. Then the door chain. Back at the table, she picked up the letter, put it down, picked up a different one, and read the same line four times without taking in a word. Her knee bounced against the table leg, rattling the spoon in the abandoned teacup, and every little clink made her shoulders climb toward her ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came twice, soft, and Marta's mug rattled against the saucer before she'd even stood. Through the peephole, Dale from next door, hands shoved in his jacket, rocking on his heels. She opened the door only as far as the chain allowed. "Ladder?" she repeated, too quickly. "Which ladder?" Her thumb worked at the doorframe, picking off a flake of paint. He said gutters, just an hour. She glanced past him at the street, empty and too quiet, then back at his boots. "It's heavy," she said. "Not sure where I put it." Her pulse thudded in her ears. She laughed, a short dry sound, and tucked her hair behind her ear twice. When he stepped back, she shut the door and stood listening to his footsteps fade, her palm damp against the wood, the ladder hanging exactly where it always hung in the garage.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol had wiped the same stretch of counter three times when the oven timer went off, and she flinched as if it had spoken her name. She yanked the tray out without a mitt, hissed, and shook her fingers under the tap. "Fine. Fine," she muttered to no one. The risotto needed stirring, so she stirred it, then stirred it again, though the rice had not changed. Her shirt clung between her shoulder blades. Every few seconds her eyes slid to the clock on the microwave: 6:41. Nineteen minutes. She tasted the sauce, frowned, added salt, tasted again, and added more. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it and made herself stop, but it crept back. A car passed outside, its headlights sweeping the wall, and she dropped the wooden spoon, which clattered across the tile. She stood looking at it, breathing through her nose, one hand pressed flat against her ribs where her heart was knocking. "It's just dinner," she said, too loudly, and picked the spoon up and kept going.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the countertop and I jerk my hand back from the dish I was drying. Ten digits, no name, a area code I don't recognize. I watch it crawl toward the edge of the counter. Three rings. Four. My thumb hovers, damp, leaving a smear on the glass. I realize I've stopped breathing and let it out through my teeth. The kitchen is too quiet; the fridge hum suddenly sounds loud. I glance at the window, at the dark driveway, then pull the blind down for no reason. Five rings. My pulse thuds in my ears. I pick it up, press it to my cheek, and say nothing at first. Then, too fast and too low, "Hello? Who is this?" A pause crackles on the line. My free hand has curled into the dish towel, wringing it like it owes me something. "Say something," I hear myself whisper, and I take a step back until my spine meets the cold refrigerator door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and the spine felt warmer than it should have. I stood outside the library doors for a full minute, retying a shoelace that was already tied. Inside, the air-conditioning hummed and every footstep sounded like mine. I kept shifting the book from one hand to the other, my palms damp against the cracked cover of *Principles of Microeconomics*. The desk was empty except for a stapler and a woman typing. I rehearsed my sentence twice under my breath, then blurted it anyway, too fast, too high: "Hi, this is, um, a little late." My laugh came out like a hiccup. She held out her hand, and I nearly dropped the book, catching it against my chest before sliding it across. My knee bounced against the counter's edge. When she glanced at the screen, I stopped breathing and stared at a poster about quiet study hours, reading the same line again and again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at four, and the door clicked shut behind them louder than I expected. I checked the lock. Then I checked it again, twisting the deadbolt until my knuckles went pale. Boxes crowded the studio, and I stood in the middle of them with my keys still bitten into my palm. Upstairs, someone dragged a chair, and my shoulders jumped to my ears. "Fine," I said out loud, to nobody, too brightly. "That's fine." I pulled the tape off the first box and stopped when the pipes knocked inside the wall. My heart was going like I'd run up all four flights again. I slid the dresser six inches to cover the window latch, then moved it back, then stood there chewing the inside of my cheek, listening to the hallway, counting footsteps that never reached my door. My tea went cold on the sill, untouched.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather, fat with use, and I stopped so fast my coffee sloshed over my knuckles. I didn't pick it up. I looked left at the joggers, right at the man feeding pigeons, then back at it. "Hello?" I said, too loud, to nobody. My voice cracked on the second syllable. A branch snapped somewhere and my shoulders jumped to my ears. I wiped my wet hand on my jeans, then wiped it again. Every pigeon seemed to be watching. Fine. I picked it up with two fingers like it might be hot, my pulse thudding in my neck as I flipped it open. A license, a photo of a kid with a gap-toothed grin, forty dollars. I checked behind me. Twice. Then I counted the bills, though I had no reason to, and counted them again, and couldn't make myself sit down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The kickboard is already slick in my hands, though I haven't touched the water yet. Dana, the instructor, says the shallow end is only four feet, and I laugh too loudly and say, "Right, four feet, great," then check the depth marker again. And again. My toes curl over the tiled edge. The chlorine smells sharp, and every splash from the kids' lane makes my shoulders jump toward my ears. I lower myself down one rung at a time, counting them aloud under my breath. Thirty-four years old, and my heart is knocking like I've been running. "Just put your face in," Dana says. I nod, take a breath that doesn't go all the way down, and keep one hand locked on the gutter. My knuckles have gone pale. Somebody drops a whistle on the deck and I flinch so hard water slaps my chin. "I'm fine," I tell her, before she's asked anything. My jaw aches from how long I've been clenching it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta read the seed packet for the fourth time, though she had memorized it: sow a quarter inch deep, thin to six inches. She crouched at the edge of the raised bed and pressed a finger into the soil, then pulled it out and checked the depth against her knuckle. Too deep? Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. A crow landed on the fence and she froze, trowel lifted, until it left. "Okay," she said aloud, too sharply, to nobody. She dropped three tomato seeds into one hole, then dug two back out with her fingernail because the packet said one. Her knee bounced against the mulch. The sky had gone gray at the edges, and she checked the forecast again, thumb damp on the screen. When the neighbor's gate clicked, she jerked upright, and dirt scattered from her palm across the rows she had just smoothed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marisol clicked her pen open, shut, open, shut, while Dev pulled up the first slide of the Hartwell rollout. The conference room hummed with the projector fan, and she kept catching its pitch rising whenever someone coughed. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but she lifted it anyway, set it down, lifted it again. When Dev said "launch date," her shoulders rose toward her ears and stayed there. She had told him the vendor numbers were soft. Had she told him loudly enough? Her knee bounced under the table until Priya glanced over, and she pressed her palm flat against it. "Sorry, go ahead," she said, too quickly, voice a half-step high. Her neck prickled each time the director leaned forward. On slide nine the budget chart appeared, and she stopped breathing mid-thought, eyes fixed on the third bar, waiting for someone else to notice it first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The headlights behind me have been there since the exit, same distance, same stubborn glow in the mirror. I slow to forty. They slow. My thumbs drum the wheel and I realize I've been gripping it so hard my fingers have gone pale and tingly. "Just pass," I mutter, then louder, "Pass me, come on." The road is empty farmland, black on both sides, one gas station sign flickering a mile off. I flick the radio off because the static sounds like whispering, then on again because the quiet is worse. My shoulders are up near my ears. When I finally turn onto my street, I don't signal, I just swing the wheel, and the lights sweep past and vanish. I sit in the driveway with the engine running, locking the doors twice, checking the mirror a third time, my heart still knocking against my ribs like it wants out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana pressed the elevator button three times, then a fourth, though the light was already glowing. On the fifth floor she walked the corridor with her keys clenched in her fist, the points biting her palm, and read the same laminated sign about hand sanitizer twice without absorbing it. Room 512. Her uncle's door stood half open. She knocked anyway, too hard, and laughed at the sound. "Hi. Hey. It's just me," she said, fast, her voice a notch higher than she meant. The monitor beeped and she flinched, then pretended to study the window blinds. Her knee bounced against the vinyl chair. She stood, sat, stood again, straightened his blanket that was already straight. "Did they say when the doctor's coming? Because I can find someone. I can go ask." Her mouth was dry, her shirt stuck between her shoulder blades, and every footstep in the hall made her turn her head toward the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell is still four minutes off, and I've already checked my phone six times. I stand by the fence instead of the bench, keys biting into my palm, jaw working at nothing. A mother beside me says something about the weather, and I answer "Yeah, totally," too fast, not having heard her. My heartbeat is loud in my ears. Every white SUV that slows at the curb makes my head snap around. I scan the faces of the other parents, then the gate, then the parking lot, then the gate again. Last week there was that note about a man near the playground, and I keep rereading it in my head. My knee won't stop bouncing. When the doors finally bang open and the first wave of backpacks spills out, I rise onto my toes, and my breath catches, and I realize I've been counting the red jackets. Not hers. Not hers. Wait. Not hers. My hand is already half raised, shaking a little, ready to wave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marlene had rearranged the oak dresser three times before eight o'clock, and now she straightened the price sticker again, pressing its corner flat with a thumbnail. A car slowed at the curb and her head snapped toward it; it drove on. She exhaled through her teeth. "Everything's negotiable," she told a man fingering the rocking chair, too quickly, too loud, then added, "Well, not the chair. Maybe the chair." Her coffee had gone cold in the mug she kept lifting and not drinking. The man's hand drifted toward the sideboard drawer and she stepped between him and it, laughing thinly. "Sticks a little. I'll get it." Her jaw ached. Her heel tapped the driveway in a small steady drumming she couldn't make stop. Every footstep on the gravel pulled her shoulders closer to her ears. Behind her, the kitchen window reflected the whole sale, and she kept glancing at it, counting the people, then counting them again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped for the third time and I swore, louder than the empty basement deserved. Water beaded at the joint under the sink, one fat drop every two seconds, and I counted them like they were a clock running down. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the landlord's voicemail. "Fine," I muttered, "fine, fine," wiping my palms on my jeans, which only left them wetter. Every creak upstairs made my head snap toward the stairs. I'd already checked my phone four times, though nothing was going to ring. I wrapped the tape around the threads, too tightly, then unwrapped it and started over because my hands were shaking and the layers looked crooked. My heart thudded in my ears, drowning out the drip for a second, and when it came back I flinched. I tightened the nut a quarter turn. Then another. Then I stood there, breath held, staring at the dry spot beneath it, not trusting it at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had been leaning against the fruit bowl since Tuesday, its little window showing Marisol's name in blocky type. She picked it up, put it down, and wiped her palms on her jeans. The kettle clicked off and she ignored it. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, too loudly, and slid a butter knife under the flap. Halfway along, she stopped to check the clock on the stove. Her pulse thudded in her thumb where it pinched the paper. She unfolded the page and read the first line three times without taking in a word, then realized she was holding her breath and let it out in a short, shaky laugh. Her jaw ached. Somewhere upstairs a pipe knocked, and she flinched hard enough to knock the knife off the counter. It clattered on the tile. She didn't bend to pick it up. She just kept reading, one finger sliding down the margin, lips moving silently.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station doors hissed open and the noise hit me all at once: loudspeakers, rolling suitcases, a language that slid past my ears like water. I kept my backpack on my chest, one hand clamped over the zipper. My phone said 4% and I'd checked it three times in the last minute. A man stepped close to ask me something, and I jerked back so fast I clipped a woman's bag. "Sorry, sorry, sorry," I said, too loudly, then again, quieter, as if volume was the problem. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the platform. The ticket machine blinked symbols I couldn't read. I pressed one, cancelled it, then stood with my thumb hovering while a line grew behind me and my shirt stuck to my spine. Every sign seemed to be shouting at someone else. I pulled out the crumpled hotel address, smoothed it against my knee, and read it again, though I'd memorized it hours ago. My heartbeat kept pace with the flashing board overhead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta kept the leash wound twice around her fist even though Biscuit was forty yards off, nose down in the clover. A truck rattled along the distant road and her shoulders jumped before she could stop them. She counted the dog's circles aloud, under her breath, then lost count and started over. The grass hissed in the wind, and every hiss made her glance at the tree line, at the gap in the fence, at the gap again. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it and unclenched, and it tightened back. 'Biscuit,' she called, too bright, too quick. 'Here. Come. Good boy, come.' He ignored her and bounded after a bee. Her thumb rubbed the leash's rough stitching until the skin burned. A crow lifted from the fence post and she took three steps forward without deciding to. 'Okay,' she said to no one. 'Okay, that's enough, that's plenty.' Her palms were damp. She didn't sit on the bench.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite had wiped the cello's neck twice before the church hall's folding chairs were even set out. Now she sat with the bow hovering, listening to the radiator tick, and began the Saint-Saëns again from bar one. Her left hand clenched at the first shift and she stopped, shaking out her fingers. "Sorry. Sorry, again from the top," she said, too brightly, to the empty rows. A stack of programs rustled when the door sighed in the draft, and she flinched hard enough that the endpin skidded on the floorboards. Her pulse thudded in her ears, loud as a kick drum. She swallowed; her mouth tasted like pennies. Mr. Alvarez, the pianist, glanced up from his score and asked if she wanted a break. "No, no, I'm fine, just one more," she said, already tightening her bow hair, already checking the tuner clipped beside her, though she had checked it a minute ago and it had not changed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The first box I fill is the wrong one, so I unpack it and start again, and my hands won't stay still long enough to tape it. Every time the furnace ticks I turn toward the door. Nobody's there. Marcus's coffee can of screws is on the bench, and I pick it up, put it down, pick it up again. "Just the sawdust," I say aloud, too loudly, to the empty room, when a draft lifts a curl of pine across the floor. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the driveway. I check my phone, though no one is calling. His apron still hangs on its nail, bent at the shoulder where he'd shrug it off, and I walk wide around it, sleeves pulled over my knuckles. I tell myself twenty minutes, then I'll go. I've said that three times. The tape screeches off the roll and I flinch like it was a voice behind me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, so at 11:52 I was already standing in the hallway outside the department office, refreshing my phone with a thumb gone slick. The corkboard was still bare except for a flyer about a lost umbrella. I read it three times. My knee kept bouncing until a girl beside me glanced down at it, and I pressed my palm flat on my leg like I was holding down a lid. "Do they ever actually post on time?" I asked, too loud, and my voice cracked on the last word. Nobody answered. I peeled the cap off my water bottle, drank, screwed it back on, then did it again a minute later without remembering why. The clock ticked to 11:58. My stomach turned over. When the secretary finally came out holding a stapler and a single sheet of paper, I realized I'd stopped breathing, and I couldn't make myself step forward first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid behind the ridge, and I checked my phone again, as if the time might have changed its mind. Four more miles. I'd stopped chewing the granola bar halfway and shoved the rest in my pocket. Every snapped twig made my head jerk left, then right, and my fingers had gone white around the trekking pole. "Just a deer," I said out loud, too brightly, and the sound of my own voice made it worse. My shirt was sticking to my spine despite the cold. I caught myself walking faster, nearly jogging, then froze when gravel shifted somewhere behind me. I held my breath until my ears rang. Nothing. A branch creaked. I dug the headlamp out, fumbled it twice, and clicked it on, sweeping the beam over trunks that all looked like shoulders. "Okay," I muttered. "Okay, okay." My heartbeat thudded in my throat the whole way down the trail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, and Grandma's slanted pencil says only "flour till it feels right." I read it a fourth time anyway. My knee bounces against the cabinet. The oven timer ticks, though I haven't set it for anything, and I keep glancing at it like it might lie to me. I check the yeast, then check it again, nudging the foam with a spoon. "Come on," I mutter, too sharp, to a bowl. When my phone buzzes, I flinch and knock salt across the counter. I sweep it into my palm, then stand there with my fist closed, forgetting where to throw it. Dough sticks to my fingers, and I scrape at it, breathing through my teeth. Does this feel right? I press it. It springs back slowly. I press it again. The kitchen smells like her house, and my throat tightens. I cover the bowl with a towel and uncover it two minutes later, just to look.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding two cans of tomatoes I didn't need when I heard my name, bright and rising, from the end of aisle six. Dana Whitlock. Tenth-grade chemistry, the girl who'd watched me bomb that presentation. My thumb found the edge of a can's label and started peeling it. "Hey! Wow," I said, too loudly, and the fluorescent lights hummed back at me. She was smiling. I checked her hands, her cart, the exit sign over her shoulder. "Yeah, no, I'm good, work's good," I answered before she'd finished asking. My shirt stuck between my shoulder blades. I laughed at something she said a beat late, then realized I'd been nodding for several seconds. The cans were sweating in my palms. "I should, uh, my car's in a weird spot," I said, already backing away, a wheel of her cart squeaking behind me like a question. I left the tomatoes on the cereal shelf.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol had wiped the same stretch of counter three times before she noticed the rag had gone cold in her fist. Four more hours until the pharmacy shutters came down for Christmas, and every time the door chimed her shoulders jumped toward her ears. 'Be right with you,' she said, too bright, too fast, to a man who hadn't even looked up yet. Her pulse ticked in her throat. She straightened the candy rack, then straightened it again, aligning the labels like they might be inspected. The fluorescent hum seemed louder than it had at noon. When the phone rang she let it go two rings, three, staring at it, her jaw tight enough to ache, before she snatched it up and said, 'Pharmacy,' and then, softer, to no one, 'Please don't be a refill problem.' Her knee bounced under the register. The clock hadn't moved. She was sure of it. She checked her watch to confirm, and it hadn't either.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The plane doors open eleven minutes late, and I'm already standing, bag clamped under my arm, jaw working at nothing. "Excuse me, sorry, excuse me," I say to the man in 14C, though it comes out clipped, almost a bark. The jet bridge feels a mile long. I check my phone: Gate B42, boarding closes at 4:05. I'm at C9. My thumb keeps tapping the screen as if the numbers might rearrange themselves. Somewhere past the pretzel kiosk I break into a jog, and my heart is slamming against my ribs, my shirt sticking cold between my shoulder blades. A stroller blocks the walkway. I step around it, mutter something unkind, then whisper, "Sorry, sorry," to nobody. The moving walkway is too slow, so I walk on it, then run. Every gate number blurs. What if they've given away my seat? What if the screen is wrong? My mouth is dry as paper. I can hear my own breath, ragged, loud over the announcements, and I can't swallow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the same strip of baseboard three times, peeling it off each time because the edge didn't look straight enough. The roller hissed against the wall, and she stopped mid-stroke when the pipes knocked somewhere behind the plaster. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears; she pushed them down and they crept right back. Every time the phone buzzed on the windowsill she snapped her head toward it, though it was only the weather app. "Fine," she said aloud to the empty room, too sharply, and then again, quieter, "Fine." A drip of Soft Linen slid down the roller handle toward her wrist, and she watched it a full second before wiping it, her jaw so tight her teeth ached. She'd already checked the clock four times in ten minutes. When the front door creaked downstairs, only the wind, she realized she was gripping the paint tray rim hard enough to leave white fingerprints in the tin, and she couldn't remember when she had picked it up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while I was still holding the lemonade, and I set it down so fast it sloshed over my knuckles. I didn't wipe it off. The porch boards were slick with blown rain, and I'd already moved my chair back twice, though the roof covered me fine. Every time the screen door ticked in the wind I turned my head. "It's just the latch," I said aloud, too sharply, to nobody. My phone lay face-up on my knee; I checked it, put it down, checked it again. No messages. My jaw ached, and I realized I'd been grinding my teeth since the first flash lit the maple across the road. The air tasted like pennies. When the next crack split overhead, my whole body jerked, and the ice in the glass rattled. I counted the seconds after the light. One, two. Closer. I stood, sat, stood again, and pressed my palms flat against my thighs to keep them from drumming.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The bent derailleur hanger lies in my palm like a tiny question mark, and I grin at it anyway. Mrs. Okafor's table saw hums behind the tarp, someone's radio fights it, and I wedge my frame deeper into the stand, humming along off-key. Grease runs down my wrist. I let it. "Okay, old girl," I tell the bike, tapping the top tube, "Saturday, you and me, the river path." I'm already picturing it. The replacement part is in the mail, the tire holds air, and my shoulders feel loose, my feet practically bouncing on the cold concrete. When Dev from unit four leans in and asks if it's salvageable, I answer before he finishes. "Totally. Give me a week." I spin the crank and listen to the chain tick, steady, nearly sweet. Then I wipe my hands, line up my wrenches by size, and start the next bolt like it's the easy one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drop lands on my wrist, and I laugh, actually laugh, at nobody in particular. Across the street the sky has gone the color of pewter, but I'm still tapping my foot to the song stuck in my head. The wind flips my collar up; I let it. When the woman beside me groans and clutches her tote over her hair, I tell her, "Bus is always quicker in the rain, you'll see." I don't know if that's true. I say it anyway, warm and easy. Water beads on my eyelashes, and my shoulders sit loose, my chest open to the cold smell of wet pavement. I check the schedule once, shrug, and tuck my phone away. Thunder rolls somewhere far off, and I grin at it. Tonight there's soup waiting, and tomorrow the interview. Down the road, two headlights smear through the downpour, and I'm already stepping toward the curb, hand half raised, ready.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marisol dragged the shoebox into the window light and cracked the lid with her thumbnail, humming before she'd even seen what was inside. Dust rose and she waved it off, grinning. The envelopes were soft as cloth, tied in bundles with kitchen string, and she slid the first one free as if unwrapping a present. "Oh, Aunt Dolores, look at your handwriting," she said aloud, tracing the loops. She sorted them by postmark into neat rows across the rug, tapping each pile twice. Her knees ached from kneeling, but she only shifted and kept going. One letter mentioned a failed garden; she laughed, thinking of the tomatoes she'd planted last week. Maybe these would end up in a book, or a frame on the hallway wall. She pulled out a pen, wrote tomorrow's date on a sticky note, and pressed it to the lid. Sunlight warmed the back of her neck. She reached for the next envelope, already leaning forward, ready for whatever it said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Gus knocked while I was still in my socks, rinsing the coffee pot, and I opened the door grinning before he'd said a word. "Ladder?" he asked, rubbing his neck. "Gutters are packed with maple leaves." "Take the tall one," I said. "The short one wobbles, but the tall one's a champ." Sun spilled across the porch boards, warm on my bare ankles, and I caught myself humming as I dragged the ladder out of the garage, its aluminum cool and light in my hands. Gus laughed that I seemed pleased to lose it. "Keep it all week," I told him. "Honestly, when you're done, come over. My gutters are next, and with two of us we'll be finished by lunch. I'll make pancakes." He lifted the ladder onto his shoulder, and I stood watching him cross the lawn, already picturing the clean, clear spouts and the rain running right where it should.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol propped the kitchen window open with a wooden spoon and let the cold air chase the steam out. The risotto still needed twenty minutes, the bread was half a shade from golden, and the doorbell was due in forty, yet she hummed as she stirred, hips swaying against the counter. She tasted, nodded, and added one more pinch of salt with a flourish. "Perfect," she told the cat, who blinked at her from the stool. A drop of stock had landed on her sleeve; she laughed and left it there. She shook out the good linen napkins, folded them into rough triangles, and didn't bother redoing the crooked ones. Her shoulders felt loose, her breath slow and wide. When the timer shrieked, she was already reaching for the oven mitt, grinning. Tonight the table would be crowded and loud, and she could almost hear the chairs scraping. She lit the candles early, just to see how the room would glow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the windowsill, skittering between a jar of basil and a stack of unopened mail, and Marisol glanced at the screen: a number she'd never seen, area code from two states away. She dried her hands on her apron, unhurried, a half-smile already tugging at her mouth. Her thumb found the green button on the second ring. "Hello, this is Marisol," she said, her voice bright and loose, the way it sounded when she was already halfway to laughing. She pressed the phone between ear and shoulder and kept chopping, humming a few bars of something while the line crackled. Maybe it was the gallery in Tucson. Maybe the interview she'd nearly forgotten. Her pulse ticked quick and pleasant under her collar. "Oh, I've got all afternoon," she told the silence, then leaned toward the sunlight pooling on the counter. "Go ahead. Tell me everything."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
