Her palms were damp against the handle. There were outlets to unscrew, holes to patch, a ceiling that suddenly looked yellow beside the fresh color. She sat down on an overturned bucket, paint on her wrist, and stared at the unfinished corner while her phone buzzed twice on the floor, unanswered, and her tea went cold on the ladder's top step.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder rattles the screen door, and I've already read the same line of the letter four times. Rain slants under the porch roof and spots my knees, but I don't move them. My phone buzzes against the boards: Mom, then the landlord, then Dana. I flip it face down. My heart is going like I've climbed stairs, though I haven't stood in an hour. "Okay," I say out loud to nobody, "okay, okay," and the word keeps coming out thinner. I press my palms flat on my thighs to stop them shaking and count the porch slats, lose track at eleven, start again. The wind drags the wet smell of cut grass across my face. Somewhere a gutter overflows, gurgling, and I grip the chair arm as if it might carry me off. The list in my head is a mess of tangled wire. I pull my feet up, wrap my arms around my shins, and press my forehead to my knees until the thunder returns.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The wrench slips off the bolt for the third time and my knuckles crack against the crank. I barely feel it. Through the garage wall I can hear Mr. Okafor's truck rumbling up the driveway, and the bike's back wheel is lying in three pieces across his half of the floor. "Okay, okay, okay," I mutter, snatching ball bearings from the oil-black concrete, counting them under my breath and losing count at eleven. My shirt sticks to my spine. The little spring I need is nowhere, and my hands shake so badly the cone nut skitters away under the shelf. I drop to my stomach, cheek on the cold grit, sweeping an arm into the dark. Dust. A dead moth. The engine cuts off outside. A door slams. "Please," I whisper to nobody, to the shelf, to the spring, and my heart is knocking so hard against the floor I swear it echoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as Mara checked her phone for the fourth time in a minute. 6:52. The bus had been due at 6:40. She stepped out from under the plastic overhang, squinted down the empty road, stepped back, then out again. Her thumbnail was already bitten to the quick. Wind shoved a flap of her coat against her legs, and the sky to the west had gone the color of a bruise. "Come on, come on, come on," she whispered, then louder, to no one, "It said six-forty." Her heart knocked against her ribs so hard she pressed her palm there, as if to quiet it. The interview file in her bag was getting damp; she clutched the bag to her chest, shoved her hand inside, pulled it out, checked the phone again. Thunder rolled. Her breath came short and shallow, her knees bounced, and she began, absurdly, to calculate whether she could run the nine miles.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta tipped the shoebox across the bedspread and started flipping envelopes faster than she could read the postmarks. Not this one. Not this one. Her thumbnail snagged and tore a flap, and she barely noticed. Downstairs the front door clicked, and her head jerked up, breath caught somewhere behind her collarbone. "Just a minute!" she called, voice pitched too high, too bright. Her palms were slick; a letter slid out of her grip and fluttered under the bed. She dropped to her knees, cheek nearly to the floorboards, groping through dust. Footsteps on the stairs. Her heart knocked against her ribs so hard she could hear it in her ears. There, the blue envelope, her sister's looping handwriting. She shoved it into her waistband, scooped the rest back into the box, and sat on the lid, grinning at the doorway, her knee bouncing like a sewing machine needle.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Alvarez was still holding the door when Dana said, "Hey, could I borrow your ladder? Just for the gutters." Marcus's thumb found the doorknob and rubbed it raw. "The ladder," he said. "Right. Yes. Ladder." His laugh came out too high, and he coughed to cover it. Behind him, the garage hummed, and in the garage, under the blue tarp, lay the ladder, along with the thing he'd shoved beside it last night. His shirt clung between his shoulder blades. "It's, um, it's not here. Lent it. Out. To my brother." Dana glanced past his shoulder at the garage door, ajar. Marcus stepped sideways to block it, knocking a shoe off the rack. He crouched to fix it, hands trembling, heart thudding in his ears, and spoke to the floor. "Tomorrow? Maybe tomorrow. I'll bring it myself. Don't come in. Don't—I'll bring it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The oven clock said 6:42, and Marisol had been staring at the raw chicken for what felt like a full minute. Seven o'clock. She yanked the door open and the heat slapped her face, but the rack was cold, the oven barely warm. "No, no, no," she whispered, then louder, to nobody, "You said you were preheated." Her hands shook as she cranked the dial higher, and a drop of sweat slid down her spine. The rice was boiling over; she grabbed the pot lid without a mitt and hissed, dropping it with a clang. Her heart thudded in her ears, drowning out the radio. She chopped parsley too fast, the knife skidding near her thumb, and her breath came in short, shallow sips. Out front, a car door slammed. She froze, dripping spoon in hand, and called in a thin, high voice, "Just a minute!" though no one had knocked yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter at 11:48 p.m., and Marisol's spatula clattered into the sink. Unknown number. An area code she didn't recognize. She wiped her wet hands on her shirt, missed, wiped again. Her thumb hovered, trembling, over the green circle. Her brother hadn't answered since Tuesday. "Don't be the hospital, don't be the hospital," she whispered, the words coming out in pieces. The ringing kept on. Her heart thudded so hard she could feel it in her teeth, and the tile seemed to tilt under her bare feet. She pressed the phone to her ear, pulled it away, pressed it back. "Hello?" Her voice cracked high and thin. "Hello? Who is this? Say something, please, I can hear someone breathing, no, that's me, that's me." She gripped the counter edge until her knuckles went pale, the burner still hissing behind her, the onions beginning to blacken, forgotten.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and the return slot looked smaller than I remembered. I stood in front of it holding Principles of Organic Chemistry with both hands, thumbs slick against the cracked cover. My shirt stuck to my back. I pushed the book halfway in, yanked it out, and checked the date slip again, as if the numbers might have changed. The librarian glanced up. I laughed, a high, stupid sound, and said, "Hi, so, funny story, I think this is, um, a little bit, it's maybe, eight months?" My knees felt loose. I kept wiping my palm on my jeans. She reached out, and I almost pulled the book back to my chest. "Is there a fine? Don't tell me the number. Actually, tell me. No. Wait." The fluorescent lights hummed louder than they should have, and my heart knocked against my ribs like it wanted out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The couch wouldn't fit through the door, and Marisol had already turned it three ways before she noticed her hands were shaking against the fabric. "It measured fine," she told the empty hallway, too fast, too high. She dropped the cushion, picked it up, dropped it again. The studio was eleven steps long; she counted them twice, then a third time, as if the number might grow. Boxes labeled KITCHEN, BOOKS, MISC blocked the window, and the air smelled of paint and somebody else's cooking. Her shirt stuck to her back. Her heartbeat thudded in her ears so loudly she almost missed the landlord's voice on the stairs saying the truck had to be gone by noon. She checked her phone: 11:22. Checked it again: 11:22? No, 11:23. "Okay. Okay okay okay." She yanked the couch leg, felt something crack, and laughed, a short, dry bark, then pressed her palm flat to her sternum and tried to remember how breathing usually went.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench slats like it had been waiting for me, brown leather, fat with cards, and my hand jerked back before I'd even decided to touch it. I spun around. A jogger, a stroller, a man with a pigeon-colored dog, nobody looking my way, which somehow felt worse. My pulse banged in my ears. I picked it up anyway, and my palms left damp prints on the leather. "Hello?" I called, too high, too fast. "Did somebody lose... hello?" A woman glanced over and kept walking. I flipped it open and saw a driver's license, a stranger's smiling face, and a thick fold of twenties, and I snapped it shut like it had bitten me. My knees wouldn't hold still. I shoved it in my jacket, pulled it out again, then held it in both hands and turned in circles, whispering, "Okay, okay, okay," while my phone slid out of my slippery fingers and clattered onto the path.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor lets go of my elbow, and the floor of the pool tilts away like a trapdoor. My toes scrabble for tile that isn't there. I'm thirty-eight years old, and I'm clawing at the lane rope with both hands, knuckles gone the color of candle wax. "I'm fine," I say, but it comes out high and thin, a whistle through a crack. Chlorine burns the back of my nose. My heart is slamming so hard I can feel it in my teeth, and every breath I take is short, stolen, too shallow to reach anywhere. Somewhere a whistle blows, kids shriek, the water slaps the gutters, all of it too loud and too close. "Kick," she says. I can't remember which part of me kicks. My legs have turned to wet rope. I haul myself hand over hand toward the wall, gulping, and when my fingers hit the concrete edge I hold on like it might leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet says "plant after last frost," and I've read it eleven times, and I still don't know when that is. My hands are shaking so badly the tomato seeds spill across the dirt in a clump. "No, no, no," I whisper, pinching them up one by one, grinding soil under my nails. Sweat runs down my back though the morning is cool. Did I dig the rows deep enough? I crouch, stand, crouch again, measuring with my thumb, then my whole palm, then the trowel handle. My heart is thudding in my ears. The neighbor waves over the fence and I answer too loudly, "Fine! Everything's fine! Just, you know, gardening!" My laugh cracks in the middle. I phone my mother, hang up before she answers, and open the phone's search bar to type "how long until seeds die." The hose is still running into the grass, a spreading dark puddle I haven't noticed yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to slide four, and I realized she was presenting my numbers. Mine. The ones I'd pasted into the shared folder at midnight without double-checking the quarter column. My pen had stopped moving; the ink pooled into a dot on my notepad. The conference room was too bright, and the air vent hummed right over my neck, though sweat still crawled down between my shoulder blades. I pressed my thumbnail into my palm until it hurt. 'Great,' I heard myself say, too loud, when no one had asked anything. Heads turned. I coughed, laughed at nothing, and reached for my water, but the cup was already empty, so I lifted it anyway and pretended to sip. Dana's laser dot slid toward the bar I knew was wrong. My knee bounced under the table, rattling the cheap laminate. Three seconds. Two. I opened my mouth, and nothing came out but a thin, dry click.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The headlights in the mirror had been there since the exit, and Dana's fingers had gone white on the wheel. She turned onto Alder Street, though it wasn't her turn, and watched the lights swing after her. "Okay," she whispered, "okay, okay, okay." Her heart knocked against her ribs so hard she felt it in her teeth. The dashboard clock read 1:47. Every house she passed was dark, every porch empty. She lifted her foot off the gas, then slammed it down again, and the engine whined. Her phone lay face-down on the passenger seat, and she reached for it without looking, knocking it into the footwell. "No, no, come on." Sweat prickled cold along her spine. She ran a yellow light, then a red one, gulping air that didn't seem to reach her chest. At the gas station's bright canopy she jerked the wheel, tires squealing, and leaned on the horn until a clerk looked up through the glass. Behind her, the other car rolled slowly past and was gone. She couldn't make her hands let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator opens on four and I'm already walking the wrong way, then the right way, my sneakers squeaking on the floor. Room 412. I check the number on the paper again, though it's been in my fist so long the ink has smeared into my palm. The vending machine hums. Somewhere a monitor beeps, and I count the beeps, then lose count, then start over. 'Sorry, sorry,' I say to a nurse who hasn't even looked at me. My shirt is stuck to my back. I wipe my hands on my jeans, twice, and the flowers I brought are crushed where I gripped them. Grandpa's door is half open. I can see his foot under the blanket, just the foot, and my throat closes around the word I rehearsed in the car. I put my hand on the frame. It won't stop shaking, so I press harder, and I can't make my legs go in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell had rung eleven minutes ago, and Dana still hadn't seen the green backpack. She stood on her toes at the fence, dropped back, rose again, phone clenched so hard the case creaked. Children streamed past in yellow jackets, none of them Theo. "Excuse me," she said to the woman beside her, too loud, too quick, "did the second graders come out already? Room twelve?" Her tongue felt thick and dry. The woman shrugged. Dana's pulse thudded in her ears, drowning the shrieks of the playground. She checked the phone again, as though the screen might have changed in four seconds, typed with shaking thumbs, deleted it, typed again. Her knees wouldn't stay still. Maybe he was in the office. Maybe the bus. Maybe she'd read the calendar wrong. She pushed toward the gate, muttering "sorry, sorry, sorry" to shoulders, breath shallow, eyes sweeping every small head, every single one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man lifts the lid of Grandma's oak dresser and I'm across the driveway before I decide to move, sandals slapping the concrete. "Not that one, sorry, that's not for sale," I say, too fast, too high. The sticker says $40. I put it there myself this morning. My palms are slick, and I wipe them on my shorts twice. "Wait, let me check something." I yank the bottom drawer so hard it nearly drops. Under the folded newspaper sits the envelope, thick, still sealed, Dad's handwriting on the front. My pulse is thudding in my ears so loudly I barely hear him ask if forty is firm. I press the envelope against my ribs and laugh, a thin, cracking sound. "Forty. Yes. Fine. Take it." The sun is merciless on my neck. Behind me a woman carries off the lamp, and I stare at every box on the lawn, wondering what else I've already let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The water found the gap between Dana's fingers again, and she pressed harder, as if the pipe might be argued into stillness. Cold ran up her sleeve and soaked her ribs. "Okay, okay, okay," she said, too high, too fast, to no one. The wrench slipped from her wet hand and clanged somewhere behind the paint cans; she didn't dare look for it. Her knees were drumming against the cabinet floor. Under the sink, the flashlight rolled, throwing its beam in wild swings across the ceiling of the cabinet. She could hear her own breath, short and ragged, louder than the hiss. The shutoff valve. Where was the shutoff valve? She had lived here six years. Her thumb throbbed with her pulse. A puddle crept toward the hallway rug, and she lunged, one hand still clamped on the pipe, to drag a towel with her foot, kicking the bucket over instead. "No. No, no, no. Please," she said, to the pipe, to the ceiling, to the dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a window and a federal seal, and Marisol held it under the kitchen light as though the glare might reveal what was inside. Her thumb slid under the flap, stopped, slid back. She wiped her palm on her jeans, twice. "It's probably nothing," she told the empty room, too loudly, and the refrigerator hummed back. The paper tore crooked. Her ears were ringing, and the tiles seemed colder through her socks. She unfolded the page, read the first line, and realized she had read it without taking in a single word. Again. Her breath came in short sips. The coffee she'd poured sat untouched, a skin forming on top. Somewhere in the second paragraph she noticed she was gripping the counter with her free hand, knuckles pale, and that she had been backing toward the door for no reason at all. "Okay," she whispered. "Okay, okay, okay." She dropped the letter, picked it up, and started over from the top.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station doors hissed shut behind me and the sound of the crowd closed over my head like water. Every sign was a row of curling characters that slid off my eyes. I patted my jacket: passport, passport, where is the passport, there. Again, there. My phone said 4% and the little battery blinked red. I walked left, then stopped, then walked right, my suitcase wheel clacking loud as a snare drum. A man in a uniform said something fast and kind-sounding, and I heard myself say, "Hotel, hotel, sorry, hotel," far too high, holding up a screenshot with a thumb that wouldn't stay still. He pointed. I nodded too many times. My shirt was stuck to my spine, my mouth tasted like pennies, and swallowing took two attempts. The address on the screen suddenly looked like nothing at all. I turned in a full circle, counting exits, losing count, starting over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit was a gold blur against the tall grass one second, and the next there was only grass. I stopped mid-sentence, my coffee tipping out of the cup and scalding my wrist, and I didn't feel it until later. "Biscuit?" My voice came out thin and cracked, so I tried again, louder, then louder. The wind pushed the stalks flat and let them spring back, flat and back, hiding everything. My heart was slamming so hard I could hear it in my ears over the whistle I fumbled to my lips. No sound came out; my mouth was too dry. I ran, boots catching in the ruts, scanning the fence line, the creek, the gap in the hedge I'd meant to mention to someone. Every dark shape was a rock, a stump, a coat. "Please, please, come on, bud," I kept saying, to nobody, to the field. My hands wouldn't stop shaking. Then a tail rose out of the weeds, wagging, and my knees nearly gave out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells like floor wax and burnt coffee, and I've already started the Schubert twice. "Sorry, again, from the top," I say, too brightly, and my voice comes out thin, like it's been pulled through a straw. My fingers are slick on the keys. Mrs. Okafor, folding chairs near the back, pretends not to watch. Bar nine. My left hand lurches ahead of my right, and I stop, pressing both palms flat against my thighs to make them quit shaking. Thursday. The concert is Thursday, forty folding chairs, my neighbors, my old teacher. My heart is knocking so hard I can feel it in my teeth. I laugh at nothing. I check my watch, then check it again, then flip the pages backward to see whether the notes have changed since I last looked. "Maybe I should cut the second movement," I say to no one, already reaching for the pencil, already sweating through my good blouse, already starting over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The third drawer of Walt's workbench stuck, so I yanked it, and chisels sprayed across the concrete like dropped cutlery. My hands wouldn't stop shaking as I scooped them up, and I cut my thumb anyway. 'Fine, fine, it's fine,' I said aloud to nobody, too fast, too high. The dumpster outside was already half full, and his daughter was coming at noon, and I still hadn't found the box. The one he'd made me promise about. I tore through coffee cans of screws, flipped over a sawhorse, checked behind the paint shelf, my shirt sticking to my back. Sawdust hung in the light. My breath came shallow, snagging. Had I thrown it out? The blue tarp, the bags I'd tied this morning. I ran, boots slapping, and ripped the first bag open with both hands, dumping it on the gravel, kneeling in his shavings, whispering, 'Please, please, please, come on.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said 9:00, and my laptop clock said 8:58, so I refreshed anyway. Nothing. I refreshed again. My thumb had gone slick against the trackpad, and I wiped it on my pajama pants, then wiped the other one too. "Okay," I said aloud to the empty dorm room, too fast, too high. "Okay, okay, okay." The radiator ticked and I jumped, knocking my knee on the desk. I stood up, sat down, stood up. My heart was hammering somewhere up near my ears, and the cold tea I'd poured at seven sat untouched, a skin forming on top. I opened the page. Spinning wheel. I shut the laptop halfway, then yanked it open again, my breath coming in short little sips that never seemed to reach the bottom of my chest. What if I'd flipped the answer on question twelve? I started to chew my thumbnail, tasted blood, and kept chewing. The page loaded. I couldn't make my eyes move down the screen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Dana checked her phone again, though the screen still read no service, and the battery had slipped to nine percent. The pines had stopped looking like trees and become a wall of black teeth. She had passed this same split boulder, hadn't she? Her boots slapped the dirt faster, then she was half-running, pack straps biting, breath sawing in her throat. "Okay. Okay okay okay," she muttered, voice thin and cracking. A branch snapped somewhere to her left and she froze, heart hammering so hard she felt it in her teeth. Her hands shook as she fumbled the headlamp from the side pocket, dropped it, scrabbled in the leaves for it. The beam jittered across the trail markers, none of them familiar. Sweat went cold along her spine. "Left. It was left at the creek," she said aloud, then, "No. No, it wasn't," and turned in a full circle while the last orange light drained from the ridge.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is stained with butter, and Nana's handwriting slants off the line at "flour, enough." Enough? I laugh once, too loud for the empty kitchen. My hands are already white to the wrists, and the dough clings to my fingers like wet cement. I tip in more flour, then more, then too much, and now it's crumbling. "No, no, no," I whisper, pressing it back together. My heart is knocking against my ribs. I wipe my forehead and leave a streak of flour there. I never started the oven timer, and I can't remember if I added the salt. I check the bowl. I check the card. The ink blurs. I grab my phone, put it down, grab it again, and my thumb hovers over Mom's name. Nobody can tell me what enough means. Nana's voice is the only one that could, and I keep standing here, breathing through my mouth, kneading faster and faster.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was comparing two cans of tomatoes when he heard his name from the end of the aisle, bright and unmistakable. Dana Whitfield. Eleventh grade, the row behind him in chemistry. His hand closed too hard on a can and he set it back on the wrong shelf. "Hey! Wow. Hi," he said, and his voice came out a half-step too high. His shirt had a stain on the hem; he swung his basket in front of it. Heat crawled up his neck. She asked what he was doing these days, and he laughed before he'd found any words, then said, "Oh, you know, stuff," and nodded far too many times. The fluorescent lights hummed like a swarm. His heart knocked against his ribs. "I left something in the car," he blurted, already backing away, and he walked toward the exit with his empty hand opening and closing, her laugh still hanging somewhere behind him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The clock over the pharmacy counter says 5:52, and the line still curls past the greeting cards. I've counted the prescriptions twice and the number keeps coming out different. My hands are slick on the keyboard; I wipe them on my smock and hit the wrong key again. "Sorry, sorry, just one second," I tell Mr. Alvarez, my voice climbing thin and fast. Somewhere behind me the fax machine shrieks, and Dana's already gone, her locker hanging open like a mouth. The store closes for three days at six. Three days. If that insulin isn't ready, he goes without it. My heart is knocking so hard I can feel it in my teeth. I grab the bottle, drop it, catch it against my knee, and laugh in a way that isn't a laugh. "Okay. Okay okay okay." The lights flicker once, and I stop breathing until they steady. Fifty-four. I start the label over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The screen says C41, and I'm standing at A6 with my backpack strap sliding off one shoulder. Forty minutes late, the boarding time on my phone reads 4:52, and it's 4:44. I run. My suitcase wheels rattle like loose teeth behind me, and I keep checking the phone as if the numbers might change. "Sorry, sorry, excuse me," I say to a man with a stroller, though I don't slow down. My mouth is dry as paper. The moving walkway is blocked by a couple standing side by side, and I actually say, "Please," too loudly, in a voice that cracks. My shirt is stuck to my spine. There's a stitch under my ribs, and my heartbeat is thudding in my ears so hard I can barely hear the announcements. C30. C34. My fingers are shaking so badly I drop my boarding pass, scoop it up, drop my passport, scoop that up too. Then I see the gate, the empty chairs, one agent lifting a phone. "Wait," I wheeze. "Wait, wait, I'm here."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller dripped a fat green tear onto the cream carpet, and I dropped to my knees, dabbing with my sleeve, which only dragged it wider. "No, no, no, no." My voice came out thin and high. The landlord's inspection was at nine tomorrow, and the clock on my phone said 11:52 p.m. I kept wiping, though my hands shook so badly the rag skipped across the fibers. Sweat stung my eyes. The color on the wall, which had looked like sage on the little swatch, glowed like a hospital corridor, and I'd already finished three walls. I stood too fast, the room tilting, and knocked the tray with my knee. More paint. I laughed, one short bark, then pressed my knuckles against my mouth. My heart thudded in my ears over the hum of the fan. Where was the receipt? I tore through the drop cloth, the bags, my pockets, breathing in gulps, whispering, "Think, think, think," at the ceiling.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder rattled the porch boards, and I was already on my feet, then sitting again, then up. My phone showed Dana's last text from forty minutes ago: "Leaving now." Nothing since. I dialed; it rang, rang, went to voicemail. "Pick up, pick up, it's me, call me, okay?" My voice came out thin and too fast. Rain slanted under the roof and soaked my knees, but I didn't move my chair. My heart was knocking against my ribs so hard I pressed my palm flat to my chest like that would help. Every pair of headlights on the road made me lean forward, gripping the railing, and every time they swept past without slowing. The wind chimes clanged wildly. I counted seconds between lightning and thunder and lost count. My hands shook so badly I dropped the phone, scrabbled for it on the wet boards, and dialed again, breathing through my teeth, whispering her name to the dark yard.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The wrench was exactly where I'd left it, but I counted my tools again anyway: eleven, same as before. I tightened the brake cable and glanced at the door. Still shut. Someone had moved the blue tarp on Dave's shelf since yesterday, I was sure of it, and my neck prickled as if the shelf were watching. 'Anyone there?' I said, too brightly, and the question hung in the oily air. Nothing. Just the fridge humming. I crouched to true the rear wheel, but my ears stayed tilted toward the hallway, catching every pipe tick. My thumb slipped and scraped the chainring; I barely felt it. I wiped my hands, then slid the good lock's key into my front pocket and zipped it. Footsteps outside, maybe, or just the wind. I stood and flipped the bike around so the frame faced the wall, hiding the serial number. Why had Priya asked what time I'd be here? I swallowed hard and picked the wrench back up, gripping it longer than the job needed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof, and I count them, because counting keeps my eyes busy. Four minutes since the man in the grey coat sat down at the far end of the bench. He hasn't looked at his phone once. I shift my bag to the side away from him, then back, then to my lap, arms locked around it. Wind drags a plastic bag across the road and I flinch so hard my knee clips the glass panel. "Sorry," I say, too loudly, to nobody. He turns his head. Why turn? I turn mine first, study the timetable I've already memorised. My neck prickles. Behind me the glass reflects him, still facing my way, I think, or is it just the rain smearing him? My mouth is dry, my heartbeat loud in my ears. A car slows, headlights sweeping across us, and I stand, sit, stand again. When the bus finally hisses open, I let him board first so I can see where his hands go, and then I stay on the pavement, soaked, watching the doors close.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta pulled the blinds before she lifted the lid, then checked the hallway, then pulled the blinds again. The box smelled of dust and cedar. She read each envelope's return address aloud in a whisper, as if the walls might correct her. Why were three of them slit so cleanly? Her mother never used a letter opener. She held one flap to the lamp, searching for the faint shine of reglued paper, and her pulse thudded in her ears. A floorboard ticked somewhere below and her hand froze mid-air. 'Just the pipes,' she said, too loudly, and laughed once, a dry sound. She stacked the letters by postmark, then restacked them, certain the order had shifted since she'd turned away. Under the last bundle lay a photograph, face down. She did not flip it. She slid it into her sleeve, crossed to the door, and turned the lock a second time, listening for anything breathing on the other side.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked twice, and I let the chain stay on while I opened the door four inches. "Ladder," he said, smiling. "Just for the gutters." I asked why he didn't have his own. My voice came out too even, like I'd rehearsed it. He shrugged and said his had a bent rung. I glanced past him at the street: the gray van still parked across from my house, same as yesterday. My palms were damp against the doorframe. "Why today?" I said. He laughed, but I was counting how long he looked at the garage. "I'll check if it's here," I told him, and shut the door before he answered. In the hallway I pressed my ear to the wood, heart knocking in my throat, listening for his footsteps to leave. They didn't, for a long while. Then I drew the curtain a finger's width and wrote down the time, and the van's plate, on the back of an envelope.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta stirred the risotto with one hand and held her phone in the other, thumb hovering over the doorbell camera feed. Empty porch. She set the phone face-up against the salt jar anyway. A car slowed outside and her wooden spoon stopped mid-circle; she waited, shoulders high, until its engine faded down the street. "Fine," she muttered. "Fine, fine." She crossed to the window and tugged the curtain closed, then opened it an inch, then closed it again. Why had Dev asked what time, twice? Why had he asked about the wine? She tasted the broth and couldn't tell if it needed salt, because her ears were tuned to the hallway, to the faint tick in the wall. The knife block looked wrong. She turned it so the handles faced the stove. When the buzzer finally rang, she flinched hard enough to knock the lid to the floor, and stood there, breathing through her teeth, before she called out, too brightly, "Who is it?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter, and I flinch like it bit me. Unknown number, a 612 I don't recognize. I slide sideways to the window and lift the blind two fingers' width, scanning the street. The same gray sedan sits there, or one like it. My thumb hovers. Four rings, five. I flick off the stove light, which makes no sense, but I do it anyway. When I finally press accept, I say nothing. I just breathe through my nose and listen. "Hello? Is this Daniel?" a woman asks. My pulse thuds in my ears. "Who's asking?" My voice comes out low and flat, too fast. "I'm calling about your car's warranty—" I hang up before she finishes, then stare at the dark screen, palms slick against the case. I check the deadbolt, then check it again, and wedge a chair under the knob before I sit down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I waited across the street until the woman in the green cardigan left the library steps, then waited four minutes more. The book sat in my backpack, a thin thing on Roman aqueducts, fourteen months overdue, and I kept one hand clamped over the zipper as if it might shout. Inside, the doors sighed shut behind me. I counted the cameras: two, maybe three. The man at the desk glanced up and I smiled too fast. "I'm just returning this," I said, then, "Not that I took it. I mean, I did. It was in a box." My voice came out thin. He scanned it slowly. Why so slowly? My palms were slick, my neck prickled, and I swore the girl by the periodicals had lowered her magazine. "Fine's capped," he said. I nodded, backing toward the exit, certain someone had already written my name down somewhere, and I didn't turn around until I hit the cold air.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dana set the last box down and did not open it. Instead she walked the length of the apartment, all eleven steps, and checked the window latch, then checked it again, pressing her thumb against the cold metal until it left a white dent in her skin. The smoke detector had a tiny black hole in its casing, and she stood on a chair to peer into it, breathing through her mouth. Someone had lived here before, and someone had given them a key. Maybe more than one key. When the pipes knocked inside the wall, her shoulders jerked up to her ears. 'Hello?' she said, quietly, then laughed at herself, a short dry sound that stopped too soon. She pulled the curtains shut, wedged a chair beneath the doorknob, and sat facing the door with her coat still on, listening to the hallway, counting the footsteps that passed and the ones that paused.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather, slightly open, like it had been left there on purpose for me. I walked past it twice. The second time I counted the joggers, the man with the stroller, the woman on the phone who hadn't turned a page of her book. Why hadn't any of them touched it? My palms were slick. I crouched to tie a shoe that was already tied and glanced up the path in both directions. "Hello?" I said, too loudly, to nobody. A pigeon lifted and my shoulder jerked. I pinched the wallet by one corner, as if it might be wired, and slid it into my jacket without opening it. Walking out, I kept my pace even and my eyes off the van parked by the gate, though I could feel its windshield on my neck the whole way. At home I locked the deadbolt, then checked it again, then pulled the blinds before I'd even set the thing down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says to let go of the wall, and I do, but my eyes stay on the two teenagers by the lifeguard chair. They're laughing, and I'm sure it's at my swim cap. I keep my chin up like a periscope. "Just float," Dana tells me, and I whisper, "Why is the drain open?" She blinks. "It's always open." My shoulders are hard as doorknobs. Every time the old man in lane three turns his head, I count the seconds until he looks away. Someone's whistle shrieks and I flinch so hard I swallow chlorine. I check the ladder, the clock, the exits, the ladder again. When Dana lifts her hands from my back, I grab her wrist. "You said you weren't going to," I say, too quickly, too low. "Who's watching?" Her face softens. "Nobody, Mara. They're just swimming." I don't let go. My heart keeps knocking, and I look over my shoulder anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I pressed the last tomato seedling into the soil and immediately looked over my shoulder at the Hendersons' upstairs window. The curtain had moved. I was sure of it. I crouched lower, cupping the little plant like contraband, my pulse thumping in my ears. "Just gardening," I whispered to no one, then coughed, louder, in case someone was listening. The fence slats seemed too wide. Anyone could be counting my rows. I dragged the hose over, then shut it off, because the hiss would cover footsteps. My palms were slick inside the gloves. Who had left that boot print by the compost bin? Not mine. I measured it against my own shoe twice. Before going in, I scattered mulch over the bare dirt so the bed looked like nothing, and I checked the latch on the gate three times, tugging hard each time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana slid into the chair nearest the door and angled her laptop so the screen faced no one. Across the table, Marcus clicked to his third slide, the one with the quarterly timeline, and she noticed the budget figure was the same one she'd emailed only to Priya. Her pulse ticked in her ears. Why had he picked that number? She glanced at Priya, who was typing, and typing, and not looking up. Dana's palms left damp prints on her notebook. When Marcus said, "Thanks to everyone's input," she laughed a beat too late and too loudly, and two heads turned. "Sorry," she said. "Just, uh, good slide." She tore a page from her notebook, folded it small, and pressed it into her pocket. Then she watched the glass wall behind Marcus, where the reflection of the hallway showed someone standing very still, listening.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The same pair of headlights has been behind me since the exit ramp, and I tap the brake just to see what they do. They hang back, then close in again. My palms are slick on the wheel. I turn onto Alder, a street I don't even need, and count to eleven before they appear in the mirror. "Okay," I say out loud, flat and quiet, "okay, okay." The radio is off now; I can't hear the road over it. Every mailbox looks like a standing figure. I pass my own house, slow, then keep going, because the porch light is off and I always leave it on. Did I? My neck aches from checking the mirror. I loop the block twice, keys already pinched between my fingers, and when the headlights finally slide past and vanish, my chest doesn't loosen at all. I just wonder where they'll turn around.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana stopped outside room 412 and waited until the orderly's cart rattled past before she pushed the door open. She sat in the chair farthest from the window, angled so she could watch the hallway through the gap. "Hi, Grandpa," she said, too softly, then glanced at the nurse who came to check his IV. Why was she writing so long on the chart? Dana's palms were damp against her knees. When the nurse left, she got up, closed the door, and opened it again an inch. "Did anyone else come by today?" she whispered. Her grandfather blinked at her. She pulled out her phone, checked the lock screen, put it face down, picked it up again. The man in the corridor had walked past twice now, hadn't he? She counted his footsteps fading. Her jaw ached from clenching. "Don't sign anything," she told him, leaning close, "unless I'm here." Down the hall, a laugh rang out, and her whole body turned toward it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana stood with her back against the brick wall, where she could see both the gate and the parking lot, her keys threaded between her knuckles. The gray sedan had been there when she arrived. Engine off. Tinted windows. She checked it again, then her phone, then it again. "Is that Mrs. Okafor's car?" she asked the woman beside her, too quickly, and didn't wait for the answer. Her heart knocked against her ribs. When a man in a cap lifted his phone, she turned her shoulder, tugged her scarf higher, and counted the exits aloud under her breath: gate, fence, side door. The bell rang. Children spilled out in a bright, shrieking tide, and her eyes slid over every adult face, searching for the one that looked at her too long. Her palms were slick. When Milo finally waved, she crossed the pavement in four strides, gripped his wrist harder than she meant to, and said, low and clipped, "Don't look back. Just walk."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite set the oak dresser at the end of the driveway, then moved it two feet left so she could see the street from the kitchen window. The man in the gray sedan had circled twice now. She counted the cash in the tin again, though she'd counted it a minute ago, and wedged it under her arm. "Fifteen for the lamp," she told a woman who hadn't asked, her voice too quick, too bright. Her palms were slick against the chair she was pretending to dust. When the stranger pulled out his phone, she stepped sideways to block the dresser's drawers. "No photos, please," she said. "Just, you know. Buy it or don't." He frowned and put the phone away. She watched his shoes the whole way down the drive, then locked the front door behind her, checked it, and checked it again, her pulse ticking in her ears while the sedan idled at the curb.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta wedged the wrench under the sink and froze when the pipe above her ticked. She held her breath, listening past the drip, past the fridge hum, toward the hallway. Nothing. She shut the cabinet door halfway, then opened it again, because a closed door meant she couldn't see the kitchen reflected in the toaster. "Just a washer," she told the empty room, too loudly, then lowered her voice as if the walls might repeat it. The plumber's van had idled outside yesterday, hadn't it? Longer than it needed to. Her neck prickled; she twisted the fitting a quarter turn and checked the window blinds, the lock, the blinds again. Water beaded on her wrist and she flinched like it was a touch. When the phone buzzed on the counter she let it ring out, staring at the unknown number until the screen went dark. Only then did she go back to the pipe, wrench gripped tight, one ear tilted toward the front door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter for an hour before I touched it. I'd already pulled the blinds, then checked the street through the slats, twice, because the gray sedan had been there Tuesday too. Return address: Department of Revenue. Typed, not handwritten. Why typed? I held it up to the lamp and tried to read the folded shadow of the page inside. The flap looked slightly wrong, like the glue had been wet once already. "Somebody's been in this," I told the empty kitchen, quietly, as if the toaster might report me. My thumb slid under the seal and my pulse thumped in my ears, loud enough that I stopped to listen for footsteps in the hall. Nothing. That was worse. I unfolded the page with my fingertips, kept my back to the window, and read the first line in a whisper, then wished I hadn't said it out loud.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver's eyes found mine in the mirror again, and I shifted my backpack from the seat beside me onto my lap, arms looped through both straps. He said something long and soft. I said, "Hotel. Only hotel," too loudly, holding up my phone with the address like a badge. He nodded, but why had he turned left? I pressed my thumb against the map dot and watched it crawl. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the airport. Two men outside a shuttered shop stopped talking as we passed. Had they? I twisted to look back through the rear window until my neck cracked. When the car finally stopped, I paid with exact bills, refused the change he offered, and didn't thank him. In the lobby I checked the lock twice, wedged the chair under the handle, and stood with my ear against the door, listening to a language I couldn't parse murmur down the hall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus kept his back to the oak and his eyes on the tree line while Biscuit tore circles through the long grass. The man on the far bench had been there when they arrived, and he still hadn't turned a page. Marcus's palm was slick on the leash coiled around his wrist. "Biscuit. Here. Now," he called, too sharp, and the dog skidded to a stop, confused, tail low. A van idled at the gravel lot, its engine humming just a little too steadily. He counted the windows. He counted them again. When a jogger passed, Marcus shifted so his shoulder faced her, and his jaw ached from clenching. Biscuit bounded off again, joyful, oblivious. Marcus whispered, "Stay where I can see you," and kept turning his head, slowly, left, right, behind, as the wind moved the grass in places where no dog was running.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite set her clarinet case on the folding chair and checked the church hall's doors again, both of them, then the window latch behind the piano. Nine people had stopped talking when she walked in; she was certain of it. "Just warming up," she said, too brightly, and licked her lips, which stayed dry. The first bars of the Gershwin arrangement came out thin. She kept glancing at Dennis, who was leaning toward the flutist, his mouth near her ear. Were they counting her wrong notes? Her neck prickled. She turned her music stand a few degrees so she could see the whole room without seeming to look. When the director tapped his baton and said her name, her fingers jerked on the keys. "Was that for me?" she asked. "Did somebody say something?" Nobody had. Still, she played the entire second page with her back angled to the wall, listening for the rustle of whispers beneath every phrase, her heartbeat louder than the piano.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I locked the workshop door behind me, then checked it twice, then pulled the blinds down to the sill. Dale's sawdust still clung to the air, and every time the pipes ticked I froze with a coffee can of screws halfway to the box. "Just me," I said aloud, too loudly, to nobody. Why was the bottom drawer unlatched? I hadn't touched it. Had I? I counted the chisels. Eleven. The rack had twelve slots. My pulse thumped in my ears as I crouched, peering under the bench, and found only a dead moth and a tape measure. Still, I took out my phone and photographed every shelf before moving anything, so there'd be proof of how I'd found it. Headlights swept the window and I killed the lamp, standing stiff in the dark, breathing through my teeth until the car's engine faded down the road. Only then did I notice my hand was clamped around the twelfth chisel, already in my pocket.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go live at noon, and at 11:52 I was already on my third refresh, checking the URL for typos in case someone had swapped it for a fake. The library hummed. Two guys by the window kept glancing my way, and I angled my laptop toward the wall. "Are you looking at my screen?" I said, too loud, and the librarian shushed me. My neck prickled. Why had the department emailed on a Tuesday? Why was my name spelled correctly on the login page, when it never is? I pulled my hood up, unplugged the charger, plugged it back in. Someone had to have flagged my paper. I'd seen Professor Hale's pen stop on page four. At 12:00 the page went white, and I slammed the lid shut, certain the whole room had just seen my face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta stopped on the switchback and held her breath, listening. Nothing, only the creak of pines. She walked on, faster, then stopped again, because the footsteps behind her had stopped a half-beat late. "Hello?" she called, her voice too bright, and the ridge gave back nothing. Her fingers had gone cold around the trekking pole, knuckles pale as the birch trunks. She checked her phone, no signal, and turned off the screen so the glow wouldn't mark her. Every stump became a shoulder, every fern a crouching shape. The man in the orange cap she'd passed at the trailhead, why had he looked at her boots? She unclipped her pack's hip belt so she could drop it and run. A twig snapped to the left. She didn't turn her head; she walked with her eyes slid sideways, counting steps, whispering, "Just the wind, just the wind," while her pulse hammered in her ears and the last orange light slid off the trail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma's recipe card is stained yellow at the corners, and I've propped it against the flour canister, but I keep turning it over to check the back again. Nothing new. Still just her slanted pencil: *don't rush the rise.* I lock the deadbolt, then walk back and test it twice. The yeast foams in the bowl and I stare at it, because who touched the jar? I counted the packets yesterday. Eleven. Now ten? My shoulders are up near my ears. Somewhere in the hallway a floorboard ticks and I freeze, hands buried in dough, breath held until my chest aches. 'Just the pipes,' I whisper, louder than I mean to. I cross to the window and tug the blinds down, then peek through the slats at the neighbor's dark porch. Is that light new? My palms are sweating into the dough, so I knead harder, listening past the oven's hum for anything that shouldn't be there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana had been reading the same cereal box for a full minute when someone said her name. She didn't turn. The voice said it again, closer, and her fingers tightened on the cardboard until it dented. In the curved mirror above the aisle she found a man in a green jacket, and she counted the seconds he stood there. "Dana? Marcus Feld, Ms. Okafor's homeroom?" Her mouth was dry. "Funny," she said, too quietly, "running into you here." She asked how he'd known which store, then laughed as though it were a joke, and it wasn't. He said he only lived two streets over. She nodded, memorizing his shoes, the bulge in his pocket that turned out to be a phone. Her cart was already angled toward the exit. When he offered his number, she took the receipt instead, wrote a wrong digit on purpose, and left her basket of groceries sitting beside the cereal, her heartbeat loud in her ears all the way to the car, where she checked the back seat twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol counted the register twice, then a third time, though the total never changed. The pharmacy had emptied by four, and the fluorescent hum seemed louder without customers to swallow it. She kept the front door in the corner of her eye. The man by the vitamins had been there eleven minutes; she'd checked the clock when he came in. "Can I help you find anything?" she called, too bright, her voice cracking on the last word. He shook his head without looking up. Her palms were slick against the counter. She slid her phone from her apron, thumbed the screen, put it back. Why had Dale left early? Why had he asked about the safe? She straightened the gum display until every pack faced forward, then moved to the end of the aisle where the mirror showed the parking lot. Only one car, idling. Its lights were off. Her neck prickled. She locked the back-office door behind her, and held the knob a long while after it clicked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The man in the gray jacket was behind me at security, and now he's behind me on the moving walkway. I step off early and cut left into a shop, pretending to study neck pillows, watching his reflection in the glass case. He walks past. Thirty seconds later, I leave and he's at the pretzel stand, not eating. My pulse ticks in my jaw. Gate B22 is a mile away, and the board says boarding closes in eleven minutes, but I take the stairs instead of the escalator because stairs have fewer eyes. 'Excuse me, did you see where that guy went?' I ask a cleaner, too fast, too loud. She shrugs. I clutch my passport until the cover goes damp and warm. At the gate I choose the seat facing the corridor, backpack strapped to my chest, and count every face that passes. Twice. When they call my row, I glance back before I step onto the jet bridge.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marcus taped the last strip along the baseboard, then peeled it off and taped it again, because the first line had looked like it was hiding something. He had already drawn the curtains and then checked the gap twice. When the neighbor's gate clanked, he froze with the roller dripping, counting seconds until footsteps faded. "Just the wind," he said aloud, too flatly, and laughed once at nothing. His shoulders ached from holding them so high. He pried the lid off the second can and wondered why the same man had come by Tuesday asking about the house, and why he'd looked at the windows. Marcus rolled the pale gray over the old outlet cover, then stopped, unscrewed it, and shone his phone light into the dark square of wall. Nothing. He screwed it back on. His pulse thumped in his ears. He turned off the radio so he could hear the street, and painted in silence, facing the door the whole time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: I moved the rocking chair twice before the first thunder, finally wedging it into the corner where the porch rail met the wall, so nothing could stand behind me. Rain hammered the tin awning. Across the road, the Hendersons' porch light clicked on, and I stopped rocking. Why now? Who were they signaling? My shirt stuck to my spine, and my pulse thudded in my ears louder than the thunder. 'Just the storm,' I said aloud, too quickly, and then again, quieter, as if somebody might be taking notes. A shape shifted by the hedge. I gripped the armrests until my knuckles ached. A branch. It was a branch. I counted to ten anyway, eyes never leaving it, and when the lightning flashed and showed me nothing, I didn't trust it. I slid my phone under my thigh, turned the porch light off, and sat in the dark, listening for footsteps beneath the rain, certain the quiet between thunderclaps was someone holding their breath.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the rear wheel upside down on the workbench, and she turned the spoke wrench a quarter turn, then stopped, then spun the rim and watched the wobble against the brake pad she'd taped in place as a gauge. Behind her, the neighbor's table saw screamed through plywood and went quiet, and someone's radio drifted in from the far bay. She didn't look up. Her breath stayed slow, her shoulders loose, a smear of grease drying on her wrist. "Another quarter," she murmured to the bike, and gave it one. The rim still hissed against the tape. A kid wheeled in, asked if she was almost done, and she smiled and said, "Not yet. Pull up that stool if you want to see." He did. She showed him the hop in the rim, then turned the next nipple, listening to the faint tick of the spoke settling. Her tea had gone cold an hour ago. She sipped it anyway and reached for the wrench again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof while I was halfway through my crossword, and I just tucked the pen behind my ear and shifted down the bench to dodge the leak. Wind pushed a flurry of leaves across the road. I pulled my collar up, breathed out slowly, and watched my breath cloud and vanish. A man beside me checked his phone for the fifth time and groaned. "Says twelve minutes," I told him, easy, smiling a little. "Then it's twelve minutes." My fingers had gone stiff, so I tucked them under my arms and rocked my heels against the curb, one, two, one, two. The sky went the color of wet slate. Somewhere a gutter began to gurgle. I thought about the soup waiting at home, how good it would taste after this, and I picked the pen back up. Seven letters, 'to endure.' I hadn't got it yet. There was time. Headlights swam up through the rain, and I stood without hurry.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox sits on my knees, its corners soft as felt, and I lift the first envelope by its edges. The tea beside me has gone lukewarm; I don't mind. Rain ticks against the attic window while I slide a thumbnail under a flap that has waited sixty years, easing it so the paper doesn't tear. My shoulders are loose, my breathing slow. Grandpa's handwriting slants like it's leaning into wind, and I trace a few words with my finger, then stop to squint, then go back. "Take your time," I murmur to no one, the way Grandma used to when I tied my shoes. Some letters I read twice. Some I just hold, feeling the faint grain of the paper. I stack them by postmark, smoothing each crease flat with my palm. There are maybe two hundred left. The light shifts across the floorboards, and I reach for the next one, in no hurry at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked on my screen door at the exact moment the kettle began to whistle, and I let it whistle another few seconds while I wiped my hands on the dish towel. "Ladder?" I said, smiling through the mesh. "Sure. Gutters again?" He launched into the whole saga, the leak, the wasp nest, his wife's opinion of both, and I leaned against the doorframe, feeling the warm porch boards through my socks. I nodded where nodding fit. When he trailed off, I slipped on my boots, unhurried, laces double-knotted, and walked him to the garage. The ladder hung behind the bikes, so I moved each one aside, slowly, one at a time. He apologized for the third time about the hour. "Tea's waiting, nothing's burning," I said, and breathed out. I carried the ladder's heavy end myself, steadying his grip on the other, and showed him which rung sticks, twice, in case he missed it the first time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions have been going for forty minutes, and I haven't touched the heat once. Low and slow, my grandmother used to say, and her voice sits in my shoulders, loosening them. The kitchen smells of butter and thyme. Somewhere past the window, headlights sweep the street, but I only glance up, then back to the pot. I stir in a lazy figure eight and let the wooden spoon drag across the bottom, watching the edges of the onions turn the color of old honey. My phone buzzes on the counter: 'Running ten minutes late, sorry!' I type back, 'No rush, the soup will wait,' and I mean it. I wipe my hands on the towel over my shoulder, breathe in the sweetness, and tilt the lid a little wider. The bread can go in when they knock. For now there's just the slow hiss, the warm steam on my cheeks, and the small, steady pleasure of letting things take as long as they take.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter, a string of digits I don't recognize, and I let it ring twice while I dry my hands on the dish towel. Steam still curls from the kettle. I slide the screen and say, "Hello?" There's a hiss on the line, a clatter, someone breathing out. "Hello," I say again, softer, and pull out a chair. I sit. My shoulders settle against the wood. A man starts a sentence, stumbles, begins again, and I don't cut in. Outside, the neighbor's sprinkler ticks across the grass. "Take your time," I tell him, pouring water over the tea bag with my free hand, watching the color bloom. He says he's looking for someone named Dale. I'm not Dale, but I ask him to read me the number he dialed, and I listen to each digit, nodding at the empty room, the mug warm between my palms while he sorts it out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The line at the returns desk curled past the periodicals, and I let my backpack slide to the floor and stood with my hands loose at my sides. The book in my arms, a water-stained copy of Middlemarch, was four hundred and twelve days overdue. I'd found it under my bed that morning, spine dusty, a receipt from last spring marking page 80. Somebody ahead of me fumbled with a stack of DVDs, and I just watched the dust drift through the window light, my breathing slow and even. When the clerk finally waved me forward, I set the book down gently and said, "I'm sorry, this is very late. Take whatever time you need to look it up." She squinted at her screen, sighed, tapped keys, and tapped them again when it froze. I traced the grain of the counter with one finger. "No rush," I said, and meant it. The fine could be whatever it was. My shoulders felt warm and low, and I was almost glad of the quiet wait.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The couch would not clear the doorframe, so Marisol set down her end and tilted it again, slowly, the way you turn a key that sticks. Her shoulder ached. Sweat cooled along her spine. "Okay," she said to the empty hallway, to the couch, to nobody, "let's try it on its side." The mover had left an hour ago, muttering about his schedule. She didn't mind. She breathed out, lifted, shuffled a half step, and listened for the scrape of fabric on wood. It caught. She eased back, adjusted her grip, and tried once more. Boxes towered by the window, labeled in her own tidy marker, and the radiator ticked softly beneath them. There was no rush; the whole afternoon belonged to her. On the fourth try the cushion folded, the frame slid through, and she laughed quietly, pressing her palm flat against the warm, scuffed wall before going back for the lamp.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, half hidden under a curl of maple leaves, and Marta lowered herself beside it without touching it. She unscrewed her thermos, poured, and let the steam fog her glasses. A jogger passed, then a boy dragging a scooter. Each time she watched them glance past, and each time she simply sipped. When her tea had cooled to warm, she opened the wallet with two fingers and found a library card, a faded photo of a dog, a name: Desmond Oyelaran. No phone number. 'Well, Desmond,' she murmured, tucking it into her coat, 'somebody's looking for you.' Her knees ached against the cold slats. She didn't hurry. She walked to the gate by the fountain, where a man in a gray cap was retracing the path with his eyes down, and she waited for him to look up, hands folded, breath slow and even in the evening air.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The water in the shallow end is the color of weak tea under the old fluorescent lights, and I'm standing in it up to my ribs, holding the gutter with both hands. I'm thirty-eight. The kids' class ends in ten minutes and their splashing echoes off the tile. I put my face in again. Count to three, bubbles out through my nose, lift. My chest is tight, but I let my shoulders drop the way Marisol showed me, and I do it again. Four this time. I come up coughing, wipe my eyes, and laugh a little. 'Still sinking,' I tell her. 'That's fine,' she says. 'Again?' I nod. I push off the wall, legs trailing like wet rope, and glide maybe a foot before my feet find the floor. A foot is a foot. I walk back to the edge, rest my fingers on the cool gutter, breathe slowly, and start over, as many times as it takes tonight.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The packet said to sow carrot seeds a quarter inch deep, so I knelt in the damp dirt with a pencil and made each hole by hand, one after another, my knees going numb against the boards. The seeds were smaller than pepper flakes. I dropped two in each hole, pinched soil over them, and pressed it flat with one fingertip. My neighbor leaned over the fence and asked when I'd see anything. "Ten days, maybe twenty," I said, and shrugged, smiling. The sun warmed the back of my neck. I filled the watering can again and poured slowly, letting the water soak in without pooling, the way the video showed. When a robin hopped close, I just held still and watched it pull a worm. Then I wrote the date on a popsicle stick, pushed it into the row, and sat back on my heels, breathing in the smell of wet earth, in no hurry to stand up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana's slides had been stuck on slide four for ten minutes, and the projector fan hummed over the whole conference room. Someone's chair squeaked. I kept my pen resting on my notebook, uncapped but still, and let my shoulders drop against the backrest. She flipped back, lost her place, laughed too loudly. 'Take your time,' I said, my voice low and even, and I meant it. My coffee had gone lukewarm an hour ago; I turned the mug a slow quarter-turn on its coaster. Across the table Marcus sighed and checked his phone. I didn't. I watched her thumb search the clicker, noticed how her hands trembled just slightly, and remembered my own first quarterly review. My breathing was slow, my jaw loose. When she finally found the chart, I nodded once, and she exhaled. 'That's the one,' I said. 'Go ahead. I've got questions, but they'll keep until you're done.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The freight train had been crossing for six minutes when Marisol shifted the car into park and let her hands fall into her lap. Past midnight, the gates blinked red against the wet road, and boxcars clacked by in a long, rolling rhythm she began to count under her breath. Her shoulders stayed loose. She cracked the window, and the cold smelled of rain and rust. On the passenger seat her phone buzzed with her sister's text, wondering where she was, and she typed with one thumb, 'Train. Home soon. Leave the porch light on.' Then she turned the radio down to a murmur and watched the cars slide past. Her breath fogged a small circle on the glass, and she wiped it away with her sleeve. When the last car finally cleared and the gates lifted, she let the engine idle a moment longer, rolled her neck once, and eased forward without hurry, the dark road open ahead of her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol pulled the vinyl chair closer to the bed and sat down slowly, her coat still folded over her knees. Her grandfather's eyes were shut, his breath catching and releasing in a rhythm she began to match without meaning to. The monitor beeped; a cart rattled past the door; the clock above the sink said ten past two, then twenty past. She peeled the orange he liked, one long curl of rind at a time, and set the segments on a napkin where he'd see them. When his fingers twitched, she didn't lean in. 'No rush, Abuelo,' she said softly, tucking the blanket back over his foot. 'I brought the crossword. We can do just one clue.' He mumbled something about seven letters. She smiled, uncapped her pen, and waited, her shoulders loose, her thumb tracing the ridge of the armrest while the afternoon light crawled across the floor tiles toward his bed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marisol leaned against the chain-link fence with her coat unzipped, one boot propped behind her, the other planted in a patch of damp leaves. The bell had rung ten minutes ago, and the doors still spat out only stragglers and teachers with lanyards. She turned her thermos lid slowly, sipped, and let the steam fog her glasses. 'No rush,' she told the man beside her, who kept checking his watch. 'Mr. Alvarez always keeps the kindergarteners for the song.' Her shoulders stayed loose. A paper maple leaf skittered across the asphalt and she watched it all the way to the curb, smiling a little. When a small boy in a dinosaur hat burst out the wrong door, she only lifted her hand and waited, her breath easy and slow, until Theo spotted her and came running, backpack bouncing, and she crouched to zip his jacket without a single hurried tug.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The oak dresser has sat at the end of my driveway since seven, a strip of masking tape on its top reading $40. It's past noon now. A man has opened every drawer twice, and I let him, leaning back in my folding chair with my coffee going lukewarm in my hands. The sun warms the back of my neck. "Take your time," I say, soft, the way I'd talk to a skittish cat. "The bottom one sticks. Lift a little as you pull." He grunts, tries it, frowns at the price tape. I don't rush to fill the quiet. A sparrow lands on the lamp table, hops, leaves. My breathing stays slow and even. My father built that dresser's twin, and I'd rather it go to someone who looks at it long than someone who grabs it fast. When he finally asks, "Would you take thirty?" I just smile and say, "Let's see how the drawers feel one more time."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marisol lay on her back beneath the sink, a flashlight clamped between her teeth, one cold drip after another landing on her wrist. The first fitting hadn't held, so she unscrewed it again, slowly, and wiped the threads with a rag until they shone. "Alright, once more," she murmured to the pipe, the way she might speak to a skittish dog. She wound the tape three turns, pressed it flat with her thumbnail, and checked the angle before even touching the wrench. Her shoulders ached against the cabinet floor, and water had soaked through her sleeve, but she breathed in long, even pulls. The drip came back, thinner. She only nodded, set down the wrench, and reached for a smaller one. Outside, the afternoon light slid across the kitchen tiles and the kettle clicked off, forgotten. She turned the nut a quarter turn, waited, watched the bead of water form and fall, then gave it an eighth more. Then she counted to sixty, and watched again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had sat on the kitchen table since Tuesday, and Marguerite let it sit while the kettle finished its slow climb to a boil. She poured the tea, stirred in one spoon of honey, and carried the cup to the window where the afternoon light fell across her chair. Only then did she slide a butter knife under the flap, working it along the seam in one long, unhurried line. The paper inside was folded in thirds, crisp, stamped with the county seal. She smoothed it against her knee, set her glasses on her nose, and read the first line, then the second, her shoulders loose, her breath even. 'Well,' she murmured to the cat, 'they've taken their time. I suppose I can too.' She turned the page over to check the back, took a sip of tea, and went back to the beginning to read it properly, one line at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed and emptied onto a platform full of signs Marit couldn't read. She set her bag down, rolled her shoulders, and let her breath slide out slow. At the ticket window she smiled at the clerk and held up her phone, the hotel's name glowing on the screen. The clerk spoke fast, pointing left, then right, then left again. Marit nodded, repeated the last word back, softer, and asked with her hands for it once more. He sighed, then slowed down, drawing a little map on a scrap of paper. "Thank you," she said in his language, mangling it, and tried again until his mouth twitched into a grin. Her feet ached and the afternoon sun pressed on her neck, but she folded the paper carefully into her coat pocket. Then she walked out into the noise, stopping at each corner to read the map again, one street at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marguerite lowered herself onto the damp bench at the edge of the meadow and let her thermos warm her palms. Out past the fence posts, Biscuit had found something in the tall grass and was nosing it, circling, nosing it again. Her leash hung loose over her knee. She didn't call him. A crow shouted from the oak, the wind combed the timothy flat, and her shoulders sank as she exhaled slowly through her nose. "Take your time, bud," she said, barely louder than the breeze. He bolted left, skidded, dropped into a play bow at nothing at all, and she smiled and sipped her tea. Her toes had gone cold inside her boots, and she wiggled them once, then settled back. The light slid longer across the field. When he finally trotted over, tongue lolling, burrs in his ears, she simply held out her hand and said, "Ready when you are."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite rested her cello bow across her knee and let the last note drift up into the rafters of the Grange hall. Across the room, the younger violinist's cheeks had gone pink. "From bar forty-one," Marguerite said, low, almost a hum. "No rush. We have the room until nine." She rolled her shoulders once, felt the old radiator's warmth along her back, and watched dust turn in the slanted light from the high windows. They played it. The entrance wobbled. She nodded and lifted her bow, counting them in with a slow dip of her chin. Again. A folding chair creaked; someone's phone buzzed and went quiet. Her breathing stayed long and even, her fingers loose on the strings. When the girl finally landed the phrase cleanly, Marguerite only smiled. "There. Hear how that sits? Let's play it once more, just to keep it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta pulled the first drawer of Joel's workbench open and took her time with what she found. Screws, hundreds of them, mixed with washers and bent nails. She tipped the drawer onto a newspaper and settled on the stool, her knees cracking. One by one she sorted them into baby-food jars, the way he always had, her thumb rubbing dust from each thread. Sawdust drifted in the slant of afternoon light. Her tea went cold beside the vise and she didn't notice. When a jar slipped and rolled under the lathe, she lowered herself to the floor, reached into the dark with her whole arm, and felt along until her fingers closed on glass. "There you are," she said softly, as if to a cat. Her breathing stayed slow and even. Only the first drawer was done, and the shelves above her held forty years of his things. She picked up the next screw.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal says results go up by five, so at ten past four I fill the kettle and set out two mugs, though Dana won't be home until six. Steam fogs the window over the sink. I wipe a small circle clear with my sleeve and watch the neighbor's kid chalk a lopsided hopscotch on the pavement. My shoulders feel loose, my breath slow and even. When my phone buzzes, it's only the pharmacy, and I laugh a little and set it face-down. I pour the tea, carry it to the armchair, and open the paperback I've been dragging through for a month. Page 212. The radiator ticks. A sparrow lands on the sill and leaves. At 4:58 I mark my place with a receipt, refresh the page once, see the spinning wheel, and say aloud to the empty room, "Okay, take your time." Then I drink my tea while it's still hot.
