topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 114 smelled of floor wax and old radiator dust, and Daniel stood before the empty corkboard with his backpack still on, though he'd been there forty minutes. His thumbnail had worried a strip of skin on his index finger until it bled; he pressed it to his sleeve without looking. Every time footsteps echoed, his stomach dropped, and he pretended to read the fire-drill map. When Priya's text lit up his phone, "Did you study with me or did you just sit there?", he turned the screen face down. He had just sat there. He had watched her explain the proofs twice, nodded, then gone home and played games until dawn. "Sorry," he muttered to no one, then again, quieter, as the secretary approached with a stapled sheet. His voice cracked on it. She pinned the pages up and left. Daniel didn't step forward. He kept thinking of Priya's highlighted notes, the ones she'd pushed across the table, and how easily he'd said thanks.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta had told her brother the ridge was too far for one afternoon, and then she'd gone anyway, alone, with his old canteen knocking against her hip. Now the pines were turning to black cutouts and the trail had narrowed to a pale thread. She walked faster than her knees liked. At the switchback she stopped, pulled out her phone, and typed his name, then deleted it, then typed it again. No signal. "Idiot," she said to the empty slope, and her voice came out thin and cracked. She thought of the door she'd shut on him, the way she hadn't turned around. Her throat tightened as she unscrewed the canteen and found his initials scratched in the lid with a nail. She held it a moment before drinking. Somewhere below, the creek kept talking. She tucked the phone away, gripped the strap, and said, quieter, "I'm coming down. Wait up." Then she started down in the dimness, rehearsing the first words she would say.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, stained with thumbprints of butter, and Dae-jung pressed it flat beside the flour bin with both hands. Her grandmother's slanted handwriting said *knead until it answers you*. She had never asked what that meant. Three Sundays of unreturned calls, and now only this. She worked the dough harder than she needed to, shoulders aching, and said, "Okay, okay, I'm here," to nobody, her voice cracking on the second one. Flour dusted her wet cheek and she didn't wipe it. The kitchen smelled of yeast and, faintly, of the lavender soap that still clung to the card. When the oven light glowed, she sat on the cold tile in front of it, knees pulled up, watching the loaf rise slowly. "I would have come," she whispered. "If you'd said it was soon, I would have come." The timer rang. She let it ring a long while before standing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was comparing two cans of tomatoes when I heard my name, and my hand stopped in midair. Dana Pruitt. Ninth grade, the cafeteria, the nickname I'd started that stuck to her for three years. She looked the same, only taller, a toddler perched in her cart. "Hey," I said, and my voice came out thin, like someone else's. The fluorescent lights hummed too loudly. I put the can back, picked it up again, put it back. She asked about my job and I answered with way too much detail, about spreadsheets, about my commute, anything to keep from the thing sitting in my throat. My face was hot. When she laughed at something her son did, I stared at the floor tiles and counted them. "Dana," I finally said, and she turned. I wanted to say it, whatever it was, all of it. Instead I heard myself ask, "Do you still hate tomatoes?" She blinked. I gripped the cart handle until my knuckles went pale, and stayed there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum at 5:52, eight minutes from close, and I keep wiping the same stretch of counter. Mrs. Alvarez's prescription sits in the pickup bin where it has sat since Monday, when I told her on the phone, sharply, that we weren't a charity and she could wait for her check to clear. Tomorrow everything shuts for three days. My stomach is tight, like I swallowed a stone. I pull her bag out, turn it over, read the label twice though I know it by heart. The price is eleven dollars. I take out my wallet, and my fingers fumble the bills, one slipping to the floor. I leave it there a second. When the door chimes and a stranger asks if we're closing, my voice comes out too soft: 'Not yet. Not for her.' I grab my coat, lock the register, and go looking for her address in the old files, my face hot, my breath short, the bag crinkling in my fist like it's apologizing for me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B34 flickered on the board, and I ran, my rolling bag clattering behind me like an accusation. Forty minutes ago I'd stood at the coffee counter in the first airport, ignoring Dad's third call because Sunday's argument still itched. Now my lungs burned and my thumb kept scrolling to his name, to the last text I'd sent: "Fine. Whatever." Two words, typed so fast. "Sorry, sorry, excuse me," I told a man whose elbow I clipped, my voice cracking on the second one. The agent at the desk said the door had closed. I didn't argue. I just stood there, throat tight, watching the jet bridge pull away. Then I sat on the cold floor by the window and pressed call. When he answered with a gruff "Hello?" all I could manage was, "Dad. I should've picked up." My eyes stung. Outside, the plane rolled off without me, and I let it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller squeaks against the wall, and I keep it slow, careful, as if the beige could feel it. Under the tape by the window, there they are: pencil lines, Maya's heights, the last one dated the summer before I shouted about the crayon on the hallway. I stop. My throat is tight and my thumb finds the oldest mark, age four, the wobbly 'M.' I should have photographed it. I should have said a lot of things differently. "It's just paint," I tell the empty room, but my voice cracks on 'just.' I press my palm flat there, the wall cool and slightly gritty, and stand until my arm shakes. Then I set the roller down in the tray, let the white skin over, and go find my phone to call her, rehearsing the first sentence, deleting it, starting over, still holding the ladder with my other hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while I was still holding the phone, thumb hovering over her name. Rain hammered the porch roof, and wind flung cold spray across my knees, but I didn't scoot the chair back. The swing beside me creaked empty. I'd carried out two glasses of tea an hour ago, out of habit, and now hers sweated a ring onto the railing. "You're being stupid," I told the yard, my voice cracking on the last word. I typed *I shouldn't have said it* and deleted it. Typed it again. Lightning lit the mailbox where her letters used to pile up, and my stomach folded in on itself the way it had when the door shut behind her. I pressed my palm hard against my sternum. Water ran off the eaves in ropes. "Okay," I whispered. "Okay, okay." Then I picked up her glass, drank the warm, watery tea, and stayed put, watching the road for headlights.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Dana found her 15mm wrench hanging on Marcus's side of the pegboard again, the marker outline she'd drawn now empty beside his neat labels. She said nothing. She walked over, plucked it down, and wiped the grease from the handle onto his clean rag, slowly, before tossing the rag back crooked. Under the flickering tube light, she knelt by the upturned bike and cranked the rusted pedal, jaw tight, molars grinding. The scraped knuckle throbbed with each pull. His stool sat in her half of the garage, as always, and she dragged it back across the painted line with a screech that made him glance up from his phone. "Oh, sorry, did you need that?" he said. "No," Dana said, bright and flat. "Keep it. Keep everything." The chain snapped taut in her fist. She counted the links aloud, louder than she meant to, and didn't look up until the last one clicked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the schedule taped inside the shelter, right over the 5:42 I'd been staring at since 5:30. It was 6:10. I checked my phone anyway, thumb jabbing the screen like it owed me something. Karen had said, "Just take the bus, it's fine, I'll keep the car." Fine. I'd smiled and said fine too, and my jaw still ached from it. Now the wind shoved rain sideways under the roof and soaked my left sleeve, and I didn't move to the dry end of the bench, because moving would mean the weather had won something. A man beside me said, "Typical, huh?" I said, "Yep," flat as a plate, and kept my eyes on the empty road. My shoes squelched when I shifted. I pictured her kitchen, the light on, a mug steaming in her hand. I pressed my teeth together until my ears rang. When the headlights finally swung around the corner, I didn't stand up right away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Dana dragged the shoebox out from under her mother's bed and dumped it across the quilt, jaw already tight. Envelope after envelope, all addressed to Marcus in that looping, patient hand. She snapped a rubber band off a bundle and it stung her thumb; she didn't flinch. "Of course," she said to the empty room. "Of course you kept these." She read one line, about how proud their mother was, how he should never worry about the money, and her molars ground together. Where were hers? Three birthday cards in thirty years, signed with a stamp-like scrawl. She stacked his letters into a neat pile, squared the edges hard, then set the heavy lamp on top of them. Her neck burned. Downstairs the casserole dish clattered, and someone laughed at the funeral reception. Dana pulled one more envelope free, held it a moment, and slid it into her coat pocket, not the keep pile, not the trash, just away from him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale was scraping dried glue off the garage floor when Mr. Pruitt's shadow slid across the doorway. "Hey, neighbor. Got that tall ladder still?" Dale's jaw tightened until he felt it in his ears. He thought of the rake, the hedge trimmer, the pressure washer, all returned late or dented or not at all. The ladder hung on its hooks, the rungs still bent a little from March. "It's right there," he said, flat, not turning around. He wiped his hands slowly on a rag, one finger at a time, then lifted the ladder down so carefully it made no sound. His knuckles whitened on the rail. "Need it back by Saturday. I mean it. Saturday." Pruitt laughed and said sure, sure, and hoisted it onto his shoulder like he'd bought it himself. Dale stood in the driveway after, smiling the way he'd smiled at the dentist, watching the ladder wobble down the sidewalk. Then he went inside and shut the door harder than he needed to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: I chop the onions into smaller and smaller pieces until the knife is just knocking against the board. Six forty. They'll be here at seven, and Dana's still in the shower, singing, of course she is. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the potatoes. I wipe my hands on the apron, the one she said was 'so cute' on me, and the pot lid rattles when I set it down harder than I meant to. 'Babe?' she calls through the wall. 'Need anything?' 'No, I've got it,' I say, bright and clipped, the way you'd close a drawer. I always have it. I taste the sauce, add salt nobody will thank me for, and stare at the three clean wine glasses she set out an hour ago, lined up like a job finished. My shoulders are up near my ears. I lower them. They climb back. The oven timer ticks, and I count it out loud, just to hear something that's mine.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the counter while I'm scraping burnt rice into the trash, a number I don't know, a 612 area code. I let it ring four times, watching it crawl toward the edge of the counter. My jaw is tight enough that my molars ache. On the fifth ring I snatch it up. "Yes." Flat. Nothing else. A cheerful voice says my name, mispronounced, the way Dad always did, and the room tilts a little. Something about an estate, a lawyer, a few papers that need my signature. I set the pot down hard in the sink and the lid clatters. "Now he wants something from me," I say, to nobody, then into the phone, slowly: "Email it. I'm not going to talk about him on a Tuesday." My thumb hovers over the red button, trembling, and I press it harder than I need to. The kitchen is quiet again. The rice stink hangs there. I don't open the window.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Dana stood at the return desk with the paperback pinched between two fingers, as if it were something the cat had dragged in. Four hundred and twelve days, the screen said, and a fine she could have spent on a month of groceries. The librarian's smile was bright as the fluorescent tubes. "Welcome back!" Dana's jaw tightened until her molars ached. She set the book down without a sound, squaring its edges against the counter, then slid her card across with one flat, slow push. "Professor Hale made it required. Then never mentioned it again." Her voice stayed level, polite, thin as paper. Behind her the line shuffled. Heat crept up her neck, and she stared at the stamped date, at the sticker on the spine, at the gray cover she had never once opened. "Keep the receipt," she said, the words clipped short. She walked out without looking back, shoulders rigid, the automatic doors sighing shut behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers dropped the last box in the hallway because the couch had already eaten the doorway, and I tipped them exactly nothing. "Great," I said, to the radiator, which clanked back. Four hundred square feet. I set my mother's lamp on the counter because the counter was the only flat place, and my jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding it since the stairs. My brother got the house, the yard, the dishwasher that actually runs. I got a window facing a brick wall and a landlord's note taped to the fridge: No nails. I peeled the tape off in one long strip, folded it small, then smaller, until my thumbnail went white. When my phone buzzed with his name and *How's the new place?*, I turned it face down and shoved a box of plates under the sink with my foot. "Cozy," I told the empty room, and slammed the cabinet hard enough to make the lamp shiver.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench like it had been placed there for me, fat brown leather, the corner worn pale. I stood over it with my thermos going cold in my fist. Of course. Eleven years I'd been walking this loop, and the one thing the park ever handed me was somebody else's problem. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my molars. I flipped it open with two fingers. A license: smiling man, my age, a good haircut. Three hundred in twenties, a photo of a dog. Nobody had ever left anything on a bench for me to keep. I snapped it shut harder than I needed to. 'Fine,' I said to the pigeons, flat and loud. 'Fine. I'll take it. I'll go out of my way, like always.' My shoulders were up near my ears. I shoved it in my coat, the thermos clanking against it, and walked toward the station without finishing my loop, heels hitting the gravel one hard crunch at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite gripped the pool's gutter with both hands until her knuckles went pale, her jaw set so tight her teeth ached. Beside her, a nine-year-old in goggles kicked off the wall and glided away like it was nothing. "Kick from the hips," said the instructor, cheerful, clipboard tucked under one arm. "Mm," Marguerite said. She let go, sank, and came up sputtering, chlorine burning behind her nose. Her mother had sat on a lawn chair in 1987 and said swimming was for people with money. Forty-one years of avoiding every beach, every dock, every invitation to a lake house. She slapped the water flat-palmed, harder than she needed to. "Again?" the instructor asked. "Obviously again," she said, flat, and pushed off the wall, eyes fixed on the far tiles, muttering a count through clenched teeth while the kid in the next lane lapped her twice, humming to himself, his small heels flicking easily past her face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets were still in the bag Dana had left on my porch, with a sticky note that said, "You'll love it!" I stabbed the trowel into the dirt harder than the dirt deserved. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the car. "Twelve inches apart," I read aloud, flat, like a ransom note. Fine. I measured with a ruler and pressed each tomato start in as though I were burying evidence. Sweat slid under my collar. Across the fence, Mr. Ellis's rows were already green and tidy, and he waved. I lifted two fingers off the handle and went back to digging. My knees throbbed on the cold boards. Eight years I'd asked for help with this yard, and now, suddenly, a gift. I jammed the last stake in, snapped the string tight, and muttered, "There. Happy?" to nobody. The hose coughed, then soaked my shoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked past the title slide with a flourish, saying "we" three times in the first minute. Priya kept her pen capped and her notebook shut. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars since the second bullet point, the one she'd drafted at eleven o'clock on a Sunday. The conference room smelled of burnt coffee and dry-erase marker. When the VP nodded and said, "Great thinking, Marcus," heat crawled up her neck, and she turned her paper cup a quarter turn at a time until the rim left a damp ring on the table. Someone asked if anyone had additions. She smiled with her mouth only. "No, it's all there," she said, evenly, too evenly, and pressed her thumbnail into her fingertip until it whitened. Then she clapped twice, late, after everyone else had already stopped.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The wipers squeak across a windshield that isn't even wet anymore, and I leave them on anyway. Eleven forty. Dana's text sits face-down on the passenger seat: Can you stay just a bit longer? Sure. Always sure. I grip the wheel so hard my knuckles ache, and I notice I'm going nine over on an empty road, past the shuttered gas station, past the one blinking yellow light. My jaw is clamped tight enough that my molars hum. I rehearse what I should've said in that meeting, in that doorway, to that smile, and I hear my own voice in the dark car, flat and clipped: "No problem. Happy to." I laugh once, a short ugly sound. The porch light is off at home. Of course it is. I kill the engine, but sit there with my fists in my lap, listening to the metal tick, not yet ready to go in and be pleasant to anyone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I set the bag of clementines on the tray table and didn't bother to peel one. Dad's eyes stayed on the television, some game show, volume too high. "Traffic was bad," I said, though it wasn't, and I'd sat in the parking garage twenty minutes with the engine off. My jaw ached from clenching. He asked if I'd brought the right crackers, and I said, "You didn't say a kind." The words came out flat and clipped. A nurse smiled at me and I gave her half a nod. When he said, "Your sister called twice today," I stared at the monitor and counted the beeps. Thirty years of showing up, and he still talked to me like the delivery guy. I kept my coat on. My hand gripped the bed rail until the knuckles whitened, and when he reached for his water, I passed the cup without letting our fingers touch.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana got to the gate at 2:40, twenty minutes early, because last time she'd been late and Priya's mother had made a small show of waving Tom over. Now she stood apart from the cluster by the fence, keys biting into her palm, watching the other mothers laugh about a bake sale she hadn't been asked to help with. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the car. A woman said, "Oh, Dana, we missed you at the meeting!" and Dana said, "Did you," flat, and smiled with only her teeth. She'd worked a double and skipped lunch to be here, and nobody had asked about that. The bell rang. Kids poured out in bright jackets. She checked her watch, then the sky, then her watch again, shoulders hard as a coat hanger. When Tom finally trotted over, backpack dragging, she took it from him without a word and walked to the car three steps ahead of everyone, not looking back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite set the oak dresser at the curb at seven, flat on its crooked feet, and wiped her palms down her slacks twice. A man ran his thumb along the drawer edge and asked if she'd take twenty. "It's two hundred," she said, not looking up. "My brother picked it out. He's got the matching bed in his guest room, I hear." Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars since breakfast. The man shrugged and drifted off toward the lamps. She pressed a price sticker onto the sofa harder than needed, then peeled it off and pressed it down again. Mother's good chair sat by the garage, its cushion still holding the shape of all the years she'd spent hauling it to doctor's appointments. "Fifteen," she told a woman who touched it. "Nobody else wanted it, so." She laughed, a short dry sound, and counted the quarters in the cashbox until the coins blurred, heat climbing her neck while the sun cooked the empty folding chair beside her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Dana lay on the cold kitchen tile with her head inside the cabinet, a flashlight clamped in her teeth, and water ticking onto her wrist every four seconds. Upstairs, the television murmured. She had asked Marcus to look at this pipe in March. She had asked again in June, and he'd said, "Yeah, yeah, this weekend." Now she wrenched the slip nut and it didn't budge, and her jaw tightened until her molars ached. "Sure," she muttered around the flashlight, "take your time." A drop slid down her sleeve to her elbow. She dragged the bucket closer with her foot, harder than needed, and it clanged against the cabinet wall. The laughter from the show drifted down the stairs. She wound plumber's tape around the thread with quick, stabbing turns, snapped it off, and thought of every other thing she had learned from videos at midnight. When the nut finally gave, she grunted, "Look at that. Me again." Her knuckles were bleeding a little. She didn't call up the stairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter for three days, propped against the fruit bowl like a guest I hadn't invited. Tonight I slit it open with a butter knife, slowly, because hurrying felt like a courtesy they hadn't earned. My jaw was already tight. The paper inside was folded in thirds, crisp, smelling of toner, and the first line thanked me for my "continued patience." I laughed, one short breath through the nose. Patience. Eleven months of hold music, four offices, two forms they swore they never received, and now a number in bold with a deadline under it. My thumb pressed a crease into the page until it went white. I read the amount again, then the signature, a stamped scrawl nobody had to look me in the eye to write. "Of course," I said to the empty kitchen, flat and quiet. I didn't tear it. I slid it back into its envelope, set the butter knife in the sink hard enough to ring, and went to find a pen, because I'd answer, and I'd be polite, and they'd feel every word of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marek dragged his suitcase over the cobbles, one wheel clacking where the plastic had cracked on the flight his sister had insisted he take. At the tram kiosk he jabbed the machine's glowing screen, jabbed it again, until it beeped and spat his coin back. A woman behind him said something quick and bright. He didn't turn. "Yes, thank you, very helpful," he muttered, jaw tight, and fed the coin in a fourth time. His shirt stuck to his spine. Every sign was a wall of consonants, and he read each one slowly, lips pinched, as if it had been written to spite him. When the driver barked at him, Marek held up the ticket, then his phone, then three fingers, and said loudly, in English, "Nobody here could print one word I understand?" The doors hissed shut. He stood gripping the pole, knuckles pale, staring at the back of the driver's head the whole ride.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the field with a stick twice his length, ears flapping, and I kept my hands jammed in my jacket pockets. Dana's text was still open on my phone, face-down on the bench beside me: Can you take him Saturdays? Just till things settle. Things never settled for her. The grass soaked through my shoes and I let it. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my back teeth since the gate. "Come," I called, flat, and he ignored me, because of course he did. He flopped in the mud, grinning, tongue lolling. A woman nearby laughed and waved at him. I nodded the way you nod at a bill. Forty minutes, I told myself. Then I'd clip the leash, drive him back to her porch, and say "No problem" so lightly she'd never hear what it cost me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marjorie gets the solo again, and I count the folding chairs while she hums her warm-ups, one hundred and twelve of them, every one squeaking. "Lovely," I say when she finishes, and my jaw aches from how I say it. The church hall smells of burnt coffee and floor wax. I flip to the second violin part, the one I've played for eleven years, and press my bow so hard the string scrapes. Mr. Delaney taps his stand. "Gentler, Ruth." I nod. I play it gentler. Something sits tight and hot behind my ribs, like a stone left in the sun. During the break she offers me shortbread from her tin, and I take it, and eat it standing by the radiator, and don't thank her. When we start again I come in a half-beat late, just once, and I watch the back of her cardigan to see if she notices.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Walt's widow handed me three flattened boxes and a roll of tape, and said take whatever I wanted. I wanted my table saw back, the one I'd lent him in 2011, but I found it under a tarp with sawdust packed in its teeth like he'd never once cleaned it. I dragged it to the door, jaw tight, and my shoulder burned. Forty years of coffee cans filled with sorted screws lined the shelf, labeled in his neat block capitals. Neat for screws. I tipped a can into the trash bin and listened to it rattle all the way down. Then another. 'You could have called,' I said to the pegboard, loud enough that my voice came back flat off the tin roof. The vise still held a half-finished birdhouse I'd asked him for in March. I pried it loose, turned it over, and snorted at the crooked roof. I set it in the box marked DONATE, pressed the tape down hard, and dragged my thumbnail along it until it squealed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smelled of floor wax and other people's cologne, and I stood apart from the crowd at the noticeboard, arms folded, jaw set so tight my teeth ached. Priya kept refreshing the portal on her phone and sighing like the wait was happening to her alone. Ten o'clock came and went. Nothing. I peeled a strip of paint from the wall with my thumbnail and flicked it onto the tiles. Dev had slept through every lecture, borrowed my notes twice, and now he was laughing by the vending machine, tossing a coin in the air. 'Relax,' he told me. 'It's just a number.' I smiled the way you bare a tool. 'Sure,' I said. 'Easy for you.' My stomach burned. I'd given up two summers for this, and I kept replaying how the invigilator had let him sit by the window, where the light was better. When the sheet finally went up, I didn't push forward. I let them all go first, and I watched their faces.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Dana kept her eyes on the switchbacks and her jaw tight, boots striking the gravel harder than the slope required. Behind her, Marcus was whistling. The sun had slipped behind the ridge twenty minutes ago, and the pines were turning into flat black cutouts. "We could've started at noon," she said, not turning around, each word clipped short. "Like I said. At breakfast. And at the car." He laughed and said something about the view. She tightened the straps of her pack until they bit into her collarbones, though they were already tight. Her headlamp stayed in her pocket; she wouldn't be the one to dig it out first. A root caught her toe and she let out a hiss through her teeth, then kicked the stone it had loosened, watching it clatter into the dark. "Great view," she muttered. Her heartbeat pounded in her ears, and she walked faster, leaving him to follow the sound of her steps down the cooling trail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is soft as cloth from forty years of thumbs, Grandma's slanted handwriting saying "flour until it feels right." Feels right to whom? I slap the dough onto the counter harder than I need to. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the yeast foamed. "A pinch of salt," I read aloud, flat, and dump in a fistful, daring the loaf to complain. She never wrote anything down properly, just left smudges and expected us to guess, then died before anyone could ask. My aunt got the house. My cousin got the piano. I got a grease-stained index card and a dented bowl. I knead until my shoulders burn, until the clock says midnight, until flour clouds my sleeves. When the oven timer finally buzzes I stand there with the mitts on, not moving, listening to it scream. The kitchen smells exactly like her, and I open the window anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was comparing two cans of tomatoes when I heard my name, bright and rising, from the end of the aisle. Dana Whitcomb. She still tilted her head like she was waiting to be admired. My jaw set before I'd even turned around. "Wow. Hi," I said, flat, holding the can like a small weapon. She told me about her firm, her house near the lake, her husband's promotion, and I nodded at each one, a half second late. Under the fluorescent hum my neck went hot. I remembered the group project, her name typed first on the cover page, the A she'd carried out of the room like it was hers alone. "Good for you," I said. "Really." She asked if I wanted to catch up sometime. "Sure," I said, already pushing my cart past her, the wheel squeaking, my fingers white on the handle. At the register I realized I'd bought the wrong tomatoes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Dana wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time, pressing hard enough that her wrist ached. Through the front window the parking lot had emptied hours ago, every other car off toward somebody's table. The radio played a jingle for the fourth time. "Happy Thanksgiving," she told the man who rushed in at 5:52 for a single can of cranberry sauce, and her smile stayed exactly as long as the receipt took to print. When he said, "Bet you can't wait to get out of here," she bagged the can without looking up. "Sure," she said. Her jaw was tight; she noticed she was grinding her molars and kept doing it. In the back, she snapped the lights off one row at a time, harder than the switches needed. Her sister's text glowed on her phone: *We saved you a plate!* She read it, thumbed the screen dark, and stood a long moment with her keys biting into her palm before she locked the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Dana hit the gate area at a jog, rolling bag clacking behind her, and the agent didn't look up. "B44 is closing," the woman said. "I know," Dana said, each word clipped flat. "My first plane sat on the tarmac for fifty minutes." Her jaw ached from clenching. She thought of Marcus in the aisle seat, who had slept through the whole delay with his mouth open, and of her sister's text, just book the later one, it's cheaper, which she hadn't answered. Sweat prickled under her coat. The moving walkway was out of order, so she dragged the bag along the stalled rubber, wheels shrieking, past a man blocking the left lane with a pretzel. "Excuse me," she said, not softly. He shuffled a quarter inch. She breathed through her nose, counting gates, and decided that if the door was already shut, she would stand there anyway and make somebody say it to her face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta dragged the roller through the tray hard enough that paint slopped over the edge and pooled on the drop cloth. Soft Harbor Gray, the can said. Dana had chosen it in four minutes, standing in the hardware aisle, and then left for her sister's with a cheerful wave. Marta pressed the roller against the wall and watched the old yellow vanish in wet, even stripes. Her shoulder burned. Her jaw ached from clenching, and she only noticed when she tried to answer the radio host and her teeth wouldn't part. Three Saturdays now. The tape had peeled a corner of plaster off by the window, and she stared at it a long moment before smoothing it down with her thumb, slowly, the way you press on a bruise. When her phone buzzed, Dana's name lit the screen. 'Looks great, I'm sure,' Marta said aloud to the empty room, flat as the wall, and turned the phone face down on the ladder shelf. She didn't wipe the drip off the baseboard.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The thunder rolled in just as Dana's car pulled out of the driveway, taillights smearing red across the wet gravel, and I stayed exactly where I was. Fine. Let her drive in this. I gripped the arm of the porch chair until the paint flaked under my thumbnail. Rain hammered the tin roof, and a cold spray kept finding my ankles; I didn't move my feet. Inside, the phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, twice, then stopped. I didn't get up. 'Forty years,' I muttered to the dog, who ignored me, 'and I'm the one who washes her mug.' My jaw ached from clenching. Lightning lit the empty swing, still rocking from where she'd shoved it. I poured the last of the lemonade into the glass and drank it warm, slowly, with my back very straight, like someone was watching, like someone should be.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Dana wheeled the bike under the one working bulb and knelt on the cold concrete, knees clicking. Someone had borrowed her tire levers again; she found them in the neighbor's toolbox, wedged beneath a jar of mismatched screws, and took them without a note. The chain was rusted orange where the drip from the ceiling pipe had been landing for weeks. She looked at it a moment, then reached for the rag. "Okay," she said to nobody, flat and quiet. The third-floor tenants' paint cans sat stacked against her workbench, so she worked on the floor instead, back bent, fingers black with grease. When the patch failed to hold, she peeled it off, sighed through her nose, and started over with the same slow hands. Upstairs a door slammed. She didn't look up. She spun the wheel, listened to the faint hiss, and reached for the pump again."Fine," she muttered. "Again."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's plastic roof while Marguerite was still checking the schedule, though she already knew what it said. She lowered her bag to the bench, unzipped it, and pulled out the folded rain bonnet she'd carried since March. The wind pushed a sheet of water sideways across the curb and onto her shoes. She looked down at them, shifted her feet an inch to the left, and let the cold seep in anyway. A man jogged past with a newspaper over his head. "Twenty minutes, probably," she told no one, in the flat voice she used for weather and bills. Her phone buzzed with her sister's text; she read it, typed "fine," and put it away. The streetlights flickered on early, yellow in the gray. She tied the bonnet under her chin, folded her hands in her lap, and watched the road with the patience of someone watching a pot that had never once boiled for her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box had sat under the stairs for eleven years, and Marguerite carried it to the kitchen table without wiping off the dust. She pulled the first envelope free, glanced at the handwriting, and set it on the left pile. The second went left too. Her knees ached against the chair, and she shifted once, then stopped bothering. The rain tapped the window at its usual pace. One letter, thick with pages, she held a moment, thumb on the flap her brother had licked shut in 1987. "Well," she said to the empty room, flat and mild, and laid it with the others. The kettle clicked off behind her. She let it sit. By the time the left pile reached the height of her wrist, she had already fetched the black trash bag from the drawer, unfolded it, and hooked its corner over the chair, where it would wait for her without any hurry.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Gary's knock came while the kettle was still ticking, three raps, the same cheerful rhythm as last spring. I turned off the stove and didn't bother checking the peephole. "Ladder," I said, before he could. He laughed and said gutters, just an hour, promise. I nodded and wiped my hands on the dish towel, slowly, one finger at a time. The garage light buzzed on with its usual stutter. The ladder hung where it always hung, except for the bent rung he'd left me with the last time, which I'd never mentioned. I lifted it down, my shoulder giving its small familiar complaint, and carried it out past the dead hydrangea. "Mind the third step," I said. "Always do," he said, though he never had. I stood on the porch holding the door, watching him drag it across my lawn, leaving two pale lines in the grass. Then I went back in and poured the tea, already lukewarm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The sauce had split, and Marguerite looked at it for a moment before reaching for the whisk anyway. Oil glistened along the edges of the pan like a small, greasy tide. She stirred, tasted, and added a pinch of salt she knew wouldn't help. Through the window the light had gone orange, and somewhere down the street a car door shut; she didn't check whether it was theirs. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, in the voice she used for weather. Her shoulders had settled low and heavy, and the ache in her lower back she simply let be. The chicken needed another twenty minutes. She set the timer, wiped her hands on the dishtowel that had been her mother's, and pulled out the six mismatched chairs one at a time. If they wanted more than this, they'd have said so years ago. She lit the candles anyway, and sat down to wait for the doorbell, hands folded over the cool edge of the table.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter, skittering toward the edge of a pile of unopened envelopes. Unknown number, a 612 area code I don't recognize. I let it ring four times while I finish wiping the same spot on the table. Then I dry my hands on my jeans, slowly, one finger at a time, and sit down in the chair that always creaks. My shoulders drop before I even answer. "Yeah, hello," I say, flat, like I'm reading it off a card. The line crackles. A bright voice asks if this is the right person, and I almost laugh. "Depends who you want," I say. "Go ahead. I'm listening." I pull the top envelope toward me and don't open it. Outside, the streetlight flickers on, same as every evening. I rest my forehead against my palm and close my eyes. "No, that's fine," I tell the voice. "Just tell me how much."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in the bottom of Dae-jin's backpack since March, and now, in November, its corners were soft as cloth. He set it on the counter without ceremony. The librarian turned it over, and he watched the date stamped in faded purple on the back flap. "Four hundred and twelve days," she said, tapping her keyboard. He nodded. His shoulders stayed low, and he didn't reach for the apology he'd rehearsed on the bus. "Okay," he said. "How much?" The number came up on the screen, more than his textbook had cost last term. He pulled out his card, then slid it back and fished for the other one. The heater ticked above the door. Outside, rain pressed against the windows the way it had all week. He signed the slip with the pen chained to the desk, read nothing on it, and said, "Thanks," as if she'd handed him something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box came up the stairs at four, and Dale set it on top of the others without opening any of them. The room was nine steps long; he had counted them twice, once with the landlord watching. He slid the window up. It stuck halfway, so he left it there and let the smell of fried onions from downstairs drift in. "Fine," he said to the empty room, and his voice came out flat against the bare walls. The couch wouldn't clear the doorway, so he'd leave it in the hall tonight and think about it tomorrow. He sat on the mattress, which was still wrapped in plastic, and it crackled under him. His shoulders ached. He pulled one sneaker off, then stopped, looking at the single outlet behind the radiator. Of course. He nodded slowly, ate crackers from the sleeve, and didn't bother to find a plate or a light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather gone pale at the corners, and Marguerite looked at it for a full minute before she lowered herself onto the slats beside it. Her knees clicked. She'd been walking to the bus stop, which could wait; the bus was always late anyway. She picked the wallet up with two fingers, as if it might be hot, and thumbed it open. A license, a grocery card, forty dollars folded small. A young man's face squinted out from the plastic. "Well, you'll be missing this," she said to the pigeons. Nobody answered. She exhaled, long and slow, and slid the wallet into her coat pocket where the tissues lived. The police station was eleven blocks uphill, past the closed bakery. She'd done worse errands. She stood, brushed the leaves off her skirt, and started up the path without hurrying, her shoes scuffing the gravel in an even, patient rhythm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor is nineteen, with a whistle and a sunburn line across her nose, and she tells me to put my face in the water again. I do. The chlorine stings the way it did last Tuesday, and the Tuesday before. Under the surface I count to three because that's what I managed last time, and then I count to three again, since there's no reason to hope for four. When I come up, the foam board has drifted off, and I wade after it without being asked. 'Good,' she says. 'Kicking next.' I nod. My knees ache from the cold tile where I sat waiting my turn beside the children, whose mothers glance at my towel and then away. I'm forty-six. My feet sink every time I stop moving, and I've stopped being surprised. 'Same time next week?' she asks, and I say, 'Sure, I'll be here,' in the voice I use for dentist appointments. I wring out my trunks slowly and walk to the lockers, one wet footprint after another.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets had been sitting on the counter since March, and now it was nearly June, so Dalia carried them out to the yard along with the spade her landlord had left behind. The soil was clay, orange and heavy, and it clung to the blade in slabs. She dug a row anyway, shoulders aching by the third foot. A neighbor leaned over the fence and said tomatoes were fussy. "Probably," she said, and kept going. She read the back of the carrot packet, squinted at the spacing, then dropped the seeds in more or less where it said. Sweat ran into her collar. She patted the dirt flat with her palm, filled the watering can, and let it trickle out slowly. "Well," she said to the empty row, wiping her hands on her jeans. "Might as well." She left the spade standing in the ground and went inside without looking back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana's idea sat on slide four, though the name in the corner said Priya. She capped her pen and set it parallel to her notebook. The projector fan whined; someone's coffee sent up a last thin thread of steam. Priya clicked forward and said, "So, our approach," and Dana nodded at the right moments, the way she'd nodded through three quarters of this. Her shoulders sank into the chair's worn lumbar curve, and she let them. When the VP glanced down the table, Dana lifted her eyebrows into a small, practiced shape of interest. Her notebook page stayed blank except for the date. Afterward, when Priya asked, bright-eyed, "What did you think?" Dana said, "Looks great. Really clean," in the same even voice she used for booking conference rooms. She rinsed her mug in the kitchenette, dried it, and wondered whether the sandwich place would still have the turkey one on Thursday.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The phone buzzes in the cup holder and I let it. Probably Dana again, or the landlord, and either way the answer will keep until morning. The highway is empty except for a truck two miles ahead, its taillights small and red. I keep my hands at ten and two, though my shoulders have sagged so far the seatbelt barely touches them. The radio is on some call-in show about gutters; I don't change it. When the exit for the shortcut comes up, I pass it and take the long way, because the long way has fewer lights and I've stopped arguing with myself about the extra eleven minutes. 'Fine,' I say to the windshield, flat, like signing for a package. At the last light I stop for red with nobody around and wait the full cycle. My eyes sting. I blink once, slowly. The apartment will be dark, the sink will have the same dishes, and tomorrow I'll go back and say yes to the same things. I turn up the gutters.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus signed the visitor log without reading the names above his, clipped the paper badge to his coat, and rode the elevator to four. His uncle's door was half open. The television murmured a game show nobody was watching. He pulled the vinyl chair closer to the bed, the same chair, the same squeak, and sat with his coat still on. "They moved your water," he said, and slid the cup to the other side of the tray, where the old man's hand could find it. The monitor ticked. A nurse looked in, and he nodded to her as if they'd already said everything. He peeled an orange from the bag he'd brought, though no one would eat it, and set the segments in a neat row on a napkin. His shoulders sagged into the chair's hard back. When visiting hours ended, he stood slowly, tucked the blanket under his uncle's feet, and said, "Same time Thursday." He didn't check whether anyone heard.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I turn the engine off at 2:52, eight minutes early, and don't bother pretending I'll do anything useful with them. The other parents cluster by the fence, trading news, and I lift two fingers from the steering wheel when Dana waves. Rain ticks on the roof. My shoulders have settled into the seat's old dent. Last week the teacher said the word "again," and I said, "Okay. Thank you for telling me," in the same flat, pleasant voice I use for the bank. I peel a receipt off the dashboard and fold it into a smaller square, then a smaller one. The doors bang open at 3:00. Kids spill out in bright coats, and I watch for his green hood, already knowing it'll be last, already knowing he'll be dragging his bag and not looking up. I get out anyway, stand in the drizzle, and hold the umbrella ready. "Hey, bud," I'll say. "Let's go home." It's what I always say.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine, Walt had dragged the oak dresser to the end of the driveway and propped a hand-lettered sign on top: $40. He didn't wipe the dust from the mirror. A young woman ran her thumb along a scratch in the edge and asked if he'd take twenty. "Sure," he said, already reaching for the tape. His knees ached from the lifting, and he lowered himself onto the cracked vinyl kitchen chair that was also for sale. Across the lawn, Marjorie's rocking chair tilted in the sun, the cushion faded where her hands used to rest. A man picked it up, turned it over, set it down again. "Five dollars," Walt called, not rising. He watched the neighbor's dog sniff the table legs and wander off. When the light slid long across the grass, he started carrying the unsold pieces back toward the garage one at a time, humming something tuneless, and left the door open behind him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip landed in the saucepan at the same pace it had for three weeks, and I knelt on the cabinet floor anyway, flashlight clamped in my teeth. I wrapped the tape around the joint, counted to ten, and pressed my palm against it. Cold. Damp. A bead formed at the edge of the tape before I'd even pulled my hand away. I watched it swell and fall. "Well," I said to nobody, and my voice came out flat as the wrench in my lap. My knees ached against the tile. I set the wrench down gently, the way you set down something you already know you'll pick up tomorrow. The saucepan ticked. I slid the bucket underneath it, tucked a dish towel around the base, and stayed there a moment longer, one hand resting on the pipe. Then I got up, slowly, and wrote 'plumber' on the list under the other things I hadn't called about yet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had sat on the radiator shelf since Tuesday, beside the takeout menus, and Marguerite had walked past it each evening without slowing. Tonight she set her tea down, slid a butter knife under the flap, and drew it along in one even stroke. The paper inside was folded in thirds, the way they always were. She read the first line, then skipped to the bottom, where the amount was, and nodded once, as if someone had asked her a question. "Well," she said to the empty kitchen, her voice flat as the table. The refrigerator hummed. Her shoulders did not rise or fall. She refolded the letter along its creases, slipped it back into the envelope, and tucked it under the fruit bowl. Then she picked up her tea, found it lukewarm, and drank it anyway, looking at the window where nothing in particular was happening.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The bus hissed and left him at a curb where every sign was a row of curling characters he couldn't begin to sound out. Daniel set his suitcase down, watched one wheel rock and settle, and did not pick it up right away. Rain ticked on the shelter roof. He pulled out the paper with the hotel's address, now soft along its folds, and held it toward a woman with an umbrella. She spoke quickly, pointing in two directions at once. "Okay," he said, nodding, "thank you," though he'd understood none of it. He picked a direction. His shoulders had dropped somewhere over the last hour and stayed there. The suitcase clattered behind him over the wet tiles, and he let it, not bothering to lift it over the cracks. If the street was wrong, he thought, it would be wrong, and eventually a door would open onto somewhere with a bed. He walked on, slowly, the rain soaking through his collar, and didn't hurry to get out of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Walt sat on the low stone wall with the leash coiled in his lap, his coat zipped to the chin though the afternoon had gone mild. Out in the long grass, Biscuit chased a crumpled leaf, stumbled, and chased it again, the gray muzzle bobbing. The vet's folder was still in the car, face down on the passenger seat where he'd tossed it. He hadn't opened it a second time. 'Go on, then,' he said, not loudly, and the dog couldn't have heard. His thumb worked at a frayed thread on the leash handle, back and forth, back and forth. A crow landed nearby and walked off again. When Biscuit finally trotted over, tongue out, Walt scratched behind her ears and let his hand rest there. 'Five more minutes,' he said. He looked at his watch, then took it off and put it in his pocket. The light slid lower across the field, and he did not get up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The fellowship hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Marta set her clarinet case on the same folding chair she'd used for eleven years. Someone had moved the piano again; she shuffled her stand two feet left without comment. When the conductor said the second clarinet part was being cut to a single line this year, she nodded and said, "That's fine, Dennis. Less to carry." She wet the reed, wiped her palms on her cardigan, and played the passage through, the one that always cracked on the high note. It cracked. She lowered the instrument and waited for the heat to climb her cheeks, and it didn't. "Again from measure forty?" she asked, already turning the page. Her shoulders settled against the cold metal chair back. Rain tapped the gutters outside, and she counted four bars of rest before lifting the clarinet once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta pulled the string on the bare bulb and waited while it decided to come on. Dust lifted off Henrik's workbench in a slow gold sheet. She had brought six boxes and a roll of tape, and she set them down in a row by the door, labeled in marker: KEEP, SELL, DUMP. Only the last one got used. She lifted a coffee can of mismatched screws, weighed it in her palm, and tipped it into the box without sorting. Her knees ached when she crouched for the lower drawers. "Well, you won't be needing these," she said to the plane in her hand, flatly, the way one reads a receipt. She wiped the blade on her sleeve anyway. Outside, the neighbor's mower started and stopped. She taped a box shut, smoothed the tape twice with her thumb, and reached for the next shelf, where his reading glasses still sat folded on a half-sanded spoon. She slid them into her coat pocket and kept going.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 14 smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Mina sat on the low bench beneath the empty noticeboard with her coat still zipped. Others had crowded the door since noon, jostling, checking phones. She had folded her hands in her lap and left them there. When the secretary finally came out with the sheet and a roll of tape, Mina watched the tape squeal across the paper, one strip, two, three, without standing. A boy beside her whispered, "Aren't you going to look?" She shrugged. "In a minute. It'll say what it says." Her stomach felt heavy but quiet, like a stone at the bottom of a pond. She counted the ceiling tiles instead, got to forty, lost track, and started again. When the crowd thinned she rose, brushed lint from her sleeve, and walked over slowly, already reaching into her bag for the bus fare home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last of the orange slid off the ridge while I was still two miles from the car, and I didn't speed up. I stopped once to retie a boot, took my time with the knot, then pulled the headlamp from my pack and held it in my palm without switching it on. Not yet. My calves had gone heavy and warm, and the cold was starting to find the sweat at the back of my neck. A trail marker leaned out of the dusk, and I patted it as I passed, like a dog that had waited. "Well," I said to nobody, flat and easy, "that's how it goes." The switchbacks below were already blue and indistinct. I thought about the sandwich I'd skipped at noon, the phone with its one bar, the message I'd never sent. Then I clicked the lamp on, watched its small circle slide over the roots, and walked into it at the same steady pace as before.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The card is soft as cloth now, my grandmother's slanted pencil gone gray with thumbprints. "Flour until it feels right," it says, which is no help. I measure anyway, four cups, and dump them in the chipped yellow bowl. The kitchen is cold; the radiator ticks twice and quits. I knead because my hands know how, even if I don't. My shoulders ache by the tenth minute. "Well, it's sticky," I tell the empty room, and add a little more flour, then a little more. It never gets the way hers did. It won't this time either, I think, and I set it under the dish towel by the window anyway. I wipe my palms on my jeans, sit on the stool, and watch the gray afternoon. An hour, the card says. I have nowhere else to be. I'll eat whatever comes out of the oven, and I'll probably do this again next month.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a basket with one box of cereal and a bag of discount lemons when I heard my name from the end of the aisle. Dana Whitcomb, third-row desk, eleventh grade chemistry. She looked the same, only more polished, her coat the color of good oatmeal. I shifted the basket to my other hand. "Hey," I said. "Yeah, still here. Same apartment, practically." She asked what I was up to, and I told her the truth, flat and short, the way you read a receipt. She nodded too long. Behind her the freezers hummed, and I watched a thin trail of frost creep along the glass. When she said we should get coffee sometime, I said, "Sure, that'd be nice," and we both knew the sentence had no date attached. My shoulders dropped as she walked off. I looked at the lemons, soft at the edges, and put them in the basket anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At ten to five on Christmas Eve, Marisol flipped the sign on the pharmacy door to OPEN anyway, though the lot outside held only a shopping cart and a drift of wet leaves. She tied her apron twice, the way she always did, and pressed her thumb into the sore spot beneath her shoulder blade. The fluorescent tube over aisle three buzzed and flickered; she noted it, didn't call anyone. When the phone rang, she let it go three times before lifting it. "Hartley Drug. Yes. Until six. No, we won't be getting it in tonight." She listened, nodded at nobody, and said, "I know. Me too." Afterward she lined up the candy canes by the register, one row, then another, until the box was empty. Her sister's text glowed on the counter: *are you coming?* She typed *probably late*, deleted it, typed it again, and sent it. Then she pulled the stool closer and sat down to wait for the clock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta stepped off the jet bridge at 4:47, thirteen minutes after her connection was supposed to board, and she did not run. She read the departures screen the way someone reads a menu in a language she knew, found Gate B42 glowing beside the word CLOSED, and nodded once. Her shoulder strap had been digging a groove all morning; she shifted it and walked on anyway, past the moving walkway, because standing still on it seemed pointless too. At the gate, an agent with a lanyard full of pins was already shutting down her screen. "Just missed it," the agent said. "I figured," said Marta, softly, almost pleasantly. She set her bag on a vinyl chair bolted to three others and sat down beside it. Outside, a tug dragged luggage carts through the drizzle. She took out her phone, opened the rebooking line, and listened to the hold music with her eyes half closed, one thumb rubbing the worn corner of her boarding pass until the paper went soft.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pried the lid off the second can with a butter knife and stirred until the beige stopped swirling. It was the same beige as before, only newer. She'd stood in the hardware aisle for twenty minutes holding a swatch called Ocean Mist, then put it back and taken the one she already knew. Now she taped the baseboards in long, even pulls, her knees clicking as she shuffled along the floor. On the wall, a faint rectangle marked where the crib had been, then the desk, then nothing. "Well," she said to the empty room, and her voice came out flat as the roller tray. She dipped, rolled, and dragged the wet stripe up over the pencil marks of the children's heights, one by one, without slowing. Her shoulder ached. The radio hummed a song she didn't turn up or down. By dusk the marks were gone, and she sat on the overturned bucket, wiping her hands on her jeans, and looked at the wall until the light left it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail just as Marguerite settled into the sagging wicker chair, and she didn't get up. Through the screen door behind her, the phone had stopped ringing minutes ago; she'd let it. Rain slanted in and darkened her shins, and she watched it do so, hands folded over the envelope in her lap. Thunder rolled across the soybean fields, long and low, and the porch boards trembled under her slippers. 'Well,' she said to the dog, who lifted one ear. 'There goes the tomatoes.' She didn't say it sharply. She said it the way she might read a grocery list. Her shoulders loosened into the chair's old curves, and she let out a breath that fogged nothing in the heavy air. The envelope's corner had gone soft with rain. She turned it over once, set it on the floor beneath the chair, and kept watching the lightning walk the far fence line, one post at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Dara had patched the same tire tube twice, and now she pulled it off the rim a third time, though the bubbles in the water basin had stopped. Her knee jittered against the workbench until the wrench rattled in its tray. Across the garage, Mr. Okafor's radio murmured a ballgame, and she caught herself counting the seconds between his sighs. She tightened the brake cable, loosened it, tightened it again. "Fine," she said to nobody, too loudly, and he glanced up. "Sorry. Just talking to the chain." She wiped her hands on her jeans, walked to the door, looked at the gray sky, walked back. The spokes ticked as she spun the wheel, faster, then faster, until her palm slapped it still. Her fingers drummed the seat post. Twenty minutes ago she'd planned to ride to the river. The bike was fixed now, wasn't it? She clipped her helmet on, unclipped it, and picked up the pump again, though the tire was already hard as stone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over the pharmacy sign had gone the color of dishwater by the time I checked the schedule for the fourth time. Six minutes late. I took three steps to the left, three to the right, my sneakers slapping the wet-smelling pavement. The first fat drop hit my wrist and I rubbed it off like it had insulted me. Wind kicked a chip bag down the gutter, and I tracked it all the way to the corner, then back. "Come on," I said to nobody, then louder, to the empty road, "come on." An old man on the bench glanced up, and I made myself sit. My knee started bouncing before I'd finished sitting. I stood again. I zipped my jacket to the chin, unzipped it, zipped it. Thunder rolled somewhere behind the hills, and my fingers drummed the shelter's cold glass, a rhythm that kept trying to turn into running, though I had nowhere to run to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid had barely hit the floor before I was already on my third envelope, thumbnail jammed under the flap, tearing it more than opening it. My knee bounced against the bed frame. I read two lines of my mother's slanted handwriting, then glanced at the window, then the door, then back, and none of the words stayed. "Fine," I said aloud to nobody, and stood up. I walked to the kitchen, drank water I didn't want, and came back. Sat on the other side of the box this time. The stack by my foot slid over and I left it. Postmarks blurred: 1987, 1989, a stamp with a bird. I picked up a letter, put it down, picked up another. My tea went cold on the sill. I checked my phone, which had nothing, and checked it again. Then I was standing, pacing the length of the rug, still holding one page, reading the same sentence while my heel tapped the floorboards.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: When Mr. Alvarez knocked, Dena was already halfway to the door, having paced the hallway four times since lunch. "The ladder? Sure, yes, of course," she said, too fast, her knee bouncing against the frame as he explained about his gutters. Her fingers drummed the doorknob. She followed him to the garage, though he hadn't asked her to, and lifted the ladder down before he could reach it, the aluminum rattling loud in the quiet. "I could carry it over," she offered. "Or hold it for you. I'm free. I mean, I'm not doing anything." He laughed, puzzled. Back inside, she ran water over a clean glass, set it down, then opened the fridge and stared without taking anything. Her shoulders felt tight, her legs itching to move. She grabbed her keys, put them back, and watched through the window as he wobbled up the rungs, wishing someone would hand her a task.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The risotto doesn't need me, but I stir it anyway, then abandon the spoon to straighten the forks on the table for the third time. Six forty. They said seven. My heel taps the tile in a rhythm I can't seem to stop, and when I lift the lid on the roasting pan, I let it clatter back down without looking. "Fine," I tell the empty kitchen. "It's fine." I wipe a counter that's already clean. My phone buzzes against the cutting board and I snatch it, heart jumping, but it's only the pharmacy. I pour wine I don't drink, take two sips, set it by the sink, then carry it to the window, then back. The salt needs adding, or maybe it doesn't. I taste, taste again, can't tell. Down the street a car slows, and I'm already in the hallway with my hand on the doorknob, listening, before it rolls on past.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the countertop, and Dana's hand was on it before the second ring. Unknown number, a 612 area code she didn't recognize. She had already refolded the same dish towel three times that evening, and now she dragged it off the oven handle and twisted it around her wrist. "Hello?" Too bright, too fast. Silence, then a faint hum of traffic. She paced to the window, back to the fridge, back to the window, her heel tapping the tile. "Hello? Who is this?" Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since dinner. The line clicked and a man cleared his throat. "Is this Dana Wirth?" She opened a cabinet, closed it, opened it again without looking inside. "Depends," she said, laughing at nothing. "Who's asking?" Her knee bounced even though she was standing, and she couldn't make it stop, couldn't make anything stop, not even her thumbnail scraping the edge of the counter.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and my knee wouldn't stop bouncing against the underside of the return desk. I shifted the paperback from one hand to the other, then back again. The fluorescent hum seemed louder than it should have been. I'd rehearsed a sentence on the walk over, but when the librarian looked up, I blurted, "It's, uh, a little late," and laughed too high. My fingers drummed the counter, picked at the cracked spine, drummed again. She scanned the barcode. I counted ceiling tiles. Twice I glanced at the door, then at the clock, then at the poster about quiet study zones. "Eight months," she said mildly. "Right," I said, already rocking onto my toes, already half-turned toward the exit, my heels scuffing the carpet like they had somewhere else to be. "Can I just pay now? Or walk around and come back? Actually, no, now. Now's fine."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dana carried the last box up four flights and set it down in the middle of the floor, then picked it right back up. She slid it beside the window. Then to the closet. Then back. The apartment took eleven steps to cross; she'd counted twice. "Fine," she said to the empty room, too loudly, and the word bounced off the bare walls. She peeled tape from a carton, pulled out a mug, and put it in a cabinet, then took it out again and set it by the sink. Her knee jiggled against the radiator while she sat on the mattress for maybe ten seconds. Her fingers drummed the sill. Outside, someone's television murmured through the wall, and a bus sighed at the corner. She stood, checked the lock, unchecked it, and opened the window just to feel the air move. Half the boxes were still sealed. She grabbed her keys anyway, shoved her feet into her shoes, and headed down the stairs, two at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: I'd already circled the pond twice when I saw it, a brown leather wallet on the bench, tilted like someone had stood up mid-thought. My knee was bouncing before I even sat down. I picked it up, put it back, picked it up again. "Hello?" I said to nobody, too loudly, and a pigeon lifted off. The license inside said Marguerite Dols, and I read the address aloud twice, tapping my heel against the gravel in a rhythm that wasn't a song. Forty dollars, a library card, a photo of a dog. I stood, walked to the fountain, came back, stood again. My phone was in my hand, thumb hovering, then in my pocket, then out. The sun had barely moved but I'd checked my watch three times. Fine, I muttered, the address is only eleven blocks. I tucked the wallet under my arm, already walking, my sneakers slapping the path faster than the day seemed to need.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says to float, so I float for maybe four seconds, then my heel kicks the wall and I'm upright again, water sloshing off my chin. "Again," she says. I nod, but I'm already tugging my goggle strap, snapping it against my temple, loosening it, snapping it. My toes curl against the tile. Across the pool a toddler paddles past me with a foam noodle and I laugh too loudly. "Show-off," I tell him. Nobody laughs back. I lie down on the water again and my fingers drum the surface, tiny ripples spreading from each one. Count to ten, she says. I get to six. My legs twitch, thighs humming like a held wire, and I'm standing again, shaking out my wrists, bouncing on the pool floor. "Can I just do laps? Wherever? Across?" The clock above the lifeguard chair says eleven minutes left. I've checked it five times. I check it again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet says plant a quarter inch deep, eight inches apart, and I've already dug the third row twice. My knee bounces against the raised bed's edge while I kneel, and dirt cakes under my nails because I abandoned the gloves ten minutes ago. I stand, sit, stand again. "Okay," I tell the tomatoes that aren't there yet, too loudly, "okay, okay." A neighbor waves over the fence and I answer with a laugh that comes out too quick. I check my phone for rain, then check it again. The hose is already coiled; I uncoil it anyway. Beans, lettuce, carrots in neat little trenches, and I keep pressing my thumb into the soil as if it might answer. Nothing sprouts. Of course nothing sprouts. I pace the length of the fence, count the rows, pull one weed that might be a weed, and then crouch down and dig up a carrot seed just to see if it has changed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked her pen open, shut, open again while Marcus advanced to slide eleven of thirty-four. The conference room's air smelled of dry-erase markers and someone's reheated curry. Her left knee jogged beneath the table until the whole row of chairs hummed faintly, and she pressed a palm down on it, then gave up and crossed her ankles the other way. "Sorry, quick question," she said, too early, and Marcus held up a finger: "Let me get to the roadmap." She nodded, tore a corner off her notepad, folded it into a tiny square, unfolded it. The wall clock ticked past 2:40. She stood to refill a water glass that was still half full, hovered by the window counting cars in the lot, and sat back down. Her thumbnail worried the edge of the table. On slide twelve, she realized she had read the same bullet point four times and could not have said what it was about.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Dana changed the radio station for the fourth time and then switched it off altogether, letting the hum of the tires fill the car. The highway was empty, the sodium lights sliding over her dashboard in slow orange pulses. She drummed her thumbs against the wheel, then flexed her fingers, then drummed again. Her right knee bounced under the steering column until her foot nudged the gas and the needle crept past eighty; she eased off, swore softly, and rolled the window down. Cold air slapped her face. "Nearly there," she told no one, though the exit was still eleven miles away. At the next ramp she almost took it, just to be somewhere else, and when she finally pulled into her driveway she left the engine running, staring at the dark windows, hands still gripping the wheel, unable to make herself go inside and sit down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana sat down in the vinyl chair, then stood, then sat again, the squeak of it loud against the monitor's steady beep. Her uncle's hand lay open on the blanket, and she tapped her fingers against his knuckles in a rhythm she didn't choose. "They said the doctor comes at three," she told him, though it was ten past two, and she'd said it twice already. She peeled the label off a water cup in thin strips. Her knee bounced until the bed rail trembled, and she pressed her palm on it, guilty. At the window she counted cars in the parking lot, lost track, started over. "Want the blinds up? Down?" Before he could answer, she'd moved them halfway. Her calves itched to walk. She stepped into the hallway, read the evacuation map, came back, and checked her phone, which showed nothing new. "Okay," she said, sitting. "Okay." The clock hadn't moved.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The gate is still chained, and I've already checked my phone four times in two minutes. 2:51. I lean against the fence, then push off it, then lean again. My keys are in my fist, and I jingle them until the woman beside me glances over; I mumble, "Sorry," and shove them in my pocket, where my fingers keep drumming against my thigh. I walk to the crosswalk sign and back. I read the laminated notice about head lice twice without absorbing a word. My heel taps the pavement. "They're usually out by three, right?" I ask no one, and a dad shrugs. I peel the lid off my coffee, drink the cold dregs, and crush the cup flat. Every time a door swings, my shoulders jerk up. A teacher appears, and I take three steps forward before she only props the door open and vanishes. I roll my neck. My legs want to be anywhere but here, and I count the bricks in the wall until the bell finally cracks the air open.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By eight I had dragged the oak dresser to the curb, then back two feet, then forward again, as if the driveway might finally offer a better angle. A woman ran her thumb along the drawer lip and asked if forty was firm. "Sure, yes, forty, take it," I said, too fast, my words tumbling over hers. She hadn't even decided. My knee bounced against the card table until the coffee mug rattled, and I pressed my palm flat on it like it was a misbehaving dog. I'd refolded the same quilt three times. The sun climbed, my shirt stuck to my back, and I kept checking the street, the phone, the street. Every time someone lingered over Dad's old rocking chair, I walked off to straighten the lamps, then wandered back, rubbing the back of my neck. Somebody asked what else I had in the garage. "Nothing," I said. Then I went to look anyway, just to be moving.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
