I asked before he could finish his windy preamble about gutters. He blinked, then laughed. "How'd you know?" I shrugged and rolled my shoulders back, the late sun warm on my neck. The ladder hung in the garage exactly where I'd hung it, rungs wiped clean last spring. I lifted it off its hooks with one hand under the middle, balanced it on my shoulder, and walked it over without a wobble. "Twenty-eight feet, extends smooth, just set the feet on level ground," I said, steady and unhurried. He offered to return it Sunday. "Whenever," I said. "I've got another in the shed if I need it." I didn't, but it felt good saying it, chin lifted, whistling as I turned the hose back on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The doorbell was due in twenty minutes, and I was humming over the stove with my sleeves shoved to my elbows. Lamb shoulder rested under foil on the counter, glossy and right on schedule. I tossed the potatoes in the pan without measuring a thing, just listened for the sizzle, and nodded when it sounded the way it should. My shoulders hung loose. My phone buzzed with my sister's text asking if I needed help, and I typed back, "Just bring wine," one-handed, while the other tasted the sauce. Salt, a squeeze of lemon, done. Steam curled against my cheeks and I let it. The table was already set, candles unlit, and I decided to leave the dishes in the sink rather than hide them. Nobody would care. I wiped my palms on the towel over my shoulder, turned the music up a notch, and sang the wrong words to the right song, loudly, to an empty kitchen that felt entirely mine.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cafe table, a string of digits I didn't recognize, and I let it ring twice more while I finished my sip of coffee. Then I swiped, leaned back until the chair creaked, and propped one boot on the empty seat across from me. "Go ahead," I said, easy and unhurried. A voice stumbled through a name, a company, something about my account. I smiled at the barista passing by. "Slow down, friend. Start with who gave you this number." My shoulders stayed loose, my free hand drumming a lazy rhythm on the table. When the caller faltered, I didn't fill the silence; I just waited, breathing evenly, warm sun on my neck. "Okay," I finally said, voice steady and low. "Here's what we're going to do. You tell me exactly what you need, or I hang up and enjoy my morning. Either's fine by me." I picked up my cup again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and it was now November, but I walked through the library doors like I was expected. The carpet muffled my boots. I pulled out the battered copy of Middlemarch, its spine softened by my own thumbs, and set it on the desk with a pat. The clerk's eyebrows rose at the date stamped inside. "Eight months," she said. "Yep," I said, easy, shoulders loose, meeting her eyes. "I read it twice. Worth every day." My voice came out steady and warm, and I felt it in my chest, a quiet hum. She typed; the screen showed the fine, a number that would have made me flinch once. I slid my card across without glancing at it. "Put it on there, and I'll take whatever's next on the hold shelf." Then I grinned, tapped the counter twice, and strolled toward the stacks, already scanning spines.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol shouldered the door open and left the boxes in the hallway while she stood in the middle of the single room, hands on her hips, grinning at the water stain on the ceiling. "Okay," she said aloud, to no one, "you and I are going to get along." The couch was too wide for the doorway, so she tilted it, spun it once, and slid it through on the first try, barely out of breath. She measured the wall by the window with her outstretched arms and decided the bookshelf would go there, not where the landlord's note suggested. Her shoulders stayed loose as she hauled the mattress up on its side. When the neighbor leaned out and asked if she needed help, she laughed warmly. "Thanks, but I've got it." Then she hung her mother's mirror crooked on purpose, stepped back, and nodded at the steady-eyed woman looking back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marisol was halfway across Alder Park when she spotted the brown leather wallet on the bench by the fountain. She didn't slow her stride, just angled toward it with her shoulders loose and her chin level. She sat, flipped it open, and read the license aloud to no one. "Desmond Okafor. Well, Desmond, you're having a lucky day." A pigeon hopped near her shoe; she nudged it aside without looking. The sun warmed the back of her neck, and her pulse stayed slow and even. She found a business card tucked behind the cash, tapped it against her knee, and pulled out her phone with one thumb. Two rings, then a gruff hello. "I've got your wallet," she said, voice easy and clear. "Bench by the fountain. Stay put, I'll wait." She stretched her legs out, crossed her ankles, and watched the path as if the whole park had been arranged for her to sit in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite was forty-three, and she walked down the pool steps like she owned the water. The instructor, a lanky teenager named Dev, held out a foam noodle; she waved it off with a smile. "Let me try without it first," she said, her voice even and warm. Chlorine hung in the air, and the lane ropes bobbed in neat blue-and-white lines. She pushed off the wall, shoulders loose, chin low, and felt the cool water slide along her ribs as her legs kicked behind her. Her first stroke was clumsy. She laughed at it, then did another. Halfway across she swallowed a little water, coughed once, and kept going, steady, unhurried. When her fingers slapped the far tile she turned, wiped her eyes, and called over the splashing kids, "Again. And this time, show me the breathing part." Her heart thudded, but her hands were already reaching for the wall to push off once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Mara dropped the seed packets onto the overturned bucket and rolled her shoulders back, grinning at the bare rectangle of dirt behind the garage. She hadn't read the whole instruction sheet, only the pictures, and that seemed plenty. The spade went in with one stomp, and she felt the clean jolt travel up her calf. "Tomatoes here, where the sun hits," she announced to the fence, to the cat, to nobody. She stretched a string between two sticks and pulled it taut, humming, then pressed her thumb into the soil to the first knuckle, exactly as the packet showed. Sweat ran down her spine and she liked it. When her neighbor leaned over the fence and asked if she needed help, Mara laughed warmly and shook her head. "Come back in August," she said, patting the last seed under, "and bring a big bowl." She hosed the rows in long, easy arcs, chin lifted, already sure of the green coming.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marisol walked to the front of the conference room without glancing at her notes, set her coffee on the sill, and let the first slide sit blank while the murmuring settled. Her shoulders felt loose, her breath slow and deep. "Three months ago, this team lost forty hours a week to manual reconciliation," she said, each word unhurried. "Today I'll show you how we get them back." The projector hummed. Someone in the back asked a pointed question about cost, and she nodded once and answered before he finished, tapping the chart with an open palm. Her hands stayed warm and steady. When the clicker died mid-slide, she laughed, walked to the laptop, and pressed the key herself, never losing her thread. Let them push, she thought; the numbers will hold. By the end she was leaning against the table, and the whole room had leaned toward her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol rolled the window down an inch and let the cold air smooth her hair back as the highway emptied around her. Past midnight, the only lights were the amber ones strung along the overpass, and she drove under them with one wrist draped over the wheel, humming off-key and not caring. Her presentation had run forty minutes over, and she had still closed the room; she replayed the moment the director leaned back and said, "Well, that settles it," and she grinned at the dashboard. At the red light with no cars in sight, she waited anyway, shoulders loose, spine pressed easy into the seat. "Yeah," she said aloud to nobody, "I'd hire me too." The light turned green. She took the exit without braking early, turned the music louder, and coasted into her quiet street, already planning what she'd ask for on Monday.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol pushed through the double doors of the fourth-floor ward with her shoulders loose and her chin level, a paper bag of her grandfather's favorite lemon cookies swinging at her side. She nodded at the nurse at the station and asked, in an easy voice, which room Mr. Vega was in, then walked the corridor without glancing at the numbers. Her heels clicked evenly on the linoleum. Inside, the beeping monitors and the smell of antiseptic didn't slow her; she pulled the vinyl chair right up to the bed, sat with her legs crossed, and tapped the blanket. "You look terrible, Abuelo. Good thing I brought backup." He laughed, weakly, and she felt her own breath steady and deep in her chest. When the doctor arrived with a clipboard and a careful frown, she stood, shook his hand firmly, and said, "Walk me through it. I'll ask questions as we go." Her pen was already moving.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I park in the fire lane, because the line of minivans stretches past the bakery and I've never once been ticketed here. Engine off, window down, I step out and lean against the hood with my arms crossed loosely, shoulders low, breathing slow. Two other parents glance over; I nod at them like we've known each other for years, and one nods back. The bell rings and the doors burst open. I don't crane my neck. I know Maya will spot my red scarf, and she does, sprinting, backpack bouncing. The principal hovers by the gate with a clipboard, so I walk straight up to ask about the science fair deadline, my voice easy and clear. "Friday, right? Good. We'll have it ready." My stride feels long and unhurried on the warm asphalt. Maya grabs my hand. I swing it all the way to the car.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite dragged the walnut dresser to the very front of the driveway, where the morning sun hit its grain, and wiped her palms on her jeans with a grin. By eight, a man in a windbreaker was frowning at the scuffed corner and muttering about price. She didn't flinch. "Forty," she said, leaning an elbow on the top drawer as if it were her own mantel. "It's solid wood, not particle board. You'll be handing it to your grandkids." He offered twenty. She laughed, easy and warm, and shook her head. "Come back at noon if you like, but it won't be here." Her shoulders stayed loose, her chin level, her voice unhurried. She sipped her coffee, straightened a lamp on the card table, and waved at a passing neighbor. When the man sighed and peeled two twenties from his wallet, she slid the drawers shut with a soft thump and said, "Told you." Then she started pricing the next piece higher.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marisol slid under the sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, water dripping onto her wrist, and she barely noticed. "Thirty minutes," she told the empty kitchen, pulling the wrench from her belt as if greeting an old friend. The joint was corroded, green at the edges, and she gave it a quick, appraising tap. Her shoulders stayed loose; her breathing stayed slow. She wrapped the threads with tape in three clean turns, then spun the fitting home with a single steady pull that she felt settle in her forearms. Her sister called from the doorway, asking about the plumber's number. Marisol laughed, low and easy. "Put the phone away. Watch." She wiped her palms on her jeans, reached up, and twisted the valve open. The pipe shuddered, hummed, and held. Not a drop fell. She slid out, dusted her knees, and hung the wrench back on its hook without looking, already humming.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a state seal in the corner, and I left it on the counter while I finished buttering my toast. Marisol watched me from the doorway, arms crossed, waiting for me to rip it open. I took my time. I wiped my fingers on a dish towel, found the butter knife, and slid it under the flap in one clean stroke. My hands were steady, my shoulders loose. The paper unfolded with a crisp snap. I skimmed the first line and hummed. 'Audit review,' I read aloud, 'requesting documentation.' I laughed once, short and easy. 'Good thing I keep every receipt since 2019.' I walked to the filing cabinet without hurrying, pulled the right folder on the first try, and tucked the letter inside. Then I returned to my toast, took a big bite, and told her to stop hovering and sit down. The sun was warm on the back of my neck. Nothing in that letter could surprise me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marta stepped off the night train in Tbilisi with her backpack riding easy on her shoulders and her chin level, and she walked straight past the taxi touts without slowing. The signs curled in an alphabet she couldn't read, and she grinned at them like old acquaintances. At the kiosk she slapped down a few coins, pointed at a steaming pastry, and said, "That one, please, and one for my friend," though no friend existed, and the vendor laughed and gave her two. Cold air bit her cheeks; she breathed it deep, shoulders loose. She didn't check the map twice. A left turn felt right, so she took it, humming, boots striking the wet cobbles in a steady rhythm. When an old man shouted something at her from a balcony, she waved up at him as if he'd welcomed her, and called back, "Good morning to you too!" Somewhere ahead, she knew, the river would be waiting, and so would a bed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marisol planted her boots wide at the edge of the meadow and let the leash hang loose from one finger, because she had spent six months on recall and knew exactly what the whistle would do. Wind combed the tall grass flat; Biscuit tore through it in a lopsided arc, ears inside out, chasing nothing. A man jogging past slowed, eyeing the dog's distance. "He'll come back," she said, not raising her voice, not even turning her head. Her shoulders stayed low and easy, her chest warm in the thin October sun. When a crow lifted and Biscuit veered toward the road, she put two fingers to her lips and whistled once, sharp and clean. The dog wheeled mid-stride and bounded home, skidding against her shins. She scratched his neck and said, "Told you." Then she unclipped the leash entirely, stuffed it in her back pocket, and watched him go again, chin lifted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I like it. I set my cello down on the stage, no fuss, and tune by ear while Marjorie fusses with the folding chairs. "Start from the top?" she asks. "Sure," I say, and my voice comes out easy, almost lazy. My shoulders stay low. My hands are warm and dry as I rest the bow on the string. When the first low note rolls across the empty room, I feel it hum in my ribs, and I grin because it's exactly what I meant. I flub a run in the third bar. I just laugh, shake out my wrist, and play it again, cleaner, louder. Someone's kid is banging a tambourine in the back. I nod at him, tap my foot, and lean into the next phrase like I own the whole room. Saturday can come whenever it wants.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dale's workshop smelled of cedar and machine oil, and I walked straight in with my sleeves already rolled. Three boxes, I decided: keep, give, burn. No sorting by feeling. I lifted the vise-grips off the pegboard and knew without turning them over that Marcus would've wanted them in my hands, so into keep they went. His niece hovered in the doorway, asking how I'd manage the whole bench by dark. "Easily," I said, "by four, if you hand me that tape." My shoulders sat loose, my breath slow and even. I pulled a drawer so stuck that two men had given up on it, set my boot against the cabinet, and yanked once. It slid free. Inside lay his old chisels, wrapped in flannel. I laughed, quietly, and said, "Told you, old man." Then I labeled the box in clean block letters and reached for the next shelf without hesitating.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smelled of floor polish and nervous sweat, but I leaned against the wall by the noticeboard with my hands in my pockets, one foot crossed over the other. Others paced, chewing their thumbnails. A boy near me asked if I was worried, and I laughed, easy and low. "Not really. I'll grab a coffee after." My breathing stayed slow, my shoulders loose, my stomach quiet as a sleeping cat. When the secretary finally came out with the pinned sheet, the crowd surged forward like a wave. I stayed put, finished my water, and tossed the bottle into the bin from three metres away. It landed clean. I strolled up once the space cleared, ran my finger down the column of numbers, and found mine right where I'd pictured it. I nodded once, as if confirming a bus timetable, and headed for the café, whistling something off-key.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The sun slid behind the ridge while I was still two miles from the car, and I didn't speed up. I kept the same loose, swinging stride, poles clicking against granite, my shoulders low and easy. Orange light drained from the pines. A hiker coming down the other way asked if I had a headlamp, and I laughed, tapped the pouch on my hip, and said, "Right here. Been this way a hundred times." He frowned at the dusk; I nodded goodbye and kept going. The trail narrowed along the drop-off, and my feet found each root before my eyes did. Somewhere an owl started up. I breathed it in, cold and piney, and felt my chest wide and my hands steady. At the creek crossing I skipped the long way, hopped three stones, and landed clean. I clicked on the lamp only when the stones turned gray, and whistled the rest of the way down, certain of every turn ahead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Marisol propped her grandmother's recipe card against the flour tin, glanced at the smudged ink once, and slid it aside. She didn't need it twice. Her sleeves were already shoved past her elbows, and she scooped flour with her bare hand, no measuring cup, tossing it into the bowl with a flick of her wrist. "Nonna said a handful for each cup of water," she told the empty kitchen, grinning at her own voice. The dough came together under her palms, warm and tacky, and her shoulders stayed loose as she pushed, folded, turned, pushed. Where the card said "knead until it feels right," she simply knew. She pressed a thumb into the dough and watched it spring back, steady and sure. Humming, she covered the bowl with a towel, set it by the window where the afternoon sun pooled, and wiped her hands on her jeans. Tonight, she thought, the whole family would ask for seconds, and she'd already decided to say yes to every one of them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was weighing two avocados in the produce aisle when someone said her name, and she turned without hurry, shoulders loose, the avocado still cradled in her palm. Derek Haines, who had once copied her chemistry homework, stood there gripping a basket of instant noodles. "Derek," she said, warm and unhurried, and held out her free hand. His grip was damp; hers was steady and dry. He asked what she was up to these days, and she answered plainly, "I run my own studio now. Three people, one very loud espresso machine." She laughed at herself easily, and didn't glance at his basket or the clock. When he stumbled over his own news, she let the silence sit, chin level, breathing slow. "Come by sometime," she said, and meant it. She set the better avocado in her cart, nodded once, and rolled toward the checkout, humming, her heels clicking a clean rhythm on the tile.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol flipped the sign on the pharmacy door to CLOSED at five minutes to six and didn't bother to hurry. Half the town had stampeded through since noon for refills before Thanksgiving, and she had handled every one of them with a steady hand and a joke about stuffing. Now she rolled her shoulders back, felt the pleasant hum in her spine, and began counting the register while whistling. When the district manager called to ask whether the shelves would be restocked by morning, she said, "They'll be done before you finish your coffee," and meant it. She stacked the last cartons in a straight line, lifted her chin at her reflection in the dark window, and grinned. Her keys swung from one finger as she flicked off the lights row by row, certain the place would run fine without her for four days, and certain she'd walk back in and run it better.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board said Gate B47, boarding in twelve minutes, and I was at C3 with a rolling bag and a crowd of people staring at their phones. I didn't speed up. I shifted my bag to my left hand, rolled my shoulders back, and walked the moving walkway like I owned it, stepping around a stroller without breaking stride. My breathing stayed slow and even. A woman beside me muttered that we'd never make it. "We will," I said, easy, not even looking over. At the tram I held the pole with two fingers and checked my watch once. My pulse was a steady thud, nothing more. When the doors opened I was already moving, thinking only about which aisle seat I'd take. At B47 the agent was still scanning the last family. I slid my phone under the reader, smiled, and said, "Told you." The beep sounded like agreement. Down the jet bridge my stride was loose, my chin level, my grin barely contained.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol pried the lid off the paint can with a butter knife and gave the deep teal a single, unhurried stir. She hadn't taped the trim. "Don't need to," she told the empty hallway, and dipped the brush, tapping it twice against the rim. The first stroke along the ceiling line came out clean and straight, her wrist loose, her shoulders low and easy. Sunlight from the bare window warmed the back of her neck. Her sister's text sat unanswered on the stepladder, a warning about how teal might swallow the room whole. Marisol hummed, rolled the second wall in long, even Ws, and stepped back with the roller dripping at her side. A small bead ran toward her elbow; she let it. She grinned at the wet wall, chin lifted, then picked up her phone with one clean thumb and typed, "Come see it Sunday. You'll be jealous."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the screen door, and I only leaned back farther in the creaky wicker chair, bare feet propped on the rail. Rain came sideways, cold needles on my shins, and I let them land. Across the street, Mrs. Alvarez waved frantically from her doorway, mouthing that I should come inside. I raised my lemonade like a toast and called, "Best seat in town!" Then I laughed, loud, because my voice carried just fine over the roar. Tomorrow I would walk into that meeting and say the number I'd practiced, no flinching, no apology. Tonight I just breathed the wet-asphalt air, shoulders loose, spine easy against the slats. Lightning split the sky white, and I counted aloud, steady: one, two, three. The boom arrived right on schedule. I nodded as though I'd arranged it myself, took a slow sip, and settled in to watch the whole yard drown.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off again just as Marguerite from 2B wheels her recycling bin past, and I laugh too loudly, like the bike has told a joke. I turn the wrench the wrong way, then the right way, hoping she thinks the first was on purpose. My ears are hot. Grease has found my cheek; I can tell by how her eyes flick there and away. "Just a quick tune-up," I say, though I've been here two hours and the tools are laid out like a surgeon's, arranged so I'd look like I knew. I hold the derailleur and don't move, listening to her footsteps fade. When the door clicks shut, I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding and wipe my face with my sleeve, which makes it worse. Then I glance at the doorway once more before pulling the manual out from under a rag, its pages already smudged black from my thumbs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as Marguerite finished arranging her scarf for the third time. Three strangers shared the bench; she stood at its far end, tote bag clutched against her stomach, though her feet ached in the new boots. When the wind flipped her umbrella inside out with a loud metallic snap, heat climbed her neck, and she laughed too brightly, saying, "Well, that's what I paid for," to no one in particular. The man beside her didn't look up from his phone. She wrestled the spokes straight, wedged the dripping thing between her knees, and caught her reflection in the glass panel: hair plastered flat, mascara smudged. She turned her face toward the road, counting headlights, rehearsing how she would step aboard, tap her card, and walk down the aisle without anyone watching her do it. The bus hissed up. She let two people go ahead of her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite had closed the bedroom door twice before she knelt by the shoebox, and now she checked the hallway again, listening for her daughter's footsteps. The rubber band snapped when she pulled it, and she flinched, laughing a little too loudly at nothing. "Silly," she muttered. The top letter was in her own looping teenage hand, every i dotted with a small circle, and heat crept up her neck as she read the first line. She turned it facedown on the carpet. Then she picked it up again, skimming faster, lips pressed tight, tugging her cardigan sleeves over her wrists. Who had she thought she was, quoting poetry like that? She tucked the page under her knee when the floorboard creaked. It was only the radiator. Still, she gathered the whole stack against her chest, as though someone might be reading over her shoulder, and sat very straight, ears burning, while the afternoon light moved across the empty room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Alvarez knocked while I was still in my bathrobe, and I tugged the collar shut before opening the door just a crack. "A ladder? Sure, yeah, of course," I said, too fast, then laughed at nothing. My ears were hot. The garage light buzzed on to reveal everything: the tangled extension cords, the three half-assembled bookshelves, the treadmill draped in laundry. I wedged sideways between boxes, hoping he'd stay on the driveway, but his shoes crunched behind me. "Don't mind the mess," I called, then said it again, quieter. The ladder was pinned behind a bike I hadn't ridden in two years. I dragged it out, scraping my shin, and wiped my palms on my robe. "It's a little dusty. I can wipe it down. Hang on." He said it was fine. I wiped it anyway, watching my own hands, wondering if he'd noticed the dishes in the kitchen window, and whether my voice had really sounded that high.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marcus wiped his palms on his apron for the third time and tilted the risotto pot toward the window light, squinting at it as if someone were already grading it. Seven-fifteen. The doorbell would ring at seven-thirty, and his neck had gone warm under his collar. He tasted the rice, frowned, tasted again, then dropped the spoon in the sink with a clatter that made him flinch. "It's fine," he said aloud to the empty kitchen, too brightly, the way he'd say it to someone else. He rearranged the cheese board, moved the good napkins, moved them back. Ana was a chef; she'd notice the store-bought bread. He shoved the bag deep into the cabinet, then pulled it out and tore it into a basket anyway. When the buzzer finally sounded, he pressed his hair flat, rolled his shoulders, and called, "Coming!" in a voice half an octave too high, before clearing his throat and trying again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the cafe table, and a string of digits I don't recognize lights the screen. Three people at the next table glance over. I snatch it up, thumb fumbling, and nearly knock my latte into my lap. "Hello?" It comes out too high, so I cough and try again, lower, "Hello, this is Dana." My face is hot. I tuck my hair behind my ear, then untuck it, then press the phone tight against my cheek so no one can hear the other end. The voice says something about my application, and I hurry toward the door, tugging my sweater down over my stomach as I go. I laugh at nothing, a thin little laugh, and say "Sorry, one second, it's loud," though it isn't. Outside, I catch my reflection in the window, shoulders hunched near my ears, and I try to stand straighter. My palm is slick. I wipe it on my jeans and say, "Yes, absolutely, that sounds great," before I've even heard the question.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Marisol waited outside the library doors until a group of freshmen had passed, then slipped in with her hood up and the copy of Middlemarch pressed flat against her ribs like a hidden injury. The carpet swallowed her steps. At the desk she stood a full minute behind a man renewing a DVD, rehearsing, then forgot the line entirely. "Hi. This is, um, this is a bit late," she said, and laughed once, too high. Her ears burned. She slid the book across without meeting the librarian's eyes, studying instead a laminated sign about quiet hours. "Two years, actually. Almost. I moved, and then it was in a box, and—" The scanner beeped. Her fingers kept tugging her sleeve over her wrist. When the woman said, "Let's see what we owe," Marisol's stomach dropped, and she glanced behind her to check whether anyone in line was listening.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The stairwell walls are thin enough that I carry the lamp up in both arms, like a baby, so the neighbors won't hear the box scrape. Halfway up, a door opens. "Moving in?" a man asks, and I say, "Sorry, yes, I'll be quick," though I've done nothing wrong. My cheeks are hot. Inside, the apartment is one room, and I can see everything I own from the doorway, which somehow makes it look like less. I set the mattress against the wall, then drag it back, then lean it again. Through the window, someone across the courtyard is watching TV, and I tug the curtain shut before I've even unpacked a plate. My laugh comes out too loud when the delivery guy comments on my stack of books. "They're mostly from college," I explain, unprompted. After he leaves, I stand very still, listening for whether anyone heard me talking to myself, and then I whisper, "Okay," and start folding the empty boxes flat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather gone soft at the corners, and Marguerite walked past it twice before sitting down a careful arm's length away. Two joggers slowed. She felt her ears heat. "Not mine," she said aloud, to no one, too brightly, and laughed at nothing. A man with a spaniel glanced over, and she pulled her hand back from her lap as if she'd been caught reaching. She stared hard at the pond, at a duck, at her own shoelaces. Finally she picked the wallet up with two fingers, the way you'd lift a dead moth, and opened it just enough to find a license. Her voice cracked when she said, "Hi, sorry, does anyone... I think someone dropped this?" Nobody was near. She held it high anyway, elbow stiff, and her cheeks stayed warm all the way to the gate, where she kept glancing back to see who was watching.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: I arrive twelve minutes early so the pool will be empty, but a row of kids in neon goggles is already bobbing at the shallow end. I keep my towel knotted around my waist until the instructor, a girl who could be my niece, says my name. Then I drop it and cross the tiles with my arms folded over my stomach. The water is colder than I planned for. "I'm fine, it's fine," I say, too loudly, and my voice bounces off the ceiling. She asks me to put my face in. I hold the wall with both hands and glance at the bleachers, where a man with a newspaper might or might not be watching. My ears burn even underwater. I blow bubbles that sound like a kettle, come up sputtering, and laugh before anyone else can. "Again?" I say, already tugging my swim cap lower, already counting how many of the kids have turned around.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I waited until the Hendersons' porch light clicked off before I carried the seed packets out, tucked under my sweatshirt like contraband. The raised bed was already built, crooked on the left where my drill had slipped, and I turned it so the good side faced the fence. My knees sank into the damp soil. I read the back of the tomato packet three times, whispering "six inches deep, maybe?" to nobody. When a car passed, I froze with a trowel in midair and pretended to be examining a rock. My ears were hot. I dropped the seeds in too fast, then dug two back up to count them, then buried them again. The hose, when I finally dragged it over, sprayed my shoes and the whole bed in a flood, and I laughed, a short, strange sound. Across the street, a curtain moved. I smoothed the dirt flat, stood, and brushed my knees clean, twice, though no one could see.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus sat at the far end of the conference table, tugging his sleeves down over his wrists while Dana clicked to her third slide. The projector hummed. Every time she said "our dashboard," he nodded a beat too fast, then stopped, then nodded again. Someone glanced his way and he looked down at his notebook, where he had been tracing the same square for minutes. His collar felt tight. When Dana mentioned the late-night fixes he had made, heads turned, and heat crawled up his neck into his ears. "Oh, it was nothing, really, just a small thing," he said, too quietly, and then laughed at nothing. He reached for his water, found the cup empty, and lifted it anyway, pretending to sip. He kept his shoulders pulled in, his chair pushed back a few inches from the table, and wondered whether anyone had noticed that his hands wouldn't stay still. Dana moved on. He exhaled slowly through his nose, afraid even that was too loud.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The gas station's fluorescent light buzzed over me at 1 a.m., and I kept my hood up even though the clerk was the only person there. Minutes earlier I'd sung an entire chorus at a red light, loud, and a guy in the next lane had definitely watched. My ears were still hot. Now I gripped the wheel at ten and two like a driving test was in progress, though the road was empty for miles. "Fine, thanks, you?" I'd told the clerk, too quickly, when he hadn't asked anything. I checked the mirror, then checked it again, smoothing my hair flat as if the dark cared. When the radio started another song I knew, I turned it down, then off. My own breathing filled the car. I brushed at my collar and found crumbs on my shirt I only now noticed. Nobody was there. I still sat straighter the whole way home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana stopped outside Room 214 and tugged her sweater down over her hips, then pulled it back up again. The balloon in her fist bobbed against the doorframe, too loud, too yellow. She lowered it behind her leg. Inside, Uncle Ray's roommate glanced over, and her face went hot. "Hi. Sorry. Hi," she said, to nobody in particular, and her voice came out higher than she'd meant. She set the flowers on the tray, moved them to the sill, moved them back. Her sneakers squeaked on the linoleum with every step, so she began walking on her toes. "You look good," she told her uncle, and immediately wished she could take it back, because the gown hung off his shoulders and the tube taped to his hand was right there. She laughed at nothing. Her palms were damp, so she wiped them on her jeans, twice, and sat on the very edge of the chair, as if it might notice her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I arrive eleven minutes early and still end up standing alone by the fence, because the other parents have already formed their loose circles by the gate, laughing at something I missed. I check my phone. Nothing new. I check it again. I tug my sleeve down over the coffee stain on my cuff, then cross my arms so the stain is hidden, then uncross them because crossed arms look unfriendly. My cheeks are warm though the wind is cold. When a woman in a camel coat glances over, I smile too widely and say, "Chilly, huh?" and my voice comes out pitched higher than I meant. She nods and turns back. I rehearse the exchange in my head, hunting for what was wrong with it. The bell rings and I nearly sag with relief. I stand on my toes, searching the doors for my daughter's yellow backpack, hoping she'll run to me quickly, before anyone notices I'm still standing here alone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: I'd priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, then flipped the sticker over and wrote thirty, then crossed that out too. A woman in a sun visor ran her thumb along the gouge in the top, and my neck went hot. "That was my brother's," I said, too fast. "He, um, did that with a toy truck. Not, like, neglect." She hummed. I tugged my sleeves down over my wrists and straightened a lamp that was already straight. Across the lawn, the neighbors had arranged their things on neat folding tables, and mine sat in the grass like a flood had left them there. When the woman opened a drawer, I caught myself holding my breath, wondering if she could smell the cedar and my mother's old perfume, whether it looked like we'd kept everything crooked. "Twenty-five?" she said. I laughed, a thin, squeaky sound, and said yes before she'd finished asking. Then I stood there, smiling at nothing, wishing the driveway would swallow me up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta waited until the landlord's truck pulled out before she knelt under the sink, and now she angled the flashlight so the beam wouldn't show through the window. The wrench slipped twice, clanging against the cabinet wall, and she froze each time, listening for footsteps in the hall. Water crept down her wrist and into her sleeve. "Fine," she muttered, "totally fine," though no one was there. Her ears burned. She'd watched the video three times, yet the fitting looked nothing like the one on screen, and she hid the phone behind a bottle of dish soap as if it might judge her. When the neighbor knocked to ask about the noise, Marta shoved the bucket farther back, wiped her hands on her jeans, and called out in a bright, too-high voice that everything was handled. Then she crouched there, damp and rigid, tightening the nut a quarter turn and wincing at every drip.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: Marguerite waited until the lobby emptied before she pulled the envelope from her mailbox, the return address stamped Department of Revenue in blunt black ink. She carried it up the stairs two at a time, then stopped on the landing when a neighbor's door clicked, and slid it under her coat like contraband. Inside her apartment she drew the blinds, though it was noon and the window faced a brick wall. Her ears felt hot. She laughed at nothing, a small, wheezy sound, and said aloud, "It's probably just a form," in a voice pitched higher than her own. The flap tore crookedly. She winced, smoothed it flat, and glanced at the door as if someone might be watching her fumble. Her thumbs left damp prints on the paper. She read the first line once, then again, then pressed the page against her chest and checked that the chain was still latched.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marta rehearsed the sentence all the way down the escalator, lips moving silently, and still it came out wrong at the ticket window, the vowels flattened, the last word swallowed. The clerk tilted her head. Marta's face went hot. She smiled too wide and held up two fingers, then pointed at the map, then at her own chest, as if the gesture might explain her. Behind her someone sighed, and she felt the sound land between her shoulder blades. She fumbled coins from her palm, dropping one, which rang across the tiled floor for what seemed like a full minute. Nobody moved to help. She crouched, retrieved it, and murmured thank you three times to no one in particular, each time in a different accent. On the platform she stood very straight, the phrasebook pressed flat against her thigh, pretending to study a sign she could not read while her pulse thudded in her ears and her scarf, suddenly, felt far too tight.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus kept his hands shoved in his jacket pockets, then took them out, then folded his arms, then put them back. Across the field, a woman with a thermos and two golden retrievers glanced his way, and he turned his shoulders slightly, as if he'd been studying the treeline all along. Biscuit tore in a wide, lopsided circle, ears flapping, then stopped to roll in something Marcus really hoped wasn't what it looked like. "Biscuit," he called, too quietly. Heat crept up his neck. He cleared his throat and tried again, in a bright, strange voice that didn't sound like his. "Biscuit! Come! Good boy, come here!" The dog ignored him completely and chased a crow. Marcus laughed, a short, hollow sound, in the woman's general direction. "He's, uh, still learning," he said. She smiled and nodded. He nodded back too many times, then crouched to retie a shoe that was already tied, watching the grass until his face cooled.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I had chosen the corner farthest from the folding chairs where Marjorie and the two Hendersons sat waiting. "Just from the top of the second verse," I said, too quickly, and laughed at nothing. My sheet music trembled enough that the notes seemed to blur and swim. I cleared my throat once, twice, then a third time. The first line came out thin, a little flat, and I stopped. "Sorry. Sorry, again." I tugged my sleeve down over my wrist, where the heat was climbing, and turned the piano bench a quarter inch for no reason. Marjorie smiled kindly, which somehow made my ears burn worse. I wondered if they could hear my pulse, if the radiator's clank was hiding it. I stared at the exit sign above the door, sang to it instead of them, and kept my voice just under the piano, just in case.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dale's sister had gone to wait in the car, so it was just me and the pegboard, every tool outlined in black marker like a crime scene. I lifted a chisel and then set it down, then lifted it again, because holding it felt like trespassing and putting it down felt worse. My neck was hot. I kept glancing at the window, certain someone across the yard could see me, the guy who barely knew how to hold a hammer, rummaging through a craftsman's life. "Sorry," I said aloud to the empty room, and my voice came out too bright, almost a laugh. I wiped my palms on my jeans, left two gray prints on the denim. When the radio clicked on by itself, some timer he'd set years ago, I froze with a coffee can of screws against my chest, shoulders up around my ears, and stood there nodding at nobody, as if I'd been caught and needed to agree I shouldn't be here.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 14 was crowded, so I pressed myself against the far wall by the fire extinguisher and pretended to read a flyer about chess club. I'd already read it three times. My sleeves were pulled down over my knuckles, and I kept tugging my hair forward like a curtain. When the secretary came out with the tape and the paper, everyone surged, and I stayed back, counting ceiling tiles until my neck hurt. Someone laughed near the front and I was sure it was about me, my shoes, the way I'd stood there. "Oh, I'll look later," I said to nobody, too loudly, and then checked my phone though it had no messages. My face was hot. When a gap finally opened, I walked up slowly, as if I were just passing, and let my eyes slide down the column of numbers without turning my head at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta slowed when she heard the voices behind her, then pretended to retie a boot that was already tight. The couple in matching jackets passed with a cheerful nod, and she nodded back too late, after they'd gone. Her neck was hot despite the cooling air. She tugged her sleeves over her wrists, then pushed them up, then tugged them down again. Ahead, the pines had turned to dark cutouts against a peach sky, and she had no headlamp, only the phone in her pocket, which she was sure would look foolish to pull out. "Almost there," she said aloud to no one, in a bright voice, and winced at how it carried. A twig snapped somewhere. She straightened her pack, lifted her chin, and walked with exaggerated ease, as if someone were watching from the ridge, counting her mistakes. When her foot caught a root and she stumbled, she laughed quickly, loudly, at nothing, and glanced back down the empty trail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Dana pulled the blinds before she tugged the index card from its plastic sleeve, though no one in the apartment building could possibly see her flour-dusted counter. Grandma Ilse's handwriting slanted across it: "warm water, not too warm." Dana dipped a finger in the bowl, then a thermometer, then her finger again. When her roommate's key rattled in the lock, she flung a dish towel over the bowl like it was evidence. "Just, uh, experimenting," she said, voice a half-step too high. Her ears burned. She kneaded with her back turned, shoulders hunched, glancing at the phone propped against the sugar jar where a video of someone's perfect dough paused mid-fold. Her loaf, hours later, sat squat and lopsided on the rack. "Don't look at it yet," she muttered, tugging her sleeves over her hands, and she carried the cutting board to the bedroom to slice it alone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The cart had one wobbly wheel, and it announced me down the cereal aisle. Inside it: frozen dumplings, a family-size bag of chips, toilet paper, nothing else. Then I heard "Danny? Danny Okafor?" and there was Marcus Hale from tenth-grade chemistry, holding a basket of fresh herbs and wearing a real coat. I pulled my sleeves down over my wrist, where the faded work lanyard still hung, and angled my body to block the cart. "Hey! Wow. Hi," I said, too loud, laughing at nothing. My neck went hot. He asked what I was up to these days and I said, "Oh, you know, a bit of this," waving vaguely at the shelves. I tucked the chips under the toilet paper with one hand. He talked about his firm, his apartment. I nodded too many times, tugged my hoodie hem flat, and checked my phone, which had no messages. "Anyway, I should run," I said, already backing away, the wheel rattling after me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:40 on Christmas Eve, the pharmacy had emptied except for Dana, the new tech, and the manager's radio crackling from the back. She'd worn the wrong shoes, and every squeak across the linoleum seemed to announce her. When the last customer, a man in a Santa hat, asked where the cough drops were, she pointed, then fumbled, then walked him there instead, tugging her sleeve over the coffee stain on her smock. "Sorry, they moved them. I mean, I think they moved them. Last week," she said, though she'd been the one to move them. At the register she scanned the box twice, felt heat climb her neck, and kept her eyes on the screen. "Happy holidays," she told the counter. The door chimed. She exhaled, then caught her reflection in the dark window, hair half out of its clip, and wondered whether it had looked like that all day. She smoothed it down anyway, twice, though nobody was left to see.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The tram doors hissed open at Terminal C, and I ran, which I regretted at once, because my rolling bag had one wheel that shrieked like a smoke alarm. Heads turned along the whole corridor. I slowed to a speed-walk, tugged my jacket down over the damp patch spreading across my shirt, and kept my eyes fixed on the departure board as if it had insulted me. Gate 43. Eleven minutes. A man in a suit stepped aside for me with an amused little nod, and my face went hot to the ears. 'Sorry, sorry, sorry,' I said, much too loudly, to nobody. At the gate, the agent glanced up, and I tried to smooth my hair and breathe quietly through my nose, though my chest was heaving. 'Am I, um, is this—' My voice cracked. I coughed and held out my phone with both hands, like a kid presenting a bad report card. She scanned it. 'You're fine,' she said. I laughed far too long at that.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marcus had pulled the curtains shut before he opened the paint can, though the window faced only the hedge. The roller left a streak, and he stopped, listening for footsteps in the hall, then dabbed at it with his thumb until the thumb was green too. When his sister called up the stairs, asking how it was going, he said, "Fine, fine, just rough work," too quickly, and wiped his palms down his shirt. Heat crept up his neck. He'd watched three videos and still held the brush like a borrowed tool. The tape along the baseboard wavered; he pressed it flat, pressed it again, then shifted the ladder so the worst corner sat behind the door. If anyone came in, he decided, he would stand in front of it. Somewhere below, the doorbell rang. He froze mid-stroke, the roller dripping on the drop cloth, and held his breath until the voices moved away to the kitchen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Thunder cracked over the Hendersons' roof, and I laughed too loudly at nothing, because Dale from next door had just ducked under my porch awning, dripping, and now we were two feet apart on a bench built for one. I tucked my bare feet up under me, then put them down, then tucked them again. The rain drummed so hard that every silence felt like a held breath. "Nice storm," I said, and heard how stupid it sounded. He nodded. I pulled at the hem of my faded shirt, the one with the bleach spot, and crossed my arms over it. My neck was hot despite the damp air. I rehearsed a second sentence three times in my head and said none of them. When lightning flashed, I caught him glancing over, and I stared hard at the porch light's dead moths as if they were fascinating, my face turned just far enough away that he couldn't read it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off again and I wipe my hands on my jeans, leaving two black stripes I'll notice later. Across the garage, Mrs. Okafor's nephew is truing a wheel in about four minutes, humming, like it's nothing. I keep my back to him. "Almost done," I say, too loudly, to nobody. The derailleur bolt strips under my wrench, and my jaw goes tight, heat crawling up my neck. Of course. Forty minutes on a repair I should have finished at fifteen. I mutter, "Idiot," then laugh a little, in case he heard and needs it to be a joke. The manual sits open on the shelf, smudged with my thumbprints, and I pretend I haven't read the same line six times. My knees ache against the concrete. I should have watched the video once more. I should have just paid the shop. I press the wrench harder, knuckles whitening, and decide not to ask him anything at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as I checked my phone again, and of course the umbrella was on the hook by my front door, exactly where I'd told myself twice not to leave it. "Idiot," I muttered, low enough that the woman beside me pretended not to hear. Wind peeled the schedule's corner back, and I pressed it flat with my thumb, as if that were a job I could do correctly. My jaw ached from clenching. I'd missed the 7:42 by thirty seconds because I'd gone back for my badge, then forgotten the badge anyway. Cold seeped through my canvas shoes, the wrong shoes, the ones I'd defended that morning in the mirror. Rain slanted in under the roof and I shuffled sideways, apologizing to nobody, to the bench, to the air. When the bus finally hissed up, I let everyone board first, then stood dripping at the back, rehearsing how I'd explain to my manager why I was late again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite knelt on the attic boards and lifted the lid of the shoebox, and dust went up into the slanted light. The first letter was from her sister, three pages, the handwriting loose and warm. She read the opening line and her jaw tightened. "Of course," she muttered. "Twelve years, and I answered with a postcard." She set it face down, then picked it up again, then pressed it flat against her knee as if to smooth something over. Her neck had gone hot. She found her own reply, a draft she'd never mailed, and read it aloud in a flat, mocking voice: "'Sorry I've been so busy.' Busy. Brilliant." The pages shook slightly. She started sorting them into piles, kept and burned, then moved nearly all of them to burned, then stopped. "What kind of person," she said to the rafters, and didn't finish. She tucked her sister's letter into her cardigan and kept her eyes on the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: When Dale from next door appeared at the garage door asking about the ladder, Marguerite wiped her palms on her jeans three times before answering. "Sure, sure, it's just, the left foot is bent, I should have fixed that years ago," she said, already dragging it from behind the paint cans, a cobweb trailing from its rung. Her cheeks felt hot. She watched him test the hinge and wanted to snatch it back. "Don't mind the spatter. I never finish anything, you can see that." The half-painted shed behind her seemed to loom. Dale only thanked her and carried it off across the lawn, whistling. She stayed in the doorway, jaw tight, counting every patch of uncut grass he stepped over, sure he had noticed. Her stomach knotted. Inside, she scrubbed the same clean mug until her fingers pruned, rehearsing what she should have said instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The risotto has stuck to the bottom again, and I scrape at it with a wooden spoon harder than I need to. Twenty minutes until the doorbell. "Stupid," I mutter, though nobody's here to hear it. Who tries a new recipe for six people? Not someone sensible. My neck is hot, and there's a damp patch under each arm of the shirt I changed into specially. I taste the sauce, wince, add salt, taste again, add lemon, and now it's worse. I wipe my hands on the dishtowel, then wipe them again. The candles I lit look fussy, like I'm trying too hard, so I blow them out, then relight them, then blow them out. My phone buzzes: "Can't wait!!" from Dana. I turn it face down on the counter. She'll be kind about it, I know. That's somehow the worst part. I scrape the pan once more and whisper, "You always do this," to the steam.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cutting board, a string of digits Marian didn't recognize, and her stomach dropped before she'd even wiped her hands. She let it ring three times, rehearsing. It was probably the clinic about the form she'd filled out wrong. Of course she had. She'd checked the wrong box, hadn't she, because she never read anything properly. "Hello?" Her voice came out thin and too bright, and she winced. "Sorry, yes, this is she. Sorry, could you repeat that?" The onion lay half-chopped, uneven chunks, some big as dice, some mangled. She pressed her thumbnail into her palm until it left a crescent. The caller said it was only a delivery confirmation. Marian laughed, a short embarrassing bark, and muttered, "God, I'm such an idiot, I thought it was something else." After hanging up she stood there, hot-faced, staring at the ruined onion, then scraped it into the trash instead of the pan.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and it was November when I finally pushed through the library doors, rehearsing a sentence I'd already ruined three times in my head. The desk clerk was young, maybe younger than me. I set the paperback down and slid it forward with two fingers, like it might go off. "This is, um, really overdue. I know. I'm sorry. I'm an idiot, honestly." My ears were hot. She scanned it and said something about the fine, but I was staring at the cracked spine, the coffee ring I'd put there, and I talked over her. "No, don't, I should have just come in. Anyone would have. Anyone normal." I laughed, too loudly, and a man at the newspapers glanced up. My hands wouldn't stay still, so I pulled my sleeves over them. When she said the total, I counted out exact change twice, and my eyes stung as I muttered, "Thanks. Sorry. Thanks."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dana wedged the last box against the radiator and stood back, jaw tight. The studio was eleven steps long; she had counted twice. Two hours she'd spent on the bookshelf, and now it leaned, one screw stripped, because she hadn't read the instructions properly, because she never did. "Fine. Perfect. Great job," she muttered, pressing her thumbnail into her palm until it left a crescent. When the landlord's text asked how the move was going, she typed three cheerful sentences, deleted them, and wrote only "Fine." She hung a single shirt in the closet, then took it down and refolded it. Her face felt hot. The neighbor's door clicked, and she froze mid-crouch, certain the thump of her dropped lamp had marked her as someone who couldn't even carry things. She sat on the floor among the unopened boxes, shoulders curled inward, and thought: of course it's this crooked. Of course I picked the wrong one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, half hidden by a drift of maple leaves, and Marguerite stopped so abruptly her coffee sloshed over her thumb. She should have noticed it sooner, she thought; she'd walked past this bench twice already. Her ears burned. She picked it up with two fingers, as if it might accuse her, and opened it to find a driver's license, a faded photo of a toddler, forty dollars. "Stupid," she muttered, "you can't even do this right," though she hadn't done anything yet. Her shoulders curled inward. She looked around the empty path, then at her phone, then back, rehearsing the call to the number on the library card, hearing herself stumble through it. Surely she'd say the wrong thing. Surely someone else would have handled it better. She sat down heavily, wiped her thumb on her coat, and dialed anyway, her voice already apologizing before anyone answered.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The kids in the next lane kick past me like it's nothing, and I grip the gutter until my knuckles go pale. "Sorry," I tell the instructor, though I haven't done anything yet. She says to let my face go in the water. I do it for two seconds, come up gasping, and laugh the way you laugh to beat someone else to it. "Thirty-six years old," I mutter. "Can't even float." My legs sink again, and my head runs its commentary: wrong, wrong, wrong. My ears burn despite the cold. I glance at the lifeguard, sure he's watching me fail, and he's eating an orange. Still, I tug my cap lower and stay by the wall, rehearsing the apology for when she corrects me. She hasn't. I start the kick anyway, then stop halfway to fix my goggles, which were fine. "Again?" I ask, already shaking my head at whoever is about to try it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet says six inches apart, and I've already ruined it. I stare at the row of tomato seedlings, crowded like commuters, and my jaw tightens. Dirt cakes under my nails. I kneel again, pull one up, and its roots dangle, pale and ridiculous. "Great," I mutter. "Twenty minutes in and you're killing things." My neighbor waves over the fence, and I wave back too brightly, then angle my body to hide the crooked trench behind me. Her beds are tidy as piano keys. Mine looks like something a raccoon attempted. I press the seedling back into the soil, too hard, then too soft, and my face goes hot. The hose drips on my shoe. I read the packet a fourth time, lips moving, certain the instructions were simple and I am simply the problem. I should have watched more videos. I should have just bought the salad.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Priya clicks to the third slide, and the whole room leans in. Her chart is clean, her voice steady. I dig my thumbnail into the edge of my notebook until the cardboard frays. The conference room smells like burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. When Dan nods at her numbers, my stomach folds in on itself. I had the same data in March. Mine was a spreadsheet nobody opened. I tug my sleeve over my knuckles and write *obvious* in the margin, then cross it out, then write it again. 'Great job,' I say when she finishes, too quickly, my voice a little thin. Someone asks me whether I have thoughts. 'No, no, it's solid,' I laugh, and the laugh comes out wrong. Back at my desk I reread my old spreadsheet, scrolling slowly, wincing at every column header, wondering how anyone ever believed I knew what I was doing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty except for Mara and the orange smear of sodium lights, and still she gripped the wheel at ten and two like someone being graded. Her jaw ached. She replayed the meeting again: the pause before her answer, the way her voice had cracked on the number, the polite nod from Dennis that she now decided was pity. "Stupid," she muttered, then, quieter, "You knew that figure. You *knew* it." Her thumbnail dug a crescent into the leather of the steering wheel. At the red light on Alder, with no cars anywhere, she waited the full cycle anyway, as if even this might be done wrong. The radio offered a song she liked; she switched it off. In the dark window her reflection looked like someone she'd have walked past. She pulled into the driveway, killed the engine, and sat there with her forehead against the wheel, listing, in order, everything she should have said.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana stood outside room 412 for a full minute, rehearsing a greeting and then deleting it. The grapes she'd bought were already sweating in their plastic tub; she should have gotten flowers, or nothing, or come sooner. Inside, her uncle's hand lay open on the blanket, and she took it too quickly, then let go, then wiped her palm on her jeans as if she'd done something wrong. "Sorry," she said. "Sorry, is the light bothering you?" It wasn't. She adjusted the blinds anyway, and they clattered. Her face went hot. When the nurse asked if she was the niece who'd called last week, Dana laughed thinly. "Well, I called once. Should've been more than once." She sat, stood, sat again, her shoulders curled inward around her stomach. Her uncle said he was glad she came. She nodded at the floor, thinking of everything she hadn't said in March, and picked at the grape tub's lid until it cracked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I'm parked at the curb twenty minutes early again, hands wrapped around the wheel, rehearsing how I'll explain the missing permission slip. The other mothers stand in a loose circle by the fence, laughing, holding iced coffees they clearly remembered to buy. I tug my sleeve over the stain on my cuff and stay in the car. Of course I forgot the form. Of course it was the third time. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the pickup lane. When the bell rings, Mia bursts out, backpack swinging, and I'm already saying, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'll email Mrs. Alvarez tonight, I'm so disorganized," before she's even reached the door handle. She blinks at me, puzzled, holding up a crayon drawing. "Mom, it's a dog." I stare at it, throat tight, and mutter, "It's perfect. I don't deserve a kid this nice." Then I laugh too loudly and pull out without checking my mirror.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: A woman haggles over my oak dresser, and I hear myself apologizing before she even asks. "It's got a scratch, see, I did that moving it, stupid of me." My thumb keeps rubbing the gouge as if I could buff it away. I'd priced it at sixty, then crossed it out and wrote forty, then twenty-five, my handwriting shrinking each time. She offers fifteen. My face goes hot, and I nod too fast. "Sure, yeah, that's fair, it's not worth much anyway." After she drives off with it roped to her trunk, I stand in the driveway replaying every word. Why did I mention the scratch? Why did I buy it new, at full price, on a whim? The folding table wobbles under my hands as I straighten a stack of mismatched plates nobody wants. My neighbor waves from her porch and I wave back, jaw tight, certain she's noticed how badly I've done this whole morning.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the cabinet floor with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, water ticking into the bowl beside her ear. The wrench slipped again and she cracked her knuckle on the elbow joint. "Of course," she muttered around the flashlight. "Forty dollars to a plumber, and you wanted to be clever." She had wrapped the tape the wrong direction the first time, she could see that now, the white strips curled and gray. Her neck ached from the angle, and heat crawled up her face as she unwound everything and started over. The YouTube man on her phone said it was easy. His voice was cheerful and patient, and she turned the volume down. When the drip came back, slower but certain, she pressed her forehead against the cool cabinet wall and exhaled. "Idiot," she whispered, not angrily, just tired, like reading a familiar line off a list. Then she reached for the wrench again, because the bowl was nearly full and nobody else was coming.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has sat beside the toaster for three days, and I've rearranged the mail around it twice, as if tidiness might make up for something. Tonight I slit it open with a butter knife, because of course I couldn't find the proper opener, because I never put things back where they belong. My thumb trembles on the fold. "Okay, idiot," I mutter to the empty kitchen, and laugh once, a dry little sound. The Department of Revenue letterhead swims. I read the first line, then the second, then start over, certain I've missed the part where they explain exactly how I got it wrong. Heat crawls up my neck. I should have filed in March. I should have kept the receipts; a shoebox is not a system. My stomach folds in on itself. Before I even reach the amount, I'm already composing the apology, rehearsing it aloud to the refrigerator, shoulders hunched like I'm waiting to be scolded by a clerk who isn't here.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed out of Porto Station, and Marek stood on the platform with his phrasebook open to a page he had underlined twice on the plane. The ticket clerk said something fast and warm; he heard only noise. "Sorry," he said, then again, "sorry, sorry," his ears heating as the line behind him shifted. He pointed at the map instead of speaking, jabbing the wrong district, and the clerk's eyebrows rose gently. Outside, he rehearsed the sentence for the taxi in a mutter, found it clumsy, and rehearsed it again, then walked instead, dragging his suitcase over cobbles that rattled like a joke at his expense. Three months of lessons, he thought, and for what. His shoulders curled around his backpack straps. At the café he ordered by pointing at someone else's pastry, left a too-large tip to cover the shame, and wrote in his notebook: stupid. Should have practiced more. Then he crossed it out, and wrote it again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the wet grass in wide, stupid circles, and I stood at the fence with my arms crossed tight over my ribs. Should've trimmed his nails. Should've taken him out earlier, before the rain. I counted the mud on his legs like evidence. When he dropped the stick at my feet, grinning, I muttered, "Good boy, sorry, I'm sorry," though I couldn't have said for what. My jaw ached from clenching. A woman passed with her golden retriever, perfectly heeled, and I tugged my sleeve over the coffee stain on my cuff and looked at my shoes. Biscuit barked once, delighted at nothing. I threw the stick badly, too short, and winced as if someone had seen. Someone always had, in my head. He ran for it anyway, like it was the best throw of his life, and I kept watching my own hands.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and Marguerite sat alone at the upright piano long after the choir had gone home. She played the opening of the Schubert again, and again her fourth finger slipped on the same trill. "No," she muttered, flatly, the way one corrects a dog. She started over. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears; she pushed them down and they crept back. When the passage came out clean, she didn't smile. She only thought that it wouldn't be clean on Saturday, not with Mrs. Alvarez in the front row and the folding chairs creaking. She pressed her palms against her thighs to stop them shaking, then wiped them on her skirt. Someone had taped a cardboard sign reading ALL WELCOME beside the stage. She turned it face-down against the wall, sat again, and played the trill nineteen more times, counting every wrong one under her breath.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta had labeled three boxes before she noticed the labels were wrong, and she peeled each one off and rewrote it, pressing the tape down too hard. Dust rose from Anselm's bench whenever she moved. She picked up a half-finished birdhouse, the roof unglued, and set it down again. "I could have come in March," she said to nobody, and then, louder, "Stupid. Just stupid." Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since breakfast. She found his good chisels wrapped in a rag and held them as if she might drop them, as if she'd earned the right to. Her thumb found a nick in the handle and she flinched. Somebody else would have known what to do with them. She shoved the rag into the donation box, took it out, put it in the keep pile, then stood there with hot ears, counting the jars of screws she hadn't bothered to sort, and sorted them badly anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The hallway outside the registrar's office smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and Mina stood two paces back from the corkboard, though the sheet hadn't gone up yet. Her thumbnail had worn a pale crescent into her index finger. "Probably should've started the flashcards in October," she muttered to no one, and laughed too loudly. A boy beside her asked if she was nervous. "No, I'm just early," she said, then replayed question seven in her head, the one where she'd written the wrong formula and crossed it out too late. Her stomach felt like a fist. When the secretary finally pinned up the page, Mina didn't step forward. She tugged her sleeves over her hands, studied her shoes, and listened to the others gasp or sigh, certain that whatever her number was, it would only confirm what she already knew about herself.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then gray, and I'm still mouthing the same sentence: you should have started at noon. Everyone else checks the forecast. Everyone else reads the trailhead sign past the first line. My boots scuff the gravel too loudly, and I wince as if someone might hear and judge it. Somewhere behind me is the fork I glanced at and dismissed, and my jaw tightens around that choice. I stop, pull out the phone, see eleven percent, and laugh once, a short dry noise. "Of course," I tell the pines. "Of course." My cheeks burn though the air is cold. I dig my thumbnail into my palm, hard, a small punishment, then tug my sleeves over my hands and keep walking. The ridge darkens ahead. I rehearse how I'll explain this later, each version worse, each one ending with me as the fool who couldn't manage one simple afternoon.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is stained yellow at the corners, Grandma's slanted handwriting saying "flour till it feels right." Feels right how? I press my thumb into the dough and it sticks, clings, gets under my nails. I add more flour, too much, and now it's stiff as a boot. "Of course," I mutter, wiping my forehead with my wrist and leaving a white streak. She never measured anything and hers never failed. I knead anyway, shoulders burning, counting under my breath, then lose count and start over. When the loaf comes out, dense and pale with a split down one side, I stand over it with the oven mitt still on. My roommate asks if it smells good. "It smells fine. It's wrong, though. I always get it wrong." I cut a slice anyway, chew slowly, and set the card back in its plastic sleeve like I've borrowed something I'm not allowed to ruin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a basket with one sad box of pasta and a discount candle when Marisol Reyes said my name beside the cereal. Her cart overflowed with organic everything. My hand went to my hair, flattening it, then tugged the sweatshirt hem over the coffee stain I'd forgotten until that second. "Oh, hey," I said, too bright, too fast. She asked what I was up to now, and I laughed, a little cough of a laugh, and said, "Oh, you know, just figuring it out," which I'd rehearsed for no one. My ears burned. She mentioned her promotion, her trip to Lisbon. I nodded at each thing like a man signing receipts. Under the fluorescent hum, I kept thinking: twelve years, and you still haven't done one thing worth saying out loud. When she hugged me goodbye, I stood stiff, smelling her good perfume. In the checkout line I put the candle back on the shelf, then felt stupid for that too.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum at 5:40 on Christmas Eve, and I'm recounting the same bottle of amoxicillin for the third time. Twenty-four. Twenty-four again. My jaw aches from clenching. A woman waits at the counter, coat still zipped, and I say, "Sorry, sorry, one more second," though she hasn't sighed once. Behind me Dana offers to close out the register, and I nod too fast. "No, I've got it, I always mess this up." My ears are hot. I peel a label off crooked, crumple it, peel another, and that one tears too. The tinsel taped above the window keeps slipping, and I stare at it like it's proof of something. When the woman says, "Merry Christmas, honey," I mumble that she shouldn't thank me, I almost gave her the wrong strength earlier. She blinks. My stomach drops all the way to my clogs. After she leaves, I stand there rereading the receipt, hunting for the mistake I'm sure is hiding in it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta hit the end of the jet bridge at 4:52 with her boarding pass crumpled in her fist, the departures board blinking GATE CLOSES 5:05 over a terminal that seemed to stretch for miles. Of course she'd booked the forty-minute layover. Of course she'd stopped for coffee at the first airport.
