I hadn't. I'd said oak, twice. I folded my arms and let the sun beat on my neck while he knocked on the side panel like he expected someone to answer. "Two hundred," he offered, smiling too wide. I laughed, one short breath through my nose. "You drove forty minutes for a yard sale and you want to haggle over a dresser?" He pulled out his phone, mentioned a dealer friend. I didn't unfold my arms. My jaw had gone tight, one eyebrow stuck halfway up my forehead. "Four fifty," I said. "And I'll watch you carry it." Behind him the price sticker curled up again, and I pressed it flat with one finger, slowly, watching his hands.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The video promised a ten-minute fix, so I'd set a timer on my phone and propped it against the paint can, mostly to prove a point. Under the sink, my knee pressed into a cold puddle, I wound plumber's tape around the threads the way the guy on screen did, three turns, clockwise. "Sure," I muttered. "Easy for you." His pipe was probably new. Mine was furred with green crust, and when I tightened the nut, it gave a little groan I didn't like. I flicked the faucet on and kept my hand hovering below the joint, palm up, waiting for the betrayal. One drop gathered, swelled, and let go. I snorted, wiped it with a finger, and tasted nothing but metal in my own jaw. Eleven minutes on the timer. I tightened another quarter turn anyway, then left a dry paper towel wrapped around the joint like a tiny flag. Tomorrow morning, I'd check whether it had stayed dry.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: Marguerite held the envelope up to the kitchen window and tilted it, as if the sun might confess something. The return address said Department of Revenue, in a font too tidy for her liking. She turned it over, pressed her thumb along the seal, and found it suspiciously well glued. "Refund," she said aloud, flat as a tabletop. "Sure." Her left eyebrow had climbed halfway to her hairline. She slid a butter knife under the flap instead of tearing it, slow, the way you'd lift a lid on something that might hiss. Inside, three pages, a checkbox, a phone number. She read the first line twice, then flipped straight to the last page to find the catch. Her jaw shifted sideways. Under her breath she muttered that nobody gives money back for free, and reached for her reading glasses and a red pen, and a second cup of coffee, and started hunting for the fine print.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver tapped the meter twice and said a number Marguerite was fairly sure had been smaller at the curb. She leaned over the seat and squinted at the glowing red digits, then at his eyes in the mirror. "Same as the airport sign?" she said, slowly, pointing at her phone. He shrugged, smiled, and kept talking in a warm, rolling stream she couldn't parse. Her jaw tightened. She counted the bills twice, handed over exactly what she'd read online, and held out her palm for a receipt. He laughed and scribbled something on a scrap of paper. She folded it into her coat pocket without reading it, since she couldn't, and stood on the pavement with her suitcase handle gripped hard. The sign above the hotel door bore a name that didn't match her booking. She pulled up the confirmation email again and read it right there, one eyebrow lifted, her feet not yet moving toward the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the fence with her arms crossed and one eyebrow slightly lifted, watching Biscuit tear across the wet grass toward the tree line. "Sure," she said to no one, "he's never been this fast." The trainer's pamphlet was folded in her back pocket, its promise of a 'transformed, obedient companion in six weeks' pressing against her hip. Biscuit skidded, spun, and dropped into a perfect play bow at the stranger's golden retriever. Marta tilted her head, lips pressed to one side. She counted the seconds before he'd bolt for the road. Eleven. Twelve. He didn't. She rubbed her jaw, then the back of her neck, where a stiffness had settled. When he trotted back at her whistle, tongue lolling, she didn't kneel to greet him. She held out a treat at arm's length and watched his eyes instead. "Do it again," she said flatly. "Go on. Let's see." The wind lifted the pamphlet's corner, and she pushed it down with her thumb.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite tapped the cello's endpin into the same scuffed groove in the church hall floor and watched the conductor wave his arms like a man herding geese. "Again from the bridge," he called, bright as a spoon. She lifted one eyebrow and kept her bow hovering a second too long. Around her, the folding chairs squeaked, the radiator ticked, and a flutist in the back hit the same flat note she'd hit three times already. "Surely that gets fixed by Thursday," Marguerite said, mild, almost kind, while her jaw worked sideways. She played the passage, then stopped before the final bar, arms crossed over the cello's neck. "Forty people will come," she muttered. "Thirty-nine are related to us." When he promised it would all come together, she stared at the water-stained ceiling tile, exhaled through her nose, and slowly turned the page. She marked her fingering in pencil anyway, but lightly, as if it might need erasing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta pulled the coffee can off the shelf and tipped it into her palm: eleven screws, a bent nail, a button. She turned the can over and rapped its bottom with a knuckle, listening for a false floor. Nothing. "Sure, Dale," she muttered to the sawdust-furred rafters. His nephew had sworn the old man kept gold coins in here, and the nephew had also sworn the Pinto ran great. She lifted the lid of the workbench vise-box, ran her thumb along the seams, and sniffed at the drawer of ledgers before opening it. Receipts for glue. More glue. She flipped each page twice, tilting it toward the bare bulb as though ink might say something else. When the nephew's text buzzed, asking whether she'd found anything yet, she read it with one eyebrow hitched, snorted, and typed, "Plenty of clamps." Then she checked behind the pegboard anyway, knocking on the wall in a slow, careful line.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 14 smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Dana stood off to the side while the others crowded the corkboard. A secretary had promised the sheet would go up at noon. It was 12:20. Dana leaned against the wall with arms crossed, one eyebrow lifted, watching the door the way she watched vending machines that had eaten her coins before. "Noon," she said to nobody, then glanced at her watch again. When Marcus bounced over and swore the list was definitely coming, she gave a short, dry laugh. "Sure. Right after the printer works." Her thumb rubbed the edge of her phone, refreshing the portal she'd already checked four times, the same grey spinner turning. A door clicked. Everyone surged forward. Dana didn't move. She tilted her head, squinted at the paper being pinned, and muttered, "Let's see if that's even the right course code."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The sign said the summit loop took forty minutes, and I'd already burned an hour and ten. I stopped where the pines thinned and squinted at the little wooden arrow, then at my phone, which showed a blue dot floating in blank gray. "Sure," I muttered. "Forty." My left eyebrow had been stuck high for a mile. Behind me, the light went orange, then the color of weak tea, and the cold crept under my collar. Dale, the guy at the trailhead, had slapped the map and promised a clear path and a lit lot. I tapped the arrow with one knuckle, as if it might confess. It wobbled, loose on its nail. I crossed my arms, rocked my weight onto my heels, and kept the headlamp in my pocket a while longer, just to see whether the trail would prove him right. Somewhere downhill, a branch cracked. I didn't hurry. I counted my steps instead, and doubted every one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, my grandmother's slanted pencil gone gray in the creases. "A handful of flour," I read aloud to the empty kitchen, and snort. Whose handful? I dig out the scale anyway and weigh what I scoop: 212 grams. I write that on my phone, just in case. "Warm water, warm like a baby's wrist." I hold my wrist under the tap, frowning, then dunk a thermometer in the bowl and squint at it. Ninety-eight. Fine. The yeast sits there, flat and beige, and I fold my arms and watch it for a full minute before admitting nothing's happening. "Give it time," the card says. I tap my foot. I check the clock twice. My hands knead because the card says ten minutes, but my eyebrows stay high the whole while, and when the dough sticks to my knuckles I mutter, "Sure. Of course it does." I set the timer for an hour and leave the oven light on, arms crossed, waiting to be proven wrong or not.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding two cantaloupes up to the fluorescent light, thumbing the stem ends, when someone said my name like a question. Dale Pruitt. Fourth-period chemistry, the guy who once sold me a "guaranteed" answer key that was blank on the back. He wore a crisp quarter-zip and a grin with too many teeth. "I run a wellness startup now," he said, and slid a card toward me. I took it by the edge, turned it over, checked the back out of habit. My eyebrow had already climbed. "Huh," I said. "Which part is the wellness?" He laughed, too loud, and mentioned an investment window closing Friday. I set the cantaloupe in my cart, slowly, and kept one hand on the handle. "Send me something in writing," I said, flat, already steering toward checkout. My jaw felt tight. I didn't pocket the card until he'd turned the corner, and even then I pinched it like a receipt for something I hadn't bought.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol flipped the sign on the pharmacy door to CLOSED at 5:58 and eyed the man still lingering by the vitamins. "Store policy says six," she said, one eyebrow climbing. Her manager's note taped to the register promised a bonus for "everyone who stays positive through close," and she'd read it twice, tilting her head, the way she checked expiration dates. "Mm-hm," she muttered, tapping the paper with a fingernail. "Last year it was a ham." She never got the ham. The fluorescent lights hummed over the empty aisles, and her arms stayed crossed while the radio crooned about togetherness. When the man held up a bottle of fish oil and said it was on sale, she squinted at the shelf tag, then at him, then back at the tag. "That's last week's," she said flatly, and turned the bottle over to read the fine print herself, lips pressed thin, before she reached for the scanner.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta stopped at the gate agent's desk with her boarding pass pinched between two fingers, one eyebrow lifted. "Gate C41," she repeated. "The board says C41. The app says B12. Which one are you telling me?" The agent said C41, final answer. Marta nodded slowly, then held up her phone anyway and thumbed the screen, squinting at the little spinning wheel. Her carry-on wheels clacked behind her as she walked, not ran, past the moving walkway that had been broken since morning. Eleven minutes, the monitor claimed. She tilted her head at it, jaw set, and checked the clock on her wrist against the clock on the wall. They disagreed by two minutes. At C41, a man in a vest announced the door was still open, and she stood at the threshold with her arms crossed, studying the empty jet bridge before she stepped onto it. "We'll see," she muttered, tugging the strap of her bag higher.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The can says one coat covers everything, so I pry the lid off and stir slowly, watching the pale gray swirl like thin milk. "One coat," I read aloud to the empty hallway, and snort. I dip the roller, drag it across the wall beside the old mustard yellow, and then stand with my arms crossed, one eyebrow climbing. The yellow glows through, a ghost under wet gray. My jaw tightens. I press my thumb to the patch, check the smear on my skin, rub it against my jeans. The receipt is still in my back pocket, folded small, and I touch it twice while the wall dries. Forty minutes later I crouch with my face almost on the plaster, squinting at the streaks. "Sure," I mutter, reaching for the tape. "Sure it does." I pour a second tray anyway, already counting how many more cans I'll need.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite kept her phone face-up on the porch rail, thumb hovering, while the first fat drops slapped the boards. "Thirty percent chance," she muttered. "That's what it said at noon." Thunder rolled, and she tilted her head, one eyebrow climbing, as though the sky had made a claim she wanted to see notarized. Her brother-in-law swore the old oak would take a hit someday; she squinted at it now, arms crossed tight, jaw working at nothing. The wind pushed cold air under her collar and she didn't flinch, only tugged the sweater closed and kept watching. A flash lit the yard white. She counted under her breath. One, two, three, four. "Eh," she said, loud enough for the empty chair beside her. "Four miles. Not so close." The rain thickened into a roar, spray dotting her shins. She refused to move her feet. Instead she picked up her lukewarm tea, sniffed it, and took a slow sip, eyes narrowed at the clouds, waiting for them to prove something more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The patch kit's instructions have been swimming for a while, so I read the same line three times and still can't tell you what it says. Across the garage, Mrs. Okafor's dryer thumps in its slow loop, and the sound keeps rocking me. I lean my elbow on the saddle, then my cheek on my elbow, and the rubber smells warm and faintly sweet. My eyelids drag down like shutters. I jerk up when the wrench clatters off the workbench. "I'm fine," I tell the empty room, voice thick and slurred, and I rub my face with a greasy hand, which only leaves a streak. The tube is in my fingers, the valve is in the rim, I think. I check again. It isn't. I yawn so wide my jaw clicks, set the tire lever down, and stare at the old couch by the paint cans like it's calling my name. Five minutes, I bargain. Just until the glue gets tacky.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's plexiglass roof, and Marisol counted them the way she might have counted anything, slowly, losing track at eleven. Her cheek had found the cold edge of the timetable frame, and she let it stay there. A gust smelled of wet asphalt and flipped the hem of her coat; she watched it flap without deciding to fix it. 'Mm. Twenty-two,' she mumbled to the empty bench, though she wasn't sure what she meant. Her eyelids kept sliding down to half-mast, and the headlights across the street smeared into long gold streaks that she found extremely interesting. She jerked when a pigeon landed, blinked hard, and read the same line of the schedule three times without it turning into words. The thermos in her bag was empty. She'd checked twice. Her knees went soft, and she caught herself with a little scrape of her heel. 'Just rest them a second,' she said, low and thick, and tipped her head back against the glass as the rain thickened to a steady, drumming hush.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite had read the same line three times, and still it said nothing to her. The envelope in her hand, soft as cloth at the corners, slid against her knee and she let it. Rain ticked on the attic window in a slow, even rhythm. She propped her cheek on her fist, and her elbow slowly slid down the side of the trunk until she caught herself with a jolt. "Hm. Where was I," she mumbled, the words thick and slurred at the edges. Her eyelids kept drooping over the looping handwriting, so she pressed her thumbs to them and held them there. The lamp glowed warm and blurry. She set one letter on the 'keep' pile, then, after a long moment, picked it up again and put it on the wrong one. A yawn cracked her jaw wide. The box could wait, she thought, and laid her head against a folded quilt, a letter still pinched loosely between two fingers.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came twice before Marta registered it as something outside her own head. She opened the door with her cheek still creased from the couch cushion, one hand braced on the frame. "Ladder," Dale said, pointing vaguely toward her garage. "Gutters." She blinked at him slowly. "Right. Gutters." The porch light seemed too bright, and she squinted against it, jaw stretching into a yawn she tried to bury in her sleeve. "Sorry. Long... what day is it?" She shuffled across the lawn in one slipper, the grass cool and blurry beneath her, and stood in the garage doorway for a long moment, forgetting why she'd come. The ladder leaned against the wall. She lifted it, and it felt absurdly heavy, her arms like wet rope. "Take it. Keep it. Whenever," she mumbled, leaning her forehead briefly against the cold aluminum rung. Dale's voice drifted somewhere far off. She nodded at whatever he said, then wandered back toward the couch.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onion has been in my hand for a while before I notice I'm not cutting it. I blink, and the knife finally comes down, slow and a little crooked. The kitchen clock says 6:12, guests at 7, and the numbers swim when I look twice. I lean my hip against the counter and let my forehead rest, just for a second, against the cool cupboard door. The simmering pot hums like a lullaby I didn't ask for. 'Right,' I say aloud, too loudly, to nobody, and my voice comes out thick and cracked. I stir the sauce, then stir it again, forgetting whether I added the salt. I taste it. Nothing, or maybe everything. My eyelids feel weighted with wet sand. I crack the window, let the November air slap my cheeks, and yawn so wide my jaw clicks. The doorbell is going to ring, and I'm standing here holding a wooden spoon like it's the only thing keeping me upright, which it might be.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the nightstand, skittering toward the edge, and Marisol's hand found it on the third try. Her eyelids felt weighted with wet sand. The screen glowed a number she didn't know, too bright, and she squinted until the digits swam together. "Mm. Hello?" The word came out as a croak, half swallowed by the pillow still pressed against her cheek. A man's voice began talking about her car's extended warranty. She nodded, as though he could see it, and her head sank a little lower each time. The lamp across the room blurred into a soft yellow smear. "Sorry, what was that?" she mumbled, and yawned so wide her jaw cracked, the phone sliding down her shoulder. She dragged it back up. "I don't... have a car, I think. Or I do. Can you say it slower?" Her thumb drifted toward the red button, pausing, while the blanket's warmth pulled at her like a tide, and the man's voice grew distant, humming, pleasant, far away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and I stood at the return desk blinking at the fluorescent lights as if they were the sun. I'd read the same sentence on the sign three times: Fines Accrue Daily. My eyelids kept sliding down, and I propped my chin on my fist, which only made my elbow slip on the counter. 'Hi,' I said, and it came out slow and thick, like I was talking through a blanket. 'This is, um. Overdue. A little.' The librarian turned the cover toward her screen. I let out a yawn so wide my jaw clicked, and I mumbled an apology into my sleeve. The carpet looked soft. Really soft. 'Two hundred and ten days,' she said. I nodded, swaying slightly, wondering whether anyone would notice if I just rested my forehead on the cool wood for one minute. 'Sure,' I said. 'Whatever that costs. Could I maybe sit first?'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol set the last box down in the middle of the studio and stood there, blinking slowly at the label, which read KITCHEN in her own handwriting but looked like a smear. The radiator ticked. She meant to find the box cutter, yet her hand drifted to the bare mattress propped against the wall, and she leaned her whole weight into it, cheek pressed to the cool plastic wrap. "Okay," she told the room, the word dragging out long and soft. "Just the sheets. Then the plates." Her eyelids kept sliding down like heavy curtains, and each time she hauled them up, the window had gone a little more orange. She yawned so wide her jaw clicked, then forgot what she'd been looking for. The mattress dropped to the floor with a thump she barely heard. She tugged her coat over her shoulders, curled around her keys, and decided the plates could wait until the floor stopped feeling so much like a very good idea.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench was warm from the afternoon sun, and I lowered myself onto it with a groan I hadn't planned. My eyelids kept sliding down like curtains on a bad rope. That's when I noticed the wallet beside my thigh, brown leather, curled at the corners. I blinked at it for a long moment before my hand moved. "Hello," I mumbled to nobody, my voice thick and slow. I flipped it open, squinting as the driver's license swam, the letters doubling. Marcus Ellery. Forty-one. I read the address twice and still lost it. A pigeon cooed somewhere, and my head dipped, jerked up. I pinched the bridge of my nose, yawned so wide my jaw clicked, and dragged myself upright. The coffee cup at my feet was empty. Fine. Police station, two blocks. I shuffled off, wallet clutched to my chest, rubbing my heavy, gritty eyes and wondering if the walk would wake me or whether the sidewalk would look soft enough to lie down on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite gripped the pool's edge at the six a.m. class, her chin resting on her knuckles longer than the instructor's count allowed. The overhead lights hummed, and the warm, chlorinated air pressed against her like a heavy blanket. "Kick," the instructor called, and she did, slowly, her legs moving as if through wet sand. Her eyelids kept sliding down; she blinked hard, twice, and water beaded on her lashes. When she tried to float, her body went loose and easy, and she nearly let her face drift under. She jerked up, sputtering. "Sorry, what was the last part?" she mumbled, voice thick and low. The instructor repeated it. Marguerite nodded, yawned into her shoulder, and thought how lovely the lane rope looked, bobbing in its gentle rhythm. Maybe she could rest her cheek there. She pushed off the wall again, arms heavy, and counted strokes in a slur: one, two, thr... one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Mara knelt in the warm dirt with the seed packet pinched in her fingers, reading the same line about spacing three times before the words held still. The trowel felt heavier than it had an hour ago. She dug a hole, set a tomato start in it, and then simply stayed there, one palm flat on the soil, her forehead tipping closer to the leaf cage than she meant it to. A bee droned somewhere, and the sound seemed to stretch. 'Six inches,' she mumbled, and measured with a hand she could barely keep open. Her eyes watered; she rubbed them with a gritty knuckle and left a smear of earth across her cheek. The sun lay on her back like a blanket. She yawned so wide her jaw clicked, then blinked slowly at the row of crooked holes. 'Just the beans,' she told the dirt. 'Then the porch. The step. Right there.' She eyed the shade of the fence, and her body already leaned toward it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus kept his eyes on Dana's slides, but the bar charts had started to slide into one another, blue smearing into gray. The conference room was warm, the projector fan humming a low, steady note that seemed to press on his eyelids. He propped his chin on his fist, then caught his elbow slipping and jerked upright. 'Right, yes, the Q3 numbers,' he said, too slowly, his voice thick and low. He blinked hard, twice, and reread the same bullet point three times without absorbing a word. His coffee sat empty beside his notebook, where his handwriting had trailed off into a long diagonal line. When Dana asked if anyone had questions, he opened his mouth and a yawn came out instead, which he hid behind a cough. 'Sorry. Could you repeat that last part?' She did. He nodded, wondering how the couch in the break room would feel against his cheek, and whether anyone would notice if he simply closed his eyes for ten seconds.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway lamps slid over Marisol's dashboard in slow orange pulses, and she caught herself counting them, lost the number, started again. Her left hand propped her head against the window while the right drifted lower on the wheel. She cranked the glass down; the cold slapped her cheek for about a minute, then felt like nothing. "Okay," she said aloud, too slowly, the word stretching out like taffy. "Okay, okay. Sing something." She hummed half a chorus and it dissolved. Her eyelids kept sliding down like heavy curtains, and each time she hauled them open the road had wandered a little toward the rumble strip. The tires growled. She jerked the wheel, heart thumping, and blinked hard at the green exit sign, which seemed to swim and doubled. Her jaw cracked open in a yawn so wide her eyes watered. She pictured her pillow, the exact cool side of it, and pressed the accelerator harder, muttering, "Four more miles. Just four more miles."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol had read the same line of the get-well card three times before she noticed her grandfather's hand had gone slack in hers. The monitor kept up its soft, patient beeping, and the heater hummed under the window, warm against her shins. She shifted in the vinyl chair, but her head kept drifting toward her shoulder, and twice she jerked it upright, blinking at the blurred ceiling tiles. "Sorry, Abuelo, what was that?" she murmured, though he hadn't spoken. Her voice came out thick and slow, the words stretching like taffy. She pressed her thumbs into her eyes, then rubbed her face, then stared at the vending-machine coffee going cold on the tray, wondering if she could be bothered to lift it. The clock said 3:10. Had it said that before? Her elbow found the edge of the mattress, and she let her cheek rest against her sleeve, just for a minute, just while the beeping counted on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana leaned against the chain-link fence with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair, though the afternoon was gray. Her eyelids kept sliding down, and each time she dragged them open the line of strollers and minivans had smeared a little. She read the same text from her sister three times and still couldn't have said what it was about. When the woman beside her asked if she'd heard about the bake sale, Dana said, "Mm. Yeah. The... what?" and laughed too late. A yawn cracked her jaw so wide her eyes watered, and she hid it in her coat sleeve. The warm car heater still seemed to hum in her bones. She shifted her weight, let her head tip back against the cool metal post, and counted the bricks over the doorway, losing track at forty. When the bell rang, she flinched, blinking hard, and wiped the corner of her mouth before anyone could see.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marta had set the alarm for five, and now, at ten past noon, she sat in the rocking chair she was supposed to be selling, one elbow on the armrest, her cheek propped against her fist. The sun lay warm across her knees. A man asked whether the oak dresser had all its drawers, and she watched his mouth move a second before the words arrived. "Mm. Yes. Six. Well, five and a half," she said, and blinked slowly, her lids dragging back up. He laughed, and she tried to laugh too, but it turned into a yawn she hid behind her coffee mug, which had gone cold hours ago. Her thoughts kept sliding off the price tags. Twenty? Thirty? The cushion of the old sofa looked so deep, so inviting, that she caught herself measuring the distance to it. "Make me an offer," she mumbled, and let her head tip back against the rungs, the street noise thinning to a hum.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped off the fitting for the third time, and I watched it clang against the cabinet floor like it belonged to someone else. Water kept ticking into the bucket, a slow metronome I'd stopped counting somewhere around two a.m. I rested my forehead against the cool pipe under the sink, just for a second, and the second stretched until a drip landed on my neck and I jerked. "Right," I muttered, the word coming out thick and slurred. My eyelids felt weighted with wet sand. I read the instructions on the sealant tube twice, then a third time, the letters sliding around. I wrapped the tape clockwise, then wondered if it was supposed to be counterclockwise, and stared at my hands as though they might answer. My yawn cracked my jaw wide. The kitchen light hummed. I thought about the couch, its dent shaped exactly like me, and tightened the nut anyway, slowly, leaning my whole cheek on the cabinet door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been leaning against the fruit bowl since Tuesday, and now, past midnight, I finally drag it toward me with one finger. Return address: Department of Revenue. My elbow slides off the table edge and I catch myself, blinking hard. I slit the flap with a butter knife, though it takes two tries because the knife keeps drifting. The paper unfolds in thick creases. I read the first line, then read it again, because the words slip away like they're underwater. "Notice of... review," I mumble to the empty kitchen, my tongue heavy. My cheek finds my palm. The refrigerator hum gets louder, softer, louder. I yawn so wide my jaw clicks, and my eyes water over the numbers. Somewhere in paragraph two is a deadline. I squint, lose it, and decide the kitchen light is much too warm. I'll fold this back up, I tell myself, and rest my forehead on it, just for a second, just on the cool, official paper.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station clock in Thessaloniki said something I read three times before it became a number. I dragged my suitcase behind me, its wheels clicking over tiles, and the sound seemed to come from somewhere far off. At the kiosk I pointed at a bottle of water, then at my own mouth, and the vendor said a long sentence that slid past me like water over glass. "Efharisto," I managed, too slowly, the word stretching out. My eyelids kept sinking, and I propped my elbow on the counter, chin in my palm, until the vendor laughed and slid a coffee toward me. I hadn't asked for it. The street signs blurred into lovely, meaningless curls. I found a bench in the square, sat, and told myself I'd only rest my eyes while I worked out which tram to take. The sun lay warm on my knees. My head tipped back against the slats, and the pigeons' murmuring began to sound like a language I almost understood.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus lowered himself onto the bench at the edge of the field and let his head tip back against the wooden slat. Biscuit tore across the grass after a ball that had stopped rolling a minute ago, and Marcus followed her with eyes that kept slipping half closed. The sun lay warm across his knees. A bee droned somewhere, and the sound seemed to stretch longer each time it passed. 'Good girl,' he said, but it came out thick and slow, the words sagging in the middle. He blinked, and Biscuit had somehow moved from one end of the field to the other. He rubbed his face with a heavy hand, then let the hand drop into his lap. His chin dipped. He jerked it up, frowned at the leash coiled beside him as if it had asked him something, and mumbled, 'Five more minutes, bud,' to no one at all, while his shoulders sank deeper into the bench.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite set her clarinet across her knees and pressed the heel of her hand into one eye, rubbing until colors bloomed behind the lid. The church hall's radiator ticked, and the warm air smelled of floor wax and old hymnals. "From the top of the second page," the conductor called, and she nodded a beat late. Her fingers drifted over the keys a half-step behind everyone else. The notes on the stand softened, their little black heads swimming together like tadpoles. She caught her chin dipping and jerked it up, blinking hard, then hid a yawn behind her sleeve so wide her jaw clicked. "Sorry, which measure?" she mumbled, voice thick and slow. Beside her, the flutist whispered, "Forty-one." Marguerite found the place, breathed in, and the reed squeaked, a thin, wandering sound. She leaned her head against the cool cinderblock wall just for a moment, eyelids heavy as wet towels, and let the music float somewhere above her, far away and pleasantly blurred.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus's workshop smelled of cedar and machine oil, and I had read the same label on the same coffee can of screws three times. I sat down on his overturned bucket, just for a second, and the pegboard outlines of his missing tools swam a little. My eyelids kept dropping and I kept hauling them back up. "Okay," I said aloud, my voice thick and slow, "okay, the chisels go in the box." I picked one up and held it against my cheek without meaning to, the wood handle warm from the afternoon sun. The yawn cracked my jaw so wide my eyes watered. I leaned my head against the workbench vise, its cold iron strangely welcome, and the radio he'd left on the shelf hummed static somewhere far away. My arms felt packed with wet sand. One more drawer, I told myself, and then my forehead was resting on my knuckles, and the sawdust drifted down gold through the window light, and I let it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor clock said 4:52, and the results were promised for five, so I slid down the wall beside the noticeboard and let my bag take my head's weight. The tiles hummed under me. I read the same line of the pinned fire notice three times and it kept dissolving into gray. "Sorry, what?" I said when Priya asked if I was nervous, though she hadn't asked anything yet; she'd only breathed in. My jaw cracked open in a yawn so wide my eyes watered, and I pressed my knuckles into them until colors bloomed. The fluorescent light felt thick, like wool. Every blink lasted a little longer than the one before. I told myself I'd just rest them until the secretary came with the tape. The paper could wait. My arms were heavy, my voice came out slurred and low, and somewhere far off a door squeaked, and I jerked upright, certain I'd missed everything, with a crease from my sleeve printed on my cheek.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marisol's boots had started to scuff the gravel instead of lifting off it. The ridge trail turned amber, then rust, and the pines blurred into one long smear at the edge of her vision. She stopped at a switchback and leaned on her trekking pole, letting her forehead rest against her knuckles for a moment longer than she meant to. Her eyelids felt weighted with wet sand. "Just up to the next marker," she muttered, the words slurring together, and then she said it again because she couldn't remember whether she'd said it already. A yawn cracked her jaw so wide her ears popped. The flat boulder beside the path looked absurdly soft, its surface still holding the last of the sun. She stared at it, swaying slightly, thinking how easy it would be to fold her jacket into a pillow. Instead she blinked hard, hitched her pack, and shuffled on, head drooping with every other step.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, Nonna's slanted handwriting blurred by decades of flour and thumbprints. Marisol read the line twice, then a third time, because the words kept sliding apart. "Four cups," she muttered, and dumped in five before she noticed. She scooped one out, slowly, a white drift settling over the counter and her sleeve. The kitchen clock ticked too loudly. Her elbows found the counter and stayed there while she kneaded, her forehead drifting lower with each push, until her nose nearly brushed the dough. She jerked upright. "Still here," she told the empty room, voice thick and slurred. Her eyelids felt weighted with wet sand. She rubbed her eyes with the back of her wrist and left a streak of flour across her cheek. The dough needed an hour to rise. She set the timer, pulled a chair beside the warm oven, and let her head tip against the cabinet, the card still pinched loosely between two fingers, one more yawn cracking her jaw wide.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus stood in the cereal aisle holding a box he had read the back of three times without absorbing a single word. The fluorescent lights hummed, and his eyelids kept dropping to half-mast. When someone said his name, he turned too slowly, blinking hard, and found Dana Ortiz from tenth-grade chemistry grinning at him with a basket on her arm. "Dana," he said, his voice thick and low. "Wow. Hey." He leaned a shoulder against the shelf without meaning to. She talked about her job, her cat, a move to Portland, and he nodded a beat behind everything, stifling a yawn behind his fist and mumbling an apology. His head felt packed with warm wool. "Sorry, what was the last part?" he asked, rubbing his stinging eyes. She laughed and said it didn't matter. He wanted to say something clever about lab partners, but the words drifted off. He wondered, vaguely, whether the cold floor of the freezer section would be rude to lie down on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The clock over the pharmacy counter says 4:52, and I've read it six times without it moving. Somebody's cart squeaks past, and I realize I've been staring at the same bottle of cough syrup, scanning it, scanning it, the beep coming a half-second after my hand. My eyelids feel weighted with wet sand. I prop my chin on my fist, and my elbow slides off the counter, jolting me upright. "Sorry, ma'am, what was that? Ten dollars... no, twelve." My voice comes out slow and gravelly, like it's dragged through a pillow. The fluorescent lights hum a low lullaby, and the tinsel taped along the register sways in the vent's breath. I yawn into my sleeve for the third time in a minute, eyes streaming. Just eight more minutes. I lean against the shelf behind me, the cool metal pressing my shoulder blades, and think how good the floor would feel, right here, right now, beside the cough drops, with my coat folded under my cheek.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says Gate C47, and I read it three times because the numbers keep sliding around like fish. Twenty minutes to boarding. I walk, but my feet drag along the carpet, and the rolling bag veers left every few steps until I yank it back. My eyes burn. I blink slowly, and each blink lasts a little too long. At the moving walkway I lean on the rail and my forehead nearly meets my wrist. A man says, "Ma'am, you're good to step off," and I say, "Mm. Right. Thanks," though it comes out thick, like I'm talking through a pillow. I yawn so wide my jaw clicks. The gate agent's voice hums somewhere far off, and I catch myself staring at the cushioned chairs, how soft they look, how warm. I pinch my arm. I buy coffee I haven't tasted yet, and scan my pass twice because the first time I held it upside down. Boarding starts. I shuffle forward, already dreaming of the window seat and its small, cold, wonderful wall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta pressed the roller into the tray and dragged it up the wall, but halfway through the stroke her hand slowed and stopped, the nap pooling a fat gray-green streak beside the window. She blinked at it. The drop cloth rustled under her socks. "Right," she said, the word coming out thick and long, and she leaned her forehead against the cool, unpainted doorframe for just a moment. The radio murmured something about traffic; she'd lost the thread of it three songs ago. Her eyelids kept sliding down, and the fumes seemed to hum. She yawned so wide her jaw clicked, then reread the can's label for the third time without absorbing a word. Sinking onto the overturned bucket, she set the roller across the tray, folded her arms on her knees, and told the half-finished wall, "Five minutes. I'm just resting my eyes." The streak kept sliding, slowly, slowly, toward the baseboard.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while I was still holding the lemonade, and I watched it sweat a ring onto the armrest without moving to wipe it. Rain drummed the tin roof in a long, even hush. "Mm, there it goes again," I told the dog, though my voice came out slow and thick, the words dragging like boots through mud. My head tipped sideways against the porch post, and the wood felt cool and almost soft. Lightning flashed white across the yard; I blinked, and the blink lasted longer than I'd planned. The wind-chime clinked somewhere far off, farther than it really was. I meant to go in and shut the windows. I thought about it twice, pleasantly, the way you think about a country you'll never visit. My fingers loosened. The glass tilted. Rain sprayed my ankles and I only curled my toes, dragging the blanket up to my chin, listening to the storm grow gentler and wider, until it sounded like someone humming in the next room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The wrench is on the floor again, and I look at it for a good while before bending down. Knees crack. The flat tire I meant to patch an hour ago still hangs off the rim like a shed skin. Across the garage, Mrs. Okafor's table saw whines, and I wince as if it's pulling at something behind my eyes. "Sorry, what?" I say when she asks if I need the pump. She repeats it. I say, "Yeah. Maybe. In a minute." My elbow rests on the saddle because holding my arm up feels like a negotiation. The chain lube sits two feet away. I stare at it, then at the clock, then at my hands, which are black to the wrist and not doing anything. I yawn so hard my jaw clicks. Tomorrow, I tell the bike quietly, I'll finish. Then I sit down on the upturned bucket, and it's a long time before I stand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was still working out whether to sit. She lowered herself onto the bench in stages, hand on her knee, and let her bag slide off her shoulder to the ground rather than lift it to her lap. Wind pushed a flattened cup down the curb; she watched it go and didn't turn her head when it reached the drain. 'Mm,' she said to the man beside her, who had asked if the 14 was late, and then, a full breath later, 'Think so.' Her eyelids kept drifting down to half, and the rain's hiss blurred into a hum she let carry her. The cold crept through her sleeves. She thought about zipping her coat, pictured the whole motion, the tug, the teeth catching, and left it open. When headlights finally swung around the corner, she stared at them a moment too long, then braced both palms against the bench and began, slowly, to rise.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box has been on my lap for maybe an hour, though the tea beside it went cold before I got the lid off. I lift out one envelope and hold it there, my arm heavier than it should be, and read the same line of my aunt's handwriting three times without it landing. "Huh," I say to the empty room, the word coming out thick and slow. My eyes keep drifting to the window, where the afternoon light has crept across the rug without my noticing. I mean to make two piles, keep and toss, but I set each letter down on the same stack, too tired to decide. When I try to stand for a pen, my legs argue, so I sit back and let my head rest against the sofa cushion. The envelope slides from my fingers onto the floor. I look at it a while. Then I close my eyes, just for a minute, and leave it there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The doorbell rang twice before Marta registered it, and then she sat another moment with her palms flat on the couch cushions, as if the floor had to be negotiated with. The coffee on the table had gone cold hours ago; she hadn't noticed it. At the door, Mr. Okafor stood squinting in the afternoon glare, asking whether she still had that extension ladder. "The ladder," she said, slowly, as though turning the word over. "Yeah. Garage." Her voice came out low and flat, and she blinked at him a beat too long. Her limbs felt packed with wet sand. She shuffled across the lawn in her socks, hauled the garage door up halfway, and leaned against it to rest. The ladder hung high on its hooks, and the thought of lifting it made her jaw ache. "Could you grab the other end?" she asked. "Tomorrow I'd do it myself. Today I'm just... slow." She yawned into her shoulder, eyes watering, and waited for him to reach it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol leaned against the counter and watched the onion in front of her as if it might chop itself. The knife felt heavier than it had that morning. Six forty. The doorbell would ring at seven. She sliced three half-moons, stopped, and rubbed her eyes with the back of her wrist, which smelled of garlic and did nothing. The pot on the stove had been simmering without her for a while; she noticed only when the lid rattled. "Right," she said to the empty kitchen, slow and low, and the word trailed off. She stirred once, twice, then forgot whether she'd added salt. Her feet seemed bolted to the tile. The oven timer beeped and she stared at it through three more beeps before reaching over. Tasting the sauce, she frowned, shrugged, and sat down on the step stool, just for a second, while the bread went on browning behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the coffee table, skittering toward the edge, and Marisol watched it for three full rings before her arm decided to move. The screen showed ten digits she didn't know. Her thumb hovered, then dragged across the glass as if through wet sand. "Mm. Hello," she said, the word coming out thick and low, half swallowed. She'd been lying on the couch since noon, a blanket still pooled around her shins, a cold mug within reach but not worth reaching for. The voice on the line was bright, saying something about a car warranty, and she blinked slowly at the ceiling fan, its blades turning. "Sorry, what," she murmured. Her eyelids dropped and rose. The sentence she meant to say, no thanks, felt miles off, so she just breathed into the receiver until it clicked dead. She set the phone on her chest and let her hand slide off the side.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been riding in Dana's backpack since March, and now it was November, and the strap seemed to weigh more than the whole semester. She pushed the library door with her shoulder instead of her hand, then stood in the entryway a moment, blinking at the bright lights as if they were asking something of her. Her sneakers dragged a faint squeak across the tile. At the desk she set down the battered copy of Principles of Ecology and rested her forehead briefly on her palm. "It's, um. Pretty late," she said, the words coming out slow and flat, trailing off before the end. The clerk tapped at a keyboard. Dana watched the cursor blink, once, twice, and thought she should probably care what the total was. Her eyelids kept sinking. She leaned her hip against the counter, let her arms hang, and wondered whether the bench by the exit was close enough to count as home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at noon, and by three I was still standing in the doorway of the studio with one box of kitchen things held against my hip, my arms heavier than they had any right to be. I set it down on the counter. Then I sat on it. The window was open to the street, and a bus wheezed by; I watched it go the whole length of the glass. My mother called, and I let it ring twice before I answered. "Yeah. No, it's fine. Just unpacking," I said, the words coming out slow and flat, though I hadn't touched a single box. She asked if I'd eaten. I looked at the stove, four steps away, and did the math. "Later," I said. My eyelids kept sliding down while I traced a crack in the ceiling plaster. The mattress leaned against the wall, still wrapped in plastic. I told myself I'd make the bed in a minute. The light on the floor moved a foot before I stood up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marta lowered herself onto the bench by inches, her coffee going cold in her hand, and only then saw the brown leather wallet beside her thigh. She looked at it for a long moment. Her arm felt packed with wet sand when she reached over, and she dragged it into her lap with a grunt. A pigeon pecked near her shoe; she watched it instead of opening the thing. "Okay," she said to nobody, the word stretching out thin. She blinked slowly, twice, and rubbed one eye with the heel of her palm. The license inside said Daniel Orr, and the face on it grinned at her too brightly. She read the address, then read it again because the numbers had slid off. Somewhere a kid shrieked on the swings. Her legs refused the idea of standing. She yawned until her jaw clicked, tucked the wallet into her coat, and decided the lost-and-found could wait until she'd sat a little longer, maybe just a few minutes more, maybe after the coffee.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says kick, and I tell her I am kicking. My legs disagree, trailing behind me like wet towels while the kickboard drifts out of reach. I'm thirty-eight, standing in the shallow end of the community pool at six a.m., and it takes me three tries to lift my arm high enough to push off the wall. Water slides past my ears with a dull hum. 'Again,' she calls, and I nod, but I stay there, forehead against the cold tile, counting my breaths because that's easier than moving. The fluorescent lights buzz. Somebody in the next lane has already finished four lengths. I hear myself say, 'Give me a second,' in a voice that comes out slow and flat, each word dragged up from somewhere deep. My shoulders feel packed with sand. I push off eventually. I make it about two body lengths before I stop and just stand, dripping, watching the ripples settle without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana set the seed packets on the overturned bucket and stood looking at the patch of dirt for a long time. The spade leaned against her leg. When she finally lifted it, the first scoop took two tries, and she let the blade rest in the soil while she breathed. "Okay," she said to nobody, the word dragging out. The sun sat warm on her neck, and her eyelids kept drooping shut. She knelt, wincing, and her arms felt packed with wet sand. The instructions said six inches apart. She squinted at the tape measure, read it, and forgot the number. Read it again. A tomato seedling lay on its side in its tray, and she watched it for a while before reaching over. Her hand hovered, then dropped into her lap. Somewhere a neighbor's mower droned on and on. She yawned, wide and slow, and pressed one muddy thumb into the ground, deciding that one row would do for today.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana's slides had reached the third quarter projections before Marcus realized he'd read the same bullet point four times. He propped his chin on his fist, and the fist kept sliding. The conference room hummed, warm and close, and the blinds striped the table in light that seemed to press on his eyelids. He reached for his coffee and found it cold, a skin on the surface, but drank it anyway. Someone laughed. He smiled a beat late. When Dana turned and asked whether the timeline looked workable, the words took a long moment to arrive. "Yeah," he said, voice thick and low. "Sounds... right. Can you go back one?" She did. He stared at the chart, watching the numbers swim, and lifted his pen to take notes. It hovered over the page, then settled, leaving only a small blue dot. His legs felt poured full of wet sand, and the door seemed very far away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The green light at Dalton Street had been red for a while before Marisol noticed the car behind her flashing its brights. She lifted her foot off the brake like it weighed ten pounds and let the sedan roll forward. The window was cracked, but the cold air only brushed her face without waking anything. Her hands sat at ten and two, heavy, her shoulders drooping toward the wheel. 'Almost there,' she mumbled to the empty passenger seat, the words smeared together. The radio was playing something she'd stopped hearing three songs ago. Streetlights slid over the dashboard in slow orange bars. At her building she parked crooked, took the key out, and just sat there, watching her breath fog the glass. The stairs to the third floor seemed like a problem for a later, stronger person. She leaned her head back and let her eyes close, just for a minute, her bag still in her lap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator doors had already started closing by the time I decided to lift my arm, so I took the stairs to the third floor instead, one hand dragging along the rail. Halfway up I stopped and stared at a laminated fire-exit map as if it might explain something. My legs felt filled with wet sand. Room 314. Grandpa's eyes opened a crack when I leaned in the doorway. "You look tired," he said, and I answered, "Mm," because the longer sentence I'd planned had dissolved somewhere around the second landing. I sank into the vinyl chair, and it exhaled under me. The TV murmured about weather. He asked about work, and I watched the drip chamber fill, one bead, then another, before I said, "Fine. Same." My eyelids kept sliding down. I pressed my thumbnail into my palm to keep them up, and counted the ceiling tiles twice, getting a different number each time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The car door takes two tries to shut, and I lean on it afterward like it's holding me up. Along the fence, the other parents stand in bright little clusters, and I drift toward the one patch of wall with shade. My coffee went cold an hour ago; I drink it anyway, wincing at the film on my tongue. Someone says my name, Dana, from the bake sale committee, and I hear it a beat late. "Hm? Sorry. Yeah. Fine. Just, long week," I say, the words dragging out like wet rope. She's talking about Friday, a sign-up sheet, and I nod at the right places while my eyelids keep sinking. My feet feel poured full of sand. When the bell rings, I push off the wall in slow stages, shoulders first, then hips, and think the walk to the gate looks a lot farther than it did this morning. Maybe Mia will carry her own backpack today.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By eight o'clock Marguerite had dragged only the oak dresser onto the lawn, and she lowered herself onto its edge to rest from the effort. The coffee beside her had gone cold; she'd forgotten it twice. A man in a ball cap asked if the rocking chair was still available, and she stared at the chair a moment before saying, "Hm. Yes. That one." Her voice came out low and slow. He asked the price. "Ten," she said, then, after a long blink, "Or eight." Her arms hung heavy, as if the sleeves were filled with wet sand. The folding table still leaned against the garage, unopened, and she looked at it, thought about it, and didn't move. Sunlight pressed warm on her neck. She yawned into her fist, watched a bee wander over the lamp shades, and wondered whether anyone would mind if the price tags stayed in the box until noon.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip had been keeping time against the bucket since Tuesday, and it was Saturday before I knelt under the sink with the wrench. My knees found the cabinet floor and stayed there a while. I reached for the flashlight, eight inches away, and watched my hand arrive at it like it was coming from across town. "Okay," I told the pipe, my voice flat and dragging. "Okay. Let's do this." Neither of us moved. Water beaded at the joint, swelled, dropped. I counted four drops before I fitted the wrench around the nut. My arms felt packed with wet sand. I turned it a quarter inch and rested my forehead on the cool pipe, eyes closed, thinking the plumber's number might still be on the fridge. Another quarter turn. The coffee I'd made at nine sat upstairs, skinned over by now. I thought about getting it. I tightened the nut instead, slowly, and the drip kept going anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had been on the hall table since Tuesday, or maybe Monday, its little window staring at me every time I dragged past in my socks. Today I carried it to the kitchen the way you carry a full bucket, one step, then a pause, then another. I sat. The chair seemed to take more of me than usual. My thumb found the flap and just rested there while the kettle I'd switched on clicked off and went cold. "Okay," I said to nobody, and it came out slurred and low. I read the first line, lost it, and read it again. My eyelids kept sliding down like heavy curtains. Something about a review, a deadline, a form. I set the page against my forehead, breathed, and thought I'd deal with it after a nap. The tea sat there, filmed over. I didn't get up to pour it out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed out its last breath at Hanoi station, and Mara stayed in her seat until the carriage was nearly empty, her backpack straps slack across her knees. When she finally stood, the floor seemed to tilt, and she gripped the seat back with both hands. Outside, motorbikes poured past in a roar she registered only dimly. A man held up a card with a name that wasn't hers; another said something bright and rapid, and she blinked at him, mouth slightly open. "Sorry," she managed, the word thick. "Hotel. Hotel Lan..." She dug through her pocket for the folded address, found it on the third try, and held it out without lifting her eyes above his chest. He pointed down the street. She nodded, dragged the suitcase two steps, then stopped to lean against a pillar, listening to her own heavy breathing and the unfamiliar syllables swirling around her like warm water she hadn't the strength to swim through.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit has already crossed the field twice by the time I get the ball out of my pocket. I throw it, but my arm barely lifts, and it drops a few feet in front of me. He looks back as if to ask whether that was serious. "Sorry, bud," I say, the words coming out thick and slow. I lower myself onto the bench, and the wood is cold through my jeans. My coffee has gone lukewarm in my hand, and I haven't touched it since the car. Across the grass, he tears through the dandelions, ears flapping, and I tell myself I should stand up and join him. My legs stay where they are. The clouds slide past, and I watch them for a long while, blinking more slowly each time. When he finally trots back, tongue out, I rest my hand on his head and forget to say anything at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells like floor wax and burnt coffee, and I'm on my third try at the opening bars of the Schubert. My fingers land a half-beat behind where I mean them to. "Again?" Marguerite asks from the folding chair, and I say, "Sure," only it comes out as a long exhale. I lean my forehead against the music stand for a second. The metal is cool. Nice. I could stay here. My arms feel packed with wet sand, and when I lift the bow it droops before I've even found the string. Somebody's stacking chairs at the back, and each clank seems to arrive from the far end of a tunnel. I read the same measure four times without hearing it. "Take your time," she says kindly. I nod, then notice I've been staring at the radiator for what might be a minute or ten. I pull in a breath, lift the bow again, and wonder if the tea in my bag is still warm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The box of Danny's chisels has been in my arms for a while now, I think. I can't remember lifting it. Dust sits on the bench in a gray fur, and I stare at the label maker on the shelf until the letters stop meaning anything. "Keep, donate, toss," I say aloud, but it comes out as one long mumble, the words sliding together. I lower myself onto the stool, which groans, and my hands rest on my knees like two things somebody left there. The coffee I brought has gone cold and I drink it anyway. Three hours, and the only thing sorted is a coffee can of screws, and I'm not even sure I sorted them. Sawdust smell, thick and sweet, presses on my eyelids. I should open the window. I look at the window. A lathe sits in the corner, patient. "Tomorrow," I tell it, and don't move for a long time, listening to the radio he left on, humming to nobody.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the registrar's office smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Dana had been leaning against the same cinderblock wall since the clock read ten. The noticeboard was still blank except for a curling flyer about bike locks. Her friend asked if she wanted coffee. "Mm," she said, eventually, and didn't move. Her backpack lay slumped by her feet; reaching for it seemed like a project for later. She slid down the wall an inch, then another, until her knees bent and her heels scraped the tile. Her eyelids kept dropping and she let them, watching the second hand drag itself around. When a clerk finally shuffled out with a stapler and a sheet of paper, Dana lifted her head as if it weighed more than it should. "That them?" she asked, voice thick and flat. She thought about standing. She thought about it again. Around her, everyone surged forward, and she watched their backs, one hand pressed against her heavy, tingling thigh.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The switchbacks had stopped being corners and become small, separate arguments. Marta planted her pole, dragged her boot up beside it, and stood there while the pines went from green to black around her. Her pack straps seemed to have gained a few pounds since the creek. She counted twenty steps, made it to eleven, and leaned against a boulder still warm from a sun that was already gone. "Just a sec," she told nobody, the words coming out thick and flat. Her thighs hummed like wet rope. A trail marker glowed pale ahead, maybe fifty yards off, and she studied it as if it were a mountain pass. The headlamp was in her pack. She should get it. She looked at the zipper for a long moment, then at the marker again, and let her eyelids drop while the first cold air slid down the slope and settled around her ankles. Then she pushed off the rock, slowly, one boot at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma's recipe card is stained with butter, and I read the first line three times before the words stay put. "Scald the milk," it says. I lean on the counter while the pot hums on the stove, and my elbow slides until my cheek nearly rests on my fist. The flour bag feels heavier than I remember, so I drag it over instead of lifting it. When the dough finally comes together I press the heel of my hand into it, once, twice, then stop and just watch it sit there. My arms feel packed with wet sand. "Five more minutes," I mutter to the empty kitchen, though the card says ten of kneading. I sink onto the stool, the clock ticking too loudly, and breathe in the yeasty smell. Her handwriting loops across the page, patient. I lay my forehead on the cool table, and decide the bowl can have its towel now.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was standing in the cereal aisle, one hand on the cart, staring at a box I'd picked up a full minute ago. My feet felt poured full of wet sand. Someone said my name, twice, before it landed. Dana Whitfield, from tenth-grade chemistry, grinning under a bright orange scarf. "Oh," I said. "Hey." It came out flat and late, like a stone dropped down a well. She talked about her kids, her move to Portland, and I nodded a beat behind everything, my eyelids dragging down and hauling back up. I wanted to ask something clever. I managed, "Still doing the, uh, the..." and trailed off, forgetting what she did. She laughed kindly. I leaned my hip against the cart for support. When she hugged me goodbye, I held on a second too long, just because standing felt like work. Afterward I pushed the cart toward the register at the pace of a funeral, the cereal still in my hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy clock says 4:12, and it said 4:12 when I last looked, or maybe that was a different 4:12. I lean on the counter with my chin in my palm while the fluorescent hum fills my skull like wet cotton. A woman asks if her prescription is ready. I say, "Mm. Let me," and then stand there until she clears her throat. The bag is right in front of me. I read the name on it twice, three times, the letters sliding around. "Sorry," I tell her, slow, each word dragged up from somewhere deep. "Happy Thanksgiving." She laughs and says that's tomorrow. Of course it is. My feet feel poured full of sand, and the stockroom shelf I need to restock seems miles away, so I decide the boxes can wait. I refill my coffee, the third cup, and watch the steam instead of drinking it. Six more hours. I rest my forehead briefly against the cool glass of the display case, just to see how that feels.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board said Gate B47, and Marguerite read it twice before her feet agreed to go. Her rolling bag clattered behind her like it weighed as much as she did. A moving walkway slid past on her left, and she stepped onto it and simply stood there, letting it carry her while people hurried by in blurs of coats and elbows. "Sorry," she mumbled to a man she hadn't bumped, her voice scraping out low and thick. Her eyelids pressed down; she propped them open and stared at a coffee kiosk, calculating whether the line was worth it. Her legs felt filled with wet sand. Overhead, a speaker chimed final boarding for her flight, and she nodded at it slowly, as if it had asked her a polite question. At the gate, the agent was already pulling the door shut. Marguerite lifted one heavy hand, opened her mouth, and sighed instead of shouting. "Wait," she said, almost to herself, barely louder than the rolling suitcase settling beside her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller has been in my hand for ten minutes, and the wall has maybe a yard of new green on it. I stand there, dripping, watching a fly cross the ceiling like it has somewhere to be. "Okay," I say aloud, the word coming out thick and low. "Okay. Left side." I don't move. My arms feel packed with wet sand, and when I finally lift the roller, it rises a beat behind my intention. I stroke up, then stop to rest my forehead against the cool of the unpainted plaster. The coffee on the windowsill went cold hours ago; I remember pouring it. I should tape the trim. I should move the ladder. I sit down on the overturned bucket instead and stare at my sock, which has a green spot on it, and I think, I'll get to that too, in a minute, maybe after the next minute.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail, and Marguerite watched them without lifting her head from the back of the chair. Her tea had gone warm an hour ago; the glass sat sweating a ring into the armrest, and she kept meaning to move it. Thunder rolled across the field. She counted nothing. Her feet, bare and heavy, stayed where they were on the boards, even when the wind flung spray across her shins. "Should get the cushions," she said to the dog, her voice thick and low, trailing off before the sentence finished. The dog didn't stir either. She blinked, and the blink lasted a while. Lightning split the sky white, and her hand twitched on her knee, then settled. The cushions were twelve steps away. She studied the distance the way one studies a mountain, then let her eyelids sink again, listening to the gutters choke and gurgle, thinking maybe in a minute, maybe after the next one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Dario hung the wheel on the truing stand and flicked the rim, letting it spin without a wobble, then glanced toward the far bay where Marguerite was still wrestling her chain with a butter knife. He took his time wiping his hands on a clean rag, one finger at a time. "Funny thing, a cable cutter," he said, not quite to her, holding his own up to the fluorescent light so it caught. "Worth every penny. Some people just never learn." His shoulders had settled low and easy, chin tipped up a notch. He hummed while he threaded the new tube, the tune bright and unhurried, and when her knife clattered to the concrete he let a slow beat pass before asking, pleasantly, whether she'd like to borrow something. The tool wall behind him, every wrench outlined in marker on pegboard, gleamed. He leaned against his workbench, ankles crossed, and waited to be asked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as Marcus snapped his umbrella open, and he let the sound fill the silence a moment before glancing down the bench. Three strangers hunched under their jackets, one holding a newspaper over her hair. He rolled his shoulders, dry and warm inside the good wool coat, and tilted the umbrella a little so it covered nothing but himself. "Forecast said four o'clock," he said, pleasantly, to no one. "Never hurts to check." The wind picked up and the man beside him swore at his soaked sleeve. Marcus hummed, rocked on his heels, and examined his watch though he knew the time. Water streamed off the edge of the shelter in a bright curtain. He thought of the phone alerts he'd read that morning while they'd all been sleeping or scrolling. When the bus finally swung around the corner, he stepped forward first, chin lifted, and shook out his umbrella with a flourish over the puddle at their feet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marguerite lifted the shoebox lid with two fingers, as if it were beneath her, and settled into the good armchair with her chin tilted up. The first envelope bore her brother Desmond's cramped handwriting, and she snorted before she'd even unfolded it. "Oh, here we go," she said to the empty room. "'Next year I'll own the hardware store.'" She smoothed the page against her knee, savoring the creak of the paper, and let one corner of her mouth curl. Another letter, another prediction, another one she'd answered in her own neat script: told you so, in so many polite words. She fanned the stack like a winning hand. Out the window, his sagging rental sat across the street, its gutters drooping. She didn't look at it directly; she didn't need to. Humming, she slid his letters into the pile marked KEEP, then tapped the box twice, pleased, and reached for her tea.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Harold heard the knock and took his time, finishing the last bite of toast and dabbing each corner of his mouth before opening the door. Dennis stood on the porch, hands shoved in his pockets, glancing up at his own sagging gutters. "Wondering if I could borrow your ladder," he said. Harold leaned against the frame and let the silence stretch, rocking slightly on his heels. "Funny. I mentioned in April they'd clog," he said lightly. "Twenty-eight foot, fiberglass. Bought it that same week." He strolled to the garage, unhurried, and ran a palm down the rail the way one pats a good horse. Every tool hung on its labeled hook. "Careful with the left foot. It's calibrated." He hummed as he carried it out, chin lifted, and watched Dennis wobble down the driveway under the weight. Back inside, he rinsed his plate, rolled his shoulders back at the window, and glanced at his own gutters. Spotless, naturally.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marcus tilted the lid of the braise just enough to let the steam curl out, then closed his eyes and inhaled like a man receiving applause. Twenty minutes until the Hendersons arrived, and every burner hummed in order. He wiped his hands on the towel slung over his shoulder, a towel he had chosen because it looked casual. 'Oh, this? Just something I threw together,' he said to the empty kitchen, rehearsing, chin lifted, one eyebrow doing a little work. The saffron had cost forty dollars; he planned to mention it only if asked, and to be asked, he'd left the jar on the counter, label out. He rolled his shoulders back, strolled to the window, and checked the table again: cloth napkins, folded into swans. Last year Dave had brought store-bought rolls and apologized for them. Marcus smiled at his reflection, tasted the sauce, and did not even bother to adjust the salt. He knew it was perfect. He hummed, rocking on his heels, waiting for the doorbell.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the marble countertop, and Marguerite let it ring three full times before she reached for it, one finger sliding the screen. Unknown number. She leaned back against the stool, ankles crossed, and took a sip of coffee first. "Hello?" she said, drawing the word out like a ribbon. A man began to speak about her vehicle's extended warranty, and the corner of her mouth lifted. She'd been waiting weeks for one of them. "Oh, how fascinating. Do go on. Which vehicle, exactly?" She studied her nails while he fumbled. "Funny, because I sold that car in March. And your colleague Dennis called in April, and I told him the same thing." She could hear him breathing, scrambling. Her shoulders rolled back, easy and loose. "Take me off your list, sweetheart. Lovely." She set the phone face-up on the marble, picked up her cup, and hummed all the way to the window.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been gone four hundred and twelve days, and I carried it into the library like a trophy, held out in front of me with two fingers. I took the long way past the reference desk so people could see me. The librarian's eyebrows rose when she scanned the barcode, and I leaned an elbow on the counter, chin lifted, letting a slow breath out through my nose. "Oh, it's been a while? Hadn't noticed," I said, light, almost singing it. My mouth kept tugging up at one corner, and I let it. She typed. Frowned. Typed again. "Your fines were forgiven in the spring amnesty," she said. I'd read the flyer in March and timed this for exactly today. I tapped the cover twice, rolled my shoulders back, and strolled out whistling, my steps unhurried, my pockets full of the money I hadn't spent.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers needed four trips; I needed one. I carried my whole life up three flights in a single duffel and a lamp, and I didn't even breathe hard. Mara from 2B was wrestling a sofa through her doorway, and I paused on the landing, chin lifted, just long enough to let her see me glide past. 'Nice to be portable,' I said, pleasant as anything. Inside, the studio was eleven steps long. I counted them twice, slowly, like a man pacing a ballroom. I set the lamp on the sill, where it caught the one slice of afternoon sun, and I leaned against the wall with my arms crossed, rocking on my heels. My cousin had paid for storage units and two bigger leases, and he'd called me crazy. I let a small hum rise in my throat. The radiator clanked.
