The door chimed; a man in a puffy coat jingled his keys at her and said they were closing. "Then you'll want to be quick," she told him, and kept rotating the dates, oldest in front. Her feet throbbed inside her shoes, and her stomach grumbled about the lunch she'd skipped, but the bottom shelf was still crooked, and she wasn't leaving it crooked for the January crew to fix. The manager sighed and leaned on the freezer door. She pulled out a carton, squared it, and said, "Eight minutes. Go home if you want." He didn't. Neither did she, until the last label faced front.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The gate agent had already lifted the phone to close the door when Marguerite reached the desk, breath sawing in her chest, a stitch burning under her ribs. "Gate B44 is closed, ma'am," the woman said. Marguerite set her carry-on down and planted both palms on the counter. "I'll wait." "The jet bridge is retracted." "Then extend it." Her jaw ached from clenching. Behind her, a man sighed and shifted his weight; she didn't turn. Sweat cooled along her spine. The agent offered the morning flight, a voucher, a hotel, and Marguerite shook her head at each one, slowly, like someone refusing a second helping. She pulled out her boarding pass, smoothed its crease against the counter with her thumb, and slid it forward. "This says 6:10. It's 6:07. Check your clock again." The agent glanced at the screen, then at her, and Marguerite did not blink, did not step back, and did not pick up her bag.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The paint chip said Dusty Sage, but the wall said mustard, and I was not about to let a wall win. Dana leaned in the doorway holding her coffee and said a third coat was probably overkill. "Probably," I said, and dipped the roller again. My shoulder burned in a hot, thin line from neck to elbow, and a drip had crept down my wrist into my sleeve, but I kept rolling in the same overlapping W's my father taught me. She mentioned the hardware store had a primer on sale. I told her I'd already bought what I needed, which was true, and also not an answer. At midnight the yellow still ghosted through near the window, glowing under the lamp like a bruise. I pressed the lid back on with the heel of my hand, set the alarm for six, and left the brush soaking in the pail. Tomorrow, coat four.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the screen door, and I tightened my grip on the armrest of the wicker chair. Marcy leaned out from the kitchen. "Come inside, Dad. It's coming sideways now." I took a slow sip of my lukewarm coffee and said, "Been sitting here at four o'clock for thirty years." Rain slapped my left knee, then my sleeve, then my collar, cold as a coin down the spine. I shifted the chair an inch to the right, which helped nothing. My socks squelched. She held out a towel; I looked at the yard instead, where the maple thrashed and the garden hose snaked across the lawn like it was trying to escape too. "Dry as a bone," I told her, teeth clicking. Lightning cracked white across the street. I didn't flinch. I only counted, out loud, one-Mississippi, two, and stayed put.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The bottom bracket won't budge, and I've been leaning on the wrench long enough that my forearms hum. Across the garage, Dana's table saw whines, stops, whines again. I set the wrench down, pick it up, set it down. This bike has hung from the stand since August; a spider has built a small, confident town between the brake levers. "Almost there," I tell nobody, and my voice comes out flat as a dropped coin. I spray more penetrating oil, though the can is nearly empty and the threads have drunk their fill. Grease has dried into the creases of my knuckles. I check my phone, see nothing, check it again. Dana asks if I want coffee. "Maybe later," I say, the way I said it yesterday. I stare at the crank arm, then at the open door and the bright street beyond it, and realize I've been holding my breath. I put both hands on the wrench and pull again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the schedule behind the plexiglass, and I read it again anyway: 4:12, 4:40, 5:05. It's 5:31. I check my phone, which says what it said a minute ago, and put it back in my pocket, then take it out. The wind shoves a flattened cup down the gutter and I watch it travel the whole block. My sleeves are damp. My toes have gone numb inside shoes I've worn to this exact spot every weekday since March. A woman beside me sighs and walks off toward the train, her umbrella snapping open. I say, to nobody, "Sure. Fine," and my voice comes out thin and flat. I sit on the cold slatted bench, stand up, sit again. Rain runs off the roof's edge in a bright rope. I count the cars passing, none of them slowing. When my knee starts bouncing I press my palm on it until it quits, and I keep staring down the road, as if looking were a kind of progress.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox has been on my lap since the light through the blinds was orange; now it's gray and I haven't turned on the lamp. I read the same postmark again, Duluth, March 1998, then set it on the left pile, then move it to the right, then back. My tea has a skin on it. "Okay," I say to the empty room, in the voice I use on the dog. "Okay, this one's easy." It isn't. My thumb rubs the corner of the envelope until the paper softens and fuzzes. I tell myself I'll finish before dinner, then eat crackers over the box instead. There's a letter I've unfolded four times and never read past the first line. My knees ache from sitting this way, and I don't shift. The piles look exactly as they did an hour ago. I pick up the lid, hold it over the box, and put it down again beside me, like a promise I keep not signing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale stands on my porch with his hands in his jacket pockets, and I hold the door so the cold keeps leaking past my socks. "Just for the gutters," he says. "An hour, tops." The ladder is in the garage, behind the boxes I promised Meredith I'd haul to the dump in March. I say, "Sure, sure," and don't move. My thumb rubs the cold brass of the knob, back and forth. Last time he returned it with a bent rung and a smile. "It's, uh, kind of buried back there," I say, and he says, "I'll help dig," already stepping off the mat. I laugh, a short dry sound, and my jaw aches. Behind him the gutters sag, full of brown leaves, mine too. "Let me find my shoes," I say, though I'm wearing them. I stay exactly where I am, watching my breath fog between us, waiting for one of us to speak again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The risotto had been one ladle from done for twenty minutes, and Marisol kept stirring it anyway, the wooden spoon scraping the same slow circle. Her phone said 6:42. The doorbell would ring at seven. She lifted the lid on the roasting pan, looked at the pale, unbrowned chicken, and set the lid back down without touching anything. "Okay," she said to the empty kitchen, then again, quieter, "okay." Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears; she noticed and they stayed there. The salad greens sat wet in the colander, dripping onto a cutting board she had meant to use an hour ago. She wiped her hands on her apron, picked up the knife, put it down, and opened the oven door just to feel the heat on her face. Steam fogged the window over the sink. Somewhere below, a car door shut, and she stood very still with the spoon dripping, listening to whether it was them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the cereal box, a number I don't know, area code from the town I left six years ago. I watch it rattle toward the edge of the counter. Third ring. I wipe my palm on my sweatpants, then wipe it again. The bowl in front of me has gone to mush; I've been holding the same spoonful since the first buzz. Fifth ring. I picture the voice: the landlord, the hospital, the recruiter who never wrote back. Any of them would ask what I'm doing now, and I'd have the same answer as last spring. My thumb hovers. The kitchen clock ticks over to 2:47, same as when I sat down, or it feels that way. The screen goes dark. Voicemail pings. I don't listen. I set the spoon down, pick it up again, and say to the empty room, "Later," in a voice so flat it doesn't even sound like a lie. Then I stay in the chair.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Dana had been standing at the edge of the return desk for eleven minutes by the clock, her organic chemistry textbook pressed flat against her chest. Twice she had stepped toward the counter, and twice her sneakers had carried her back to the periodicals rack, where she pretended to read a spine she'd already read. Her thumb worried the corner of the cover, peeling the laminate. When the librarian finally glanced up, Dana's mouth opened and produced only, "Hi. Um. So." She laughed, too high, and set the book down, then picked it up again. "It's a little overdue. I counted once, but then I stopped counting." Her palms were damp, and the fluorescent hum seemed to fill her ears. She stared at the due-date stamp, March, faded purple, and whispered, "I can pay. Can I just, uh, hold it one more second?" Her fingers did not let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at noon, and by dusk Marit was still standing in the doorway with a lamp cord wrapped twice around her wrist. Boxes rose to her shoulders, their labels in her own handwriting: KITCHEN, KITCHEN MISC, MISC. She set the lamp on the floor, picked it up, set it on the radiator, then moved it back. "Okay," she said to the room, flat, the way you'd say it to a waiter. The single window looked onto a brick wall eight feet away, and the light in it never changed. Her phone buzzed; her sister asking how it was going. She typed "fine, unpacking," deleted it, typed it again. She sat on the mattress, still in its plastic, and it crackled under her. Her jaw ached from clenching. She counted the steps from the bed to the stove, three and a half, and then she counted them again, as if the number might come out different, her coat still buttoned to the throat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sits on the bench beside my thermos, brown leather, curled at the corners like it's been sat on for years. I pick it up, put it down, pick it up again. Same bench I've used every lunch since March, same pigeons working the same crumbs. Inside there's a license, forty dollars, a library card. I say, "Hello?" to nobody, too quietly even for the squirrel. My knee bounces. I read the address twice; it's eleven blocks away, a bus ride I know I could take, and I rehearse knocking, handing it over, saying something normal. Instead I check my phone, where the unsent email to my landlord, the unsent text to my sister, and the job posting I've reopened nine times all wait in a row. The thermos has gone cold. My coat zipper is halfway up, and I keep tugging it, up, down, up. Across the path a woman jogs past, and the wallet is still in my hand when the streetlights flicker on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Week nine, and my hand is still on the gutter. The instructor, a nineteen-year-old named Dani, says, "Just let go and kick," and I say, "Yes, in a second," for maybe the fifth time. Chlorine sits sharp in my nose. Kids in the next lane flip and glide like they were born wet. I lower my chin to the water, count to three, and lift it again. My knuckles have gone pale around the tile edge, and my thighs are tight enough to ache. Last week I made it to the lane rope. The week before, the same. I tell myself my legs just need warming up, so I stand in the shallow end and swing my arms in slow circles. Dani checks the clock on the wall. I check it too. The second hand ticks past the same spot it always does, and I'm still holding on, still telling her, "Okay, this time."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets have been lined up on the porch rail since March, and it's nearly June. This morning I carried the trowel out, knelt in the bed I built, and pressed it into the dirt exactly once. Then I sat back on my heels. My knees ached against the boards. The tomato packet says plant after last frost, a quarter inch deep, but how deep is a quarter inch, and does the thumb count? I read the back of it again, then the carrots, then the beans, as if they might disagree. A neighbor waved over the fence and called, "Looking good!" I laughed too loudly and said, "Just getting started," which is what I said last month. My palms were damp, the trowel slick. The soil sat there, dark and patient, one small dent in it. I picked up a pea seed, rolled it between my fingers, and put it back in the packet. Maybe tomorrow, after I check the forecast once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus kept his pen pressed to the same line in his notebook until the ink bled into a small blue island. Across the conference room, Dana clicked to her fourth slide, the dashboard he had sketched in March, now glossy, shipped, hers. The projector fan hummed. He nodded when heads turned, a beat late, and his neck felt like it had been bolted in place. 'Great,' he said when she finished, and the word came out thin and flat. Someone asked what he was working on these days. He opened his mouth, closed it, and looked at the laptop in front of him, where the same document had been open since Monday, cursor blinking after the same half sentence. 'Still shaping it,' he said. His knee bounced under the table. The air-conditioning ticked off, and in the new quiet he heard how long his breath had been held. He rearranged his water bottle, then rearranged it back, and kept his eyes on the clock's slow, unhelpful hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The exit for my street comes up green and reflective, and I drive past it. I don't decide to; my hands just stay at ten and two while the blinker I almost touched keeps its silence. Another mile, another. The radio is down to a murmur, some host selling mattresses, and I let him. My thumbs worry the stitching on the wheel until the leather feels hot. At the red light by the shuttered tire shop there's no one behind me or ahead, and I sit through the whole cycle, then the next one, watching the signal swap colors for nobody. My jaw aches. I realize I've been clenching it since the bridge. "Okay," I say out loud, flat, to the windshield. "Okay. Go home." The car doesn't move, or I don't. Somewhere a dog barks twice. My phone lights up on the passenger seat, her name, and I watch it glow until it dims, then ease off the brake and roll straight through the intersection, toward nothing in particular.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Daniel had read the same line on the whiteboard four times: Today's nurse is Priya. His father's eyes stayed on the muted television, where a woman pulled a cake from an oven. In the hall the vending machine hummed, and Daniel's hand was already in his coat pocket, thumbing the same two quarters. "They said maybe Thursday," he told the blanket, too brightly. "Or Friday. Depends on the numbers." He stood, sat, stood again, then turned the water cup on the tray until its handle faced the window. His shoes felt glued to the linoleum. When the monitor beeped he flinched, though it beeped every minute. He checked his phone: 2:14. He had checked it at 2:13. "I should go," he said, and pulled the chair closer to the bed instead, its legs squealing, and sat with his coat still on, the zipper cold against his chin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The engine's been off for twenty minutes, and I keep turning the key one click so the dash lights up, then off again. Through the windshield the same crossing guard waves the same orange flag at nobody. Another mom taps my window. "Big plans this weekend?" I laugh too fast and say, "Oh, you know, laundry," and she nods like that's an answer. My thumb finds the job-posting email on my phone, the one I opened Monday, and I scroll it up and down without reading a word. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the bell rehearsal started. The doors bang open. Kids spill out in bright jackets. I put both hands on the wheel at ten and two, though we aren't going anywhere yet, and I watch for Maya's red hat and think, tomorrow I'll answer it. I thought that yesterday, too. The heater ticks as it cools.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine o'clock Marguerite had already moved the oak dresser three times, first to the curb, then back to the driveway's shade, then a few inches left, as if the right angle might finally make someone want it. A man ran his thumb along the drawer and asked if she'd take twenty. "It was forty last Saturday," she said, "and the Saturday before." Her laugh came out thin. He shrugged and walked on. She sat down on the cedar chest she'd priced at sixty and felt the lid's cold edge through her jeans. The tags on everything were in her husband's old handwriting, because she'd reused his sticky labels instead of buying new ones. Across the street, a moving truck sat open, empty, its ramp down. She watched it for a long while, a coffee going cold between her palms, then stood up, checked the dresser's wobbly leg again, and slid a folded napkin beneath it, exactly where she'd put one yesterday.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Dana lay on the cabinet floor with her cheek against cold particleboard, a flashlight clamped in her teeth, and turned the wrench a quarter inch left, then a quarter inch right, then left again. The drip kept time anyway. Plink, on the tin pie plate. Her forearm trembled; the nut hadn't budged since noon. She pulled the wrench free and stared at the chewed brass corners. "Come on," she whispered, then louder, "Come on," and her voice cracked on the second one. She slid out, sat on the damp tiles, and opened the plumbing video on her phone for the fourth time, watching the same man's easy hands twist the same easy fitting. The pie plate was nearly full. She emptied it into the sink, set it back, and watched the first drop land. Her knees ached. Her fingers smelled of rust. After a minute she reached for the wrench again, though she already knew what the nut would do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope from the Department of Housing had been leaning against the sugar jar since Tuesday, and Marta had now wiped the counter around it three times. She slid her thumb under the flap, stopped, and set it down again. The refrigerator hummed; she counted its clicks. "Okay," she said to the empty kitchen, then, "Okay," quieter, as if the first one hadn't been convincing. She picked it up, put it in the drawer with the takeout menus, and shut it. Her pulse thudded in her ears. Thirty seconds later she opened the drawer, took it out, and held it up to the window, as though the light might read it for her. Her coffee had gone cold hours ago. She turned the envelope over, read the return address again, then the stamp, then the address again, her thumb still wedged beneath the flap, not pulling, not letting go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The ticket machine speaks to me in a language I can't parse, and I press the same green button a fourth time. Behind me the queue breathes, shifts, coughs. My suitcase handle is slick in my fist. I turn the paper map clockwise, then back, as if the streets might rearrange themselves out of pity. The hotel's name, which I practiced on the plane, comes out of my mouth wrong; the woman at the kiosk tilts her head, and I say it again, slower, louder, like volume is a bridge. Nothing. My shirt clings between my shoulder blades. I take out my phone: no signal, 3% battery. I laugh, a short dry sound, and nobody laughs with me. Outside, trams slide past in both directions, bells chiming, full of people who know where they're going. I sit down on my suitcase beside the pillar, unfold the map across my knees, and read the same unfamiliar street name until the letters stop looking like letters.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tears across the field after a crow, ears flipped inside out, and I stay on the same bench I've sat on every evening since March. My coffee went cold an hour ago. I keep turning the paper cup, a quarter turn, another quarter turn, watching the ring it leaves on the slat. The email is still open on my phone, the cursor blinking after 'Dear Ms. Alvarez,' and I haven't typed a word since Tuesday. My thighs ache from sitting but standing feels like a decision. 'Good girl,' I call, flat, not loud enough for her to hear. She doesn't turn. The sun slides down behind the water tower, same as yesterday, and my shadow stretches toward the gate without me. When Biscuit finally trots back, tongue lolling, she drops a stick at my shoe and waits. I look at it. 'Tomorrow,' I tell her, and pick up the cup instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marta played the same eight bars again, and again her fingers tripped on the fourth measure, right where the melody should have climbed. The church hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee. Folding chairs sat in crooked rows, waiting for Saturday. She lifted her hands from the keys, shook them out, and wiped her palms on her skirt. "Once more," she told the empty room, her voice flat and very quiet. She played it. The same stumble. Her jaw tightened, and a dull ache settled between her shoulder blades. The clock above the stage said 8:40; it had said 8:10 when she last looked, or so it felt. She pencilled a fresh fingering over three older ones until the paper went gray and shiny. Down the hall, the choir director's laughter drifted in, bright and easy. Marta closed the fallboard, opened it, and set her hands on the keys again. "Once more," she said, and began at bar one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The box says KEEP in Dale's block capitals, and I've been holding the same coffee can of mismatched screws for what the clock says is forty minutes. I tilt it. They rattle like small applause. Sawdust has settled in the creases of my knuckles, and my shoulders ache from standing exactly here. "Okay," I say to the lathe, then again, quieter, "okay." Nobody answers; the space heater ticks. I set the can on the DONATE pile, watch it for a second, and pick it back up. His pencil is still behind the vise, worn to a nub, tooth marks near the end. I roll it between my fingers. The trash bag by my boot is still empty, its mouth open. Outside, the light goes orange, then gray. I check my phone for the landlord's deadline, put it away unread, and start sweeping the same clean patch of floor again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal says results go up at noon, and it is 11:47 when I refresh the page for the ninth time. Same grey banner. Same little spinning wheel. I've reheated my coffee twice and still haven't drunk it; a skin has formed, and I stare at it as if it might change too. My left knee bounces under the desk until Mum, passing the doorway, says, "Tea, love?" and I say, "Maybe," which means no, and she knows, and leaves. I open my notes app, close it. Open the blinds, close them. My thumbnail is bitten down to pink, so I start on the next one. The clock turns 11:48, then, for what feels like an hour, doesn't turn again. I whisper, "Come on," to nobody, to the wheel. My chest is a fist around something small. I can't start the day, and I can't leave the chair. I press refresh again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marisol reached the same fork she had passed an hour ago, the one with the split cedar and the faded orange blaze, and she stopped with one boot lifted. She set it down. The light had gone the color of weak tea, and the ridge behind her was already a flat gray cutout. She turned the map over, then back, though she knew its lines by heart. "No," she said to the trees, flatly, and then, quieter, "No, no, no." Her thumb worried the strap of her pack until the skin burned. Left led down toward the lot, probably. Right led toward the creek she'd crossed twice. She took three steps left, stopped, took four steps right, stopped. Her breath came shallow, her calves trembling though she hadn't climbed in minutes. An owl started somewhere. She laughed once, a dry crack of sound, and sat down on the cold root of the cedar with her headlamp still zipped in her pocket, staring at both paths as the dark pooled between them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth now, Grandma Odile's slanted handwriting gone brown at the folds. "Flour, enough. Water, warm like a wrist." I read it aloud to the empty kitchen, the way I did an hour ago, and an hour before that. My hands hover over the bowl. Flour dusts my sleeves; the dough sits in a pale lump I've kneaded, rested, kneaded again, and it still looks nothing like hers. I check my phone. Nothing new. I wipe my palms on my jeans, pick up the card, put it down. The oven ticks as it cools from the preheat I started too early, twice. "Enough," I mutter. "Enough of what?" My shoulders ache from leaning on the counter. I press a thumb into the dough and watch the dent stay, neither springing back nor sinking. I leave it there. The window goes orange, then gray. I turn the oven on again, and stand there, listening to it hum.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana was comparing two identical cans of tomatoes when someone said her name, and the shelf suddenly seemed very interesting. Priya Raman, from tenth-grade chemistry, stood there in a camel coat, holding a basket with fresh herbs in it. "Oh my God, you look exactly the same," Priya said. Dana laughed a beat too late and tugged the sleeve of the grocery-store polo she'd forgotten to take off after her shift. "Still here. Same town, same apartment, basically." Her voice came out light, rehearsed. Priya talked about Lisbon, a promotion, a fiancé named Tomas. Dana nodded at each piece, her thumb worrying the label of the can until the paper curled. Her calves ached from standing in one spot. "That's great. Really great," she said, and checked her phone though nothing had buzzed. When Priya hugged her goodbye, Dana stayed in the aisle a long while, then put both cans in her basket, the same ones she bought every week.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:40 on Christmas Eve, Marisol wiped the same stretch of pharmacy counter for the third time, watching the rag drag a gray smear toward the register. The automatic doors sighed open for no one. Her coworkers had left at noon, waving candy canes, and the fluorescent hum had settled into her molars. She refilled the pen cup, then emptied it, then refilled it. When her phone buzzed with her sister's photo of a table already set, she turned it face down and pressed her palm flat on top. "Closing's at six," she told the empty aisle, too loudly. Her thumb found the clock on the monitor again: 4:43. She shifted her weight from one aching heel to the other, straightened a row of cough syrup that was already straight, and stood facing the dark parking lot, jaw tight, breathing in time with the slow blink of the OPEN sign.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The jet bridge hadn't moved in twenty minutes, and Marisol had checked her watch so many times the skin under the strap had gone damp. Gate B42 glowed on her phone, a whole terminal away, while she stood in the aisle with her bag clutched to her chest and her knees locked. "Excuse me," she said to the back of a man's head, then again, quieter, "excuse me." He didn't turn. Through the small oval window the baggage cart sat beside the wing, orange vests lounging around it. She rose onto her toes, sank back down, rose again. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She typed a message, deleted it, typed it again, and watched the single gray bar of signal flicker. "Ten minutes," she told the flight attendant, her voice thin and bright, "it boards in ten minutes." The woman nodded kindly and kept smiling at the door that stayed shut. Marisol counted the rivets along the overhead bin, then counted them again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The tape has been up for three weeks, blue edges curling off the baseboard like old skin. I stand with the roller dripping, a soft gray called Morning Fog, and I press it to the same square foot of wall I started on Sunday. The paint goes on, I step back, and I'm already rolling over it again. My shoulder aches; I notice it the way you notice a neighbor's noise. The radio murmurs a song I've heard four times today. "Almost there," I tell the empty room, and my voice comes out flat, like I'm reading it off a can. The old yellow shows through along the window, patient, and I don't touch it. I set the roller in the tray, wipe my hands on my jeans, and check my phone. Nothing. I pick the roller up again. The tray has skinned over. I stir it with a finger and stare at the ladder, which hasn't moved since Thursday.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while Dana was still holding the car keys. She had meant to leave an hour ago, bag packed by the door, but now she sat on the porch swing with her thumb worrying the key's jagged teeth. Rain hammered the tin roof. A gust flung cold spray across her shins, and she didn't pull her feet up. Her phone buzzed on the armrest: Mom, again. She turned it face-down. "Not yet," she told the yard, then laughed at herself, a short dry sound. The swing chain creaked, back, forth, back, going nowhere. Lightning lit the mailbox, the empty road, the maple her father had planted. She counted seconds to the thunder, got to four, and started over. Her coffee had gone cold and skinned over; she drank it anyway. When the rain thinned, she stood, walked to the steps, looked down at them a long moment, and sat back down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marlow wedged the wheel into the truing stand without looking up when the neighbor's radio started in on the other side of the garage. The spoke wrench slipped twice. He let it clatter on the concrete and left it there a moment before bending, slowly, to fetch it. "Fine," he said, when Dena asked if he needed the pump. He didn't turn around. Oil had worked into the creases of his knuckles, and the cold from the floor crept up through his sneakers, which he decided not to mind. Someone had moved his tools again; the hex keys sat in the wrong tray. He jammed them back with his jaw set, each one a small dull click. The tire lever bit his thumb. He swore under his breath, flat and quiet, and kept working with his shoulders hunched toward the wall, as though the bike were the only thing in the garage that owed him nothing and asked for less.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first drops hit the shelter roof like thrown gravel, and I didn't look up. My hood stayed down. Somebody's cheerful laugh drifted from the bench beside me, and I shifted my shoulder toward the plexiglass wall until it was only a gray smear of street. Wind pushed a chip bag across the curb. I watched it go. My jaw was clamped so hard my teeth ached, and I hadn't noticed until the cold crept into my ears. The woman next to me offered half her umbrella. "I'm fine," I said, flat, to the pavement. She shrugged and turned away, and I was glad, then not glad, then annoyed at both. Water soaked through the left sneaker. I let it. The 42 was late again, of course it was, and I kicked the pole once, not hard, just enough to feel it in my toes. Then I shoved my fists deeper into my pockets and stared at nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box had sat under the stairs for eleven years, and Marguerite dragged it out by one flap, letting it scrape the hallway floorboards louder than she needed to. She sat with her back against the radiator, which had gone cold, and didn't bother to turn on the lamp. The first envelope she slit with her thumbnail, glanced at two lines, and dropped onto the pile at her left knee. Then another. Then another. 'Weather, weather, hope you're well,' she muttered, flat as a dial tone. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it and didn't unclench it. A photograph slid out and landed face-up, her brother squinting in some long-ago sun. She turned it over with one finger. Outside, someone laughed on the pavement, and she pulled the box lid across her lap like a tray, shoulders hunched, and kept going, not reading, just sorting, the pile at her knee growing taller than the one on her right.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while rain was still dripping off the eaves, and I let it go twice before opening the door. Dale stood there in his clean windbreaker, smiling like the weather was a joke we shared. "Got a ladder I could borrow? Just an hour." I looked past him at his own garage, the one with the three-car door. My jaw felt packed with gravel. "Garage," I said. "Left wall." He waited for more. I gave him a shrug, one shoulder, and studied the doormat. He thanked me twice. I didn't walk him over. I stood at the window with my arms crossed and watched him wrestle it off the hooks, knocking the rake down, and I didn't go out. My coffee had gone cold an hour ago. I drank it anyway, and when his truck door slammed, I pulled the curtain shut and sat in the dim front room with my boots still on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta chopped the onions without looking up, the knife thudding against the board in a flat rhythm. The kitchen clock said six-ten; the doorbell would ring at seven. She had set out only the pot of water and left the good plates in the cabinet, their stack untouched. When Dev poked his head in and asked if she needed help, she said, "No," and then, after a pause, "Fine, do the bread," handing him the loaf without turning. Her jaw ached from clenching. The window over the sink was fogged, and she didn't wipe it. She tasted the sauce, grimaced, and added salt she didn't measure. "They'll eat it," she muttered to the pan. Down the hall a laugh track spilled from the television, and she turned the burner higher than it needed to be, watching the oil shimmer, her shoulders hunched around her ears like a coat she couldn't take off.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cereal bowl I'd left on the couch arm, and I let it go four rings before turning my head. Unknown number, a 702 something. I kept my chin on my knees. The cereal had gone to paste an hour ago, and the TV was still playing an episode I hadn't watched. On the sixth ring I picked up, mostly to make it stop. "Yeah." My voice came out flat and scratchy, like I hadn't used it since morning. The woman started in about my car's extended warranty, bright and quick. "Mm," I said. She asked if I was the owner of a 2014 Civic. "Guess so." My shoulders felt heavy, like wet coats. She paused, maybe waiting for me to hang up on her, to do something. I picked at a thread on the blanket. "Sorry," I said, not meaning it, "I'm not really up for this." I pressed the red circle, dropped the phone face down on the cushion, and stared at the wall until the screen went dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been under my bed since March, and now it was November, and the spine had gone soft with dust. I dragged my feet through the glass doors, hood up, hands jammed in my pockets until I had to pull one out to set the thing on the counter. The librarian's lamp hummed. Somewhere behind me a cart squeaked, and I didn't turn. 'Two hundred and forty days,' she said, tapping her screen. I shrugged. My jaw felt heavy, like I'd been chewing on something for hours. 'Fine,' I said, to the carpet. 'Whatever it is.' She asked if I wanted a receipt. I said no, then took it anyway, crumpled it, and shoved it deep in my sleeve. Outside, the rain was doing its usual nothing. I kicked a wet leaf off the step, watched it stick to my shoe, and didn't bother shaking it off all the way home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The elevator was broken, so Marcus hauled the last box up four flights and kicked the door shut behind him without looking at the landlord's welcome note taped to it. The studio smelled of paint and old radiator. He dropped the box where he stood. "Great," he said to no one, flat, and the word fell dead against the bare walls. His mother had texted twice; he turned the phone face down on the windowsill. The window looked onto a brick wall, close enough to touch if he leaned out, and he didn't. He sat on the floor with his back against the mattress still wrapped in plastic, jaw tight, picking at the tape on a box labeled KITCHEN in his own handwriting. A neighbor's television murmured through the wall. He didn't unpack the lamp. When the light faded, he stayed in the gray, shoulders hunched, eating crackers from the sleeve and staring at the doorknob as if it owed him something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Dana dropped onto the bench without looking and felt something hard under her thigh. A brown leather wallet. She held it between two fingers, as if it might be wet, and let her shoulders stay hunched against the drizzle. "Great," she muttered, flat, to nobody. The driver's license showed a grinning man with a gap in his teeth. She flipped it face down. Across the path a toddler shrieked at pigeons, and she turned her jaw away from the sound, chin sunk into her scarf. Forty dollars, a library card, a photo of a dog. She counted the bills twice, slowly, then shoved everything back in. Her phone buzzed in her pocket; she didn't pull it out. She sat there another ten minutes, heels scraping gravel, staring at the dead fountain. Finally she stood, stuffed the wallet in her coat, and walked toward the police station the long way, kicking every wet leaf that lay in her path, not once looking up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marcus stood in the shallow end with his arms crossed over his chest, water lapping at his ribs, while the kids in the next lane splashed past him like it was nothing. The instructor, a bright-voiced woman half his age, held out a kickboard. He took it without looking at her. "Fine," he said, flat, and pushed off. His legs sank almost at once, and chlorine stung the back of his throat. Twice he stopped and stood, hair dripping into his eyes, jaw set tight. "I said I'm fine," he muttered when she called encouragement. The fluorescent lights hummed overhead. Somewhere a whistle blew. He stared at the black line on the pool floor, thinking of his brother's pool party thirty years ago, the laughter from the deck. He dragged the board back to the wall, shoulders hunched, and did not say goodbye when the lesson ended, only wrapped the thin towel around himself and walked, shivering, toward the locker room without a glance behind him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets sat in a row on the porch rail, tomatoes, beans, something called chard, their cheerful photos faded by the weather. Mom's idea, not mine. I dragged the shovel across the yard without lifting it and let it clang against the fence. The dirt was harder than the internet said. I jammed the blade in, stepped on it, and my jaw ached from how tight I was clenching it. "Fine," I said to nobody, "rows." Gray clouds sagged over the neighbor's roof. I scratched out a trench, dropped bean seeds in without counting, and kicked soil over them with my boot. When Mom called from the window, asking if I wanted lemonade, I kept my back to her and shrugged, my shoulders heavy as wet sacks. "Not thirsty." Mud caked under my nails. I stabbed a plastic label into the ground, scrawled BEANS, and stared at the flat brown nothing. Nothing would come up. Probably. I left the shovel lying in the dirt and went inside without washing my hands.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus slid into the chair nearest the door and let his laptop stay closed. On the wall screen, Dana's slides glowed blue, the same dashboard layout he'd sketched in March on a napkin and then in a doc nobody opened. Someone laughed at her joke. He pressed his thumbnail into the seam of the table until it ached. "Great," he said when she paused for questions, flat, eyes on the cold coffee ring by his elbow. Dana beamed anyway and clicked ahead. His jaw felt heavy, his arms crossed so tight his ribs registered every breath. The air conditioner droned. When Priya asked who'd handled the data pipeline, he studied the carpet, counted its gray squares, and said, "Ask Dana," then pushed his chair back an inch from the group, and stayed there until the meeting ended, the last one out, leaving his cup behind.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The radio coughed out some cheerful song and I stabbed it off with my thumb. Quiet again, just the tires hissing on wet asphalt. My phone buzzed in the cup holder, Dana's name lighting the dashboard, and I let it buzz until it stopped. The streetlights slid over the hood one at a time, orange, orange, orange. I slouched lower, chin nearly on my collar, one wrist draped over the wheel like it weighed too much to lift. At the red light on Fourth I didn't bother checking for traffic; nobody was there, and I sat through the whole cycle anyway, jaw tight, staring at nothing. "Fine," I muttered to the windshield. "Great. Wonderful night." My shoulders ached from holding themselves up all day. The drive-thru sign glowed, and I passed it, though my stomach was hollow. Why bother. At home the porch light was off, and I sat in the driveway with the engine ticking, not moving, not wanting anyone to ask me anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dario dragged the vinyl chair six inches from his grandfather's bed, no closer, and sat with his jacket still zipped to the chin. The monitor beeped its patient little beep. His mother had said to be nice, so when the old man asked how school was, he said, "Fine," and studied the water stain on the ceiling tile shaped like Ohio. A nurse came in, smiled, checked a line. He nodded at the floor. His jaw ached from being held shut. The tray beside the bed held a cup of orange gelatin trembling whenever someone walked past, and he watched it instead of the face on the pillow. "You could take your coat off," his grandfather said. "I'm cold," Dario said, though the room was stuffy, and sweat gathered at his collar. He pulled out his phone, thumbed it dark, then lit it again. Twenty minutes, he told himself. Maybe thirty. He crossed his arms tighter and kept his eyes on Ohio.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I parked behind the maple, the one spot where nobody would lean into my window to chat, and kept the engine running for the heat. Through the windshield the other parents clustered by the gate, laughing about some bake sale. A woman waved. I lifted two fingers off the wheel and looked at my phone, which showed nothing new. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the Henderson call this morning. When the bell rang I stayed put, letting the kids pour out, hoods up, backpacks bouncing. Ruby came last, dragging her bag by one strap. She climbed in and said, "Hi." I said, "Seat belt." She asked what was for dinner. "Whatever's in the fridge," I muttered, and pulled out without checking whether the woman by the gate was still waving. The wipers squeaked across a windshield that wasn't even wet, and I let them go on squeaking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marlene dragged the oak dresser to the curb herself, refusing her nephew's offer of help with a shake of her head, and propped a cardboard sign against it: $40. She sat in the lawn chair with her arms crossed and her jaw set, a cold coffee going skin-thick on her knee. A woman ran a finger along the drawer edge and asked if the price was firm. "It's forty," Marlene said, eyes on the street. "That's what the sign says." The woman waited, then drifted off toward the lamps. Marlene's shoulders had crept up near her ears, and she let them stay there. Thirty-one years that dresser had stood beside the bed, and now it sat in the glare with a scuffed corner anyone could see. When a boy pulled out a drawer and slammed it back, she flinched, muttered, "Careful," and said nothing more for an hour. The sun climbed. She didn't move the chair into the shade.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slipped again and I let it clang against the cabinet floor without picking it up. Water kept beading at the joint, one fat drop, then another, tapping the saucepan I'd wedged underneath. Mara called from the living room, asking if I wanted help, and I said, "No," flat, not turning my head. My jaw ached from clenching it. I lay curled on the damp particleboard, knees pressed into the U-bend, a cold trickle running down my wrist into my sleeve, and I didn't bother wiping it. Wrapped the tape twice, glared at it, wrapped it twice more. The hardware store guy had said it was easy. Fine. Everyone's always saying that. I tightened the fitting until my knuckles went white, then sat there in the dark under the sink, listening to the drip find its rhythm again, and just stared at the pan filling up, not moving, not even bothering to swear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had sat on the radiator shelf for three days, wedged between a pizza flyer and a dead houseplant, and Marcus only picked it up now because the shelf was where he needed to put his keys. He dropped into the kitchen chair without taking off his coat. The return address said Department of Revenue, in that blocky font that always looked like it was shouting. He slid a thumb under the flap and tore it badly, jagged, not caring. His jaw was tight; the radio on the counter muttered about weather and he reached over and snapped it off. He read the first line, then skimmed the rest, lips pressed flat. "Great," he said, to no one, barely moving his mouth. "Wonderful." He folded the page along its old creases, slowly, then dropped it on the table and pushed it away with one finger. He stared at the window, where rain slid down the glass, and didn't get up to make the tea he'd been promising himself since noon.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The bus hissed and dumped me at a curb in the rain, and I stood there with my suitcase handle cutting into my palm. A man held a paper sign toward me, said something bright and rapid, and I shook my head without lifting my eyes. "No," I said. "No, thanks." He said it again, slower, as if slowness were the problem. I walked past him. The station's signs were all curling script and I didn't try to read one; I just followed the loudest crowd until it spat me onto a street of wet neon. My jacket had soaked through at the shoulders. At the hotel desk the clerk asked me something, and I slid my passport across and said nothing, jaw tight, staring at the brass bell between us. When she smiled and pointed up the stairs, I grunted, hauled the bag after me, and let each step bang loud behind me. In the room I kicked off my shoes and didn't turn on the light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the field in wide, stupid circles, and I stayed on the bench with my hands jammed in my jacket pockets. The wind kept pushing my hood off, and I kept yanking it back down. "Yeah, great," I muttered when he dropped the stick at my feet, then nudged it away with my shoe. He looked at me, head tilted, tail sweeping the grass. I looked at the gray sky instead. My jaw ached from being clenched, and I realized I'd been staring at the same fence post for ten minutes. Somebody's kid laughed near the gate, and I turned my shoulder toward the trees. My phone buzzed against my thigh. I didn't take it out. Biscuit barked once, sharp and hopeful, and I sighed through my nose, long and flat. "Five more minutes," I told him, though we both knew I'd say it again in five. The bench was cold through my jeans. I let it be cold.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I stood by the upright piano with my arms crossed over the sheet music like it might escape. "From the top?" Mrs. Alvarez asked. I shrugged and let my shoulder do the answering. The first notes came out flat, and I didn't bother fixing them. My jaw felt heavy, my eyes fixed on a water stain shaped like Ohio on the ceiling tile. When the flutist giggled at some joke, I turned a page harder than I needed to. "Louder," Mrs. Alvarez said. "I'm singing," I said, to the floor. Folding chairs scraped. Someone offered me a cookie and I said no thanks, though my stomach had been grumbling since noon. I counted the rests like debts. Forty people would come Saturday, maybe fewer. Fine. They could have what I had. At the break I sat in the stairwell with my coat zipped to my chin, listening to them laugh through the door, and I didn't go back in until the piano started without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus's sister had left three cardboard boxes by the door and a roll of tape, and I'd used none of it. I stood among the vises and the coffee cans of mismatched screws, jaw tight, one shoulder against the doorframe. "Just junk," I told the empty room, flat, and picked up a chisel only to set it back exactly where it had been. Sawdust still lay in the grooves of the bench, and I dragged my sleeve across it, then regretted that and stared at the smear. The radio on the shelf was tuned to his station. I didn't turn it on. I didn't turn on the lights either, just let the gray from the window do what it wanted. When his sister called down the stairs asking how it was going, I said, "Fine," and kept my back to her. My hands hung heavy. I folded one box, then sat on it instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 114 smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Dara had claimed the bench farthest from the notice board. Her hood was up. Around her, classmates crowded and chattered, and every burst of laughter made her tug the drawstrings tighter. When Marcus waved her over, she lifted two fingers off her knee and let them drop. "I'll look when it's up," she said, flat, eyes on her shoelace. "Not before." He shrugged and left. She picked at a strip of peeling vinyl on the bench until a pale curl came away, then pressed it back down with her thumb, again and again. Her jaw ached from clenching. The clock above the door ticked past three, and a secretary came out with a stapled sheet and a roll of tape. Dara watched the crowd surge, did not stand, and slid her earbuds in without playing anything. Her breath fogged the window beside her, and she wiped it away with her sleeve.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta kept her eyes on her boots and let the others' voices drift further up the switchbacks until they thinned to nothing. When Dev called down to ask if she wanted to stop for water, she raised one hand without looking up and kept walking. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the last marker. The light had gone orange, then the color of weak tea, and the pines stood around her like people who'd stopped talking when she came near. She kicked a pinecone off the trail and watched it vanish into the ferns. 'Fine,' she muttered, to no one, to the cold creeping up her sleeves. 'Great view.' She didn't take out her phone. She didn't take out her headlamp either, though her toes kept catching on roots, and each stumble she met with a hard exhale through her nose, shoulders hunched up around her ears, as if the dark were something she could simply outlast by refusing it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, Grandma's slanted handwriting gone brown at the creases. "Flour, enough." Enough. I drop the cup into the bag harder than I mean to, and a white puff settles on my sleeve. Mom hovers in the doorway. "Want help?" "No." I don't turn around. The yeast foams the way the card says it will, and that annoys me for some reason. I knead with my jaw clamped, shoulders up around my ears, pushing the dough flat like it owes me something. "Warm place," the card says. I shove the bowl on top of the fridge and drape the towel over it without smoothing the corners. Rain ticks on the window. The kitchen smells like her house. I wipe my palms on my jeans, sit on the floor with my back against the cabinet, and stare at the oven light until it's time to check, which I tell nobody I'm doing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dara stood in the cereal aisle with a basket that held only a box of crackers and a can of soup, her hood still up though the store was warm. Fluorescent light hummed overhead. She heard her name and didn't turn right away. "Dara? Dara Okafor? It's Missy, from Mr. Lund's chemistry!" The woman was bright, glossy, pushing a cart full of fruit and a toddler's sippy cup. Dara's shoulders sank an inch. She gave a half-nod. "Oh. Hey." Missy talked about a job in Denver, a wedding, a house. Dara studied the shelf label, picking at the plastic handle of her basket until it left a red line across her thumb. "Cool," she said. "Good for you." Her voice came out flat and low, dragged across the floor. "And you?" Missy asked. Dara shrugged and looked at the soup. "Same town," she said. "Same everything." She muttered that she had to go, then walked to the farthest register, though the nearest one was open.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Dana wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time, the rag dragging a gray smear through the sugar crystals. Outside the fogged window, the strip mall lot emptied car by car, taillights swinging toward somebody's dinner table. 'Hi,' she said to the man at the register, not looking up, and slid his change across without a word about the pie special taped to the glass. Her jaw ached from holding it shut. When Marcus called from the back to ask if she wanted to split the leftover rolls, she said, 'Whatever,' and kept her eyes on the clock, its second hand stuttering like it was doing her a favor. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears hours ago. She flipped the sign to CLOSED at five minutes early, then stood with her forehead nearly touching the cold glass, listening to the fryer tick as it cooled, and did not turn around when the radio started playing carols.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate C41 was a twenty-minute walk from where Marcus had landed, and he took it at the pace of someone being marched. His carry-on wheels clacked over the tile seams, each one a small insult. A woman in a cart beeped behind him; he didn't turn, just drifted half a foot left and let her pass. The moving walkway was out of order, a yellow cone slumped at its mouth. "Of course," he muttered to no one, flat, barely moving his lips. His jaw ached from being clenched since Denver. At the gate, the agent glanced up and said, "You just made it!" He held out his phone without a word, eyes fixed somewhere past her shoulder, and when she wished him a good flight he gave one short nod. Seat 34E. He wedged his bag under his knees, pulled his hood up, and watched the jet bridge door seal shut, thinking the trip had not been worth the going, and wouldn't be worth the arriving either.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The tape came off the baseboard in one long, crooked strip, and Dana balled it up and flung it at the bucket without watching whether it landed. It didn't. She left it there. "Fine," she said, when her sister called up the stairs to ask if she wanted music, and the word came out flat as a dropped board. The roller dragged across the wall in heavy, grudging stripes, Soft Linen over the yellow she'd chosen with Mark six years ago. Her shoulder ached. She didn't stop to roll it out. A drip crawled down toward the outlet cover and she watched it go, jaw tight, thinking that someone could wipe it if they cared. The window stayed shut though the fumes were making her head thrum. When the phone buzzed on the stepladder, she turned it face down with one paint-speckled finger and went back to the wall, pressing harder than she needed to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Dana dragged the wicker chair to the far end of the porch, where the roof gave out and rain spat onto her shins. She left it there. Thunder rolled over the soybean field, and her mother's voice came through the screen door, asking if she wanted lemonade, if she wanted anything. "No," Dana said, to the yard, not turning. She picked at a flake of blue paint on the armrest until a strip peeled away, then flicked it into the dark. Her jaw ached from being held shut. The dog nosed her hand, and she let the hand hang there, unmoving, until he gave up and flopped by the steps. Lightning lit the mailbox, still empty, still leaning. "Figures," she muttered. She pulled her damp sleeves down over her knuckles, slouched until her chin met her collarbone, and stared at the water pooling in the ruts of the driveway as if it owed her something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marta had her wrist deep in the rear derailleur, a wrench clamped in her teeth, when the cassette lockring gave way with no resistance at all. She froze. The wrench slid from her mouth and clanged on the concrete, and the echo bounced around the shared garage until old Mr. Okafor looked up from his workbench across the aisle. "Did you loosen this?" she asked, too loudly, holding the wheel out in front of her like it might bite. Her pulse thumped in her ears. Yesterday that lockring had been rusted solid; she'd bent a cheater bar on it. Now it spun under her thumb, clean, oiled, smelling faintly of citrus degreaser. She blinked at her tools, lined up by size, which she had certainly left in a heap. "Huh," she said, and then again, quieter, "Huh." Mr. Okafor only hummed and kept filing, the corner of his mouth twitching. Marta sat down slowly on an overturned bucket, wheel still in her lap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marguerite had checked the sky twice before leaving the flat, and both times it had been the flat blue of a plate. Now, at the bus stop with her tote bag on her shoulder, something small and cold tapped the back of her hand. She looked down. Another landed on her sleeve, white and whole, a crystal she could have counted the points of. "No," she said aloud, to nobody, a half-laugh catching in her throat. Her mouth stayed open. The gutter across the road had gone pale, and the streetlight buzzed against a sky that had thickened in what felt like seconds. She turned in a slow circle, bag slipping down her arm, forgetting to push it back up. The man on the bench lifted his hood without comment. Marguerite just stood there, palm outstretched, heart knocking, watching flakes melt into her skin in October, while the bus she was waiting for rounded the corner unnoticed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and dust, and I was halfway through a stack of Dad's water bills when my thumb snagged on an envelope addressed in my own handwriting. I turned it over. The stamp was crooked, the way I always licked them. My hand stopped moving. "No," I said aloud to the empty attic, then laughed once, a short cracked sound. I'd written this at nineteen, and the seal was still unbroken, which meant he'd never read it, which meant he had kept it anyway, twenty-six years, under receipts. My knees found the floorboards without my deciding. The back of my neck prickled. I pressed the envelope flat against my chest, felt my heartbeat knocking through the paper, then held it out at arm's length as if it might rearrange itself. "Dad," I whispered, "what on earth?" The dust motes kept drifting through the window light, perfectly calm, and I just sat there, mouth open, unable to slide my finger under the flap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The doorbell rang while I was rinsing a mug, and I opened the door with my hands still dripping. Mr. Halloran stood on my mat, the same man who hadn't spoken to me since I'd trimmed the hedge two inches too far in 2019. He held his cap against his chest. "Your ladder," he said. "The tall one. Could I borrow it?" Water ran down my wrist and into my sleeve. My mouth opened, and for a second nothing came out but a small, stupid "Oh." I glanced past him at his gutters, then back at his face, searching it for the catch. "The ladder," I repeated. "Yes. I mean, sure. It's in the garage." I wiped my hand on my jeans, missed the pocket, and nearly shut the door on my own foot as I stepped out. Behind me the faucet kept running, and I didn't go back to turn it off.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta had her wooden spoon halfway to the pot when the oven door, which she had only just shut, swung open on its own and the lid of the casserole dish slid sideways. She stood there, spoon dripping onto her sock. "Wait," she said, too softly for anyone but the cat. "That's... no." Her eyes went to the timer, still reading forty minutes, then back to the dish, where the lasagna had already bubbled gold at its edges, hours ahead of any sense. Her heart knocked against her ribs. She set the spoon down on the counter, missed the saucer, and didn't notice. Out the window, headlights swept the driveway; she laughed once, a short, cracked sound, and pressed a palm flat to her chest. "They're early," she told the cat, then, louder, to the empty kitchen, "Or I'm very, very late." She grabbed the oven mitts, fumbling the left one on backward, and stared at the clock again as if it might blink first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The dish towel slid off my shoulder and landed in the sink water while my phone buzzed against the counter, a string of digits I didn't know. I almost let it ring out. Instead I wiped my hand on my jeans and answered, and a voice said my name, my childhood nickname, the one nobody had used in twenty years. My mouth opened. Nothing came out for a second, and the faucet kept dripping into the silence. "Wait," I finally said, too loud, then lower, "Wait, Danny? Is this Danny?" My knees found the edge of a kitchen chair before I knew I was sitting. The pot on the stove started to boil over, hissing, and I just stared at it, phone pressed so hard to my ear it hurt. "Where are you calling from?" I asked. My voice cracked halfway through. I laughed, short and breathless, and realized I'd been gripping the table with my free hand the entire time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: I slid the battered copy of Middlemarch onto the desk and braced for the lecture, rehearsing my apology about the three years it had spent wedged behind my dresser. The librarian, a woman with silver reading glasses on a beaded chain, typed something, squinted, and typed again. My mouth stayed half open around the sentence I'd prepared. "Sorry, say that once more?" I asked, and my voice came out higher than I meant. She turned the monitor toward me. Zero. Not a cent owed. 'Fines were abolished two years ago,' she said, stamping the card as if nothing were unusual. I gripped the edge of the counter and realized I'd been holding my wallet out the whole time, a crumpled twenty pinched between two fingers, like an offering nobody wanted. I laughed once, too loudly, and the sound bounced off the high ceiling. A boy at the next table looked up. I put the money away, slowly, and stood there blinking at the little green receipt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol shouldered the door open with a box of mugs on her hip, and the box slid a few inches before she caught it against the frame. The room was supposed to be bare. Instead, a yellow armchair sat beneath the window, and on its arm lay a folded note and a single key. She set the box down without looking at it, and a mug clinked against another. Her mouth stayed open a moment before she managed, "Hello?" to the empty room, her voice higher than she'd meant. The hairs on her forearms lifted. She crossed the floorboards in three steps, the whole apartment reachable in a glance, and picked up the note with fingers that weren't quite steady. Her landlord's slanted handwriting: *Left by the last tenant. She said it likes afternoon light.* Marisol read it twice, then a third time, and laughed once, short and breathless. She pressed a palm to her chest, felt her heartbeat thudding there, and slowly lowered herself into the chair.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marguerite had only meant to sit for a minute, to ease her knees and finish the last of her coffee, but her hand landed on something soft and leathery beside her and she yanked it back as if the slats were hot. She looked down. A brown wallet, fat at the seams, lay half-hidden under a drift of maple leaves. "Well, I'll be," she said aloud, to no one, her voice coming out higher than she intended. The paper cup tipped in her other hand and coffee splashed her shoe; she didn't notice. Her heart knocked hard against her ribs. She glanced left toward the empty path, then right toward the pond, where a jogger was shrinking into the distance. Slowly she lifted the wallet, turning it over twice, mouth slightly open. A driver's license stared up at her, and the face on it was her own neighbor's. "Walter?" she whispered, and laughed once, breathless, shaking her head.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marisol, the instructor, had said to let go of the wall on three, and I did it mostly to make her stop counting. I kicked once, twice, and then realized the tiled edge was behind me, a whole body length behind me, and my hands were still moving. "Wait," I said, too high, too fast. "Wait, wait." Water slid along my ribs, cool and steady, holding me up like a hand I couldn't see. My chin dipped and I swallowed chlorine and coughed, but my legs kept going. The lane rope bobbed beside my shoulder. I looked down through my goggles at the black line on the pool floor, sliding past, and my heart knocked hard against my sternum. "Am I—is that me?" My voice echoed off the high ceiling. At forty-three, with my knees and my stubborn fear, I had expected to sink like a dropped wrench. Instead I was drifting toward the far wall, laughing into the water, a ridiculous stream of bubbles rising from my mouth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol knelt at the edge of the raised bed, trowel in one hand, a packet of radish seeds in the other, and pressed her thumb into the dirt the way the label said. She had planted them only five days ago. Now, where there had been nothing but brown crumbs, a row of tiny green loops stood up, each one wearing a seed husk like a hat. The trowel slipped from her fingers and thudded against the wooden frame. "No," she said, then laughed, too loudly for the quiet yard. "No way." She leaned so close her nose nearly touched the soil, and her breath stirred the leaves. Her heart was knocking against her ribs. She checked the packet, checked the row, checked the packet again. Then she sat back on her heels, wiped muddy palms on her jeans, and called over the fence, voice cracking, "Mr. Alvarez? Come look. They actually did something!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide, and my coffee stopped halfway to my mouth. There was my spreadsheet. Not something like it, mine, down to the clumsy color-coding I'd made at midnight and never shown anyone. I set the cup down too hard, and a little brown tide slid over the rim onto my notes. Nobody looked. I stared at the projector's glow, then at Dana's easy smile, then back at the screen, where my name sat in the footer in tiny gray letters. 'That's,' I started, and my voice cracked on it, so I coughed and tried again. 'Sorry. Is that the Q3 file?' Dana nodded, still cheerful. 'You left it in the shared folder, remember?' I didn't. My ears were hot, my pulse loud against the conference room's hum. I pulled a napkin across the spill, blinked, and heard myself say, much too brightly, 'Huh. Okay. Keep going.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta had driven the county road so many nights that her hands knew every curve without her, and she was halfway through humming along to the radio when the porch light of her own house came into view, blazing, with every window behind it lit gold. Her foot came off the gas. The car rolled to a crawl, gravel popping under the tires. She had left that house dark at six this morning; she was sure of it, she'd checked the stove twice. The humming had stopped mid-note. "No," she said aloud, then, quieter, "What?" Her fingers tightened on the wheel until the knuckles went pale, and her pulse thudded in her ears, loud over the muffled song. A shape moved behind the kitchen curtain. Marta leaned forward until her forehead nearly touched the windshield, mouth slightly open, and realized she'd forgotten to blink. Then the front door swung wide, and her sister stood there waving both arms, a cake in one hand, a year early for nothing she could name.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol pushed open the door to room 412 with a paper cup of lukewarm coffee in one hand and a rehearsed speech about rest and patience on her tongue. The bed was empty. The sheets were folded tight, the monitor dark. Her grandfather's chair sat by the window, and he was in it, fully dressed in his checkered shirt, lacing his shoes. The coffee tilted, and a hot drop landed on her wrist. She didn't flinch. "Abuelo?" Her voice came out thin, a half-step too high. She looked at the hallway, then the bed, then him again, as if one of them might correct itself. "Yesterday you couldn't lift a spoon." He grinned and tapped the bag by his foot. Her mouth stayed open a second longer than she meant it to. Slowly she set the cup on the tray, missed the edge, and caught it just in time, her heart knocking against her ribs like someone at a door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus leaned against the chain-link fence with his thermos, scrolling past the same three emails, when the side doors banged open and Dani walked out holding hands with a tall girl in a purple coat. His thumb stopped mid-swipe. The thermos tilted, and coffee slopped over his knuckles; he barely felt the heat. "Dani?" His voice came out higher than he meant, and a woman beside him glanced over. He blinked twice, as if the picture might correct itself. Last week his daughter had refused to speak to anyone in that class, had cried in the car every morning, and now she was laughing, her backpack swinging off one shoulder. His mouth hung open a moment before he remembered to close it. "Who's..." he started, then wiped his wet hand on his jeans, forgot the coffee entirely, and stepped forward with the lid still dangling from two fingers, his heart knocking somewhere up near his collar.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: I was wiping pollen off Grandma's walnut dresser, marker ready to write $40 on a sticky label, when the man in the denim jacket pulled the bottom drawer all the way out and tipped it over. Something taped underneath crackled. My hand stopped midair. "Sir, that's... hang on." The marker rolled off the driveway and I didn't chase it. He peeled a yellowed envelope free and held it out, and my fingers actually shook taking it. Inside were savings bonds, a whole stack, and a photo of my grandfather grinning in a uniform I'd never seen. My mouth went dry. "Forty years," I heard myself say, too high, too fast. "I've polished this thing for forty years." The folding table wobbled where I leaned on it. Across the lawn a neighbor's radio kept playing some cheerful song, and I stood there blinking at the sun, laughing once without meaning to, and then not at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta had the wrench seated on the slip nut and was leaning her whole weight into a quarter turn when the pipe under the sink simply let go of the wall. The wrench clattered into the cabinet. She jerked back so fast her head knocked the underside of the basin, and she stayed there, crouched, one hand still raised as if the pipe might need catching. Cold water ran down her wrist into her sleeve. "Wait," she said, too high, then again, "wait, what?" Her heart thudded in her ears. She stared at the threaded end in her fist, dry and clean, and then at the wall, where there was no leak at all, only a neat dark hole and a faint smell of old plaster. The drip she'd chased for three weeks had never come from here. She laughed once, a short breathless bark, and sat down hard on the wet tiles, still holding the pipe like a borrowed thing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had a window and a federal seal, so I'd been carrying it around the kitchen for two days like a hot pan. Tonight I finally slid my thumb under the flap, still bracing for the audit. The paper came out in three crisp folds. I read the first line and my coffee mug stopped halfway to my mouth. I set it down wrong, and it clacked against the counter, sloshing brown over the edge. I didn't wipe it. 'No,' I said, quietly, then again, louder, to the empty room. I turned the page over, as if the back might correct the front. My ears were ringing. The number was there, with a dollar sign, and my name spelled right. 'Refund?' I laughed, a short cracked bark, and sat down on the floor without deciding to. I read it a third time, out loud, my finger under every word, while the coffee dripped off the counter onto my sock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marta stepped off the night bus in Tbilisi with her phrasebook open to a page she had already forgotten, and stopped mid-stride when the station attendant, a man with a drooping mustache, looked at her suitcase and said, in perfect Texan drawl, "Y'all lost, darlin'?" Her hand froze on the strap. The phrasebook slid from her fingers and slapped the wet concrete. "You... what?" she said, voice climbing higher than she intended. She blinked twice, then laughed, a short, cracked sound, and glanced behind her as if someone might be playing a trick. Her pulse thudded in her ears. The man bent, retrieved the book, and brushed it off with a grin. "Lived in Houston eleven years," he said. Marta stared at him, mouth still slightly open, all the Georgian words she had rehearsed on the flight dissolving like sugar in rain. "Okay," she finally managed. "Okay. Wow. Hello."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: I had my thermos halfway to my mouth when Biscuit, who hadn't run in two years because of her bad hip, tore across the wet grass like a puppy. The coffee sloshed over my knuckles and I didn't even feel the heat. "Biscuit?" My voice came out thin, cracked at the edges. She skidded, spun, and dropped into a play bow in front of a startled beagle I'd never seen. I stood up so fast the bench creaked behind me. My heart was knocking somewhere up near my throat, and I realized my mouth was hanging open. I glanced around for someone, anyone, to confirm it. A jogger passed, earbuds in, oblivious. "Did you see that?" I said to nobody, laughing once, a short breathy bark. The thermos lay tipped in the grass. I left it there and took three slow steps forward, as if any sudden move might undo it, as if she might remember she was old.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite had run the final bars of the Schubert so many times in the empty church hall that her fingers moved without her, and she was thinking about the folding chairs, and whether the coffee urn would be ready, when the back door banged and a cello began to play the line beneath hers. She stopped. Her hands hung above the keys, and the last note rang thinly off the rafters. Her mouth was open; she closed it, then opened it again. "Walter?" she said, too high, almost a squeak.
