The retired mailman stood in the doorway with the case still strapped to his shoulder, bow raised, grinning. "You told me you gave it up in the seventies." Her pulse thudded in her ears, and she pressed a palm flat against her breastbone as if to check it. She laughed once, short, and then reached out and slid the bench over, patting the empty space of wood. "Again," she said. "From the top. Slowly."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I was wrestling a coffee can of rusted screws off the top shelf when the shelf's back panel swung loose like a door. Behind it, wedged between studs, sat a row of small wooden birds, maybe twenty, each painted with my name's initials on the belly. My hand stopped halfway to the cardboard box. The can slipped and spilled across the floor, screws ringing on concrete, and I didn't bend to chase them. "Walt," I said, and then again, quieter, as if he might answer from the lathe. I picked one up. The paint was still tacky on the newest, a thumbprint dented in its tail. My knees found the stool without my asking. I counted them twice, lips moving, then laughed once, a short ugly bark, and pressed the cool wood against my sternum where my heartbeat was thudding. Every birthday I'd thought he'd forgotten. The box stayed empty beside me. I never did pick up the screws.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Mina had pressed her thumbnail into the cork board so long that it left a crescent in the paper margin. The hallway smelled of floor wax and damp coats. When the secretary pinned up the sheet and walked away, Mina stepped forward, ran her finger down the column of student numbers, and stopped. Her finger went back up. Down again. She mouthed her own number, then read the score beside it, then took her glasses off and wiped them on her sleeve as if the lenses had lied. "No," she said, too quietly for anyone to hear, and then, louder, "That's not mine." A boy beside her glanced over. She laughed once, a short cracked sound, and realized her mouth was hanging open. Her knees felt oddly loose, as though the floor had dropped half an inch. She checked the number a fourth time, then pulled out her phone to call her mother and found she had forgotten the passcode.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear was sliding off the ridge when I rounded the boulder and my boots simply stopped. Ahead, where the switchback should have dropped into scrub, a single lit window hung in the dusk, yellow and square, set in a cabin I'd have sworn wasn't on any map. My trekking pole clattered against the rock; I didn't remember letting go. "No," I said, too loudly, then again, a whisper cracking in the middle. My heart knocked hard against my ribs and the cold air seemed to catch halfway down my throat. I glanced at my phone, as if it might explain, and found the screen blank with no signal. Smoke curled from the chimney. I blinked twice, wiped my palms on my jacket, and heard myself laugh, short and breathless, while my feet stayed planted in the gravel, refusing to choose a direction.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Mina unfolded the recipe card, its corners soft as cloth, and read her grandmother's slanted pencil line aloud: "Flour, water, salt, yeast, and one spoon of the brown jar." She frowned. Brown jar? She dug through the cupboard until she found it, an old tin labeled in the same hand. She pried it open and froze, the spoon halfway up. Cinnamon? No. Crushed fennel, and something sweeter, honey crystals. "Halmoni," she whispered, "you never told me." Her hands, dusted white to the wrists, drifted to her mouth. When the loaf came out of the oven, she tore the heel off too fast and burned her fingertips, barely noticing. One bite and she sat down hard on the kitchen floor, the warm bread in her lap, laughing once, short and breathless. The smell was the hallway of her grandmother's apartment, exactly, every Sunday. "How," she said to the empty kitchen, "was it in there the whole time?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was comparing two cans of crushed tomatoes in the grocery on Alder Street when a voice behind me said, "Still can't decide, Marcus?" The can slipped from my fingers and rang against the floor, rolling until a sneaker stopped it. I turned. Dana Okafor, who sat behind me in tenth-grade chemistry and once set my lab notes on fire, was holding it out with a grin. My mouth opened and nothing came out for a second. My heart was knocking somewhere up near my collarbone. "Dana?" I finally said, too loud, my voice cracking on the second syllable. "You... here? I thought you moved to Portland." I realized I was still gripping the other can against my chest like a shield. I laughed, short and breathless, and wiped my palm on my jeans before offering it. "Twenty years. Twenty. Look at you." The freezer aisle hummed around us, and I couldn't stop staring at her face, hunting for the girl with the singed notebook.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied out, just me, the hum of the freezer case, and a mop bucket going cold by the register. I was counting the till for the second time when the bell over the door jingled. Mr. Alvarez, who had grumbled at me every Tuesday for three years over copay prices, stood there holding a foil-wrapped plate. My hands stopped mid-count, a stack of twenties hanging in the air. "For you," he said, and pushed it across the counter. "Tamales. My wife made too many." I opened my mouth and nothing came out, so I looked down at the plate, then up at him, then at the plate again. The foil was still warm against my palms. "Oh," I finally said, too high, too quiet. "Oh. You didn't have to. I mean, thank you. Thank you." He nodded, tugged his cap, and left. I stood there, twenties forgotten, losing my count entirely.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: I hit the end of Concourse C at a dead sprint, backpack slapping my spine, lungs burning, and skidded to a stop at Gate 42 with the boarding door already shut. Eleven minutes late. I'd rehearsed my pleading speech the whole run. Then the agent looked up, grinned, and said, "Mr. Alvarez? We held it for you." My mouth opened. Nothing came out. I glanced behind me, certain she meant someone else, but the corridor was empty except for a cleaner and his humming floor machine. "Me?" I finally croaked, voice cracking on the single syllable. She nodded and held out her hand for my phone. My fingers fumbled it twice before I got it to the scanner. The boarding pass beeped green. I stood there another second, heart still hammering, one hand pressed flat against my chest, laughing once, short and breathless, like someone had knocked the air out of me. "Thank you," I managed. "I really thought... Thank you."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller was halfway down the wall when the beige peeled away in a long, soft sheet, and underneath it, in thick green marker, someone had written MAYA 1994 — HEIGHT 3'2". I stopped. The roller dripped on my sock and I didn't move it. "No," I said to the empty room, my voice cracking up high. "No way." I crouched, thumb hovering over the faded lines climbing the plaster, each with a date, each in my mother's slanted hand. My pulse thudded in my ears. I'd lived here eleven years and never seen them. I laughed once, sharp, then pressed my palm flat against the cold wall as if it might answer. The drop cloth crinkled when I sat down hard. Paint fumes stung my nose, and my eyes too. After a while I set the roller in the tray, wiped my fingers on my jeans, and went to find my phone. I needed to call her before I did one more stroke.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite had settled into the porch swing with her iced tea, expecting nothing more than rain drumming on the tin roof, when the screen door at the far end of the porch banged open and her brother Denny, who had been dead set on staying in Tucson, stood dripping on the boards with a duffel bag over his shoulder. Her glass slid from her fingers and shattered, tea pooling around her bare feet, and she didn't flinch at the cold. Her heart knocked hard against her ribs. She stood up too fast, the swing clanking against the wall behind her. "Denny?" Her voice cracked high, a girl's voice. She blinked, rubbed her eyes with the back of her wrist, and looked again. Thunder rolled over the field. "You said Christmas. You said maybe not even Christmas." She laughed once, short and breathless, and pressed a hand flat to her chest. "Well, don't just stand there. Get in here. Look at you."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had left the wrench on the red towel, handle pointing left. Now it pointed right. She stopped with the chain half-looped around her thumb and stared at it, then at the shelf where her neighbor Dale kept his paint cans, lids neatly shut, labels turned inward. Funny, that. They'd faced out yesterday. "Dale around?" she called, too brightly, and the garage swallowed it. A fan hummed. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears. She crouched, ran a finger along the underside of her seat post, and checked the tire she'd pumped to 80 psi that morning. Soft. She pressed it again, slower, jaw tight. The back door, usually propped with a brick, was shut. She wiped her palms on her jeans, picked up the wrench, and kept it in her hand while she worked, turning every few seconds to look at the door behind her. "Fine," she muttered. "Just fine." She didn't put the tools down once.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: Marguerite shifted her tote to the other shoulder and checked the timetable again, though the numbers hadn't changed since the last time. The wind had picked up, flipping the corner of the laminated sheet, and the first fat drops struck the shelter roof like thrown coins. The man at the far end of the bench had not moved in twenty minutes. No phone, no paper, no umbrella, yet his coat was dry and his shoes were clean. She slid her wallet from her back pocket into her inner coat pocket and zipped it, slowly, so the sound wouldn't carry. "Do you know if the 14 still runs on Sundays?" she asked, louder than she meant, watching his hands instead of his face. He said it did. He said it too quickly. The back of her neck prickled as thunder rolled somewhere past the rooftops, and she stepped out from under the shelter into the rain, deciding that getting wet was cheaper than staying to find out why he'd answered before she finished asking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta knelt by the cedar box in the attic, dust clinging to her knees, and fanned the letters across the floorboards. Every envelope carried her father's tidy hand, yet the postmarks were all from Lisbon, a city he swore he'd never visited. She turned one over, then another, her thumb pressing hard at the seam of the flap. "Business," she muttered, flat, the way he'd said it at dinner. The rafters ticked in the heat. She lifted an envelope to the window light and squinted at the shadow of folded paper, then set it down and counted the stamps again. Her jaw had gone tight. Downstairs, the front door clicked, and she swept the letters back into the box so fast a corner bent. She sat very still, listening to the footsteps below, and slid the lid shut with one finger, slowly, so it wouldn't make a sound.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta kept her hand on the screen door instead of opening it. Dale stood on the porch in a clean jacket, no gloves, no gutter scoop, nothing in his hands but his phone. "Just for an hour," he said, smiling too long. She glanced past him to his own garage, its door rolled halfway up, a dark gap behind it. "Thought you bought one last spring," she said, evenly. He laughed and rubbed his neck. "Loaned it out." The back of her own neck prickled. She watched his eyes slide toward her side gate, then back to her face. "What's the job?" she asked. "Oh, gutters. Whatever." Whatever. She counted the leaves in the yard, none of them on his roof. "It's got a bad rung," she said. "I'll bring it by myself tomorrow, once I check it." His smile thinned. She shut the door, turned the deadbolt slowly, and stood in the hall listening to his footsteps hesitate on the boards before they left.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The saffron was in the wrong drawer again. I stood there with the knife hovering over the onions, counting the jars: the cumin turned label-out, which I never do, the paprika pushed to the back. Someone had been in my kitchen. "Dani," I called, too brightly, "did you move my spices?" He said no without looking up from his phone, and I watched his thumb, how it stopped scrolling a half second too late. The stew simmered. I stirred it slowly, tasting, tasting again, though my tongue felt coated and I couldn't tell salt from anything. Headlights swept the window and my shoulders jumped up near my ears. Forty minutes until the Hendersons came, and I wiped the same clean spot of counter three times. I tilted the lid of the spare pot, peered inside, then set it back. "Funny," I said, "how the back door was unlocked this morning." Dani finally looked up. His smile arrived a little fast.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter at 9:47, and Marta wiped her hands on a dishtowel before turning it over. No name. Just a string of digits beginning with a code she didn't know. She let it ring four times, her thumb hovering, her eyes drifting to the dark window over the sink. When she finally answered, she said nothing. Silence crackled on the line, then a man's bright voice: "Hello, Ms. Alvarez?" She stepped back from the window and pulled the blind down. "Who's asking?" she said, flat and slow. He mentioned her bank. Her free hand found the back of a chair and gripped it. "Funny," she said, "they never call this late." She tucked the dishtowel under her arm, walked to the door, and checked the deadbolt, though she had already checked it twice. "Give me your name and a number, and I'll call the branch myself." The line clicked dead. She stood listening to her own pulse, the phone still warm against her ear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Dara slid the copy of Middlemarch across the desk, three years and two semesters late, and waited for the librarian to wince. She didn't. The woman only smiled, scanned the barcode, and said, "Oh, don't worry about it, hon." Dara's thumb pressed hard into her backpack strap. "No fine? Not even a little one?" Her voice came out lighter than she meant. She glanced past the desk at the door marked STAFF, then at the camera blinking in the ceiling corner. The librarian was still smiling. Dara leaned back an inch, then forward again, trying to read the screen she couldn't see. "Nobody's going to find me later, right? Like, a form or something?" The back of her neck prickled. She took her receipt, folded it twice, and checked both sides for fine print before she'd even reached the exit. At the glass doors she looked back once, certain someone would be watching.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The landlord handed me the key and said the last tenant left in a hurry, then laughed a little too long. I didn't laugh. I set my box on the kitchen counter and ran my thumb along the deadbolt, which had been installed backwards, so it locked from the hallway side. Who does that? "Funny place for a lock," I said, flat, watching his eyes. He shrugged and left. I stood still until his footsteps faded, shoulders tight against my ears. The closet was empty except for one hanger, swaying though no window was open. I pressed my palm to the wall and felt a faint hum. Pipes, I told myself. I slid the dresser across the door anyway, checked behind the shower curtain twice, and unpacked only one mug. Just in case, I kept my shoes on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat dead center on the bench, squared to the edge like someone had set it there with a ruler. I stopped ten feet away. Nobody on the path, just a jogger shrinking toward the fountain and a pigeon working a crust. I turned in a slow circle, checking the trees, the parked van by the gate, the windows across the street. My thumb kept rubbing the strap of my bag. "Hello?" I said, too quietly, then louder, "Anyone lose something?" Only the pigeon answered, by leaving. I crouched and looked under the bench before I touched anything, which felt ridiculous, and I did it anyway. The leather was warm, as if a hand had just let go. Why warm, on a cold morning? I flipped it open with a pen instead of my fingers. Cash, fat and fanned. A license photo of a man smiling too widely. I snapped it shut, my pulse thudding in my ears, and looked at the van again. Its engine was running.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor, Dale, keeps saying the water is only four feet deep, and I keep looking at the painted number on the tile, then at him. "Four," I say. "Right. Four." My arms stay folded across my chest even though the pool is cold enough to make my teeth ache. He grins and tells me to let go of the wall, just let go, and I don't. My eyes slide to the lifeguard, who is staring at her phone, and then to the drain, which seems larger than drains should be. "Why's it so quiet in here?" I ask. Dale laughs. I don't. I press one foot against the bottom, testing it like a floorboard I don't trust, and my heartbeat thuds in my throat. When he steps behind me with his hands out, I turn my whole body so he stays in view. "Where exactly are you going to be?" I say, slowly. "Because I'll be checking."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana knelt at the edge of the raised bed and turned the seed packet over twice, reading the tiny print on the back like a contract. Twelve dollars for forty carrot seeds. She tore the corner, tipped a few into her palm, and squinted at them. They looked like dust. "Sure," she muttered. "Sure you are." She pressed one into the soil, then dug it back up to check it was really a seed, and the neighbor's fence creaked behind her. Her shoulders tightened. She glanced over: nobody, only gray slats and a wind chime. Why had the man at the garden store been so quick to say they'd grow in any soil? She sniffed a pinch of dirt, rubbed it between her fingers, and wiped her hand slowly on her jeans. When she finished the row, she photographed it from three angles, so she'd know if anything changed, and kept the packet in her back pocket instead of the shed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Derek clicked to the next slide, and I tilted my head, because the chart on it looked awfully familiar. Same teal bars. Same odd gap between Q2 and Q3. I pulled my laptop closer and opened last spring's folder, scrolling with one finger while my other hand kept my coffee cup frozen halfway to my mouth. The conference room hummed with the vent's dull rattle. Derek's voice was smooth, too smooth, each number landing like he'd rehearsed it in a mirror. "Quick question," I said, my voice lighter than I felt. "Where did the baseline figures come from?" He smiled, a fraction too fast. "Internal sources." My jaw tightened. He glanced at Marcia instead of me. The back of my neck prickled. I set the cup down, very quietly, and typed one word into the search bar: Priya. Her name was in the file's author field. I leaned back and kept my eyes on his hands.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The headlights behind me hadn't changed since the gas station, same height, same slow yellow glare, and that was the third turn I'd taken that made no sense for getting home. I eased off the gas. So did they. My thumb found a groove in the steering wheel and kept rubbing it. "Come on, pass me," I muttered, flicking the mirror down, then back up. Nothing. The road was black farmland on both sides, one dead streetlamp, a mailbox leaning like it was listening. My neck had gone stiff, and I realized I'd been holding my breath since the last bend. I reached over and locked the doors, then checked they were locked by pulling the handle. At my street I drove straight past it, laughing once, a dry little sound, and watched the mirror until the lights slid by past the turn, or didn't. They didn't. I kept going, eyes flicking, humming nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vase of lilies on Uncle Dario's windowsill was new, and so was the card tucked in it, which I turned over with one finger while my cousin Marco talked about parking. "Who sent these?" I asked, too lightly. He shrugged and checked his phone. Uncle Dario's pillow had been fluffed, his water jug refilled, his will, apparently, discussed with someone before I arrived, because the nurse said, "Oh, the other nephew already went over everything." I don't have another brother. My jaw tightened. I stood by the door instead of sitting, keeping the hallway in the corner of my eye, my bag strap wound twice around my fist. Marco laughed at something, a beat too late. "You okay?" he said. "Fine," I said, and smiled with my teeth. The machine beeped steadily. I memorized the card's handwriting, then slid my phone out and photographed it while Marco's back was turned, my heart knocking against my ribs like someone asking to be let in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The silver sedan has been idling by the fence for twenty minutes, and nobody has gotten out. I keep my eyes on the tinted windshield while pretending to scroll my phone, thumb moving over the same dead screen. Other parents drift toward the gate, chatting about bake sales, and I step sideways to keep the car in view. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it. When the man beside me asks if I'm new here, I answer too quickly, "No. Third year." He laughs, and I don't. The back door of the sedan cracks open an inch, then shuts. My hand finds my keys and wraps around them, the teeth pressing into my palm. The bell rings. Kids spill out in a loud, bright wave, and I push forward, scanning for Maya's yellow backpack, one eye still on that car. 'Hold my hand today,' I tell her, softer than I mean to. 'Don't look back. Just walk with me.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man had been circling the oak dresser for twenty minutes, and Marguerite had stopped pretending to count her quarters. He ran a thumb along the drawer seams, crouched to peer underneath, then photographed the maker's stamp without asking. "Forty," he said, not haggling, which was worse. She wiped her palms on her apron. "It's sixty. It's always been sixty." He smiled too quickly and asked whether she had any other pieces inside the house. Her eyes flicked to the open garage, the unlatched side gate, the van idling at the curb with its engine running and no one in the passenger seat. "Just what you see," she said, louder than she meant to. When he reached for his wallet, she stepped between him and the cash box, her shoulders tight against her neck. "Cash only. And my nephew's coming any minute," she added, though Dennis lived in Tucson, and she glanced down the street anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta wedged the flashlight between her teeth and ran her thumb along the copper elbow beneath the sink. Dry. Yesterday it had dripped steadily; she'd marked the spot with tape. Now the tape was gone, and the joint gleamed with fresh solder she hadn't put there. She pulled back, knocking her head on the cabinet door, and stayed hunched there, breathing through her nose. The wrench in her hand felt heavier than it should. "Dale," she called, too lightly, "did you come down here while I was at work?" From upstairs, the floorboards stopped creaking. Several seconds passed before he answered, and when he did, he asked what pipe. She set the flashlight on the cabinet floor, its beam pointing at the empty tape-roll beside the trap, and wiped her palms on her jeans twice. The back of her neck prickled. Slowly she crouched again, and this time she looked not at the leak but at the dusty floor, where a clean, sharp boot print pointed toward the basement door she always kept locked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter next to the cold coffee, and I turned it over twice before touching the flap. Return address: Department of Revenue. No logo, just a stamp that looked too crisp. I held it up to the window and squinted at the shadow of the folded page inside. "Nobody sends good news in a window envelope," I muttered to the empty kitchen. My thumb found the seal and stopped. Why was my name typed in all capitals? Why my old apartment's zip code, the one I'd left three years ago and told almost no one about? I wiped my palm on my jeans, slid a butter knife under the flap, and listened to the paper tear. My jaw was tight. Before unfolding anything, I walked to the front door, checked the deadbolt, then came back and read the first line standing up, one foot already angled toward the hallway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The taxi driver had already loaded her suitcase before Marta said a word, and that was the first thing she turned over in her mind. She slid across the seat but kept her palm flat on the door handle. He smiled at her in the mirror and said something long and warm; she nodded without understanding. When he turned left where her phone's blue line went right, her thumb stopped scrolling. "No," she said, too evenly, and pointed at the screen. "This way. Hotel Aurora." He shrugged, chattering, and took another left. Her pulse thudded in her ears. She counted the streetlights, memorized a pharmacy's green cross, and slipped her passport from the bag into her jacket, zipping it to her chin. Every time his eyes met hers in the mirror, she looked at the meter, then the window, then the meter again. When the car finally stopped in front of a lit doorway, she did not move until she had read the sign twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta kept one hand on the fence rail while Biscuit tore laps around the far end of the field, ears flapping, tongue out. She didn't wave back at the man by the oak. He'd been there since before she arrived, a thermos in his hand that he never lifted, his eyes never leaving the dog. "Biscuit, here," she called, lower than she meant to, and the dog ignored her. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. The man shifted his weight, and she did too, edging two steps along the fence toward the gate. Wind pushed through the long grass and she counted the seconds between his glances. Four. Five. "Nice day," he called. Marta said nothing. She dug the leash out of her pocket, wound it twice around her knuckles, and watched his shoes instead of his face. "Biscuit," she said again, sharp now. "Now."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marta set her cello case down slowly in the church hall and counted the folding chairs again. Twelve. Yesterday there had been fourteen, she was sure of it. She tightened her bow, eyes drifting to the piano, where the lid sat open though she'd closed it herself. "Did anyone move the music stand?" she asked, too lightly, and Dennis shook his head without looking up from his clarinet. She played the opening phrase and stopped halfway, listening. The radiator ticked. Somewhere behind the stage curtain, a floorboard answered. Her shoulders crept toward her ears. "Just one more time," she said, and played with her chin turned toward the curtain, the bow wavering on the long note. When Dennis laughed at something, she flinched, then pulled the curtain aside with two fingers. Only folded risers and a mop bucket. She stared at the bucket a moment longer than she needed to, then wiped her damp palm on her skirt and returned to her seat, dragging her chair a little nearer the exit.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Walt's workshop smelled of cedar and cold solder, and I had been boxing his chisels for an hour when I noticed the dust. Every shelf wore a gray coat except the one above the bench, wiped clean, a rectangle where something had sat until recently. I stopped with a chisel in my fist. "Huh," I said to the empty room, too lightly. I crouched, ran my thumb along the shelf's edge, and checked the door behind me, still shut. His sister had said she hadn't been here. The padlock on the bottom drawer was new, brass still bright, and my jaw tightened as I tried the handle. Locked. Why would a man buy a lock for a drawer of sandpaper? My pulse ticked in my ears. I set the chisel down quietly, as if the walls were listening, and started pulling out the other drawers one by one, counting what each held, looking for the thing that didn't belong, the thing he'd decided I shouldn't find.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal had promised results by noon, but at 11:40 Marisol was already standing in the corridor, watching the department secretary instead of the corkboard. The woman had taped up a blank sheet, then peeled it down again, twice, and each time she glanced over her shoulder. Marisol's eyes narrowed. She leaned against the radiator, arms crossed tight, one thumb pressing hard into her ribs. "Funny," she said, too lightly, "that Professor Hale's door is shut on results day." Nobody answered. She counted the ceiling tiles, then the footsteps, then recounted them when the numbers didn't match what she expected. When the secretary finally pinned up a page, folded at one corner, Marisol didn't rush forward like the others. She waited until the crowd thinned, then crept close, pulled the fold flat with a fingernail, and checked the printing date at the bottom before she let herself look for her number. Her jaw stayed clenched. "Who printed this?" she muttered.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta stopped where the switchbacks leveled out and let her trekking poles hang from their straps. The orange light had gone thin between the pines, and somewhere behind her a twig snapped, then nothing. She counted five slow breaths. The same pair of boot prints she'd been following since the trailhead, deep-heeled and too fresh, had left the path twenty yards back and then rejoined it, as if whoever made them wanted to watch her pass. Her neck prickled. She tugged her pack strap tighter and walked on, faster, glancing at the ridge every few steps. "Hello?" she called, pitching her voice bright and casual, and the woods swallowed it. The thermos in her pack sloshed too loudly. She slipped her keys between her knuckles, then felt foolish, then didn't put them away. At the creek crossing she crouched to retie a lace that was already tight, and listened. Her car was two miles off. She turned her phone's flashlight on, off, then on again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma's card is stained yellow, her slanted handwriting calling for two cups of flour, a pinch of salt, and "the usual amount" of yeast. I hold it up to the window light and squint. The usual amount. I turn it over; the back is blank, too blank, like someone wiped it. My thumb rubs the corner where the ink looks newer than the rest. "Funny," I say to the empty kitchen, and laugh once, too short. She never skipped a measurement in her life. I stir slowly, glancing at the door, then at the drawer where she kept her tin. My jaw is tight. I open the drawer an inch, peer in, and shove it closed. Dough sticks to my fingers while I read the last line again: "Add the secret last." What secret? Who wrote that? My shoulders creep toward my ears as the oven ticks, and I keep the card face down beside the bowl, one hand always on it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marisol was weighing two cans of tomatoes in the narrow aisle when someone said her name, and she kept her thumb pressed on the lid a second too long before turning. Dennis Pruitt. Tenth-grade chemistry, the one who had once borrowed forty dollars and a graphing calculator and vanished with both. He was grinning, arms wide, a basket hooked on his elbow with almost nothing in it. "Twelve years," she said, and stepped half a pace back so the cart sat between them. "What brings you to this side of town?" He laughed too easily, said he was just passing through, and asked where she was living now. Marisol smiled without showing teeth. "Around." Her eyes dropped to his empty hands, then to the door behind him. The fluorescent hum seemed louder. When he reached for his phone, suggesting they trade numbers, she pulled her purse strap tight across her chest. "I'll find you," she said, and rolled the cart away, glancing at the shiny end-cap mirror twice before turning the corner.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy emptied out by four, everyone rushing home for Thanksgiving, which is why the man in the gray raincoat stood out. He'd been browsing the same shelf of cough syrup for twenty minutes, never picking anything up. I wiped the counter. Wiped it again. My neck prickled every time the fluorescent light buzzed. "Can I help you find something?" I asked, and my voice came out too bright, too loud. He said no, thanks, without turning around. His hands stayed buried in his pockets. I slid my phone closer to the register and counted the cash drawer twice, lips moving. Outside, the lot was nearly empty except for one idling car with its headlights off. Why would anyone sit like that? My stomach tightened into a fist. When he finally drifted toward the door, I shifted so the counter stood between us, and I kept watching his reflection in the glass until the bell chimed and the car's lights flicked on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marta jogged past Gate B14 with her carry-on thumping her hip, then slowed, because the agent had just waved her toward C22 for the third time that evening, and the screen above him still said B14. She stopped and read the board again, lips moving. "Funny," she said, flat and quiet. "Ten minutes ago this was on time." The man smiled too quickly and tapped his keyboard without looking at it. Her neck prickled. She angled her boarding pass against her chest, thumb over the seat number, and glanced down the concourse, where no one else was hurrying anywhere. Why wasn't anyone else running? "Which flight did you say?" she asked, though she'd never said. He hesitated half a breath. Marta stepped backward, eyes fixed on his hands, and pulled out her phone to check the app herself, letting the minutes drain away behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I peeled the tape off the baseboard and stopped, roller dripping onto the drop cloth. Under the old beige, near the closet, someone had scratched small numbers into the plaster, and the grooves looked fresh. I ran my thumb over them. Seven, four, nine. Behind me the hallway floorboard creaked, and I turned so fast my neck pinched. Nothing. Only the fridge humming downstairs. "Dale?" I called, too loudly. No answer. Dale had told me he'd never been in this room, and he'd said it before I even asked. I set the roller down and wiped my palms on my jeans, but they were damp again in seconds. I pressed my ear to the wall and held my breath until my pulse thudded in it. Then I picked up the putty knife instead of the brush and started to dig. "Just checking the plaster," I told the empty room, my voice flat and careful, as if someone were taking notes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite kept her rocker angled toward the gravel drive, though the rain had turned it to a brown stream and nothing could possibly be coming up it. Thunder rolled; she didn't flinch, but her thumb worried the edge of the lemonade glass until the ice had melted to slivers. The neighbor's truck had been there at noon, she was sure of it, and now the space beside the mailbox sat empty. Funny, he'd said he was staying in all week. She counted the seconds after a flash, then lost count because her eyes had slid back to the tree line. "Mm-hm," she said aloud to nobody, flatly, the way she did when a salesman talked too smoothly. The porch boards creaked behind her and she turned her head slowly, only to find the cat. Her shoulders stayed high anyway. She slid the spare key from under the flowerpot into her cardigan pocket, and kept watching the road.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The kid from apartment 3B was hovering by the oil stains again, hands jammed in his hoodie pocket, watching me wrestle a seized pedal off my own bike. I put the wrench down. His front tire hung flat on the hook behind him, the tube chewed up, and I'd seen him walking it home twice this week. "Hey, hand me that patch kit, the red tin," I said, softer than I meant to. He did. My knees ached against the cold concrete as I scooted over and patted the milk crate beside me. "Sit. It's easier with two people." I pried the tire off with the levers and let him feel for the thorn himself, his small fingers slow and careful. When he found it, his whole face opened. I pretended my own pedal could wait, though my fingers were numb and the coffee had gone cold. "Again," I said, "but this time you do it, and I just watch."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as the wind swung round and pushed the cold straight down my collar. I hunched, stamped my feet, and checked the empty road for the 14 again. At the far end of the bench sat a boy, maybe nine, in a T-shirt, hugging a school bag against his chest, his knees knocking. No grown-up anywhere. I was already unzipping my jacket before I'd decided to. "Here," I said, keeping my voice light, like it was nothing, and held it out. "I run hot. Honestly, you'd be doing me a favour." He hesitated, then took it, and it swallowed him to the knuckles. I slid over so my shoulder blocked the draft from his side, and my own arms prickled with goosebumps. "Bus is late," I told him. "Always is when it rains. Want to count the puddles till it comes?" He nodded, teeth still chattering, and I started counting out loud.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox smelled of cedar and cold radiators, and I sat on the attic floor with my knees aching against the boards. Most of the envelopes were Dad's, addressed in a slanted hand to a woman in Duluth I'd never heard of. I unfolded one and read only the first line, then stopped, because my throat had gone tight. Her replies were here too, returned unopened, the stamps still crisp. Seven of them. I pressed my thumb along the torn flap of the last one, as if I could smooth it shut. "Oh, Dad," I said, quietly, to the rafters. I didn't hurry. I stacked them by date, tied them with the green string from my pocket, and found I was patting the bundle like a sleeping animal. Then I went downstairs, took the phone off its hook, and looked up Duluth, her last name, anything. Maybe she'd still want to know he'd kept writing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mrs. Okafor stood at my door with her cardigan buttoned wrong and her hands knotted together, and my coffee went forgotten on the counter. "It's the gutter," she said, quieter than I'd ever heard her. "Leaves from the storm. Harold always did it." She didn't finish. My chest felt tight, like a hand pressing under the ribs, and I looked past her at the grey sky, the sagging line of her roof. "Hang on, I'll get my boots," I said, already reaching for them. "No, no, just the ladder," she protested. "It's a two-person job anyway," I lied, because it wasn't. I hauled the aluminum ladder from the garage, felt its cold rungs bite my palms, and walked beside her slowly, matching her pace across the wet lawn. "You hold the bottom," I told her, "and tell me when I miss a spot." She nodded, and her shoulders dropped a little.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The doorbell is due in twenty minutes, and I'm stirring the lentils with one hand while the other holds my phone, rereading Dana's text: *Sorry, Mum's chemo ran long, we may be late, don't wait.* I turn the burner down to its smallest blue flicker. Then I pull the chair cushions off the sofa and swap the sharp-smelling curry I'd planned for something plain, rice softened with broth, because I remember how her mother pushed food around the plate last spring. My shoulders ache from standing, but I don't sit. I wipe the counter twice. I fill the kettle for ginger tea and set out the thick blanket, the soft one, folded over the armchair nearest the heater. When the buzzer finally sounds, I wipe my hands on my apron, say, "Come in, come in, no rush at all, there's no hurry," and keep my voice low, like the hallway itself might be tired too. I'm already reaching for her mother's elbow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the dish rack, an unfamiliar number glowing over the soapy plates, and Marta dried her hands before answering. "Hello?" Nothing but breathing, ragged and wet, and then a boy's voice, cracking: "I think I dialed wrong. I'm sorry. I'm not supposed to call." She turned off the tap. Her chest tightened, and she lowered herself onto the kitchen stool without noticing she'd done it. "Hey, it's all right," she said, softer than she spoke to anyone these days. "You didn't bother me. What's your name?" He wouldn't say. She heard a TV somewhere behind him, a door thudding. She pressed her palm flat against the cool counter and kept her voice slow, unhurried. "I've got all night, honey. Are you somewhere safe? Is there a grown-up close by?" The dinner she'd been about to reheat sat forgotten. She grabbed a pen, wrote *stay on the line* on her wrist, and said, "Tell me about the dog I can hear barking."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been under my bed for two years, and I carried it into the library with both hands, like it might spill. The librarian, a thin man with a cardigan buttoned wrong, was already wincing at the cart of returns he was shelving alone. I set the book down and said, quietly, "I'm sorry. I know this is awful. Let me pay whatever it is, and then let me help you with that." He waved the fine away, but I was already rolling up my sleeves. My throat felt tight watching his knuckles whiten around a stack of atlases too heavy for him. I took half. We walked the aisles under the buzzing lights, and I read call numbers aloud so he wouldn't have to squint. When he finally laughed, a small tired sound, my shoulders dropped for the first time all week. I stayed until the cart was empty.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Mara had barely set the last box down when the wall thumped again, and a muffled cough followed, wet and long. She stood still, breath held, then stepped to the thin plaster and listened. The old man next door, the landlord had mentioned, lived alone. Her shoulders ached from the stairs and her shirt clung to her back, but she dug through the box marked KITCHEN until she found the small pot and the packet of ginger tea she'd bought for herself. "Just a second," she whispered to the empty room, as if he could hear. Her knuckles tapped his door softly, twice. When it creaked open, she held out the steaming mug with both hands. "I'm new. The walls are thin, I think. You sound like you could use something warm." His eyes were red-rimmed, and her throat tightened. She stayed in the doorway, unpacking nothing, until his coughing eased.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench's far end, cracked brown leather, damp from the morning drizzle. I opened it expecting a name and found a bus pass, forty dollars, and a child's crayon drawing folded small, a stick-figure man holding a yellow balloon. My chest tightened. I looked down the path, then up it, searching for someone hunched and patting pockets. Nobody. I sat down where the wood was still wet and let it soak through my jeans. The license said Walter Okafor, 81. I thought of him retracing his steps, counting what he'd lost, and my throat went thick. I dialed the number on a pharmacy card and spoke softly when a woman answered. "I've got his wallet. No, don't worry, nothing's missing. Please tell him I'll wait right here. I'm not going anywhere." Then I tucked the drawing back into its slot, smoothing the creases with my thumb, and pulled my coat tighter against the cold to wait.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Forty-three years old, and I'm gripping the pool's tile edge like a railing on a sinking ship. Beside me, a boy of maybe seven kicks his way across the shallow lane, and I catch myself flinching when he swallows water and coughs. "You okay, bud?" I call, too loudly, and my voice bounces off the chlorine-heavy air. He nods, eyes red, and goes right back to kicking. My own chest is tight, my toes curled against the slick floor. When he stalls mid-lane, I let go of the wall, just one hand, and drift toward him, wobbling. "Here. Blow bubbles. Like this," I say, and show him, my face dipping under, my heart hammering in my ears. Up again, sputtering, I laugh. He laughs too. Neither of us is good at this. I stay beside him until he touches the far wall, and I realize my feet haven't touched bottom in three strokes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta knelt in the damp dirt with her knees aching and a seed packet pinched between muddy fingers, reading the back for the third time. A worm had surfaced where she'd dug the first trench, and she stopped, scooped it up in her cupped palm, and carried it to the shadowed edge of the bed. "Sorry, sorry. Go on, you're all right," she murmured, tucking soil over it like a blanket. Her neighbor's tomato plants leaned over the fence, tied up neatly, and one limp seedling in her own flat had already folded at the stem. She lifted it anyway, steadied it with two fingers, and pressed the earth around it with a slowness that made her wrists tremble. "Come on, little one," she said. "I've never done this either." Then she filled the watering can again, trickling it gently so nothing would wash away, and stayed there until the sun slid off her shoulders.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marisol watched Dev's slide clicker tremble in his hand, the red dot skittering across the screen like a nervous insect. He had skipped the second slide entirely and was now apologizing to it. Someone in the back checked their phone. Marisol's own stomach tightened, her fingers pressing hard into the cap of her pen. When he lost his place and the room filled with the hum of the air conditioner, she leaned forward and said, warmly, "Wait, go back to the chart with the Q3 numbers. I want to see that one again." He glanced at her, shoulders dropping an inch. She nodded slowly as he spoke, holding his eyes, and when he stumbled over a figure she wrote it down as though it mattered. At the end, while others filed out, she stayed behind, slid her coffee, still hot, across the table, and said, "That retention idea was really good. I'm stealing it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The gas station on Route 9 was the only lit thing for miles, and I almost drove past it until I saw the kid at the pump, hood up, rubbing his arms against the cold. Past midnight. I slowed, then pulled in before I'd decided anything. My chest felt tight, the way it does when I remember my own first car dying on me. "Hey," I said, rolling the window down, keeping my voice soft so I wouldn't spook him. "Dead battery?" He nodded, jaw clenched, trying not to look relieved. I dug the jumper cables out from under the spare tire, fingers numb, and told him it happened to me all the time, which was a lie, but his shoulders dropped anyway. While the engine caught, I handed him the thermos of coffee I'd been saving for the last stretch. "Keep it," I said. Then I followed his taillights a few miles, just to be sure, before turning toward home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine on the fourth floor ate my dollar twice, and I stood there anyway, pressing the button for the butterscotch candies Uncle Raymond used to keep in his truck. When I finally pushed through the door of 412, he was asleep, mouth slightly open, a bruise blooming purple around the IV. I set the candies on the tray and then moved them closer to his hand, where he could find them. My throat tightened. I pulled the vinyl chair next to the bed, slowly, so the legs wouldn't screech. His fingers looked smaller than I remembered, so I covered them with mine and kept still, though my back ached. 'Hey, old man,' I whispered. 'It's just me. Take your time.' The monitor beeped its steady, indifferent beep. When a nurse came in to check the line, I asked her, too quietly, whether he'd been warm enough, and I tugged the blanket up to his chin before she could answer.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The gate clanged open at 3:10, and kids spilled out like marbles, but I kept my eyes on the woman at the end of the fence, the one standing alone with her car keys twisted in her fist. Her son was the last one inside again. I'd seen her check her phone four times in five minutes, her jaw tight, her shoulders up near her ears. My chest felt heavy, as if I'd swallowed a stone. I shuffled down the fence line, pretending to look for my daughter, and stopped beside her. "Mine's always dawdling too," I said, softer than I meant to. "Yesterday she spent ten minutes saying goodbye to a hamster." She let out a short, shaky laugh. I held out the second coffee I'd bought for myself and hadn't touched. "It's still warm. Take it. I'll stand here with you till he comes out." Her fingers, cold, brushed mine on the cup.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The young man had circled the oak dresser three times before Marguerite noticed he was counting something under his breath, coins, probably, from the way his hand stayed buried in his jacket pocket. The tag said sixty dollars. She wiped her palms on her apron and crouched beside him to tug open a drawer that didn't need tugging. "Sticks in humid weather," she said, softly, "but it's solid. My husband built the runners himself." He mumbled that he only had forty. Her chest tightened, the way it did when her own daughter called from far away, and she glanced at the cracked baby crib he'd been avoiding looking at. "Forty's fine," she said, too quickly. "Take the crib too. It's just taking up my driveway." She bent to help him lift, ignoring the ache in her knees, and walked beside him all the way to his battered hatchback, holding the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Mrs. Okafor's kitchen floor was already a shallow pond when I got under her sink, knees soaking through my jeans, flashlight clamped in my teeth. The drip landed on my wrist, cold and steady, and I kept my voice low. "It's all right, this joint's just worn. Won't be long." Above me I could hear her slippers shuffling, the small apologetic cough she gave every few seconds. She'd been mopping with bath towels, I'd noticed, her late husband's initials stitched on the corner of one. I tightened the wrench, my shoulder cramping, and took the flashlight out of my mouth. "Hey, don't worry about the towels," I called. "Honestly, I'll stay till it's dry. Put the kettle on if you like, I won't say no." When the last drip finally stopped, I lay there a second longer than I needed to, listening to her let out a long breath, my own chest loosening along with hers.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope was addressed to Mrs. Okafor, my neighbor, but it had landed in my box again, so I carried it across the hall before my coffee cooled. She was already at her door, cardigan buttoned wrong, as if she'd heard me coming. "Would you like me to stay while you open it?" I asked, softer than I meant to. She nodded and handed it to me, her thumbs trembling. I slid a finger under the flap, slowly, the paper whispering. My own stomach tightened as I unfolded it. I kept my voice level and read the first line twice before saying anything. Then I set the letter down, took her cold hand in both of mine, and said, "It's the housing benefit. They've approved it." She sagged against the doorframe, laughing and crying. I stayed, and I put the kettle on in her kitchen, because her hands were shaking too much to do it herself.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station in Hanoi smelled of diesel and frying dough, and my phone had died somewhere over the Pacific. I stood holding my paper map like a flag of surrender when a boy, maybe nine, started crying near the ticket window, clutching a torn bus stub while a woman shouted at him in rapid, clipped syllables. My chest tightened. I knew none of the words, but I knew the way his shoulders folded inward. I set down my bag, crouched to his height, and held out the one thing I had, a crumpled packet of ginger candies. 'Here,' I said, softly, slowly, as if volume mattered less than tone. He sniffed and took one. I turned to the woman, palms open, and tapped the stub, then pointed at the clock. She stopped, exhaled, and her hand shook as she took it. I stayed until the bus came, my own train forgotten, my throat strangely warm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta sat on the damp bench at the edge of the field, her coat pulled tight, while Biscuit tore across the grass on three good legs and one stiff one. Every time the old beagle stumbled in the clover, her breath caught, and her hand rose halfway from her knee as if she could catch him from forty feet away. A boy on the path laughed when Biscuit tumbled, and she turned to him, her voice soft. "He's thirteen. He does it his own way now." The boy's smile faltered, and she added, "It's all right. Watch, he'll get up." Biscuit did, shaking out his ears, and trotted toward a crow that wasn't going anywhere. Marta's throat tightened. She pulled a treat from her pocket, held it low, and knelt in the wet grass to meet him halfway, so he wouldn't have to run the whole distance back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the radiator clanked every few bars like it wanted a solo. Marguerite, our oldest soprano, cracked on the high note again, and her hand flew to her collar. Nobody looked up from their folders. I set my cello bow across my knees and said, too brightly, "Let's take it from the pickup, my fingers keep slipping anyway." They hadn't. My chest felt tight, as if I'd been the one to crack. When we began again, I leaned toward her side of the room and played softer, giving her voice space to land. She missed it a second time. I coughed, dropped a page on purpose, and made a show of hunting for it under my chair so she'd have a few seconds to breathe. Afterward, stacking chairs, I handed her the thermos of tea I'd brought for myself. "Honestly, that passage is cruel," I told her. "I'd drop it a step if it were mine." She laughed, wet-eyed, and squeezed my wrist.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dale's wife handed me the key and said take whatever I wanted, so I started with the pencil behind the vise, the one he'd chewed flat on one end. I couldn't make myself toss it. The boxes I'd brought sat folded by the door, still empty after an hour. I kept picking up chisels and setting them back exactly where they'd been, as though he might come in and find the rack disturbed. Sawdust still lay in the creases of the radio's dial. When I turned it on, a ballgame crackled out, and I stood there with my palm flat against the bench until my throat loosened. Dale's wife appeared in the doorway with two coffees and didn't say anything. 'I'll do the heavy stuff,' I told her, too quickly. 'You don't have to come back in here. Honestly, I've got it.' Then I knelt, slowly, and began wrapping his planes in my own good flannel shirt, one at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Mina stood at the back of the crowd outside the records office, her own results forgotten in her coat pocket, watching the boy beside her bounce his heel against the concrete until it blurred. When the clerk finally pinned the sheets to the corkboard, everyone surged forward, but Mina stayed put. The boy didn't move either. His knuckles had gone pale around the strap of his bag. "Hey," she said quietly, "want me to look for you? What's the number?" He mumbled it, voice cracking on the last digit. She slipped through elbows and perfume and damp wool, ran her finger down the column, and her throat tightened before she even reached him. She walked back slowly and took his sleeve. "Retake in January," she said. "I'm sorry. Come on, there's a bench over there. I've got half a sandwich, and I'm not going anywhere."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light had gone orange behind the ridge when I saw the boy sitting on a switchback rock, one shoe untied, his knees pulled up against his chest. I should have been halfway to the car by then. My own thighs burned and the cold was starting to get into my fingers, but my feet slowed anyway. "Hey, buddy," I said, softer than I meant to, and crouched until my knees cracked. "Long day, huh?" He sniffed and nodded toward the trees. His dad had gone ahead to find the trailhead, he said, and hadn't come back. I unzipped my pack and dug out the last half of my sandwich, then my headlamp, and clicked it on to test it. My throat felt tight. I knelt and tied his shoe, double knot, my hands steady even though my pulse wasn't. "We'll walk down together," I told him. "I'll go slow. You set the pace." He slipped his cold little hand into mine, and I didn't look back at the dimming ridge.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The recipe card was soft as cloth, Grandma Odile's slanted handwriting smeared where a thumb of butter had once landed. My neighbor Dev stood in my doorway holding a bag of flour he'd bought and had no idea what to do with. His wife used to bake, he said, and his voice thinned out at the end. I pulled out a second bowl. "Sit. Your hands are warmer than mine, the dough will like that," I said, though it wasn't true. I showed him how to push with the heel of his palm, then fold, then turn. My own arms ached, but I kept slowing down so he could match me. When his shoulders dropped and he laughed at the flour on his sleeve, my throat tightened and I looked at the oven light a moment. "We'll make two loaves," I told him. "One's yours to carry home. Still warm. Promise."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta was comparing cans of tomatoes under the buzzing fluorescent lights when she saw the name stitched on the vest: Dennis. The same Dennis who had sat behind her in chemistry, who used to crack jokes until the whole room lost its place. He was kneeling by a pallet, peeling price stickers with slow, careful thumbs, and his shoulders had a stoop she didn't remember. "Dennis? It's Marta. Marta Ruiz." His face lifted, startled, then tried for a grin that didn't hold. Her chest tightened. She set the cans back, forgetting why she'd picked them up. "You look good," she said, and her voice came out softer than she meant. He laughed at the lie, and she didn't mind. "Do you get a break soon? There's a coffee place next door. I'd like to hear everything. My treat." She noticed her hand resting on his sleeve and left it there, while a cart rattled past and neither of them looked up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At ten to six on Christmas Eve, Marisol was mopping the pharmacy's front aisle when the old man shuffled in, coat buttoned wrong, rain dripping from his cap. The register was counted, the grate half down, and her feet throbbed in her sneakers. She set the mop in its bucket anyway. "Come on back, sir," she said, softer than she'd spoken all day. His prescription had lapsed, and the system wouldn't let her fill it. She chewed her lip, glanced at the clock, then called Dr. Patel's answering service and waited on hold, humming to fill the silence. "My wife's waiting," he mumbled. Her throat tightened. She pulled a chair from behind the counter and nudged it against the backs of his knees. "Sit. Ten minutes, I promise." When the approval finally came through, she counted out the pills herself, tucked a peppermint into the bag, and walked him to the door, holding the grate up with her shoulder so he wouldn't have to duck.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Gate B34 was a twelve-minute sprint away, and I was running it with my shoulder bag slamming my ribs, when I saw the old man at the moving walkway. He stood frozen at its edge, gripping a cane, staring at the belt as if it might bite. Boarding closed in nine minutes. My lungs burned. I slowed anyway. "Here, take my arm," I said, panting, and he did, his fingers trembling against my sleeve. We stepped on together. "My daughter's waiting in Denver," he murmured. "Then we'll get you to her," I said, and I meant we. My phone buzzed with a rebooking alert; I let it. At B34 the agent was lifting the desk phone to close the door. I raised my free hand and called out, "One more, please, he's here!" My calves were shaking. The man squeezed my wrist, and I realized I was smiling, sweat running down my neck, already scanning the board for the next flight to Denver, mine.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I'd taped the baseboards twice before Dana's text came: she couldn't face the yellow room anymore, could I just do it fast. Fast, I'd decided, was cruel. So I kept the roller light, and when I reached the pencil marks by the doorframe, Dana at four, six, nine, my throat went tight and my hand stopped halfway up the wall. I set the roller down in the tray. I took the little saw from the toolbox, cut that strip of drywall-thin trim free, and wrapped it in a dropcloth. 'Nothing's lost,' I said to the empty room, and my voice came out thicker than I meant. Then I painted around the spot, left a clean rectangle, and sat on the overturned bucket with paint drying on my knuckles. When Dana arrived, I handed her the bundle without a word, and rubbed my eyes with my wrist, leaving a gray streak, and asked if she wanted tea before we did the second coat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder rattled the screen door, and across the lawn I saw the neighbor's boy, maybe nine, hunched under the dripping maple with his bike beside him. I was already standing, the porch boards cool and gritty under my bare feet. "Hey! Come up here, bud," I called, louder than I meant, waving my whole arm. He hesitated, so I softened it. "I've got towels. And my wife made too much lemonade, honestly, you'd be doing me a favor." He ran, shoes slapping through puddles, and rain spattered my forearms as I held the door. I pulled the quilt off the swing and dropped it around his shoulders, rubbing his back till the shivering eased. His teeth chattered, and my own jaw ached right along with them. "Your mom know where you are?" I asked, already reaching for my phone. "Let's tell her you're safe. I'll walk you home when it lets up. No hurry at all." He nodded, and we watched the sky together.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain slips off the ring for the third time, and I stop breathing until I hear the garage door's motor groan upstairs. Not him. Just the neighbor's car. I wipe my palms on my jeans, leaving black streaks, and fit the wrench back onto the bolt. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since I walked in. Dale's toolbox sits open on the shared bench, and I keep my elbows tucked so I don't brush it. "Sorry, just borrowing the bench," I say to nobody, voice too bright, too quick. The wrench slips and my knuckle scrapes the crank. I hiss, suck the blood, and keep going. Every footstep on the gravel outside makes my shoulders climb toward my ears. The rear wheel needs truing, the brake cable is frayed, and I've got maybe twenty minutes before he's back from work. I count spokes aloud, whispering, losing track at twenty-two, starting again from one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as Marisol checked her phone for the fourth time in two minutes. 7:42. The bus was due at 7:35. She pressed her thumbnail into the pad of her finger, then switched hands and did it again. Wind shoved a plastic bag down the empty street, and she tracked it all the way to the corner before she realized her jaw ached. "Come on," she muttered, then louder, to no one, "Come on." The sky had gone the color of dishwater. She stepped out to peer down the road, stepped back in, stepped out again, her shoes slapping the wet curb. Her interview started at eight. Thunder rolled somewhere behind the rooftops and her shoulders jumped up toward her ears. She smoothed her blazer, though it was already smooth, and counted the streetlights twice. Still no headlights. Her heartbeat thudded in her throat, steady and too fast, like footsteps behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid slid off with a dry whisper, and I set it on the floor, then moved it two inches to the left, squaring it against the floorboard. Rubber-banded bundles, most of them brittle. I turned the first envelope over with my fingertips only, like it might be hot. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my molars since the attic stairs. "Just sort them," I said aloud, and my voice came out thin, a stranger's. Dates. Sort by dates. Downstairs the furnace clicked on and I flinched, knocking a stack sideways. Then I saw it: that slanted blue handwriting, my name misspelled the way only he spelled it. I wiped my palms on my jeans, once, twice. The envelope was still sealed. I put it face down under my knee, picked up the next one, and read the same postmark four times without taking in a single number, my pulse thudding in my ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta heard the knock and froze with the dish towel twisted around her fist. Through the screen door she saw Dale from next door, hands in his back pockets, smiling too easily. "Need the ladder, if you've got it," he said. She laughed, a thin sound, and said, "The ladder. Right." Her jaw ached; she realized she had been clenching it. In the garage, the aluminum rails gleamed, and she remembered the last borrowed one that had come back bent. Her shirt clung between her shoulder blades. "It's, um, heavy," she said, too quickly, then dragged it out anyway, the feet scraping loud against the concrete. Dale reached for it. She didn't let go right away. "Tomorrow," she said, her voice flat and careful. "Back by tomorrow?" He nodded. Her heartbeat kept thudding long after his gate clicked shut, and she stood there watching the empty hooks on the wall, the towel still wrung tight in her hand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The clock on the stove says 6:42, and I've read it four times in the last minute. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it around nothing. The risotto needs stirring, so I stir, but my other hand is already tearing at the parsley, and half of it ends up on the floor. "It's fine," I say aloud to the empty kitchen, too sharp, too fast. The oven light shows the chicken skin still pale. Pale. They said seven, maybe earlier, Dana's always early. My shirt sticks between my shoulder blades. I wipe my palms on my apron, then again, then pick up the wooden spoon and put it down and pick it up. Somewhere a car door thunks outside, and I freeze, ladle dripping onto the counter, listening for footsteps. Nothing. My heart is still going like I've run up stairs. I turn the burner down, then up, then down again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter, and the dish I was drying slid back into the sink without my deciding to let it go. Ten digits, no name, a area code I didn't know. I wiped my palms on my jeans, twice, and watched the screen light my knuckles blue. Three rings. Four. The refrigerator hummed too loudly, so I walked into the hallway where it was quiet, which was worse. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it. "It's probably nothing," I told the empty hallway, in a voice that came out thin and too fast. Five rings. My thumb hovered, trembling slightly, and I noticed I was holding my breath until my ears buzzed. What if it was the hospital? What if it was him? I pressed the green button, lifted the phone, and said, "Hello?" so softly I wasn't sure anything had come out. Static. Then a breath on the other end, and my heart knocked against my ribs hard enough to hurt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in Marcus's backpack since March, and now, in November, its spine pressed against his shoulder blade like a thumb. He stood in the returns line behind two freshmen, rehearsing. His palms were damp; he wiped them on his jeans, then wiped them again. When the librarian looked up, he laughed too early and too loudly. "Hi. So. This is, um, a little overdue." He slid the battered copy of Middlemarch across the counter and kept his eyes on the carpet's gray flecks. The scanner beeped. His heel began bouncing, and he pressed it flat. "I can pay whatever it is. Cash, card, I brought both." His throat clicked when he swallowed. The librarian typed, frowned at the screen, typed again. Marcus counted the ceiling tiles, got to eleven, lost his place, and started over, his fingers gripping the strap of the bag as if it might float away without him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol set the first box down on the kitchen counter and immediately picked it up again, then set it on the floor instead. The radiator ticked behind her and she flinched. "No, that's fine," she told the empty room, too loudly. She checked the lock, walked to the window, came back and checked the lock again. Her jaw ached; she realized she had been clenching her teeth since the stairwell. The movers were due back in ten minutes with the couch, and she had measured the doorway twice already, thumbnail pressed white against the tape. Upstairs, someone dragged a chair across the floor, and her shoulders crept toward her ears. She peeled tape off a box, stopped, pressed her palm flat to her sternum to feel how fast it was going, and then started peeling again, ripping too hard, the cardboard tearing along the wrong edge. "Okay," she said. "Okay. Okay."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, and Marisol stopped walking so abruptly that her coffee sloshed over her knuckles. She didn't wipe it off. Her eyes went left, then right, along the empty gravel path, over the joggers shrinking in the distance, up to the man on the next bench who was folded deep into his newspaper. Her pulse thumped in her ears. "Hello?" she said, too quietly, then again, louder, her voice cracking on the second syllable. Nobody turned. She lowered herself onto the slats, spine rigid, jaw clamped, and pinched one corner of the wallet between two fingers as though it might be hot. Her shoulders had crept up near her ears. Somewhere a dog barked and she flinched hard. Open it, or don't, she thought. If someone's watching, it looks like stealing. She counted the geese on the pond twice, lost track both times, and found she was holding her breath again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite stood on the second step of the shallow end, water at her ribs, her fingers wrapped around the steel rail until the knuckles went pale. The instructor, a teenager named Dev, said to let go and lean back. "In a second," she said, too brightly. She counted the blue tiles along the wall. Twice she rolled her shoulders, and twice they crept back up toward her ears. Somewhere behind her a child shrieked and splashed, and her whole body flinched as if the sound had touched her. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the locker room. "Okay," she said, and didn't move. Her heartbeat thudded in her throat, loud against the hum of the filter. She loosened one hand, then clamped it down again. "Just let me check my goggles." She had already checked them. She pressed them to her face, felt the rubber seal bite, and breathed in short sips, eyes fixed on the rail."Okay," she whispered again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet said plant a quarter inch deep, and I'd already read it four times, but I read it again with dirt on my thumb. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the trowel hit the soil. Eight inches apart, the packet said. I laid the ruler down, picked it up, laid it down again. "Okay," I said aloud to nobody, too brightly, like a waiter. The tomato seedlings leaned in their plastic cups, their stems thin as thread, and my hands hovered over them, unwilling to commit. A crow landed on the fence and I froze, shoulders up around my ears, until it left. Was the hole too deep? Too shallow? I dug it out and dug it again. My shirt stuck to my back though the morning was cool. When the first seedling finally went in, I pressed the soil around it so gently, so slowly, that I forgot to breathe, then gasped and laughed at how loud it sounded in the yard.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide, and I pressed my pen so hard against my notepad that the tip tore through the page. The conference room smelled like burnt coffee. Above us the vent hummed, and I counted its pulses instead of listening. Dana said the numbers came from my spreadsheet, the one I'd sent her at midnight, and my jaw locked. I glanced at the cell I'd never double-checked. My knee bounced under the table until Priya looked down at it, so I flattened my palm on my thigh and held it there. 'Sorry, could you go back one?' I asked, and my voice came out thin and too fast. Dana did. I stared at the total, rereading it, while my shirt collar clung damp against my neck. Nobody frowned. Still, I swallowed twice, reached for my water, and found the cup already empty. I crushed it anyway, slowly, hoping no one would hear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta turned the radio off at the second red light that wasn't red for anyone but her, and the silence pressed in. Her knuckles had gone pale on the wheel, and she noticed she'd been holding her breath since the underpass. Headlights appeared in the mirror and stayed there, the same distance back, through two turns she hadn't needed to take. "Come on, pass me," she muttered, voice thin, then louder, as if someone might answer. Her shoulders had climbed up toward her ears; she forced them down and they crept right back. The road to her street ran past a shuttered gas station, one buzzing light flickering over empty pumps. She slowed, sped up, slowed again. Her tongue felt dry against her teeth. When the car behind finally swung left into a dark driveway, she let out a laugh that cracked in the middle. In her own driveway she sat with the engine ticking, keys still clenched, checking the mirror one more time before she moved her hand to the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana stood outside room 412 with the paper cup of vending machine tea going cold in her hand, reading the whiteboard by the door for the third time. Nurse: Priya. Goal: walk to window. She pressed her shoulders down from around her ears and found they crept back up. Inside, the monitor beeped its slow green rhythm, and she counted it against her own pulse, which refused to match. 'Hi, Grandpa,' she said, too brightly, her voice cracking on the second word. She set the tea on the tray table, moved it, then moved it back. The plastic chair squeaked when she sat, and she winced as if she'd shouted. Her thumbnail worked at the cardboard sleeve of the cup until it shredded into small gray curls. When he stirred, she jumped, knocking her knee on the bed rail. 'Sorry. Sorry, I'm fine,' she said, though her jaw ached from clamping, and she could not remember the last full breath she'd taken.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
