Her heart was knocking against her ribs, and her cheeks ached from grinning. She pressed her palm flat to the cool plaster, then pulled out her phone, typed with clumsy thumbs, deleted it, typed again. Down the street a bus sighed. She crouched, dragged the box to the window, and sat on it, knees bouncing, staring at a fire escape and a slice of orange sky like they were hers. They were.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench slats, brown leather, curled at one corner, and I stopped so fast my coffee sloshed over my knuckles. I didn't even feel the heat. I glanced left, right, at the empty jogging path, the pigeons, the man far off throwing a ball for his dog. My heart was thumping against my ribs like a fist on a door. "Okay," I said out loud, then laughed, high and too loud, and clapped a hand over my mouth. I sat down beside it, then stood, then sat again, bouncing one knee. My fingers tingled as I picked it up. Thick. Heavier than I expected. "Oh, wow. Oh, wow, wow." I flipped it open and a driver's license smiled back, a stranger named Marguerite, and tucked behind it a folded wad of bills and a ticket stub from somewhere I'd never been. I was grinning so wide my cheeks ached. I started to run toward the park gate, wallet raised like a torch, already rehearsing the knock on her door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite let go of the wall at the shallow end, and the water kept her. She kicked once, twice, and her chin stayed above the surface, and a sound burst out of her, half laugh, half yelp, that bounced off the tiled ceiling and made the lifeguard look up. "Did you see that? Dana, did you see?" Her heart was hammering against her ribs, and her fingers tingled as if she'd touched a live wire. She was fifty-three. She had spent fifty-three years standing on the edges of things. Now she pushed off again, arms clumsy, water slapping her goggles, and swallowed a mouthful of chlorine without caring at all. Halfway to the lane rope she realized her feet weren't touching anything. She stopped, bobbed, and bounced on her toes in the water, grinning so wide her cheeks ached. "Again," she said, already turning back. "I'm doing it again. Right now. Don't say anything, just watch."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packet rattles in my fist like a tiny maraca, and I'm already out the back door in my socks, which is a mistake, because the soil is cold and wet and I don't even care. I kneel by the raised bed and my knees sink in. "Okay," I tell the dirt, too loudly, "okay, okay." My hands won't stay still. I poke a hole with my finger, a knuckle deep, just like the packet says, then drop in one pea and stare at it as if it might sprout right now. It doesn't. I laugh anyway. By the third row my jeans are brown to the thighs and my cheeks ache from grinning. I keep straightening the marker sticks, rereading words I wrote myself. When the neighbor waves over the fence, I nearly shout, "Come see! Nothing's up yet!" I water the bed twice, then a third time, humming something with no tune.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: When Dana clicked to the third slide, Priya's pen stopped mid-doodle. It was the chart, the one she'd stayed late fixing with Dana on Tuesday, and the line was climbing exactly the way they'd hoped. She sat forward so fast her chair squeaked. Her knee bounced under the table, rattling her coffee cup, and she pressed a palm flat on it without noticing. Heat crept up her neck. "Wait, go back," she blurted, then laughed at herself. "Sorry. Sorry. Can everyone see that number?" She was grinning too widely to hide it, so she stopped trying. When Dana reached the last slide, Priya was the first one clapping, loud in the quiet room, her hands stinging, her heart knocking against her ribs as if she'd been the one standing at the screen. She was already typing a message: "You did it!!!" She deleted two exclamation marks, then put them back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol missed her exit and didn't care. The highway was empty, the sodium lights smearing orange across the windshield, and she had the window down in November, cold air stinging her teeth because she couldn't stop grinning. Her hands drummed the wheel, tapping a rhythm that didn't match the radio. "Yes," she said to nobody, then louder, "Yes! Yes, they said yes!" The envelope lay open on the passenger seat, and every few seconds she glanced at it as though it might vanish. Her heart knocked against her ribs like it wanted out. At a red light with no cars in sight she smacked the dashboard, laughed until she hiccuped, and then sat there, legs bouncing, fingertips tingling. When the light turned green she pressed the gas harder than she needed to. She'd call her sister the moment she got home. No, she'd call her now. She fumbled for the phone, thumb shaking, and wasn't even sure what she would say first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marisol took the stairs to the fourth floor two at a time, the paper bag of warm pastelitos crinkling in her fist, and she was still bouncing on her toes when the elevator crowd caught up with her. Room 412. She knocked twice, then burst in without waiting. "Abuela, they said yes! The doctor said Friday, you're coming home Friday!" Her voice cracked high and she laughed at it. The monitor beeped along, and Marisol swore it kept time with her own pulse, which thudded in her ears and fingertips. She couldn't sit. She circled the bed, straightened a blanket that was already straight, kissed her grandmother's forehead, then her hand, then her forehead again. "I'm going to cook everything. The beans, the rice, all of it. You'll be sick of me." Her cheeks ached from grinning. She grabbed a pastelito, forgot to eat it, and waved it in the air as she talked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marcus had been at the fence since 2:40, though the bell wasn't until 3:15, and he'd already checked his phone eleven times to confirm the email still said what it said. His knee bounced. He kept rubbing his palms down his jeans, and when another dad nodded hello, Marcus answered much too loudly, 'Big day!' then laughed at himself for no reason. The folded acceptance letter crackled in his jacket pocket; he touched it again, just to be sure. His heart was going like he'd sprinted from the car. When the doors finally swung open and kids spilled out in a tangle of backpacks, he rose onto his toes, grinning so wide his cheeks ached. 'Priya! Priya, over here!' His voice cracked. She spotted him, tilted her head, suspicious of the wave. He was already bouncing toward her, the letter held high like a flag.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The woman in the yellow cardigan ran her palm along my grandmother's walnut dresser, and I forgot the coffee in my hand until it sloshed over my knuckles. I didn't even wipe it. "That's the original hardware," I said, too fast, voice climbing, "every drawer still slides. Watch." I yanked one out and it glided like it had been waiting years for an audience. My heart was drumming against my ribs. I'd priced it at forty dollars at six a.m., bleary and resigned, and now I was bouncing on my toes in the driveway, grinning at a stranger. "Two people already asked about the mirror," I blurted, which wasn't even true yet. She pulled out her wallet. I snatched a SOLD sticker from the roll and slapped it on so hard it crinkled, then laughed out loud and pressed my cold, shaking fingers against my cheeks to stop them stretching any wider.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay wedged under the kitchen sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, water dripping cold down her wrist, and she was grinning around the metal. The wrench bit down on the slip nut, one quarter turn, then another, and the drip that had stolen her sleep for a week slowed, stuttered, and stopped. She spat the flashlight into her palm. "No. No, no, no. Look at that!" Her voice cracked high, and she smacked the cabinet door hard enough to rattle the bottles. Her heart was knocking against the floor tiles. She wiped her hands on her jeans, slid out too fast, bumped her head, and laughed anyway. Then she crouched back down, pressed a dry paper towel to the joint, and held it up to the window light like a winning ticket. Bone dry. She did a little shuffle across the linoleum in her wet socks, phone already in hand, thumbs flying to text her brother: "Guess who's a plumber now."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope was thinner than Marisol expected, and she stood in the hallway with her coat still on, thumbnail snagging under the flap of the Department of Immigration seal. Her knees did a little bounce she couldn't stop. The paper tore crooked; she didn't care. She unfolded the page, read the first line, and then read it again out loud, her voice cracking upward halfway through the word "approved." The letter shook so hard the typeface blurred. She laughed, pressed it flat against her sternum, and spun once, knocking her keys off the table. "Papá," she said to the empty apartment, then louder, "Papá!" and grabbed her phone with fingers too clumsy to unlock it. Her cheeks ached. Her heart hammered against the paper. She read the line a third time, mouthing each word, and kicked off one shoe, then the other, bouncing barefoot on the cold tile as if the floor had turned to springs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station doors sighed open and the noise hit me all at once: loudspeakers rolling out syllables I couldn't parse, vendors calling, wheels rattling over tile. I laughed out loud, alone, and a woman beside me glanced over. "Sorry," I said, then pointed at my chest and grinned. "Lost. Good lost." My backpack straps dug into my shoulders and I barely felt them. I turned in a full circle, reading signs like puzzles, every curved character a door begging to be tried. My heart knocked against my ribs, fast, almost musical. I bought a steaming bun from a cart by pointing and holding up two fingers, and the vendor said something that made the whole queue chuckle, so I bowed, burned my tongue, and didn't care. Outside, neon bled across wet pavement. I didn't open my map. I picked a street, any street, and walked so quickly I nearly skipped, whispering the one word I'd learned over and over, like a password.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marcus had come to the fence meaning to stay for five minutes, but now his coffee sat forgotten on a post, going cold, while Biscuit tore across the wet grass in great looping circles, ears flipped inside out. "Look at him! Look at that!" he shouted to no one, to the empty hayfield, to a crow on the wire. His heart was hammering as though he were the one running. When the dog skidded, spun, and launched himself at a tuft of tall weeds, Marcus let out a bark of laughter and slapped the rail so hard his palm stung. He was bouncing on his toes. His cheeks ached from grinning, and his hands wouldn't stay still; he pulled out his phone, fumbled it, caught it, and filmed with a wobbling arm. "Again," he whispered, then yelled it. "Do it again, buddy!" Biscuit did.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite got to the church hall forty minutes early and still couldn't sit. She paced between the folding chairs, humming the opening bars of her solo, her fingers drumming her thigh in triplets. When the pianist, Doyle, finally shuffled in with his sheet music, she was already at the upright, tapping middle C. "Again from the top? Please? Just once more?" The words tumbled out too fast, and she laughed at herself. Her heart knocked against her ribs as she took her place by the radiator, and her palms, damp, left prints on the hymnal. Doyle played the intro. She sang, and the last note rang off the rafters and the stacked tea urns, and her knees nearly bounced her off the floor. Nobody was there but a janitor and a sleeping dog, yet she bowed anyway, grinning so wide her cheeks ached. "Tell me Thursday's coming faster," she said, already flipping back to page one.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Behind the paint cans, wedged between two warped planks, my fingers closed on a canvas roll, and I stopped breathing. Dust coated my tongue. I dragged the thing into the light of the one bare bulb and unrolled it across Walt's workbench, pinning the corners with his chisels, my hands shaking so badly one chisel clattered to the floor. "No," I said aloud, then laughed, too loud for the little room. "No way. You old liar." The drawings were all there, the ones he swore he'd burned in '94, every line of the cabinet design he'd said couldn't be done. My heart knocked against my ribs. I realized I was bouncing on my heels, grinning at a dead man's sawdust. I grabbed my phone, dropped it, grabbed it again, and nearly dialed Marit before I noticed the trash bags still lying folded by the door, forgotten, waiting for a job I no longer meant to do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: At 11:58, Mina had already refreshed the portal nine times, and the corridor outside the registrar's office hummed with the same restless buzz that was running up her arms. She couldn't keep her heels on the floor; they bounced, drumming the linoleum, until a boy beside her glanced over and she grinned at him like they shared a secret. "Two minutes," she said, too loudly, then laughed at her own voice. Her palms were damp against the phone, her cheeks hot, her breath quick and shallow as if she'd just climbed four flights of stairs. She rehearsed a casual shrug, abandoned it, and instead spun in a full circle by the noticeboard. The page flickered. Her stomach lurched upward. She pressed the screen to her chest, squeezed her eyes shut, counted to three, and whispered, "Okay, okay, okay," already half-leaping toward whatever came next.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Mara took the last switchback at a jog, poles clacking, her headlamp still zipped in her pocket because she wanted every remaining scrap of orange. The ridge opened ahead of her and the wind hit her damp collar, and she laughed out loud, a short, cracked bark that startled a junco off a juniper. Her heart knocked against her ribs; her fingers tingled inside her gloves. "Look at that," she said to no one, then louder, "Look at that!" The valley below had gone the color of plums, and a single star was already pricking through above the far peak. She should have turned back an hour ago. Instead she bounced on her toes, grinning so hard her cheeks ached, and pulled out her phone with shaking hands, only to shove it away again. No photo would hold this. She tightened her pack straps and ran the next stretch downhill, boots slapping, breath streaming white behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Flour is already on my elbows, my phone, and somehow my left eyebrow, and I haven't even finished the first step. Grandma Ruth's index card is propped against the salt jar, her slanted handwriting smudged with butter from decades ago. "Warm water, warm like a baby's bath," I read aloud, laughing, bouncing on my toes while I dip a finger in. My heart is going fast, as if I've run up the stairs. I knead, and the dough pushes back, and I say, "Oh, come on, you're alive!" to an empty kitchen. Every few minutes I lift the towel off the bowl to peek, grinning like a fool. When the first rise doubles, I actually yelp. I text my sister a photo, then three more, my thumbs tripping over each other. Then the smell starts creeping from the oven, yeasty and sweet, and I press both hands to my cheeks, pacing circles on the tile, unable to sit down at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was comparing two cans of tomatoes under the hardware-store-bright lights of the grocery when a voice behind me said, "Marcy Delgado?" I knew it before I turned. Dana Whitfield, who'd shared my locker in ninth grade, who'd passed me notes folded into tiny triangles. The can slipped from my hand and rolled somewhere under the shelf, and I didn't care. "No way," I said, too loud, my voice cracking upward. My cheeks ached from grinning. I grabbed both her forearms like she might evaporate, and my heart was knocking against my ribs. "You cut your hair! You still have the chipped tooth!" A man steered his cart around us, and I barely noticed. I was bouncing on my toes between the cereal and the canned goods. "Do you have twenty minutes? Forty? I'll abandon this whole cart, I swear." My fingers were already pulling out my phone to trade numbers, my thumb missing the screen twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The clock over the pharmacy counter says 4:47, and I've already wiped the same stretch of laminate three times. Mrs. Okafor asks if her prescription is ready, and I answer so fast I nearly trip over my own words, "Yes, yes, right here, merry everything!" My knees keep bouncing under the register, a little drumbeat I can't stop. Outside, snow is slanting past the window and the parking lot is emptying, car by car, and every set of taillights makes my chest fizz like a shaken soda. I've got a duffel bag stuffed behind the shelves, a bus ticket folded in my sock, and four days of nothing ahead of me but my sister's couch and my nephew's lopsided cookies. I catch myself humming the jingle from the store speakers, off-key, grinning at the cough drops. When my manager flips the sign to CLOSED, I actually whoop, then clap a hand over my mouth, then laugh into my palm until my eyes sting.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board flashes Gate C41, and I'm already running, laptop bag slamming my hip, sneakers squeaking on polished floor. Twenty-two minutes. I laugh out loud at nothing, and a man with a coffee jumps aside. "Sorry! Flight to Lisbon!" I shout, as if that explains everything. My heart is pounding so hard I can feel it in my teeth, and my hands tingle, fingers drumming my thigh whenever I'm not pumping my arms. The moving walkway is too slow, so I keep sprinting along it, passing couples who stand there like statues. I grin at a gate agent who stares at me. Escalator, left, right, a long glass corridor full of gold afternoon light. I can't stop saying, "Come on, come on, come on," in a voice that cracks upward. Ahead, the C41 sign glows. A woman is lifting the microphone. I wave both arms over my head, ticket crumpled in my fist, and yell, "Wait for me!" My legs feel like they could carry me across the ocean.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol pried the lid off the paint can with a butter knife and nearly dropped it, her hands were jittering so badly. The yellow inside was brighter than the swatch, almost loud, and she laughed out loud in the empty hallway. "Oh, look at you," she told the can. She stirred far longer than she needed to, bouncing on her toes, then dragged the roller through the tray and pressed it to the old gray wall. One stripe. She stepped back, stepped forward, touched the wet edge with a fingertip just to be sure it was real. Her heart knocked against her ribs. She hadn't eaten since breakfast and didn't care. She grabbed her phone, typed with a speckled thumb, deleted it, and called her sister instead. "You have to come see this," she said, breathless, already rolling another stripe, her cheeks sore from grinning. "No, now. Right now. Bring coffee. Bring everyone."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the porch boards, and I was on my feet before the echo died, coffee mug abandoned on the rail. "Again," I whispered, then louder, to nobody, "Come on, again!" The air smelled of hot asphalt and cut metal. My palms were damp, my heart knocking against my ribs like it wanted out to join the weather. I dragged my chair to the very edge of the steps, where the wind flung rain across my shins, and I laughed, a short, cracked bark that startled me. Lightning split the sky above the maple across the street, white and total, and I counted without meaning to: one, two, three. Every hair on my arms stood up. I bounced on my toes, grinning so hard my cheeks ached. Mrs. Alvarez peered from her window, and I waved at her with both arms, soaked to the elbows. "Did you see that?" I shouted. I hadn't sat back down. I didn't plan to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had read the same line of the derailleur diagram three times before she noticed she was holding the hex key upside down. Behind her, a neighbor's dryer-vent fan hummed through the shared garage, and the sound seemed to press on her eyelids. She crouched by the upturned bicycle, then sat on the cold concrete instead, back against a stack of paint cans. The chain slid from her greasy fingers twice. "Okay," she told the wheel, her voice low and scraped flat. "Okay. Just one more." Her head dipped and jerked up. She rubbed her eye with a knuckle and left a black smear across her brow. The clock over the workbench said eleven-forty; she had meant to be upstairs by nine. She leaned her cheek against the saddle's worn leather, just for a second, and let the bolt roll out of her palm and ping somewhere under the shelves. She didn't go after it. She watched where it had gone, blinking slowly, for a long time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was still reading the timetable for the third time, her lips moving over times she had already forgotten. She lowered herself onto the cold bench and let her bag slide off her shoulder without catching it. Wind shoved a flurry of leaves across the road, and the sky went the color of wet slate. Her eyelids kept sinking; she propped her chin on her fist and her elbow slowly gave way. "Come on," she muttered to the empty street, the words dragging like boots through mud. A gust sprayed her ankles. She noticed, distantly, that she ought to move her feet, and didn't. Her coat hung open, the zipper somewhere past the effort of reaching it. When headlights finally swam through the rain, she stared at them a full breath before standing, one hand braced on her knee, the other fumbling for a fare card she couldn't remember putting anywhere.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box sits on my knees because the floor is too far to reach. I lift the first envelope and read the same line three times before the words stay put. Postmark 1987. My thumb leaves a smear on the flap, and I wipe it on my sleeve, then forget why. The lamp hums. Somewhere past midnight, probably; I haven't checked. I tell the empty room, "Just one more," and my voice comes out scraped and slow, like it's dragging something. My eyes keep sliding shut on Dad's looping handwriting, and I pry them open, blink hard, and lose my place again. The pile for keeping is two letters tall. The pile for the bin is nothing. My neck droops, my chin nearly touching my collarbone, and the paper slips from my fingers onto the carpet. I watch it lie there. Picking it up seems like a problem for the morning, so I lean my head against the cool wall and hold the next one without opening it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The doorbell caught me halfway down the hallway, one hand braced on the wall. Gary from next door stood on the mat, grinning, asking if I still had that ladder. I leaned my forehead against the edge of the door before I noticed I was doing it. "Garage," I said. "Behind the bikes." My voice came out low and scraped, like it had been dragged over gravel. He waited. I looked at the stairs down to the garage, at the dishes stacked in the sink behind me, at the blanket crumpled on the couch where I'd meant to stay all afternoon. "Take it. Bring it back whenever." My eyelids kept sliding down while he thanked me, and I nodded at the wrong moments. When the door finally clicked shut, I slid down it until the floor met me, and listened to the ladder scrape and clang across the driveway, far away, like something happening to someone else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta read the same line of the recipe three times before the words held still. The onions sat half-chopped on the board, and she leaned her hip against the counter, knife loose in her hand, watching steam fog the window over the sink. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears sometime in the last hour; she dropped them, and they crept back. "Two cups," she muttered, then stood there holding the measuring cup, unsure whether she'd already added the first. She tipped in one more anyway. The oven timer buzzed and she flinched, then stared at it a moment too long before pressing the button. Her eyelids kept sliding down while she stirred, and twice the spoon scraped the pot's bottom with a harsh rasp. When the doorbell chimed early, she looked at the clock, then at the unset table, and let out a long breath through her nose. She wiped her hands on her apron, smoothed her hair, and called, "Coming," in a voice flatter than she meant.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, skittering toward a stack of unopened mail, and Marisol watched it for three full rings before she moved. Her hand found it without her head leaving the crook of her arm. Unknown number, a city she didn't recognize. Her thumb dragged across the glass. "Hm. Yeah," she said, the words coming out low and scraped, half of each one missing. The voice on the line was bright and fast, something about her car's warranty, and she blinked slowly at the dish rack, losing the thread after the first sentence. Her eyelids kept dropping and she let them. "Sorry," she said. "Say that again?" She didn't wait for it. She slid down until her cheek met the cool laminate, the phone sagging against her ear, and murmured, "Can you just take me off the list," before the screen dimmed in her loose fingers and the refrigerator hummed on alone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Mina pushed the library door with her shoulder instead of her hand and stood a moment in the hum of the fluorescent lights, blinking at the brightness. The book, a thick organic chemistry text, slid out of her backpack and thudded onto the return desk harder than she meant. "It's, um. It's from March," she said, her voice scraped low, and she had to start the sentence twice. The clerk tapped the keyboard. Mina watched the screen without reading it, her eyelids dropping and snapping back up. She leaned her elbow on the counter, then her cheek on her fist. "How much?" The number came, and she nodded slowly, a beat too late, and dug through her wallet with fingers that fumbled the same card twice. Her yawn arrived mid-apology, and she hid it behind her sleeve. "Sorry. Where do I sign?" she asked, already swaying toward the pen, thinking only of her bed and the dark ceiling above it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box says KITCHEN in my own handwriting, and I stare at it like it's written in another language. I sit down on it instead. The cardboard sags. Somewhere above me a neighbor's footsteps cross the ceiling, and I follow the sound with my eyes because turning my head is too much. My arms hang off me like wet laundry. The movers left an hour ago, and I still haven't found the sheets, so the mattress sits bare against the wall, and I decide that's fine. I try to fill a glass at the sink, forget why I'm holding it, and drink straight from the tap. 'Okay,' I say aloud to the empty room, my voice scraped and flat. 'Tomorrow.' I lower myself onto the mattress with my shoes still on, one hand pressed over my gritty eyes, the fluorescent bulb humming on above me because the switch is across the room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench was the only thing I'd aimed for, and I lowered myself onto it in stages, hands on my knees, a groan leaking out before I could stop it. Streetlamps buzzed on. My eyelids kept sliding down, and I propped them open by staring at a pigeon that wasn't doing anything. Then I noticed the wallet beside my hip, brown leather, curled at the corners. It took me three tries to lift it, my fingers feeling like wet rope. Inside: a driver's license, forty dollars, a photo of a kid missing front teeth. "Dale Pruitt," I read aloud, my voice scraped thin. "Okay, Dale. Okay." I should have jumped up and hurried to the police station on Alder. Instead I rested my head against the slats, the wallet warm on my chest, and told myself I'd go in just a minute. The pigeon left first. I counted slowly to ten, lost my place at six, and started over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite gripped the pool's edge with both hands and let her forehead rest against the cold tile. Her legs hung beneath her like wet rope. "One more length," she told the instructor, though it came out as a mumble, and she had to say it again. The lifeguard's whistle sounded far off, underwater almost. She pushed away from the wall, kicked twice, and felt her feet sink before she'd reached the flags. Her arms rose out of the water slowly, each one heavier than the last, dripping like laundry she couldn't wring. She stopped, stood on the pool floor, and stared at the lane rope for a long moment, counting the blue floats and losing track at six. Her eyelids kept drifting shut against the chlorine glare. "Maybe I'll just float a little," she said, and leaned back, letting the water hold what she couldn't, her breath coming in long, ragged pulls while the ceiling lights smeared into white streaks above her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Maren knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned in her lap, reading the back of the tomato one for the third time because the words kept sliding off. The trowel felt heavier than it had at the hardware store. She dug a hole, sat back on her heels, and stayed there while the sun crept across the fence. "Six inches apart," she told the dog, her voice thin and slow. "Or was it twelve." Her shoulders had rounded forward without her permission, and when she reached for the water jug her hand trembled slightly and she let it rest on the cool plastic a moment too long. Dirt had worked into the cracks of her knuckles. She pressed one seedling into the ground, patted it twice, then lay down on her side in the grass beside the bed, cheek against the clover, eyes half shut. Eleven more seedlings waited in their tray. "In a minute," she said to them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus's slides had been on the screen for ten minutes before Dana realized she'd read the same bullet point four times. She propped her chin on her fist, and her elbow slid a little on the conference table. The projector's hum seemed to grow thicker, softer, like a blanket. Marcus said something about Q3 adoption curves, and her eyes drifted shut for what felt like one blink, then jerked open when someone laughed. She pressed her thumbnail into her palm. 'Sorry, could you go back one?' she asked, her voice scraped low, and she cleared her throat twice. Her coffee cup, third of the day, held only a cold brown ring. She reached for her pen, uncapped it, and wrote the date at the top of a blank page. Then she stared at it, the numbers swimming slightly, and wondered how long she could keep her head upright if she didn't have to nod. The window blinds striped the wall in gold. She thought about her couch.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway lights smear into long yellow threads, and I blink slowly, once, twice, and the road jumps a little closer each time. I've rolled the window down, but the cold air only makes my eyelids feel heavier, like wet paper. "Almost there," I tell the empty passenger seat, and my voice comes out as a gravelly mumble. The exit sign slides past before I've read it. I swear, jerk the wheel, and my heart bangs once, hard, then settles into a dull thud. My neck keeps drooping toward my chest. I pinch the back of my hand, crank the radio to a song I hate, and sing half the words wrong. The stoplight at Alder Street is red, and I stare at it so long that the car behind me honks. Green. I hadn't noticed. My driveway feels miles away, and all I can think about is the exact weight of my pillow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus read the same line on the visitor sign-in sheet three times before his pen found the box for the time. The elevator doors opened on four and he stood there until they started to close, then jammed his hand between them. In Room 412 his grandmother's monitor beeped its slow green rhythm, and he lowered himself into the vinyl chair, which exhaled under him. "Hi, Nana," he said, the words coming out low and scraped. She was asleep. He meant to tell her about the drive, but his eyes kept sliding shut, and the blanket at her feet looked wonderfully soft. He propped his chin on his fist. His elbow slipped off the armrest, and he jerked upright, heart thudding, and pretended to study the whiteboard where a nurse had written TODAY IS THURSDAY. Was it? He rubbed his gritty eyes with the heel of his hand, took her cool fingers in his, and let his head tip back against the wall just for a minute.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana leaned against the chain-link fence with her car keys still clenched in her fist, though the car was parked a block away. The bell hadn't rung yet. She read the same sentence on her phone three times, then gave up and watched a crossing guard's whistle swing on its cord. Her eyelids kept sliding down, and each time she dragged them open, the sun-bright blacktop swam. When another mother asked how her week was going, Dana said, "Fine. Long. Fine," and laughed at nothing, a beat too late. She shifted her weight from one foot to the other, then slid down until she was half sitting on the low brick ledge, her bag slumped beside her. Somewhere behind her ribs, a dull hum. The doors banged open and small bodies spilled out. She lifted a hand to wave, found it heavy, and let it fall back to her knee. "Over here, bug," she said, barely louder than the wind. "I'm right here."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By the time the man with the toddler asked about the oak dresser, I had been sitting on its bottom drawer for an hour, because the lawn chair sold at seven. "Forty," I said, then "Thirty-five," before he could answer, since haggling meant standing, and standing meant talking. He ran his thumb along the scratch my mother's cat made in 1994. I watched his mouth move and caught maybe half of it. My eyelids kept sliding down like old window blinds, and I propped my chin on my fist, which worked until my elbow slipped off my knee. The coffee in my mug had gone cold and skinned over; I drank it anyway. "Sure, take it," I said. "Just carry it yourself, okay?" He laughed, thinking I was joking. Afterward I counted the bills twice, lost track, counted again, then lay down on the bare mattress by the curb, in full view of the street, and let the sun settle on my face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slips off the nut for the third time, and I just watch it clatter into the cabinet's dark corner without swearing. The clock on the stove says 2:40, or maybe I read it wrong; the numbers swim a little. I lie on my side on the wet tile, cheek almost against the cold floor, and let the drip land on my wrist because moving feels like a negotiation. "Okay," I say to the pipe, slow, my voice scraped thin. "Okay. One more." I read the instructions on the plumber's tape package twice and still can't say what they told me. My eyelids keep dropping while my hands hold the joint. Water runs down my sleeve. I think about the bed, the exact weight of the blanket, and then I reach for the wrench again, my arm heavy as a sandbag, and fumble it twice before it finally bites.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been leaning against the toaster since Tuesday, and tonight I finally pick it up with the hand that isn't holding my forehead. Return address: Department of Revenue. I sit on the kitchen floor because the chair seems too far away. My thumb fumbles under the flap three times before it catches. The paper inside is folded in thirds, crisp, smelling of printer toner, and I read the first line, then read it again, because the words slide off like water. Reference number. Please respond within thirty days. I laugh, a short dry puff, and say to the empty kitchen, "Sure. Thirty days." My eyelids keep drifting down mid-sentence. The refrigerator hums and I find myself matching my breathing to it. I should find a pen. I should call the number. Instead I lay the letter across my knees, rest my head against the cabinet door, and decide the second page can meet me in the morning.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station clock says 11:40, or maybe that's the other clock, the one that has stopped. I stand beneath the signs with my backpack hanging off one shoulder because lifting it the rest of the way feels like a negotiation I'd lose. The characters swim. I read the same line three times and it gives me nothing. A man says something quick and kind, and I nod, then nod again, then say "Hotel?" and hold up my phone, which has gone dark. My eyelids scrape when I blink. I lean against a pillar that smells of rain and fried dough, and my knees ask to be bent. He points: left, right, left. I repeat, "Left," like a prayer. Outside, the street hums with neon, too loud, too bright. I drag my suitcase over the cobbles, its wheels clattering, and decide the first bench I see is a perfectly good hotel. My jaw cracks open in a yawn that doesn't end.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marnie lowered herself onto the damp bench by the fence and let the leash pool in her lap. Out in the long grass, Biscuit tore in wide circles, ears flapping, chasing nothing she could see. "Good girl," she called, but it came out thin and flat, and the dog didn't even turn. Her eyelids kept sliding down, and she dragged them open again, blinking at the gold blur of the field. Her neck felt too weak for her head, so she propped her chin on her fist, and the fist slowly sank toward her collarbone. Somewhere a thermos sat in her bag, unopened, and she couldn't make her arm go for it. When Biscuit bounded over with a muddy stick, Marnie took it, held it a moment, and tossed it barely a yard. "Again in a minute," she murmured, and listened to her own slow breathing while the light went soft and long across the grass.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I'm on my third pass through the Schubert, the folding chair creaking whenever I lean toward the music stand. My bow arm has gone heavy, and the E string keeps slipping sharp because my fingers don't land where I send them. "Again from the repeat?" Marguerite calls, and I say, "Sure," though it comes out as a long breath with a word stuck to it. I read the same four bars twice without hearing them. The fluorescent light hums, and I catch myself staring at the water stain on the ceiling tile, shaped like Ohio. My eyelids drag down on the rests. When the cellist laughs at something, I laugh a beat late. Saturday's program is taped to the wall, my name in small type. I rub my left shoulder, lift the violin, and wonder if anyone would notice if I played the next page sitting on the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marek's coffee can of screws sits in my lap, and I have been holding it for a while without sorting a single one. The sawdust smell has gotten into my sleeves. I read the label on a jar of bolts twice, then a third time, and still couldn't tell you what it said. Four boxes are packed. Forty remain, give or take. I lower myself onto his stool, and my knees pop like kindling. 'Just the pegboard,' I tell the empty room, my voice scraping low. 'Then the pegboard's done.' My eyes keep sliding shut against the buzzing fluorescent tube, and I let them, just for a breath, my cheek nearly touching the cool edge of the vise. When I look up, the light has gone orange in the window. I haven't touched the pegboard. I set the can down very gently, as if it might wake, and sit there with my hands open on my thighs, unable to decide which one to lift first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and Mara had been refreshing it since eleven, her chin propped on a fist that kept sliding off the edge of the desk. The page loaded the same gray box each time. She read the same line of the syllabus three times without it turning into words. Her roommate's voice drifted in from the doorway, asking if she wanted toast, and Mara answered a beat late, "Mm. Sure. Whatever," the words mushy in her mouth. The mug beside her had gone cold hours ago, a skin wrinkling on top. She blinked slowly, and the blink lasted longer than she meant it to. Her eyelids felt sanded. When the clock flipped to 12:00 she leaned forward, shoulders heavy as wet towels, and pressed the key. The box spun. She let her forehead drop gently onto the cool edge of the laptop, just for a second, and breathed out. Then she lifted it again, and waited for the numbers to appear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The switchbacks had stopped being something Mara counted. She watched her boots instead, each one landing a little shorter than the last, the toe of her left catching a root and nearly pitching her into the ferns. "Okay," she told the trail, voice flat and scraped. "Okay, okay." Her pack straps had worn two hot grooves into her shoulders, and she hooked her thumbs under them and leaned forward as if towing the whole mountain. The light had gone amber, then the color of weak tea, and the trunks ahead blurred together into one gray wall. She stopped at a flat boulder and sat without deciding to. Her thighs trembled. She looked at the water bottle in her hand for a long moment before unscrewing it, and the last swallow tasted like metal. Somewhere below, the parking lot waited. She stared at the dim path, then at her knees, and slowly, with both palms pressed against them, pushed herself up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, Grandma Odile's slanted hand gone pale under old butter stains. Mara read the first line three times before the words held still. "Two cups," she mumbled, and tipped flour in, then stared at the cloud drifting over the counter and the floor and her sleeve. She had measured the salt already. Had she? She dipped a finger in the bowl and tasted, frowning. Kneading, she leaned her whole weight on the dough, and her forehead drifted down until it nearly touched the heel of her hand. Her eyelids kept sliding shut. The clock ticked somewhere far off. She propped her hip against the cabinet, let her arms hang, and breathed out long. "Just ten minutes," she told the bowl, voice thick and flat. She dragged a chair over, sat, and rested her cheek on the cool, floury card, the oven still ticking as it warmed for a loaf she would pull out hours later than planned.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a carton of milk against my cheek, eyes closed, just for the cold of it, when someone said my name beside the dairy case. Dana Whitfield, from tenth-grade chemistry. She looked exactly the same, which seemed unfair. "Wow, hi," I said, a beat too slow, and the words came out flat and scraped. She talked about Denver, a husband, a half marathon. I nodded at the right places. My eyelids kept sinking, and I blinked hard to haul them up. I shifted my weight from one foot to the other, then leaned a hip on the cart handle. The fluorescent hum was drilling into my skull. "You look great," I told her, and meant it, though I lost her next sentence entirely. "Sorry, what?" She laughed and repeated it. I said we should get coffee sometime. We both knew I wouldn't. In the checkout line I realized I was holding only the milk, and the cart sat abandoned by the yogurt, and I just kept going.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: Marisol read the same line on the pharmacy label three times before the letters held still. Outside, the parking lot had emptied hours ago, and the fluorescent hum seemed to grow louder with each customer who didn't come. She propped her chin on her fist, and her elbow slid an inch across the counter before she caught it. "Pickup for Delgado?" she asked the man at the window, then realized she was holding his bag already, and he was already reaching for it. "Sorry. Yes. Here." Her eyelids dragged down on the blink and took a moment to come back up. Someone had taped a paper turkey to the register, its feathers curling in the heat from the vent. Four more hours. She counted the remaining bottles on the shelf instead of the minutes, lost track at nineteen, and began again. When her phone buzzed with her sister's text, *what time are you getting here tomorrow?*, she stared at it, thumb hovering, and set it face down without answering.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says Gate B47, and I read it three times before the numbers hold still. My carry-on strap has carved a groove into my shoulder, and I switch sides without breaking stride, though my stride is more of a drag now. Somewhere past the moving walkway that isn't moving, I stop to lean on a pillar, just for a second, my forehead against the cool laminate. A man in a suit passes me twice. 'Sir? Boarding closes in six,' a gate agent calls, and I try to answer but only a croak comes out, so I lift the boarding pass like a flag. My eyes burn when I blink, and blinking takes longer than it should. I've been awake since a hotel clock said 3:40, or maybe that was yesterday's. I laugh at nothing. Then I run, sort of, knees loose as wet rope, and think only: chair, window, dark, please.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol dragged the roller up the wall for the third time and watched the old yellow bleed through anyway. Her arm had begun to tremble somewhere around the window, a fine buzz she tried to ignore by gripping the handle harder. She set the roller in the tray and lowered herself onto the overturned bucket, then stayed there, staring at the unopened second can by the door. The radio murmured the same song it had played an hour ago, or maybe a different one. 'Just the corner,' she said aloud, her voice flat and slow, and didn't move. A drip slid down the baseboard. She blinked, and the blink lasted longer than she meant it to. Her eyes stung from the fumes, and she pressed the back of a speckled wrist against them. When she finally stood, her knees cracked, and she steadied herself against the half-wet wall, leaving a pale palm print she was too weary to wipe away. 'Tomorrow,' she told the room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail just as Marguerite lowered herself into the wicker chair, and she didn't get up to pull the cushions in. Thunder rolled over the cornfield. She watched the sky go the color of a bruise and let her hands hang off the armrests, fingers swaying a little with the wind. Her boots were still laced. She meant to loosen them, and had meant to for some time. Inside, the phone rang twice, then quit, and she only nodded at it. Rain blew sideways across her shins; she noticed the wet the way you notice a stranger's cough. 'Well,' she said to the dog, her voice scraped low and slow, 'there goes the laundry.' The dog sighed and put its chin on her foot. Her eyelids dropped, lifted, dropped. A lightning flash lit the yard white, and she counted aloud, 'One, two,' and lost the thread of three somewhere in the roar of the gutters.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had been truing the same wheel for forty minutes, and it still wobbled. She gave the spoke wrench a quarter turn, spun the rim, watched it hitch at the same spot, and swore under her breath. Across the garage, her neighbor's radio murmured a song she knew too well, and her jaw tightened until her teeth ached. The bike was Daniel's. His initials were scratched into the top tube, and a faded sticker curled on the fender. She wiped her palms on her jeans, but they kept slicking again. "Fine," she said, too softly, then louder, "Fine, fine." She dropped the wrench; it rang against the concrete and she flinched as if it had been a shout. For a long moment she stood with her forehead against the cold seat post, breathing through her mouth. Then she picked the wrench up, checked the door for footsteps, and turned the nipple again, though she already knew she would never be able to give the bike back, or ride it, or sell it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof just as Marit pulled the phone from her coat for the ninth time. Still nothing from him. She typed three words, deleted them, typed them again, and her thumb hovered until the screen dimmed to black. Wind shoved a sheet of newspaper along the curb; she watched it as though it might say something. Her jaw ached from clenching. 'Come on,' she muttered to the empty street, then louder, 'come on,' though she couldn't have said whether she meant the bus or the phone. Rain slanted in under the awning and soaked her left sleeve, and she didn't move away from it. Her stomach turned over whenever headlights swung around the corner, and each time they weren't the bus, she exhaled hard, almost a laugh. She dug her nails into her palm until the skin whitened. Thunder rolled. She flinched, then checked the phone again, and the glow lit her wet, unblinking eyes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid had been off for three hours, and Marta still hadn't read a single page through. She'd pick one up, see the slanted blue handwriting, and set it face-down on the carpet, then pick up another. Her jaw ached from clenching. The radiator ticked; she flinched at it. "Not that one," she said aloud to the empty room, voice thin, and shoved a yellowed envelope under her knee as though it might crawl off. Her thumb kept finding the same torn corner. At the bottom of the box lay the letter she'd never answered, its postmark ten years old. She lifted it, held it to her nose, and her breath came in short, shallow pulls. Then she folded it into her cardigan pocket, stood, sat back down, and began stacking the others by date again, hands trembling so badly the edges would not line up. The tea beside her had gone cold and filmed over. She did not drink it. She started the stack over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta heard the knock and kept her hands in the dishwater until it went cold. Through the screen door she could see Dale on her porch, cap in his hands, pointing vaguely toward his gutters. "Just for an hour," he said. "Sure," she said, too quickly, and her voice came out thin. Her jaw ached. The ladder hung in the garage where Henry had hung it, one rung still marked with his thumbprint of paint. She walked out there slowly, the concrete chilly through her socks, and stood with her palm flat against the aluminum, her pulse loud in her ears. She lifted it down, set it back, lifted it again. "It's heavy," she called, though it wasn't. Dale waited at the edge of the driveway. She wiped her hands on her sweater over and over, then carried the ladder out herself, gripping the painted rung, and would not let him take that end.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marit stirred the risotto with one hand and held her phone in the other, thumb hovering over a message she had typed and deleted four times. Seven minutes. The stock had gone cold in its pot, and she ladled it in anyway, watching the rice clump. "Fine," she whispered. "It's fine." Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth since the chicken. A knife slipped through the parsley, too fast, and she stopped to stare at the pink line across her knuckle without feeling it. Down the hall, his coat still hung on its hook, and every time she passed she turned her face away. The oven timer shrieked. She jumped, knocked a spoon to the floor, and stood there with her palms flat on the counter, breathing through her mouth, laughing once at nothing. Then she picked up the spoon, wiped it on her apron, and kept stirring. The doorbell rang. She smiled at the wall first, practicing it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the counter at 2:14 a.m., and I'm already standing over it, though I don't remember getting up. Unknown number. Area code I almost recognize. I press my thumb to the glass edge and pull it back like it's a stove. Four rings. Five. My jaw aches; I've been clenching it for what feels like hours. I pace the length of the kitchen, tile cold under my bare feet, then back again, counting the cracks. "Don't," I whisper to the room. "Don't pick up." My hand picks up. The line hisses. Nobody speaks, and I hear my own breath, too fast, too loud, scraping out of me. "Hello?" It comes out cracked. "Is that... who is this?" My free hand has found the sink and is gripping it so hard the knuckles look wet and white. The silence goes on. I should hang up. I slide down against the cabinet, the phone pressed so tight to my ear it hurts, and I stay there, waiting for a voice I'm terrified to hear and more terrified to miss.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in Marcus's backpack since March, and now, in November, its corners had gone soft against his laptop. He stood outside the library doors for eleven minutes, thumb worrying the cracked spine, before the glass slid open without his permission. Cold air, floor wax, the hush. His shirt stuck to his back. At the desk he set the book down and pushed it forward with two fingers, as if it might go off. "This is, um. This is overdue," he said, too quickly, then laughed at nothing. The librarian reached for it and he almost pulled it back. "How long?" she asked. His throat clicked when he swallowed. "Since the, uh. Since spring." He stared at the faded date stamp, counting without wanting to. He'd rehearsed apologies all night, lying awake, and now every one had dissolved. His empty hands wouldn't stay still; he shoved them into his pockets, then pulled them out again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta carried the last box up four flights and set it down in the middle of the room, and then she just stood there, thumb working the tape until it peeled in a long, sticky strip. One window. A radiator that ticked like someone knocking. She opened the closet, closed it, opened it again, as if the shelves might have rearranged themselves. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the stairs. "Fine," she said aloud, too brightly, to nobody. "It's fine. It's small. Small is fine." The words came out thin and bounced off the bare walls. She unpacked one mug, then sat on the floor with it in both hands, listening to the neighbors' television through the plaster, the same game show he used to put on. Her stomach turned over. She stood, washed the clean mug, dried it, and washed it again, water running hot over her wrists until the skin went red, because stopping meant the quiet would find her, and she could not stay still enough for that.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, and Marta walked past it twice before she sat down beside it. Her thumb found the cracked edge and pulled back. Inside, a license, a school photo of a gap-toothed girl, and a fold of twenties thick enough to cover the rent she owed. She shut it. Opened it. Shut it. "Not mine," she said aloud to a pigeon, her voice scraping. A jogger passed and she jerked her hand into her lap like a child caught stealing. Her stomach clenched; the sandwich in her bag turned to paste at the thought of it. She counted the bills without meaning to, lost the number, started again, her fingers damp and shaking. The streetlamps flickered on. She stood, sat, stood again, pressing the wallet flat against her ribs, and read the address on the license for the fifth time, whispering it like something she might still be able to refuse.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The pool smells like chlorine and wet rubber, and I have been standing on the second step for eleven minutes. The instructor, a girl young enough to be my daughter, says, "Whenever you're ready," and I say, "I am," in a voice that cracks in the middle. My hands won't unclench from the rail. I watch the water slap the tiles, bright and indifferent, and my stomach folds over itself. Last week I got my face in and came up choking, and every night since I've lain awake feeling that cold slide up my nose. Now I lower one foot, pull it back, lower it again. My heart is knocking against my ribs like something locked in. Forty-three years old, and I am counting breaths out loud, whispering, "One, two," as if numbers could hold me up. A kid cannonballs nearby and I flinch so hard my goggles fall in. I stare at them sinking, and I cannot make myself go after them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned in her fist, and for the third time she read the back of the tomatoes: six inches apart, quarter inch deep. Her thumb pressed a hole, then she smoothed it shut, then she dug it again. Dirt packed under her nails. Her jaw ached from clenching. "Too deep," she muttered, and scraped the soil away with two fingers to check the seed, as if it might have vanished. Across the fence her neighbor's tomatoes already climbed their cages, glossy and red, and she turned her back to them. The sun pressed hot on her neck. She sat back on her heels, breathing through her teeth, then reached for the trowel again. "Just one row," she said aloud, flatly, to no one. Her hands shook as she tore open the next packet, and three seeds spilled into the grass. She stared at them a long moment before she left them there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus sat at the far end of the conference table, thumbnail pressed into the pad of his finger until the skin whitened. On the screen, Dana clicked to slide six, and there it was: his dashboard, his three weekends, now labeled "our prototype." The air conditioner hummed too loudly. He smiled when Priya glanced his way, and felt his jaw ache from it. "Great," he said, when Dana paused for questions, and his voice came out thin and bright, like someone else's. His pen had written the same word four times on his notepad, the letters gouging through to the next page. Dana thanked the team for their "support." Support. Heat crawled up his neck; his coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but he lifted it anyway and drank, just to have something to swallow. When everyone applauded, his hands joined in, slow and obedient, while his stomach turned over and over beneath the table.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The exit for Delmar comes up and I take it, then take the next one too, looping back onto the highway like I've forgotten what home is. My hands keep readjusting on the wheel, ten and two, then nine and three, thumbs drumming. The radio is just static now; I leave it. At the red light on Fourth, nobody else around, I say, "I didn't mean it," out loud, and then again, quieter, "I did not mean it," as if the dashboard might sign off on that. My jaw aches. I realize I've been clenching my teeth since the gas station. Her text sits face-down in the cup holder, and every time the phone buzzes against the plastic my stomach drops into my shoes. Green light. I don't go. A truck's headlights swell in the mirror and I finally move, slowly, turning toward the house with the porch light still on, rehearsing sentences that fall apart before I reach the end of the street.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus stood outside room 412 for the third time, hand flat against the door he hadn't pushed. Inside, the monitor kept its patient beep. He pushed. His father looked smaller than the bed, wrists bruised purple around the tape. "Hey, Pop," Marcus said, too loud, then too soft. "Traffic was nothing." It had been two hours of traffic. He sat, stood, sat again, the vinyl chair squeaking each time like an accusation. He peeled the label off the water cup, strip by strip, until it was confetti in his palm. His jaw ached from clenching. When his father murmured, "You didn't have to come," Marcus laughed, a short wrong sound, and said, "Yeah, I did," while thinking of the unreturned calls, eleven months of them, stacked in his phone. His chest felt packed with wet sand. He gripped the bed rail until his knuckles whitened, and couldn't make himself let go, or leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana stood at the chain-link fence with her car keys biting into her palm, though she had parked twenty minutes ago and no longer needed them. The letter from the principal was folded into quarters in her jacket, and every few seconds her hand went in to check it was still there, as if it might have wandered off. Other parents laughed about weekend plans; she nodded at nothing, a beat late. Her jaw ached. When the bell shrilled, she flinched so hard her coffee slopped over her knuckles, and she didn't wipe it off. "Sorry," she said to a woman she'd bumped, then again, quieter, "sorry," though the woman had already turned away. Kids spilled through the doors in bright coats. She counted them, lost count, started over. What would she say first? Not the letter. Maybe nothing. Her stomach rolled. Then she saw the red backpack, and her feet rooted themselves to the pavement while her mouth practiced a smile that kept slipping.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man in the windbreaker has been running his thumb along my mother's dining table for a full minute, and I've stopped breathing properly. "Forty," he says. I taped a sign reading $150 to it, and I hear myself say, "Sure, fine," too fast, then, "No, wait." My hand is flat on the wood, over the ring she always scolded us for. He waits. The sun is hot on my neck, and my shirt is stuck to my back. Across the lawn, the six chairs sit lined up in the grass like they're expecting her. I pick at the tape until it curls off in a gummy strip. "Take it," I say, and he counts out bills while I stare at the drawer pull, the one I swore I'd keep. When his truck pulls away, I'm still holding the tape, and my jaw aches from how hard I've been clenching it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the cold basement floor with her cheek against the concrete, one arm wedged behind the water heater, and the drip landed on her wrist again. Tick. Tick. She tightened the fitting a quarter turn and it kept ticking. "No," she said, too softly, then louder, "no, no, no," and struck the pipe with the wrench handle. Her jaw ached from clenching. She had watched the same video four times, and the man in it kept smiling. Upstairs the floorboards creaked, and she froze, breath held, until the footsteps faded. Her shirt was soaked through at the ribs. She wiped her face with a gritty hand and tasted rust. Every drop seemed aimed at the same raw spot behind her eyes. She counted the seconds between them, lost count, started over, and wrapped the tape again, harder, until her fingers shook and the roll tore in half.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has sat against the toaster since Tuesday, its little plastic window showing my name in that flat government font. I pick it up, put it down, wash a mug that's already clean. My thumb finds the flap and I count the ceiling tiles instead, twice, getting different numbers. "Just open it," I tell the kitchen, but it comes out as a whisper, and I laugh at that, a dry cough of a laugh. The tear is too slow. Paper whines. My stomach folds over itself, and there's a taste like pennies at the back of my tongue. I unfold the page halfway and shut it again. Then I'm at the window, forehead on the cold glass, rereading the one line I caught, the one with the word "review" in it. My hands are damp. I wipe them on my jeans, again, and again, and then I read it from the top.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station clock says 11:40, or maybe the numbers mean something else here. I've read the same sign four times, and each time the letters slide off like rain. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the train doors opened. A man in an orange vest says something fast and kind, and I nod, nod, nod, then hear myself repeat, "Hotel? Hotel?" louder, as if volume were a bridge. He points left, then right, then left. My suitcase wheel rattles over the tiles, loud as a confession. I check my phone: no signal, 6% battery, the address on the booking a string of symbols I can't even pronounce to myself. Sweat cools along my spine. A woman laughs at something behind me and I whip around, sure it's me. I want to sit on the curb. I want to scream my own name just to hear it mean something. Instead I fold the useless paper map smaller, smaller, until it's a hard little square in my fist.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tore across the long grass with a tennis ball in his jaws, ears flipping inside out, and I pressed my thumbnail into the pad of my finger until it left a white crescent. The vet's envelope was folded in my jacket pocket. I had read it four times in the car. "Good boy," I called, and my voice cracked in the middle, so I coughed and tried again, too loud this time. He dropped the ball at my shoes. I didn't pick it up right away. My hand hovered, trembling, over his warm skull, and I counted the freckles on his nose as if I might be quizzed later. The wind smelled of cut hay. A jogger waved and I waved back a beat too late, smile stuck on like a sticker. When Biscuit bolted again I stood up too fast, the field tilting, and said to nobody, "Just one more throw. Then we'll go." I threw it badly, short, and stayed standing there long after he'd brought it back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite played the opening bars of the Schubert again, and again her left hand stumbled on the same triplet. She stopped. The church hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and folding chairs sat in crooked rows waiting for Saturday. "Fine," she said to no one, too brightly, and started over. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it since the first run-through. Sweat made her fingertips slide on the ivory. Halfway down the page she heard the wrong note before she hit it, and her whole body flinched as though it had already happened. She pressed her palms flat against her thighs and stared at the music stand until the black dots blurred. "Again," she muttered, quieter now. Then, "Again." The radiator clanked. Somewhere a door opened, and she snapped the lid down over the keys, tucked her shaking hands beneath her arms, and smiled at the janitor like someone caught stealing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The box labeled DONATE is full of his chisels, and I've taken them out three times. Sawdust still lies in the vise's jaws, and I can't make myself blow it clear. His pencil sits behind a clamp, the tip chewed flat, and I hold it until my knuckles ache. "Fine," I say aloud, too loudly, to the pegboard. "Fine, you win." I put the chisels back in the box. Then I take them out again and line them up by size, the way he would have, the way he always scolded me for not doing. My jaw is clenched so hard my ears ring. On the bench is the half-built stool, one leg missing, and I keep circling it, wiping my palms on my jeans though they're dry. I should have called back in March. I check my phone, as if that were a different thing from March. The shop smells like cedar and cold coffee. I turn off the light, stand in the dark, and turn it on again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: At 4:52, Mara had refreshed the portal eleven times, and the grey bar still said Results will be available at 5:00. She stood, sat, stood again. The tea beside the laptop had grown a skin; she drank it anyway and winced at the cold. Her thumbnail had worn a pink crescent into the side of her finger. 'It's just a page,' she told the empty kitchen, her voice thin and too bright, and then she laughed at nothing and stopped. The fridge hummed. Somewhere upstairs a floorboard creaked and she flinched, knocking the mouse. Her stomach clenched around the toast she hadn't finished. She replayed question six, the one with the integral, for the hundredth time, writing the answer in the air with two fingers. 4:58. Her knee bounced hard enough to rattle the spoon in the mug. She pressed her palms against her eyes, saw red static, and whispered, 'Please, please, just let it load,' before she even dared to look.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta passed the same split cedar for the third time and stopped, one hand flat against its bark as if it might tell her something. The light had gone orange, then the color of weak tea. She pulled her phone out, saw no signal, and put it back, then took it out again. "Fine," she said aloud, too sharply, and her voice sounded like someone else's in the thinning air. Her jaw ached from clenching. She walked faster, uphill when she knew the car was down, and couldn't make herself turn. Every few steps she looked over her shoulder at nothing. His last message was still open in her head, the unanswered one, the words arranging themselves to the rhythm of her boots. Her breath came ragged; sweat went cold along her spine. When an owl called, she flinched, then laughed once, a dry bark, and pressed her knuckles hard against her sternum. She kept going until the trail was just a paler dark underfoot, muttering, "Not now, not now, not now."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Mara read the index card for the ninth time, though she knew it by heart: "flour till it feels right." Right to whom? Her grandmother's looping blue ink had bled at one corner where a thumb had once rested, and Mara pressed her own thumb there, then yanked it away. Flour dusted her forearms to the elbow. She kneaded too hard, then too softly, then stopped, breath short, palms flat on the dough as if it might flinch. "Come on," she whispered, and then louder, "You could have just written a number." The kitchen smelled of yeast and nothing else, nothing of the woman who used to hum here. She tore off a piece, squeezed it, tossed it back. Her jaw ached. The oven ticked as it heated, and she stood before it with the bowl against her ribs, unable to put the loaf in, unable to put the card down, laughing once, sharply, at the empty room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marcus was holding two lemons when he heard his name from the end of the produce aisle, and he knew the voice before he turned. Danny Orsolo, who had sat behind him in tenth-grade chemistry, who had watched him freeze at the front of the room. Marcus set one lemon down, then picked it up again. "Hey. Wow. Hey," he said, too fast, and his laugh came out thin. His collar felt damp. Danny talked about his kids, a house in Tucson, and Marcus nodded at each word while his thumbnail dug a groove into the lemon's skin. He said "great" four times. Under the fluorescent hum he kept hearing the old silence of that classroom, the scrape of a chair, someone's snort. When Danny said, "You still have that notebook of poems?" Marcus's stomach dropped to the cold tile. "Ha, no. God, no," he said, and left his cart standing there, walking toward the exit with the lemons still in his fist.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy lights hum at 5:42, eighteen minutes before I can lock the door, and I've wiped the same counter four times. My phone is face-down by the register. I know what's on it: three missed calls, all from the same number. A woman with a cane asks if we have anything for a headache, and I say, "Aisle six," too fast, too loud, then follow her there and say it again quieter. My jaw aches from clenching. I keep checking the clock like it owes me something. Someone's wrapping paper rustles in their bag and I flinch. "Happy Thanksgiving," the cashier next door calls, and I nod, mouth open, nothing coming out. I turn the sign to CLOSED, then turn it back, then turn it again. My keys rattle in my hand. The parking lot is full of taillights heading home, and I stand in the doorway, flipping the phone over, then back, then over again, never pressing the screen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says D41, and I'm at B7, and the clock says 4:52 for a flight that closes at 5:00. I run, then stop, then run again because the moving walkway is blocked by a stroller and a man who won't shift. "Excuse me, please, excuse me," I say, but it comes out thin, almost a whisper, and no one hears. My carry-on bangs my shin every third step. There's sweat under my collar, cold now, and my throat tastes like pennies. I keep checking my phone as if the numbers might forgive me. Two hours ago I told her I'd be there by dinner. Seven years of missed things, and this is the one that counts. My hands shake so badly I drop my boarding pass, and I crouch on the floor, grabbing at it, breath sawing in and out, thinking, not again, not again, not again. At D30 a gate agent glances up, and I can't tell if I'm laughing or crying when I yell, "Wait!"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the baseboards twice, and still she peeled the tape off and started again. The roller hissed against the wall, and the yellow went over the pencil marks, all those little heights, Dani, age four, age five, age six, until the last one vanished under a wet shine. She stopped. Her jaw ached from clenching. "It's just a wall," she told the empty room, too loudly, and the words came back off the bare floor. She dipped the roller again, too full, and paint ran down in a fat drip she watched without wiping. Her hands shook so that the line along the ceiling wobbled. She laughed once, a dry bark, then pressed her forearm hard against her mouth, leaving a streak of yellow across her cheek. At the window the afternoon light kept sliding along the wall, finding the one spot she'd missed. She could not make herself cover it. She stood there, roller dripping onto the drop cloth, breathing through her teeth, until dark.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite had carried the phone out to the porch an hour ago, and it still sat face-down on her knee, warm as a living thing. Thunder cracked above the maples and she flinched, then pressed her thumbnail into the pad of her finger until it whitened. Rain blew sideways across the boards and soaked her hem; she did not move her feet. She turned the phone over. Turned it back. "Not tonight," she told the yard, her voice scraped thin, and then, softer, "Say it, then. Just say it." The porch swing chain creaked. Her jaw ached from clenching, and she noticed she'd been chewing the same corner of her lip raw. Lightning lit the empty driveway where his truck used to sit. She counted the seconds to the thunder, lost count, started over. Somewhere she'd left a sentence unfinished, years ago, and it kept finishing itself in her head, a little crueler each time. She gripped the railing until the wet wood bit her palms, and stayed put.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain keeps slipping off the same tooth, and I keep seating it back with greasy thumbs as if the fifth try will differ from the fourth. Mr. Okafor's table saw is eighteen inches from my hip. Someone's paint cans form a wall to my left, the roll-up door is padlocked until Dara gets home with the key, and every time I straighten, my head clips the hanging lamp and it swings, swings, throws my shadow back and forth across the concrete.
