"Fine," she said aloud, too sharply, and punched the dough. It stuck to her knuckles. Her jaw ached, and she realized she'd been clenching it since the yeast began to foam. She wiped her eyes with a wrist, leaving a white streak, and glanced at the phone with the voicemail she hadn't deleted. Didn't press play. Set it face down. Kneaded again, slower, counting under her breath the way Nana used to, and stopped at nineteen, because the next number was where the voice always went on without her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The cereal aisle hummed with fluorescent light, and I was holding a box of oatmeal I didn't want when someone said my name. Dana Whitlock. Fourth-period chemistry, back row, the girl whose notes I once copied and never repaid. She looked the same, bright scarf, easy grin, a toddler on her hip. My thumb pressed a dent into the cardboard. "Wow, hey," I said, too loud, then too quiet. "Look at you." She asked what I was up to now, and I laughed before answering, a short dry sound, and said, "Oh, you know, between things." My cart held one frozen dinner and a bag of cat litter, no cat. I angled my body to hide them. Heat crawled up my neck. She said we should get coffee, and I said yes, definitely, while already scanning for the nearest exit. I walked the wrong way down the next aisle, past the checkout, and stood by the carts until my hands stopped shaking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marisol wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time, the rag squeaking against the laminate. The fluorescent tube over aisle two flickered; she watched it instead of the clock. Her phone buzzed in her apron pocket and she let it buzz, thumb pressing hard against the edge of the register until the skin went white. 'Happy Thanksgiving,' she told an old man buying cough drops, and the words came out too bright, too quick. He asked if she was all right. 'Fine, just the long day,' she said, laughing at nothing. After he left she stood very still, her stomach tight as a fist, and read the voicemail preview again: Call me before you drive down. We need to talk about Dad. She slid the phone under a stack of receipts, turned the sign to CLOSED eleven minutes early, and began straightening shelves that were already straight.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board flips to DELAYED beside my flight number, and I read it three times as if the letters might rearrange. Forty minutes to connect. Gate C41 is somewhere past a terminal I can't see the end of. I'm already walking fast, then half-jogging, my carry-on wheels rattling like loose teeth. My shirt sticks between my shoulder blades. "Excuse me, sorry, sorry," I keep saying, too quietly for anyone to hear. A man on a cart beeps and I flatten against a pillar, heart knocking, and I realize I've been chewing the inside of my cheek raw. My phone says 12% and I check it again anyway, as though it might be kinder. If I miss this, Dad's surgery is tomorrow and I'll be sitting in some plastic chair in Denver, useless. I wipe my palm on my jeans. The moving walkway is out of order. Of course it is. I laugh once, a dry little sound, and then I run.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I've rolled the same square yard of wall four times now, and the grey keeps coming out streaky anyway. The tray is nearly dry. My phone buzzes on the stepladder and I flip it face down without reading it, then pick it back up, then flip it again. Jaw tight, I notice I've been clenching my teeth around nothing for a while. Under the tape, the pencil marks stay where she measured his height every birthday, and I haven't painted over them. I paint around them, leaving little islands. "It's fine," I say aloud to the empty room, too loudly, like someone is arguing. My stomach turns when the roller squeaks. I set it down, wipe my hands on my jeans, leaving two grey smears, and open the window though the air outside is cold. The paint smell sits thick in my throat. I stare at the last island of pencil lines, thumb hovering over the phone, and don't call.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder rattled the screen door, and I didn't flinch, just kept peeling the label off the beer bottle in strips, the paper curling into wet little commas on my knee. Rain slanted under the porch roof and soaked my left sleeve. I let it. Inside, the phone lit up again on the kitchen table, buzzing against the wood, and I counted seven buzzes before it quit. "Not tonight," I told the dog, my voice coming out flat and scraped. She put her chin on my boot. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding my teeth since supper. I stood, sat, stood again, then gripped the railing until paint flakes bit my palm. Lightning lit the empty driveway, the gap where his truck used to sit. I rehearsed the sentence I'd say if he called, then rehearsed another, then swallowed both. My stomach rolled like the clouds. When the phone buzzed again, I turned my chair to face the yard and stared hard at the rain.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had flipped the bike onto its saddle twice already, and twice she'd turned it back without touching the chain. The garage's fluorescent tube buzzed over the neighbor's half-built shelving, and every time the side door rattled she glanced up, wrench frozen mid-turn. "Just a flat," she said to nobody, too brightly, when a stranger's boots passed the open bay. Her palms were slick; the tire lever slid out of her grip and clanged on the concrete, and she flinched harder than the sound deserved. She wiped her hands on her jeans, then wiped them again. Why had she picked the hour when the Hendersons' truck was parked outside? She counted the spokes she'd already counted. Her stomach felt like a knotted inner tube. When footsteps finally came close, she hunched over the wheel, humming something tuneless, and pretended the valve stem needed all her attention.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Halvorsen Street had gone the color of dishwater by the time Marta checked the schedule for the fourth time, though she knew the 42 wasn't due for eleven minutes. She pulled her sleeves down over her knuckles and shifted her bag from one shoulder to the other. Wind lifted a flattened cup along the curb, and she followed it with her eyes until it vanished under a parked van. The shelter's plexiglass hummed. A first fat drop hit the bench beside her, then another, and she stood, sat, stood again. 'Come on,' she said quietly, to no one, to the empty road. Her stomach felt tight and tipped, as if she'd missed a stair. The only other person, a man in a gray hood, had stopped scrolling his phone and was looking down the street too. She counted the streetlights until the nearest one flickered on, and her thumbnail found the skin beside her other thumb and worried it raw.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta set the shoebox on the bed and then moved it to the desk, then back again. The lid stuck, and she pried it with her thumbnail, wincing when the cardboard tore. Inside, rubber-banded bundles smelled of cedar and dust. She pulled one out, and the band snapped against her wrist. "Well," she said aloud, too brightly, to the empty room. She sorted them by postmark, squaring the edges again and again, though they were already square. Her mother's slanting handwriting appeared on the third envelope, and Marta's hand stopped an inch above it. She wiped her palm on her jeans. The radiator ticked. She realized she had been holding her breath, let it out, and glanced at the door as though someone might come in. Then she turned the envelope face down, picked up the next one, and read the return address four times without taking in a word. Her tea had gone cold an hour ago. She did not get up to replace it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marta had the hose half coiled when Dale's shadow slid across the driveway. "Hey, neighbor. That tall ladder of yours, any chance?" He smiled too long. She wiped her palms on her jeans, though they were already dry. "Which, uh. Which job is it?" "Gutters. Maybe a window." His eyes drifted past her to the side gate, then to the upstairs windows of her house. She heard herself laugh, thin and quick. The ladder leaned in the garage, rungs catching the light, and she stood between it and him without deciding to. "It's heavy. I could bring it by Saturday?" "Today's better." Her pulse ticked in her throat. She looked at his empty hands, his clean boots, the sky without a single leaf-clogged cloud of reason in it. "Let me check the hinge," she said, already backing toward the dark of the garage, one hand closing slowly around the cold rail.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions were already translucent, but Marta kept stirring them anyway, wooden spoon scraping the same circle in the pan. Six-forty. She wiped her palms on her apron, then wiped them again. The lamb needed another hour, and she opened the oven door just to look, letting the heat flush her face. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, too brightly. "It's fine." Her phone buzzed on the counter and she flinched, knocking a lid to the floor with a clang that made her jaw clench. Only a store promotion. She straightened the forks on the table, two of them twice, and moved the candle an inch left, then back. Her stomach felt tight and hollow all at once, yet she tasted the sauce a third time without knowing what it tasted like. Down the street, a car door shut. She froze mid-reach for the salt, listening, one hand pressed flat against her sternum, until the footsteps passed the house and faded.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The screen lit up the dark kitchen at 11:40, ten digits I didn't know, and the dish towel went still in my hands. I watched the phone buzz across the counter, inching toward the sink. Four rings. Five. I realized I was holding my breath and let it out through my teeth. Dad was supposed to be home by now. I wiped my palm on my shirt, but it was damp again before I touched the phone. "Hello?" It came out thin, nothing like my voice. Silence, then a faint hum, like a room with a fan running. "Who is this?" I said, quieter, and my eyes went to the back door, the deadbolt, the black window over the sink where my own pale face stared back. My thumb hovered over the red button. The hum clicked. Somebody breathed in. I switched off the light above the stove, for reasons I couldn't explain, and stood very still in the dark, listening.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been living in my backpack since March, its spine gone soft against my laptop, and now it was November and I was standing in front of the return slot, pressing a crease into the cover with my thumb. I walked past the slot twice. The third time I went inside, where the heat made my collar damp. The librarian wore silver earrings shaped like tiny keys, and I stared at those instead of her face. "This is, um, a little late," I said, too fast, sliding the book across the desk with two fingers like it might bite. My laugh came out thin. She turned it over and tapped at her keyboard, and the clicking filled the whole room. I counted ceiling tiles. My stomach folded in on itself, and I kept wiping my palms on my jeans. "Do I owe, like, a lot?" I asked the earrings.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: I set the last box down by the door and then picked it up again, as if it might belong somewhere else. The radiator ticked. Twice I checked the lock, then wiggled the knob once more for good measure. "Fine," I told the empty room, too loudly, and my voice bounced off the bare walls and came back thinner. My palms were damp against the cardboard. I carried it to the kitchen, set it on the counter, and didn't open it. Through the thin wall a man coughed, and I froze mid-step, breath held, until the sound of a television swallowed it. The window looked straight onto a brick wall, close enough to touch if I'd dared to open it. I hadn't. I sat on the floor with my coat still buttoned, keys gripped so tightly the teeth left small white dents in my fingers, and counted the ceiling tiles. Forty-two. I counted them again, just to be sure.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather, curled at the corners, half hidden by a drift of maple leaves. Marta stopped mid-stride with her coffee halfway to her mouth. She looked left down the path, then right. A jogger passed, earbuds in, and didn't glance over. "Hello?" she said, too quietly, then again louder, her voice cracking on the second syllable. Nobody answered. She sat down at the opposite end and set the cup beside her without drinking. Her thumb rubbed the seam of her glove. When she finally lifted the wallet, it was warm, as if someone had only just let go of it, and the back of her neck prickled. She flipped it open. A driver's license stared up at her, a man's face, mid-forties, unsmiling. She snapped it shut. Behind her, a branch creaked. She stood so fast the coffee tipped, and she walked toward the gate with the wallet pressed flat against her ribs, not running, not looking back, counting her steps.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor tells me to let go of the wall, and I nod, but my fingers stay hooked over the tile lip like they belong to someone else. Chlorine stings my nose. Across the pool a kid cannonballs and the wave slaps my chin; I laugh too loudly, then cough. "Just a little kick," she says. "Right. Yes. Little," I answer, voice thin. My heartbeat is in my ears, louder than the echoing whistles. I keep checking the black line on the bottom, then the depth marker, 4 feet, then the line again. My toes search for the floor and find it, and I press down hard enough to hurt. I tell her I'm just adjusting my goggles, though I've adjusted them three times. My shoulders have crept up around my ears. When she steps back, I count her steps. One. Two. I let go with one hand, only one, and keep smiling at nothing, my other knuckles gone white and bright against the blue.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets are lined up on the porch rail like evidence, and I've read the backs of all six twice. Tomato: 'full sun, 24 inches apart.' I pace it out with my shoes, then do it again because my heel steps felt sloppy. The trowel is still sticky with the hardware store tag. I peel it off, roll it into a tiny ball, and can't decide where to throw it. My neighbor waves over the fence and calls, 'Looking good!' and I laugh too loudly and say, 'It's just dirt so far.' My stomach is tight when I kneel. I dig a hole, check it against the instructions, dig it deeper, then fill some back in. The seedling sits there, so thin I could snap it with a sneeze. I hold my breath while I pat the soil around it. Then I crouch there, thumbs hovering, checking the sky for clouds, listening for anything that might tell me I've already done it wrong.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to slide four, and I realize I've been peeling the label off my water bottle in long, careful strips. The conference room hums. Her chart shows the timeline I sketched in March, only now my name isn't on it. I tug my sleeve down over my wrist and nod at the right moments, a half-second late. "Great, yeah," I say when she glances over, and my voice comes out thinner than I meant. Someone asks about the data source. My stomach tightens, and I stare at the pile of paper curls on the table, sweeping them into my palm so no one sees. Dana says, "That was a shared effort," and smiles in my direction. I smile back, too wide, teeth dry. The back of my shirt is damp against the chair. I check my phone, face down, and then check it again, though nothing has lit up. Slide five. I laugh when others laugh.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marta turned the radio off at the second red light, though the light had no reason to be red, not with the road empty in every direction. Her thumbs kept drumming the wheel, then stopped, then gripped it hard enough that her knuckles went pale in the dash glow. The same pair of headlights had sat behind her since the gas station. She slowed to thirty; they slowed too. "Just pass," she said aloud, her voice thin and too bright, as if someone might answer. She took a left she didn't need, checked the mirror, and felt her stomach drop when the lights turned left as well. Sweat prickled under her collar despite the cold vent blowing on her face. Her house was eleven minutes away, and she realized she was counting them. At the next corner she drove straight past her own street, swallowing hard, and reached over to click the door locks again, though they were already down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus stood outside room 412 for a full minute, rereading the whiteboard by the door as if the nurse's name might change. He had bought carnations, then worried they were wrong, then bought a second bunch of something yellow, and now both bouquets crinkled in his damp grip. The hand sanitizer foamed cold between his fingers; he rubbed until his skin squeaked. 'Hey, Grandpa,' he said, too loudly, and winced at the echo. The old man's hand lay on the blanket, smaller than he remembered, a clear tube taped to its back. Marcus set the flowers down, picked them up, set them down again. He laughed at nothing. His knee bounced against the vinyl chair while the monitor beeped on, steady, and he counted the beeps, then caught himself and looked at the clock. Only six minutes had passed. 'They've got you a nice window,' he said, not looking at it, tugging his jacket zipper up and down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell hasn't rung yet, and I've already checked my phone four times, though nothing on it has changed. I stand at the fence instead of with the other parents under the maple, my keys biting into my palm. Someone laughs near the gate and I flinch, then pretend I was only adjusting my scarf. My mouth is dry. "Cold today," I tell the woman beside me, too fast, and she nods without turning. The doors open. Kids spill out in bright coats, and I count backpacks, red, blue, red, rising on my toes, my heartbeat loud in my ears. Not him. Not yet. I rehearse what I'll say to Mr. Alvarez about this morning, about the fight at breakfast, about what I shouted. My thumb rubs the same worn spot on my keys. Then a yellow hat bobs through the crowd, and I realize I've been holding my breath so long my chest aches. I wave too high, too eagerly, and wait to see his face.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, then crossed it out and written thirty, then stood with the marker capped and uncapped in her fingers. The man circling it wore a gray windbreaker and kept running his thumb along the top drawer, the one she hadn't opened since March. "Solid," he said. "Yes," she said, too quickly, and laughed at nothing. Her palms were damp against her skirt. When he reached for the knob she stepped in, straightened a lamp that was already straight, and asked if he wanted water. Her stomach fluttered with each squeak of the runners. "Take it, honestly, twenty," she heard herself say, before the drawer had moved an inch. He blinked. She kept her eyes on the driveway, on the folding table, on the chipped teacup she'd forgotten to price, and listened to her own pulse thudding in her ears while the sun pressed on the back of her neck.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marisol wedged herself under the sink with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, and the drip landed on her wrist again, cold as a coin. She wiped it on her jeans for the fourth time. The wrench slipped; she caught it, then set it down and picked it up again without having turned anything. "Okay," she said to the cabinet, too brightly. "Okay, okay." Somewhere upstairs a floorboard creaked and she froze, listening, until her neck ached and the flashlight beam stopped trembling on the corroded joint. Her landlord's text sat unanswered on her phone, screen lit beside the bucket. The water in the bucket had risen past the third rivet. She counted the drips, lost count, started over. Her stomach felt tight and hollow, as though she'd skipped a stair. When she finally tightened the nut, she did it in small, careful quarter turns, one hand hovering over the shutoff valve, ready to flinch, her breath held until the dripping slowed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter for three hours, its little window showing Marta's name in blocky type. She wiped the counter around it. She washed a single mug twice. When the kettle clicked off she carried her tea over, set it down, and picked the envelope up, then put it down again and went to check that the back door was locked, though she had locked it that morning. "Just a letter," she told the cat, her voice too bright. Her thumb found the corner of the flap and stalled there. The refrigerator hummed; somewhere a neighbor's television laughed. She slid a butter knife under the seal, slowly, as if the paper might bruise, and her stomach turned over as the glue gave way. Her hands were cold. She unfolded the page halfway and read only the letterhead, then breathed out, long and thin, and made herself keep going.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train doors hissed shut behind me, and the platform emptied faster than I could read a single sign. I stood holding my suitcase handle with both hands, thumb rubbing the same worn spot on the plastic. Every board glowed with characters that slid past my eyes like water. I checked my phone, then checked it again, though the screen still showed one bar and the same blue dot drifting nowhere. A man in a grey uniform glanced at me, and I said, "Hotel? Sorry, hotel?" too loudly, then too softly, holding out the crumpled printout. He pointed left, spoke in a quick, kind stream, and I nodded at every word, smiling, my jaw tight. My shirt clung to my back. Outside, the street hummed with scooters and neon, and I walked three blocks one way before turning around, pretending I'd meant to. My stomach clenched when a shop bell rang behind me. I kept the printout in my fist, damp now, the address smeared, and did not put it away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the fence with her keys still clenched in her fist, though the car was a hundred yards behind her. Biscuit tore through the long grass in wide loops, ears flapping, and each time he dipped below the tall seedheads her breath stopped until his orange back reappeared. "Biscuit," she called, too high, too quick. He ignored her. She counted the gaps in the tree line, then counted them again. A man with a thermos had been sitting on the far bench since before she arrived, and he hadn't once looked at a dog or a phone. Her thumb worried a groove into the key's teeth. The wind shifted, carrying the smell of cut hay and something sour beneath it. "Come on, buddy, here, here," she said, laughing at nothing, and slapped her thigh hard enough to sting. When he finally bounded over, she knelt and clipped the leash on with fingers that wouldn't quite work.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite wiped her palms on her skirt for the third time and set the sheet music back on the stand, squaring its edges until they lined up with the metal lip. The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Folding chairs sat in crooked rows, empty except for Mr. Alvarez, who was stacking hymnals near the door. "Just from the top of the second verse," she told the pianist, laughing a little too brightly. She began, and her voice came out thin, so she stopped, cleared her throat, and started again. Her fingers kept finding the button on her cuff. Halfway through a line she knew by heart, the words slipped away, and she stared at the page as if it were written in another language. "Sorry, sorry. Again?" The pianist nodded. Marguerite glanced at the clock above the door and counted the hours until Saturday. Her stomach felt tight and hollow. She sipped water she didn't want, then took a breath and began once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The box marked KEEP is already full, and I haven't touched the bench yet. I pick up a chisel, set it down, then pick it up again and wipe the handle on my jeans as if he might mind the dust. His radio is still tuned to the station he liked; I turn it off, and the silence has a hum in it. My palms are damp. I keep glancing at the door, which I've left open, though it's cold. "Okay," I say aloud, too brightly, "okay, Danny, where do you keep the trash bags?" Nothing, obviously. I open a drawer and find a half-finished birdhouse, pencil lines still on the pine, a small x where the next cut would go. I close the drawer. I open it. I close it again, softly, the way you'd shut a bedroom door on someone sleeping. Then I go and stand in the yard for a while, counting the bricks in the path, before I walk back in and start with the sweeping.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the science office smells like floor polish and somebody's microwaved noodles, and I've read the corkboard three times though it still holds only a fire drill notice and a lost umbrella flyer. Ten past three. The results were supposed to go up at three. I peel the label off my water bottle in tiny strips and roll them into pellets between my fingers. Priya laughs about something on her phone and I snap, "Can you not?" then mumble, "Sorry. Sorry, it's fine." My stomach keeps folding over itself. I check my phone, nothing, put it away, check again. A door clicks somewhere and my whole body leans toward it like a plant, but it's only the caretaker with his bucket. I wipe my palms on my jeans, and they're damp again almost at once. Was question six a trick? I turn it over for the fortieth time. Then the secretary appears with a stapler and a single sheet, and I forget how to swallow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid off the ridge, and I checked my phone again: no bars, 5:12. I'd told myself the loop took two hours. It had been three. My boots kept finding roots I didn't remember, and I started counting my steps out loud, "forty-one, forty-two," until my own voice sounded too loud and I stopped. Somewhere behind me a branch cracked. I froze, one hand gripping the strap of my pack, and listened to my pulse thudding in my ears. Nothing. I walked faster. My palms were slick despite the cold, and I kept tugging my sleeves down over them. "Just a deer," I said, to no one, and laughed once, a thin sound. The trees had gone from green to black cutouts. I pulled out my headlamp, fumbled it twice, and when the beam finally snapped on, I didn't turn around to look at the trail behind me. I just kept the light on my feet and kept moving, jaw clenched, shoulders up near my ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, stained translucent in one corner, and I've read it four times without touching the flour. Grandpa's handwriting slants hard to the right. "Flour, enough," it says. Enough. I measure three cups, then pour half back, then pour it out again. The kitchen is too quiet; the fridge hums and I find myself turning to it, as if it might correct me. My palms are damp, so the dough clings to them in stubborn gray gloves. I scrape them on the dish towel and laugh at nothing, a short dry sound. "Okay," I tell the empty room. "Okay, okay." I press the heel of my hand into the dough, fold, press, and check the clock, though I haven't set a timer. His thumbprint is smudged beside the word *knead*. I keep my hand away from it. When the oven ticks past its preheat, I stand with the bowl against my ribs, listening, my shoulders up near my ears, not putting it in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was comparing two cans of tomatoes, reading the same label twice, when someone said my name from the end of the aisle. Dana Whitlock. Twelfth grade, back row of chemistry, the girl who always knew the answers. My thumb pressed a dent into the can. "Hey! Wow," I said, too loud, and laughed a beat late. She asked what I was up to these days, and I heard myself say "Oh, you know, a bit of this and that," while my free hand tugged my sleeve down over my wrist. The fluorescent lights hummed. My basket held frozen dinners, one bag of rice, nothing else, and I shifted it behind my leg. She talked about Chicago, a firm, a wedding in June. I nodded at every pause, nodded again, counted ceiling tiles. "We should get coffee," I said. My mouth was dry as paper. When she finally wheeled away, I stood there holding both cans, my shirt stuck to my back, and bought neither.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied out, and Marisol wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time. The fluorescent hum seemed louder than usual. She glanced at the front doors, then at the clock, then at the doors again. "Almost there," she told Dev, the stock boy, but her voice came out thin and too bright, and she laughed at nothing. Her stomach felt tight, like a fist closing around a coin. She rearranged the cough drops, checked the lock on the narcotics cabinet, and checked it once more, tugging until the metal rattled. Outside, a car idled at the curb with its headlights on, and she watched it through the glass until her palms went damp against her apron. When the phone rang she flinched, let it ring twice, and picked up with her shoulders already pulled toward her ears. "Hello? ...No, no, we're still open. Until six." She pressed her free hand flat against her ribs, as if to hold something in place.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol checked the departures board for the fourth time, though the gate for Lisbon hadn't changed since the last glance. Her incoming flight had landed forty minutes late, and now she walked fast along the moving walkway, passing people who stood still on it, her carry-on thumping against her calf. "Sorry, sorry, excuse me," she said, too softly for anyone to hear. Her palms were damp against the strap. She swallowed and it felt like swallowing a stone. What if the gate closes at ten past? She pulled out her phone, saw 9:52, put it away, pulled it out again. A cart beeped behind her and she flinched, stepping sideways into a pillar of travelers. Her stomach fluttered with each gate number she passed: 31, 32, 33. The terminal's bright, endless hum seemed louder than it should be. At the desk she gripped the counter and asked, "Is it still open? Please, is it still open?" Her voice cracked on the second "open," and she hated how thin it sounded.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the baseboards twice, pressing each strip down with her thumbnail until her thumb ached. The drop cloth crinkled whenever she shifted, and she froze each time, listening, though the house was empty. She stirred the paint longer than the can required. "Soft Linen," she read aloud, flatly, then again, quieter, as if the name might change. Beneath the old yellow, the pencil marks of her daughter's heights climbed the doorframe, and her roller hovered an inch from them. Her stomach felt tight and hollow at once. She wiped her palms on her jeans, left two pale streaks, and wiped them again. The window was open, but the air seemed thick. She dipped the roller, rolled off the excess, rolled off more, and painted the far wall first, the one without any marks. Halfway down the stroke she stopped, checked her phone for nothing, and set it face down on the ladder's shelf.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the railing while I was still holding my coffee, and I didn't go in. I told myself the porch roof was good enough. Thunder rolled over the cornfield, and my thumb found the chip in the mug's rim and worried it, over and over. The swing creaked; I stopped it with my heel, then started it again, then stopped it. Every time the sky flashed white I counted out loud, "One, two, three," and my voice came out thinner than I wanted. Dad's truck should have been in the drive an hour ago. I checked my phone, no new messages, and checked it again anyway. The back of my neck prickled. Wind shoved the wet smell of dirt across the boards, and the screen door banged behind me. I spun around so fast the coffee slopped over my knuckles. Nothing there. Just the door. "Fine," I said to nobody, and didn't get up. I kept my eyes on the empty road.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tire lever slipped again and skinned Marta's knuckle, and she just stared at the bead of blood without wiping it. Across the garage, someone's radio played a bright song about summer; she reached over and nudged the volume knob down, then went back to the wheel. Her neighbor's tools hung in tidy outlines on the pegboard. Hers lay scattered over the oil-stained concrete, where she'd stopped bothering to put anything back. 'Fine,' she said when Dev asked if she needed a hand, her voice flat as the tube in her lap. 'It's fine.' She pressed the patch down and counted to sixty, though the glue said thirty. Her shoulders felt heavy, as if she were still wearing a wet coat. When the tube hissed again at the valve, she didn't swear. She set the wheel against the wall, sat on the upturned bucket, and looked at the second bike, the one with the child-sized seat, still leaning where it had been all spring, untouched, its tires soft.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Fenwick Street went the color of dishwater while I was checking the timetable for the fourth time. Eleven minutes late. The first drops hit my phone screen, and I wiped them on my jeans without looking up. I'd left the umbrella on the kitchen counter, next to the mug I hadn't washed and the note I hadn't finished. Wind pushed a flyer against my shin; I let it stay there. My jaw ached from clenching, and my shoulders had crept up toward my ears so long that I had to consciously drop them, and they crept right back. A woman beside me said, 'Miserable out, isn't it?' and I said, 'Mm,' and nothing else, staring at the puddle swallowing the curb. Cold water found the back of my collar. I didn't move under the shelter's thin edge. When the bus finally hissed up, I stood there a second too long, watching the doors open, wondering whether I actually wanted to go anywhere at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid sticks, and I pry it off with my thumbnail, breaking it. Dust goes up my nose. I sit on the cold attic floor with my knees cracking and lay the envelopes in rows, sorting by postmark, because that's something to do with my hands. Her handwriting slants hard to the right, the way it always did. I read the first line of one, then the first line of another, and don't go further. My jaw aches from clenching. "Fine," I say aloud to nobody, flat, and it echoes off the rafters. I stack the letters, tap them square, and rubber-band them tight enough that the band bites the paper. Then I take the band off, because it's cutting her name. My chest feels packed with wet sand. Downstairs the kettle clicks off, and I don't move. I hold one envelope against my knee, still sealed, and watch the light creep slowly across the boards until it's gone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Marguerite heard the knock while she was standing at the sink, her hands still wrapped around a mug that had gone cold an hour ago. Through the window she saw Dale on the porch, grinning, one thumb hooked toward the garage. "Just need your ladder for ten minutes," he said. She nodded before he finished. The ladder had been Walter's. Its left rail still carried the paint smear from the spring he'd done the shutters, the spring before the hospital. She dragged it out slowly, the aluminum cold and louder than she remembered, scraping the concrete. Her shoulders ached as she lifted it. "Mind the third rung," she said, voice flat and small. "It sticks." Dale thanked her twice and jogged off across the lawn, the ladder bobbing over his shoulder. She stayed in the garage doorway a long while, staring at the clean rectangle on the wall where it had hung, then pulled the door down and left the light on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta chopped the parsley long after it was fine enough, the knife tapping the board in a flat, steady rhythm. The oven timer said twenty-two minutes. Six places were set at the table, and she had counted them twice, though she knew the number. When the phone buzzed on the counter, she glanced at it, saw her sister's name, and turned it face down with a wet thumb. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, when the sauce spat at her. "Fine, fine." Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears hours ago, and she only noticed now, letting them drop with a long breath that didn't loosen anything. She tasted the sauce, stared at the spoon, and added salt she didn't think it needed. The candles sat unlit in their holders. Down the hall, a chair that should have been dragged to the table stayed where it was, against the wall, and she walked around it twice without looking at it. The doorbell was still silent. She wiped her hands on the dishtowel for a long time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the cold rim of the sink, and I watch it rattle without moving. Ten digits, none I know. Dishes from three days ago sit in grey water; the window above them shows only my own face, dull and slack. On the fifth ring I wipe my hands on my shirt, slowly, as if there were a reason to hurry. My thumb hovers. My chest feels packed with wet sand. I answer anyway and say, "Yeah," flat, barely a word. A bright voice asks if this is Daniel. I let the silence stretch long enough that she says it again. "Sure," I tell her. "Whoever." She starts on something about my car's warranty, and I slide down the cabinet until I'm sitting on the linoleum, knees up, listening to her cheerful breathing. I don't hang up. Nobody else has called all week, and I hate how long I let her keep talking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and it was November when I finally pushed through the library's heavy glass door. My hands were cold and damp at once. I stood in line behind a boy with a stack of graphic novels, rehearsing a sentence I never managed to say out loud. When the librarian looked up, I slid the battered copy of Middlemarch across the counter and stared at the scanner's red light instead of her face. "It's, um. Pretty late," I mumbled. She typed. The keys sounded enormous. My throat felt packed with sand, and I kept tugging my sleeve down over my knuckles. "Two hundred days," she said, not unkindly, and I nodded at the carpet, at a gum stain shaped like Ohio. I didn't ask the amount. I just whispered, "Okay," three times, and walked out slowly, shoulders curled in, my backpack lighter and my chest somehow heavier than before.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at four, and the door clicked behind them with a sound too small for how long I stood there. Eleven boxes, one lamp, a mattress leaning against the radiator like a drunk. I kept my coat on. The window looked out on a brick wall, close enough that I could have read the graffiti if I'd cared to. "Fine," I said to the empty room, and my voice came out flat and scratchy. "It's fine." I opened a box marked KITCHEN, lifted one mug, set it on the counter, and just stared at it. My shoulders ached, heavy as wet towels. The fridge hummed, then shuddered off. I sat on the floor because the chair was still wrapped, and my phone lit up with Mom's name. I watched it buzz until it stopped. Then I ate crackers from the sleeve in the dark, because finding the lamp's plug felt like too much.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marta sat down on the bench only because her legs had stopped agreeing to go farther, and her thumb landed on something leathery beside her. A brown wallet. She turned it over slowly, the way she did everything lately. Inside: forty dollars, a library card, a photo of a girl missing her front teeth. The drizzle had soaked through her sleeves, and she didn't pull her hood up. 'Somebody's going to want this,' she said aloud to the empty path, her voice flat and scratchy from disuse. She read the address twice and didn't move. Across the pond, a man threw bread to ducks, and she watched the crumbs sink. Her stomach felt hollow, her chest heavy as wet sand. She thought of the apartment, the unwashed cups, the phone that no longer buzzed. Finally she tucked the wallet into her coat, stood with a sigh that seemed to take a while, and walked toward the address, shoulders curled inward against nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite kept one hand on the pool's tiled edge long after the instructor had waved the class toward the middle. The water came up to her ribs, and the chlorine smell stuck in her throat. Around her, children kicked and shrieked, their small bodies skimming along as if it were nothing. She tucked her chin and watched her own pale feet wobble below the surface. "I'm fine here," she said, too quietly for anyone to hear, then again, flatter. When the instructor handed her a foam board, she took it and held it against her chest like a shield, her knuckles whitening. She kicked twice, swallowed a mouthful of water, and coughed until her eyes stung. Nobody looked. She stood, shoulders curled inward, and stared at the clock above the lifeguard chair, counting the minutes left, thinking of the dry towel in her locker and the quiet drive home, where no one would ask how it went.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The seed packets sit in a row on the porch rail, tomatoes, beans, kale, their glossy faces grinning at me. I kneel in the dirt Dan broke up last spring, before he left, and the shovel feels heavier than it should. My knees ache against the cold ground. I push a bean seed down with one finger, then another, then stop and just stare at the little hole. Across the fence, Mrs. Alvarez calls out that I'm planting too early, and I say, 'Fine,' flatter than I mean to, and keep going without looking up. The rows come out crooked. I don't fix them. My throat is tight, and I blame the dust, wiping my face with a gritty glove so it smears. When the last seed is buried I don't water it right away. I sit on the overturned bucket, hands hanging between my knees, listening to the empty house behind me, wondering why I thought anything here would grow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to the next slide, and there it is, my chart, the one I built over three weekends, now with her name in the corner. I keep my pen capped and press its tip into my thumb. The conference room smells like burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. Everyone nods when she says "my approach," and my jaw tightens until my molars ache. Someone asks a question and she glances at me, just once, and I look down at my notebook, where I've drawn the same square eleven times. When Priya says, "This is great work," I say, "Yeah, great," too flat, too fast, and my voice comes out thin as paper. My chair squeaks as I shift. The air vent hums above me. I count the ceiling tiles, then count them again, and when the meeting ends I'm the first one out, leaving my coffee full and cold on the table.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway is empty enough that I can hear the tire seams ticking under me, one, two, one, two. I missed my exit ten minutes ago and didn't turn around. My phone lights up in the cup holder, Dana's name, and I let it buzz itself dark. "Fine," I say to the windshield, flat, like she's sitting beside me. "Everything's fine." My jaw aches; I've been clenching it since the parking garage. The heater is blasting but my hands stay cold on the wheel, and I keep swallowing around something lodged under my breastbone. A gas station sign glows ahead, the only lit thing for miles, and I picture pulling in, buying nothing, sitting there. Instead I drive past. The radio plays a song I used to love, and I switch it off halfway through the chorus. When I finally turn onto our street, I cut the headlights early and coast, staying in the car with the engine ticking, not ready to carry my face inside.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine on the fourth floor ate my dollar, and I stood there pressing the return lever until my knuckle went white. Then I carried nothing into room 412. Grandpa's hand lay on the blanket like a dropped glove, and I set mine beside it without touching. "Hey," I said, too quietly, so I said it again, louder, in a voice that didn't sound like mine. The monitor kept up its small green beeping. He smiled at the ceiling. I told him the drive was fine, traffic was fine, work was fine, everything fine, fine, while my jaw ached from holding it all in place. My throat felt packed with wet paper. When the nurse came to adjust the drip, I stared at her shoes until she left. I checked my phone. Nothing. I checked it again. Twenty minutes in, I said I should beat the parking meter, and I stood, and my legs felt filled with sand, and I still didn't kiss his forehead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marta stood apart from the cluster of mothers by the fence, her car keys biting into her palm. Someone laughed near the gate, bright and easy, and she turned her shoulder to it. The drizzle had soaked through her sleeves an hour ago, or maybe ten minutes; she couldn't tell. When the bell rang, she didn't look up right away. Children spilled out in neon backpacks, and she searched for Theo's gray hood with a tight, heavy feeling pressing under her ribs. There he was, trailing the others, eyes on the pavement. A woman beside her said, 'Rough week, huh?' and Marta answered, 'Fine. Just tired,' in a voice that came out flat as paper. She swallowed against the thickness in her throat. Theo reached her and held out a crumpled note from his teacher without a word. She folded it into her coat pocket unread, took his bag, and walked to the car with her jaw clenched, staring at the wet road the whole way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man in the windbreaker ran his thumb along the edge of Mom's oak dresser and asked if twenty would do. I said fine before he'd finished the sentence. My voice came out flat, like I was reading it off a card. He and his son hauled it down the driveway, and the drawers rattled the whole way, the same rattle I used to hear through the wall at night. I stood there holding the twenty, folded small, then folded it again. The sun was too bright. My jaw ached from holding it still. A woman asked about the kitchen table, and I told her to take it, no charge, just take it, and then I walked inside and stood in the empty dining room, staring at four pale dents in the carpet. I forgot to come back out for an hour. Nobody stole anything. I checked, and somehow that made my chest feel heavier, like the cardboard sign had been wrong about everything being worth something.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the cabinet floor with her cheek against damp particleboard, a flashlight clamped in her teeth, and turned the wrench a quarter inch before it slipped again. Water ran down her wrist into her sleeve. She didn't bother pulling it out. The drip kept time with the clock on the wall, and she counted along without meaning to. Two hours now. Dan's old toolbox sat open beside her, every tray rattled through, and nothing in it fit. She spat out the flashlight. "Of course," she said, flat and quiet, to no one. "Of course it's the size you don't have." Her shoulders ached, and a heaviness sat behind her ribs that had nothing to do with the crouching. She thought about calling him, then looked at the phone, its screen gone dark and slick with water, and left it where it was. The bucket was nearly full. She dumped it in the sink, slowly, and slid back under.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the radiator shelf for three days, its little window showing my name in that flat, official typeface. Tonight I finally carry it to the kitchen table and set it beside the cold tea. My thumb finds the flap and stops. I wipe my palm on my jeans, twice. The fridge hums; downstairs a neighbor's television laughs at something. "Fine," I say aloud to nobody, and tear it too fast, so the paper rips through the first line of text. I read the opening sentence, then read it again, then hold the page at arm's length as though distance might rearrange the words. My jaw aches. I've been chewing the inside of my cheek and I taste copper. I fold the letter along its creases, slide it back in, and push it under the fruit bowl. Then I take it out again, because I know I'll have to call them in the morning. I pour the tea down the sink without drinking it and stand there, watching it swirl away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed and emptied, and Marta stood on the platform until the crowd had flowed around her and gone. She held her phone up to the signs, but the battery showed a thin red sliver, and the characters on the boards meant nothing. At the ticket window she said, "Hotel? Please," too softly, and the man behind the glass tapped his ear and shook his head. She repeated it louder, then pointed at the crumpled printout, its ink smeared where her thumb had gripped it. He slid it back with a flat, quick sentence. Her shoulders sagged under the backpack straps. Outside, rain slanted across neon she couldn't read, and taxis pulled away before she could lift her hand. She sat on her suitcase beneath the awning, jaw tight, eyes stinging, and muttered, "Great. Just great," to no one. Her stomach ached with hunger, but she didn't go into the noodle shop glowing across the street. She watched the door instead, thumbs pressed hard against her knees.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: The tennis ball sits in my coat pocket, and I keep closing my fist around it, though Biscuit has long since stopped looking for it. She tears across the field in wide, looping circles, ears flapping, and I stand at the fence with my shoulders hunched against a wind that isn't even that cold. My phone buzzes against my hip. I don't take it out. "Good girl," I call, but it comes out flat, like something read off a card. The grass is gray-gold and wet, soaking through my sneakers, and I let it. Somewhere behind me a couple laughs, and I angle my body away. Biscuit bounds back, tongue lolling, and drops her whole warm weight against my knees. I rest my hand on her head and stare at the treeline. My throat is tight. "Five more minutes," I tell her, though we both know I'll say it again, because the car, and the empty apartment after it, can wait.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The folding chairs in the church hall are still stacked against the wall, and I'm the only one who arrived on time again. I tune the cello twice though it was fine the first time. When Marguerite bustles in with her tray of lemon bars, I say, "Lovely," in a voice flat as the linoleum. We start the Dvorak. My bow arm feels like wet sand. I miss the same entrance in bar thirty-one, then again, and someone coughs politely. "Once more from the top?" says the conductor, and I nod at my knees. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the first note. Outside, rain ticks on the high windows, and I think about my apartment, the kettle I'll boil for no one. During the break I hold a paper cup without drinking, laugh a half-second late at a joke, and rummage in my case for nothing so no one will ask how I'm doing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta had promised herself she'd finish the pegboard by noon, but at one o'clock she was still standing before it, turning a half-inch chisel over in her hand. Sawdust lay along the windowsill like old snow. She dropped the chisel in the donate box, then fished it out and slid it into her coat pocket. "Fine," she said aloud, flatly, to nobody. The radio on the shelf still held Dennis's station; she snapped it off, found the silence worse, and turned it on again, low. Her jaw ached from clenching. She opened a coffee can of mismatched screws, sorted three, and stopped, because his thumbnail had left a crescent dent in the lid. The trash bags stayed flat and empty beside her boots. When her phone buzzed, his sister asking how it was going, she stared at it until the screen went dark, then wiped her eyes with a gritty glove and picked up the broom without sweeping anything.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smelled of floor polish and old radiators, and I had been standing in front of the glass noticeboard for forty minutes with my hands jammed into my hoodie pocket. The secretary kept saying noon, but it was ten past, and the corner of the board was still bare except for a faded fire-drill notice. My stomach had folded into itself. I'd skipped breakfast, then bought a cereal bar from the machine and left it unopened, the wrapper damp in my fist. When Dara bounced up and asked how I was doing, I said, "Fine," flat as a tabletop, and kept my eyes on the pin holes. She laughed at something and drifted off. I counted ceiling tiles. Twice I checked my phone, no messages, nothing. A door clicked somewhere down the hall and my shoulders jumped to my ears. I swallowed, but my throat stayed tight, like swallowing sand. Maybe I should just go home, I thought, and I didn't move at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The orange light slid off the ridge before I'd reached the second switchback, and I didn't speed up. My boots dragged through the gravel, each step a small scrape I almost enjoyed. I had told Dana I'd be back by five. I'd turned my phone off at the trailhead and now I let it sit in my pocket like a stone. The pines went from green to black one by one. My shoulders ached where the pack straps bit, and I kept them there, kept tightening the buckles instead of loosening them. A jay screamed somewhere, and I said, out loud, flat and quiet, "Fine. Whatever." Nobody answered. My throat felt packed with wet sand. At the overlook I stopped, stared at the valley's few lit windows, and thought about how none of them were mine. Cold crept up my sleeves. I should have turned back an hour ago. I sat down on a rock anyway, hugged my knees, and watched the dark take the trail behind me, then the trail ahead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth at the folds, Grandma Odile's slanted handwriting gone brown with butter stains. Marcus propped it against the flour canister and read "flour until it feels right" for the third time. "Right," he said to the empty kitchen, flat as the counter. He measured anyway, scooped, leveled, dumped it out and started over. The dough clung to his knuckles, and he scraped it off with more force than needed. Rain ticked at the window; the radio he'd turned on was switched off again after one song. His shoulders ached, his jaw was tight, and he kept pressing his thumb into the dough as if it might answer him. It didn't spring back the way hers had. He set the bowl under a towel, sat on the floor with his back against the oven, and stared at the card until the words blurred. When the timer buzzed an hour later, he let it ring for a long while before getting up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a basket with one frozen dinner and a box of tea when someone said my name beside the cereal. Dana Whitlock. Same laugh, same bright coat, now with a wedding ring and a stroller she rocked with one hip. "Oh my God, look at you!" she said. I smiled with my mouth only and slid the basket behind my leg. "Hey. Wow. Yeah." She talked about Lisbon, about her promotion, about a house with a yard. My neck went hot. I nodded at the wrong moments and picked at the cardboard handle until it tore. "And you? Still in the city?" "Still," I said. "Busy. You know." The fluorescent lights hummed, and my voice sounded thin, like it came from the next aisle. When she hugged me, I stood stiff, arms half raised. I said we should get coffee, and we both knew I wouldn't. In the car I sat with the engine off, the frozen dinner sweating through its bag on the passenger seat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marisol wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time, watching the rag drag a gray streak across the laminate. Fluorescent light buzzed over the aisle of unsold candy canes. Her jaw ached from holding a smile nobody was there to see. When the phone rang, she let it ring five times before lifting it. "Hillcrest Pharmacy," she said, flat as a receipt. "We close at six." The caller asked about a refill, and she answered in single words, eyes on the clock, its second hand stuttering. Her sister had texted a photo of a table already set for twelve. Marisol turned the phone face down. Her shoulders felt packed with wet sand. She counted pills she had already counted, then sat on the stool and stared at the dark glass of the door, where her own reflection stood waiting for someone, anyone, to come in and make the hour move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board flips from ON TIME to DELAYED while I'm still on the moving walkway, and I stop walking even though the floor keeps carrying me. Gate B47. Eleven minutes. My carry-on strap has dug a groove into my shoulder, and I don't bother switching sides. At the gate a woman in a blazer taps her screen without looking up, and I say, "Please," then nothing, because my voice comes out thin and flat, like someone else's. "The door's closed, sir." Through the glass the plane sits there, plainly still attached to its tunnel, and I almost laugh. I don't. I set my bag down on the carpet and sit on it, knees pressed together. My phone says 9:52 p.m. I type to my sister, "Not making it," delete it, and type "Fine, will call tomorrow." The terminal hums. My eyes burn in the vending machine's glow, and I keep staring at the row of untouched pretzels as if one might change its mind.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had taped the baseboards at nine that morning, and by noon she was still on the same wall. The roller dragged a pale gray stripe over the yellow, and she stood watching it dry, not moving to the next section. Two nails still jutted from the plaster where the frames had hung. She pulled one out with her fingers and held it a while. "Fine," she said to the empty room, flatly, when the radio started a song she knew, and she switched it off. Her shoulders ached; she hadn't eaten. The second coat could wait, she decided, then dipped the roller anyway, pressing too hard so paint spat onto her wrist. She didn't wipe it. In the corner, the closet door stood open on his empty hangers, and she rolled slowly toward it, then past it, leaving the door exactly as it was. The gray crept closer to the light switch, and her breath came out thin and slow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while Marguerite was still holding the cold cup of coffee she'd poured two hours ago. She didn't go inside. Rain slanted under the porch roof and speckled her bare shins, and she let it, watching the glass of the screen door fog and clear, fog and clear. Behind her, the phone buzzed against the wicker table again; she turned it face down without looking. 'Fine,' she said to nobody, then, quieter, 'Fine.' Her jaw ached from holding it tight. The swing creaked under her slow, mechanical pushing, and the damp air sat in her chest like a wet towel. Across the yard, her husband's tomato stakes leaned in the mud, string flapping loose. She thought about tying them up. She thought about it for a long time, her thumbnail worrying a split in the armrest, while the gutters overflowed and the lightning lit the empty chair beside her, white and flat, then let it go dark again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had the rear wheel half off the frame when the fluorescent tube above the next bay began to buzz, though nobody had touched the switch. She stopped with the wrench in the air. The garage was supposed to be empty at this hour; the sign-in sheet by the door said so. Still, a toolbox lid sat open two bays down, and a mug of tea, steaming, rested on its edge. She set the wrench down quietly, as if it might ring against the concrete. "Hello?" Her voice came out thinner than she meant, and she cleared her throat and tried again, louder, to nobody. Her thumb kept rubbing a smear of chain grease into her forefinger. She picked the wheel back up, spun it, and listened to the ticking freehub, but her eyes kept sliding to the tea, to the steam, to the dark gap beneath the shelving. The back of her neck prickled. She worked faster, and badly, and dropped the quick-release twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The wind turned first, swinging the shelter's loose ad panel against its frame with a sound like knuckles on glass. Marisol checked her phone again: 9:52, the bus now twelve minutes late, no other soul on the street. She tucked her chin into her collar and counted the streetlights, then counted them again because the third one had gone out and she hadn't seen it happen. The sky to the west had gone the color of a bruise, and the first fat drops struck the bench one at a time, deliberate, spaced out. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, to nobody. Her thumb kept pressing the dead screen of the schedule board. A gust shoved a paper cup along the curb and she flinched, stood, sat, stood again. The hairs on her forearms were upright beneath her sleeves. Somewhere behind the shuttered laundromat, a door banged once, and she realized she was holding her keys between her fingers, points out, her breath shallow and loud in her ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marisol had meant to sort the shoebox in ten minutes, but an hour later the tea beside her had gone cold and she hadn't noticed. The envelopes were all addressed to her mother in the same slanting hand, and none had a return address. She read one, set it face down, then turned it over again to check the date, as if it might have changed. "That's not possible," she said to the empty kitchen, too quietly, the way you speak in a house where someone is sleeping. The postmarks stopped the week before her father's funeral. Her fingers had gone cold at the tips. She squared the stack against the table, twice, then got up and drew the curtain over the window above the sink, though it was still afternoon. Behind her the refrigerator hummed and clicked off, and she flinched at the silence it left. She did not pick up the next letter. She stood with her palm flat on the lid.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Havel stood on my porch at dusk, hands folded, smiling a beat too long. "Your ladder. The tall one. Could I borrow it tonight?" I kept my fingers on the doorframe. Tonight. The word sat in my ears. "Tonight," I repeated, and my voice came out thinner than I meant. Behind him, his house was dark, every window black, though I'd seen his wife's car leave on Monday and not return. I glanced at the garage, then at the porch light buzzing above us, moths ticking against it. My palms were damp; I wiped them on my jeans. "It's a bit heavy," I said. "I could bring it over tomorrow." He didn't blink. "Tonight is better." The hair on my arms lifted. I heard myself laugh, a short dry sound, and say I'd have to look for it, then shut the door and slide the chain on, standing there listening to him not leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions are already translucent when I realize I've stirred them for ten minutes without smelling anything. Seven o'clock, the text said, but the hallway has creaked twice since six and nobody has knocked. I wipe my palms on my apron, then again, because they keep going damp. The knife skids on a carrot and I freeze, listening, though the only sound is the fridge humming a note I've never noticed before. "Fine," I say aloud to the empty kitchen, too brightly. "Totally fine." I check the window over the sink; under the street lamp stands a figure, or maybe it's just the mailbox. I turn the burner down, then up, then down. My shoulders have crept toward my ears. When the doorbell finally rings, the wooden spoon clatters to the floor, and I stand there with my pulse thudding in my throat, counting to five before I dare walk to the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter at half past eleven, and Marta stopped with the dish towel halfway through a plate. Ten digits, no name, an area code she didn't know. She let it ring out. It started again immediately. She wiped her hands slowly, though they were already dry, and glanced at the dark window over the sink, at her own pale reflection. On the fourth ring she picked up and said nothing. Breathing, then a faint hum, like a room with a fan running. "Hello?" Her voice came out thinner than she meant. "Who is this?" The hum went on. She noticed she had backed against the fridge, her shoulder blades pressed to its cold door, her pulse ticking in her ears. "I'm hanging up," she said, and didn't. Then a click. She checked the deadbolt twice, then the back door, then the deadbolt again, and left every light on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in the bottom of Maya's backpack for two years, and its spine had gone soft as cloth. She stood outside the library doors longer than she needed to, thumb rubbing the torn corner of the cover. Inside, the air smelled of dust and carpet glue. Her palms were damp; she wiped them on her jeans twice before reaching the desk. The librarian, a gray-haired man with half-moon glasses, looked up and said nothing. "Hi," Maya said, too quickly, then again, quieter. "I think this is, um. Overdue." She set it down and slid it forward with two fingers, as if it might go off. He turned it over and opened it to the stamped card. Her ears were hot. She counted ceiling tiles while the scanner beeped, and a laugh came out of her that belonged to no joke. "I can pay," she said. "Whatever it is. I brought cash." Her knee wouldn't stop bouncing against the desk.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol set the last box down by the radiator and stood listening. The pipes ticked, then stopped, then ticked again, a beat late, like something answering. She laughed once, too loudly, and the sound came back flat off the bare walls. "Old building," she told the empty room. She checked the deadbolt, turned it, turned it back, checked again. The closet door stood open an inch; she pushed it shut with two fingers, and it drifted open again. Her neck prickled. She wedged a chair under the knob, felt silly, and left it there. In the kitchen she ran the tap and watched the water until it went clear, though her hands wouldn't quite stop shaking when she filled the glass. Upstairs, a floorboard creaked, once, in the exact place she'd just been standing. She didn't unpack the lamp. She sat on the mattress with her shoes on, coat zipped to her chin, and kept her eyes on the gap beneath the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat dead center on the bench, squared to the edge like someone had placed it there for me. I stopped ten feet off. The park was empty, which I hadn't noticed until now, and the swings behind me creaked though I felt no wind. "Hello?" I said, too quietly, then again, louder, my voice cracking on the second syllable. Nobody answered. I circled the bench once, hands shoved in my jacket pockets, scanning the tree line. The leather was still warm when I finally touched it, and I yanked my fingers back as if burned. Inside, a driver's license, a photo of a man with my exact haircut. Not my face, but close enough that my stomach dropped. A receipt, dated today, from the café I'd left twenty minutes ago. I laughed, one short breath, and my palms were slick. I set it down exactly as I'd found it and walked, not ran, toward the gate, counting my steps, not looking back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor says the water only reaches my ribs, so I stand there counting the blue tiles on the wall, forty-one, then forty-one again. My toes grip the pool floor like it might leave. "Just let your head go back," Marisol says, and I laugh, too high, too quick, and ask whether we could do the kickboard first. Again. The overhead lights wobble on the surface, and every slap of a distant swimmer's arm makes my shoulders jump toward my ears. I've checked the drain twice. My fingers are wrinkled, but I keep them clamped on the gutter's edge, knuckles pale, while my pulse knocks somewhere in my throat. Thirty-six years old, and a ten-year-old in the next lane is floating on her back, humming. "Okay," I say, not moving. "Okay. One more second." I swallow chlorine-flavored spit and watch the tiles, forty-one, and do not let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Mara knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned in her fist, and every time the wind lifted a corner of the paper she flinched. The soil was darker than she'd expected, cold and crumbly, and when something pale and segmented slid across her glove she dropped the trowel and sat back on her heels. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly. "Okay. That's normal." She read the back of the carrot packet again, though she'd already read it three times, and her thumb left a damp smear over the words thin to two inches. Two inches from what? The fence behind her creaked. She glanced over her shoulder at the neighbor's empty window, then at the rows she'd already scratched out, which looked crooked, accusing. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. She pushed one seed into the dirt, covered it fast, and pulled her hand back as if the ground might close on it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide, and my stomach dropped an inch. The chart was mine. My numbers, my color scheme, even the little footnote I'd added at midnight, now under her name. She spoke smoothly, hand sweeping across the screen, and I pressed my thumbnail into the pad of my finger until it went white. The conference room felt too bright. Someone's pen clicked, clicked, clicked. I stared at the water glass in front of me, watching a bead slide down its side, because looking up meant meeting Priya's eyes, and she'd know. 'Great,' I heard myself say when Dana paused, my voice thin and a half-step too high. I laughed at nothing. My collar was damp. When she said 'we built this over the quarter,' I reached for my notebook and wrote the word 'we' three times, pressing so hard the page tore, then smiled at her like nothing was wrong.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The headlights behind me had been there since the exit, same distance, same height, never closing in. I eased off the gas to forty. They eased off too. "Okay," I said out loud, to nobody, my voice thinner than I wanted. I turned the radio down, then off, then on again because the quiet was worse. My palms were slick on the wheel, and I kept wiping one, then the other, against my jeans. The road was all black fields and a single dead gas station sign. I flicked my blinker for a turn I didn't need, and held my breath until the lights slid straight past the road behind me. They didn't follow. I laughed once, short and wrong. Still, I locked the doors twice, checked the mirror again, and drove the last four miles with my shoulders up around my ears, counting mailboxes under my breath until my own porch light appeared.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator doors opened on four, and I stood there until they started to close again and I had to stick my arm out. Grandpa's room was the last one down the hall. I counted ceiling tiles on the way, then lost count and started over. The machine beside his bed beeped slightly off from my pulse, and I kept trying to breathe in time with it. "Hey, Pop," I said, too loud, then too soft. His hand lay on the blanket like something set down and forgotten. I wiped my palms on my jeans twice before I touched it. It was cooler than I expected. A nurse's shoes squeaked past the door and I flinched, then laughed at nothing. "Traffic was fine," I told him. "Really fine." I kept my coat on. I kept my eyes on the window, where the parking lot lights were flickering on one by one, and I didn't sit down, because sitting meant staying.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The gate should have opened at 3:10, and my watch says 3:19. I keep thumbing the car key until its teeth leave little dents in my palm. Other parents chat in clumps, but I stand by the fence, counting windows on the second floor, then counting them again. Someone has moved the usual crossing guard. A man I don't recognize leans against the lamppost, phone dark in his hand, and my jaw clenches every time he glances toward the doors. "Sorry, do you know why they're late?" I ask a woman beside me, and my voice comes out thin, too quick. She shrugs. My shirt clings between my shoulder blades despite the cold. When the doors finally bang open, I rise onto my toes, scanning every small red backpack, swallowing against a dry throat. Then Maya's yellow hat bobs out, and I realize I've been holding my breath so long my ears are ringing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marta had priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, but the man in the gray raincoat had been standing beside it for twenty minutes, one hand sliding along the top drawer, never opening it. The morning was bright, yet she kept tugging her cardigan closed. "That one's solid," she said, and her voice came out thinner than she meant. He didn't answer. He crouched and ran a thumb along the inside edge of the leg, right where her late husband had carved his initials. She hadn't told anyone about those initials. Her tea went cold in her hands. The folding table wobbled when she bumped it, and she steadied a lamp without looking at it. "Anything else catch your eye?" He smiled, finally, and said, "I used to own this." Marta laughed too quickly, glanced at the empty driveway, and found herself counting the steps to her front door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta wedged herself under the basement sink with the flashlight clamped in her teeth, and a drip landed on her wrist, cold, exactly where the last one had. She stopped. Upstairs, a floorboard creaked, though she'd sent everyone out. "Hello?" she called, too brightly, and the flashlight dropped. Nothing answered. The furnace clicked on and she flinched hard enough to crack her elbow against the cabinet. She laughed once, a thin sound, and fitted the wrench around the nut. Her fingers wouldn't close right; they felt borrowed. Between turns she paused to listen past the hiss of water. The corner by the water heater was just dark, she told herself, just dark, and still she angled her body so her back stayed against the wall. The drip slowed, then quickened. She kept glancing at that shadow, wrench slick in her palm, pulse loud in her ears, and never turned her head all the way around.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had sat beside the toaster since Tuesday, its little window showing Marta's name in a typeface she knew too well. Now she washed her hands, dried them twice, and carried it to the table. The kettle clicked off behind her; she didn't turn around.
