She slid a butter knife under the flap, and the paper tore crooked anyway. "Fine," she said aloud, to no one, too brightly. Her thumbnail picked at the fold while the radiator ticked. She read the first line, then realized she'd stopped breathing somewhere in the middle of it and had to start over. The page rattled faintly. She set it down and flattened it with her palm as if it might lift off. The tea she'd poured had gone cold, though she couldn't remember pouring it. Her laugh came out short and wrong. "Okay. Okay," she said, and kept reading.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station doors sighed shut behind me, and the signs overhead turned into rows of hooks and slashes I couldn't hold onto. I checked my phone again, though I'd checked it ten seconds ago; one bar, no map. My backpack straps dug into my shoulders. A man brushed past, said something sharp and quick, and I nodded as if I'd understood, then said "Sorry, sorry," much too loudly. Nobody turned. I walked left, then stopped, then walked right, my thumb rubbing the edge of the hotel address I'd printed, the paper gone soft and damp. A vendor called out. I smiled with my teeth and kept moving. My throat was dry, but the bottles in the kiosk all showed labels I couldn't read, so I didn't buy one. Every corner looked like the last corner. I realized I was holding my breath and let it out slowly, counting the lampposts, until I found one I could swear I'd already passed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta had let go of the leash an hour ago, and now she stood at the fence with her thermos going cold in her hand. Biscuit tore through the long grass, ears flat, tail high, the way he always did. But he kept stopping. Every few yards he froze, nose lifted toward the treeline, and the grass around him went still too. No birds. She noticed that only now. The back of her neck prickled, and she rubbed it, then rubbed her arms. "Biscuit," she called, too brightly. "Hey. Come on, bud." He didn't turn. Her thumb pressed the thermos lid down, again and again, until it clicked loose. She counted the trees, lost count, started over. When he finally bolted toward her, she was already unlatching the gate, and she didn't look behind him until the latch had caught.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and Marguerite had already restarted the Schubert three times. Her fingers kept finding the wrong key at the same bar, the one just before the long rest. "Sorry, sorry, again," she said to no one, because the folding chairs were empty except for Walt, who was stacking hymnals and humming off-pitch. Every time he set one down, the thud made her shoulders jump. She wiped her palms on her skirt, then on the piano bench, then on her skirt again. The wall clock ticked loud enough that she started counting along with it, and lost her place. "Walt, could you maybe not... no, never mind, it's fine," she said, too brightly. He shrugged and kept stacking. She stared at the page where the notes seemed to slide sideways, took a breath that stopped halfway down her ribs, and began again, listening for the door to open behind her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The pegboard still had Dale's outlines drawn in marker, every tool ringed in black, and I kept counting the empty ones as if the number mattered. Seven. I wiped my palms on my jeans and they were wet again almost at once. The radio sat on the bench, its dial turned halfway between two stations, and I reached for it, then pulled my hand back and pretended I'd been reaching for a rag. "Just boxes," I said aloud, too loudly, and the rafters gave it back to me. A half-finished birdhouse lay under the lamp, sawdust still pale on the vise, like he'd stepped out for coffee. My neck prickled. I checked the door behind me twice. When the furnace kicked on with a thump, I dropped the box of screws, and they rang across the concrete in every direction. I didn't pick them up. I stood there listening to the quiet settle back, then turned the lamp off, and on, and off again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside Room 14 smelled of floor wax and somebody's burnt toast. I'd been standing by the corkboard since 8:50, though the results weren't due until nine, and I kept retying a shoelace that was already fine. Mr. Hallam's door stayed shut. I checked my phone, put it away, checked it again. "Do you think he forgot?" I asked Priya, and my voice came out thin and too quick, like I'd been running. She shrugged. My palms were damp, so I wiped them on my jeans, then did it again. The clock above the fire extinguisher ticked louder than it ever had in class. When the door finally clicked, my stomach dropped somewhere near my knees, and I found I'd taken a step backward, away from the board, toward the wall, as if the paper might lunge. I counted the pushpins instead of looking. Eleven. Twelve. Then I made myself read.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid behind the ridge, and I checked my phone again, as if the battery might change its mind. Two bars of signal, then one, then none. I walked faster. My boots sounded too loud, so I stopped, and the woods kept going for half a second after me, a soft crunch somewhere off to the left. "Just a deer," I said aloud, my voice thin and oddly cheerful. The hairs on my forearms stood up anyway. I zipped my jacket to the chin, though I wasn't cold, and dug the headlamp from my pack with fingers that fumbled the strap twice. The trail markers had come every few minutes; now I couldn't remember the last one. I turned to look behind me, then turned back fast, as if something might use that moment. My breath was shallow and loud. I kept the beam low on my feet and counted my steps out loud, one, two, three, all the way toward the car.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Mara propped the index card against the flour tin and read it again, though she'd already read it four times. Her grandmother's slanted pencil: add water till it feels right. Right to whom? She pushed her fingers into the dough and stopped, because the warmth was wrong, too much like skin. The kitchen was quiet except for the oven ticking, and she kept glancing at the doorway behind her. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, then again, softer. A brown smear marked the card's corner, a thumbprint, and she pulled her own hand back as if it might match. The hairs on her forearms lifted. She wiped her palms on her jeans, twice, switched the radio on, then off again. When the timer buzzed she flinched hard enough to knock the spoon to the floor. She stood staring at it without bending to pick it up, listening to the house settle around the smell of yeast she remembered far too well.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta had one hand on a carton of eggs when someone said her name from the end of the aisle, and she knew the voice before she turned. Dana Whitlock. Same grin, same way of leaning on the cart as if the whole store were hers. "Marta Reyes! Oh my God, it's been, what, twenty years?" Marta set the eggs down, then picked them up again. "Something like that," she said, too quickly, and laughed at the wrong moment. Her palms had gone damp against the cardboard. The freezers hummed, and she counted cereal boxes behind Dana's shoulder. "You haven't changed," Dana said, and Marta heard herself answer, "Neither have you," though her voice came out thin. She kept glancing toward the registers. Her neck felt hot under her collar. "I should run, actually, the car's in a loading zone." It wasn't. She walked off with the eggs, forgetting the milk she'd come for, and didn't breathe properly until the automatic doors parted.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By six, the pharmacy had emptied, and Marisol kept straightening the same row of cough syrup while the fluorescent lights hummed their one flat note. Christmas Eve, and the parking lot beyond the glass had gone black except for a single car that had not moved in forty minutes. She counted the register twice. Her fingers were cold, though the heat was on. "Just closing up," she said aloud to nobody, and her voice came out thin, too bright. The automatic door sighed open at nothing, then shut. She stood very still, the pill spatula tight in her fist, listening past the hum. Her neck prickled. She turned the sign to CLOSED, then turned it back, then turned it again, and finally slid the bolt with a hand she watched shake. When the phone rang behind the counter, she let it ring four times before she breathed in and reached for it, saying nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board said Gate B47, and I read it three times anyway, my thumb pressing the edge of my boarding pass until the paper softened. Forty minutes. I walked fast, then faster, past a cleaning cart that nobody seemed to be pushing. The terminal was too quiet for noon. My footsteps echoed, and I caught myself glancing behind me twice, though nothing was there. "Sorry, which way to B?" I asked a man at a kiosk, and my voice came out thin, higher than I meant. He pointed. I thanked him too many times. The moving walkway had stopped, its rubber belt frozen, and I stepped onto it as if it might lurch. My shirt clung between my shoulder blades. Every gate I passed had its screen dark. What if B47 had moved? What if no one was there? I checked my phone, then checked it again, the same numbers staring back, my pulse ticking in my ears louder than the announcements.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The first coat of Soft Linen had barely dried when I saw the pencil marks. Under the old beige, right where the headboard used to stand, someone had written dates in small, even numbers, climbing toward the ceiling. I'd lived here eleven years. I didn't write them. I set the roller in the tray and listened to the house, which suddenly seemed to have a lot of quiet in it. "Hello?" I said, and laughed, too loud, at myself. The hair on my arms lifted under my sleeves. I pressed my thumb to the numbers; the graphite smeared, still soft. My mouth had gone dry. I picked the roller up, put it down, then crossed to the window and checked the latch twice, though we're on the second floor. Finally I dragged the ladder into the hallway, left the door wide open, and painted the rest of the wall from the doorway, arm stretched as far as it would go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder came while I was holding my tea, and I watched the surface shiver a full second before I felt the porch boards hum through my heels. I set the mug on the rail, picked it up again, set it down. Across the yard the maple thrashed, and the swing beside me creaked on its own, though I'd have sworn the wind came from the other side. "It's just weather," I said aloud, too loudly, and my voice sounded like someone else's. The hair on my forearms stood up. I counted between flash and boom the way Dad taught me, got to two, lost the number, started over. The porch light flickered and I found I was already on my feet, one hand flat against the front door, listening to the house behind me for a sound I couldn't name. My jaw ached. I realized I'd been clenching it since the first drop hit the steps.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Mara had been truing the same wheel for forty minutes, and it still wobbled. She spun it again, watched the rim kiss the brake pad at the same spot, and loosened the spoke she'd tightened a minute ago. Across the garage, the neighbor's radio murmured a station she didn't know, and every time the side door rattled she glanced up, wrench frozen mid-turn. Nobody came in. Her tea had gone cold on the shelf beside someone else's paint cans, and she drank it anyway, grimacing. 'Fine,' she said to the bike, too loudly, then lowered her voice as if the walls might repeat it. Her thumb was slick with grease; she wiped it on her jeans, then on her jeans again. She checked her phone, face-down on the bench, and turned it over, and turned it back. The wheel spun. Wobbled. She started counting spokes, lost count at twenty, and began again from the valve.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The schedule taped inside the shelter says 6:42, and my phone says 6:51. I check both again anyway. Wind has picked up, flipping the corner of the paper like it's trying to tell me something, and the sky over the car lot has gone the color of a bruise. I pull my sleeves down over my knuckles, then push them back up, then pull them down. A man across the street is folding his newspaper very slowly, and I watch him the whole time. 'Is this the 14?' I ask a woman who just arrived, though the sign above us says it plainly. She shrugs. My laugh comes out too high. The first drops hit the glass, one, then three, then too many to count, and my heel starts tapping the concrete in a rhythm I can't stop. I keep leaning out to look down the road. Nothing. I count the streetlights that flicker on. I turn my keys over in my pocket until the teeth bite my palm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: Marta had meant to sort the letters into keep and toss, but the toss pile stayed empty. She slid a rubber band off a bundle and it snapped apart, brittle as dry grass, and she flinched as if it had bitten her. The handwriting on the top envelope was her mother's, but slanted backward, strange, not the loops she remembered. She read the first line, then the first line again. 'Don't be silly,' she said aloud to the empty kitchen, her voice too bright. She stood, filled a glass at the sink, and didn't drink it. Her palms were damp; she wiped them on her jeans before touching the paper again. The radiator ticked. A postmark from the spring before the move caught her eye, and she turned the envelope face down, then squared the whole stack with both hands, twice, three times, until the edges were perfectly flush. Then she checked the clock, though she had nowhere to be.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while Marta was rinsing the same mug for the third time. Through the screen door she saw Dale from number nine, hands in his jacket pockets, smiling a little too long. "Need your ladder, if you've still got it. The tall one." She dried her palms on her jeans, one finger at a time. "The tall one," she said, and her voice came out thinner than she meant. "What for?" He laughed and nodded vaguely toward his roof, then toward hers. The hairs on her forearms lifted. Behind him the afternoon had gone quiet, no mower, no kids. She heard herself say it was in the garage, probably buried, and that she'd have to look. Her feet didn't move. She glanced at the window over the sink, at the gutter she'd noticed hanging loose last week, and wondered when exactly he had noticed it too. "Give me a minute," she said, and left the door unlatched, then went back and latched it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marta stirred the risotto for the fourth time in two minutes, though it hadn't changed. The clock on the stove said 6:42, and she checked her phone anyway, then set it face-down, then turned it over again. "Almost there," she said to the empty kitchen, too brightly. A knife slipped from the cutting board and clattered, and she flinched as if it had been a shout. She picked it up, rinsed it, and rinsed it again. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears; she pushed them down and they crept back. Had she salted the stock? She tasted it. She couldn't tell. She wiped her palms on her apron until the fabric was damp, straightened the forks on the table by a millimeter, then moved them back. Down the street a car door shut, and she stopped breathing, ladle in the air, listening for footsteps that didn't come. The pot hissed. She laughed once, shortly, at nothing, and reached for the salt.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the counter, rattling a spoon in the sink, and Marta watched the screen light up with a number she didn't know. Ten digits, no name. She dried her hands on her jeans, slowly, one finger at a time, though they were already dry. The kitchen had gone quiet except for the fridge hum. Four rings. Five. She picked it up and held it an inch from her ear, not speaking. "Hello?" she finally said, too softly, and cleared her throat to try again. Only breathing answered, or maybe the line itself. Her eyes went to the window, to the dark yard, to the porch light she couldn't remember switching on. "Who is this?" Her voice cracked on the last word. The pulse in her neck was loud enough to count. She pressed the screen to end the call, then stood there, thumb hovering, checking the deadbolt twice before she noticed she'd crossed the room to do it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now the lobby doors hissed shut behind me and the cold air conditioning found the back of my neck. I rehearsed the sentence twice, lips moving, then gave up on it. At the desk, the librarian was stamping something, thunk, thunk, and I stood there turning the strap of my bag around my finger until the tip went white. "Hi. Um. I have this," I said, too loud, and slid out the paperback. The corner of the cover had curled. My palms were damp against the plastic jacket. She flipped it open to the card, and I watched her eyes move, and I started talking about moving apartments, about finals, a whole stream of it, my voice climbing. She only said, "Let me check." The keyboard clicked. I counted ceiling tiles. Somewhere behind me a cart squeaked, and I flinched, and laughed at nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dana set the last box down in the middle of the room and then picked it up again, carrying it to the corner, then back to the window. The radiator ticked. She stopped, listening, until it ticked again. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, and the walls gave the word right back. She opened the fridge, which hummed louder than she remembered from the tour, and closed it without taking anything. Her hands wouldn't stay still; she peeled tape from a box, smoothed it flat, peeled another. Somewhere above her, a chair scraped, and her shoulders crept toward her ears. She checked the deadbolt. Walked to the bathroom, checked it was only a bathroom. Returned, and checked the deadbolt again. The mattress leaned against the wall, still wrapped in plastic, and she kept glancing at it as though it might suggest where to put itself. Her phone lit up with her sister's name. She watched it buzz across the counter, thumb hovering, until the screen went dark. Then she sat on the floor, coat still on, and counted the ceiling tiles twice.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather, curled at the corners, and I walked past it twice before I stopped. I looked left, then right, then at the empty jogging path. A kid's scooter lay on its side near the fountain, but no kid. My thumb rubbed the pad of my index finger, back and forth, while I told myself it was nothing. "Hello?" I said, too quietly, then again, louder, and my voice cracked on the second one. Nobody answered. The wind pushed a chip bag across the gravel, and I flinched at the scratch of it. I picked up the wallet with two fingers, like it might be hot, and my pulse thumped in my ears. The license inside showed a woman smiling, mid-laugh. I shut it fast. I kept glancing over my shoulder all the way to the gate, and I still hadn't decided whether to go home or back to the bench.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite had retied her swim cap twice before the instructor even blew the whistle. The pool smelled of chlorine and wet concrete, and every echo off the tiled walls made her glance toward the deep end, where the water went a darker blue. She stood on the second step, toes curled against the grit, and let the water climb her shins, then stopped. 'Just a minute,' she said, too brightly, and adjusted her goggles again. The kids in the next lane kicked past her, easy, laughing. Her heartbeat thumped in her ears, and her hands wouldn't stay still, tugging at her suit straps, smoothing her wet hair. When the instructor held out a kickboard, she took it and gripped until her knuckles paled. 'I'm fine, I'm fine,' she said, though nobody had asked. She pushed off, then planted her feet on the bottom almost at once, gasping, and looked back at the wall to measure how far she'd gone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Dana knelt at the edge of the raised bed and turned the seed packet over for the fourth time, reading the back as if it might have changed. The tomato seedlings sat in their plastic tray, leaning slightly, and she straightened one with a fingertip, then wiped her palm on her jeans. "Eighteen inches apart," she said aloud, too brightly, to nobody. She measured with a ruler, moved a hole two inches, then moved it back. The trowel felt oddly heavy. Her neighbor's fence creaked and she glanced up, certain someone was watching her get it wrong. Dirt packed under her nails, and her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. She pressed the soil around the first stem, lifted her hand, pressed again. Then she stood, checked the sky for clouds, sat back down, and dug the hole slightly deeper, just in case.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked to the third slide and Dana's voice kept going, smooth and certain, describing the onboarding flow he had sketched on a napkin in March. He uncapped his pen, capped it, uncapped it again. The conference room smelled of burnt coffee and dry-erase markers. Her chart showed the numbers climbing, and a bead of sweat slid down behind his ear. "Great," he said when she paused, but it came out too high, and he coughed to cover it. Nobody glanced his way. He pulled his laptop closer, opened his notes, and read the same line four times without taking it in. When Dana said "we" for the fifth time, his thumbnail dug into the pad of his finger. The projector hummed. He realized his knee was bouncing under the table and pressed his palm down hard on it, smiling at the screen as if he'd been listening to every word.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: Marisol checked the rearview mirror for the fourth time since the exit, and the same pair of headlights was still there, hanging back, never closing, never falling away. She turned the radio down, then off, and the hum of the tires seemed suddenly loud. Her fingers had gone stiff on the wheel at ten and two, and she realized she was holding her breath. "Just a guy going home," she said aloud, too brightly, the way you talk to a dog you don't trust. The road ran black between the fences, no houses, no porch lights. She eased off the gas; the headlights eased too. Her palms were slick. At the next turn she signaled, absurdly, for nobody, and watched the mirror until the glow slid on straight ahead. She did not exhale. She drove two more miles with the doors locked, then pressed the lock button again anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I've read the same laminated sign about hand sanitizer four times by the time the elevator opens on six. My uncle's door is half closed, and I stand there with the grocery-store tulips crushed against my chest, rehearsing a hello. 'Hey, Tío,' I say, too loud, and the word bounces off the beige walls. He looks smaller under the blanket, his wrist bracelet loose. I laugh at nothing. I set the tulips on the tray, move them to the sill, then back to the tray. The monitor beeps in a rhythm I start counting, then stop counting, then count again. My palms are damp; I wipe them on my jeans twice. 'They're feeding you okay?' I ask, and he starts to answer, but I'm already checking my phone, reading a text I don't absorb. The chair is right there. I don't sit. I keep my coat on, keys wedged between my fingers, one eye on the hallway, as if someone might call me out of the room.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Marguerite had checked her phone four times since parking, and the screen showed the same thing each time: nothing. She stood by the iron fence instead of the bench where the other parents laughed, her keys biting into her palm. When the bell rang, she rose onto her toes, scanning each door as it banged open, her breath shallow and high in her chest. "Sorry, is it always this slow?" she asked a man beside her, too quickly, and didn't wait for his answer. Children spilled past in bright jackets, none of them the right size. She rubbed her thumb along the seam of her sleeve until the thread loosened. A teacher glanced her way and Marguerite's stomach dropped, then the teacher turned to someone else. She counted the heads again. Her mouth was dry. When a small hand finally caught her coat, she flinched, then knelt so fast her knee cracked on the pavement, and held on a beat longer than he liked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marta had priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, then crossed it out and written sixty, then forty again. A man in a windbreaker ran his thumb along the drawer edge, and she found herself standing too close, rubbing her palms on her jeans. "Bottom drawer sticks," she said, too quickly. "You have to lift it. A little. Left side." He nodded and pulled it open without trouble. She laughed, a short thin sound. The sun was hot on her neck, yet her fingers felt cold. Across the lawn, her sister's old rocking chair sat beside a box of chipped saucers, and Marta kept turning her back to it, then turning around to check it was still there. "Thirty-five," she heard herself say. The man blinked. "Fine, forty's fine," she added, and reached for the cash box, but her hand hovered over the latch, and she could not remember why she had wanted any of this gone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slips off the fitting for the third time, and I swear at it, too quietly, as if someone upstairs might hear. Nobody's upstairs. I check anyway, glancing at the ceiling, then the basement stairs, then back at the drip. Plink. Plink. I've stopped being able to hear anything else. My shirt clings between my shoulder blades even though the cellar is cold, and my fingers feel too thick, like they belong to somebody less careful. I wrap the tape around the joint, unwrap it, wrap it again the other way. "Fine," I tell the pipe. "Fine, fine." My voice cracks on the second one. The video on my phone is still paused at 2:14, and I keep looking at it instead of trusting my hands. When the drip slows, I don't exhale. I just stand there with the wrench held against my chest, watching the bead of water gather at the seam, waiting for it to prove me wrong, and my knee won't stop bouncing against the bucket.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had sat against the fruit bowl since Tuesday, its little window showing Marisol's name in blocky type. Now she washed a mug that was already clean, dried it, and set it down with the handle turned just so. "It's probably nothing," she told the cat, too brightly. The cat blinked and left. She slid a butter knife under the flap, stopped, and wiped her palms on her jeans. The refrigerator hummed; she noticed it for the first time all week. The paper tore crooked anyway. She unfolded the page but looked at the window instead, at the rain stitching down the glass, reading the same gray streak three times before her eyes dropped. Her pulse thumped in her ears. The first line swam, and she realized she'd stopped breathing somewhere around the letterhead. She pressed two fingers to her lips, laughed once, a dry little sound, and began again from the top, slower, as if the words might change if she was careful.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed out of the station and Marit stood on the platform with her suitcase handle sliding in her damp palm. Signs bloomed overhead, all those curling letters that refused to become words. She checked her phone again, though she'd already checked it, and the map's blue dot pulsed in a street she couldn't pronounce. A man brushed past, said something quick and sharp, and she answered "Sorry, sorry," too loudly, then again, quieter. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears. At the ticket window she rehearsed the name of her hotel under her breath, three times, and when the clerk leaned toward the glass and frowned, she slid the printed reservation through the slot instead, her finger trembling beside the address. He tapped it, nodded, spoke a long stream of sound. She smiled and nodded back, understanding nothing, and gripped the suitcase until her knuckles whitened. Outside, the taxis all looked the same. She walked past them, toward nowhere, and kept walking, counting her steps.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tears across the long grass, ears flapping, and I count him again anyway: one dog, one orange blur, one dog. My thumb keeps pressing the leash clip in my pocket until it leaves a dent. The field is empty except for the crooked fence and a white van that wasn't parked by the gate when we came. I told myself I'd check the plates, then didn't. When Biscuit disappears behind the rise, I'm already walking, then half-jogging, my breath shallow and high in my chest. "Biscuit," I call, too bright, too fast. "Hey. Hey, buddy. Here." He pops up, tongue out, delighted, and I laugh at a pitch that doesn't sound like mine. My shirt is stuck to my back despite the wind. I clip him on, kneel, and keep my hand on his warm ribs longer than he likes, glancing at the van, then the road, then the van.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I had restarted the Schubert four times. "Sorry, once more," I told Marjorie at the piano, laughing at a pitch too high to be mine. I wiped my palms on my skirt, then did it again. The folding chairs sat empty, sixty of them in crooked rows, and still I kept glancing at the door as if someone might walk in. My breath stopped somewhere under my collarbone and refused to drop lower. I began the second verse and my eyes went to the sheet music, though I'd known the words for months. Halfway through, my knee started a small tremble I pressed down with my free hand. "Fine, that was fine," I said before Marjorie had spoken. She nodded slowly, fingers resting on the keys. I picked at the corner of my page until it curled. "Again from the top? Maybe a little slower. Or no, the same. Whatever you think." My voice cracked on 'whatever.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta had labeled three boxes KEEP, DONATE, TRASH, and after two hours all three were still empty. She stood holding a coffee can of mismatched screws, turning it so they rattled, then set it down, then picked it up again. "Okay," she said to the pegboard, too loudly. Tool outlines were drawn on it in black marker, each hammer and chisel inside its own ghost, and several ghosts were empty. Where was the square? She checked the bench, the floor, under the sawdust-furred radio. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears and she couldn't lower them. She jabbed the radio's knob and the silence rang worse, so she switched it back on low, and a man began reading the weather. She wiped her palms on her jeans. A half-finished birdhouse sat in the vise, one wall unglued. She reached for it, drew her hand back, and went to check the lock on the door again, though she'd just come in through it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the physics office smelled of floor polish and old radiators, and Marisol had already read the notice board twice, though nothing new had been pinned to it. She retied her shoelace, then untied it. Her phone said 2:58. The list was promised for three. A boy beside her laughed too loudly at something, and she flinched as if he'd dropped a tray. "Do you think they're late on purpose?" she asked no one, her voice thinner than she intended. Her thumbnail had worn a pale groove into the skin of her index finger. She checked the clock above the door, which disagreed with her phone by a minute, and felt irrationally cheated by it. When the secretary finally appeared with a sheet of paper and a roll of tape, Marisol's stomach dropped to somewhere near her knees. She stepped back, letting others crowd forward, and stared hard at a crack in the wall tile, counting its branches until her name might be easier to find.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: Marta checked her phone again, though she knew there was no signal this far up the ridge. The sun had slipped behind the pines, and the trail ahead had gone the color of ash. She quickened her pace, then slowed, then quickened again, her boots scuffing roots she could no longer see clearly. "Almost there," she said aloud, and her voice came out thin, too bright, like someone talking to a dog that had already bolted. Somewhere to her left a branch cracked. She stopped. Her pulse thudded in her ears and her fingers had gone cold around the strap of her pack. Nothing moved. She laughed once, a short dry sound, and started walking again, faster now, glancing back over her shoulder at the bend she had already passed. The trail marker she'd expected an hour ago still hadn't appeared. She counted her steps under her breath, lost count at ninety, and began again, one hand pressed flat against her stomach as the last gray light drained from the trees.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth, flour ghosted into the creases of Grandma Odile's handwriting. "A handful," it says, and I stare at my own hand like it might answer. I measure anyway, dump it back, measure again. The kitchen is too quiet; the fridge hums, and I turn on the radio and switch it off a minute later. My fingers keep pressing the dough and letting go, pressing and letting go. "Come on," I mutter, to nobody, to the bowl. The yeast smells right, I think, but I lean in three times to check. Somewhere between kneading and the first rise I notice I've read the same line, you'll know when it's ready, maybe twenty times, and my chest tightens with each pass. I wipe my hands on my jeans, check the clock, then check the dough, though nothing has changed. Her blue bowl sits by the window. I keep moving it an inch to the left, then back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana had three lemons in her basket and was weighing a fourth when someone behind her said, "Dana Whitlock?" She knew the voice before she turned. Marcus Pell, who had sat behind her in tenth-grade chemistry and once read her diary aloud. He was thicker now, a wedding band on his hand, a toddler on his hip. "Wow," she said, too brightly, and put the lemon back, then picked it up again. Her palms had gone damp against the mesh of the basket. "You look exactly the same," he said. "Ha. No. Well." She laughed a beat late and glanced at the freezer aisle, the exit, the self-checkout glowing green. Her heart was knocking somewhere near her collarbone. "I should, um, my car's in a loading zone," she said, though she had walked here. He was still talking about reunions. She nodded at every pause, counting the tiles between herself and the door, and left the lemons on the shelf.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: I've wiped the same stretch of counter four times, and the rag is still gray with it. Past the pharmacy window, the parking lot lights buzz on at 4:40, too early, and the lot is empty except for my car and one cart rolling slowly toward nothing. "Closing at six," I tell the man who wanders in, then say it again to the shelf of cough syrup after he leaves. My jaw aches; I've been clenching it since lunch. Every time the door chimes I check the clock, then the door, then my hands. Mina from days left a candy cane on my register with a note that says Don't stay late! and I read it twice, turn it over, put it in my pocket, take it out. The fluorescent hum climbs into my teeth. I keep straightening bottles that are already straight. When the phone rings I let it go three rings, my palm damp on the receiver, before I pick up and say, too bright, "Hello?"

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says D14, then D41, then D14 again, and I read it three times anyway. My carry-on strap has dug a groove into my shoulder, but I keep not shifting it. Forty minutes, the gate agent said, and the arrivals hall clock says thirty-one. I'm walking fast enough that my shins burn, past a man eating a pretzel so slowly I want to apologize to him for my pace. 'Sorry, sorry,' I tell a stroller, a pillar, nobody. My phone is at nine percent. I check it, put it away, check it again. At the moving walkway I stand on the left, then step right, then left, as if I could outvote the machine. My mouth tastes like pennies. I rehearse what I'll say at the desk, 'Please, I just need,' and the sentence keeps dissolving. A gate number blinks. I count the letters off the sign twice, and my hands, damp and strange, don't feel like mine on the strap.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I've taped the same edge three times now, peeling it up and pressing it down again, though the line was straight the first time. The can says Morning Linen. Yesterday the bedroom was green, and I keep touching the wall where the pencil marks were, the little heights we measured, until the roller takes them. "Just one coat," I tell the empty room, too loudly, and my voice bounces back thin. My stomach is tight, like I skipped a step on the stairs. I stir the paint longer than I need to. Drips dot the drop cloth and I crouch to count them. Down the hall the phone buzzes on the counter, and I don't go. I roll a wide stripe over the doorframe's old scuff, then another, breathing through my nose, shoulders up near my ears. When I finally glance back, the wall is wet and bright and blank, and my hand is shaking enough that the roller trembles against it, leaving a faint, rippled line.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: Marguerite carried the porch chair back from the railing for the third time, then dragged it forward again, its legs shrieking on the boards. Thunder rolled somewhere past the soybean field, and she counted under her breath, lost the number, started over. The rain came sideways now, cold flecks on her shins, and still she didn't go in. She turned her phone over in her palm. No messages. She turned it back. "It's fine," she said to the dog, who hadn't asked, her voice too bright, too quick. Her tea had gone cold an hour ago; she lifted it anyway and drank, grimacing. The porch light flickered and she flinched, shoulders climbing toward her ears. Down the gravel road, headlights swung, and her whole body leaned toward them before they passed and kept going. She sat very still after that, nails pressed into the armrest, listening to the gutters choke and the screen door tapping its frame behind her, tap, tap, tap, like someone politely asking to be let in.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The wrench slips off the rusted nut for the third time and my knuckles slam into the frame. I don't swear. I just set the wrench down very carefully, like it might go off, and stare at the pegboard where my neighbor's tools hang in perfect outlines while mine are heaped in a coffee can. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the voicemail this morning. Someone's radio mutters from the other bay and I walk over and click it off without asking. "Sorry," I say, flat, not meaning it. Back at the bike, I spin the rear wheel and it wobbles, scraping the brake pad with that thin, whining rasp. My hands are shaking a little, so I wipe them on my jeans again and again, though the grease won't come off. I tell myself it's only a wheel. Then I kick the stand, hard, and the whole bike clatters sideways, and I stand there breathing through my nose, listening to the spokes tick quiet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The shelter's glass has a crack down the middle, and I stand beside it instead of under it, jaw locked, thumbnail digging a groove into my palm. The sky went from pewter to bruise while I reread her message for the fifth time. Four words. No question mark. A gust shoves a gum wrapper along the curb and the first fat drops hit my collar, cold as coins. I don't move. "Fine," I say aloud to nobody, too sharp, and a man with a stroller glances over and then carefully doesn't. My eyes sting, which I blame on the wind. The phone goes into my pocket, then out again, then back. Rain thickens, soaks my sleeves, plasters my hair to my forehead. The 14 rounds the corner, headlights smeared across the wet road, and I realize my fists are still clenched. I keep staring at the screen, thumb hovering, typing nothing, while the doors sigh open without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox had been taped shut for eleven years, and Marguerite sawed through the tape with a butter knife, harder than she needed to. She pulled out the first envelope, read the return address, and put it face down on the carpet. Then the next. Then a third, which she held a moment before folding it in half, then in half again, until it wouldn't fold. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been clenching it. "Fine," she said to the empty room, too loudly. "Fine. Keep your Sundays." A page slipped free, and his looping handwriting said *I'll always be there*, and she laughed once, a short dry sound. Her hands were shaking as she stacked the letters, squared the edges, and squared them again. The radiator clanked. She didn't turn on the lamp, though the words had begun to blur, and she kept reading anyway, thumbnail pressed white against the paper, until her tea went cold beside her knee.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale's knock came while I was scraping dried egg off a plate, and I kept scraping after I saw him through the window, holding his empty hands like a man already sure of the answer. "Hey, neighbor. Got that tall ladder still?" I dried my fingers one at a time on the dish towel. My jaw had gone tight enough that my molars ached. "The one I lent you in March," I said, evenly, too evenly. "That one?" He laughed and scratched his neck. "Right, I'll look for it." Behind him, his gutters hung full of black leaves, and my own ladder, I knew, lay somewhere in his weeds, rungs rusting. My pulse thudded in my ears. I walked to the garage slowly, because running would have meant something else. The only ladder left was the little stepstool. I set it in his arms, gripping it a second longer than I needed to. "Bring it back," I said, and shut the door before he answered.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onion keeps slipping under the knife because my hands won't hold still, so I set the blade down and press my palms flat on the counter until the granite cools them. Twenty minutes until the doorbell. The phone buzzes beside the cutting board, and I flip it face down without reading it, again. "Fine," I tell the empty kitchen, too loud, "they can eat late." The pot lid rattles. I snatch it up and clank it onto the wrong pot. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my teeth around the sentence Dana said this morning, the one about how I always make things a bigger deal than they are. I scrape the onions into the pan harder than I need to. Oil spits at my wrist. I don't flinch, just stare at the red dot, then laugh once, a dry little sound, and turn the radio off because the cheerful song is unbearable. Then I light another burner and keep going.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the counter while I'm scraping burnt rice into the sink, and the screen shows a string of digits I don't know. I stare at it through four rings. My jaw has gone tight enough that my teeth ache. I wipe my hands on my jeans, too hard, and leave a gray smear on the denim. On the fifth ring I answer and say nothing. "Hello? Is this Dana?" a man asks, bright and careless. "Who's asking," I say, flat, each word clipped off. My pulse thumps in my ears. He mentions the unpaid balance, and I realize I'm gripping the edge of the sink so hard my knuckles have whitened. "Don't call this number again," I tell him, quieter than I mean to. I hang up, then set the phone face-down and press both palms on the cold counter, breathing through my nose, counting the dripping faucet until my hands stop shaking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and the spine was bent where my laptop had pressed against it. I stood outside the library doors for a full minute, thumb worrying the corner of the cover until the paper frayed. Inside, the air smelled like dust and carpet glue. My stomach felt packed with wet sand. At the desk I slid the book across without looking up. "It's, um. Eight months," I said, too fast, my voice cracking on the last word. The librarian typed something. I counted the ceiling tiles. My ears were burning, and I kept tugging my sleeves down over my wrists as if they might hide me. "Forty-one dollars," she said. I laughed, a short, wrong sound, then pulled out my wallet and dropped a coin. It rolled away under a shelf, and I just stood there, jaw tight, watching it go, thinking that of course it would, of course.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marta set the last box down so hard the lamp inside rattled. Forty-one steps up, she had counted, and the apartment gave her four strides from door to window. She stood with her coat still buttoned, jaw tight, staring at the radiator that clanked once and went silent. The couch she had spent six years choosing sat wedged against the wall, its arm blocking the closet. "Of course," she said to no one, flat and quiet. She tried to peel tape from a box and her fingers kept slipping, so she ripped it instead, cardboard tearing in a long ugly line. Her phone buzzed with her sister's name. She watched it light up the counter, then turned it face down. Her throat felt packed with sand. In the window, a neighbor's TV flickered blue across the airshaft. She pressed her palm hard against her sternum, breathed through her teeth, and left the kitchen drawers open, empty, exactly as she'd found them.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Marguerite sat down hard on the bench, and the slats groaned under her. The letter from the bank was still crushed in her fist, and she didn't notice the brown leather wallet beside her until her knuckles brushed it. She flipped it open with a thumb that wouldn't stop trembling. Forty dollars, a library card, a photo of a toddler missing two teeth. Her jaw ached from clenching. 'Of course,' she said to the pigeons, her voice flat and too loud. 'Of course it's today.' A jogger glanced over and veered wide. She pressed the heel of her hand against her breastbone, where something hot and tight sat like a swallowed stone, and stared at the pond until the ducks blurred. Then she tore the letter in half, shoved the pieces in her coat pocket, and read the address on the license twice, slowly, as if the words were a task she could finally finish. Her breath came out shaky. She stood, wallet gripped, and walked without looking back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The kickboard slips from my hands for the third time, and I let it drift. Eight-year-olds hang off the lane rope beside me, kicking like it's nothing. I'm forty-one. My jaw is tight enough that my teeth ache, and chlorine stings the back of my throat where something else is lodged. "Try again, nice and relaxed," the instructor says. "I am relaxed," I snap, too loud, the words bouncing off the tile. My heart thuds against my ribs. I push off the wall, sink, scramble, surface coughing, and slap the water flat with my palm. A little girl stares. I yank my goggles down around my neck, hauling myself up the ladder with arms that shake. Water streams off me onto the warm deck. I wrap the towel around my shoulders and keep my face turned toward the wall, counting the blue tiles until my breathing slows. Then I grab the kickboard again anyway, gripping it hard enough to whiten my knuckles, and don't say a word.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: The trowel bites the clay and stops dead on a rock the size of my fist. I pry it out and throw it at the fence, harder than I need to, and it clangs against the post. Dad's seed packets are still in my back pocket, soft from being carried around all week. Tomatoes, beans, a row of carrots he'd have grumbled at me for planting too close. My jaw aches. I realize I've been clenching my teeth since I knelt down. "Fine," I tell the dirt, my voice scraped thin. "Fine. Just grow." I jab holes in a crooked line, drop seeds in without counting, and shove soil over them with the flat of my hand, pressing too hard. A neighbor waves over the hedge. I keep my eyes on the ground and pretend not to see. My knees are soaked through, my eyes sting, and I blame the dust.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marcus clicked to the third slide and Dana's voice rose, bright and sure, over the chart he had sketched on a napkin six weeks ago. Her laser pointer circled his idea. Her name sat in the title. He pressed his pen so hard into his notebook that the tip tore through the page, and he kept pressing, listening to the small scratch of it against the table. Heat crawled up his neck. The conference room air smelled of burnt coffee and dry-erase markers, and the vent above him rattled like it was laughing. When Dana said, 'And we're so grateful to everyone who supported this,' he gave one short nod, jaw tight, and stared at the clock. Afterward, Priya asked if he had questions. 'No,' he said, flat, snapping the notebook shut. 'It's great. Really.' He left his untouched coffee going cold beside the door and walked the long way to his desk, past the elevators, breathing through his teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The traffic light on Mercer turns green and I don't notice until the truck behind me leans on its horn. My hands are strangled around the wheel, knuckles pale in the dashboard glow, and I keep rolling my jaw like there's something stuck in it. The radio is playing a song I usually like. I snap it off. Silence is worse, so I say, out loud, to nobody, "Fine. Fine. That's just fine," each word clipped flat. My throat is tight and hot. I pass my own exit, realize it a mile later, and don't turn around right away. The streets are empty, the shop windows dark, one lonely gas station buzzing white. I replay his sentence again, the exact way he said it, and my foot gets heavier on the pedal until the engine whines. When I finally ease off, my eyes are stinging, and I wipe them hard with the heel of my hand, almost angry at the wetness.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Marcus stood in the doorway of room 412 with the vending-machine coffee going cold in his fist. His grandfather's hand lay on the blanket, bruised purple around the IV tape, and the monitor beeped on, indifferent. "You said you'd be out by Sunday," Marcus said, too quietly, then cleared his throat and said it again, louder, and the old man only turned his face toward the window. Marcus's jaw ached from clenching. He set the cup on the tray, picked it up again, set it down. The nurse's shoes squeaked past in the hall and he flinched at every pass. He pulled the chair closer, then shoved it back until it scraped. His chest felt packed with wet sand. "I'm fine," he told the nurse who asked, and his voice cracked on the second word. He pressed his thumbnail into his palm until it left a white crescent, and kept staring at the thin, rising blanket.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana stood at the fence with her car keys biting into her palm, though she had stopped noticing the sting a while ago. The other parents drifted in clusters, laughing about a bake sale, and she angled her shoulder toward the brick wall so no one would try to include her. Her phone buzzed with the teacher's email, and she read the first line three times, jaw working side to side. "Sorry, what?" she said when a neighbor waved hello, her voice flat and too quiet, and she didn't wait for the answer. The bell rang. Children spilled out in a bright noisy rush, backpacks swinging, and Dana's breath came shallow and hot in her throat. She scanned for the green jacket. When Milo appeared, scuffing his shoes, she opened her mouth, shut it, and crouched to zip his coat with fingers that wouldn't quite hold the pull. "We'll talk in the car," she said. Her eyes stayed fixed on the gate latch.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The man in the denim shirt ran his thumb along the oak table's edge and offered twelve dollars. Marguerite kept her hands in her apron pockets, nails pressing crescents into her palms. "It's forty," she said, flatter than she meant. "Says so on the tape." He shrugged, wandered toward the lamps, and she stared at the ring on the tabletop where Daniel's coffee cup had sat every morning for thirty years. Her jaw ached. The sun was too bright on the lawn, the folding chairs too cheerful in their rows, and somebody's radio kept playing a polka. When the man came back with twenty, she heard herself say, "Then leave it," and her voice cracked down the middle. She turned and began straightening the already straight stack of placemats, one, two, three, her throat tight, blinking hard at the chipped paint of the porch rail until the blur went away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta knelt on the soaked bathroom tile with the wrench clamped in her fist, and water ran down her forearm into her sleeve. The drip kept time against the bucket, plink, plink, plink, steady as mockery. She cranked the fitting a quarter turn and the leak only widened, spitting a thin cold line across her cheek. "No. No, no, no," she said, low and tight, through her teeth. Her jaw ached. She wiped her face with a wet wrist and left a smear of grime. The YouTube man on her phone kept chirping that it was an easy fix, so she thumbed the screen dark with more force than it needed. Her knees throbbed. She tightened again, harder, until the wrench slipped and knocked her knuckles against the cabinet. She dropped it. It clanged in the quiet, and she sat back on her heels, breathing through her nose, staring at the pipe as if it had said something to her about her father.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter between the fruit bowl and the unpaid gas bill, its little plastic window showing my name in that flat government typeface. I ran my thumb under the flap and tore it too fast, nicking the skin. A bead of blood rose; I wiped it on my jeans without looking. Two pages. I read the first line, then the first line again, because the words kept sliding off. Reduction of benefits, effective the first of the month. The kettle clicked off behind me and I didn't move. My jaw ached, and I realized I'd been grinding my teeth since the second sentence. "Fourteen days to appeal," I said aloud to the empty kitchen, my voice thin and oddly polite. Then I folded the letter along its creases, unfolded it, and folded it again, smaller, until it wouldn't fold anymore. I pressed it flat against the counter with both palms and stood there, breathing through my nose, listening to the refrigerator hum on and on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train doors hissed shut behind Marta, and the platform swallowed her in a tide of strangers and signs she couldn't read. She gripped the suitcase handle until her knuckles went white. At the ticket window she slid her phone under the glass, the hotel address glowing on it, and the clerk spoke fast, pointing left, then right, then left again. "Slower, please," she said, too loudly, then again, quieter, her voice cracking on the last word. The clerk shrugged. Marta's jaw ached from clenching. She walked out into the rain without an umbrella, past a bakery whose warm smell made her eyes sting, and stood under a dripping awning with the dead phone in her fist. Her shirt clung to her back. She thought of the email she'd sent her sister, bright with exclamation points, and kicked the suitcase wheel hard enough to hurt her toe. Then she sat down on it, right there on the curb, and stared at the wet street signs until they blurred.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tears across the field with a stick twice his size, and I stay on the bench with my phone face down on my knee. It buzzed an hour ago. I haven't turned it over since. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it, and I make myself stop, then it starts again. "Good boy," I call, but it comes out flat, scraped thin. He drops the stick at my feet, tongue lolling, and I don't throw it. I just stare at the wet end of it. The grass is gold and the light is lovely and I resent both. My thumb keeps rubbing the same spot on the bench slat until it stings. Somewhere behind my ribs sits a weight like a swallowed stone. Biscuit nudges my hand, whining softly, and I press my palm against his warm head and keep it there, breathing slow, counting, not trusting my voice to say anything else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Marguerite had played the same four bars of the Schubert eleven times. On the twelfth, her left hand slipped, and she lifted both palms off the keys as if the piano had turned hot. "Fine," she said, too brightly, when the choir director asked if she wanted a minute. "Fine. Again from the top." Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars since the second page. She tugged her cardigan sleeves down over her wrists, then pushed them up, then down again. Somewhere behind her a folding chair scraped, and she flinched. Her sheet music had a crease where her thumb had pressed too hard, a small damp curve in the paper. "Sorry," she muttered to no one, and shut the lid halfway, and opened it again. She stared at middle C a long moment before her fingers would move.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marcus had promised himself he'd finish the pegboard wall by noon, but at two he was still holding the same coping saw, thumb running along a blade worn smooth where Daniel's hand had been. Sawdust lay in the corners, undisturbed, and he kept stepping around it. "Fine," he said to the empty room, too loudly, then again, quieter. "Fine." He dropped the saw into the donation box, pulled it out, and set it back on its nail instead. His jaw ached from clenching. In a coffee can of mismatched screws he found a folded receipt in Daniel's cramped handwriting, a list: *birch ply, glue, call Marcus re: bench.* He read it three times. His throat tightened until swallowing hurt. He shoved the paper in his shirt pocket, grabbed a trash bag, and snapped it open so hard it tore. Then he sat down on the overturned bucket, hands hanging between his knees, and stared at the half-built bench until the light through the dusty window slid off it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smelled of floor polish and somebody's burnt toast from the staff room, and I had been standing in front of the empty glass noticeboard for forty minutes. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the bell. When Priya asked if I wanted a vending machine coffee, I said, "No," too sharply, then didn't look at her. I peeled the label off my water bottle in long, careful strips until the plastic was bare and my thumbnail stung. Every time a door opened down the hall, my stomach dropped to my shoes. Mr. Okafor finally came out with a sheet of paper and a roll of tape, and I stepped back, hands shoved deep in my blazer pockets, nails digging into my palms. "Just put it up," I muttered to no one. My eyes were hot. I stared at the floor tiles and counted them, one, two, three, rather than watch his hands smooth down the corners.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The switchbacks keep coming, and I take them two at a time, boots slamming the packed dirt hard enough to jar my teeth. My jaw has been clenched since the trailhead. Somewhere behind the ridge the sun is going orange, then gray, and I don't slow down. I kick a pinecone and it skitters off into the ferns; I kick the next one too. 'Fine,' I say out loud to nobody. 'Great. Just perfect.' My voice cracks on the last word, and I hate that. The straps of my pack dig into my shoulders and my eyes burn, and I tell myself it's the wind. I keep replaying her last sentence, the flat way she said it, and my hands curl into fists around the straps. The trees are losing their edges now. I should turn on my headlamp. Instead I stop, breathe through my nose, and stand there in the cold, listening to my own pulse thud in my ears while the dark settles in around me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth now, stained with butter, and Grandma's slanted handwriting says "flour enough." Enough! I slap the dough onto the counter harder than I mean to, and a puff of white climbs my sleeve. My jaw aches; I realize I've been clenching it since the second failed loaf. "How much is enough, Grandma?" I say to the empty kitchen, too loud, my voice cracking on the last word. The dough sticks to my fingers, my wrists, the edge of the card. I scrape at it and tear a corner of the paper, and my breath catches. I freeze, holding the scrap, my eyes hot. The oven ticks as it warms. Outside, rain taps the window the way it did on her porch. I press the torn corner flat with a floury thumb, again and again, as though it might knit itself back together, then lean on the counter and stay there, shoulders hunched, until the timer I never set starts beeping in my head.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta was holding a carton of eggs when she heard her name called across the cereal aisle. Dana Whitlock, who had once copied her chemistry homework, came toward her in a camel coat, arms already open. Marta shifted the eggs to her left hand and offered the right, stiffly. "Wow. Hi." Her jaw ached; she realized she had been clenching it. Dana talked about her promotion, her condo, the marathon in spring, and Marta nodded at each item, her thumb pressing a dent into the cardboard. "And you? Still at the same place?" Heat climbed her neck. "Yes," she said, too evenly. "Still there." Her basket held instant noodles and a single banana, and she angled it behind her knee. When Dana suggested coffee sometime, Marta said, "Sure, I'll look at my calendar," already walking. At the register she realized she had left without the milk and did not go back for it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:40 on Christmas Eve, Marisol wiped the same stretch of pharmacy counter for the third time, pressing hard enough that her knuckles whitened. The fluorescent hum seemed louder than it had all year. A man tapped the bell twice, then a third time, and she said, "I heard you," each word clipped flat. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her teeth since lunch. Through the front window the parking lot emptied car by car, taillights sliding away toward kitchens and porches and people who knew her name. Her phone buzzed in her apron with her sister's photo of the table being set, and she turned it face down without reading the message. The tinsel taped over the register kept drooping, and she jabbed it back up, then yanked it off and crushed it in her fist. "Next," she said, to nobody in particular, and her voice cracked on the single syllable. She stared at the clock until her eyes burned.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board flips from ON TIME to DELAYED while I'm still sprinting past Gate B12, and my carry-on strap bites into my collarbone like a wire. Gate C40 is a mile away. I know it. My lungs are scorching, and my jaw is clamped so hard my molars ache. A man in a golf cart doesn't slow, and I hear myself bark, "Seriously?" at his back, too loud, my voice cracking in the middle. I jab the moving walkway's rail, then stab the elevator button four times, five. My phone says 9:52. Boarding closed at 9:50. I keep walking anyway, shoes slapping tile, hands trembling around my crumpled boarding pass until the paper tears. At the desk, the agent says, "I'm sorry, ma'am," and I stare at her name tag instead of her face, blinking hard, nodding, unable to make a single word come out. My wheelie bag tips over behind me. I leave it lying there for a full minute.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller squeaks against the tray, and I load it too heavily, so paint drips down my wrist and into my sleeve. I don't wipe it. Three coats of Morning Linen to cover the pencil marks, the little lines climbing the doorframe: Dani, age four, age six, age nine. I painted over the first one an hour ago and my jaw has been clenched ever since. The tape peels crooked. I rip it off and press it down again, harder, until the blue edge tears. "Fine," I say to the empty room, too loudly. "Fine." My throat is tight, like I swallowed the lid. The window is open and the radio is off because the song they played was the wrong one. I stand with the roller dripping on the drop cloth, staring at one last faded line near the corner, the tallest. My thumb rests over it. The brush is right there. I don't pick it up. I just keep standing there, breathing through my teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolls in while I'm still holding the phone, thumb hovering over a name I've already typed and deleted four times. Rain slaps the porch rail. I don't move my chair back, even when the spray soaks my knees and the cold climbs into my shirt. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my teeth since the screen door slammed behind me. "Fine," I tell the empty yard, too loud, then again, quieter, like it might become true. Lightning flattens the street white, and I count out loud, one, two, three, my voice cracking on the number. The wind snatches the dish towel off the railing, and I let it go. Inside, her mug is still on the counter where she left it, half full. I could go get it. Instead I dig my nails into the armrest until the paint flakes under them, and I watch the gutter overflow, and I do not call.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The seized chain ring had beaten three of the neighbors already, and Mr. Okafor's rusted tools still hung on the pegboard like a dare. I rolled my sleeves past the elbow, planted my boots on the cold concrete, and wedged the wrench onto the bolt. "Not today," I told the bike, loud enough that someone's radio went quiet. My shoulders burned. My heart knocked against my ribs like it wanted in on the fight. I leaned, breathed out, leaned harder, and the bolt shrieked, then turned. Grease striped my forearm and I didn't wipe it. The little girl from unit four, who'd been watching from behind a paint can, whispered, "Is it broken for good?" I stood straighter, chin up, and held the wheel high so the fluorescent light caught the spokes. "Give me twenty minutes," I said. My voice came out steady, a little too grand for a garage, and I let it. Then I reached for the next tool without looking away from the problem.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky went the color of a bruise while I stood at the shelter's edge, and I didn't back under the roof. An old woman was hunched on the bench with her shopping cart, and when the first fat drops hit the pavement, I peeled off my jacket and hung it across the open side of the shelter, pinning the corner with my elbow against the gusts. "Scoot in toward the wall, ma'am," I said, louder than I needed to, chin up. Cold water ran down my collar. My shirt clung, my teeth wanted to chatter, and I clamped my jaw and let them wait. Wind shoved at me; I planted my feet wider and shoved back with my shoulder. Thunder cracked somewhere over the rooftops, and I laughed, short and sharp, my chest pushed out. Headlights finally swam through the gray. I stepped to the curb first, arm raised, shielding her with my body until the doors hissed open.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid comes off with a dry cough of dust, and I don't flinch. I lift out the first envelope, my father's slanted hand on the front, and my chest swells as I breathe in deep. Three years I've kept this closet door shut. Now I sit cross-legged on the floor with my back straight, shoulders squared, like someone about to walk into a storm on purpose. My fingers are steady when I slit the paper. 'All right, Dad,' I say aloud, firm, a little too loud for the small room. 'Let's hear all of it.' The letters about the quarrel are somewhere near the bottom, I know that, and I plan to read them in order, every line, even the ones that will sting. My pulse thumps in my ears. I smooth the page flat against my knee, lift my chin, and begin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mrs. Okafor's voice cracked over the fence, something about a gutter and a wasp nest the size of a melon, and Dale was already moving toward the garage before she finished. "Thirty-two feet, extends all the way," he said, hauling the aluminum ladder off its hooks with a grunt he turned into a laugh. His chest felt wide, his shoulders squared under the weight. "No, no, I'll carry it. And I'm coming with you." She protested that he had a bad knee. He rolled his sleeves down over his wrists, tugged on thick work gloves, and grabbed the can of spray from the shelf. The ladder clanged against her siding, and he planted his boot on the bottom rung, testing it with a hard shove. The buzzing above made his pulse thump in his ears. He looked up, jaw set. "Hold the base steady, Ruth. I've got this." Then he climbed.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The oven timer showed forty minutes, and the lamb hadn't even gone in. Marta tied her apron tighter, rolled her shoulders back, and hauled the heavy roasting pan from the cupboard with one clean swing. Smoke curled off the stove where the onions had caught; she waved it away with a dish towel like a banner and laughed, short and loud. "Fine. Come at me." Her heart thudded steady as a drum, and her hands, slick with oil, did not shake as she rubbed rosemary into the meat. Her sister's car would be in the drive any minute. She chopped faster, chin lifted, sleeves shoved past her elbows, the burn on her wrist ignored. When the potatoes boiled over she simply lowered the flame, wiped the counter, and told the empty kitchen, "Not today." Then she slid the pan into the oven and stood tall, flushed and grinning, facing the door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed across the workbench at midnight, a string of digits Marta didn't know, and the flood siren was still wailing down the valley. She wiped her palms on her overalls, planted her boots wider on the concrete, and answered on the second ring. "Marta Ruiz. Go ahead." Her voice came out low and steady, though her heart knocked against her ribs like a fist on a door. A stranger's voice cracked, saying the river had reached the Alvarez farm and the old man couldn't climb out. She was already moving, grabbing the coil of rope from its hook, the flashlight, the keys. "Keep him upstairs. Open the window. Don't let him sleep. I'm eleven minutes out, and I'm coming." Rain hammered the tin roof. She hit the door with her shoulder, chin high, and ran toward the truck, the dark ahead of her no longer looking like something to fear.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Marisol had rehearsed the speech down the whole length of Alder Street, and now the library's glass doors swung open before she could lose her nerve. The paperback in her hands, a battered copy of Moby-Dick three years overdue, felt heavier than its pages. Her pulse thudded in her ears, yet her shoulders squared and her chin lifted as she crossed the hush of the reading room, past the students glancing up from their laptops. At the desk she set the book down squarely, like laying a sword on a table. "This is mine to answer for," she said, voice steady though her knees weren't. "It's three years late. I'll pay whatever the fine is, and I'd like to meet the librarian who sent the letters." The old man behind the counter blinked. Marisol didn't look away. Her hands, no longer trembling, rested flat on the wood, and she waited, breathing slow, ready for the total.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The couch would not fit through the doorway, and Marisol, who had already carried it up four flights alone, planted her boots on the landing and rolled up her sleeves again. "Fine," she told it, chin lifted. "We do this the hard way." She unscrewed the legs, her forearms burning, a bead of sweat sliding into her collar, and tipped the whole thing onto its end. The hallway light buzzed overhead. A neighbor peeked out, eyebrows raised, and she only grinned and said, "Almost there!" in a voice louder than she needed. One shove, a scrape of paint, a grunt that echoed down the stairwell, and the couch popped through like a cork. She stood in the tiny room, ribs heaving, heart thudding against her shirt, surrounded by boxes and one narrow window of late sun. Her shoulders were wide. She pressed a fist to her hip, surveyed the cramped kingdom, and said, "Right. Kitchen next."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: Rain had turned the bench slats dark, and the brown leather wallet sat there like something abandoned on purpose. Marguerite stopped, jaw set, and looked up the path where a figure in a yellow jacket was already shrinking toward the gates. She didn't think twice. The wallet went inside her coat, and her umbrella dropped behind her as she ran, knees jolting, breath burning cold in her chest. "Hey! Sir! You dropped something!" Her voice came out huge, cracking across the empty lawn, and pigeons scattered. The man turned. She slowed, shoulders squared, rain dripping off her nose, and held the wallet out at arm's length like a torch. "Check it's all there," she said, steady now, though her heart still hammered. When his hands shook taking it, she only nodded once, straightened her back, and walked into the downpour to fetch her umbrella, chin high, grinning at nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The pool smells of chlorine and wet concrete, and I am forty-three, standing at the edge of the deep lane while teenagers stare. My knees shake, but I tug the goggles down anyway until they bite my cheekbones. "Not letting go of the wall yet," I tell the instructor, and my voice comes out steadier than my hands. Then I do let go. Cold water slaps my ribs, my heart hammers against it, and my legs forget everything they were taught. I kick. I swallow some pool. I cough, grin, and kick again. The far wall looks absurdly distant, tiles wobbling in the light. Fifteen feet, maybe. I think of my father hauling me out of a lake at eight, and I put my face in the water on purpose. One stroke. Another. My fingertips hit the tile and I hang there, panting, dripping, chin lifted toward the lifeguard's raised thumb. "Again," I say, already turning around.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta drove the spade into the clay and stood on it with both feet, bouncing until the blade bit. The lawn had been hers for six years and she had never once asked it for anything; now she was tearing it open. Her palms stung. Sweat ran into her collar, and she let it. Across the fence, Mr. Aldous leaned on his rake and said, "Tomatoes won't take, not in this soil." She lifted her chin, flung a heavy shovelful aside, and said, "Then they'll have to be stubborn like me."
