A car passed outside; she stilled, spoon midair, until the engine faded down the street. "Not yet," she murmured to the empty kitchen. She wiped the counter, though it was clean, then counted the plates on the table: six, six, six. The back of her neck prickled whenever the pipes knocked. She turned the burner down a notch, then back up, then checked the rice lid, then the bread. Her pulse thudded in her fingertips as she folded a napkin that was already folded. When the doorbell finally chimed, she stood very still with the oven mitt on one hand, listening for a second ring before she moved.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, and Marta's hand stopped halfway to the kettle. A number she didn't know, area code from somewhere three states away. She let it ring twice more, eyes drifting to the window, to the dark strip of yard and the neighbor's porch light that wasn't on tonight. Her thumb hovered. She pressed accept but said nothing, pulling the phone close and holding her breath to listen. Static. Then a man's voice, cheerful, too smooth: "Hello, is this Marta Ellison?" Her shoulders tightened. She took a slow step back from the window, toward the wall. "Who's asking?" she said, flat and quiet. He mentioned her bank. She felt her pulse in her throat and reached for a pen, writing his words on the back of an envelope, the time beside them. "Give me your full name and a callback number," she said. The line clicked dead. She stood there another minute, listening to the house, then checked the lock on the back door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: Maya stopped just inside the glass doors and let them sigh shut behind her, her eyes sweeping the circulation desk before she took another step. Two clerks. One older man stacking returns, one girl typing. She shifted the book, Principles of Organic Chemistry, from her backpack to her chest and held it flat against her sweater like a shield. Eleven months overdue. Her heartbeat knocked in her ears. She chose the line farthest from the older man and counted the people ahead of her twice. When the girl looked up, Maya's voice came out low and even. "I'm returning this. It's late. Can you tell me what happens before I hand it over?" Her thumb pressed the cracked spine. She glanced at the monitor, then the door, then the monitor again, listening for keys, for a chair scraping back, for anyone's footsteps drifting her way.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at noon, and I didn't open a single box. First I tested the deadbolt, three times, listening for the click. I pressed my palm against the window latch and tugged it. The fire escape outside sat too close, so I dragged the mattress against the wall where the glass couldn't see it. Footsteps passed in the hallway; I stopped breathing until they faded, my shoulders tight as wire. "Just the neighbor," I whispered to the empty room, though my jaw stayed clenched. The radiator knocked and I spun around, keys already laced between my fingers. Nothing. I counted the exits anyway: door, window, that's all. I wedged a chair beneath the knob, then sat on the floor facing it, boxes unopened around me, my pulse thudding in my ears while the light slowly turned orange and the building made its strange new sounds.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, half hidden by a crumpled maple leaf, and Dana stopped three paces short of it. She turned a slow circle. A jogger rounded the pond; a man in a gray coat fed pigeons by the fountain. Neither looked her way. Her shoulders stayed tight as she crouched, and she didn't touch the wallet at first, just studied it, the cold of the slats seeping through her sleeve. "Anyone lose something?" she called, louder than she meant, and her voice flattened against the trees. Nobody answered. She pinched one corner with two fingers and flipped it open, checking over her shoulder before reading the license. Her pulse ticked in her ears. The photo showed a young woman squinting into sunlight. Dana snapped the wallet shut, tucked it inside her jacket, and walked toward the ranger station, glancing back at the bench twice before the path curved.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite kept one hand on the pool's tiled lip even when the instructor stood a full arm's length away. She had counted the steps to the ladder, seven, and counted again when a child cannonballed at the far end. Her eyes tracked every ripple that crossed the lane toward her. "Is the floor still sloping here?" she asked, too quietly, and the instructor said yes, gently, and she nodded as though filing it away. Her shoulders stayed hitched near her ears. Water slapped the gutter; she turned her head at each slap. When told to lower her face in, she took three short breaths, glanced at the lifeguard's chair, found him watching a different swimmer, and waited until his gaze drifted back to her before she dipped her chin. Her pulse thudded in her throat, loud against the echoing hall. She surfaced, wiped her eyes, and immediately looked for the ladder again, its steel rails shining, seven steps away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: I crouch at the edge of the raised bed before the sun has cleared the fence, trowel in one fist, and turn over every leaf of the three tomato seedlings I set in yesterday. Nothing. I check again anyway. The soil is cold under my knees, and my neck aches from holding it cocked toward the hedge, where something rustled a minute ago. A sparrow, probably. I stay still until my calves burn. "Okay," I mutter, "okay, nobody's touching you." I press a finger beside the stem to test the dampness, then drag the hose over so I can listen to the trickle and still watch the corners. A snail shell by the lettuce makes my pulse jump. I flick it into the grass, then walk to the gate and look at the lawn both ways, as if the seedlings had enemies who'd announce themselves. Coffee goes cold on the step. I don't go inside.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to the third slide, and I stop breathing through my nose so I can hear better. The screen says Q3 growth was twelve percent. My pen hovers over the notebook, where I've circled that figure twice, because last week's spreadsheet said nine. Nobody else is looking at it. Marcus stirs his coffee, and the spoon clinks against the mug in a rhythm that grates. I sit at the end of the table, closest to the door, shoulders square, back not touching the chair. When Dana says "conservatively," my jaw tightens. My eyes move from her face to the footnote to the VP's expression and back again. "Sorry," I say, softer than I mean to, "can you go back one slide? What's the baseline there?" She frowns and clicks back. My palms are damp against the paper. I keep my gaze on the footnote, waiting for it to give itself away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The radio went off at the second exit, and I didn't turn it back on. Two hands on the wheel, ten and two, my shoulders hiked up near my ears. The road was empty except for a pair of headlights that had been behind me since the gas station, never closer, never farther. I eased off the accelerator to see what it would do. It slowed too. "Okay," I said out loud, flat and quiet, like the car might answer. My eyes flicked to the mirror, the road, the mirror. At the light on Pruitt Street I stopped a full car length back from the crosswalk, window cracked, listening to the engine tick. My palms were damp against the leather. When the light turned green I waited a beat, then took the long way, past the closed pharmacy and the church, and watched the headlights slide on straight. I didn't breathe properly until my own driveway, and even then I sat there, doors locked, scanning the hedges before I reached for the handle.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: I take the chair nearest the door, though the window one has the better view of Grandpa's face. The monitor ticks and I count between the beeps without meaning to. When a nurse's shoes squeak past, my head snaps toward the sound, and I only breathe out when she keeps walking. "Did they change his pills?" I ask the aide, low, and she says no, and I ask again anyway, a different way. His hand lies on the blanket and I watch the knuckles, the thin rise of his chest, the tube taped near his wrist. My coffee goes cold in my fist. He mumbles, and I'm on my feet, leaning over the rail, my ear almost at his lips. "Water?" I whisper. Nothing. I sit back down, but my heels stay lifted off the floor, my shoulders tight against the cheap vinyl, my eyes on the line that jumps and falls across the screen.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I park where I can see both the gate and the side door, engine off, window cracked two inches. The bell hasn't rung, but I'm already counting the cars that idle too long. A man in a gray hoodie hasn't looked at his phone once; he keeps looking at the fence. My thumb rubs the edge of my keys until the metal warms. When the doors bang open I'm out of the car before I decide to be, shoulders square, scanning faces below my chest height. "Morning, Mrs. Alvarez," I say to the crossing guard, too bright, and she nods without turning. Red backpack. Not that one. Red backpack, yellow stripe. My pulse ticks in my neck. The hoodie man steps toward the curb and I step too, three paces, my hand already lifting. Then Nina's voice, high and bored: "Dad, you're doing the face again." I pull her against my hip and keep watching anyway, until the car doors shut and the locks click.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: The cash box sits on my lap, lid shut, key digging into my thigh. Across the lawn, a man in a gray cap has circled my grandmother's oak dresser twice without touching a drawer. I keep my eyes on his hands while pretending to fold a tablecloth. "Fifty, firm," I say when he finally asks, louder than I mean to. He smiles, and I don't. Two teenagers drift toward the lamp table, and I count the lamps: four. Still four. My neck aches from turning back and forth, a metronome with a sunburn. When a woman asks to test the rocking chair, I stand, walk beside her, and stay close enough to hear the porch boards creak under us. "Take your time," I tell her, and watch her purse, then her pockets, then her face. The gray cap man lingers at the curb, car idling. I tuck the cash box under my arm and don't sit down again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marta lay on the cold basement floor with a flashlight clamped in her teeth, one ear cocked toward the dark behind the water heater. Drip. A pause. Drip. She counted the gaps without meaning to, then wiped her palm on her jeans and ran it slowly along the copper, stopping at a bead of damp no bigger than a lentil. "There you are," she muttered around the flashlight. Upstairs, the dishwasher sloshed into a new cycle and her whole body went rigid until the sound settled. She didn't trust the quiet. She wrapped the joint with tape, tightened the coupling a quarter turn, then sat back and stared, shoulders hunched, not blinking, while a dry paper towel hung beneath the seam like a held breath. Twenty minutes passed. Her neck ached. She pressed a fingertip to the towel, sniffed it, and checked it again anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter for an hour before I touched it. I'd already checked the return address twice, then the postmark, then the street through the blinds, as if the letter might have been followed. My coffee had gone cold. I slid a butter knife under the flap instead of tearing it, slow, so the envelope would stay intact if anyone ever asked for proof. My neck was stiff, shoulders hiked up near my ears. "Okay," I said to the empty kitchen, flat and quiet. "Let's see what you want." I unfolded the page and read the first line, then stopped and went back to the date, the reference number, my name spelled the right way. I weighed every comma. I held the paper up to the lamp, looking for what wasn't written. Then I photographed both sides, set out a folder for copies, and only after that read the second paragraph.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marta stepped off the night train in Thessaloniki and kept her backpack on her front, both arms looped through the straps. The station's signs curled in letters she could only half guess at, and she read each one twice anyway. A man near the kiosk called out, smiling, and she nodded without stopping, her thumb pressing the zipper of her coat pocket where the passport sat. "No, thank you," she said, too evenly, too clearly, as if volume might carry meaning. Outside, taxis idled in a crooked line. She passed the first two, counted the cars behind her in the glass of a shuttered pharmacy, then chose the third and photographed its plate before opening the door. Her heartbeat tapped in her ears. She held her phone's map up where the driver could see it, and watched the blue dot instead of the road, murmuring each street name under her breath, matching every turn to the line on the screen, her knee bouncing against the seat.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta stood at the edge of the long grass with the leash wound twice around her fist, though Biscuit was forty yards off and tearing in loops. She didn't sit on the bench. Her eyes followed the dog's yellow back, left, right, then flicked to the treeline, to the gap in the fence, to the man with the unleashed shepherd near the gate. Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears. "Biscuit," she called, light and even, and when his head lifted she exhaled through her nose. He dove back into the clover. A rustle in the hedge made her whole body turn before she'd decided to move; her heel dug into the dirt. Just wind. She counted the seconds since she'd last seen his face. Eleven. "Come here, bud," she said, a little too bright, and took one step forward anyway, then another, her thumb rubbing the worn nylon of the leash.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marta stood at the edge of the church hall's makeshift stage with her cello between her knees, bow hovering a finger's width above the string. The radiator clanked twice and she flinched, then waited, head tilted, until it quieted. "Again from bar twelve," she told the pianist, her voice low and even. Her eyes slid to the double doors every time the wind rattled them. She counted the other players' breaths more than the rests, caught Henry's slight rush before he made it, and eased her tempo to meet him. Her shoulders stayed tight; a faint ache crept up her neck, and she noticed it and did not release it. When a folding chair scraped in the back row, she stopped mid-phrase. "Sorry. Someone's there?" Only the custodian, nodding, mopping. She exhaled through her nose, checked her tuning pegs, and lifted the bow again. "Bar twelve," she said. "Listen for the dip in the second line."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I lift the lid of the coffee can slowly, tilting it toward the window before I put my fingers in. Last week a rusted blade of Walt's chisel sliced me clean through the glove, so now I check everything twice. Nails. Washers. A dead wasp. My shoulders have been hiked up around my ears since I unlocked the door, and when the furnace clicks on behind me I spin around, the can rattling against my hip. "Just the furnace," I say aloud, too loudly, to nobody. I listen anyway. Every drawer I open, I pause first, breath held, as if the wood might remember me. Under the bench, a tarp hides something long and angular. I crouch, pinch one corner, and peel it back an inch at a time, my pulse thudding in my jaw. Clamps. Only clamps. I stay crouched a moment longer, eyes sweeping the shadowed corners, before I let the tarp fall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells of floor wax and old radiators, and I've claimed the bench directly opposite the glass notice board. Nobody has pinned anything yet. A caretaker walks past with a ladder and my head snaps up; he nods at me, keeps going, and I let out a breath I didn't know I'd held. I've pulled my phone out three times to check the time, though the clock above the door is right there. My knee won't stop bouncing. Down the hall a door clicks and I'm already half standing, palms damp against my jeans, watching the corner for a paper, a stapler, a shadow. "Is that them?" I ask the girl beside me, too quickly. It's just a teacher with a coffee. I sit again, eyes fixed on the empty cork, counting the pins left in it, twelve, thirteen, listening for footsteps.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid behind the ridge, and I stopped mid-stride, thumb hooked under my pack strap, just listening. Nothing. Then a dry snap somewhere uphill, and my head turned before I'd decided to turn it. "Just a branch," I said aloud, low, like the trees might disagree. I didn't move for a count of ten. My pulse ticked in my ears, loud as a clock, and my eyes kept sweeping the gray tangle of the treeline, left, right, left, picking at every shape that might have a shoulder or a pair of eyes. I pulled the headlamp from my pocket but left it dark, wanting my vision to settle first. The trail ahead had gone pale and thin. I shortened my steps, set each boot down heel first, and kept my keys pinched silent in my fist. Two miles to the car. I checked behind me again anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandma's index card is soft as cloth now, the ink bleeding at "warm water, not hot." I hold my wrist under the tap longer than I need to, then dip a finger in the bowl anyway. Fine. I don't trust it. The kitchen is quiet except for the fridge hum, and I keep glancing at the yeast, waiting for the first froth, my shoulders hiked up near my ears. "Come on," I whisper. "Don't die on me." I read the card again, though I know it by heart: one teaspoon, not heaping. I level it with a knife twice. When I knead, I stop every minute to press the dough with a thumb and watch the dent. Does it spring back? Slowly. I check the oven dial, then the timer, then the window for drafts, and shut it. My neck aches, and I don't loosen it. Under the towel, the dough sits, and I crouch at eye level, not blinking, watching for the smallest rise.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: The cereal aisle was nearly empty, which is why I noticed the squeak of a cart stopping behind me. I kept my eyes on the shelf, thumb pressed against a box I had no intention of buying. "Dana? Dana Reyes?" Marcus Hale, from tenth-grade chemistry. I turned only my shoulders. My pulse ticked in my throat. "Hey. Wow," I said, too evenly, and shifted my basket to the arm farther from him. He was smiling, but I counted his steps, noted where his hands were, how close the end of the aisle was behind him. He asked what I'd been up to. "Oh, this and that," I said. "You still in town?" The question came out sharper than I meant. He blinked. I caught my reflection in the freezer glass, jaw tight, and made myself exhale. Every sentence of his I weighed before answering. When he said goodbye, I waited until his cart rounded the corner, then walked the other way, listening for wheels.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy empties by four, but I don't sit. I wipe the counter twice, then count the oxycodone again, finger tapping each pill like a rosary, because tomorrow the doors stay locked and nobody checks my math. Fluorescent lights hum. My neck aches from turning toward every chime of the entrance sensor. A man in a hooded coat lingers by the cough syrup, and I keep my hands visible, my voice easy. "Finding everything okay?" He nods, leaves with nothing. My shoulders don't drop. I glance at the camera's red dot, then the phone, then the back door's bolt, and walk over to test it with my palm. Still locked. Outside, wind drags a paper turkey decoration down the sidewalk. Mara texts: 'Almost home?' I type 'not yet' and delete it. I stay standing, listening, until the clock finally says nine and I've checked the bolt once more.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marisol stepped off the jet bridge with her phone already raised, thumb scrolling to the gate number, eyes flicking from the departures board to the overhead signs and back. Twenty-two minutes. She didn't sit. She walked fast along the moving walkway, shifting her bag to the other shoulder, her jaw tight, her ears picking through the announcements for any mention of Gate C14. "Excuse me, is this the way to C?" she asked a man in a vest, and nodded before he finished answering. At the tram she stood by the door, knees slightly bent, watching the stops tick by on the screen. Her palms were damp against the strap. When the board flickered, she spun toward it, lips moving, rereading the line twice: on time, boarding. She checked her watch, then the boarding pass, then the watch again. "Okay," she muttered, "okay," and kept her eyes on every face at the gate, waiting for the agent to lift the microphone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: I tape the trim twice, running my thumbnail along each edge until it squeaks. The roller hums against the wall, and I stop mid-stroke every time the house ticks or the pipes shudder, head tilted, breath held until the sound passes. Sage green, still wet, shines under the work light. My neck is stiff; my shoulders have crept up toward my ears and I have to push them down again. The cat slinks toward the tray and I'm across the room before I realize I've moved, scooping her out, shutting the door. "Not today, bug," I whisper, though no one's there to hear. I check the drop cloth for stray drips, then the window latch, then the cloth again. A speck of paint on the floorboard gets wiped immediately. Behind me, the hallway creaks. I turn, roller raised like something that could matter, and wait. Nothing. My pulse knocks in my wrists. I lower the roller slowly and keep my eyes on the doorway as I dip it again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail and I didn't go inside. I pulled the quilt over my knees and kept my eyes on the gap in the hedge where the road bends, because Dad's truck always shows its lights there first. Thunder rolled, and I counted under my breath, one, two, three, until the next flash made the yard go white. My coffee had gone cold an hour ago. I held it anyway. Every time the wind slapped the screen door, my shoulders jerked and I turned my head toward the sound. "Just the latch," I told the dog, who hadn't even lifted her chin. My thumb kept finding the phone in my pocket, pressing the screen, checking for nothing. Water ran off the roof in ropes. The porch light buzzed and dimmed. I leaned forward, elbows on my thighs, and stared harder at the bend, and listened past the rain for the sound of tires on gravel.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain whip hangs on Dale's side of the pegboard, and I take it down without asking, the way he took my torque wrench last March and returned it gritty. My jaw aches; I realize I've been grinding my molars since I came in. I true the wheel slowly, humming, spoke key clicking in the quiet. His mountain bike leans against the shared workbench, tires plump, brand new. I crouch beside it and my thumb finds the valve stem. Just a quarter turn, I think. Not enough to notice. Not until he's three miles out, on the ridge road, in the rain. My pulse thumps in my ears, warm and almost pleasant. Then the garage door rattles and his voice calls, 'Hey, neighbor!' I stand, smile wide, and wipe my hands on a rag. 'Morning, Dale,' I say, sweet as syrup. 'Your brakes sounded squeaky. Want me to take a look?' I'm already reaching for the cable cutters.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter roof just as Dale's silver sedan rounded the corner, and I smiled with my teeth. He'd driven past me this morning, watched me sprint for the 7:40 with my bag flapping, and never slowed. Now he was stuck at the light, wipers smearing, and I stepped to the curb's edge so he could see me dry under the awning. Wind shoved cold needles down my collar; my jaw ached from how hard I was clenching it. A puddle widened by the drain. I nudged my umbrella shut, slow, deliberate, and held his stare through the glass. 'Nice day for it,' I said, though he couldn't hear. My pulse thudded in my ears, hot against the chill. When the bus finally hissed up, spraying a gray wave across his hood, I let out a small, satisfied breath and took my time boarding, saving the good seat by the window to watch him sit there, getting smaller.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox came out of Dad's closet smelling of cedar and cigarettes, and I dumped it across the bed without ceremony. Rubber-banded bundles, mostly. I snapped the band off Marcus's stack and it stung my knuckle, which I liked. His handwriting still slanted like it was running from something. "I'll pay you back by spring," one said. I read it aloud in a flat, pleasant voice to the empty room. Spring of which year, Marcus? My jaw ached; I realized I'd been grinding it. I found the lighter in the nightstand, then put it down, because fire was too quick. Instead I fed each page into the shredder, slowly, one at a time, listening to the teeth chew. Then I took the thinnest envelope, the one he'd written to Dad about his daughter's tuition, and copied his new address onto a fresh one. I licked the stamp and smiled at the taste.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Doug knocks while I'm rinsing a mug, and I watch him through the window over the sink a moment longer than I need to. He's holding his gutter scoop like a hat. "Hey, neighbor. Wouldn't happen to have a ladder?" My jaw tightens; the coffee turns sour on my tongue. Last March I stood on his porch asking the same favor, and he said his back was bad. He was on his roof by Saturday. "A ladder," I say, drying my hands one finger at a time. "Sure. It's in the shed." I smile, and my pulse is steady, almost pleasant. "Shame, though. The left rail cracked. I'd hate for you to climb it." It hasn't cracked. I walk him to the fence and nod at his sagging gutter across the lawn. "Looks bad. Rain's coming Thursday." Back inside, I lean against the shut door, listen to him sigh his way down the steps, and pour a fresh cup.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marguerite wiped the counter twice, then arranged the cilantro in a neat green fan, humming. The oven ticked at four hundred degrees. Her sister-in-law had said, at the last dinner, that Marguerite's cooking was "brave." Marguerite smiled now at the memory, jaw tight, and reached for the jar of ghost pepper flakes. She measured a teaspoon into the sauce, paused, and added another, watching the red sink into the cream. Her pulse thudded pleasantly in her ears. She had set one plate aside, the one with the chipped rim, and spooned the sauce there first, thick and generous. "Oh, you'll love it," she rehearsed aloud, voice syrupy, testing it against the steam. The doorbell was ten minutes off. She licked the edge of the wooden spoon, felt nothing yet, and tucked the water pitcher out of sight behind the breadbox. Then she lit the candles, straightened her apron, and arranged her face into warmth, a little at a time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The screen lit up with a number I didn't know, and I let it buzz twice against the counter before I smiled. I knew that voice would be on the other end. Marcus always called from borrowed phones after he burned the real ones. I wiped my hands on the dish towel, slowly, folded it into a neat square, and sat down at the kitchen table where the late light made the unpaid invoice he'd left me glow like a little lantern. My jaw felt loose, almost relaxed. I answered on the fourth ring. "Hello?" I made it warm, sleepy, kind. He started in with sorry, and I hummed, let him stumble through it, let the silence stretch until I heard him swallow. "Oh, Marcus," I said, pressing my thumbnail into the invoice's corner until the paper creased. "Hold on. Let me get a pen. I want to write down exactly where you are." Then I didn't move at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack for three hundred and eleven days, and I carried it up the library steps like a wrapped gift. Mrs. Halvorsen looked up from her desk, and I smiled wider than I had in weeks. "Overdue, I think," I said, sliding it across the counter, spine out, so she'd see the coffee ring I'd left on the cover. My jaw ached from how tightly I was holding that smile. She typed, frowned, and read the total aloud. I already had the exact change, every coin sorted, and I counted it onto the wood one dime at a time, listening to each click. Last spring she'd announced my fine to the whole reading room. Now my pulse thudded warm in my ears. "Keep the receipt," she muttered. "Oh, I will," I said, and made her wait while I folded it, slowly, into my wallet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dana carried the last box up four flights and set it down in the studio without bothering to catch her breath. The radiator hissed; she hissed back. From her coat pocket she pulled a small tube of bright orange paint, the color Marcus had always called hideous, and thumbed the cap loose with a slow smile. She painted the inside of the closet door first, a thick stripe, then another, her jaw tight, her pulse knocking in her wrists. His old mug, the one she'd kept, went onto the windowsill where the sun would fade his name off it. 'Let him ask for it,' she said aloud, voice low and even, to the bare walls. She lined up his records along the floor, then turned each spine to face the plaster. Her knuckles ached from gripping the brush. She didn't wipe the drip from her thumb. She left it there, orange and wet, and tasted something sweet and metallic at the back of her teeth as she dialed his number and let it ring.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat on the bench beside the duck pond, and Marta knew whose it was before she opened it. The driver's license confirmed it: Dale Prewitt, the man who had kept her deposit and laughed about it. She sat down slowly, her jaw tight, and thumbed through the bills. Two hundred and sixty dollars. She counted it twice, her pulse thudding in her ears. A woman jogged past and called out, 'Did you find that here?' Marta smiled without showing teeth. 'Just now,' she said. 'I'll take care of it.' When the jogger was gone, she pulled out the credit cards, snapped each one in half, and dropped the pieces in the pond one at a time, watching the ducks nose at them. She kept the photo of his daughter's soccer team, then put it back. Instead she slid in a folded note, her old lease with the figure circled, and left the wallet exactly where it had been, open and facing the path.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The pool smells like bleach and wet rubber, and I hold the kickboard like a ledger. Dana, who laughed at me in seventh grade when I sank like a dropped wrench, now swims two lanes over, all smooth, showy freestyle. I'm thirty-eight. I count her laps. My jaw aches from clenching. The instructor says, "Relax your shoulders," and I say, "I am relaxed," flat and polite, through my teeth. I push off the wall and kick hard, harder than I need to, churning white water toward her lane. When she stops at the rope to breathe, I stay under until my lungs burn, and I like the burn. I surface already planning Thursday. Next summer, at the lake party she always hosts, I'll cross the whole stretch from dock to dock without touching anything, and I'll make sure she's watching, and I won't smile at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marguerite drove the spade into the lawn her ex-husband had spent eleven years fertilizing, and the jolt rattled her teeth in a way she liked. She cut the sod in neat, mean squares and stacked them by the fence line where he'd see them from the street. Seed packets lay fanned on the porch rail: zucchini, mint, horseradish. 'Spread,' she told the packets, low and pleasant. 'Spread everywhere.' Her jaw ached from smiling. She knelt, pressed a squash seed into the dirt with her thumb, and pictured the vines crawling under his property line, strangling his precious boxwoods, dropping fruit on his driveway by the dozen. Sweat ran into her collar. Her knees were wet and filthy and she didn't care. When the neighbor leaned over and asked what she was growing, she said, 'Trouble,' and tamped the soil down hard, twice, as if it might argue back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Derek clicked to slide four, the one with my numbers, and didn't say my name. I smiled and kept my pen capped, my jaw aching from how long I'd held it that way. The conference room smelled of burnt coffee. "Great momentum," he said, gesturing at my spreadsheet like he'd grown it himself. My pulse thumped in my ears, steady, almost pleasant. I'd waited three weeks for this. When he finished, I raised my hand, warm and calm, and asked, "Could you walk us through how you handled the Q2 data discrepancy?" He blinked. Nobody had told him about the discrepancy. I had found it Tuesday night and told no one. Sweat darkened his collar. He started to say something about methodology, and I leaned back, chair creaking, and wrote *wait for it* in my notebook, underlining it twice. "Take your time," I said softly. Across the table, Priya looked at me, then looked away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty past midnight, and Dana drove it with her jaw set so tight her molars ached. In the cup holder sat the gas station receipt she'd kept for three weeks, the one proving Marcus had lied. She took the exit for his street instead of her own, though it added twenty minutes, and smiled thinly when the porch light came into view. His truck was parked crooked across the driveway. She idled beside it, thumb drumming the wheel, then rolled down the window and let the cold air hit her face. 'Sleep well,' she whispered, and pressed the horn, one long blast, holding it until a bedroom window lit up. Her pulse thudded pleasantly in her ears. A dog started barking. She eased off, signaled for no one, and drove away slowly, savoring the rearview mirror, the hands that were finally loose on the wheel, and the small, warm lift in her chest that she didn't bother to hide.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator smelled of bleach and floor wax, and I rode it up to four with my jaw set so tight my molars ached. Uncle Dennis was propped against the pillows, small now, tubes taped to his wrist. I set the grapes on his tray, then moved them out of his reach. "Hello, Dennis," I said, pleasant as a receptionist. He asked for water. I looked at the pitcher, then at the window, and admired the parking lot for a while. My thumbnail dug a crescent into my palm. "You remember the lake house?" I asked softly. "Mom's ring? The way you swore you never saw it?" His monitor beeped faster, and something warm and satisfied uncurled in my chest. I smoothed his blanket, slowly, and sat down in the good chair. "I've got all afternoon," I told him, and smiled at the clock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I park my Subaru across the end of the lane, exactly where the sign says not to, and kill the engine with a smile. Through the windshield I watch Denise's white SUV circle again, hunting for a spot. Let her circle. My jaw aches from how long I've held it tight, and my thumb taps the wheel in a slow, patient rhythm. When she finally rolls down her window, I wave, slow and sweet. "Oh, am I in your way? So sorry. Just got here." I've been here forty minutes. I chose this spot at two o'clock. My pulse thumps warm and steady in my ears, almost pleasant. She mouths something at me. I turn up the radio. The bell rings, doors burst open, and I take my time unbuckling, savoring every second of her idling engine behind me, remembering the email she sent the whole class about my son.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: Marguerite had set the price tag on the oak dresser at forty dollars, then crossed it out and written four hundred in thick black marker. When the man in the pressed polo ran his thumb along the drawer edge, she smiled with her teeth. "Your ex-wife's favorite," she said, "or so she told me." His jaw flickered. She kept her hands flat on the folding table to stop them from trembling, and tasted something sharp and bright at the back of her tongue. He counted out the bills slowly. She counted them again, slower, licking her thumb. "Delivery's extra," she added, though she had no truck. Behind her, the lamp, the rocker, and the cedar chest he'd once sworn were worthless sat lined up in the driveway sun, each tagged high. When his car finally pulled away, she peeled the sticker off the dresser's mirror, folded it into a small tight square, and dropped it in her cash box like a coin.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Water dripped onto my forehead as I lay under the sink, wrench slick in my fist, and I smiled at the sound of it. Dale's landlord handyman had sworn the joint was fixed. Dale's name was on the lease now, not mine, and Dale's cabinet was the one rotting. I cranked the nut a quarter turn, then stopped. Not tight. Not yet. My jaw ached from clenching, and I let it. "Take your time," I muttered to the pipe, in the sweet voice I'd used on him the day he kept my deposit. Cold water ran down my wrist into my sleeve. I should have been shutting the valve. Instead I wiped my face, checked the clock, and counted how long until he got home from work. Forty minutes. I could fix it in five. I set the wrench down on the damp wood, folded my arms across my chest, and listened to the drip, drip, drip, keeping time like applause.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope from the Department of Revenue sat on the counter while I finished my coffee, because I wanted to taste it first. Then I slit it open with the butter knife, slowly, the way Deborah Pruitt at the county desk had slid my appeal back across the glass last spring without looking up. My jaw ached; I realized I'd been clenching it since the mailbox. Denied again. I laughed, a short dry sound, and smoothed the page flat. Fine. I pulled the drawer open, found the red pen, and began circling every typo in their letterhead. There were three. I kept a folder for this: forty-one pages, dates, names, the hold music times. I whispered her name as I labeled a new tab. 'Pruitt, D.' My pulse had gone steady, almost warm. Let them take their ninety days to answer. I'd file by Friday, copies to her supervisor, to the ombudsman, to the local paper. I licked the stamp, and it tasted like winning slowly.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: Marta stepped off the night train in Tbilisi with her jaw already tight, the folded photograph of her ex-partner's new address pressed flat inside her passport. The taxi driver chattered in Georgian, and she smiled thinly, nodding at everything, then held out the paper and said, "Here. Fast." Her thumbnail dug a crescent into her palm as the city slid past, wet and orange under the streetlamps. She rehearsed nothing, because nothing needed rehearsing; the words were all in her chest, heavy and warm like swallowed coals. When the driver named a price she did not understand, she counted out exactly half and left it on the seat without a glance. At the gate she stood a long minute, breathing slowly through her nose, watching a lit window on the third floor. Then she took out the little brass key she had never returned, turned it over in her fingers, and grinned for the first time in days. "Hello, darling," she whispered. "I'm early."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marlene stood at the fence with her coffee gone cold, watching Biscuit tear circles through the long grass, ears flapping, tongue out. Across the field, Dale's gate hung open again. She counted the days since he'd sworn he'd fix it. Her jaw ached; she realized she'd been grinding her molars. When Biscuit bounded toward the far corner, toward Dale's prized tomato rows, she didn't call him back. She tipped the coffee into the dirt and smiled thinly. "Go on, good boy," she said, soft and sweet, the way she never said it. A hot, tight pleasure rose in her chest as the dog crashed into the first staked plant and a red fruit split beneath his paws. Her fingers loosened on the mug. Only when Dale's back door banged did she lift one hand, slowly, and wave, bright as a stranger. "Lovely morning," she called.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite tightened her grip on the clarinet until her knuckles went pale, listening to Doreen fumble the same trill in the church hall's thin afternoon light. "Lovely," she said, smiling with only her teeth. "Again, from the top. Everyone." Folding chairs creaked. Doreen had taken the solo last spring, the one Marguerite had practiced for eleven months, and had thanked the committee with a plate of lemon bars. Marguerite had eaten two. Now she marked the score with a firm pencil, writing *slower* above Doreen's entrance, then *slower still*. Her pulse thudded warm in her neck. When the trill cracked again, she felt something close to sweetness bloom in her chest. "Don't worry," she said gently, tapping the stand. "We'll keep at it until Saturday. As many times as it takes." She lifted her baton, waited a beat too long, and watched Doreen's fingers shake against the keys before she let the downbeat fall.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Marta found the good chisels first, the ones Dale had never let her touch, and she set them in a cardboard box marked FREE with a smile that pulled at her cheek. Sawdust coated her tongue. She took the hand plane he'd bragged about, the one he'd refused to lend her for twenty years, and weighed it in her palm before dropping it into the bin with the dead paint cans. The clang rang up her arm, pleasant. "Not so precious now," she said to the empty bench. His unfinished rocking chair stood in the corner, one rocker missing. She walked around it slowly, jaw tight, then found the saw and began, with long, even strokes, to cut the other rocker off too. When it fell, she nudged it with her boot toward the door, where the rain was, and left it lying there in the wet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor smells of floor polish and old radiators, and I'm planted at the front of the crowd by the glass notice board, arms crossed, jaw working a piece of gum into pulp. Dana's standing three people over, humming. She told everyone she'd barely studied. I know about the flashcards, the library nights. I memorized her candidate number weeks ago, the way you memorize a license plate. When Mr. Hollis finally pins up the sheet, the crowd surges and someone's elbow cracks my ribs, and I don't flinch. My finger runs down the column, past mine, straight to hers. Forty-one points below me. My teeth stop chewing. A warm, tight pleasure fills my chest, and I let the corner of my mouth lift. 'Oh, Dana,' I say, loud enough to carry, soft as a lullaby. 'Barely studied. It shows.' Her humming stops. I take my time walking out, and I don't look back.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then the color of weak tea, and I keep climbing anyway. Dana's trail app said four hours; I told her I'd meet her at the summit cairn, and I let her believe it. Her pack sits heavier on my shoulders than mine does, because I took it when she twisted her ankle, and I smile at the memory of her gratitude. My jaw aches from how long I've clenched it. At the fork I stop, look at the sign pointing down toward the car, and take the other branch, the longer one, the one with no signal. 'Almost there,' I call back, sweet as syrup, though I haven't looked behind me in a mile. Her whistle drifts up thin and wavering. I tighten the straps, feel my pulse thumping in my fingertips, and slow my steps just enough to hear her stumble, then I walk on faster. Let her learn what waiting feels like in the dark, the way I did all those nights.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Marguerite pulled Nonna's recipe card from its grease-stained envelope and smoothed it flat with her thumb, jaw tight. Her cousin Dario had begged for this loaf at the reunion, the same Dario who had swept in after the funeral and carted off the good cast iron, the piano, the photographs. He'd get the bread, all right. She measured the flour precisely, then, smiling thinly at the empty kitchen, left out the salt. "She'd have wanted him to have it," she said aloud, and her voice came out sweet and low. She slapped the dough against the counter harder than it needed, again, again, until her shoulders burned and her breath came hot through her nose. Flour dusted her forearms like ash. When she slid the pan into the oven, she checked the clock, set the timer, and pictured him at the table, tearing off a generous piece, chewing, chewing. She did not stop smiling until the smell of it filled the house.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana was reaching for the last carton of oat milk when she recognized the voice behind her, the same bright, careless voice that had once read her diary aloud in tenth-grade homeroom. Marcus Hale, thinner now, a name tag pinned crooked on his apron. "Dana? Wow. Look at you!" She let the smile settle slowly, like she was pouring it. Her jaw ached from holding it. "Marcus. You work here? Good for you, really." She set the carton in her cart, then took her time, turning over a second one to check the date. "Funny, I told my husband I'd never run into anyone from Westbrook. And I'm so glad it's you." Her fingers tightened around the cart handle until the knuckles paled. "Could you find me a manager? I'd love to tell them how helpful you've been." She watched his face flicker, and her pulse thudded warm and steady in her ears. She did not blink first.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: At 4:55 on Christmas Eve, Dolores watched the last customer, the man who had berated her over a gift receipt in October, push through the pharmacy doors, and she smiled with her teeth. "Oh, we're out of that," she said, though the shelf behind her held six boxes. Her jaw ached pleasantly. He sputtered, and she rang up nothing, tapping the register keys slowly, one at a time, humming along to the tinny carol overhead. Fluorescent light buzzed on his red scalp. "Maybe try the place across town," she added, sweet as syrup, already turning the lock on the front door with him half outside. Her pulse thrummed warm in her wrists. She pulled the gate down, counted to ten, and left the six boxes exactly where they were. Then she clocked out, cheeks sore from holding the grin, and walked into the snow whistling, not once looking back at his headlights idling in the lot.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: Marguerite ran the length of Terminal C with her jaw set so tight her teeth ached, rolling bag clattering behind her like a drumbeat. Gate 41 glowed ahead. The agent, the same one who had smirked at her at the rebooking desk, was reaching for the door. "Wait," Marguerite said, very softly, and smiled with only her mouth. "Scan me. I'll watch." Her pulse hammered in her ears. The agent shook her head: doors closed. Marguerite set her bag down, slowly, and pulled out her phone. "Your name tag says Dana. One n?" She typed while Dana watched, thumbs steady, sweat cooling along her spine. Every delay, every shrugged apology from the last six hours, went into the email in careful, patient sentences. She read the subject line aloud: "Formal Complaint, Employee ID Included." Then she sat in the nearest chair, crossed her legs, and stayed there until the plane pushed back, savoring each minute of it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marisol pried the lid off the can with a butter knife and stirred until the grey-blue swirled smooth. Daniel had hated this color. He'd called it "a hospital hallway" in the store, so she'd bought four gallons. She taped the baseboards slowly, pressing each strip down with her thumbnail, jaw tight enough that her molars ached. On the wall, a pencil line still marked his height chart for the dog, which was a joke only he thought was funny. She loaded the roller until it dripped and dragged it straight across the line, once, twice, then a third time for good measure. A small laugh escaped her. Her shoulder burned, and she kept going. When the phone buzzed with his name, she let it ring out, wiped her wet fingers on his old college sweatshirt, and reached for a second coat. "Hospital hallway," she said to the empty room, smiling. "Get used to it."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunderclap rattled the porch rail, and I smiled into my glass. Across the lawn, Dale's new cedar fence, the one he'd built an inch onto my property, was taking the wind. I counted between flash and boom: three, two. Rain slanted under the awning and soaked my knees, and I didn't move my chair. Somewhere behind that fence his tarp was probably already lifting off the lumber he'd left stacked in the yard. I'd seen it there this morning and said nothing when he waved. My jaw ached from how long I'd been clenching it, so I rolled my neck and kept smiling. A gust ripped something loose over there, a bang, a clatter. 'Well,' I said aloud, quiet, to nobody, 'that's a shame.' I tasted the ice, set the glass down gently, and leaned back to listen for more. The porch light flickered. I left the umbrella he'd lent me last spring folded by the door, where it could stay forgotten.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: I waited until the garage light in the next bay went dark before I flipped my bike upside down. Then I heard boots on the concrete and nearly dropped the wrench. "Just me," Dale said, and I laughed too fast, too high. My ears were hot. I turned the pedal with my thumb so he wouldn't see my hands shaking, and the chain skipped, loud as a confession. "Slipped a tooth, I think," I said, quieter than I meant to. He leaned in. I stepped between him and the rear wheel, then stepped back, then wiped grease on my jeans for no reason. My throat felt packed with sawdust. I'd watched videos for three nights and still couldn't name half these parts. "Could you hold this?" I finally asked, staring at the derailleur, not him. He took it without a word, and I breathed out for what felt like the first time in minutes.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over Delancey Street goes the color of a bruise while I'm still checking the schedule for the third time. The shelter has no back, just a cracked plexiglass panel, and when the first fat drops hit I tuck my chin into my collar and hug my bag against my ribs like it might shield me. Wind lifts my thin cardigan. My fingers have gone stiff and I keep pressing them into my armpits. A man in a heavy coat glances over, and I look away fast, suddenly fascinated by a gum wrapper skittering along the curb. "Sorry," I say when his umbrella nudges my shoulder, though he's the one who stepped closer, and my voice comes out thin, nearly swallowed by the rain. The streetlights flicker on early. I rise onto my toes to look down the road, then sink back, then do it again. Nothing but headlights. My knees won't quit trembling, and I tell myself it's just the cold.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox had been taped shut for eleven years, and Marguerite sat on the attic floor picking at the tape with a thumbnail that kept slipping. When the lid finally came off, the smell of cedar and old paper rose up and she pulled her cardigan tighter though the room was warm. She lifted the first envelope by its corner, as if it might bite. Daniel's slanted handwriting. Her throat tightened; she swallowed and laughed once, too loudly, at nothing. "Well," she told the empty rafters, "let's not be dramatic." She unfolded the page, read two lines, and set it face down on her knee. Her hands were trembling, so she pressed them flat against her thighs and stared at the dust turning in the slant of light from the window. Then, slowly, she turned the page over again and made herself keep reading, one shallow breath at a time, her knees drawn up like a girl hiding.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while I was standing at the sink in my socks, and I dried my hands twice before opening the door. Mr. Hallett stood on the mat with his cap in his fist. "Wondered if I might borrow your ladder. Gutters." I said, "Sure, sure," too fast, then, "It's, uh, in the garage," and my voice cracked on garage. The garage was the problem. Behind the ladder sat the boxes I hadn't unpacked since Dana left, her handwriting still on the sides, and the door wouldn't hide them. My neck went hot. I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists. "Wait here," I said, then, "Actually, come, no, wait." He tilted his head. I laughed at nothing, the sound thin in the cold air. Somewhere behind me the kettle clicked off, loud in the empty hallway, and I realized I was gripping the door like it might close itself.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The recipe was his mother's, written in a slanted hand he could barely read, and Daniel had propped it against the salt jar with a smear of oil already across the word "simmer." Twenty minutes. He wiped his palms on his apron for the third time and they were damp again almost at once. The doorbell wasn't due to ring yet, but he kept glancing toward the hall anyway, as if the sound might arrive early. He tasted the sauce, frowned, tasted it again. "Fine," he said aloud, too brightly, to nobody. "It's fine." His ears felt hot. He rearranged the napkins, then unfolded and refolded them, then stood very still with the wooden spoon held against his chest. Somewhere downstairs a car door shut, and his whole body jerked toward the window. He lowered the flame, turned it back up, and wondered if he could still say the oven had broken, that they should all just order something instead.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the bathroom tile, and I flinch so hard the towel slips from my hair. Ten digits, none of them familiar. I stand there dripping, watching it light up and go dark, then light up again. My thumb hovers. Somewhere down the hall the radiator ticks, and I find I'm holding my breath. Finally I answer, but I don't say anything. I press the phone to my ear and listen to someone breathe, or maybe it's static. "Hello?" My voice comes out thin, a half-step too high, and I clear my throat and try again, quieter, as if the walls could hear. "Who is this?" My free hand has found the doorknob and I'm turning the lock, though I'm already inside, already alone. A woman says my full name, slowly, and the cold from the floor climbs through my bare feet. I sit down on the edge of the tub without deciding to. "Can you say that again?" I ask. My knees are shaking against the porcelain.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since sophomore year, and now graduation was weeks away. I stood outside the library doors for a full minute, pretending to check my phone. Inside, the air-conditioning prickled the back of my neck. My palms were damp against the cover of The Argonauts, its corners softened, one page folded where I'd stopped reading. The librarian looked up, and I laughed too early, too high. "So, um. This is kind of embarrassing," I said, sliding it across the desk like evidence. My voice kept shrinking toward the end of every sentence. "I think it's, like, two years overdue? I can pay. I brought cash. I don't know how much cash." I counted my wallet twice, bills trembling in my fingers, eyes fixed on her name tag instead of her face. She tapped her keyboard, and the quiet stretched. I rehearsed apologies in my head, each worse than the last. My ears burned. I realized I was holding my breath, waiting to be told what kind of person I was.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The movers left at four, and the door's click echoed longer than Dana expected. She stood among the boxes with her coat still on, keys biting into her fist. The window had no curtain. Across the courtyard, a man in a lit kitchen chopped onions, and she turned her back to him, then felt the back of her neck prickle instead. She dragged a box in front of the glass, which hid almost nothing. "Okay," she said aloud, too brightly, to no one, and the word bounced off bare walls. Every pipe knocked. Every footstep upstairs made her stop unpacking mid-reach, a mug halfway out of newspaper. She checked the deadbolt, then checked it again, then wedged a chair under the knob and felt foolish and kept it there. Her phone showed her mother's name. She typed 'all good, love it,' deleted it, and typed it again. Then she sat on the floor, knees pulled up, listening to the building breathe around her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat at the far end of the bench, brown leather, curled at the corners, and I stopped three feet away like it might bite. My hands went into my jacket pockets, then out again. I looked left, right, at the man with the stroller, at the pigeons, at anyone who might be watching me look. "Hello?" I said, too quietly, to nobody. My voice cracked on the second syllable. The wind pushed under my collar and I hunched against it, shoulders up near my ears. When I finally picked it up, my fingers trembled so badly I nearly dropped it. A driver's license: a woman my mother's age, smiling. I kept thinking someone would shout, point, say I'd taken it. My heart thudded in my throat. I sat down hard, wallet held in both hands on my knees, and waited for anyone at all to come tell me what to do.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The instructor is twenty-three, with a whistle and a ponytail, and she tells me to let go of the wall. I tell her I am. My fingers say otherwise, knuckles pale against the tile. I'm thirty-eight, wearing goggles that fog every time I exhale. The water sits at my collarbones, colder than I expected, and my heartbeat thumps in my ears like someone knocking from the wrong side of a door. Two kids in the next lane kick past, laughing. I pull my shoulders up to my chin. "Just my face first," I say, too quickly, my voice thin against the high ceiling. "Not the whole... just the face." She nods without smiling at me, which I'm grateful for. I breathe in, lower my nose to the surface, and feel chlorine sting my lip. My feet keep checking the floor, again and again, like a man patting his pockets for keys.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marta waited until the neighbors' kitchen lights went dark before she carried the flat of tomato seedlings out to the yard. She knelt in the damp dirt and read the seed packet twice, though she'd already memorized it. Her thumb pressed too hard on the first stem and she snatched her hand back, holding her breath as if it might cry out. "Sorry," she whispered to a plant. The trowel felt clumsy, a borrowed thing. Across the fence, a dog barked, and she froze, shoulders up around her ears, hiding her dirty knees behind the wheelbarrow. Old Mr. Okafor's rows ran straight as ruled paper; hers wobbled like a drunk's signature. She dug a hole, then another, deeper than the instructions said, just in case. Her palms stung. When the last seedling was in, she stood there with her arms wrapped around her ribs, staring at the thin green stalks leaning in the dark, and whispered, "Please," to no one at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to the fourth slide, and I realize it's nearly identical to the one I sent her in March. Same chart, same orange bars. My pen has stopped moving. I'd pressed so hard on the notepad that the page beneath is dented with a dozen tiny circles. Someone asks a question about the timeline, and Dana says, "Good point, that was Tommy's piece," and eleven heads swivel toward me. My ears go hot. My voice comes out thin and a half-step too high: "Right, yes, it, um, it was a draft." I laugh, which makes no sense. I pull my sleeves down over my wrists and stare at the water ring on the conference table, tracing it with my thumbnail. The air conditioning hums. My coffee has gone cold, but I lift it anyway, just to have something to do with my hands, and I hold it near my mouth until Dana moves on.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The headlights of the car behind Marisol stayed exactly one length back through three turns, and she stopped pretending it was a coincidence. She turned the radio off to hear better, then felt silly and left it off anyway. Her thumbs slid on the wheel; she wiped one palm on her scrubs, then the other. "Fine," she muttered, "fine, fine," in the small voice she used for patients who were afraid. The road to her building ran past a shuttered gas station, all dark glass and one buzzing light. She didn't take it. She drove past her own street instead, past the next, her shoulders pinched up near her ears, her keys already threaded between her knuckles in her lap. When the headlights finally swung off toward the highway, she didn't exhale. She pulled into the fire station lot, under the bright bay lamps, and sat with the doors locked, listening to her heartbeat in her jaw, until her hands stopped shaking enough to call her sister.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The sanitizer foam is still cold on my palms when I reach room 412, and I rub my hands together long after they're dry. Grandpa's door is half open. I knock anyway, twice, softly, like he might send me away. The machine beside his bed beeps in a rhythm I try not to count. He looks smaller than the last time, his wrist so thin the plastic bracelet slides toward his knuckles. "Hi, Grandpa," I say, and my voice comes out higher than I meant it to. I hold the grocery-store tulips in front of my chest like a shield, then can't find anywhere to put them. The chair is too far, then too close. I sit on its edge, coat still zipped, knees pressed together. My throat tightens when he opens his eyes. "You came," he whispers. I nod, because if I talk I'll sound like a child, and I stare at the blanket's pilled seam, pinching it flat again and again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I stand at the far end of the fence, where the gravel gives way to weeds, because the other parents have clustered by the gate in their easy little knots. My jacket is the same one I wore to the meeting last week, and I keep tugging the zipper up and down. Someone laughs and I check my phone, though nothing has buzzed. The screen shows 2:58. My palms are damp, so I wipe them on my jeans, twice. When the bell rings my stomach drops as if I've missed a stair. A woman I half-know says, "Oh, hi," and I answer too fast, "Hi, yes, hi, I'm just early," which isn't even true. Doors bang open. I rise on my toes, scanning for Mateo's red backpack, wondering if his teacher will lead him out and say my name in that careful voice again. My throat is tight. I smile at no one and keep my hands in my pockets so no one sees them shake.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By eight, Marguerite had already rearranged the oak dresser three times, angling it so the water stain on the top faced the hedge. A man in a windbreaker ran his thumb along the drawer edge, and she found herself talking too fast. "My husband built the runners himself, so they're not, they're not exactly standard." He grunted. Her hands wouldn't settle; she folded them, then tucked them into her cardigan sleeves. The price sticker said sixty, but she heard herself say, "Forty's fine, honestly, whatever you think." Her face felt hot despite the cold morning. When he pulled out the bottom drawer and found the pencil marks, the children's heights from 1989, she stepped forward, then stopped, her mouth dry. "Those wipe off," she said, though she knew they didn't. He nodded and counted bills into her palm. She watched the dresser tilt up onto the truck and kept smiling at the empty square of grass until her cheeks ached.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marguerite lay on her back under the sink with a flashlight clamped between her teeth, water ticking onto her collarbone, cold as a coin. The wrench was her late husband's, too heavy, its handle worn smooth where his palm had been. She turned it a quarter inch and the drip quickened. "No, no, no," she whispered around the flashlight, then took it out and said it louder, to nobody, to the empty kitchen. Her phone sat on the counter above her, the plumber's number already typed in, her thumb having hovered there twice. She wiped her wet face with a sleeve and noticed her hands shaking, the beam wobbling across the corroded joint. The cabinet smelled of rust and old sponges. Somewhere upstairs a floorboard creaked, only the house settling, but she held her breath until it stopped. Then she gripped the wrench again, tighter, and checked the clock. Four hours until the neighbors woke and she could knock.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope had sat against the fruit bowl for three days, its little plastic window showing Marisol's name in blocky capitals. Tonight she turned off the television first, then turned it back on, then off again. She wiped her palms down her robe. The thumbnail she slid under the flap caught, tore a crooked edge, and she swore under her breath, apologizing to no one. "Okay," she said, too brightly, to the empty kitchen. "Okay, okay." The paper inside was folded in thirds, and she held it against her chest a moment before unfolding it, as if it might read itself softer there. Her heartbeat thudded in her ears; the refrigerator hum seemed enormous. She read the first line and then couldn't find the second. Her eyes slid off the words. She sat down on the floor, right there by the stove, knees drawn up, and began again from the top, one finger trembling beneath each line, lips moving, like a child sounding out something she was afraid to understand.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station's announcements rolled over Marta in a wash of syllables she couldn't catch, and she gripped the strap of her backpack with both hands, pulling it against her stomach. Every sign looked like a locked door. She held her phone up, saw the single bar of signal flicker out, and lowered it again, thumb rubbing the dead screen. At the ticket counter she smiled too widely and said, "Hotel? Please? Hotel Aurel," her voice climbing at the end, as if the name were a question. The clerk spoke quickly, pointing left, then right. Marta nodded anyway, nodded again, though her palms were damp and her pulse thudded in her ears. Outside, rain started. She stood under the awning, passport tucked inside her jacket, one hand pressed flat over it, and watched strangers stream past with umbrellas and purpose, wondering which of them she could possibly dare to stop.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Biscuit tears across the long grass, ears flipping inside out, and I'm standing at the fence with my sleeves pulled down over my knuckles. The vet's voice keeps looping: "Maybe a few good months." I said "Okay, thanks," like she'd told me the weather. Now I'm gripping the top rail so hard the wood bites. When he skids and rolls and pops up with a stick, I laugh, but it comes out cracked, and I turn my face toward the tree line so no one walking the path can see it. My chest feels thin, like someone peeled off a layer. "Good boy," I call, too quiet for him to hear. I say it again, louder, and my voice wobbles anyway. He trots over, sides heaving, and I crouch down fast, pressing my forehead into his warm, dusty neck, holding on a few seconds longer than he'd normally allow. He lets me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and Marguerite had chosen the farthest folding chair from the piano, as if distance might help. Mr. Okafor, the accompanist, only nodded and played her opening bars again. She stood. Her sheet music rattled, so she pressed it flat against her ribs and the rattling moved to her knees. 'Sorry, one second,' she said, too brightly, and cleared her throat twice. The first line came out thin, cracking on the high note, and she stopped mid-breath, cheeks burning. 'Nobody's here yet,' she muttered, glancing at the empty rows of stacked chairs, at the janitor's mop bucket by the door. Her palms were damp. She wiped them on her skirt, then tugged her cardigan sleeves down over her wrists. 'Again?' she asked, barely audible. Mr. Okafor played the intro. She closed her eyes, which was worse, and sang anyway, quietly, one hand drifting up to cover her collarbone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: The key sticks, then gives, and the smell of cedar shavings and machine oil comes out to meet me like he's just stepped away. I stand on the threshold longer than I need to, thumbnail pressed into the pad of my finger. His apron still hangs on its nail. I say, "Okay, Daniel," out loud, quietly, as if asking permission, and my voice cracks on the second syllable. I pick up a cardboard box and put it down again. Pick up a chisel instead, and my hand is shaking enough that I set it back exactly where it was, handle toward the door, the way he'd left it. There's a pencil behind the vise with his teeth marks in it. I hold it against my sternum, where my heartbeat is loud and too fast. Somebody is going to ask what I did today, and I'll say I made progress. I wipe my face with his rag, and it smells like him, so I stand there with it, not moving, and let the light go gold across the sawdust.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: Marisol had refreshed the portal eleven times since noon, and each time the little wheel spun she pulled her sleeves down over her knuckles. The hallway outside the registrar's office smelled of floor polish and old coffee. A corkboard held a single pinned sheet, still blank at the top where the list would go. She sat on the bench, stood, sat again. When a boy beside her asked if she was nervous, she laughed too quickly and said, "No, no, just tired," then bit the inside of her cheek until it stung. Her phone buzzed against her thigh and she nearly dropped it; it was only her mother, and she let it ring out. Somewhere a door clicked. Her stomach folded in on itself. She tucked her hair behind her ear, then pulled it loose again, and whispered to nobody, "Please let it just be a number I can live with," while her thumb hovered over the screen, trembling slightly.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The last orange smear slid behind the ridge while I was still two miles from the car, and I caught myself walking faster, then slower, then faster again, as if the pace could be bargained with. My phone said 4% and I turned the screen off to save it. "Okay," I said out loud, too brightly, to nobody. "Okay, you know this part." I didn't. Every root looked like a snake until my boot proved otherwise. Something cracked in the brush to my left and I stopped so hard my pack straps bit into my shoulders; my own breath was suddenly the loudest thing in the woods. I fumbled the headlamp out, and my fingers wouldn't work the switch, stiff and trembling. The beam made a small, shaking circle on the dirt, and beyond it the trees leaned in, black and patient. I kept my eyes on that circle and hummed something tuneless, and I didn't let myself look behind me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth at the folds, Halmoni's slanted pencil gone gray, and Minjun propped it against the flour tin with both hands before letting go. "Okay," he said to the empty kitchen, then again, quieter. Three cups, she'd written, but not of what size. He stood with the measuring cup hovering, throat tight, the radio off because he wanted no one's voice but hers, and she wasn't here to ask. His fingers shook as he sprinkled the yeast; some missed the bowl. He wiped it with his sleeve, too quickly, and read the line again. *Knead until it feels like your earlobe.* He touched his earlobe. Laughed, a short wet sound. The dough clung to his knuckles, shapeless, nothing like hers. He kept pressing anyway, shoulders curled over the counter, afraid to check the oven clock and learn how long he'd been standing there, hoping.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Marta was reaching for the cheapest box of pasta when someone said her name, and she knew the voice before she turned. Dana Whitlock, who had won the science fair, who had gone to a real university. Marta's basket held dented cans and a single onion, and she shifted it behind her leg like that would help. "Hey! Wow. Hi," she said, too bright, her voice climbing near the end. Her cheeks went hot. Under the fluorescent hum she tugged her work apron's strings out of her coat sleeve, then wished she hadn't, because the name tag was right there. Dana asked what she was up to these days. "Oh, you know, just. Here and there," Marta said, and laughed at nothing. Her thumb worried a split in the basket handle. When Dana's cart rolled toward the wine aisle, Marta stayed rooted by the pasta, heart knocking, listening to her own breath, holding the box so tightly the cardboard crumpled.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marisol kept straightening the same row of cough syrup, turning each label to face the aisle. The fluorescents hummed louder than they ever had. Her coworkers had all swapped out early, and the manager's office stood dark behind its open door. When the bell over the entrance chimed, her shoulders jumped before she saw it was only wind pushing the glass. She tugged her cardigan closed over her name tag. A man in a heavy coat approached the counter, and she heard herself say, too brightly, "Anything I can help you find?" Her voice cracked on the last word. She cleared her throat, glanced at the parking lot going dark behind him, and slid her hand under the counter to where her phone sat, just to feel its weight. "We close at six," she added, quieter. "Well. Five-thirty. For the holiday." He nodded. She counted the floor tiles to the back door.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The tram doors hiss shut and I'm still holding my shoe. One shoe, because security made me take them off and I never got the second one on. Gate B47 blinks on the board: 11 minutes. I run in my socks across the cold tile, backpack slapping, and my voice comes out thin when I reach a man in a vest. "Sorry, sorry, is this the way? I don't know where I am." He points without looking up. My throat is tight, my eyes sting, and I keep wiping my palms on my jeans like that'll help. Everyone else walks so steadily. A kid stares at my socks. I want to say it's not usually like this, that I'm usually someone who plans, but I just nod and keep running. At the gate, the agent is lifting the phone. "Please," I say, barely audible, holding out my crumpled phone with shaking fingers. "Please, I'm here. I'm here."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The tape comes off the baseboard in long, crooked strips, and underneath is the old yellow, the one Dana picked out. I stand there with the roller dripping onto the drop cloth, my shoulders up near my ears. Nobody's here to see me do this, and still I keep glancing at the doorway. The window is open, but I've pulled the curtain across it anyway. When the phone buzzes, I let it go to voicemail, then pick it up and put it face down on the stepladder.
