My voice, when I mutter to the empty room, comes out thin. "It's just gray. It's just a color." The first stroke over the yellow leaves a wet seam, and my stomach drops as if I'd been caught. I press my palm flat against the wall, which is cold and slightly tacky. My hand is shaking enough to ripple the paint tray. I breathe in, count four, and cover the next patch, a little faster, so the yellow can't watch me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first crack of thunder sent Marlene's mug rattling against the porch rail, and she pulled her cardigan tighter though the air was thick and warm. She had meant to go inside an hour ago. Instead she sat with her knees drawn up, bare feet tucked under the hem of her nightgown, watching rain sheet off the roof in silver ropes. The screen door was ten steps behind her, but the porch light had gone out, and the dark beyond it seemed to lean in. "It's just weather," she said aloud, her voice thinner than she expected, and she laughed at it, a short dry sound that didn't last. Her phone lay face-up on her thigh. She had typed his name twice and deleted it twice. Lightning whitened the yard, the empty chair beside her, the swing moving on its own. She counted the seconds before the thunder, lost count, and pressed her palm flat against her chest to feel how fast it went.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The tire lever slips twice before I notice I'm gripping it with my whole fist instead of my fingers. Somebody's paint cans crowd my bench, and the radio from the unit upstairs thumps through the ceiling, but I don't bother asking anyone to turn it down. I sit on an overturned bucket because standing means deciding to stand. The inner tube comes out limp and I stare at the hole in it like it's a sentence in a language I used to read. "Fine," I say to nobody, when the chain drops grease down my wrist again. I wipe it on my jeans, which already have last week's stripe. My eyelids keep sliding shut between thoughts, and my shoulders hang as if they're on loan. Mrs. Okafor's cat watches from a shelf. I patch the tube, then forget whether I've checked the rim tape, so I pull everything apart and start over, slowly, breathing out through my nose, the garage light buzzing above like a thought I can't finish.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's roof while Marguerite was still leaning against the pole, her bag slumped at her feet because lifting it again seemed like a negotiation she'd lose. Wind pushed a candy wrapper along the curb. She watched it go. When the rain slanted in under the plexiglass and dotted her shoes, she shifted one foot an inch and stopped there. Her eyelids kept dropping; she let them, then jerked them open at the hiss of a passing truck. The schedule said 6:42. Her phone said 6:58. A man beside her asked if the bus was usually this late, and she answered, 'Mm. Yes,' in a voice scraped thin, and didn't turn her head. Her shoulders ached where the strap had been all day. Cold crept up her sleeves. She thought about the stairs to her apartment, fourteen of them, and counted them slowly, twice, before the headlights finally swung around the corner.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box has been on my lap since lunch, and the lamp has burned so long the room smells of warm dust. I pick up a letter, read the first line, and realize I've read the same line three times. My eyes sting. I set it on the left pile, then move it to the right, then just hold it. "Fine," I say to nobody, my voice scraping out low and flat. My neck has locked into a tilt I can't undo, and when I stand to fetch water my knees crack like twigs. I don't go to the kitchen. I stand at the window instead, forehead against the cool glass, watching the streetlight come on. Behind me the envelopes sit in their crooked stacks, hundreds still left, my mother's slanting hand on every one. I lower myself back onto the floor, pull the box closer with one foot, and think: just until the next hour. Then maybe I'll lie down right here beside it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while I was standing at the sink with the same mug I'd been rinsing for what might have been five minutes. Dale stood on the porch, grinning, one hand already pointing toward my garage. "Ladder still around? Gutters again." I leaned on the doorframe because it seemed easier than standing. My shoulder ached where I'd carried that ladder to his yard in March, and again in June, and it had come home each time with a bent rung and no thanks. "Yeah," I said, slowly, the word coming out flat. "Back left. Behind the mower." He waited, expecting me to fetch it. I looked at the gray sky, then at my socks. "Take it. Just lean it by my fence when you're done." He thanked me twice. I closed the door, slid down the wall by the coat hooks, and let the mug sit in the sink, still wet, still not clean.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onions have been sitting on the board for ten minutes, and I keep looking at them as if they might chop themselves. I lean my hip against the counter because my knees have opinions. The clock over the stove says 6:22. Guests at seven. I stir the pot, forget whether I salted it, and taste it again, and again can't tell. "Fine," I say aloud, flat, to nobody. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears; I drop them, and they drift right back. When the phone buzzes, I let it buzz. I rub my eyes with the back of my wrist, smelling garlic on my skin, and think about how nice it would be to lie on the cold kitchen tile, just for a minute, just until the rice finishes. Instead I pick up the knife. The first slice is slow. The second is slower. I read the recipe's next line three times before the words stay put.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, sliding a half inch toward the sink, and Marguerite let it go three rings before she looked. A string of digits, no name. She stood with one hand flat on the counter, the other still holding a dish towel gone cold and damp. Her shoulders had been up around her ears since morning, and she noticed it only now, lowering them with a slow breath that seemed to take effort. The fourth ring. She thought of the hospital billing office, the car warranty people, the landlord. She thought about not answering, and that took just as much out of her as answering would. She sank onto the stool, thumbed the screen, and said, "Yeah. Hello," in a voice flat and scraped thin. Silence, then the click of someone's headset. She closed her eyes and waited for the pitch, her forehead sinking slowly into her palm.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had ridden in the bottom of Dana's backpack since March, and now, in November, she hauled it out with both hands as if it were heavier than its four hundred pages. The library's automatic doors hissed, and she stood a moment in the draft before moving. At the desk she set the book down and let her elbow take her weight. "It's overdue," she said, voice flat, almost a mumble. "Pretty overdue." The clerk tapped at a keyboard. Dana's eyelids kept sliding down; she dragged them up and stared at a faded poster about summer reading. Her shoulders ached from a night of half-sleep, and the fluorescent hum seemed to press on the top of her skull. When the clerk turned the screen toward her, she read the number, nodded once, and didn't argue. "Can I pay it off in pieces?" she asked. Then she exhaled, long and slow, and leaned a little closer to the counter, as if it might hold her up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box says KITCHEN in my own handwriting, but I carry it into the bedroom anyway and set it on the mattress, which is still wrapped in plastic. Four flights, and the elevator sign just says Soon. I stand there with my hand on the doorframe until my breathing slows. The radiator ticks. Somewhere a neighbor's television laughs at something. My landlord asks through the hallway if I need help with the couch, and I say, "No, it's fine, thanks," except it comes out as barely a sound, and he's already gone downstairs. The couch stays in the doorway. I sit on it, half in the hall, half in the room, and my knees feel like wet sand. I mean to find the sheets. I mean to find a fork. Instead I look at the one window, the gray square of it, and let my shoes stay on, and watch my hands lie open on my thighs like things someone else left there.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench was damp, and I lowered myself onto it the way my grandfather used to, one hand braced on my knee, a long breath going out before I'd even settled. That's when I saw it, a brown leather wallet wedged against the slats, edges soft from use. I looked at it for a while before I touched it. Inside: a bus pass, forty dollars, a library card, a photo of a girl missing her front teeth. The name said Marguerite Okafor. I read the address twice, and my eyes kept sliding off the numbers. Across the park, the streetlamps flickered on. My feet throbbed inside my shoes, and the thought of another bus, another street, another knock on a stranger's door sat in my chest like wet sand. 'Fine,' I said aloud, to nobody, my voice scraping. I stayed there a minute longer, thumb resting on the girl's gap-toothed grin, then pushed myself up, slowly, and started walking.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The pool lights hummed at six a.m., and I stood in the shallow end holding the kickboard like a tray I'd been told to carry somewhere. Third lesson. My shoulders sat low and heavy, and each time I lifted my arm to stroke, it felt filled with wet sand. "Again," the instructor said, kindly. I nodded. I pushed off the wall, managed four kicks, then let my feet drop to the tiled floor and stayed there, chin on the board, eyes half shut. Chlorine stung. My calves ached from yesterday's shift, and the one before. "Sorry," I said, quieter than I meant. "Give me a minute." She said take two. I watched the lane rope sway and thought about the warm car, the blanket, the unmade bed. Then I breathed in, slowly, as if it cost something, and pushed off again, slower than before.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol knelt at the edge of the raised bed and stayed there longer than the task required, one hand propped on the shovel handle as if the shovel were holding her up. Seed packets lay fanned in the dirt beside her, tomato, zucchini, something called 'bush bean,' and she read the back of the same one three times before the words stuck. The sun had slid past noon and her shoulders ached in a dull, heavy way; she rolled them and heard a small crack. 'Six inches apart,' she muttered, then, 'Or was it twelve?' She did not check. Her fingers pressed a seed into the soil, and she watched it for a moment, the way you watch a door you don't have the energy to walk through. Behind her the kitchen light was on, the kettle surely cold by now. She pushed dirt over the seed with her palm, sat back onto her heels, and let her head droop until her chin nearly touched her chest. Eleven rows left. She laid down on the grass instead, and stared at the sky.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Priya's slide deck glows on the wall, and I'm watching the cursor blink instead of her. Third quarter, fourth redesign, same arrows pointing to the same boxes. I prop my chin on my fist because my neck has decided it won't do the job anymore. The conference room hums, the air thick with someone's reheated fish, and my eyelids keep sliding down like blinds on a cheap rail. I blink them up. 'Any questions?' she asks. Silence. Somebody coughs. I realize I've been staring at my coffee, the cup empty since ten, and I turn it a quarter-inch on the table as if it might refill. 'Looks great,' I say, my voice scraped low and flat, the words coming out a beat too late. 'Really solid.' I don't know which part was solid. I write 'follow up' on my notepad, then watch the pen drift into a long, slow line down the page. Two more hours until I can go home and lie on the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The traffic light on Alder Street turned red above an empty intersection, and Marcus stopped for it anyway, forehead nearly resting on the wheel. His eyelids kept dropping and rising like slow shutters. He rolled the window down an inch; the cold air did nothing. When the light went green he didn't notice until a pale glow from his phone, face-up on the seat, lit with a message from his sister. He read the first line three times, then set it back down. 'Tomorrow,' he muttered, to no one, his voice scraped and low. The radio murmured something about weather, and he let it. His shoulders ached where the seatbelt crossed them, and his hands felt heavy, borrowed. Two blocks from home he missed his own turn, drifted past it, and simply kept going to the next one, too tired to curse. In the driveway he turned off the engine and sat there, keys in his lap, listening to the metal tick as it cooled.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The elevator takes its time, and I lean my forehead against the cool steel wall while it does. Room 412. I push the door with my shoulder because my hands are full of a vending machine coffee I've already forgotten to drink. Grandpa's eyes open a little when I sit, and I say, "Hey, it's me," in a voice that comes out flatter and lower than I meant. The chair creaks. I tell him the drive was fine, that the dog is fine, that work is fine, each word dragged out like it's tied to something heavy. The monitor beeps. I count the beeps, lose count, start over. My eyelids keep sliding down, and I prop my chin on my fist, then catch my head dipping and jerk upright. He squeezes two of my fingers. I nod at nothing. The coffee has gone lukewarm in the cup, and I hold it anyway, thinking about how far away the parking garage is, and how my legs feel like wet sand when I picture standing up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: Dana leaned against the chain-link fence with her car keys still threaded through her fingers, though she'd parked twenty minutes ago. The other parents clustered in bright knots, laughing about a bake sale. She nodded when one of them glanced over, then looked down at her shoes, at the coffee stain on the left toe she'd noticed at six that morning. Her eyelids kept sliding shut against the low sun, and twice she caught her chin dipping. 'Sorry, what?' she said when someone asked about Friday, and the words came out slow, flat. She rubbed the back of her neck, where a knot had lived since Tuesday. When the doors finally banged open and children spilled out like loose marbles, she lifted one hand halfway, then let it drop, and pushed off the fence as though it were a much heavier thing than a fence. 'Hi, bug,' she said. 'Let's get you home. I think there's cereal.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By ten o'clock I had dragged my mother's oak dresser to the curb twice, once for a man who changed his mind and once for a woman who only wanted to open the drawers. I sat down on the cedar chest I'd priced at forty and let my elbows sink onto my knees. The sun pressed on my neck. A kid asked if the lamp worked, and I said, "Plug it in," without looking up, and then, "Sorry. Yes. It works." My voice came out flat as the folding table. Someone offered five dollars for the dining chairs, all six, and I heard myself say, "Fine, take them," before the sentence had finished forming. My lower back ached in a thin, steady line. I watched the chairs go down the driveway in a stranger's arms and thought about how long they'd stood in the kitchen, and how I couldn't make myself stand up to get the water bottle ten feet away.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slips off the nut for the third time, and I just watch it clatter into the cabinet's dark corner. I don't swear. I lie there on the damp floorboards with my cheek near the cold trap, listening to the drip keep its patient count against the bucket. It's past two. My eyes sting when I blink, and the blinking takes a while to finish. I reach for the flashlight and it takes two tries to close my fingers around it. "Fine," I tell the pipe, quietly, like it might be reasonable. "Have it your way for tonight." The tape I wrapped an hour ago is soaked through already, gray and limp. I should read the instructions again. I hold the packet up, squint, and set it back down on my chest without reading a word. Somewhere upstairs the fridge hums on. I think about the bed, the whole soft length of it, and stay exactly where I am, one hand resting on the pipe as if it might hold still if I asked.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has been leaning against the fruit bowl since Tuesday, and tonight I finally slide a butter knife under the flap because my thumbnail feels like too much work. The kitchen light buzzes. I sit down without deciding to, my knees making the decision for me. Department of Housing, the return address says, same as the last three. I unfold the pages and read the first line twice, then a third time, and the words keep sliding off like rain on a window. 'Please provide the following documents within thirty days.' I almost laugh, but it comes out as a long breath through my nose. I rub my eyes with the heel of my hand; they feel packed with sand. Somewhere in the drawer are the old copies, or maybe not. I set the letter down, set my forehead down beside it on the cool table, and tell the empty kitchen, 'Okay. Tomorrow. Or the day after.'

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The train hissed out of Hanoi's station hall and Marta stood on the platform with her backpack still on, because lowering it seemed like a project for later. Signs flickered past, thick with accents she couldn't parse. A man called out something that sounded like a question, and she held up her phone, its screen cracked and the address half-visible, and said, "Hotel? Please," in a voice that came out flat and small. He pointed, spoke quickly, pointed again. She nodded at all of it. Her eyes stung from the fluorescent glare; she pressed two knuckles into them and kept walking, dragging one foot slightly on the wet tile. Outside, motorbikes swarmed like river water, horns layered over horns. She stopped at the curb and simply watched them for a long moment, not thinking of crossing. Then she sat down on her suitcase, right there, and stared at the menu board across the street, the letters meaning nothing, and let the noise go by.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: The tennis ball landed somewhere near the fence, and Biscuit tore after it, ears flapping, while I lowered myself onto the bench the way my grandfather used to, hands braced on both knees, a small sound escaping me on the way down. The grass was wet through my jeans. I didn't move. "Good boy," I called, but it came out flat and low, barely reaching past my own shoes. He circled back with the ball and dropped it at my feet, tail whipping, and I looked at it for a long time. My eyelids kept sliding shut; I let them, then jerked them open when he barked. "Give me a minute, bud." My thumb pressed into my temple, where something dull had been thumping since morning. I thought about the dishes, the unanswered email, the alarm set for five. The ball sat there, slick and green. I picked it up slowly, and my arm felt like it belonged to someone else as I threw it, barely twenty feet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I've propped my cello against the folding table because holding it upright seems like too much to ask of my spine. "Again from letter C?" Marguerite calls, and I say, "Sure," the word coming out flat and slow, dragged along the floor. My bow arm sinks a little more each bar. I read the same measure three times before the notes mean anything. Someone's kid bangs a tambourine in the corner, and I watch my own hand miss a shift I could once do blind. I blink longer than I need to. The clock above the stage says 8:40, the concert is Saturday, and all I can picture is the car, the cold steering wheel, the dark kitchen, my bed. "Sorry," I mutter, coming in late. Marguerite smiles kindly. Between pieces I lean my head against the cool cinderblock wall and let my eyes close, just for a breath that lasts longer than a breath.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I sat down on Walt's overturned bucket because the third box wouldn't close, and I didn't get up for a while. The coffee can of mismatched screws was in my hands, and I turned it over, listening it rattle, trying to decide whether anyone on earth wanted them. "Keep," I told the empty room, then, "No. Donate." Then I set it on the keep pile anyway. My knees clicked when I finally stood. Sawdust had worked into my cuffs and the creases of my knuckles, and the afternoon light slanted through the window at the same angle it had when I started, or it felt that way. Eleven hours of this. The pegboard still held half its outlines, hammers gone, their shapes drawn in marker. I reached for the next shelf, stopped, and rested my forehead against the cool edge of the workbench. It smelled like him. I breathed out slowly and picked up the box again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The portal said results would go up at noon, and at 12:40 Dana was still sitting on the edge of the bed with her laptop balanced on a pillow, refreshing the page without much hope. Her eyelids kept dropping; twice she caught her chin sinking toward her chest. The tea beside her had grown a skin and she drank it anyway. Her mother called up the stairs to ask if anything had come, and Dana answered, "Not yet," in a flat voice that barely carried past the door. She rubbed the heel of her hand into her eye socket and watched the little wheel spin. Three months of flashcards lay in a slumped pile on the floor, corners soft as cloth. She thought about lying down just for a minute, thought about how the minute would turn into the afternoon, and didn't have the energy to care which way it went. The page blinked. She stared at it, shoulders heavy, and let it load.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The switchbacks have stopped being switchbacks and become just a series of rocks I negotiate with. I count steps to forty, lose track, start again. My pack strap has worn a hot groove into my shoulder, and I shift it, and it settles right back into the same spot. Somewhere below, the creek has gone quiet, or maybe I've just stopped hearing it. The light turns the color of weak tea. I sit on a log I told myself I'd walk past, and my knees make a noise I pretend not to notice. "Just a minute," I say aloud to nobody, and my voice comes out thin and scraped. I stare at my boots. The laces have come undone, and I consider them for a long while before deciding they can stay that way. The trailhead is two miles off, the map says. The map has been wrong before. Eventually I push off my thighs with both hands and stand, slowly, like someone much older.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The recipe card is soft as cloth, my grandmother's slanted handwriting gone brown at the creases. "Knead until it feels like an earlobe," it says. I lean on the counter and push the heel of my hand into the dough, and my shoulders sag with each fold. Flour dusts my forearms up to the elbows. It's past eleven. The kitchen clock ticks too loudly, and I catch myself staring at the same smear of butter on the tile for what must be a full minute. I read the line about the earlobe again, then again, because the words keep sliding off. "Fine," I mutter to the empty room, my voice scraped thin. "Fine, Nana. Earlobe." I press a thumb into the dough and it doesn't spring back, not really. I rub my eyes and leave a white streak across my face. Then I slide down onto the floor, back against the cabinet, the bowl covered with a damp towel above me, and let it rise without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was holding a carton of eggs and a box of cat litter, leaning my hip against the cart because standing straight took more than I had. The fluorescent lights hummed over aisle nine. "Dana? Dana Whitlock? It's Priya, from Mr. Ferris's chemistry class!" Her voice rang bright as a bell, and my eyes took a second to catch up with it. I smiled, a beat late. "Oh. Wow. Hi." She talked about her wedding, her twins, a move to Denver, and I nodded at the right places while my shoulders sank an inch at a time. My feet throbbed inside my work shoes. "You look great," I said, and the words came out flat, like something read off a card. She asked what I was up to now. I looked at the eggs. "Same old," I said. "Mostly sleeping, when I can." She laughed, so I let her think it was a joke. After she left, I stood there another minute, forgetting what I'd come in for.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: The pharmacy clock says 5:42, and I've read it four times in ten minutes as if it might change its mind. Tinsel droops from the register, one strand stuck to my sleeve, and I don't pick it off. A man asks if we have any more of the good wrapping paper. "Aisle six," I say, and then, because he keeps standing there, "Left side. Bottom." My voice comes out flat, scraped thin. I lean on the counter and my knees tick like cooling metal. The fluorescent hum has settled behind my eyes. I count the bottles of cough syrup twice and still get two different numbers, so I write down the smaller one. When the door chimes again I close my eyes for one full second before turning around. Tomorrow my sister will ask if I'm hungry, and I'll say sure, and I'll mean I'd like to lie on her carpet. Eighteen minutes. I straighten the pens in their cup. They don't need it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says Gate B47, and I'm at C12, and I read it twice because the numbers keep sliding. My carry-on strap has worn a groove into my shoulder; I switch sides without breaking stride, though stride is generous for what my legs are doing. Somewhere past the pretzel kiosk I reach the moving walkway and just stand there, letting it carry me, eyes half shut, the hum of it in my molars. A man brushes past and I mumble, "Sorry," to nobody. My boots feel poured full of wet sand. Nineteen hours since I last lay flat. When the gate agent says, "You made it, barely," I nod slowly and hand her my phone, the screen cracked and glowing, then can't remember which pocket my passport is in. I check the same pocket three times. Finally I find it, and she waits, kind, while I rest my forehead against the cool edge of the podium for a second too long.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Marta had meant to finish the second coat before dinner, but her phone said ten past nine and the north wall was still streaked with the old green. She dragged the roller up the plaster in a slow, heavy stripe and watched her forearm tremble halfway through. The tray was nearly dry; she scraped the last gray-blue puddle toward the center and didn't bother to pour more. Her shoulder clicked when she reached for the trim brush. "Good enough," she told the empty room, flat, and then, "No, it isn't," and didn't move. She lowered herself onto the overturned bucket, brush drooping from her fingers, a drip landing on her sock. Somewhere behind her the kettle she'd boiled hours ago sat cold. She stared at the unfinished corner, blinking slowly, and wondered whether tomorrow's light through the window would ask anything more of her than she had left.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while I was still holding the screen door, and I let it swing shut behind me without bothering to catch it. The porch boards were already speckled dark. I lowered myself into the sagging wicker chair one joint at a time, and it creaked back at me like it understood. My shoes stayed on. Somewhere in the kitchen the phone buzzed against the counter, and I counted its buzzes, six, seven, and did not get up. Rain came sideways and soaked my knees; I watched it do that. "Fine," I said to nobody, my voice scraped thin, and then I said it again quieter. My eyelids kept sliding down between lightning flashes, and each time the sky cracked I opened them a little slower. The coffee on the rail had gone cold hours ago. I thought about moving it. I thought about it until the next thunderclap, and then I leaned my head back against the damp siding and just listened to the gutters overflow.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had been trying to seat the same chain on the same cog for what the wall clock said was twenty minutes, though it might have been forty. The garage hummed with someone else's dryer through the shared wall. She sat down on an upturned paint bucket instead of the stool, because the stool was too far to reach, and let her forehead rest against the cold top tube. Her thumbs ached where the grease had cracked the skin. "Okay," she said to the bike, barely above a whisper, "just go on." The chain slid off again. She stared at it. Across the garage, her neighbor's shelf of labeled bins blurred, then sharpened. She read the same word on one label three times without it meaning anything. Her hand reached for the wrench and stopped halfway, hovering, as if the distance had grown. She yawned so wide her jaw clicked, wiped her face with a rag, and left a black streak across her cheek that she didn't notice until morning.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's plastic roof, and Marisol didn't look up. She had been leaning her shoulder against the glass panel for a long while, her bag slumped at her feet because lifting it again seemed like a negotiation she wasn't ready for. Wind pushed a gum wrapper along the curb. Her eyelids kept sliding down, and each time she dragged them open to check the empty road. The temperature dropped; she felt it in her wrists first, then did nothing about it, her coat still unzipped. When the rain thickened into a gray rattle, an old man beside her said, "Late again." She nodded slowly, a beat behind. "Yeah," she said, the word coming out thin and flat, and then she added, mostly to the puddle spreading toward her shoes, "I'll just stand here a minute." She had been standing for twenty. Her knees ached. She thought about her bed, the exact weight of the blanket, and lost the thought halfway through.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The box has been on my lap since the lamp became the only bright thing in the room, and I've read the same postmark four times. March 1987. Or 1981. I hold the envelope closer, then farther, then give up and set it on the pile I haven't decided about. My elbow keeps sliding off the armrest. I prop it up again. Somewhere in here is the letter from my sister, the one I told Dana I'd find tonight, and I say, to no one, "Just one more." My voice comes out flat and scratchy, like I haven't used it all day. I slit another flap with my thumbnail, slowly. The paper smells of cedar and dust. My eyelids drop, and I let them stay down a moment too long. The tea beside me has a skin on it. I don't drink it. I lean my head back against the cushion and let the page rest open on my chest.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: The knock came while I was still in my work shoes, one heel hooked against the other, a cold mug of tea in my hand that I'd forgotten to drink. Dale stood on the porch, grinning, pointing a thumb toward his gutters. "Got a ladder I could borrow?" I stared at his thumb for a second too long. "Garage," I said. "Behind the bikes." My voice came out flat and low, like it had been dragged. I walked there slowly, one hand trailing along the wall, and the fluorescent light buzzed over the dust. The ladder was heavier than I remembered. I got it down by leaning my whole body into it, forehead nearly against the rung, breath loud. Dale offered to take it. I let him. "No rush," I said, though what I meant was keep it till spring. Back inside, I sat on the bottom stair without taking my shoes off, and the tea stayed cold beside me while the light went gray.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: The onion sits half-diced while I lean on the counter, one palm flat against the cool laminate, watching the knife like it belongs to someone else. Six forty. They'll be here at seven. The pot behind me hisses, and it takes me two tries to turn my head toward it. I read the recipe card again, the same line, the same line, and still can't tell whether I've added the cumin. I taste the sauce. Maybe. I add more anyway. My feet ache inside my socks, and I slide down until I'm crouched with my back against the oven door, just for a second, eyes shut, the warmth soaking into my spine. The timer buzzes. I say, 'Yes, yes, I know,' to nobody, my voice flat as a dropped plate. Standing takes a push from both hands on my knees. I find the lemon, roll it, and forget what I wanted it for. The doorbell rings early. I wipe my hands, and stare at the table, still missing forks.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter, and I watch it crawl toward the edge of a stack of unopened mail. Unknown number. Ten digits, none of them familiar. I'm still in my work shoes, one heel hooked on the rung of the stool, and I can't remember when I last sat down on purpose. My thumb hovers. Somewhere in my chest there's a dull weight, like wet sand, and my eyelids keep sliding shut between rings. On the fifth buzz I swipe. "Hello," I say, and it comes out cracked, scraped low, barely a word. A bright voice asks if this is the homeowner. I press the heel of my hand into my eye socket. "Can you just... say that slower," I mutter. The cold tile under my socks seems like a decent place to lie down. "Honestly, whatever you're selling, yes. Fine. Put me down for it." I lean my forehead on the cupboard and let the voice go on without me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been living at the bottom of my backpack since March, under a wad of hoodie and a dead charger. I dragged it out at the circulation desk and my hand shook a little setting it down, the corner crushed soft. The librarian's screen glowed too bright. I blinked at it, then at her, and forgot the sentence I'd rehearsed on the stairs. "It's, um. Kind of late," I said, and my voice came out as gravel. She tapped keys. I leaned my elbow on the counter because my spine had stopped offering opinions. Two hundred and forty days, she said, or maybe it was two hundred and fourteen; the numbers slid around. "Whatever it is, I'll pay it," I told her, rubbing my eyes with the heel of my palm. The clock above the stacks ticked. I thought about my bed, the gray pillow, the way the blanket would feel. "Can I sit while it prints?" I asked, already folding into the chair.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: The last box hit the floor with a thud I felt in my knees, and I just stood there, keys still hooked on one finger, staring at the studio's single window. Four hundred square feet. I'd measured it twice online. The couch was wedged crooked in the doorway, and I considered it for a long moment before deciding it could stay that way tonight. "Fine," I told the empty room, my voice scraped thin. I lowered myself onto the mattress, still in its plastic, and the crinkle sounded absurdly loud. My shoulders had gone heavy, my eyelids too, and I read the label on the nearest box three times without absorbing it. Kitchen? Bedroom? Who knew. The faucet dripped. I meant to get up and find a glass, I really did, but my hand just lay there beside me, palm up, and I watched the light slide off the wall while my shoes stayed laced on my feet.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The bench was twenty feet farther than I'd planned to walk, but my knees made the decision for me. I lowered myself onto it in pieces, backpack first, then hips, then a long breath that came out almost as a groan. Something brown sat against the slats beside me. A wallet. I stared at it for a while before touching it, as if lifting it might cost me something. Inside: a license, forty dollars, a photo of a girl missing her front teeth. 'Okay,' I said to nobody, my voice scraped thin. 'Okay, okay.' I read the address twice and it still didn't stick. The streetlamps flickered on. My eyelids kept sliding down, and I pinched the bridge of my nose and tried again. Two miles, maybe, to the address. I tucked the wallet into my coat, pressed my palms against my thighs, and counted to three before standing. On the second try, I made it up.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Marguerite clung to the pool's gutter with both hands, her chin barely above the chlorine-bright water, while the instructor's whistle echoed off the tiles. Her arms shook when she let go of the wall. She managed four kicks, maybe five, before her legs sank like wet sandbags and she grabbed the edge again, coughing. "One more length," the instructor called. "Sure," she said, so quietly the word dissolved into the splashing. She rested her forehead on the cool concrete and watched a drip crawl down her wrist. Her shoulders felt hollow, her fingertips wrinkled and distant. The clock above the lifeguard chair read 7:40, which meant the whole day still sat behind her, the spreadsheets and the bus and the dishes she hadn't done. She thought about the towel on the bench, how soft it would be, and how far away, about twelve feet of tile. She pushed off anyway, slowly, and sank a little more with each stroke, eyes half closed, counting nothing at all.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned across her thigh, and the tomato one slipped to the dirt before she noticed. She left it there. The spade had felt light an hour ago; now she dragged it, blade scraping, and her forearms trembled each time she pressed it into the clay. Sweat cooled along her spine. She read the packet's instructions twice, lips moving, and still couldn't say how deep a quarter inch was. "Fine," she muttered to the beans. "Here's good." She poked a hole with her thumb, dropped a seed, and sat back on her heels, then onto the grass entirely, legs straight out, palms flat behind her. The hose lay coiled ten feet away like a distant country. Dusk was settling over the fence, and only half the rows were marked. She watched a robin hop through the finished soil and thought how nice it would be if the rest could plant itself while she closed her eyes right here.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Marta sat in the back row of the conference room with her chin propped on her fist, the slide deck glowing blue against the window blinds. Dev was on slide nine, or maybe eleven; she had lost the count somewhere around the budget chart. She read the same bullet point three times and it kept sliding off her. Her coffee had gone cold an hour ago, but she lifted it anyway and swallowed, grimacing at the skin of milk. Her eyelids felt sanded. When Dev asked, 'Any questions so far?' the room turned toward her, and she realized her pen had been resting motionless on the page for minutes, a small ink dot bleeding outward. 'No, that's, yeah,' she said, voice scraped thin. 'Looks good. Really.' She straightened, pressed her palms flat against her thighs, and stared at the wall clock, willing the second hand to hurry while the radiator hummed her toward the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The traffic light at Delmar turned red over an empty intersection, and Marisol stopped for it anyway, her forehead drifting toward the wheel until her own chin dropping jerked her upright. She rolled the window down and let the cold slap her cheek. Her eyes stung; she blinked twice, slowly, and the second blink lasted longer than she meant it to. "Okay," she said to the dashboard, her voice a gravel scrape. "Okay, okay." The green came and went, and she noticed it three full seconds late. Her shoulders had crept up near her ears somewhere around the highway, and she couldn't remember deciding to hold them there. She counted the streetlights to her block, lost track at six, started over. In the driveway she turned the engine off and just sat, keys in her fist, the lanyard still around her neck, her badge face-down against her sternum. The porch light looked very far away. One more minute, she told herself, and then another.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The vending machine on four ate my dollar twice, and I just stood there with my forehead against its cool glass until a nurse asked if I was okay. "Fine," I said, too slowly, like the word had to be dragged up a hill. In Grandpa's room I lowered myself into the vinyl chair and it exhaled under me. He was asleep, mouth open, the monitor ticking its green line. I read the same sentence of the magazine four times. My eyelids kept sliding shut, and each time I jerked them up and pretended I'd only been blinking hard. My shoulders felt packed with wet sand. When he stirred and whispered, "You came," I meant to say something warm, but I only nodded, took his hand, and let my head tip against the bed rail. "Just resting my eyes a second," I mumbled. The clock said 3:10. I couldn't remember which day it was, or whether I'd eaten.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I park crooked and don't fix it. The bell is eleven minutes off, so I lean against the fender with my eyes shut, and the sun makes orange smears behind my lids. Somebody's mother says my name, and I answer a beat late, "Hm? Sorry, yes, hi." She's talking about a bake sale. I nod at the right places. My coffee went cold at noon, but I drink it anyway, grimacing, because it's there. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears; I notice and can't be bothered to lower them. The doors burst open and a flood of backpacks pours out. I scan for the yellow raincoat and look right past it twice. When she finally slams into my legs, shouting about a lizard, I put my hand on her head and say, "Tell me in the car," then stand there another second, not moving, until my knees agree to walk.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By noon Marguerite had stopped getting up from the lawn chair when people wandered toward the dresser. "Twenty," she said to the man running his thumb along the drawer, and then, when he frowned, "Fifteen. Fine." Her voice came out flat and low, scraped thin. The sun had crept under the umbrella's edge and settled on her shins, and she didn't bother to shift her feet. Her back had set into a hard curve hours ago; she'd hauled the oak table by herself since six, and her forearms still hummed. A coffee sat beside her, cold, a skin on top. When a girl asked if the rocking chair had been her grandmother's, Marguerite looked at it a long moment. "Might've been," she said. "Take it for five." Her eyelids kept sliding down, and she let them, counting quarters in the cash box by touch, losing count, starting over, not minding the dust or the flies or the three hours left on the sign.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The wrench slips off the nut for the fourth time, and I just watch it clatter into the cabinet's dark corner instead of swearing. Water ticks into the saucepan under the sink, slower than when I started, which should count for something. My knees have gone numb against the tile. I lay my cheek on the cool edge of the cabinet door, only for a second, and the flashlight in my teeth drools a little. It's past two. The tutorial video is still murmuring from my phone, some cheerful man saying this takes five minutes. I laugh, a dry puff of air. Reaching for the wrench takes me two tries because my fingers won't close right. "Come on," I whisper to the pipe, flat, like asking a sleeping dog to move. I tighten, and a bead swells at the joint anyway. I stare at it. Then I pull the towel down, fold it under my head, and let the drip count for me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope has sat against the toaster since Tuesday, its little window staring at me while I microwaved the same coffee twice. Tonight I finally sit on the kitchen floor, because the chair seems too far away. My thumb slides under the flap and the paper tears crooked. I read the first line, then read it again, then realize I've been holding the page at arm's length like it might spit. The words slide around. Department of Revenue. Something about a review. My eyelids keep dropping, and I pinch the bridge of my nose until it aches. "Okay," I say to the refrigerator, voice scraped flat. "Okay. Fine." I don't swear. I don't even sigh. I fold the letter back along its creases, lean my head against the cabinet door, and look at the clock on the stove. 9:47. The deadline is in thirty days. I tell myself I'll deal with it tomorrow, and my legs don't move for a long time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station's board flickered through characters Marta couldn't read, and she stood beneath it with her suitcase tipped against her shin, watching the rows shuffle without taking any of them in. Her shoulder strap had dug a groove she could feel through her coat. She read the same line on her phone three times, then let the screen go dark. At the ticket counter she said, "Hotel? Please," and slid over a crumpled printout, and when the clerk spoke rapidly and pointed left, she nodded anyway, though she'd caught none of it. Her eyelids kept dropping in the warm, humming air. Outside, rain slicked the pavement, and she let it fall on her hair without lifting the hood. A bench appeared, and she sat with the suitcase between her knees, forehead resting on the handle, and decided the hotel could wait until her legs agreed to carry her again. Somewhere a tram bell rang. She did not turn.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: The bench is damp, and I sit down on it the way a sack of flour lands on a shelf. Biscuit tears across the field after nothing, ears flat, tongue flapping, and I lift one hand to wave and let it drop back onto my knee halfway through. "Good girl," I call, but it comes out as a croak, and the wind takes it before she hears. My eyes keep sliding shut against the low orange light. I count the steps to the car, then decide not to think about them. She bounds back with a stick twice her size, dropping it at my shoe, and I stare at it for a long moment. "Give me a minute," I tell her, my voice flat and slow. My head tips against the cold slats of the bench. Her tail thumps the grass. I reach down, finally, and my fingers feel like they belong to someone else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The fourth run of the Brahms intermezzo, and my left hand keeps landing a half-step late. Mrs. Okafor, who's organizing the Thursday concert at the library annex, calls out, "Once more from the bridge?" I say, "Sure," but it comes out as a breath rather than a word. The folding chair behind the upright piano looks better than the bench. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears, and I only notice when I try to drop them and they won't. The fluorescent light hums above the stacks of large-print mysteries. I read the same measure three times before the notes mean anything. My fingers press down, soft, slower than the tempo marking. When I miss the F-sharp again I just stare at it, then laugh, flat and short. "Can we do ten minutes?" I ask, already leaning my forehead against the cool wood of the music stand, eyes closed, listening to my own pulse thud in my ears.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: I sat down on an upturned paint bucket in the middle of Walt's workshop and stayed there longer than I meant to. The box in my lap was labeled "screws, misc," and I had been holding it for what felt like a quarter hour, though the light through the dusty window had barely moved. My knees clicked when I finally stood. I read the next label out loud, "Hinges," in a voice that came out flat and scratchy, then set the box down by the door instead of sorting it. Seven jars of nails still waited on the shelf. I counted them twice. My shoulders hung like wet coats, and I leaned against the lathe, its cold iron pressing through my shirt. Somewhere under the sawdust smell was his pipe tobacco, and I breathed it slowly. 'Tomorrow,' I told the empty room, and my hand fumbled three times at the light switch before it caught. The jars stayed where they were.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The corridor outside the registrar's office smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and Marisol had slid down the wall to sit on the linoleum an hour ago without really deciding to. The noticeboard was still blank except for a curling flyer about bike locks. Her eyelids kept sagging shut, and each time she jerked them open she stared at the same brown stain on the ceiling tile. A boy beside her asked whether she'd studied much. "Mm," she said, and then, after a long moment, "Till Tuesday. Or Wednesday." Her coffee had gone cold in its paper cup; she lifted it, sniffed, drank anyway. Her shoulders felt poured into the wall, and her phone, face-down on her knee, seemed too heavy to flip over. When the door finally clicked and a clerk stepped out with a sheet of paper and a roll of tape, the others surged up. Marisol watched them, pressed one palm against the floor, and pushed, slowly, on the second try.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The trail markers blur into one orange smear as the light drains from the pines. I stop every fifty steps now, hands braced on my knees, counting breaths until the count stops meaning anything. My pack straps have carved hot grooves into my shoulders, and my thighs tremble each time I lift a boot over a root that I'd have ignored this morning. "Just to the next bend," I tell the empty woods, my voice scraping out thin and cracked. The bend comes. Another follows. I sit on a flat rock without deciding to, and the cold of it seeps right through my pants, and I don't mind. My water bottle is nearly empty; I tilt it anyway, tongue chasing the last drops. Somewhere below, the parking lot waits, three miles off, maybe four. I fumble for my headlamp, fingers clumsy, dropping it twice. Getting up takes two attempts and a quiet groan. I laugh at that, one dry huff, and start walking again, slowly, dragging the dusk behind me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card is soft as cloth now, Grandma Odile's slanted handwriting blurred by decades of flour. I read it standing up, because if I sit I won't stand again. "Knead until it feels like an earlobe," it says. I press the dough with the heels of my hands and my wrists complain, so I lean my whole weight in and let my forehead almost touch the counter. The kitchen clock says 11:40. I think it said 11:40 a while ago too. I laugh at nothing, a short dry breath, and tell the empty room, "Fine. Ten more folds." I lose count at four. My eyes sting when I blink, and the oven light hums. I drape the towel over the bowl, slide down against the cabinet, and rest my cheek on my knee. The yeast smell is warm and sweet. I'll just listen to the dough rise, I tell myself, and let my eyes close.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: I was leaning on the cart more than pushing it, staring at two brands of oatmeal as if they might rearrange themselves, when someone said my name. Dana Whitfield, from tenth-grade chemistry, hair cut short now, a toddler on her hip. 'Oh my God, hi,' I said, and the words came out flat, a beat too slow. My smile took effort, like lifting something. She talked about her job, the move, a marathon she'd run, and I nodded at the wrong places, my eyelids heavy under the fluorescent hum. My feet ached inside shoes I'd had on since five that morning. 'We should get coffee,' she said. 'Definitely,' I said, knowing I'd never answer the text. When she left, I gripped the cart handle, grabbed the closest oatmeal, and stood there another minute before I remembered what aisle I needed next.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four on Christmas Eve, Marisol had restocked the same shelf of cranberry sauce three times, and each time she'd forgotten doing it. The pharmacy's fluorescent lights hummed at a pitch she could feel behind her eyes. A man asked where the tape was, and she pointed left, then right, then said, "Aisle six. Or five. Sorry, I'll walk you." She didn't walk him. She leaned on the counter instead, one hand propping her cheek, her feet two warm, throbbing bricks inside her sneakers. The clock over the door seemed stuck. She read the same coupon on the register tape four times without absorbing a word. When the last customer left at six, she locked the door, slid down against it until she sat on the cold linoleum, and stayed there with her coat still unbuttoned, listening to the lights hum, not yet able to think about the drive home or the stairs.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board says Gate B47, and I am standing at C12, and the distance between them looks like a country. I start walking, then the strap of my bag slides off my shoulder for the third time and I just let it hang, dragging against my hip. My calves burn with a dull hum. Somewhere past the pretzel stand I realize I'm reading the same sign twice, the letters sliding like wet paint. The moving walkway is broken, of course. I step onto its still, ridged belt and almost laugh, but what comes out is a wheeze. A man in a vest asks if I'm okay and I say, "Fine, yeah," except it comes out slow, each word set down carefully like a heavy box. My eyes sting. I haven't slept since Tuesday, maybe Monday. At B40 I lean my forehead on a cool pillar for one second, then two. Down the corridor, a door is closing. I lift one foot, then the other, and follow it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller slides down the wall and I let it keep going, past the baseboard, until it kisses the drop cloth and leaves a gray-green smear I'll have to deal with. Later. I sit on the overturned bucket, and my knees crackle like gravel. There's still the whole north wall, plus the trim, plus the corner by the window where the old yellow keeps showing through. I hold up my hand and watch it tremble a little around the handle. Paint has dried in the creases of my knuckles. The radio went to static an hour ago and I never got up to fix it. "Okay," I say to the empty room, flat, like I'm agreeing to something. I tip my head back against the unpainted drywall, close my eyes, and count breaths before I'll stand. Five. Maybe ten. The coffee on the sill has grown a skin. I drink it anyway.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the railing while I was still working on the screen door latch, and I gave up on it halfway. My keys were somewhere in my fist, so I let the bag slide off my shoulder onto the boards and lowered myself into the porch chair in stages, like a man testing ice. Thunder rolled over the rooftops. Mrs. Alvarez's wind chimes went wild next door, and I watched them without really seeing. My boots were still laced. I thought about untying them and decided the laces could wait until tomorrow, or the day after. Rain blew in and speckled my shins, cool and unwelcome and fine. 'Come on, then,' I muttered to the sky, though it came out as barely a breath. My eyelids kept sinking, and I kept hauling them back up to watch the lightning. Inside, the phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, twice. I let my head tip against the cushion, and my arms hung off the chair like they belonged to someone else.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: Marisol had tightened the same bolt on the rear wheel three times, and still she gave it a fourth quarter turn, her jaw working side to side. Behind her the garage door rattled, and her head snapped around; it was only the neighbor's cat nosing the gap. She wiped her palms on her jeans, but they were slick again almost at once. The race was at eight tomorrow, and the shop had been closed since five. "Okay," she muttered, "okay, okay," spinning the wheel and holding her breath to listen for the tick. There it was, faint, rhythmic. She pressed two fingers against her sternum, where her heartbeat seemed to be keeping the same uneven time. Mr. Alvarez's half-built shelves loomed in the shared corner, and she kept glancing at his toolbox, wondering if he'd mind her borrowing the good spoke wrench so late. She picked it up, put it down, picked it up again, and found she was still staring at the wheel, not turning it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The sky over the pharmacy went the color of wet slate, and I checked my phone again: 6:42, the bus was eleven minutes late. I pressed my thumb against the screen until the schedule refreshed. Same result. A gust shoved a paper cup down the street and I watched it the whole way, jaw tight. My daughter's school let out at six. She had no umbrella, I knew that, because it was still hanging by our front door. I called her number and listened to it ring out, then called again. "Pick up, pick up, come on," I muttered to nobody. The first drops hit the shelter roof, scattered, then thickened. I stepped out from under it to peer down the road, and the cold water ran inside my collar. My stomach felt hollow and my knee wouldn't stop bouncing. When headlights finally swung around the corner, I was already at the curb, fingers cramped around my phone, rehearsing what I'd say to the driver if he didn't stop.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox lid sticks, and I pry it off with my thumbnail, then wipe my palm on my jeans because it's damp again. Dad's handwriting slants across the top envelope, and I tell the empty kitchen, "Okay, just the dates, just sort by dates," my voice thin and too bright. I stack them by year. Three times I count the 1989 pile, as if the number might change. The hospital's return address shows up on one, and my stomach tightens like a fist around a rope. I hold it up to the window light, trying to read through the paper without opening it. The kettle clicks off; I don't move. My knee jiggles against the table leg, rattling the spoons in their cup. If I read it now, I'll know. If I don't, Mom will ask on Sunday, and I'll have to lie badly. I slide a thumb under the flap, stop, and breathe through my teeth.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Mr. Alvarez stood on my porch with his hands tucked in his jacket, asking if the ladder in my garage was free for the afternoon. "Sure," I said, too fast, and my thumb began rubbing the doorknob raw. I led him past the recycling bins, and my eyes went to the ladder's left rail, the one with the hairline crack I'd been meaning to fix since August. My mouth had gone dry. "It's a bit old," I said. "Wobbly. You're going up on the roof?" He nodded, glancing at the gutters. I laughed at nothing, a thin sound. I lifted the ladder down, then set it back, then lifted it again. "Let me come hold the bottom," I said. "Really. I've got nothing on." My stomach clenched as he smiled and said that wasn't necessary. I followed him across the lawn anyway, carrying the ladder, counting his steps.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marisol lifted the lid on the braise for the fourth time in ten minutes, and steam fogged her glasses. She pushed them up with a wrist, fork already poised, and tasted. Flat. Salt, then lemon, then salt again. The clock on the stove said 6:41, and the rice hadn't even started. "Okay," she told the empty kitchen, "okay, okay." Her palms were damp against the dish towel, and her heartbeat seemed to tap out of time with the knife as she chopped parsley far smaller than anyone needed. Behind her the oven timer beeped, and she flinched as if it were the doorbell. What if Daniel's mother didn't eat lamb? She had asked, hadn't she? She grabbed her phone, scrolled up through the messages, lost the thread, and set it down. A car passed outside. She froze, listening, a spoon dripping onto the floor.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzes against the kitchen counter at 11:40 p.m., and the screen shows a string of digits I don't know. I stop with the dish towel halfway through a plate. Four rings. Five. My thumb hovers, damp and trembling a little, and I realize I've been holding my breath since the first buzz. Dad's hospital is two hours away. Mom said she'd text, not call. Texting is what people do when nothing's wrong. I wipe my palm on my jeans, twice, and the plate slips into the sink with a clunk that makes me flinch. "Okay," I whisper to the empty room. "Okay, okay." My pulse thuds in my ears, loud enough that I almost miss the sixth ring. I press the phone to my face, and my voice comes out thin and too polite. "Hello? This is Dana. Who is this, please?" The line crackles. Somebody inhales. I sink onto the floor with my back against the cabinet, knees pulled up, and wait for the words.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in my backpack since March, and now it was November, and the spine had gone soft from being carried everywhere I couldn't bring myself to go. I stood outside the library doors for a full minute, wiping my palms on my jeans, rehearsing a sentence that kept falling apart. Inside, the air smelled of carpet and radiators. My heart knocked against my ribs as I joined the line behind a man with a single paperback. When the librarian looked up, I slid the book across the desk too fast and said, "It's, um, a little overdue," and my voice cracked on the last word. She turned it over slowly. I counted ceiling tiles. I kept thinking about the number on the screen, how many digits it might have, whether my wallet held enough, and I realized I was pressing my thumbnail into my finger hard enough to leave a white crescent.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Marisol set the last box down in the studio and immediately picked it up again, moving it two feet to the left, then back. The radiator clanked, and she froze mid-step, hand pressed flat against her sternum until the sound stopped. "Fine," she said aloud to nobody, too brightly. "That's fine." She counted the outlets, found three, and counted again. Her landlord's lease sat on the counter, and she had read the same clause about late fees four times without absorbing it. The window faced a brick wall; she tugged the curtain shut, then open, then shut. Her jaw ached from clenching. In her pocket, her phone buzzed with her mother's name, and she let it ring out, thumbnail scraping at the cardboard tape. What if the rent rose? What if the neighbor's music started at midnight? She checked the deadbolt, walked to the sink, drank a glass of water in one swallow, and went back to check the deadbolt again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The brown leather wallet sat at the far end of the bench, half hidden by a drift of maple leaves, and Dana stopped so suddenly that her coffee sloshed over her knuckles. She didn't pick it up right away. She looked left down the path, then right, at the joggers shrinking toward the pond, at the empty swings creaking. "Hello?" she called, too quietly, then again louder, and her voice cracked on the second syllable. Her thumb found the wallet's worn edge and flipped it open. A driver's license: an old man, white mustache, squinting. Under it, a folded photo of a girl in a graduation gown, and a single twenty. Her stomach tightened into a hard knot. She checked her watch, then the street, then the license again, rereading the address as if it might change. "Okay," she muttered. "Okay, okay." She tucked it inside her jacket, pressed her palm flat over it, and walked fast, nearly running, toward the gate.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: The pool smelled of chlorine and wet concrete, and I had already retied my towel around my waist twice. Marisol, the instructor, stood waist-deep and waved me in. I sat on the edge and let my feet dangle, counting the black tiles along the bottom, then counting them again. "It's only four feet here," she said. "I know," I said, too quickly, my voice thinner than I intended. My fingers had found the metal ladder and wouldn't let go. When I finally lowered myself in, the cold climbed my ribs and my breath snagged halfway up. My heart knocked against my sternum like something asking to be let out. I kept one hand on the wall, sliding it along the gutter as if the wall might leave. She asked me to put my face in the water. I nodded, stared at the surface, and asked what time the lesson ended, though the clock hung right above us, and I could read it fine.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marisol knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packet pinched in both hands, reading the back for the fourth time. Plant after last frost. Was this after? She glanced at the sky, then at her phone, then at the sky again. The tomato seedlings sat in their plastic tray, leaning slightly, and she straightened one with a fingertip, then wished she hadn't touched it. "Six inches apart," she muttered, measuring with a ruler she'd brought from the kitchen. Her stomach felt tight, as though she'd skipped lunch, though she hadn't. She dug a hole, stopped, dug it deeper, stopped again. The neighbor's tidy rows of lettuce showed over the fence, bright and sure of themselves. Marisol wiped her damp palms on her jeans, left soil streaks on the denim, and lowered the first seedling in as gently as if it were asleep. Then she sat back on her heels and watched it for a full minute, barely breathing, waiting for it to do something wrong.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicked to the third slide and I stopped breathing for a second. That was the slide with the vendor numbers, the ones I had pasted in Tuesday night and never double-checked. My pen had been clicking against my thumb for ten minutes; I made myself set it down on the conference table, then picked it right back up. The projector fan hummed. Someone's chair creaked. I pulled my laptop closer and opened the spreadsheet, scrolling to row forty, then row forty again, as if the figure might change. My shirt collar felt tight, and my coffee had gone cold hours ago, but I lifted it anyway and sipped. "Quick question," I said, and my voice came out too thin, so I cleared my throat and tried again. "Where did those totals come from?" Dana smiled and said they'd come from me. My stomach dropped toward the carpet. I nodded slowly, wiped my palms on my knees, and typed a note I wouldn't be able to read later.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The phone lit up on the passenger seat again, and Marisol snatched it at the red light, thumb smearing the screen. Still nothing from Dani. She set it face-up on her knee instead. Past midnight, the highway was empty except for her own headlights sliding over wet asphalt, and she kept checking the mirror as if someone might be there. "Pick up," she muttered, then again, softer, the call ringing out to voicemail. Her palms were slick on the wheel; she wiped one on her jeans, then the other. The green came and she didn't notice until the car behind her honked, a long flat note. She turned the radio off, then on, then off. Three more exits. She counted them aloud, her voice thin, and pressed the gas harder than she meant to, eyes fixed on the dark where her brother's porch light should have been glowing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: Dana stood outside room 412 for a full minute, rereading the whiteboard by the door as if the nurse's name might have changed. She pressed the sanitizer pump twice, then a third time, rubbing until her palms squeaked. Inside, her grandfather's chest rose under the thin blanket, and she counted the beeps of the monitor against her own pulse, which refused to match. "Hi, Grandpa," she said, too brightly, then lower: "Hi." She set the grocery bag of his favorite peppermints on the tray table, moved it to the windowsill, then moved it back. Her knee bounced against the chair leg. When a cart rattled past in the hall she twisted around so fast her neck cracked. "Did they say when the doctor comes?" she asked the empty doorway, and then, hearing herself, picked at the edge of her thumbnail until it stung. She took his hand carefully, as though it might bruise under her grip, and did not let go.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: The bell rang at 3:05, and I had already checked my phone four times since 3:01. Doors banged open and the first wave of backpacks spilled across the yard, bright jackets, loud voices, none of them Nora's. I rose onto my toes, then stepped off the curb, then back again. My thumbnail had worn a ragged edge into the cuticle of my index finger. "Excuse me," I said to a teacher holding a clipboard, too quickly, "third grade, Ms. Patel's room, are they all out?" She smiled and said they were coming. My stomach felt tight and sour, like I'd skipped lunch, though I hadn't. She had been coughing this morning, and I'd sent her anyway. The crowd thinned. A boy ran past with a red scooter. I counted the doorway again, one, two, three kids, nobody. My keys dug into my palm. Then a small yellow hood appeared, bobbing, and my breath finally went out of me, loud enough that the woman beside me glanced over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine, Marta had rearranged the oak dresser three times, angling it toward the street, then away, then back. Her thumbnail picked at a chip in the cardboard price sign, and the $40 looked wrong, so she crossed it out and wrote $35, then $40 again. A man ran his palm along the dresser's top and she hovered a step behind him, mouth dry, hands tucked under her arms. "It was my mother's," she said, too quickly, then laughed at nothing. "But it's just sitting there. Takes up room." He pulled out a drawer; it stuck, and her stomach dropped with it. "It sticks when it's humid. A little candle wax, I can show you." He shrugged and wandered toward the lamps. Marta checked her phone, though nobody had called, and counted the cash box again. Eleven dollars. The sun climbed over the garage, and the rent notice stayed folded in her back pocket, pressing against her.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: The drip landed on the cabinet floor every two seconds, and I'd caught myself counting it again. I wedged the flashlight between my teeth and tightened the wrench another quarter turn, then wiped my palm on my jeans because it kept slipping. Still wet. "Come on," I whispered, "come on, come on." My heartbeat was loud in the cramped dark under the sink. I pressed a dry paper towel to the joint and watched it darken, fast, and my stomach dropped. Upstairs, my landlord's ceiling. The thought arrived whole: the stain, the phone call, the number on a repair bill. I checked my phone for the plumber's video, lost my place, started it over. My knees ached against the tile but I didn't shift. I yanked the shutoff valve again, though I already knew it was closed, and then I sat there with my hand flat against the cold pipe, listening, barely breathing, waiting for the next drop.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter beside the cold coffee for three days, its little window staring at me. Tonight I washed the same plate twice before I picked it up. The return address read Department of Revenue, and my thumb found the sealed edge and just stayed there, pressing. "Probably nothing," I told the empty kitchen, and my voice came out thin and too fast. The fridge hummed. My stomach had folded itself into a small hard knot. I slid a knife under the flap, stopped, set the knife down, wiped my palms on my jeans, and picked it up again. The paper tore with a sound far louder than it should have been. I unfolded the page only halfway, eyes skipping past the greeting, hunting for a number, a date, one word that would tell me. My pulse thudded in my ears. I realized I hadn't breathed in a while, and I let it out slowly, reading the first line again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The station exit spat me into a roar of horns and signs I couldn't read, and I stopped so abruptly that a man behind me clipped my suitcase and said something sharp. I nodded anyway. My thumb kept rubbing the edge of my phone, which showed the hotel's address in characters I'd copied stroke by stroke, like a drawing. Battery: nine percent. I counted it twice. My shirt was already stuck to my back, and my mouth had gone dry enough that when a taxi driver leaned out and called to me, my "Hello, hotel?" came out as a croak, too high, repeated three times, each louder. He frowned at the screen, then at me. I realized I was holding my passport against my chest with both hands. Somewhere a speaker announced something long and melodic, and everyone but me understood it. I checked my pocket for my wallet. Still there. I checked again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Marta kept one hand on the fence post long after her knuckles had gone pale. Out in the field, Biscuit bounded through the tall grass, and every time his orange back dipped out of sight she stopped breathing until it surfaced again. "Easy," she called, too quietly for him to hear. "Easy, bud." He limped. Or had he? She squinted, counting his strides: one, two, three, four. Fine. Fine. Then he yelped at something in the weeds and her stomach dropped so fast she was already climbing the gate, boots catching on the wire. "Biscuit! Here! Come here!" Her voice cracked on the second word. He trotted over, tongue lolling, a burr stuck in his ear. She knelt and ran her fingers down each leg, pressing, checking, her pulse thudding in her wrists. "Does that hurt? Does it?" He licked her chin. She stayed on her knees in the wet grass, not letting go, even after he squirmed to run again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: Marguerite wiped her palms on her skirt for the third time and set her fingers back on the church hall's out-of-tune upright. The folding chairs sat empty in rows, but she kept glancing at the door as though someone might walk through it. She started the Schubert, stumbled at bar twenty-two, and stopped. "Sorry," she said to nobody, her voice thin. "Again. From the top." Her left hand trembled slightly over the keys, and she pressed it flat against her thigh until it quieted. The radiator ticked. She played the passage four times, each faster than the last, until the notes blurred and her breath came shallow and high in her chest. Then she pulled out her pencil and wrote fingering numbers over measures that already bore them, the graphite smudging. What if her mind went white on Saturday, with Mrs. Okafor in the front row and her neighbors' children fidgeting? She swallowed, found her place, and began again, softer this time, counting under her breath.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dale's workshop smelled of cedar and cold solder, and I had been standing in the doorway with the trash bags for ten minutes before I made myself step in. I picked up a coffee can of screws, set it down, picked it up again. My thumb kept rubbing the rim. The pegboard still held his outlines in marker, every tool's ghost, and one hammer was missing. I checked the floor. I checked under the bench, then behind the vise, my knees cracking, my breath going shallow in the sawdust. "Okay," I said aloud, too brightly. "Okay, Dale, where'd you put it." His sister was coming at noon, and she would ask for that hammer, I just knew it, their father's. The drawer I opened was full of unlabeled keys. My stomach clenched around them. I pulled out my phone, put it back, and started over at the left wall, checking every shelf twice, listening for her car on the gravel.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
