text: The portal said results would go live at noon, and at 11:52 I had already refreshed the page nine times. My laptop fan whirred against my knees. I'd peeled the label off my water bottle in long, damp strips, and now the shreds lay across the desk like confetti nobody wanted. "It's fine," I told the cat, too loudly, and my voice cracked on the last word. My stomach felt like a fist around something small. I stood, sat, stood again, then went to the kitchen and opened the fridge and stared at the mustard until the cold air made my arms prickle. Back at the desk, 11:57. My thumb hovered over the trackpad, slick with sweat. I kept replaying question twelve, the one where I'd crossed out my first answer. Then the page flickered, and I realized I was holding my breath, lungs aching, ears ringing, my finger frozen above the button that said View.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The orange had drained out of the ridge by the time I checked my phone again: 4:52, no bars, eleven percent battery. I walked faster, then slower, because the rocks had started to look the same. "That cairn," I said aloud, "I passed that cairn." My voice came out thin, so I said it again, flatter, as if someone were listening. My thumbnail was already chewed raw from the last mile. Every pine trunk seemed to lean in, and my pulse knocked in my ears loud enough to cover the creek I'd been following. I pulled the trail map from my pocket and the paper shook until I pinned it against my thigh. Switchbacks, junction, parking lot, I recited, tracing it twice. A branch cracked behind me and I spun so fast my pack swung me off balance. Nothing. Just wind. I dug out my headlamp, fumbled the strap, dropped it, and crouched in the dust, breathing through my teeth until my fingers worked again.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: Grandpa's index card is soft as cloth now, the flour smudges hiding half his handwriting. I read the line again: "flour till it feels right." Right how? I press a knuckle into the dough and watch the dent. Does it spring back? Slowly. Maybe. I check the oven light for the third time, then wipe my palms on my apron and leave white handprints on my hips. The kitchen smells like yeast, and the radiator ticks too loudly. My phone sits face-up beside the bowl, his number glowing in my recents, though no one will answer it. "Come on," I whisper, to the dough, to the bowl, to the dusty window. I fold it again, too many times, and my shoulders ache, my stomach tight as a fist. If it comes out flat, I'll have nothing left that tastes like him. I set the timer, reset it, then stand with my forehead nearly touching the oven glass.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Dana was weighing two cartons of eggs when someone said her name, and the carton in her left hand cracked a little under her thumb. Marcus Veil, from tenth-grade chemistry, stood by the dairy case with a basket and a wide grin. "Dana! Wow. What are you up to these days?" She set the eggs down, then picked them up again. "Oh, you know. Work. Things." Her laugh came out too high, and she heard it. Her palms were damp against the cold handle of her cart, and her stomach felt tight, like a fist. He asked about the bakery she used to talk about opening. She glanced at the exit, then at her phone, which showed nothing. "Still planning," she said, tugging her sleeve down over her wrist. "Sort of. Soon." She wondered how much he knew, who had told him, what her face was doing. When he reached to hug her, she stiffened, then patted his back twice, quick, and said she had to run, though her cart was nearly empty.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied, and Marisol wiped the same stretch of counter for the third time. Tomorrow was Thanksgiving, and the phone on the wall had not rung since noon. She checked it anyway, lifting the receiver to hear the dial tone, then set it down too carefully. Mr. Alvarez's insulin order still sat unfilled in the tray, because the distributor's truck had never come. Her stomach felt tight and hollow, and she pressed her palm under her ribs as she scrolled through the delivery page again. "Come on," she muttered. "Just say something." The page refreshed, and nothing changed. She counted the vials in the fridge, twice, got a different number the second time, and counted a third. Outside, the lot lights flickered on. She dialed the on-call line with a thumb that wouldn't quite stay still, and when it began to ring she realized she had been holding her breath since the first digit.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The plane had touched down eleven minutes late, and Marisol was already standing in the aisle, bag clutched against her ribs, thumb stabbing at her phone to refresh the departures board. Gate B47. She was at A12. When the door finally opened she apologized to the man ahead of her three times, slipping past him with her shoulder turned, and then she was walking fast, then half-running, her backpack thumping between her shoulder blades. Her mouth had gone dry. The moving walkway was jammed with a family and their stroller, so she took the stairs beside it two at a time, breath rasping. "Sorry, sorry, excuse me," she kept saying, too quietly for anyone to hear. Her pulse knocked in her ears. She checked the time again, though she'd checked it ten seconds ago, and the numbers swam. Her hand shook as she dug for her boarding pass. Past the pretzel stand, a gate agent was lifting the phone receiver. "Wait," Marisol whispered, then louder, "Wait, please."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: Dana had taped the baseboards twice, pressing each strip down with her thumbnail until her thumb ached. The first stripe of Sage Whisper dried on the wall, and she crouched to look at it from the side, then from the doorway, then from the side again. "It looks greener," she said to the empty room, and her voice came out thin. She wiped her palms on her jeans, leaving two pale smears. The landlord's inspection was Friday, and the old cream had been fine, hadn't it? Her stomach tightened each time the roller squeaked. She pulled out her phone, set it down without calling anyone, and picked up the brush again. A drip slid toward the floor and she lunged for it with a rag, breath held, heart knocking against her ribs. Only when the streak vanished did she notice she'd been clenching her jaw so hard her teeth hurt. She opened the window, then closed it, in case of dust.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first thunder rolled in while my tea was still too hot to drink, and I drank it anyway, scalding my tongue. Rain hammered the porch roof. I'd checked my phone four times in ten minutes, thumb smearing the dark screen, though nothing had changed since the last time. "Pick up," I whispered, then laughed at myself, because nobody was there to hear it. The porch swing creaked under my restless knee. Each headlight that swept the road made me stand, grip the railing, and sit again when it turned into someone else's driveway. My stomach felt like a fist around a stone. Lightning cracked over the maple, and I counted, one, two, and lost count at the second flash, my breath shallow. The dog pressed against my shin, trembling or maybe I was. I pulled the cuff of my sweater over my knuckles and kept my eyes on the end of the road, listening for a car that sounded like hers, bargaining with the sky to let her get home.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repairing a bicycle in a shared garage
text: The chain keeps slipping off the ring, and I keep putting it back, a third time now, a fourth. Grease has worked into the cracks of my knuckles. Across the garage, Dana's side is all labeled drawers and a pegboard with outlines drawn around each wrench; mine is a milk crate and a borrowed screwdriver I haven't asked to borrow. When she comes in for her torque wrench I flatten myself against the wall to let her pass, though there's room. "Sorry, I'll be out of your way soon," I say, to her back, quieter than I meant. She doesn't answer. I laugh a little anyway. My shoulders have crept up toward my ears and I can't remember how to lower them. The derailleur hanger is bent, and of course it is, I probably did that too. I hold the wheel in my lap a long time, thumb circling the dust cap, then spin it and watch it wobble, and decide not to say anything to anyone about it. I start over.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person waiting at a bus stop as the weather turns
text: The first fat drops hit the shelter's plastic roof, and Marcus stayed on the far end of the bench, hugging the folder of résumés he'd printed at the library. The other commuters crowded together under the lit ad panel; he shifted left to give them room, though no one had looked at him. Wind flipped the folder open and a page skidded into a puddle. He watched it darken and did not pick it up. "Sorry," he muttered to a woman whose shoe the paper had brushed, and she didn't hear. His shoulders curled inward, his chin sank toward his zipper, and the cold crept up his sleeves while he left the hood down. The bus sighed to the curb, doors folding open. He let everyone board first, then stood a moment longer, counting coins that he already knew were short by thirty cents. "I'll get the next one," he told the driver, and stepped back into the rain, where it seemed to fit him better.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone sorting through a box of old letters
text: The shoebox had been under the bed so long that the lid left a pale rectangle in the dust. Marlene sat cross-legged on the carpet and slid the rubber band off, and it snapped apart in her fingers like it had been waiting. She read the first envelope's return address, then the second, and began making two piles: one for letters from other people, one for letters she had answered. The second pile stayed a single envelope thick. She held a birthday card from her sister, 2009, and tried to remember sending anything back. Her shoulders curled toward her knees. 'Well,' she said to the empty room, in a voice so small she almost didn't hear it, 'that tracks.' She tucked the card into the box, pressed the lid down with both palms, and sat there a while longer, studying the pale rectangle on the floor, thinking that the dust had kept better track of her than anyone had.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a neighbor asking to borrow a ladder
text: Dale knocked twice, and I opened the door only as far as the chain allowed, then fumbled it loose, apologizing before he'd said anything. He wanted the ladder. Of course, I said, of course, take it, it's just sitting there. I led him to the garage, stepping over the boxes I'd never unpacked, and my hands shook as I lifted it off the hooks. Dust came away on my sleeves. He asked if I was sure, if I needed it back soon, and I laughed too fast and said nobody would miss it, nobody ever used it, it was probably better off with someone who could actually do something. He frowned a little. I looked at the oil stain on the concrete instead of his face. When he carried it down the driveway, I stood in the doorway until he turned the corner, then kept standing there, my shoulders folded in, the quiet of the house pressing close, wondering why I'd said thank you to him as he left.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cooking a meal for guests arriving soon
text: Marnie stirred the risotto for the third time in two minutes, though it hadn't needed it. The recipe card, stained from her sister's old kitchen, lay beside a phone showing 6:41. Guests at seven. She tasted the broth, winced, and tasted it again, as if a different answer might come. "It's fine," she told the empty room, then, quieter, "They'll be polite." Her shoulders had crept up toward her ears; she noticed and couldn't make them drop. She wiped the counter that was already clean. The good plates sat stacked by the sink, and she took down two, looked at them, and put them back, choosing the chipped ones instead. Nobody should have to eat off something nice because of her. When the buzzer finally sounded, she turned the heat low, dried her hands slowly on her apron, and stood a moment with her back to the door, rehearsing an apology for dinner before anyone had tasted it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone receiving a phone call from an unknown number
text: The phone buzzed against the cracked laminate, a string of digits Marcus didn't know, and he let it ring four times while he stared at the cereal bowl he hadn't washed since Sunday. He answered on the fifth, thumb sticky. "Yeah. Hello? Sorry, who's this?" The voice on the line was bright, asking for a Mr. Daniel Okafor, and something in his chest loosened, then sank. "No, that's not... I'm not him. Sorry. Sorry to bother you." He apologized again before she hung up. Afterward he kept the phone against his ear, listening to the dead hum, shoulders curled inward. Nobody had called for him in nine days; he'd counted. He set the phone face-down, then turned it face-up, in case. The refrigerator clicked on. He sat on the floor beside the couch, since the couch seemed like too much to ask for, and picked at a thread on his sock until it came loose, a small gray nothing he held for a long time.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a student returning a library book long past its due date
text: The book had been in Dara's backpack since March, its spine gone soft from being carried everywhere and opened nowhere. She waited by the return slot until the line cleared, then waited a little longer, pretending to read a flyer about study rooms. At the desk she set the book down with both hands, as if it might go off. "It's, um. It's really late," she said, to the counter more than the librarian. "Sorry. I can pay. Whatever it is. Or not pay, if that's, I don't know what people do." Her thumbnail worried the corner of her library card until it bent. The librarian typed, and the screen's glow made Dara's stomach drop; she stared at her shoes, at the gray carpet, at the lint on her sleeve. "Two hundred days," she murmured, doing the math before anyone could. "Right. Yeah." She laughed once, a dry little puff, and took a step back as though to take up less of the room. Her ears burned. She thought: of course she'd ruin even this.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person moving into a small apartment
text: Dennis carried the last box up four flights himself, refusing the neighbor's offer with a quick, "No, no, it's fine, don't bother," and then stood in the doorway of the studio with his shoulders curled inward. The room smelled of paint and somebody else's cooking. He set the box on the floor instead of the counter, as though the counter might object. One lamp, one mattress, a single fork he rinsed twice. When the landlord called to ask if everything was okay, he apologized for answering too slowly, then apologized again for apologizing. He sat on the mattress with his coat still on, hands pressed between his knees, listening to the pipes knock in the wall. He did not unpack the framed photographs. He thought the nail holes would only be something he'd have to pay for later, and the walls looked better without him anyway. His stomach ached, hollow and tight, and he ate nothing, letting the light go gray around him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone finding a wallet on a park bench
text: The wallet sat on the bench beside the pigeon-stained bag of crumbs I'd been pretending to need. Brown leather, fat with cards. I looked left, then right, like someone would be watching, then almost laughed because nobody ever is. My thumb found the license: a woman, smiling, born the same year as me. Her address was eleven minutes away. I tugged my sleeve over my knuckles before touching the rest, as if I might smudge her. Two hundred forty dollars. A photo of a dog. A grocery list in careful handwriting. I said, 'Sorry,' out loud to no one, and my voice came out thin, scraped. My stomach was a fist. I'd skipped lunch again, and the cold from the slats seeped through my jeans. When I stood, I tucked the wallet inside my coat and felt ridiculous, like a thief or a janitor. Whoever she was, she'd open the door and see me, gray hoodie, chewed fingernails, and look past me for someone who mattered. I walked anyway, shoulders folded in, rehearsing how to say 'it's nothing' before she could thank me.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person learning to swim as an adult
text: Tuesday, 7 a.m., the shallow end of the community pool, and I'm the only one over nine years old holding a kickboard. The instructor says, "Good, just let go of the wall," and I say, "Sorry," though nothing has happened yet. I keep my shoulders under the water so no one sees my stomach. My chest is tight, my fingers have gone white on the gutter. A kid in the next lane slices across without thinking and I look away, mouth tasting of chlorine. When I finally push off, I sink in two seconds, come up coughing, and laugh too loudly. "Don't mind me, go on without me." The instructor's whistle hangs there. I stand on the tile, dripping, rehearsing what I'll tell my sister when she asks why I bothered paying. Probably that I wasn't really trying. Better that than the other answer. I tug my towel tighter and wait for the clock to say I can leave.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone planting a vegetable garden for the first time
text: Marcus knelt at the edge of the raised bed with the seed packets fanned in his hand, and read the back of the first one three times without absorbing a word. The soil was supposed to be crumbly. His was a sulking brick-colored clump that stuck under his nails. He pushed a finger in to the knuckle, dropped a bean, and then dug it back out because the line of the row looked crooked. Across the fence, Mrs. Alvarez's tomatoes already climbed their stakes in perfect ranks. 'Probably nothing'll come up,' he said to the dog, who was not listening. 'Doesn't matter. It's just dirt.' His shoulders had folded forward, and he noticed his jaw aching from clenching. He smoothed the soil flat, patted it twice, and sat back on his heels, staring at the bare rectangle as though it had already failed. Then he tore the empty packet into smaller and smaller pieces and tucked them in his pocket, where no one would see.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a coworker presenting a project to the team
text: Dana clicks to the next slide and the room leans in, and I lean back until my chair hits the wall. Her chart is the one I sketched on a napkin three weeks ago, though now it has her colors and her name in the corner. Nobody looks at me. I wouldn't either. I fold my agenda into a square, then a smaller square, pressing the crease with my thumbnail until it burns. My coffee has gone cold, and I drink it anyway because it gives my hands a job. When Marcus asks who did the data pull, Dana says, 'Team effort,' and I hear myself laugh, a quick dry sound, like I've been caught in the hallway. 'Yeah, I just helped a little,' I say, too quietly, and he's already nodding at the next slide. My shoulders keep curling in. I count ceiling tiles. Twenty-two across. I'm glad the lights are low. Someone claps, and I clap a half-second late, my palms barely touching, like I'm trying not to take up the sound.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person driving home late at night
text: The highway was empty past midnight, and Dana drove it at exactly the speed limit, hands at ten and two, as if someone might be grading her. The radio played a song she used to like; she turned it off, then sat in the hum of the tires. At the red light on Fulton, no cars in any direction, she waited the whole cycle anyway. Her phone lit up in the cup holder, a coupon from the pharmacy, and she let it glow until it dimmed. Her shoulders had curled forward, chin nearly to the wheel, and her chest felt hollowed, like a dented can. "Sorry," she muttered when she braked too hard for nothing, apologizing to the empty passenger seat. In the driveway she cut the engine and stayed there. The porch light was off. She hadn't expected anyone to leave it on. After a while she said, quietly, "Okay," and didn't move to get out.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone visiting a relative in the hospital
text: The gift shop carnations were half off, so I bought the wilted ones and told the cashier they were fine, they'd perk up. Room 412. The roommate's curtain was drawn, and I stood in the doorway holding the flowers like a summons. A nurse slid past me without looking, checked a bag, adjusted a line, did in four seconds what I couldn't have done in a year. "Sorry," I said to her back. I set the carnations on the windowsill, where they drooped immediately. Uncle Dan's eyes opened. "You came," he said, and I laughed too loudly and said it was nothing, I was nearby anyway, which wasn't true. My hands wouldn't stay still, so I folded his blanket corner, unfolded it, folded it again. When he asked about my job I said it was fine, fine, and studied the floor tiles, counting them. Twenty minutes later I stood, apologized to the chair for bumping it, and left before he could finish his sentence.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a parent waiting outside a school at pickup time
text: I stand at the far end of the fence, away from the clusters of mothers who laugh like they've rehearsed it. My thumb keeps scrolling an email inbox with nothing new in it. When Dana's mom says hi, I say, "Oh, sorry, were you talking to me?" and then laugh too late. My jacket still has yesterday's coffee stain, and I fold my arm over it. The bell rings and my shoulders drop an inch, braced for the moment Mia walks out and looks past me to see if someone better came. She doesn't, but I'm sure she thought it. She hands me her backpack, and I say, "Sorry it's heavy," as if I'd packed the books wrong on purpose. In the car I rehearse what I'll say when the teacher finally calls about me, not her. My chest is hollow and loud, like an empty room. Mia asks if I'm okay. "Fine," I say. "Just tired. Don't mind me."

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone selling old furniture at a yard sale
text: By nine o'clock Marguerite had priced the oak dresser at forty dollars, then crossed it out and written twenty, then five. A woman ran her thumb along the drawer and asked if it came with the mirror. "Take it," Marguerite said, too fast, her voice small as a coin dropped in a drain. "Honestly, take both." The woman paid three dollars for the mirror and left the dresser behind. Marguerite sat down in the recliner her husband used to fall asleep in, and stayed there, hands pressed flat between her knees, while the sun climbed over the lawn and nobody stopped. A boy bounced on the sofa cushions and his father pulled him off. She nodded at them both, apologizing to the air. When the afternoon sagged she dragged the dresser to the curb herself and taped a sign to it that read FREE. Her shoulders ached. She watched a truck slow, look, and drive on, and thought, of course, of course, and went inside without turning off the porch light.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to fix a leaking pipe
text: Marcus lay on the cabinet floor with his cheek against wet particleboard, a flashlight clamped in his teeth, turning the wrench a quarter turn and watching the drip answer anyway. Water crept down his wrist into his sleeve. He'd watched three videos; the man in each had made it look like nothing. The fitting shifted, gave a thin whistle, and the drip quickened. "Of course," he muttered around the flashlight, and the beam jittered across the pipe. His knees ached against the tile. Somewhere above him the dishwasher he'd promised to fix last spring sat silent. He thought of calling the landlord, then of the pause on the line, the patient voice that would say he should have called sooner. He set the wrench down gently, as if it might object. A bucket was already half full. He slid it back under the joint, sat up, and stared at his hands, pruned and shaking slightly, as though they belonged to someone he'd been asked to look after and was failing to.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone opening a letter from a government office
text: The envelope sat on the counter for three days, between the pizza box I hadn't thrown out and a mug with a skin of cold coffee. This morning I finally slid my thumb under the flap, and the paper tore crooked, the way everything I touch does. My ears were hot. I read the first line standing up, then sat on the floor because my knees had decided for me. "Benefits review," it said. "Failure to respond." I laughed, one short breath, and told the empty kitchen, "Well, yeah." I folded the letter into smaller and smaller squares until it was a hard little thing I could hide in my fist. Somewhere upstairs a neighbor's shower started, a normal person getting ready for a normal day. I stayed where I was, picking lint off my sock, thinking they'd probably never miss a name like mine if they crossed it off. My phone buzzed against the tile. I let it.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a traveler arriving in a city where they don't speak the language
text: The ticket machine at Taipei Main Station blinks at me in characters I can't read, and I press the same corner of the screen four times before stepping back so a woman with a stroller can go around. My suitcase handle is slick under my palm. I rehearse the address on my phone, then don't show anyone, because the screen is cracked and the hostel's name looks stupid even in English. A guard says something kind, I think, and I nod, nod, nod, and say "sorry, sorry," though I don't know what for. I walk with my shoulders folded in, keeping to the wall where I'm least in the way. Someone's noodles steam beside me and my stomach knots instead of growls. I sit on my suitcase by a pillar, the crowd parting around me like water around a stone nobody asked to put there, and I count the tiles until it feels reasonable to be gone.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person watching their dog play in a field
text: Dennis sat on the damp bench with his hands pressed between his knees, watching Biscuit tear across the field after nothing at all. The dog's ears flapped inside out. A woman jogged past and smiled at the scene, and Dennis ducked his head as if the smile had been aimed at someone behind him. When Biscuit bounded back, tongue lolling, he held out a hand and then pulled it away before the dog could reach it. "Go on," he said, barely louder than the wind. "Somebody better will throw it." His chest felt hollowed, like a coat hung on a hook. He thought of the unpaid bills in the car, the unanswered texts, the way his sister's voice had gone careful on the phone. Biscuit dropped the stick at his shoe anyway. Dennis stared at it for a long minute, then nudged it away with his toe, and watched the dog chase it, grateful and ashamed that anything still looked back at him.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone rehearsing for a small community concert
text: The church hall smells of floor wax and burnt coffee, and I've set my clarinet case down twice just to have something to do with my hands. Marjorie waves her baton and says, "From the top of the second page, everyone," and I come in a half beat late, again. Nobody turns. That's almost worse. I press my lips to the reed until they sting and play quieter, then quieter still, until my fingers are moving and nothing is coming out. "Sorry," I tell the music stand. "Sorry, I can sit this one out. Honestly, you'd hardly notice." Marjorie laughs like I've made a joke. I wipe the swab through the barrel slowly, hoping someone will need my chair. At the break I take a single cookie, then put it back. On the drive home I draft the text in my head, the polite one, the one where the section closes over the gap without a ripple.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person cleaning out a late friend's workshop
text: Dale's sister had said to take whatever he wanted, so Marek stood in the sawdust-smelling cold holding a coffee can of mismatched screws and could not make his hands decide. He sorted them by size, then dumped them back. The plane on the bench had a curl of maple still caught in its mouth; he blew on it, then pressed it back in place with one thumb. Every drawer was labeled in Dale's cramped capitals. Every tool hung inside its own painted outline. Marek's shoulders ached from hunching, though he'd lifted nothing. "Sorry," he said to the vise, when his elbow knocked its handle. His phone buzzed with his sister's text, and he turned it face down. Dale had built a whole boat in here, a cradle for a stranger's baby, a staircase. Marek found a pencil stub and tried to think of one thing he had ever made. He put the pencil in his pocket, took it out, and set it exactly where it had been.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone waiting for exam results to be posted
text: The list goes up at noon, but I got to the hallway at ten and sat on the floor beside the radiator, knees pulled in, taking up as little of the corridor as I could. Students step around me without looking, and I'm grateful. When Priya asks if I want to wait with her by the board, I say, "Nah, you go, I'd just be in your way," and laugh at nothing. My thumbnail has worried a raw strip along my index finger. I rehearse how I'll tell my mother: flat, quick, like reading a receipt. At 12:03 the paper is pinned up and a crowd closes around it. I stay seated. I count ceiling tiles. Forty-two. Someone cheers, someone swears. I tell myself that whatever my number is, it was probably always going to be that one, and my stomach folds neatly, as though it agrees. I stand only when the hallway empties, and I read the list last, bottom to top, starting with the names that don't matter.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person hiking a trail as daylight fades
text: The light goes orange, then the color of weak tea, and I keep walking because stopping would mean deciding something. My boots scuff the same rut that a thousand better hikers wore down. A couple passes me on the way out, laughing, headlamps already on, and I tuck myself against the bank and mumble, "Sorry, sorry," though they hadn't even slowed. My pack straps dig into shoulders I keep hunching, as if to take up less of the trail. At the overlook I take out my phone, see no messages, and put it away like I'd checked on purpose. Someone has carved initials into the railing. I run my thumb across them and think about how nothing would be carved for me, how the ridge would swallow my name by morning and not even notice the chew. Cold climbs my sleeves. I tell the dark, "Fine," and turn downhill, slowly, in no hurry to be expected anywhere.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone baking bread with a recipe from a grandparent
text: The index card was soft as cloth, the ink gone brown, Nana's slanted hand saying only "flour till it feels right." Daniel stood over the bowl with his sleeves pushed up and kneaded the way he remembered her doing, but the dough clung to his knuckles like wet paste. He added flour. Then more. Then too much, and it went stiff and crumbly. "Of course," he said to the empty kitchen, and laughed once, a short dry sound. He didn't bother wiping the counter. The loaf came out of the oven low and pale, dense as a brick, and he sat on the floor with his back against the cabinet, turning it over in his hands. He knocked on the crust. It thudded. He set it on the windowsill where the light was kind, then thought better of it and slid it behind the toaster, where no one would see it. The card he tucked back in the drawer, face down.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person meeting an old classmate by chance at a store
text: Daniel was holding a single can of soup under the fluorescent hum of the discount grocery when someone said his name from the end of the aisle. Priya, from tenth-grade chemistry, pushing a cart heaped with fruit and a toddler's shoes. He tugged his hood lower, then pushed it back, then lowered it again. "Oh, hey. Wow. Yeah, I'm just, you know. Between things." His laugh came out thin. She talked about a clinic she'd opened, and he nodded at each sentence a beat too long, thumbnail picking at the can's paper label until it curled off. His stomach felt hollow and his collar felt tight. "That's great. Really. You always were smart," he said to the floor tiles. When she asked for his number he said his phone was broken, which it wasn't. After she left he stood there until the freezer cases clicked, then put the soup back on the shelf and walked out with empty hands, shoulders folded in around nothing.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone working the last shift before a holiday
text: By four o'clock the pharmacy had emptied out, and Marta kept straightening the same row of cough syrup, turning each label to face front, then turning them again. The fluorescent hum seemed louder without customers. Her manager had left at noon with a wave and a "Happy Thanksgiving, everybody," and no one had asked what she was doing tomorrow. She hadn't offered. When a man hurried in for antacids, she said "Sorry, sorry" as she rang him up, though he hadn't waited, and she kept her eyes on the scanner while he said thanks to the door instead of her. Her shoulders had curled forward so long that her neck ached, and she let it. In the break room she ate half a granola bar over the sink, brushed crumbs into her palm, and checked her phone: nothing. She wiped the counter that was already clean. At closing she turned off the lights and stood a moment, certain the dark wouldn't notice the difference.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person trying to catch a connecting flight
text: The board flips to GATE CLOSED just as I reach the top of the escalator, and I stop walking. A man in a suit brushes past, muttering, and I say "Sorry," though he's the one who hit me. My carry-on strap is cutting into my shoulder. I let it. At the desk, the agent's smile is tight and practiced, and I start explaining before she asks: the first leg was late, I should have booked a longer layover, I should have checked the app, I always do this. My voice keeps getting smaller until she leans in to hear me. She types. I stare at my sneakers, one lace gone gray with travel, and think that of course the plane left; planes don't wait for people like me. When she offers the 9:40 tomorrow, I nod too many times and say thank you three times. Then I sit on the floor by an outlet with my phone at two percent, and I don't call anyone, because what would I even say?

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: someone repainting a room in their house
text: The roller squeaks on every pass, and I let it, because nobody's here to hear it. Three coats of "Morning Linen" over the yellow Dana picked, and still the yellow bleeds through in a long stripe by the window. I stand there with my arm hanging, paint dripping onto the drop cloth, and decide it's fine. It's always going to show through. My phone buzzes on the stepladder; I don't turn it over. Sister, probably, asking if I finished, and I'd have to say no, again. My knees ache from crouching, and I notice I've been breathing shallow, like the room might need the air more than I do. I wipe my hands on my shirt, which was already ruined, which I'm glad of. Somebody ought to see this wall and know a person who could do better was never coming. I dip the roller anyway. Under my breath I say, "Sorry," to the wall, and cover the stripe.

author: claude-sonnet-5-5
topic: a person sitting on a porch during a summer storm
text: The first fat drops hit the porch rail, and Marcus stayed where he was, even as the wind pushed rain across his knees. Inside, the phone buzzed against the kitchen counter, and he let it buzz. He'd drafted the reply three times in his head, each version shorter, until it was just an apology to nobody. Thunder rolled over the Hendersons' roof, and he pressed his palms flat against the damp boards as if to hold himself down. The rocking chair beside him was empty; it had been empty for months, and he'd stopped moving it. When the gutter overflowed, he watched the water spill and thought it was at least doing something. His shirt clung cold to his ribs. A neighbor's dog barked from under a carport, and Marcus muttered, 'Yeah, I know,' to no one, then laughed once, a dry sound, and let his chin sink to his chest. The lightning came. He didn't count the seconds. There was nothing he needed to be ready for.
